FULL REVIEW:
Beat it on normal. Wonderful TBS, enjoyed every second of it.
Highlights:
- Simple but pleasant isometric art design.
- You get swordsmen, knights, paladins, dwarves, elves, mages, priestesses, magic swords, fireballs, undead, orcs, kings - all the tasty cheese a proper fantasy game requires.
- Fine combat system with passive and active skills, stats, illumination bonuses, hit chance, armor, etc.
- Plenty of content and replayability. My run lasted 26 hrs and I tend to be quick. Did a "good" playthrough but one can also do an "evil" playthrough. Went for a turtling approach but I think it's also possible to play aggressively by spamming cavalry units which I never even tried out. And unless one beats the game on highest difficulty outright, one always has the option of trying to beat the next difficulty level. I played 36 out of the 42 available missions.
- Good attitude by the devs - they pay attention to people's reactions and quickly fix problems.
- Some have complained about the difficulty, but I found the game straightforward on normal. (Beat the early orc catapult siege with no problem before the devs removed the catapult. Maybe lost a unit but on normal that's no big deal.) Would recommend hard difficulty to the hardcore.
Negatives:
- Disliked only one thing about the games - the catapults. Those do something like 10 dmg per turn (depending on hits and misses and unit congestion) with no regard to range, evasion, or armor. Given that units tend to have 20-25 HP and heavily rely on healing, catapults make it possible for the enemy to instagib units at random. And generally an instagib means a restart. The only way to destroy catapults short of destroying the enemy army and crossing the map is by sniping enemy catapults with your own catapult. Which, given that catapults suffer from no range restrictions, can be done on turn 1. So I save-scummed on a couple of late missions in order to snipe the enemy catapult on turn 1 and turn a brutal mission into an easy mission. This is just bad design IMO.
Protips:
- Spam potions. I found the stun potion and the dispel potion particularly useful. The idea is to stun the enemy top honchos, and dispel the mass stuns the enemy throws at you. Healing potions on frontliners are useful on long missions in which the healers run out of mana.
- Units refuse to walk on fire, which means that one can create/block chokes by spamming liquid fire pots.
- I didn't replace any of my original swordsmen and they felt weak toward the end. If I were to replay the game I'd consider replacing the swordsmen with dwarves.
- Only hired one healer early on; but I suspect having a second one would be worthwhile. Healers do solid work in this game.
- Was not impressed with the elf unit. The lack of shield makes it vulnerable to archers. And one can't control the ent.
- Except on a few timed missions, the game favors turtling, because typically the player has healing but the enemy doesn't. I beat most missions by immediately falling into formation and then just waiting for the enemy to break upon my barricades.
Rating: 9/10, recommended to TBS fans. Pleasantly surprised by this game, big kudos & thanks to the devs.

FIRST IMPRESSIONS REVIEW:
Bought Warbanners because the screenshots reminded me of "Battle of Wesnoth", "Steel Panthers" and  "Korsun Pocket", all of three of which are great favorites of mine that I rate 10/10. "Warbanners" is clearly inspired by at least the first two.
Beat the first 3 missions and the game looks like the real deal:
- Hardcore hex-based TBS action.
- Simple yet rich combat system with few stats but tons of items, skills, and modifiers that make a huge difference.
- Party-based, can hire mercs, units gain xp.
- The graphics & music are perfectly serviceable.
Only problem I had is that I think at one point a bleeding modifier bugged out and wouldn't go away.
Overall I get a good vibe from this game. Will post full review when I finish it or quit.

Game is not easy.
I'll edit the review a bit.
So the game ramps up quickly on the difficulty scale on normal. Unlike Battle Brothers in which you can keep your sandbox players alive and carry them over from battle to battle. The characters in this game WILL die, I have tried desperatly to replay mission after mission keeping them alive, alas they die.
My reccomendation is based upon my preference for these type of games. If you enjoy hex based / turn by turn combat, then give it a try. You can always refund it within 2 hours.

If you aren't afraid of a little crushing difficulty and can get over the primitive production value, Warbanners provides satisfying and tense tactical combat.
The meat of the game is combat. Units move, atack, cast spells, and use abilities on a hex grid map. The mechanics are surprisingly in depth, despite the primitive look of the game. Trees, rocks, and buildable fortifications block routes. A range of bonuses and penalties are available, from simple buff spells to terrain and character effects. Units can throw a variety of grenade-like potions. Units also expend stamina during combat and can gain or lose morale. Fresh, inspired units enjoy stat bonuses. Tired and scared units suffer penalities, and may even try to flee combat.
Outside of the combat, you must manage your band of mercenaries. You spend the gold you get from missions to hire and resurrect soldiers, hire advisors, and purchase potions. As units gain experience, you also choose what new stats or abilities they earn as they grow.
On the world map, you choose where to go and what actions to take, although I noticed this was mostly just choosing the order you'll complete missions, and whether or not you'll engage in optional missions.
My greatest criticism may be the difficulty, which feels weird to say in 2017. I'm not trying to be a big baby, but the game can be punishing. Your mercs are often outnumbered, or outmatched. Even in an otherwise good situation, the dice rolls can easily give you the XCOM flavored frustration of missing high percent attacks while the enemies enjoy seemingly flawless turns. The brutal missions often result in at least a couple of deaths, so you are presented with a choice of either tossing their corpse in the dirt and hiring a rookie, or bringing them back with permanent stat penalities. Either decision drains your very limited treasury. Poor performances makes your team weaker, which makes further missions more difficult, resulting in more poor performances, and so on. This can create a situation where you feel hopelessly underpowered as the difficulty marches on.
Warbanners is a surprisingly deep turn based fantasy tactics game, but can be a vehicle of powerless frustration.

The inclusion of zombies in a classic style RPG is a very creative idea. This is something that I have not seen attempted before, and I think it was achieved quite well by Mr Graham Dodge. Havent completed the story yet, but has been a nice play so far.

Having played hundreds of classic JRPGs, I'm always on the lookout for a fresh experience. Zombies are still a rare appearance in classic JRPGs. "Wolfenhain", a free German RPG, implemented them in a Low Fantasy setting last year. "Galer: Plague of Heroes" is this year's High Fantasy JRPG embodiment.
If you like Final Fantasy VI (large cast of characters, dawning apocalypse scenario) and zombies, bothered to read my review and don't dislike RPG Maker (2003) games, there's a good chance this game might appeal to you.
While the story (see the game description) is executed fairly well (despite/because of a lack of major, but therefore also often unbelievable plot twists), it suffers from typos and a "doughy", seemingly unrelated beginning. If you can make it past that, though, you'll have a hard time finding another JRPG like Galer that forces you this strongly to question your heroes' success. Despair's palpable as you seem to fight a losing battle. This might be the game's greatest merit, as the heroes' victory in other JRPGs is never in any real danger (unless these games deliberately offer "bad ending" or "chaos" routes). Finally, a satisfying ending rounds out the story.
The beginning is typical JRPG fare (visit town, clear dungeon, rinse and repeat). Things get more interesting when the player is granted full control over his own home base. Here, he can change party members, forge equipment, create items and much more. A lot of systems and mechanics have been implemented compared to other JRPGs of this kind. While this is commendable, the player can find enough rare equipment in dungeons without ever having to rely on the opportunities the home base has to offer.
Speaking of implemented mechanics, there's a rather unique one: When traversing the world map, the player doesn't only fight random encounters on the world map, but also random encounters to protect the home base (either-or, so this doesn't mean twice as much random encounters). This feature creates the chance to test all characters in battle and contributes to the story scenario's flair. Furthermore, if the home base party is strong enough to scare monsters away (happens automatically), the player receives a "Wild Card" that awards, when used, a randomly created bonus. The effects range from mere money to (permanent) status-raising items, free level-ups, summons that can be used in battle and even new skills. I deem this mechanic refreshing, but easily abusable once the party members are strong enough. In any case, be prepared for a rather high random encounter rate with no way of mitigating it. Apocalypse isn't known to let the players rest.
When the home base becomes available, the player has to choose a difficulty setting. "Normal" leaves everything as it is, but "difficult" forces the player to buy food rations in order to survive overworld trips. Despite underlining the fight for survival, this feature complicates exploring the world map, so I'm glad it's purely optional. It may very well be this feature doesn't pose a problem anymore once the player is able to travel by (air)ship.
My biggest gripe with the large cast of characters is that there aren't enough meaningful battles for all of them to participate in. There are some scenarios that force the player to use certain party members, but it just isn't enough (so don't expect a "Suikoden"). Especially the game's final stage, despite being intense as hell, wastes a lot of potential in this regard (compare JRPGs like "Legends of Illarion" that force the player to use all party members by forming different parties for simultaneously - successively - fought battles). It doesn't help that many characters receive hardly any development (if any at all). The antagonists aren't anything special, but they get their jobs done. On the other hand, the main characters and their problems are likable and believable. To name a few: Paladins struggling with the fact that the god they believed in may not exist, regular people having to cope with the loss of their friends, a defector having a hard time to be (and feel) accepted - while the wheel isn't reinvented, any JRPG player will feel right at home.
Dependent on which party members the player takes (and sometimes doesn't take!) with him to certain locations, he's awarded with additional story scenes or side quests that become available. The player can discover enough hints to find most of the optional stuff, but he's likely to miss something without developer's knowledge. Most of the side quests unlock scenes from the past of certain characters, which the player can view at the home base. There are also some "one-time only dungeons" and other permanently missable things. Thus, be aware that this game can be frustrating for completionists, particularly as it doesn't offer any replay value.
Another typical problem that comes with (too) many party members: The player doesn't know which characters will be useful until the end. Should you level up your characters evenly or concentrate on a few select ones? It's definitely the latter for this game. Since there are enough (voluntary) opportunities to grind and even to buy level-ups for party members (using money earned in-game at the home base, requiring increasing amounts of money at higher levels), any player will be able to circumnavigate potential "roadblocks". The game features some unwinnable boss battles, though, a device I truly despise. This is even more aggravating considering this game could really use more boss battles in general. Fortunately, at least the ones available can be exciting and force the player to make full use of all his battle options.
Battles feature the standard RPG Maker 2003 system, which means ATB ("active time battles") like in earlier Final Fantasy games. Bars fill up for your party members, and if a bar is completely full, you can input an action. Dependent on the setting, this system either resembles real-time combat (“active”) or turn-based combat (“wait”). The wait function is fully automatic, so battles halt completely when it's the player’s turn to input an action. I really appreciate this execution, since a lot of JRPGs only halt battles when pressing “enter” or while navigating through menus.
Apart from the battles, there are several "mini games" that require to avoid or run away from zombies or to quickly fetch some things to barricade a house so that zombies can't enter. Some of these sequences are difficult, especially when the player isn't accustomed to 2D action games, but they are never unfair and instead manage to make the zombie apocalypse feel more real (also, there's only a few of them). This isn’t "The Walking Dead", where zombies don't pose much of a threat nowadays. Additionally, there are some sequences during which the player has to "perform" while being pressed for time (e.g. flee from a collapsing cave within five minutes like in "Wild Arms 1"). I don't like being pressed for time in JRPGs, but these sequences fit the game's style, and they are - once again - never unfair.
In terms of graphics and music/sound, the game seems to rely on resources from RPG Maker 2003's RTP, mixed with a few fitting original pieces. These graphical resources are, to my mind, the best ones to create a Super Nintendo JRPG flair, but as a consequence, this game looks like any other game made with RPG Maker 2003. There's room for improvement when it comes to mapping, but the overall dungeon design is mostly motivating. The developer responds quickly to bug notifications, so the game shouldn't suffer from game-breaking bugs anymore.
I enjoyed this game despite the aforementioned flaws, and I encourage any JRPG aficionado to at least give it a try. Galer isn't a masterpiece, but it's a tremendous (mostly) one-man effort, a love letter to classic JRPGs, adding a special zombie touch. Trying like Galer to tweak the formula without breaking it, that's what more classic JRPGs nowadays should try to accomplish.

TL:DR
PROS - Good nation creation, nice AI, repeatable content, lots of multiplayer compatible mods,
CONS - Late game lag makes the game slow to a grinding halt. Save Files are Cluttered.
Definitely a great game for anyone who likes empire building/strategy games.  It's got customizable nations and map creation settings so you can get a different experience (or the same experience if that's what you want) every time you play.
The main feature that makes this game so good in my opinion is the way the AI handles itself.  Unlike other strategy games (like Civilization) the AI doesn't cheat, at least not as far as i can tell.  Even without them cheating though i find that I'm frequently being outclassed by my galactic neighbors.  The game is full of micro management, which the AI can handle easily, but me and my fat fingers need more time to deal with all the little things.
Not only is the game fun on it's own, it also offers great mod support.  There's a thriving community of mods on the steam workshop for an endless supply of content, texture packs, and more.  Most mods are multiplayer compatible as well so you can play with friends if you've gottem, or solo like i do most of the time.
So what's bad?  Lag.  I've done a lot reading on the internet about Stellaris and all the cool things you can do, especially in the late game.  Unfortunately I've never been able to really appreciate those late game things as my game slows to a crawl before I can get there.  As the game progresses and all the AI build up their fleets the framerate drops significantly.  Framerate's not really an issue in a top down strategy but it makes the game time slow down as well.  What you end up with is a slow grinding halt to your game as you get fed up sitting and waiting 20 minutes for one thing to build (even on fastest speed).  I have a nice computer.  A really nice computer.  But the late game lag makes it drag so much i get fed up every time.  Usually when I hit the slow phase I quit and start a new game, which has lead to a plethora of saves cluttering up the save files (which is very uhh.... not good).  Finding a specific save is nearly impossible as they're all piled up on top of each other and listed only by species name and galactic date.  There needs to be some sort of separation as the only way to really tell them apart is to just remember how many different games you've played between the most recent and the one you want.
The only game where I can be a pacifist and can't take over any planets, but can justify genocide of the very same planet by being a xenohpobe.

This is the greatest game of all time. It has aged really well for a twelve year old game, so I wouldn't let that put you off. The graphics arent flashy, but they are remarkably sound, and the combination of a breathtaking soundtrack and impressive game mechanics and features make up for the graphics not blowing you away, because they make the game much more immersive than empty graphics do. More importantly, this game never gets boring. I've had this game for years before I got it on steam, and I never got tired of it. It really hits the sweet spot in my opinion of being easy enough to grasp and get good at while still maintaining depth of features and complexity of gameplay. The only complaint I can think of is that, similar to other Total War games, the AI is pretty unimpressive, and the game can get fairly easy. FOrtunately, I think this gets combatted fairly well by enjoyable aspects of politics, with the pope, crusades and jihads, and public order all being interesting to manage and adding additional challenge. Additionally, unlike some other total war games, it presets a separate and unique late game challenge in the Mongol invasion and the Americas. It is especially impressive in its rolelaying potential as well, as the traits characters can develop are extremely varied and interesting, with the descriptions often making me laugh. The traits are all based off of the lived experiences of the charaters, as well, rather than a generic linear leveling up system. That is to say, to make a character a better commander, you need to win lots of battles, the more difficult the better. It can be personalised as well, as if the character only fights defensive battles, then he will receive traits improving their command rating only during defensive battles. The traits also allow characters to gain either dread or chivalry, which offer separate bonuses and allow the player to actually decide whether they'd prefer their characters to be respected or feared. Would you like your kingdom to have such a terrifying reputation that almost nobody will dare to stand and fight against you? Then do dreadful deeds, like sacking cities, assassinating rivals, and executing prisoners. Alternatively, crusading or jihading, releasing prisoners, or undertaking projects for the public good, like building happiness buildings and maintaining lower tax rates, will allow your charater to gain chivalry, which carries its own benefits. That may seem like an overly long explanation, but it is just indicative of the outstanding depth this game has to offer. Total War is a series like no other, offering an incredible blend of grand strategy and exhilerating RTS elements, and no game in the series really comes close to Medieval 2, in my opinion (Rome 1 and Shogun 2 come closest, but M2TW is in a class of its own).

Don't mind my hours spent on the Steam version, because I have way more than 100+ hours on the free, web browser version itself - but now! - there's an almighty question many most probably have asked.
Well, not only that you're supporting the developers but also introducing a literal gem into your game library. In comparison with the web free version, you'll get more content on the Steam version. Since the very first GemCraft, I was amazed of how a tower defense game could be so wonderful. I've played a lot, then have focused on playing 'Chasing Shadows', which comes after 'Labyrinth'.
You might think that it's some simple, boring, sketchy tower defense games like those on Armor Games, Kongregate and so forth. Not so! This is a tower defense game made properly, with love and basically revolutionizes the genre itself!
You're presented with a field composed out of roads which lead the monsters to your orb. What
is the orb? The orb is the point you have to defend from the monsters that swarm all over, that rush towards your orb to vanquish it. If a monster touches the orb, don't fret! Yet, if you let way too many monsters at it, it will get crippled. Once your mana pool is depleted and one last monster touches the orb, it's game over. The mana acts like a shield, protecting the orb from destruction. Dropping a gem bomb (Done by pressing B (default assigned key) and dragging a gem over a spot) on the orb will decrease the banishment cost and will furthermore decrease the damage received by the monsters.
Mana is your single resource in the whole game, used in conjuring gems, towers, traps, amplifiers, combining gems as well as in gem bombs. How is mana acquired? It is acquired by slaying monsters and mining from mana shards with a tower which has a gem equipped.
Defense of the orb is done by creating gems of a respective trait (colour) and grade. The gems can be combined altogether, the traits being distributed by half if the gem has two traits (colours), you can figure the rest out. These gems can be socketed in towers traps and amplifiers or thrown as bombs. In most fields, you will encounter shrines which can be activated by dropping a gem on them. Depending on the grade of the gem dropped on it the damage will be increased, the shrine will inflict the properties on the monsters. Walls can be used to create new paths for the monsters to follow. Traps are built on the road to inflict damage especially on the swarmlings which are quite fast, while amplifiers are built next to towers to amplify damage and properties of the gem it is amplifying. The gems can also be assigned on what to target, a building or a monster. Slowly you'll gain three area-of-effect spells and three gem enchantments, with a specific cooldown. Throughout the game you'll get talisman fragments to randomly drop which you can socket into their respective slot in the panel displayed in the 'Talisman' tab.
The level of difficulty can be easily customized, by adding traits at the beginning of the level, dropping gems on the wave tablets to enrage the monsters which will yield more mana and you can also call waves in earlier which will give you mana as well.
This game also has an experience system which rewards the player with skill points at every level gained and also with every achievement, said skill points can be spent on wizard traits that enhance your playthrough. The skill points can be stashed for a starting mana pool bonus.
Not much can be said about the graphics but that everything is detailed quite nicely, the effects being absolutely wonderful and the way the vivid colours combine when mixing a gem with another of a different colour is overly pleasing.
The soundtrack gives an eerie feeling when playing, driving you to think of how deeply horrifying the story is, fitting
to the theme.
+More than 150 fields to battle on
+Eerie, atmospheric music
+Variety of gems each with its own trait
+Different modes to play
+Personalization of the challenge
+Rewarding XP system
+Lots of achievements
+Infinite replayability
+Addicting

Ok, so CrossCode is a 2D action RPG, unlike most RPGs it's a cyber RPG and not a fantasy one.
-It features a Tree system for the skills called "Circuits"
I really like the ability to choose your own path, your style. However the circuits dont let you do that.The circuit system is still incomplete and I hope it will let you pick a "style" once it's complete. Being a melee spheromancer is near impossible and being a tank is useless. This system has a lot of potential but is not fully exploited.
-Challenging bosses and puzzles
I personally really, really enjoyed this. For some people, the puzzles and the bosse fights can be extremly frustrating due to their punishing behavior.
When you die in a boss fight you have to redo the entire fight and figure out what did you do wrong and what can you do to not make the same mistake. However for some people dying over and over is not an option and they tend to give up. I see it as a way to evolve.
The puzzles can almost all be solved using reverse engineering however to solve some puzzles you will need to have great timing and understanding. I remember at the level 18 dungeon I was trying to get one of the last mine keys. I knew the key was in the room I was in, because it was the only one left, however I didn't have enough vision to see where I should throw my fire charged ball to prock the bomb and destroy the rocks. So I started throwing charged balls in all directions until I got it right after one minute. I still don't know if there was another way to solve that puzzle, but I rejoice in the method I used to solve it; this game lets you be creative (sometimes).
Monaster puzzle (ascension quest): At the last level I was really confused and spent thirty minutes trying to figure out what was going on because I completly forgot that you could use a shield in this game... You were put on a steady plate and you had to block the cannon's shots. However nobody uses the stupid ♥♥♥♥ing shield in this game so we forgot that it existed!!! Can you make it so we use the shield more??? So that it's mandatory sometimes.
-Map and Quests
The map (not the regions and everything, when I say map I mean the thing you see when you press TAB and click on map) is horrible and the quests are often unclear. The map shows you very little information and could use a massive rework (I know it's still early access) and the quest tab under synopsis should show you the location of the quest giver using a map. I take on alot of quests and when I complete one I have to start looking around for 10 minutes to hopefully find the quest giver... not fun. Also for gathering quests tell us what plants or whatever we have to destroy to get the material using an image or something similar.
-Combat
I feel like it relies too much on range combat. The use of the shield is almost always unecessary. However it is fun and enjoyable.
-Controls
I tried to play this with my logitech F310 controller and all I could say was : holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ You attack with ♥♥♥♥ing [RB] ? do you know how tiring that is??? It hurts after 2 minutess... You need to redo the controls for controllers. However the mouse and keyboard controls are fine as they are. Can you also introduce an option to jump? The automatic jump is thrash.
-Graphics
This is the last point because it didn't bother me a lot. I play on a 27 inch 1440p monitor. Once the game has been upscaled 10000x times it looks like a blurry mess.
Conclusion --> This is constructive critiscism. I want you to understand that I loved this (early access) game and that's why I bothered writing a review, if you are undecided as to wether you should pick up this game or no, I would recommend you pick it up! However I suggest waiting for the end release.

Champions and roles
Paladins provides various characters, called champions, for the players to choose during their multiplayer sessions. Each of these champions fall into one of the following categories: Front Line, Damage, Support and Flank. Being a team-based shooter, players must rely on strategy, character knowledge, coordination and teamwork in order to attain victory. Players may use VGS, along with text and voice chat to communicate. A good team will have a balanced choice of classes that will support each other during the game.
Front Line: Champions who serve as the anchor of the team, holding the front and protecting their allies. With high health pools and shielding capabilities, Front Line champions excel at blocking enemy fire and disrupting enemy objective captures.
Damage: Champions who possess reliable and consistent damage outputs or large burst damage potential. Their damage, coupled with average health pools and decent mobility, make Damage champions ideal for skirmishes and extended firefights.
Support: Champions with high utility and healing abilities, the backbone of any team. Due to their healing capabilities that keep their allies in the fight, Support champions are invaluable allies.
Flank: Champions who excel at traversing the battlefield and getting behind enemy lines, eliminating vulnerable key targets. While most Flank champions are relatively frail, having lower health pools than any other role, their excellent mobility and self-sustain provide them with the means of escape and survival.
There are 31 champions in Paladins, 6 of which are available from the start for new players to choose. Additionally, 4 champions are also temporarily accessible for free on a fortnightly rotation. Players can permanently acquire additional champions through purchases using in-game currency. More are slated for release in 2017.
Game Modes
There are different gameplay modes for Paladins:
Siege: The 'main' Paladins game mode, teams are tasked first to capture the map's central capture point and, if successful, push a payload that spawns from it to the enemy base. This mode is played in a best-of-seven format.
Payload: An attacking team is tasked with escorting a payload through an extended railroad track to push it as far as they can, or to the end goal, while a defending team thwarts their progress. A push is halted if the both teams engage in combat near the payload and it slowly moves backwards if no one on the attacking team is nearby to push it, though push progress the team has accumulated is not lost. Once time runs out or if the payload is pushed to the destination, teams switch attack/defense roles. The winner is determined by the team that pushes the payload the furthest, with the attacking team setting the bar in the first round. If the attacking team in the second round are able to push the payload the same distance as the first team, the second wins the game.
Survival: Teams try to outlast each other on a relatively small map with no respawning until the next round, all the while avoiding deathly fog that closes in from the outer edges of the map. The fog deals percentage-based damage of a champion's health and negates all healing while a champion is in it, foiling long term stall tactics. The fog starts at the edge of the map, which starts closing in after a short delay until it reaches the map's epicenter, where any surviving champion are forced to do battle. This mode is played in a best-of-six format. This game mode was removed in OB 52.
Co-op: A player versus environment game mode, a team of five face off against an AI-controlled team that possess extremely large health and high damaging attacks, as well as modified abilities. The objective in each PvE map vary from capturing an objective in a Siege game (where the mode is simplified so that only capturing the point is necessary) or a Survival game. This game mode was removed in OB 49.
Onslaught: Teams do battle over a large combat area in an attempt to take point control and earn points. Along with holding an uncontested presence on the control point, slaying enemy players also scores points for the team, akin to a team deathmatch. Killing an enemy scores the team 5 points, while holding control over the combat area earns the team 1 point per second. The first team to reach 400 points, or the team with the most points after 10 minutes, wins the game.
Test Maps: An additional game mode accessible in the casual section. Players can play untested maps that may be implemented into the game and give their rating for the map. The objective for test maps vary between Siege and Onslaught, and the maps available are rotated every major patch.
Competitive
The Competitive game mode is unlocked for players once they have unlocked 12 champions and reach a player profile level of 15. Competitive only features the Siege game mode. However, at the start of the match, players must choose their champions one by one. First one player chooses. Then, two players from the opposing team choose. Then two players from the team opposing the last choose. This continues until the last player (from the team opposing the one that has first pick) has a role. This challenges the teams to try and counter-build each other by specifically choosing certain champions. Competitive games also affects a player's Competitive rating.

This game is - in a rather unexpected way - one of the best RE games out there.
I got interested in the RE series again this May. I was interested before, but life happened, and I kind of forgot about RE. So yeah, I'm a huge fan of the series. I saw this at the mall, so I decided to buy it.
Well... WOW. This game is a blast.
After the incredible disappointments that were ORC and RE6 which were released the same year, I thought that the RE series would only go downhill. But then I played this game. And it rocks.
The gameplay is basically the same as RE6, but instead of being more action based, it's actually scary. Yeah, you hear that? SCARY. Capcom decided to stop ♥♥♥♥ing around, making the game feel more horror based than action based, which is stunning. The atmosphere is fantastic and Queen Zenobia is one of the most interesting settings for a RE game. Capcom finally heard what the fans wanted and they delivered perfectly.
The plot is great too. The characters are all memorable, the whole Terragrigia backstory is pretty interesting and it's pretty nice to have Jill back.
Another thing I really like is the way the chapters work. Every chapter contains 3 sub chapters as I call them (there are exceptions of course). The first sub chapter describes the main events of the game with Jill and Parker and the rest may either continue directly what happened with those two or describe a different POV of what happened or a flashback. I find this idea to be mildly interesting and it's done pretty well in this game.
However, this game is not perfect, and it has a lot of issues. First of all, some of the enemies and the bosses you fight are ultra cheap. What I mean is that if you don't avoid these enemies (which is pretty hard by itself), they will kill you instantly with one hit. That is just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. I know it doesn't happen too often, but it's still a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥
The raid mode is also pretty addicting and it feels very different than any other generic TPS multiplayer mode of most games nowadays.

It's one of the best RE games out there and this game puts the other RE games that came out that year to shame. Fans will love this game, no matter how die-hard of a fan you are. It's proof that a RE game doesn't have to be centered around zombies or Raccoon City to be great. I utterly recommend this game. Go play it now. You won't regret it.

*Okay, before I say you should get Deadly Premonition, I must state that you should exercise caution into buying this PC port for the game. It is a terrible port from what I've been told and have experienced. However, though I think I'm only about halfway done with the game I have only experienced 1 crash so far... thought it was game breaking until I switched to Administrator mode for the game and the compatability for win 98.*
So far... this is one of those games that's so bad that it's good... And I mean that in a way in which no matter what platform you play it on, it will have some faults, but just the fun, interest in the plot, and characters and what not are gonna get you hooked on this game. If I play a bad game it's usually to torture myself for an audience, but this is a game that is instead very enjoyable even with it's faults.
The dialogue is some of the most ridiculous you'll ever hear and it is just god damned beautiful. It feels like a B-Movie on a low budget, but the director and the actors would have fun with it if it were an actual movie (which by the way the main character while driving WILL tell you some interesting movie trivia). The characters are for the most part likable and each have their own personality.... and... tend to overexaggerate their gestures while talking (seems to be very on purpose in all of it). The music is really damn good in my opinion. When the song, "Life is Beatiful," plays it will get stuck in your head, and it always seems to play at some of the most unappropriate spots.... just... making the situation that much wierder (perhaps it plays at such spots because it what the main character, York, feels at that moment.... simplicity in life).
The controls, on the other hand.. are what set me off a bit.... So many times I wish I could walk or run while I shoot a gun or swing a crowbar, but instead I am locked in place and can only aim. Seems to be a control sceme that even older Resident Evil games suffered through. The driving in the game is very weird to me as well. You can buy new cars in the game, each with it's set of speed and steering difficulties. However, I found myself always having trouble turning or turning too hard and spinning out... or hell even parts of the road that will have the car think it's Ryu or Ken from Street Fighter doing the Hurricane Kick!
One more gripe I HAVE to mention with the game is the map. It is one of the most difficult maps I've ever had to handle for one SIMPLE reason... It cannot zoom out far enough to properly know how to get from point A to point B, unless it is directly related to a plotpoint mission. If I want to do some side missions or go to the diner or gas station, I have to either start at my car and pan up the map until I HOPE to see a path that will take me to my desired location, OR I have to flip through set locations using the left or right bumpers on my controller and then from there try to search for the location of my car. It is very annoying, tedious, and frustrating. It would have been nice to either be able to zoom out even further to see more of the map, or even if there is a way to set your own waypoints like the game does for you when you have to proceed with the plot (seriously.... if there is a way to do that and I just can't find out, please message me and tell me how! Would help me greatly!!!).
With all that has been said, I still really enjoy this game and would recommend it! Just take caution, however, that it MAY or MAY NOT work on your pc, not matter what your specs are. Youtuber and Twitch Streamer Cryotic stated he can't get this game working on his rather powerful gaming set up, and yet I'm able to play this on a rather standard laptop myself, so... you have been warned... it may not work. I took the risk and was able to fix my one crashing issue thankfully by switching the compatability and turning on admin mode. Also do NOT GET THE DPFIX JUST YET!!!! It is still in alpha and needs to be throughally updated before it will do any sort of good... Tried it, and had to reinstall the game to make it work again...
Anyhow, I talked on far too long. The bottom line is this is a good game! Give it a shot! If too afraid for the PC version, try it on xbl or psn!

A lovingly crafted old school tbs. By "old school," I don't mean lazily constructed with crappy graphics. This game is a modern nod to a time when games were judged more for their robust rulesets and gameplay, than flashy visuals. Warbanners is a deep, turn-based tactical game with light rpg elements. Set piece battles take place on a hex grid, with interactive environments. Build your mercenary company to suit your play style. Recruit ranged, melee, healers, and magic users from several fantasy races. Hire heroes that give you access to new units and buffs. Outfit your troops with potions and magic items. Your units will gain experience as you progress, leveling up and learning new abilities.

The scope of the game is focused on squad level tactics, like battle brothers. It's not an open world sandbox like BB, but the storyline for the campaign is serviceable enough. ( Saving orphans from an evil necromancer should be universally satisfying. ) The ruleset and mechanics are just deep enough to be meaningful, but not overwhelming. You'll be considering health, morale, fatigue, lines of sight, and terrain. You'll form shield walls, prepare defensive positions, and use the environment to your advantage.
Keep in mind that it's an old school tbs, not an rpg. The rpg elements are light, and only serve to make it a deeper strategy game.  I like battle brothers, but I feel like the rpg elements are wrapped around a mediocre combat system. I spend most of my time tinkering with weapons and equipment. In Warbanners, you can't mess with weapons or armor. You get a couple slots for generic potions and items, and most troops get a couple abilities that scale up with exp. The combat though, is deep and visceral. I was really surprised at how exciting the battles were. The rules and mechanics are easy to grasp, so from the start your tangling with the enemy and not the ruleset. Wargamers will absolutely approve.

This game is many times better than I was expecting. There are tons of levels, most with alterable paths. There are several difficulty levels, and - in addition to the preset difficulty levels - at the start of each map there are additional traits you can add to the map to make it more difficult while increasing the rewards gained.
There are tons of tower combinations that can be done on the fly, not forced to be chosen before you have seen the map they will be used on. There are 9 gems which can each be merged with each other in endless combinations. You can set those into powers, floor traps, and amplification towers. There are more skills, stats, upgrades, unlockables, and achievements than you will know what to do with at the start.
There are very few penalites for changing you towers around. You can drag and drop finished gems to different towers and they just need a couple of seconds to load into the tower. If you find you've made a gem you no longer need, it can be returned to your mana pool to get back 70% of its total crafting cost. There are hot keys to duplicate a complicated gem (hit D) for its crafting cost, or to upgrade one with a copy of itself (press U). You can drop gems as Bombs (with B) to destroy enemies on screen that passed your towers, or you can boost imcoming waves strength by dropping bombs on their text before they arrive.

The Binding of Isaac is a game about a young child, whose devout christian mother tries to kill him. He escapes into the basement through a trapdoor, and then must navigate through the dungeon that is the Basement. It is a 2D Top-down dungeon crawler, where you can play one of several characters. You start out in Isaac's Mothers Basement working your way throughout. The game is strange, but funny and interesting. It feels a lot like The original Legend of Zelda, though most dungeon crawlers do, and it also features co-op play so you can play with friends. I recommend this game if you enjoy adventuring through dungeons! The Binding of Isaac Rebirth is also a fun play if you want to try other games in the series.

Pretty awesome game, even in it's in development. 4/5 review
PROS:
- Nice old school pixel graphics
- Fun but challenging ARPG system. I don't think I'll be able to go back to a standard RPG with where you have to stand still and let the dice choose everything. The movement and skills are addictive.
- Ambience and atmosphere. Landscapes to explore. A perfect combination of cyber feel and traditional creatures + magic. Good story so far.
- Skill trees are flexible and forgiving. Unlike things like Diablo II, you can always change around your points, and each element uses a separate skill point bank. Part of the game is using all of your elements and neutral powers, as you get them one by one.
MIXED:
- A bit puzzle heavy for my taste so far. I have seen some similar complaints from other players. 75% of the game is traditional quests, killing, and small puzzles, but 25% are these long dungeons with chains of puzzle after puzzle. These can be fun in some moderation, but they may be a little much for traditional RPG players. Some of the puzzles are more tedious than others also (fail to jump or time something correctly, and you have to go back to the beginning, etc.).
Even with the mixed, I still definitely recommend.

I had never played the original Nier, let alone heard of it - I had never played any Drakengard games either, this game was recommended to me by a friend and I bought it based on how much he said he enjoyed it. This is easily one of the best and unique games I have ever played. A lot of its features and its willingness to push the boundaries of how usually games and stories flow really stand out.
I extremely enjoyed this game, to the point where I found it hard to stop playing it and then when I finished it, stop thinking about it. The game also has an interesting way of in-game lore, by having details that can only be discoverd not by playing the game - but by content that exists outside of it such as novellas, script reads and timelines you can find online. The story is portrayed in such a way that the only way to get the full picture after beating the game, is to read these additional lore bits - which after beating the game really makes you want to.
The game's story telling is outstanding but also frustrating at times. While the story itself reveals itself in a manner iconic to the game's creator and the Drakengard series, its built up in a way that as you progress you discover more about the overarching plot - but some parts are never explored and revealed, even with the lore outside of the game which leads to a frustrating yearning to know why. The game has strong themes which references philosophers in the concept of free will and purpose but also downright hilarious moments which sometimes seem unintentional while others were perfect at that moment.
The gameplay is unique, to the point where I havent seen many games do something like this in a long time and even then to this scale. The melding of different genres seemlessly and smoothly was done extraordinary well, although some segments were repetitive most of the game was extraorindarily fun. Its RPG skill system is probably one of the best parts, allowing the player to weight which skills are appropriate for which time and what other skills should be sacrificed through a limited slot system.
Nier:Automata is an outstanding game in nearly all of the features, with outstanding story telling, gameplay and fun-factor - my only gripes is some confusing storylines that are never ventured and some repitive parts to the game.

If there was an option for 'meh', I would. But I'll do the devs a solid for a bit and just give them a binary 'yes'.
Megabyte Punch has a lot going for it, as far as indies go. For one, it tries to emulate the fighting style and feel of the ever-so-popular Smash Bros. series of fighting games, and puts in a bit of Custom Robo meets... Mega Man into the mix. While this sounds like a dream come true, where it really fails at is the Smash Bros. part. Before we get to that, let's start with the good.
Good:
- The graphics are very well done. Nice, bright, but very cool colors, and pretty well done if a bit simplistic robot design.
- Level Design does it's job well. Damage tiles, secrets, so far so good.
- Lighthearted kid-like humor in the writing. I wouldn't be afraid to hand this to a niece or nephew.
- Music is nice.
Meh:
- Gameplay feels very static and restrained. As far as I can tell every bot has the same default attacks, and what's changed is the secondary (specials in Smash.) moveset. What's also missing from Smash are...well, smash attacks, and rolling. In-game I always try to pull off those two moves, and it just bugs the hell outta me when I can't.
Bad:
- Sound effects. No, seriously, it's annoying enough to be a problem. There is a delay when opening up some of the customization options, and it's very noticable. Same goes for some attacks, and the explosion sound repeats for each object per explosion and it sounds terrible.
- Local-only multiplayer. It's rare to find someone willing to huddle around a monitor to play some indie game, and I haven't been very lucky.
Other than that, the game is pretty nice. I can't speak for multiplayer, because of said local-only multiplayer, but it's alright to kill an afternoon with or you're just on a coffee break or somethin'. I don't think the game needs a very built computer to play on.
So, 6.5/10. Great idea, average implementation. If they fix all my gripes, This game would be an 8 or 9 easy. Hopefully we'll see that with a sequel. I'll update this review if I continue and find something else to add.

At first glance this game looks kind of boring, and when I first looked up game play videos I found a 20-minute video of pounding concrete blocks with a sledge hammer, which made this game look almost as exciting as Duke Nukem Forever.  But then I found out about the explosives missions and decided to give it a try.
I had hours and hours of fun playing missions over agin just blowing things up in different ways!  I think my favorite mission was the clock tower; if you pack the explosives just right, most of the structure goes skyward and then it rains bricks for a while afterward.
There is some strategy to the explosives, however.  In some missions you have to avoid destroying the wrong structures while others require you to avoid making a big mess.  (Or, just for the fun of it, you can go ahead and blow everything up and fail the mission.)
There is a variety of missions with different structures and different tool sets and objectives.  I found the frontloader and dumptrucks difficult to use because when you're trying to scoop up the debris it doesn't clump up nicely into the scoop, and then when you're hauling the debris, it's feather light and can slosh out of the container like water if you stop too quickly.
After completing all the missions you can replay the older missions with any tools or vehicles you like (including the explosives) and unlock special tools like the repulsor gun.
This game also supports user content, and you can download some add-ons from the developer website, including a rocket launcher.
Another fun thing you can do is edit the tool properties files and increase the explosive power of the explosives!
One problem I had with this game is that the mouse cannot be inverted, but I eventually got around that by using SakasaMouse so that I can properly pitch foward when I move the mouse forward and pitch backward when I move the mouse backward.

Gemcraft:CS is a great tower defense game, lot of content and lot of variety. It's about gems, of course, you spend mana (which also represents your life bar) to conjure more and more powerful gems in any combination of 9 flavours, each one bringing a different special ability to the final product. Then you socket these gems into stationary assets you build on the field, such as towers, traps, and amplifiers. And then, in time, you'll unlock three area-of-effect spells and three gem enchantments, all on separate cooldown. And then you'll get talisman fragments to randomly drop, and will socket and upgrade up to 15 of them into a large panel, securing a number of additional bonuses and perks. And then you'll gather xp at the end of every mission and invest them in the 25 skills available, or stash them in order to get a different kind of bonus. And then you'll move up and unlock all of the 150+ battlefields available, up to the Spiritforge. And then you'll want to try vision battlefields, where skills and talismans and all that stuff don't matter and you're alone and scared like the first time. And then you'll want to try Iron Wizard mode, with different rules to the game. And that's just scratching the surface.
On top of all that, you can drastically personalize the level of challenge: each battlefield can be played in one of three different difficulty settings, and up to 9 crippling traits can be enabled to different extents in order to make the game more engaging/unforgiving. And even then, you can increase the challenge dynamically by calling in waves ahead of time and even 'enrage' them, which is to say 'spend mana to increase number, healthpool and armor of foes in a wave'.
This little gem (hah) has a lot going for it, so if in doubt, trust a random stranger on the interwebs and buy this game!

I picked this game up because of the positive user reviews (without really knowing anything about it) and the art style (I love some good pixel art), I didn't really know anything about the game before trying it out. After having played it a bit, I have to say I absolutely love this game- it's one of the best games I've played in a long time. The core gameplay elements of this game are fun and just feel great- I would say they set a high bar in terms of quality and, as a game developer myself, they are inspirational in how a great game should feel and play.
There are a couple things that really stand out about the game:
- The controls are on point. Running and jumping around the world feels superb, I would be willing to put the controls for this game on the same level as Super Meat Boy's controls.
- The combat is good (and fun!), the combat systems are easy to learn (maybe feeling a little akward at first because of the mix of range and melee) but require enough finess that you can get noticeably better at combat.
- I like the art, some people don't like "retro"/pixel art but I think CrossCode doesn't just go for "retro" style art. The world is more detailed than what you would find in an actual SNES-Era game, but is still in the same style. I would call this art high quality pixel art, I especially love the antimation on the title screen.
- The world/lore is interesting (so far) and the game being a
is well executed and entertaining. I love how the world is used to explain and build gameplay mechanics, such as having allies, communicating with people, and more. I look foward to seeing the story continue and eventually be completed in future updates.
Beyond those specific points, I still enjoy pretty much everything else about this game (they just don't nessecarily jump out as specifically being awesome to me). The music is good, the controller support is good, leveling and equipment (allowing for a bit of flexability in how you build your character) are also good. I struggle to find anything negative about the game.
That said, there are really only two negatives I can find about the game (which honestly don't bother me at all).
- Sometimes it can be difficult to tell how high up you are in relation to other terrain/platforms (which is important for moving around). The world you are moving around in gives you 3 dimensions of freedom, however it's only represented in 2 dimensions.  I've only had this be a problem once or twice, but it's maybe worth mentioning. It really is only a minor problem, it's not nearly as bad as what you have problem encountered in other 2D/3D plaformers where it can be difficult to gauge gaps and your placement in the world.
- It's not finished :( I was really sad to see I had hit the end of the existing story content and can't wait to see the game finished (at which point I will probably replay it from scratch).
Everything said and done I would absolutely recommend this game. This is, personally, one of the best games I have played in a long time and I can't wait to see where the world and story go as the game continues to develop.

Megabyte Punch feels like a Super Smash Bros type fighter, which in reality it is, but it has a wide variety of customizations that enhance your fighting technique. With the Smash fighting mechanics I easily learned how to play this game. The customizable moves create a unique way of fighting through the campaign with each combination of custom special moves and stats. The customizing mechanics are well built and I found no problem figuring out how everything worked even without a tutorial.
While in story mode the friendly NPC's ripped on the RPG genre in a very humorous way. I found myself laughing at what they said as a person familiar with games like The Legend Of Zelda. When I got into the fighting portions of the story I found myself doing lots of circles to find all the loot scattered and hidden around the map. Each level took about an hour to finish. The story itself was very well constructed and written, with a great plot and story arch. though I didn't finish the story I was very happy with what I did get through.
While I was fighting the enemies I was exclaiming "HOLY S***!!" because the way to kill enemies is to bash them against the walls and have them explode into and through the walls. One instance where this was very apparent is when I purposefully kept hitting an enemy into a wall to increase his damage percentage to a very high percent, when I pulled my finisher move on him he demolished a huge chunk of wall. This shock factor only really happens when the walls are destructible, and for the second level all the walls were indestructible so the shock factor dissipated.
The games graphics aren't anything to fancy, they are quite dull in modeling but make up for it in color. The character recoloring was welcome in making the game very colorful, I even made my guy looking like Batman, bat wings and grey color.
The Tournament mode was a very welcome challenge. I never got past round 5 because the bots are super powerful, compared to story mode. Their damage equaled mine and had every customization that I myself could have. I found myself having as much AA damage as possible and hitting them with ariels to maximize my effectiveness in battle.

Megabyte Punch is like Megaman-lite and Super Smash Bros.-lite combined.  It does not quite have the sophisticated move sets and balancing of either game, but the combination of the two creates a fairly fun game.
The adventure/campaign mode is about 6-8 hours long, depending on how much backtracking is done in each level for rare parts and color customization items, and each boss fight is essentially bare bone Super Smash Bros. stages but with some destructable terrain.  The story is simple as well, but considering the genre and style of the game and the fun factor, it can be forgiven.  Connecting a spin kick on an enemy gives a nice satisfying feedback in slow-mo sound and visuals as you watch them fly. The level visuals are nice as your character travels to different regions. It never felt like a chore to play the game.
Given the strong foundation that this game has built, I hope a sequel would be made that expanded on the combat system through part diversity. There may be many parts but there isn't a wide variety as many share the same abilities.  They may be located in different areas of the character's body, such as double jump attached to the head instead of the shoulder, or are cosmetically different and functionally the same.  Also, the majority of abilities can be found about halfway through the game which makes backtracking for rare parts in later levels to be less rewarding. Considering that many are variations from Super Smash Bros., I wouldn't mind seeing more abilities and ideas borrowed too. For example, the shield mechanism doesn't allow rolling, which I found myself repeatedly trying to do. Basic melee combat is always at a fixed range because there are no melee weapons and parts don't extend attack range. Just adding some of these can be a massive improvement on an already solid game.
Overall though I found Megabyte Punch to be a fun and would definitely help scratch the itch for a bit of Megaman and Supersmash Bros. game on Steam. I would definitely recommend playing with a controller as it feels much better.

this is a fun game and the gamepad does work with the game now. ok first time downloaders if they run into this same problem i did. the DP.exe fix is. you need to go to your steam folder C:Drive/SteamLibary/Steamapps/common/Deadly Premonition The Director's Cut. go to folder redist. scroll down to the bottom and there should be two files. ones vcredist_x86. click on it and install it. next click on file called PhysX_SystemSoftware and install it. scroll up alittle bit half way and find file called DXSETUP and run that and install it. ok after that go back to folder Deadly Premonition The Director's Cut. right click on DP and click on properties. click on Compatibility tab up on top. click on box Run this program in compatibility mode for Windows 98/ Windows Me. dont need to check off run as administrator. click apply or ok. thats done. next right click on DPLauncher and click on properties again. click on Compatibility up on top. now down at the bottom where it says Privilege Level theres a box that says next to it Run this program as an administrator. click on that box, check it off. and now click apply and ok. and now boot up the game and have fun :) this may not fix every ones problems but if you freshly installed this game on a clean copy of Windows 7 ill guess 8 as well it should work with this method.

Games that get remade are a bit of a sticky point for reviews. I try not to allow external factors to influence my estimation, but at the same time it must be acknowledged that a superior version of the same product exists. However, I think there’s still enough daylight left between Binding of Isaac and Rebirth that the original can stand on its own, and stand tall on its stubby, misshapen legs. It was one of the most-played games on Steam for a reason, and still retains a few features that distinguish it from its successor.
On the off-chance you’ve been living under a rock inside a Faraday cage somewhere in the Himalayas, Binding of Isaac is like if Zelda was all randomized dungeons, a billion unsettling organic weapons, and lots of poop. Little Isaac’s mother has been commanded by God to sacrifice him, and to escape this grim fate he flees into the gloomy basement and tunnels of his home. There he finds horrifying cast-offs of life, amalgamations of blood and bone, and twisted visions of heaven and hell standing between him and his final fate. It’s a fever-dream of a presentation, crowned with vomit and feces.
The bizarre, grotesque themes of BoI are inescapable, and I’ve often wondered if they were more of a contributor or a liability to its success. Given the runaway popularity I can only conclude the former, and now have to face the reality of just how many gamers love peeing enemies to death. Isaac’s main weapon against the bloody fetuses and rotting children of the underhalls is his tears, upgradable through all sorts of random objects to cry farther, faster, harder, and in different ways. He can cry in a spread, in a beam, in psychic homing tears, in pee, in blood, and more. Enemies worn down by his mournful tirade explode into piles of cartoon gore and viscera that paint the dingy walls crimson.
It’s a grim game in theme and aesthetic, held together by the incredible depth and breadth of content. The first time you complete the game it’ll be on a run through six levels, but after that many more open up with their own new gimmicks and enemies. Many of your deeds unlock new items to appear from the random pool of power-ups, some with dramatic effects that make future wins more likely just with their availability. New enemies and bosses are unlocked as well, lest you think the good fortune comes at no cost. You’ll also need to manage supplies of bombs and keys for accessing certain areas, and coins that are used to purchase, gamble, donate, and achieve other ends.
Your rewards for learning the nuances of the game and growing your skill are the runs where you get a perfect confluence of items that fill entire rooms with deadly tears, or transform you into an immortal floating head of attrition, or give you direct access to the mysterious and terrifying endgame areas. The RNG is God here in the dungeons, but it is a benevolent one that will grant you power beyond measure just as often as it will snatch it away. And with a little experience, you can stack that deck in your favor, too. BoI is tuned to let you win any run, and while some will be tougher than others, some will also be utter cakewalks with instant laser tears.
Bear in mind that all of this and more is found in Binding of Isaac Rebirth, of course. I won’t mince words here, Rebirth is the superior version, but there is a case still to be made for the original. Plenty more content was added to the remake, from new levels to new enemies to entirely new systems, but they only make the game bigger, not better. OG BoI is still a very focused, comprehensible challenge with plenty to see and do. Having sunk nearly 50 hours into this version, I still find myself a little bewildered by the new, unfamiliar features of Rebirth. There’s a difference in look and feel as well, this one featuring the smooth vector looks of Flash while Rebirth has a more blended, pixelly appearance.
It’s not all good, mind you. Being a Flash game makes this one more prone to stuttering, slowdowns, and the occasional glitches. Rebirth isn’t perfect either but it doesn’t have that inescapable cheapness that Flash titles do. At other times the hit detection might get a little wonky, or in extreme cases some things might not unlock correctly. And there’s no native controller support either, which these days can be a dealbreaker for some. Still, it’s the one that helped grow the roguelike craze that has engulf Steam, and for good reason. The unique look, the compelling secrets, and the visceral fun of working through it all are in no way diminished by the remake. It’s such a bizarrely perfect mix of roguelike and bullet hell that no matter how far its successors go, there will always be a place for the original.

. A flash semi-bullet hell satirical game on Christianity.
The story goes that you are a young child named Isaac whom is stripped of fun and enjoyment in simple life after Mother has heard the voice of God demand that all things sin is removed. The objective of the game is the clear any rooms you enter of monstrosities that lie in your way as you travel deeper and deeper in the depths of your own basement, or maybe a cellar; crawling around the caves and catacombs, throughout the Depths of Nercopolis; and facing the one they call... Mom! Along the way, you find pick-ups, items, tarot cards, and pills that could do good or could do harm to Isaac as you take him on a somewhat sad (but fun!) venture to escape.
Though I had originally thought this game was kinda sad, I eventually got it, played it, and actually found myself excited over playing it over and over, unlocking a variety of cool items and using sweet powers. Just a small feedback + review after finishing chapter 4.
Since the game is currently (1st Nov 2016) still in early access mode, there are couple of unfinished things, like missing skills in the skill-tree, missing sprites for couple of NPCs and some missing content. These shall be ignored for now, as they will be fixed in the final version.
Pros:
+ Pretty fun gameplay
+ Charming art
+ Interesting enemies
+ Good mix of real time action and RPG
+ Good puzzles
+ Lots of side quests
Neutral:
- Consuming heal items takes time and leaves you vulnerable
Cons:
- Locations to finish quests often unclear
- Puzzles and bosses can get quite challenging and there's no option to choose difficulty
- Questmenu kinda hidden
- Quick access menu not very comfortable
- Low item drop rates
I think the good parts of the game are quite obvious: Apart from the nice pixel art, the gameplay is really good. Despite the pixel art, the movement is free and not tile-based and the game plays similar to titles like diablo or bastion. Apart from the Action, there's a skill tree and options for equipping the character, so it also got the fun of a RPG.
About the bad parts: I think the only real criticism would be that the game can sometimes get rather difficult. For this, I'd suggest adding an option to choose difficulty levels (easy, normal, hard) or have a option to give hints to the player (maybe in form of a shop item?). The other points are mostly nit-picking which hopefully get fixed in the final version: It sucks that the quest menu requires couple of clicks (with the gamepad) to reach. Assigning it directly to a button or the quick access menu is neccessary. Also, the quick access menu is kinda uncomfortable: Holding down a button, moving the analog stick and then also pressing another button is annoying. One of the two last steps can and should be removed for an easier access. Another thing is about the quests: Often, it is very unclear where you initially got the quest. Every place in the game is rather big and full of hidden paths, so searching around for one person is annoying. A better description ("This person is in the north-west of place XY") would be nice. What also annoyed me were really low drop rates for certain items, be it from monsters or from plants. Especially when a certain amount of items is needed for a quest and the specific item drops at 1% chance (bear tail or smth, for example), then that's rather annoying and really just grinding, which isn't very nice. Also, starting the game does take a while (20 seconds, I guess?), which feels rather long for a 2D pixel art game like this, but well, since the game runs fast after that without longer loading times, that's ok.
Well, this was mostly just me nitpicking. Overall, the game looks very promising and is pretty fun and addictive to play!
I'll edit this review with time as I and the game's development progress.

Now this is my first review so bare with me.
I have been following this game for some time and recently I finally bought it. The game is obvioulsy inspired by some old classics but it also tries to inovate a lot and brings tons of great features that help the pacing of the game, and the overall enjoyement.
You play as an avatar called Lea. She is mute, but slowly starts to get more words put into her vocabulary as the story progresses. This sparks a lot of interesting and comedical conversations  which brings me to the first great point of this game. The writing, and some of my favourite things are :
Inspect the hilarious usernames of the npc's
Ability to listen to conversations and then interrupt if there is something interesting in it, which usually results in a quest
Although the main character is mute, the amount of different expressions the character has + the supporting characters really spice up a lot of conversations.
Don't want to watch/read a cutscene ? The game has got you covered with the skip cutscene feature which can skip almost any dialogue in the game, even the important story parts, which is great for both speedrunning and people who are replaying certain areas.
Combining all of this the story is really enjoyable the whole way through.
Now, for the great mechanics.
Looking for a rare item for a quest ? Just keep killing enemies without stopping for a short time and your "rank" will increase ! The higher the rank the better the loot ! This helps a ton and can also keep areas where you are overleveled (revisiting old areas ) fairly dynamic to go through anyway, as you can try to chain as many monsters as you can.
You have the normal quests that give you a bit of exp, but the majority of the quests are really interesting and make you do things such as :
Fight sonic the hedgehog
Go into a mole hideout
Catch a smuggler
Discover landmarks etc.
Speaking of landmarks, teleporting ! Cause backtracking has never been easier !
Lets move on to the art and music.
Now I am not the best with musical terms, but this game does a really good job with the soundtrack. It is not too diverse, as you will usually be going through a whole area with just 1 song playing + the battle song, but the songs are not annoying at all even after listening to them for some time.
The pixel art in this game is gorgeous , some of the best I have seen. This is aspecially impressive seeing that its made by a small team. At certain points you are really high up from the ground and the view to down below  is great, or in the early areas of the game , the view to the first city from far away is breathtaking because it gives a sense of scale of the world.
All the animations feel extremely well, and the game should run on 60 fps on most computers, and if it doesn't , I suggest going to windowed mode and lowering the window size. The smaller the faster !
Now for the most important and best part of this game
Gameplay
Now I am gonna divide gameplay into 3 categories :
1. Platforming
- Really basic jumping platforming, but there are a lot of areas where you are just going to say : " Hmm, how do I get over there " , which usually I would say is a bad thing, but in this case it feels like a puzzle of its own.
- Party members follow you really nicely around the map. There is only a few instances where I have seen the AI fail a jump.
- Theres a quest where you jump on top of a roof to chase a goat. WHAT MORE YOU NEED ?
2. Puzzles
- As I said, platforming can sometimes be a puzzle of its own, but besides that this game features a lot of other good and interseting mechanics.
-Platforms that only move/extended when you hit a switch. At first this seems really basic and unoriginal , but you would be suprised how interesting it gets later on.
-Your balls ( weapon, not the nut part ) bounce off of terrain , which in combination with the extending/moving platforms gives some really fun puzzles, which are exteremely fun to watch when speedrunned.
3. Combat
- Skill tree with 4 elements.
- Every elements is a different part of your character Fire = demage , Cold = Defense , Electricity = Ball demage  and Wind = Health/Dodge
-You can switch between using different elements, which comes with its own costs and advantages.
-Dodge, Melee, ranged and block feature.
- Block feature features ( say that 10 times fast )  perfect blocking, aka timing your block last second to negate demage/counter enemy attacks, leaving them vulnerable.
- Dodging can not be spammed which, in my opinion ,is a good thing.
-Tough but extermely fun bosses
-Enemies tend to have a lot of recolours which is probbably the biggest negative point of the game I have found so far ( This does not mean the game is perfect ) Although, recolours tend to have different means of attacking then their previous itterations. ( For example , normal hedgehags can "spin dash" at you , while red ones can dash and jump on top of you, where you need to block one and dodge the other )
- And of course simple to learn but hard to master controls.
I give this game a 9.5/10 as it currently stands, and this is honestly my opinion and its subject to change and it does not have to affect your opinion at all.
The game is addictive and fun, if I truly talked about everything in this review, it would have taken me double the time to write this.
Thank you for  your patience, and I hope we can direct link our opinions !

But where this game is excellent, however, is the visuals, the jokes, and the story over all. The game looks great, in my opinion it is a straight upgrade from BL2. The jokes for the most part hit the spot, and this game is littered with references just like BL2. The story definitely has some weak spots, but what makes TPS stand out from BL2 is the playable character interaction. In this game, the character you play as actually responds to the people you're talking to, and each playable character will have a different reaction.
The game definitely has some weak DLC sans Claptastic Voyage (which is excellent), but for the base game, I would definitely recommend. Worth quite a few playthroughs.
