Mmm. This was my first real foray into Resident Evil, and I liked it so much that I finished the entire game in one sitting that went way er, late into the morning.
Though I have no other RE benchmark to compare it to, I thought the campaign story was really neat and well done, lots of twists that kept me guessing. Most of the characters had interesting personalities, though as a new player to the RE series with no prior background knowledge of the characters besides knowing they exist, I feel not much was done with Chris and Jill outside of them obviously being "the celebrity couple that won't admit it" in the game. I suppose you're meant to know them from previous games, but as a standalone, they ended up being the flattest characters even though you get to play the both of them and thus like them by virtue of them being an extension of "you".
I enjoyed the episodic sort of storytelling technique with a cutscene recap of the previous episode at the start of each next one as though it was a TV serial. Ammo shortages put a constant pressure on the campaign (on normal) but it was not overly scarce, so generally it was a good balance. Definitely had to use every single gun in the game and swap them in and out at times though.
I seldom play games with this kind of 3rd person angled camera, and I was afraid I'd get motion sickness at first, but as it thankfully turned out it was not an issue for me through the game. I didn't have issues aiming or shooting but did have slight issues locating the enemy at times, but by the end of the game had become accustomed enough to it.
The horror element in this game was mostly the gore/grotesque sort of horror, and not the kind of horror that keeps one awake at night from the sheer terror of a floorboard creaking in the kitchen.
There are only two, maybe three fights in the game that would really count as "bosses" with a particular strategy/way to defeat them or stay alive against, and not just giant meatbags. There were a couple fun little turret shooting sessions too.
The biggest negative, I would say, is that some quest objectives that were not marked on the map should have been. You are made to run back and forth to different parts of the ocean liner that most of the story takes place on, and the map is humongous and somewhat complex to comprehend. The story also jumps back and forth between the three pairs of characters and a fourth flashback pair, taking the player on and off the ship to different locations on a whim. Those together plus the nature of an episodic game encouraging people to take breaks between each chapter/episode, all leads to the fact that it's very easy to get lost in the ship and head in the entirely wrong direction. This can be especially bad since ammo does not respawn.
The campaign is entirely solo, the listed co-op tag is solely for Raid mode, which seems to be some sort of wave survival rubbish that I plan to never play. There is a New Game+ available after you finish the campaign, which is you keeping your characters + some extra unlocked gear and starting a new campaign with them. I probably will look toward other games in the series/franchise instead, though.

Full Review:
Do you like Smash Brothers? Of course you do! But have you ever been playing Smash Brothers and wished you were a completely customizable robot? If so, then this is the game for you. Megabyte Punch is essentially Smash Brothers between robots with customization. It's not the most original idea but it is fantastic.
For the story, you are a simple robot fighter living in a simple village till evil comes along and forces you to take action. You fight through a bunch of levels, each one containing a boss at the end, collecting parts and making money. You get a great feeling when you finally find a new kickass weapon to place on your robot, or a new ability, or an enhancement of an ability you already have. You can change up your head, torso, hip, back, left arm, right arm, left leg, and right leg, Also there are a bunch of color designs to be unlocked throughout the game that can be applied to your robot. The customization is probably this game's strongest feature. You can also complete the story mode with a friend in couch coop or compete against them in arena style matches.
Some minor complaints I would have with the game would be that the robot customization system can take some time to get used to. Also, you have to physically run to each level before starting it up. Being able to just teleport from the town to the level would save some time. These are very minor complaints and do not take away from the game to any serious degree.
Overall, this is a great game at a good price with only minor problems. If you are interested in a fighting/customization/robot game with couch coop then you should definitely give this a try.

Stellaris is the game that everyone wants to love but can't bring themselves to. The first couple of hours are extreme amounts of fun. You create your species and government and are launched into space. It's admittedly a ton of fun (at first) to play around with these governments. You could be a slaver empire who relies on conquest, a martial empire that relies on conquest, a pacifist empire that has to colonise or get conquered. This is the problem. There is not a lot to actually do and after a while the game becomes stale. However, this game has the most stable multiplayer of a paradox game I have played.

I got stellaris last year in the sales, i've recently picked it back up and its been quite a bit of fun, alot of the vanilla mechanics have been reworked and there is an extensive modding community.
All in all, i can recommend this; if you enjoyed galactic civilizations, but prefer real time play - you will like stellaris.
It runs fairly well on higher details on my ROG 750JS (2013/14 gaming laptop) - the only time ive seen it chug is when i have massive areas of revealed space constantly under survailance, usually with the ISBS Sensor stations and some ZRO dust.
Not having the dlc's will not break your experience but they do add some nice extras, most though; are cosmetic and can be safely ignored.
I will say that there is a stark lack of events/meaningful events with meaningful rewards from the anomolies and the ai has a tendency to suddenly overlook the polar opposite ethos of neighbouring empires just to up yours the player.
Ship design, while interesting; lacks dedicated hull types for heavy cruiser and carrier types, forcing you to use BB/Cruiser hulls for those ships and there is a disturbing lack of defense against fighter spam from fallen empires, the "autocomplete" ship design option is a moot point as the ai only considers the military value of the ship, not its actual effectiveness against your enemies - in short; design your own damn ships!
Managing the different factions of your empire can prove to be a bit of a challenge if very specific ethos' gain dominance, some factions can vanish entirely from time to time and it can be a bit of a tightrope balancing act at the best of times, though it is also very rewarding to have a high approval with some factions.
The planetary and sector management system is interesting, quite extensive and the sector AI has been substancially improved since the earlier releases, though im still waiting for a sector shipyard designator so i dont have to remember where all my capital-shipyards are in each sector. (biiiig hint here devs ;) )
Endgame events can be challenging, especially the war in heaven ... fallen empires are probably the heaviest hitting thing you will usually face.
Combat ai is fankly, stupid and insists on smooshing all ships into a melee, even your carriers and artillery ships.
However, most of the faults ive mentioned can be fixed with mods, it is also; as of the writing of this review (July 2nd),50% off on the summer sales... so now is the best time to get it if you want it.

Despite that, you still need to experience this perfect train wreck. It sucks in so many ways that it literally creates its own gravitational pull that sucks you in. It's like the sirens of Greek mythology- you're not supposed to listen to their song. But you do anyway, and get drawn in. And then you can't get away. Because it's just that entralling.
10/10 Would suffer again. So says Mr. Stewart.
PS: If anyone can explain to me why I keep seeing Fk's in my coffee, that'd be great.
In all seriousness, despite some of the glaring gameplay issues and clunky menus, it does create an interesting story, albeit in a cheesy B-horror/comedy style that's reminiscent of Twin Peaks. Don't approach this game with the mentality that "This is a survival horror game" because it's not. Once you decide not to take the game seriously, you'll probably appreciate it if you can handle said B-horror comedy Twin Peaks stuff.

- Vision fields to test players true strategy skills
- Level exclusive achievements to push players to the limit, strategy and/or strength wise

Cons:
- Most levels can be done with one tower (even from the start, normal mode)
- End-game grinding causes lags
- Constant HUD freeze can be frustrating at times
You can play the flash version for free just to check whether you should buy this game or not at Armor Games, but if you like tower defense games, you should buy it, even if you're a casual player.

I have a love/hate relationship with Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel. Sometimes it's extremely fun, blasting enemies, completing quests, fighting mini and full bosses, among other stuff. However, other times it's tiring, getting one shot by the same group of enemies over and over again until I get one lucky run through, after nearly dying to oxygen loss (will explain later).
Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel is like many other RPGs: it thrives on side quests. While the main storyline is interesting, making you think about Jack's role as the bad guy in the other Borderlands games, and it isn't like as I mentioned in the intro, particularly difficult, it is significantly shorter than the story from Borderlands 2. However, despite it being shorter, it still is entirely enjoyable, with no points of confusion or a lack of coherence. One major issue with it, however, is that many of them are Back and Forth type quests, where the game has you running back and forth to get something done just to turn around and run back to the original spot to do something else, fighting some enemies along the way. The side quests in The Pre-Sequel also occasionally have the back and forth issue, but also a lot of the time are in true Borderlands style: funny as hell, and you actually feel like you're doing something.
Gameplay was very enjoyable. The game, like other Borderlands, doesn't skimp on gun choice, allowing you to adjust to your playstyle without issue. Furthermore, the new Vault Hunters' abilities are all quite good too, with no one clear character being stupidly broken or stupidly underpowered. I personally played along with my friend, him going for a Lawbringer build based on damage while me going for a healing/damage oriented Athena. The Pre-Sequel, also, adds a group of items called Oz Kits. These items are used to give some bonuses to your character (such as increased gun damage, accuracy, etc) and also act like astronauts' space suits, providing Oxygen to your human characters (the claptrap character granted isn't a human, but still needs an Oz Kit)
This mechanic required you to enter into an Oxygen rich area (building, Oxygen geiser things, etc) every so often to refill your Oz Kit, with the consequence of death if you didn't. This mechanic seemed cool at first, especially with the double jump and crouch slam abilities it gave you, but eventually it just got annoying, forcing you to run to find some place to refuel, killing the heat of battle. While I never died to it, it still got annoying.
Like Borderlands 2, this game had the golden keys mechanic where you can enter codes (I believe it was in some sort of collaboration with some snacks companies that you would buy their snack for a code, but you can just find them through google) into the game to get a few items (guns and customizations) but mostly golden keys to be able to use on their Mystery Box-esque Loot Box in
.
Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel has a lot of fun and good dlc, which adds many many new quests, and even sort of like a second campaign,
If you can find it on sale with the season pass, I would definetly recommend it.
Do I recommend it? Yes. Does it have its problems? Yes, many. Despite them, however, it can be amazingly fun, even more so if you have a friend or friends who also own it to enjoy the story and game with. I would not recommend it at full price, though, pick it up when it's on sale, and preferably, as stated earlier, with the season pass, as that adds many more gameplay and playtime.

Resident Evil Revelations (from here forward known as Resilations) is a pretty solid Resident Evil game, not amazing or revolutionary, but it's enough to get your survival horror mojo going if you're a fan of the series. If you've never played a Resident Evil I recommend the HD remake of the original to Resilations.
As a Resident Evil game it fits somewhere in between Code Veronica and RE4 in terms of the horror/action/hilariously convoluted storytelling ratio. It does a good job of making itself feel like it's more challenging and is putting you in more danger than it really is and the Queen Zenobia is a pretty good location to set the game in. The early moments where the game lets the atmospheric groan of the empty ship surround you as the screen shifts every so slightly to the rhythm of the ocean are the most unnerving parts of the game. Eventually it becomes obvious that ammo and health is pretty plentiful and you're feel too well equipped by the end of the game for it to be scary or even more than a little tense.
It's pretty obvious that this is a port from the 3DS. While very impressive on that piece of hardware even an HD facelife doesn't keep it from looking dated, even the cutscenes have a stange grainy/poorly compressed look to them. It's also still apparent that it was meant to be played in small chunks. The game is split into little episodes that usually run roughly 45 minutes and end on a big cliff hanger (which usually resolves in the silliest way possible) it was obviously designed around playing on a commute or lunch hour. It even plays a little "last time on Resilations" recap before each episode like it's assuming you're not going to play the game for long periods. Playing it sporadically probably helped hide some of the games issues with backtracking. At one point you escape a flooded area and the the next episode you just dive back in and swim though it all over again.
The best parts of the game revolve around Jill Valentine investigating the Queen Zenobia, but you're constantly being pulled from that storyline the plotlines of other characters and when you're back to Jill you end up backtracking a decent amount meaning that, in an already short game, you just don't get enough of the best parts. Tht being said Resilations is overall a solid games and is still a good game even when you're not in the Jill Valentine segments. The RE4 style mechanincs for fighting are fun even if Resilations doesn't have that game's excellent level design to play around with it in. Raid mode adds some life to the short campaign although your milage may vary with it.

This is a deceptively simple one; it's essentially an image-analysis algorithm paired with a fairly rudimentary paint program.
You play as an inexplicably-green-skinned frenchman.  It's just you, a blank canvas, a collection of paints, and a slowly-depleting bank balance that serves to keep you painting.
You have to sell your art to a number of buyers who will continually mill past, commenting on your work.  Different potential clients will have different 'preferences', and if they don't like a painting they'll tell you exactly why.  Sometimes it's as simple as 'I hate pink' and sometimes it's as vague as 'why do you paint without passion?', but as a general rule your being judged not on 'quality' but on whether it meets certian compositional criteria.
The result is something that works a lot better than you might think.
Because bills are never all that aggressive in their accumulation (being French, you live entirely off of Baguettes and Wine) and the clients are very particular that you fulfil the criteria - but don't care HOW you do it - it essentially works as a series of creative virtual painting exercises.
If you're terrible at visual art like I am, it's an absolutely wonderful way to get over any hang-ups you might have about sucking.  Some of the winners of the weekly contests might be distressingly skilled but since the only people actually judging you are the ones throwing money at you for your scrawlings, the whole thing makes for a very relaxed, enjoyable experience.
Definitely a good way to spend an hour or two if you've always wanted to paint but feel you lack the talent required; those with a lot of skill might also find the specific challenges creatively fulfilling.  It's definitely worth picking up at the price point.

So I am a fan of Platinum Games, Bayonetta 1 and 2 are both some of my favourite video games and I was looking forward greatly to this title and bought it day one. Unfortunately I think as far as gameplay goes they dropped the ball on this one.
The combat for starters does not have the button combination or delayed input combos seen in games like Bayonetta or Devil May Cry, instead they follow simple hit strings that remain the same, you can combine the inputs for example X, X, Y, X but changing the button input used will simply reset your string so X(1), X(2), Y(1), X(1). Obviously this leads to a lack of depth in basic combos and what they seemed to try to do was give you 2 weapon loadouts and allow you to switch weapons on the fly. Unfortunately the combat still ends up feeling incredibly limiting because you still have at most 4 different attack strings on your load out and that is assuming you even enjoy using the other weapons. The game also has some version of Platinums love of dodge mechanics but I feel this is the weakest yet although admitedly I have not played TMNT. You dodge and can do either an AOE hitting launcher or a large damaging attack, the problem is you already have a launcher with back input + respective weapon attack. Never has dodging felt less rewarding and enjoyable, in Bayonetta Bayonetta says some cheeky quip leading to everything slowing down and you get to relentlessly attack your opponent.
The enemy AI is horrible, not much else to say about that.
The open world is completely bland (which fits the tone of the game to be fair) and unnecessary, it feels like another video game that tacked on an open world because every other video game was doing it. An episodic or stage based game would be far better and instead of crafting a huge world with random sidequests and not much else in it they could have put that development time towards making the combat (the most important part of a Platinum game IMO) more interesting.
The sound design is completely insane, the voice acting is incredible and the music some of the best I have heard in a video game which I still listen to months after release.
The story is the best part, I don't want to give anything away because without the story there is very little to justify the games cost but it is as good as they say although it does take a very long time to ramp up, to the point where upon completing the game, twice, you still won't be at the interesting parts of the plot.
I am not sure if I can recommend the game based on the story alone, however, this is ultimately a video game and people have a certain expectation when it comes to Platinum Games and their combat. However I also understand there are Nier fans who already had a game with terrible gameplay/combat and didn't care and also mostly want to see the conclusion. Ultimately though I am not a fan of the original Nier and so I can only speak for myself and players like me. Avoid this game, watch a playthrough or story summary on Youtube.
Oh I forgot, it is a bad port and Square promised to fix some of the issues a week or two after release. It is now the 26th of June and no patch has arrived but they sure as hell released the DLC on time, lol.

This is my first review/Recommendation.
Nier: Automata is one of the few games that I was hyped for 2017 and it surpassed my expectations!
At first I was like this will be another generic overhyped hack and slash game that will dissapoint when it comes out. But when I played the Demo and learned about the story of the previous games... (Drakengard and NieR Gestalt/Replicant) I was ... intrigued wondering how the story will go on.
Story:
So.... From the description of the game ("Humanity has been driven from the Earth by mechanical beings from another world. In a final effort to take back the planet, the human resistance sends a force of android soldiers to destroy the invaders. Now, a war between machines and androids rages on... A war that could soon unveil a long-forgotten truth of the world.") the plot sounds unique and trust me IT IS! It had moments that made me go like "WOW THIS IS AWESOME!", other times I laughed or smiled from the interactions between characters and the dialogues and sometimes I teared up and felt so sad! Overall it is a rollercoaster of emotions. After saying all that, someone may wonder: "Do I have to play the first games to understand the plot?" The answer is NO you don't. You can play it as a standalone game and still enjoy the story. BUT! I would still recomend to have some basic knowledge about the Nier and drakengard universe (Mostly about project Gestalt and the white chlorination syndrome).
World Build (I hope I used a correct term) :
Every place you discover/visit in Nier automata is unique and memorable and what makes it even better is the awesome soundtrack that you hear while being in those places. Seriously I would just sit the amusment park and just listen to the music! Or while I was in the dessert I would just hum along the (Nonsensial) lyrics of the song while surfing on the sand. And every time I listen to the city ruins soundtrack I get chills reminding me the destruction that was caused in the land all these years and the fact that earth is now a desserted wasteland. More over the secondary quests even though they were just escort missions or fetch quests or just go from one place to another and talk to a certain someone almost all of them were unforgetable and it gave an even better understanding of the whole world and the people who live in it. Some of them had really creepy endings or just made you sit back and think as the extintential thoughts flow in your mind...

Gameplay:
No matter how good the story of a game is if the gameplay is not impresive and is boring and clunky very few people will finish it and enjoy it. And I am so happy that Nier: Automata does NOT belong in that category! (Unlike the previous games (ok maybe NieR was not so bad either)) To begin with, the new developer of the game (Platinum Games) did an exceptional work! The variaty of weapons gives you a huge amount of possibilities and new combos to try out! Chips that are dropped from enemies help you enhance your android to your playstyle. Do you like to just sit back and shoot with your pod use ranged attack chips to boost your ranged attack power. Do you want to be tanky and survive many hits defensive chips are here for you! More over some chips enable you to see your enemies lvl and health bar or your own health bar or the mini map and by removing them you won't be able to (I just found this a really nice detail). Further more I like how the camera angles change from place to place making the gameplay less repetitive and the shooter sequances reminded me of the games I use to play on MAME 32. Finally every boss fight felt so awesome and I loved how every boss had a backstory making them more interesting and not just something that I have to destroy in order to progress further. I  should also mention the awesome soundtrack during the boss fights. (Yeah this game's sountrack is so great it's one of my favourite video game soundtracks.)
Downsides:
Even though it is my personal oppinion I think I should just mention them.
First of all when I first played as 9S the only thing I was using was his hacking ability since 9S is not capable of using two weapons and doing the combos 2B can do. Plus it is really OP: once you finish the hacking the machine you were hacking will just explode and the machines caught in the balst radius will lose half of their hp and at first I found it really repetitive but I guess they did it in order to be able to go through ending B quickly since you are doing almost the same stuff you did during Ending A but with some revelations. What is more since NieR: Automata is a jRPG that means if your numbers are bigger than your enemy's you can easily beat them or vice versa. The problem was that in some side quests the enemies were lvl 30 while I was still lvl 15 and I tried to grind (I wanted to do all the available side quests first and then do the main story quests) so I tried to grind and in the final chapters of the game I was 10 levels ahead and the game just felt so easy! I even beat a boss before it could finish all its lines! So... a tip don't overgrind and don't worry about the side quests like I did. Just finish the game and just do the side quests that seem interesting and are around your level. Lastly some say that they had problems with the PC Port of the game like crashes etc. I did not have any problems except some FPS drops but I just lowered the graphics and everything was fine (I guess it was my pc's fault). So make sure you have a good PC that can handle the game or else just get it for the PS4.
Overall: NieR: Automata is an exceptional game with astonishing story, great gameplay and superb soundtrack that you should totally play and complete it until the end!
P.S. If you did not know already. To experience the whole game you have to complete all 5 Endings. And only after completing Ending E you will have truly experienced NieR: Automata (Just saying for the people who only completed ending A).
I hope you found this Review/Recommendation helpful and have a nice day !

Basicly a multiplayer game into singleplayer. Feels like one, too (positive).
Mechanics are solid, graphics are pretty, story (so far) is amazing, there are neat little tweaks to a "classical zelda like platformer" that make it special.
Mechanism impacts are introduced through a do more than a tell, at least once you get into the less basic ones. This can sometimes make one feel a little stumped, but the feeling of "I get it now!" gets that much stronger, and it feels more... natural?
The skill tree is well made, has a mechanism (switching branches) that i've never seen done well before, and here it is.
Elemental system : check, good so far, some puzzles use the switch of elements which is very good.
Varied ennemies, with interesting attack patterns that take into account the environment (simple example : thing that spits a rock upwards that falls on your head, but if there's something above, the rock can hit it - amazingly simple yet very clever - or take penguins that interact with falling into water not by taking damage like other ennemies, but jumping out and attacking? Ok i'll stop spoiling now.) with different strategies that reward the player for using his brain a little, but not so much that it interrupts the pacing? Check.
Platforming puzzles with switches and pushing boxes and moving platforms and things that shoot at you and bombs and... check.
Sidequests that are not just plopped on, but actually feel like you have a small impact on the world, hidden chests with loot inside, backtracking, making encyclopedias of monsters and plants? Check.
Balance between combat platforming and puzzle? Check.
Epic boss battles with patterns to learn? Check.
Sentient cyborgoats? Check.
Can't wait for more updates, hits all the right buttons, must recommend. <3

Pizza Connection 2 (I knew it as Fast Food Tycoon 2) doesn't age well with its slow UI and often crashes with new operating system (set compatibility mode to Windows XP and turn on "Run the game as an administrator" help.)
However, if you can overlook those flaws, the game itself is still a great business simulation game that requires strategic thinking. I agree with some of the reviews here that mentioned about the lack of tutorial in game, so here are some beginner tips:
- If you need money, ignore the trash and open restaurants 24/7 (it will affect your restaurants' area of effect however)
- Only update the headquarter when you need to, spend money on training staff, advertising, or sabotaging opponents instead
- Only accept a proposal when you can achieve it, don't just accept anything (there're penalties)
- Training staff is important, training bodyguards? not so much, use that money elsewhere.
- Save your game, try out different restaurant design and see which one pleases most types of customer (color does matter)
- Suck at making pizzas that people like? Focus on what they like and hate (click on people, green ingredients indicate like and red means hate), then design pizza for that specific peep (kids, students, louts, etc.) You can also buy pre-designed pizzas for a price, but you can't bring over these pizzas to new map.
- When the game says to build something, actually buy and construct a restaurant from a building, not just rent one because it doesn't count (I lost a couple games because of this..)
Hope you enjoy the game as much as I do.

This game has something going for it but I'm not sure what,
CrossCode is a sort-of 'Hack n' Slash, Bullet Hell RPG' which coincidentally (story-wise) takes places inside a game of the same genre. However, fun gameplay aside it's story is questionable but enjoyable.
You play 'Lea', a blue-haired 'avatar' which is basically infiltrating an online videogame as a fake player. You're basically a sentient AI who's motive is unclear for the entire game. I wasn't sure what the whole point of the main character being in the game was and I was never told why. The game pulls the amnesia-card straight out of the hat with this story so your main character knows just as much as you do. However, the few people that do know your backstory don't speak up at all and rather take a backseat while occasionally talking. Immersion breaks after that unfortunately once you dive into an endless paradox of self-purpose but let's not get ahead of ourselves.
Characters are a mix of fantastic but also quite mundane. Most of the time you're accompanied by a French Redheaded girl named Emilie who for the most part won't shutup and her only real use is 'To stop you from being a solo-player in a RPG'. There's also some green dude that I forgot the name of because he makes an appearance like twice and then you never see him again who has so much potential to be part of the plotline but it doesn't seem like it. He acts more like a rival from Pokemon than anything else.  There isn't much relation to the main-story and the ingame characters in that regard, the only 'real' character you keep in touch with that knows about your backstory doesn't say much aside from obvious advice such as 'Log off now you imbecile, you can't play for 24 hours, that's not human'. This entire scenario to put lightly comes to a screeching halt when we nearly get proper character development and then the game slaps you in the face and says "Hi, we haven't made this part yet! But you can still grind and do stuff to set you way over the level-cap for the next dungeon so that the game loses its challenge.'
How am I still giving this game a positive review?
Because for the most part, it's fun. It's challenging and enjoyable to enough of an extend where I can recommend this game to people who like fast-paced gameplay. The gameplay/gunplay/whateverplay is amazing, borrowing a lot from 'Furi', dashing around, avoiding attacks and when getting into close-quarters it can seem chaotic. The puzzles are a mixture of difficult and relatively easy, a bunch of the Ice Temple's puzzles had me stumped up until the last one which was probably the easiest in the entire dungeon. But that's what got me hooked, the gameplay. Which is a damn shame because the story accompanying it has so many flaws but so many upsides it's hard to say whether it will live up to the gameplay and blossom into a great game or just trip and fall into the pit of forgotten games.
For what it's worth, play it as it is right now. The game appears to be getting enough updates to sustain life and it's well worth your time.

I put hundreds of hours into this game back when it was new and I had a physical copy.  Now that my disc is all scratched up, I thought it was time to switch to digital.
An excellent title, and my first Total War game.  The base game is great, the expansion is better, the battles are fun, and everything just plays well.  Plus, watching thousands of troops slaughter each other is great fun, especially when you're doing most of the slaughtering.
It's also got a great modding scene:  Third Age: Total War (Lord of the Rings), Westeros: Total War (Game of Thrones), Hyrule: Total War (Legend of Zelda), Call of Warhammer (Warhammer Fantasy, although in this case you should probably get the actual Total War: Warhammer), and many, MANY more.  Lots of these mods have been worked on for years, giving this game a lifespan way longer than its already extensive base content.
There are a few flaws, like the squalor system and rebel system.  The former you can't really control so much as temporarily limit, and if you like long games like me you may find yourself fomenting revolts in your own cities so you can massacre the population to bring squalor back down.  The latter means that you can't get a region to be 100% guaranteed to not rebel, and since the game doesn't alert you when a new rebel army pops up, you have to manually scan your empire each turn for new rebels.  A lot of these flaws would be fixed in later games, but here they're just a minor annoyance and not a deal breaker.
Anyway, this is a must-have for strategy fans.

Did you ever feel bored in a middle of 3 hour movie? Watched it because you've started it and wanted to know that maybe the ending will save you from those boredom feelings? Search no more, Borderland: TPS offers it all! Dull and boring sidequests that often just make you walk from point A to point B? We got you covered! Time-limited quests with buggy vehicle physics that will make you get stuck in some pit after driving from hangar? It's also in here! Dialogues that clearly state that you're a moron and need easy sentences to understand what's going on - like 'shoot dat guy in the face'? Oh boi, you have plenty of those. Story? To avoid major spoilers -
But since Borderlands was never heavily focused on that... we should move on to...
Do you enjoy explosions covering the whole screen? Multi-level locations where map overlaps itself? Each weapon looking the same (unless it's legendary)? That's the spirit, I knew that you're a man of culture as well. Jokes aside. The gameplay didn't change that much since Borderlands 2. They've added (some more) gravity, stomps and oxygen. Sounds cool right? Well it isn't. As much as I'd like to enjoy those features I can't because it's hard to put them into actual gameplay. If you rush towards enemies with intention to stomp them - you'll most likely die in halfway. And while we're at enemies topic. Don't expect too many new species, new models, new ways to die. Regular enemies tend to respawn so quickly that it easily becomes a pain in the rear to fight them (unless you want to grind, then it's an ideal option). Bosses? There are a few. Some of them die too fast (not only because of level/items you have) and with the others you'll struggle for 20 minutes. Locations - every each one of them tries to scream 'look at me, I'm big, open and beautiful' and while I can agree with them being big, (and often confusing) they have nothing else to offer. Vehicles? I think that there are 2 (!) locations where you can use 2 types of vehicles. One being the same as in each Borderlands and the second one being buggy thing that you wish you'd never have to use.
As a fan of franchise and having about 200 hours (only on steam) spent with the first and second Borderlands, I can only write that I don't consider The-Presequel as an official 3rd (or 1st) part of the series. 40€ is a bit much for 12 hours of gameplay, even if the game doesn't end after the 1st run - you're really unlikely gonna make yourself suffer and try to do it again and again whereas in Borderlands 2 even grinding (with friends) could be fun. Maybe I'm just getting too old for all that.
I didn't mention characters on purpose. I think their design is okay as always, beside the fact that their personalities lack a lot of depth and you just can't feel the connection to them. Their fate isn't something that you'd care about.
I'm really surprised to see so many positive reviews, guess you guys want 2K Australia (which already died because of bankruptcy) to create Borderlands 3 as well :D

Borderlands and I have had a long, storied relationship. If you bother to look at my games played (and stop that, you creep) you'll notice that I spent an embarrassing amount of time playing Borderlands 2. The weird thing is, I'm not sure if I actually liked that game.
It clearly did something right. It must have - I wasted around 160 hours of my life grinding its many environments for equipment with better numbers than my current equipment. But when I think "Borderlands 2", I really think about the fate of my character - Salvador the Gunzerker.
See, I invested a LOT of playtime into that character. At some point, I began a new game+ with him. And that, for me, was a moronic thing to do. I played a bit of the campaign all over again, and got bored until the DLC came out. Mistake. Huge, huge mistake. The DLC came out, and I wasn't at the recommended level for it.
...I struggled through it anyway.
Borderlands 2 had a fundamental flaw, you see. I'm not sure how they could address it, but basically it relies heavily on leveling, and even being one level above or below the recommended level for a mission makes it p***-easy or incredibly hard. And from there, I grew to hate a game I spent a lot of time playing.
Now, I could have started a character over, but that was a lot of time I just didn't have. I could have (and probably in retrospect SHOULD have) modified my save, but I was too proud at the time. What I really wanted was a way to bring my character up to speed with the DLC.
...At least, that's what I thought at the time. Now I realize, if I was fretting over numbers that much, how could I possibly have been enjoying the game?
Enter Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel.
Now, I remembered all this when The Pre-Sequel came out, and purposefully stayed away. But eventually nostalgia of a sort hit me, this game hit $3, and I decided to give it a go, long after all its DLC was out. Smart me, thought I, for avoiding the trap I fell into last time.
TPS (which I'm referring to this game as from now on) is a pure sequel. It's the most sequely kind of sequel I can think of. It doesn't honestly do much other than tweak BL2 in some simple ways.
TPS is BL2 with faster, more aerial combat, essentially. Whether or not TPS is worth, frankly, anything, comes down to a question: would faster combat have completely revitalized your love of BL2?
For me... I'm not sure. I feel that familiar "revisit the same f****ing area" fatigue set in and essentially ragequit the game. BUT, and this is important, I come back because the core combat is more mindless, and therefore fun, than I remember BL2 ever being. For some people, the reduction in difficulty is probably a turn-off. For me, I think it saves the game.
The writing's slightly less obnoxious (fewer BUTT STALLION LOL jokes, more "this game was developed in Australia and we're going to make sure you know that). The combat's more fun. The loot system is a little more generous with the legendary drops.
Overall, I like it.
At least, for three dollars.

This game is actually a decent game, but it resembles perfectly what the Resident Evil franchise morphed into over the years, and what Capcom actually wanted it to be: a game that appeals to new comers, while keeping the fan base happy.
They wanted to play it safe, rather than attempt to make the masterpiece 10/10 game they once used to do. It brought some elements from the original Resident Evil, such as using the tanker as an analogue to the Spencer mansion of the first game, and elements from Resident Evil 4, such as using few parts of the games as battle arenas to shoot waves of zombies and go through near death experiences, and they got some Call of Duty elements from the inferior Resident Evil 6 game, such as Chris and Jill fighting hordes of enemies while finding easily accessible ammos and health when needed.
The tone of the game is not horror, like the Resident Evil Remake, nor is it camp, like the second half of Resident Evil 4, but rather it was mostly like watching a T.V. action series such as 24. And just like T.V action series, they replay highlights of the earlier chapters to stay updated on the overall plot when playing the next chapter or when returning to the game later. They really wanted to take the story seriously, when the canon of Resident Evil really wasn't great to begin with. They could've had a basic story to create a scenario, rather than attempt to make the story the central theme of the game. At least this games had a better story than all of the other Resident Evil games (I am serious), but it is still not great, though.
The game is fun when playing the Jill segments in the tanker. It looks like the traditional survival horror Resident Evil game that Capcom could've made if they wanted to go back to the original Resident Evil formula. Unfortunately, there are many times when the game cuts away to another character in another location, turning into a pure action segment, breaking the immersion immediately for me.
My other problem is that the game is too easy. I know there is a hard mode, but I started the game out with Normal, and thought that Normal would have a bit of challenge. I didn't die as much as I thought I would. I died 12 times, and of the 12 times, I think six or seven of them are either cheap deaths or because of dumb mistakes.
I recommend playing this game, especially if you want to take the taste of Resident Evil 6 out of your mouth, and hope for a better Resident Evil. As for me hoping for a better Resident Evil, this game showed me what Capcom is going to do with the franchise: play it safe, and don't make something spectacular like the remake or RE 4.

You customize your robot with eight parts (head, core, shoulder, hip, arms and legs). Each of the parts can have additional stats or have an active ability, up to four abilities, which means you can create your own combos. You gain these by destroying enemy robots and picking up their parts.
The bosses are played in Smash-like 1v1s where you can beat them up or knock them off the map. The bosses can be as powerful as you. The game features a fun tournament mode where you can participate in a series of boss fights.
Actually, the game is very interesting for the first couple of levels because you discover many parts that have different moves. I had a lot of fun. But as you progress further, you start getting parts that have the same attributes as the ones you already have, but either as a different part type or with a different model. After about half-way through, the level platforming becomes frustrating (one level can have you bouncing around damaging floors), and the enemies get too meaty for your combos, usually this would be alright but the way enemies fly off after a combo and not die is very irritating, especially if they go into dangerous areas and you want their parts.
Tournament mode is still fun, however. The bosses can be challenging.
The game also has multiplayer, so it could be possibly be better with friends.
Overall: 7/10,  it's good for a few hours. Get it only while it's cheap!

This is an OK game. It showed potential when I first started playing it. I recently picked it up again, but found myself wanting for the end to come; the ingame credits or otherwise.
PROS:
-The Super Smash Bros. style combat system works fairly well, with the player being able to smash their opponents into the wall or off the stage.
-The game is of average length.
-The parts system is easy to understand, intuitive and interesting.
-Part designs are interesting and varied.
-There is a stage editor.
CONS:
-Stages can be 1/2~1 hour long.
-There are no checkpoints in any stage except for the boss at the end, so if you lose all of your lives, you'll have to start the entire stage all over again. (which leads to artificial playtime extension)
-I've played through the entire game yet still have no clue what the story is.
-The final boss is frustrating, with absolutely no payoff after killing him.
-Sometimes, you will die because the controls fail you.
-Wall jumping is useful on a keyboard, but definitely not on a controller.
Overall, the game is OK, but not worth a buy unless A) you're a fanatic of Smash Bros.-style games or B) it's super cheap.

This is the best tower defense game I have ever played, and I really think that 'GemCraft - Chasing Shadows' is the best tower defense game on steam. The game benefits from it's gem system, allowing you to combine your tower properties and upgrade your towers to have multiple abilities. The learning curve for this game is smooth, with only a few spikes that grab your attention to the hints on the maps that help tower noobies to learn how to take advantage of your starting materials and the environment.
Gemcraft also features RPG elements such as a leveling system along with skills and equipable fragments for the tailsman, allowing you to gain an advantage in levels that were previously too difficult to complete (this means that you can grind to help you progress through the game if you'd like). If you think that grinding might make the game too easy, there are additional handicaps that the player can set on themselves to give more EXP and shadow cores for upgrading fragments. Achievements in the game are plenty and serve as milestones, giving the player skill points as a reward and keeping the difficult of the game from becoming to troublesome at later points in the game.
Gemcraft is a huge game for a tower defense game, which is incredible since the entire game can be played on the web for free at ArmorGames. I really encourage anyone who wants to play a tower defense game to try GemCraft, it doesn't get any better than this.

Alright, alright... where to begin this review...
...no, the Review doesn't end there yet, hang on for a bit more.
Well of course anyone can say a Game is good or bad, but saying
the game is good depending on my own opinion is what matters here.
As previously mentioned, I'm in love with the Game, even without playing it to its full extent, even though it is unfinished.
And about that, honestly, the game feels like it is finished until you see that small reminder after 12 hours of gameplay "Yo, the story ends here cause Early Access you know, you can still continue through content though, glhf" that makes you feel bad because you really want to continue to learn more about the Story of the Game, which is really well written.
Good lord, I never had so much fun fighting enemies in a game in a long time. No enemy feels like its a trash mob, unless youre 5 levels above that poor little creature, because then you're likely oneshotting it anyway. There's a relatively well structured vendor system aswell, that rewards you with items that don't just boost your basic stats, but enable you to customize Lea (that's the protagonist's name, duh) to your playsytle. Want hardhitting crit balls? There you have them. Want to take like 0 damage when blocking and reflect damage to enemies? You can do just that!
(Disclaimer: said strategies are not guaranteed to work throughout the progress of the Game) The Riddles and Puzzles are great and are a lot of fun, and if you're not a fan of those, too bad, you're missing out on some good Leveldesign there.
Two words, Eargasm and Eyegasm.
The soundtracks are awesome, fitting and don't get too repetitive or boring while you're playing,
Characters have really unique characteristics to them, which makes them very enjoyable. (I'm not looking at Apollo or anything.) Also, I think it's mentionable that every single Pixel the devs put onto your screen is blessed, because everything just looks so good, even with those little colored squares being visible. Animations are smooth and very enjoyable (also oddly satisfying sometimes.) And don't get me started with the title screen, that smooth animation had me hooked for a good 2 minutes of appreciation.
Is this game worth 20 bucks? For you? Probably. For me? Oh hell yes.
Does the game offer you quality gameplay? Hells yeah.
Do the devs deserve your money? Uhh... that's likely?
Basically, if you like RPGs and can appreciate details in a game, this is
game for you.
I can assure you that CrossCode is worth the time you put into it.

Borderlands and I have had a long, storied relationship. If you bother to look at my games played (and stop that, you creep) you'll notice that I spent an embarrassing amount of time playing Borderlands 2. The weird thing is, I'm not sure if I actually liked that game.
It clearly did something right. It must have - I wasted around 160 hours of my life grinding its many environments for equipment with better numbers than my current equipment. But when I think "Borderlands 2", I really think about the fate of my character - Salvador the Gunzerker.
See, I invested a LOT of playtime into that character. At some point, I began a new game+ with him. And that, for me, was a moronic thing to do. I played a bit of the campaign all over again, and got bored until the DLC came out. Mistake. Huge, huge mistake. The DLC came out, and I wasn't at the recommended level for it.
...I struggled through it anyway.
Borderlands 2 had a fundamental flaw, you see. I'm not sure how they could address it, but basically it relies heavily on leveling, and even being one level above or below the recommended level for a mission makes it p***-easy or incredibly hard. And from there, I grew to hate a game I spent a lot of time playing.
Now, I could have started a character over, but that was a lot of time I just didn't have. I could have (and probably in retrospect SHOULD have) modified my save, but I was too proud at the time. What I really wanted was a way to bring my character up to speed with the DLC.
...At least, that's what I thought at the time. Now I realize, if I was fretting over numbers that much, how could I possibly have been enjoying the game?
Enter Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel.
Now, I remembered all this when The Pre-Sequel came out, and purposefully stayed away. But eventually nostalgia of a sort hit me, this game hit $3, and I decided to give it a go, long after all its DLC was out. Smart me, thought I, for avoiding the trap I fell into last time.
TPS (which I'm referring to this game as from now on) is a pure sequel. It's the most sequely kind of sequel I can think of. It doesn't honestly do much other than tweak BL2 in some simple ways.
TPS is BL2 with faster, more aerial combat, essentially. Whether or not TPS is worth, frankly, anything, comes down to a question: would faster combat have completely revitalized your love of BL2?
For me... I'm not sure. I feel that familiar "revisit the same f****ing area" fatigue set in and essentially ragequit the game. BUT, and this is important, I come back because the core combat is more mindless, and therefore fun, than I remember BL2 ever being. For some people, the reduction in difficulty is probably a turn-off. For me, I think it saves the game.
The writing's slightly less obnoxious (fewer BUTT STALLION LOL jokes, more "this game was developed in Australia and we're going to make sure you know that). The combat's more fun. The loot system is a little more generous with the legendary drops.
Overall, I like it.
At least, for three dollars.

I would definitely recommend this game. So far I have played almost 200 hours as of writing, and I would enjoy playing more. This game is less complicated than other paradox games, not including hoi4, so it is a great introduction to paradox's style, along with a good intro to 4x in general. It is definetly less deep than other pdox games, but that isn't a bad thing.
The combat is fairly balanced, as much as people say it is just numbers vs. numbers there is thought to combat, since you can redesign your ships to counter any opponent. (except naked corvettes, though that one doesn't matter as much, because the ai doesn't spam it, so you can choose not to as well. There is also a mod that fixes that.) Though I will add that missles are the best pick in the starting game because you can't put point defense on corvettes anymore, (because people used to spam the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of it) so missles will have no trouble beating your corvettes. As for going to war, the ai is very good about forming defensive pacts at the moment, so you may end up in a bad position because you don't have enough ships or you don't have a friend. (this is singleplayer of course) The crisises can be repetitive, but that's mostly because you only ever see two out of the three available. Creating your empire, including setting up ethics, govt., flag, traits, etc., is fun because you can get a bit more invested into say, your fungi that want to conquer everyone, I mean, invite them all to the best party ever. I do feel that the traits don't make you extremely different from other aliens, so that could be worked on. Research is interesting because it doesn't follow a tech tree when you pick something to research, it randomly picks techs from what you have available to research, which prevents you from beelining for the best stuff straight away. It also means that you don't just follow the same research strategy every game because the choices you get are different. Pop ethics aren't too important though, since factions that oppose the governing ethics rarely spawn to begin with (not enough pops to make a faction) and usually those factions die off. The factions system is fun though, because there are concrete easily seen issues that each faction cares about, and making them happy makes pops in that faction happy AND you get influence. The new traditions are basically like social policies from civ 5, with starter and finisher bonuses along with all of the traditions in the tree. If you have Utopia you get ascension perk slots when you finish the trees, which give you huge bonuses and can affect your playstyle heavily. The ai can also get traditions, though from my experience they don't seem to focused on generating unity (culture). There are two tradition trees that are worthless unless you use the specific playstyle they cater towards. Traditions could use some work in my opinion but they aren't too bad. Getting new planets gives you malices to research and the unity cost of traditions, but that's a good thing. It keeps snowballing in check while still allowing you to get big. Generally your research will outpace the malices if you build labs. Sadly, there are some features locked behind DLC like most other Paradox games, but you can take a look at the wiki to see what each one offers. I own both of the dlcs that add content besides portraits, and i haven't played the most recent update without them, (paradox releases free content with every major update) so I can't give a serious recommendation on what to buy. Either way, this is certainly a game I would recommend.

I got this in The Green Light Bundle's 'Best of' Bundle.  It took around 10 hours to get to the end, no 100%.
I heard the comparisons to Super Smash Bros. and Custom Robo and didn't believe it at first, but it got me interested in the game.  And I'm really glad I picked this up now.
So you're a super fighting robot, and it's your mission to go beat up other robots in the Levels and beat the boss at the end of the third stage of each Level.  Controls felt pretty tight.  On a controller, left stick moves, you have a button for jump, normal attacks, special attacks, and the parts menu.  You can wall jump, sprint, double jump, and have a variety of normal attacks based on tilting the stick or if you're in the air (no smash attacks here).  But the rest of the fancy stuff comes from parts.
Megabyte Punch is part exploration, part platformer, part fighter, part collectathon.  The basic premise of the game is to find the door in each stage to advance to the next section until you get to the end of the third stage and fight the boss to clear the level.  On your way, you'll fight other custom-made robots both in the field and in arenas that seal themselves off when you enter.  Like Smash, you still have to raise the unseen damage number for your enemies, and like Smash, a particularly hard hit will send them flying.  But if your foe slams into a hard surface, it explodes, leaving behind life-granting Bits or a custom part.  Or if they go into the soft blocks, they'll cut right through them and explode.  And the same applies to you.
Boss battles twist the basic formula and turns it into an itemless match of Smash.  Smack the boss around and get his damage up and then send him into the black killzones around the area a few times.  And of course, try not to burn all your lives in the process, or you'll have to start the entire level over.
I liked exploring, though outside of the forced-fight arenas, you're allowed to rush to the end.  The issue then is finding the right way to go.  The damage you take is permanent until you die and respawn, so rushing may end up being the better option for some.  You can carry a small inventory of extra parts from the robots you destroy and from there you can swap out with what you currently have on, but everything not equipped goes to your inventory at home when you go through any door.  You more or less start each stage with the clothes on your back, but you can break down any spare parts for Bits--64 of which give an extra life, and you start each Level with three no matter what.
I wouldn't say the platforming was necessarily hard, but I went with more jumps and most of the challenge was maneuvering around obstacles with enemies present, or dealing with dangers like damage plates and mines in the arenas.  Each stage is pretty big though, especially if you try to drill through the soft blocks.
Parts do a variety of things, like give you passive mobility boosts or extra jumps, or some give you special attacks you assign to Neutral, Up, Down, and Side B.  While there are a lot of parts, there aren't as many unique effects, but you could argue it's partly for aesthetics reasons too.  You can equip to your torso, head, shoulder, left and right arms each, left and right legs each, and hips.  And there are color palettes to collect too, though you can't customize each part's color--it's everything or nothing.  You can save quite a few parts and color loadouts too.
Progression in specials felt a little stagnant, but it was less "ever-powerful moves in later stages" and more "everyone is mostly on the same playing field."  The strongest special is the 25-damage Megabyte Punch, and I had a move that did 18 in the first level, though it was slow coming out.  Every move felt like it had a use, as opposed to 100 moves of which you'd use 10 at best.
Overall, if you enjoyed Adventure Mode/Subspace Emissary in Smash, you'd probably like this game.  It has local 2-4 coop for Adventure, there's Versus, and a Tournament Mode to get rare parts.  No online, but desyncs and lag would hamper enjoyment for a game like this.  Lots of parts, lots of things to beat up, great length for the price.
And I had a smile on my face from the first time I spiked one of those little robots through the ground.

GemCraft - Chasing Shadows is an outstanding tower defense game that's one of the more stimulating ways to kill time.
The main gimmick of this series is that your towers are sockets for gems, which are the source of your attacks and can be switched between towers as well as fused to combine their special effects.
The game has very complex mechanics, but it doesn't feel overwhelming as they're introduced one by one and many are optional. It's a lot of fun to get accustomed to new abilities or structures, and the game is only punishing if you want it to be.
Aside from common features such as custom targeting, fast-forward (up to 9x), mazing and calling waves early, there's many unique concepts, lots of different structures to keep things diverse, and the ideas from previous GemCraft games have been vastly improved.
Slightly annoying: demolitions are costly and limited even in the preparation phase, so if you make a mistake with wall building you may have to restart and build everything again.
Chasing Shadows' main problem is that it runs on Flash, so there's no linux support. For a flash game it runs well though, lag is only an issue at extremely high levels.
There's a lot of content. The large amount of maps is supplemented by custom difficulty modifiers and the option to continue each level in endless mode. On sale, the amount of playtime you get for 2€ is just ridiculous.

My big gripe with people who do negative reviews on brawlers is that they tend to expect way more out of these games than they should. A 2D brawler is more or less going to be 3 things: 1) coop mandatory 2) generally shallow fighting system to allow pick up and play 3) usually short. The mash x and mix it up with y is something you can expect with all brawlers (castle crashers, dd neon, foul play). When you defiant from this formula is when things go bad. Too deep of a combo system scares people from wanting to co-op with less skilled players, too long and you sacrifice fun for padding. There is one thing a brawler can do that will absolutely ruin it, making annoying/too tanky enemy types. This game never does that. 90% of attacks are blockable, all attacks are dodgable and all enemies stagger within reason. To me, this game is a solid brawler. I buy these games for the strict purpose of playing with my wife/friends and this is an absolutely solid brawler. Player types are various enough in how they play to make them interesting.
To give you an idea of who I am so you can have a good idea of whether my opinion will likely match yours, here are my favorite brawlers:
Double Dragon neon
Castle crashers
Dragons crown
TMNT iv Turtles in time
Foul play
Magicka
Here are the ones I hate:
Final exam(all enemies are tanks, and they randomly swam the screen. Super annoying, exploration based gameplay that makes exploring annoying)
Streets of Fury Ex (I actually like this game but only if the 99 credit cheat is in. It's a good example of poor brawler gameplay. Early on frustrating enemy types, enemies don't stagger when they stack, player staggers too easily and can get juggled by enemies, no healing, frustrating bosses, block it's worthless)
Rampage Knights (Roguelike brawler pretty much tells you how bad it's going to suck)
Phantom Breaker (too deep of a combat system, worthless block, non-staggering tank enemies, worthless special)

Deadly Premonition sucks. Ultimately, it fails on all levels. The setup of the story is actually pretty good. It's obviously biting off Twin Peaks. A weirdo FBI agent is sent to investigate a murder with supernatural overtones in a small town filled with wacky characters. The obvious inspirations for the game play are Silent Hill and Resident Evil. There are parts where a location transforms into a twisted nightmare version of the place and its filled with monsters and the player has to make their way through the nightmare version of the location to find clues to help the investigation. So, the combat takes place really in the protagonists mind. The combat gets really repetitive and boring really quick. There's really just one type of enemy to fight for most of the game besides bosses. Later there's another type that's even more boring and repetitive to fight. Every location ends up being the same thing. To gather the necessary clues you gotta wade through a series of narrow corridors fighting the same boring enemies over and over again. The combat is really clunky too like a Resident Evil game. There is one interesting part of this, though. At some point the legendary supernatural killer of the story, The Raincoat Killer, will track you down and the screen splits so you can also see through the killers eyes and your own point of view simultaneously. You need to hide from  him for a certain amount of time before he gives up and goes away. Usually, right after this section there will be a chase sequence that's kind of like an on-rails quick time event where you need to escape from The Raincoat Killer.  These encounters were fun the first few times, but even these interesting parts get repetitive as they are used over and over again. So, the actual combat portion of this game is a big dud. There's also a lot of driving that needs to be done in this game. It is also no fun. The cars handle terribly and they can even run out of gas. This is supposed to be an open-world exploration adventure game, but the fuel tank keeps a leash on you so its an annoying concern that made me not want to even bother with exploring the environment. Really, all there is anyway is some random collectibles to find littered around and also some side quests. So, the driving portion is also not any fun. The PC version is a really bad port too. It crashes ALL the time. I lost several hours to stupid crashes that can and will strike at any time. There was even one cut scene that would guaranteed crash the game. I had to change the compatibility mode and some other options to get past this stupid bug. The game is originally capped at 30 fps and 720p. Ridiculous! The same guy that fixed this outrage for Dark Souls did a fix for Deadly Premonition too, but like the DS one, it seems like it just plain wears off after a while and the game reverts back to ♥♥♥♥♥♥ graphics and frame rate.  I had to re-start the final boss because the game was running so horribly it wouldn't even register inputs from the controller. One thing I did find at least amusing is that if you don't have your clothes cleaned every so often, flies will start buzzing around your character because of your stinky clothes. I got a chuckle of watching cut scenes where these big fat (white?) flies were swarming around this guy. Now to the story. The setup is intriguing. There's a serial killer on the loose which brings the FBI to the small town and while there, more people get murdered. I was hooked on the setup. However, once the story starts to explain what's going on and who is behind everything the story just falls completely apart. It's just plain ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. It's like a ten year old's idea of a murder mystery. It's unbelievably bad. It's so dumb! I'm shocked and baffled that this story isn't completely ripped apart by everyone that has reviewed this absurd game. This game is also not scary, AT ALL. It fails in that department too. On the technical, atmosphere, narrative, and game play levels this game fails across the board and I definitely recommend you avoid this game.

105 hours. A regular triple A game takes about 44 continuous hours to complete if you take your time with it. While you can certainly beat this game in less time without all the side-missions, this game drags on for 105 hours if you want to 100% it. ...and when you're done, you breathe a sigh of relief.
I'm done making excuses for this game. This game features invisible shrubberies, and levitating trees and fences. Cars sometimes fall off the map, straight through the street. The game also more or less requires you to wait several days for a certain side-mission to open up. (It has to be raining during three specific hours, three times, you have to have certain specific items at these times, that you better look up in a walkthrough beforehand, and if you don't want to smoke, that can mean waiting many, many hours IN REAL LIFE. That means leaving your computer and go do the dishes. I means going to the store to buy food in real life. Oh, but the game doesn't tell you, is that the days where the side mission is said to open up, isn't the days where it ACTUALLY opens up.)
Everything that can be broken in this game, is broken. People say that it's just a "bad port". No, this is the ULTIMATE bad port. This is a nearly playable port! This is the circus freaks of bad ports, of a game that was a circus freak to begin with!
HOW TO GET IT TO RUN
In order to get this game to even get past the loader setup without crashing, you need to "repair" its PhysX file. (See description in the Steam forums.)
Then, in order to improve the graphics with custom resolutions and antialiasing, you should probably want to install the DPfix fan fix. ...but you need to edit the fix ini file to a certain resolution. (Also, if you set the details to "Ultra" in that file, the graphics will crash.)
Now you can get the intro to play, so that the game doesn't crash on start-up. There's still the issue with random crashes in-game, as well as the issue with the car sound.
In order to fix the sound, you will need to set your 7.1 or 5.1 surround headphones back to 2.0 stereo headphones in the headphone's own settings.
As for the random crashes, I have been able to establish two causes.
First of all, the game was a memory leak that will slowly but surely eat up RAM until it crashes. When this occurs depends on how much free RAM you have.
Second of all, you need to set the game file (DP.exe) to run in a Windows 98 compatibility mode. You will be able to play the game up to Chapter 6 without doing so, with only occationally buggy inventory menus as an ecceft,, but at that chapter the game will finally crash consistently.
If you experience further problems, there are talks about further fixes that you can do, such as getting the game to recognize higher memory adresses by downloading a third-party tool.
However, this will NOT fix all the crashes. Try rebooting your computer if the game starts crashing too much. Nobody knows why this is required. It could be that the game would require continuous unfragmented areas of memory in RAM.

Crosscode is one of those special games you come across only once in a while. A small, obscure indie game that hides in the nooks and crannies of the internet, hoping to be discovered.
If I were to describe this game with a sentence: Imagine a game that combines classic 2D Legend of Zelda puzzle and exploration mechanics with top-down shooter combat, and MMORPG leveling and skill tree systems.
The game world takes place in an MMORPG called "Crosscode" but is in fact a single player game. The exact place you have in this world as the protagonist (Lea) is a mystery, and an intriguing intro sequence reveals that you may have quite the past to uncover. Suffering from amnesia, the only way to recover your memories is to play and advance through the world of Crosscode, fulfilling two purposes: Completing the game, and discovering the truth about yourself.
This game exploits the best elements of an MMORPG, and eliminates the boring parts they contain. Leveling up, finding hidden items, getting loot, destroying large amounts of enemies in a short amount of time, skill-based combat that requires finesse and precision, these are all fantastic elements in Crosscode. If you master the combat system, you can wipe out enemies vastly superior to you in level, and by investing in a variety of skills, unlocked through a skilltree, you can express yourself with battle instead of words, which you'll come to find quite valuable. *wink wink*
Puzzle mechanics are not only smart and satisfying, making you feel like a smug little Sherlock, but they are just as fast paced as the combat, meaning that you'll never sit still and be bored out of your mind, or spend too much time walking around wondering what the hell is going on.
So please, buy this game. The developers deserve so much more than what they're getting. There's *passion* in this game. Just go. Buy it. Do it, do it now. Oh, and bring your gamepad.

As you read over some of these negative reviews, one thing seems to be a common theme between them: depth of the game. Now, if you're like me, a person who has never played a 4x strategy or Paradox title before, I reccommend that you ignore these reviews. It is true that Stellaris is not as in depth and micromanage-y as something like EU4 or Crusader Kings, but it is, however, a fantastic introduction into these styles of games.
Stellaris was my first Paradox title and I'm glad it was. The tutorial did a great job of explaining the basics of the game, but did lack somewhat in explaining some quality of life things that I had to find out on my own. Thankfully, online guides and the subreddit are great resources.
The game shines the most in the empire creation, I have a ton of fun picking the appearence, flag, name, ethics, government, and perks for my empire. Going from a diplomatic trader race to a "DEUS VULT" purge-xenos-in-holy-fire warmongering race keeps the replay value high.
The game is hard to put down. Espically as you start to learn the ins and outs and really take off, things snowball quite fast and you get to see your empire grow and change as you see fit. With the DLCs, leviathans give you a end-goal to work towards, ensuring you dont get bored as you progress into later parts of the game.
My biggest issue with the game right now is combat. Unfortunately, combat is severely unbalanced right now and, somehow, it is actually in your best interest to be using the starting ship class (corvette) with starting weapons as it is the quickest and most cost efficient way to wage war. Tests have been done and higher-tier weapons and ships actually get way less efficient as you progress through the tech tree. Currently(1.6 at time of writing) battleships, which are end-game ship-class, are pretty much ignored in the meta due to how they're build cost is simply not worth the damage they output. Of course, this is subject to change in future patches and there are some great mods on the workshop to balance this.
Overall, I think stellaris could do a lot of things better, like combat and to some degree, diplomacy, but I still find it a very fun game regardless. Visuals are great, the soundtrack in the background is nice, but I always prefer to listen to my own music when I play. The game is well optimized. Some friends of mine run this on older laptops with no issues.
One final feature I want to talk about that I think is really cool is the ability to run multiplayer games out of single player saves. So say you have a really fun single player game and you're allied with some AI in the game and you two are broing it up in space. Well your real friend can actually hop in that game if you choose to host it online and take over that empire. In general mutliplayer, I have had no issues so far with connecting or hosting games. Also, the game features cloud saving of games so you can pick up where you left off on another device.
So tl;dr ,
If youre new to 4x or paradox games and want to get into them, I highly reccommend Stellaris. It is a great intro to 4x games and is hard to put down once you get the hang of it. My biggest issue is combat balancing, but mods and possible future patches can address that.

I'm really not one to write reviews because I believe other people are able to better define why or why you shouldn't buy the game, but because I've burned so many hours into this, I felt I needed to speak about it.
When you load the game you're given a few options: Campaign, Tournament (the 1-player stage fighter) or Versus (the multiplayer stage fighter). You can play the campaign with up to four players, and the screen is split so you can explore on your own without trapping players in a corner (a la Gauntlet style).
Playing Campaign allows you to unlock new colors and parts for the game. The game boosts 30 color schemes and 150 parts (some of which are duplicates for different body parts).
You play through 6 worlds, each having 3 levels and a boss at the end. Each world can take about 15 - 30 minutes, depending on if you're trying to find the colors/parts or just racing for the finish. There are also two bonus levels, one of which is fairly difficult.
Story is okay, the levels are fun, the bosses are great, but it doesn't have any replay value unless you want to play with friends.
This is where the game shines. I recommend getting some parts and colors from the campaign, then playing Multiplayer with some friends.
The game has full X360 controller support, and you can change the controls to best suit you (that said, I've never changed them because they're perfect for this game).
The first time you play Multiplayer (Campaign or Versus) be prepared for about 5 minutes per player of setup time. The nice thing is you can save your Megac Set to the game, making for a quick load the next time you play together.
Once you get into Versus mode and everyone is ready, you'll enter the stage select screen. There are 15(?) stages to select, along with 3 custom stages you can create.
The Multiplayer is exactly like Super Smash Bros with no items: Just you and your abilities trying to knock your opponents off the stage.
The big downside to Multiplayer is the lack of match customization. You can only play 4-stock, no time limits. While I've never run into any problems with this ruleset, it would be nice to have a time mode, or items.
The lack of online Multiplayer prevents me from playing with a few friends, but this game is really meant to be played with people right next to you with everyone yelling at the monitor/TV.
Tournament mode is quite the challenge, but allows you to unlock a few secret parts in the game that you can't get through Campaign. There is also the task of tracking down all 30 color schemes and all 150 parts, so there's plenty of exploration to be done, and the game has a lot of replay value.
While I did mention the Campaign is lacking a little, it's still an absolute blast with several people, but the main pull will still be the customization and the Versus mode.
I look forward to any future updates or Megabyte Punch 2 (f there are any plans).
