Frontier Simulator 200X.
Do you like crafting?
Do you like terraforming?
Do you like building cozy farms?
Do you like watching skills level up by increments of 0.02 points?
Do you like having your cart and planks stolen then tricked into dying a spider's death?
Do you like stabbing your♥♥♥♥♥♥off while trying to function in a N64 like environment?
If you answered Yes to all of these, you would enjoy Wurm Unlimited (WU).  WU is the non-MMO version of Wurm Online (WO).  For those of you who missed the /v/ invasions of 2009, WO is a game managed and coded by some Viking guy that lives in the frozen Scandanavian mountnains.  WO is extremely grindy--- think like Early 00 Korean MMO levels of grind.  Fortunately, WU is a version of Wurm that is made for private servers.  You can join in custom run servers with various exp rates or create your own for solo / personal use.  The game is a frontier simulator with fantasy elements.  You must chop down trees, skip and jump, and press wild flowers.
You have a giant list of skills to develop for crafting.  Every action you do falls under a tech tree.  In order to survive, you must learn how to balance resource gathering, resource processing, and building.
The game is extremely niche.  Extremely.  Graphics are not going to improve and combat is mostly just standing near a monster and waiting to see how badly you die.  A few takeaways:
+Edit the world.  Design and build buildings wherever you want.  Set settlement tokens to "claim" land and property.
- You will need to level up considerably before you can build a grand stone palace.
+ Start your own server and play as you want.
- The base game really does require teamwork to do anything.  Playing by yourself is really... lonely.
+ Set your own server with higher EXP rates or play on private servers with raised rates.
- Building depreciation occurs while the server is on.  You will have to log in every so often to ensure your structures don't crumble to dust.
+ Depreciation can be turned off if you run your own server.
- AGain, playing by yourself is lonely.
+ Starting from scratch after you built all your roads crooked and couldn't get the slopes even is kinda fun.  Think of when you got frustrated in Sim City 2000 and mashed the Natural Disaster button.
+ Massive crafting options.
- Game is kinda ugly, haha.
+ Very challenging.
- No naked anime girls as rewards for challenges.
+ Rewards are seeing your cozy farm / town grow as the result of your efforts.
This game really really really isn't for everyone.  Watch some Let's Plays before you touch this.  I highly recommend playing a bit on your own single player server to learn the controls.  Terraforming is tricky.  This isn't Animal Crossing or Rune Factory.

As you most likely see in the other reviews for this game:
itself is quite enjoyable, but bugs and crashes can quickly sour the taste of the experience.  I, however, mostly enjoyed the game so I wanted to give it a "Thumbs Up."  If you approach the game the right way then you can really minimalize the impact of the crashes.
The game is a moderately open-word survival horror game.  The controls are a little clunky, especially the driving, but I suppose it fits the genre.  The music is whimsical and the dialogue is funny, if not at times very corny... but again the corny lines fit with the genre and the "bad horror movie from the 80s" type vibe the game gives off.  The story is enjoyable and intriguing.  A fun little aspect is that the game does it best to make the small town of Greenvale feel lived in.  That is to say:  each NPC moves around the town depending on the time of day, and the weather—so you may have to search for them accordingly.  The graphics are not very good, but they aren't
bad.  There is a user-created mod that can improve the visuals.
As mentioned, the bad side of the game really boils down to bugs and crashing.  Now as for bugs, I didn't really experience any "bugs" when I played, I did experience crashing, however.  But really, it wasn't
bad.  Here is some advice:  check out the “stickied” thread about troubleshooting.  Make sure to repair PhysX.  I personally did
install DPfix (which is a user-created, unofficial mod) because it only fixes visuals (which don’t bother me) and it may actually cause more problems than it fixes.  Lastly, be sure to save
.  Like: even if you just saved 5 minutes ago, if you reach another save point, save again.  This way if and when you get a crash, you don't have to replay a ton of gameplay.  This will help make the crashes a minor annoyance rather than a game-destroying problem.
There are also 50 side-quests in the game which actually offer rewards that are valuable in the main campaign—so you may find yourself wanting to do them even if you don’t care about achievements or “completionism.”  Many guides and such will recommend you do the side-quests during chapter-replays... I however, recommend you try to do as many as you can during initial playthroughs of a chapter.  This is because during a chapter-replay you can't save until you finish the replay, which may cause you to lose some progress if you encounter one of the aforementioned crashes.  If you try to do as many side-quests as you can during initial playthroughs, you will be free to save often preventing progress loss.  Some side-quests will require replays to do, simply because of the mechanics… for those I recommend chapter 7, because you can quickly end the chapter-replay, save, and then start it up again to do more side-questing.  Then just rinse and repeat until you’ve done everything… that’s how I did the side-quests and the occasional crashes were endurable.
In summary, the game is good, and worth the experience... in my opinion.  This is especially so if you enjoy the genre, or enjoy heavily story-driven games.  It will require some troubleshooting and some tolerance for bugs/crashing.  If you decide to follow my advice, and do a little planning and save often, the crashes that you will encounter won't set you back that badly, and you will probably enjoy the overall experience of the game.

I'm writing this late review out of gratitude to the developer and because I believe this game deserves another positive review. This game is THE defining Tower Defense game. Every other I've played has come nowhere to the enjoyment I felt playing this.
You want replayability? The game essentially never ends. You can beat the final map but you can always do better, or unlock new maps. Or replay older maps to beat it at a higher difficulty to level up.
You want customisation? This game has it. Lots of it. Play the game how YOU want, how YOU would enjoy it. Sure, at high level there are common strategies used by most but the game lets you choose alternative ways if you care more about having fun than constantly beating your past exp score.
And speaking of fun, yes, this game has all of it.
My one criticism is - believe it or not - that this game is TOO good. I worry that the sequel (and there WILL be a sequel to this amazing game) won't have anywhere near the amount to expand and improve upon that this one did. But I should really have more faith in the developer than that, as they have proved how much of a good game they can already make.

I remember a friend of mine showed me Wurm Online, the original mmo version, and I was hooked right away,
Wurm unlimited is not far off from its forefather. It carries over everything we know and love from the original and bundles it all in a nice packaged deal for those of us without the money for subscription time or even just time in general. Because this game needs A LOT of time. Thankfully being able to host your own servers or join a friend's takes away a lot of that pressure to constantly check in on your character/village.
Anyway, on to the actual review.
Graphics 7/10
Keep in mind that this game may not meet AAA graphics standards, but it has come a long way since its fledgling days.
While not super appealing at first glance, the game's low end graphics do grow on you over time and are more than enough for what the game is trying to present.
Gameplay 7/10
Wurm is one of those games that scratches a very specific itch. It covers a wide range tags such as base building, resource management, rpg elements, and a few more. Whatever it is you typically like to do in survival sandbox games, Wurm has something to cover it.
Controls 5/10
I won't lie about this one, Wurm's controls are a bit jarring at first. The game functions mostly on drop menu commands and task queues. Thankfully this can be salvaged with proper key bindings to reduce the number of mouse clicks needed to complete a task. Don't let all this throw you off right away though. A lot of the games commands become second nature once you've sank a few hours into it.
Community 9/10
This one is a bit tricky. While the community per server will always be different a lot of the over all players are from the original game. Which means new players are generally welcomed wholeheartedly and there's no shortage of people who'd be willing to show you the ropes. Wurm, at its core, is a heavily community based game in general too. Networks of villages, player run trade markets, etc. Don't be afraid to reach out and talk to other players.
tl;dr
Overall rating 7/10
Wurm is one of those games that fits into a very niche community of gamers. It may not be your cup of tea, but it is very much worth a shot.

TL;DR first for people skimming reviews. There are no plot spoilers in this review.
The game is a great overall. The music in particular does a great job of making the game an experience. The 'main' story has breaks to explore and do side quests, while keeping a sense of urgency in other places as it should. I used the "FAR" patch and I didn't have any FPS issues, but I did have some slow down because of a weak CPU in my laptop. For negatives, there are a lot of unexplained mechanics that would have been nice to have explained, like sprint. The game's difficulty settings don't feel that good/rewarding. Also, the story is pretty depressing if that's an issue.
Full-Length version below.
Game Length/Achievements
I enjoyed playing through this game. I took my time to farm the equivalent of gear that I wanted, and I did as many side quests as I could when I could. It took me about 60 hours going fairly slow to finish the main story. The game has multiple endings, but it will basically lead you from ending to ending until ending "E" where you have actually completed the main story. I will bet that some people have stopped after ending "A" or mid way to "B" thinking that there isn't much reason to play more. I spent about 70 hours to 100% the acheivements legitly minus the only part that would have had me start a new save file. For the lazy achievement hunters, there is an achievement shop after you complete the game.
Music
I'm not too picky for music, but this game has my favorite OST. The music creates quite a bit of atmosphere. There are multiple versions of many songs so that the game can change the music's intensity on demand or change the mood when of revisiting areas. It adds tons to the experience of playing Nier: Automata. Even if you decide against buying/playing the game, I would still recommended checking out the OST.
Story
I did not play or watch videos for any of the related games (the Drakengard series or Nier) and I was not spoiled on anything major in the plot. The story felt fine as a standalone, but you will be missing context for some of the collectable archives found around the world. I watched plot summaries of the games and I recommend watching one for Nier before you play Nier: Automata, as some things that happen will have a bigger impact or they will make more sense with backstory. Nier's story was maybe 6000 years before this game takes place. As for the actual story, I thought it was alright, and then it got better later into the game.
Technical Issues
From what I've read many people had technical issues for this game because of the port to PC. Reading that, I installed the "FAR" 3rd party patch before I started playing. I did not have any framerate issues. One problem I did have was that "Alt-Tab" would take the game out of full screen mode sometimes, but I learned that you can re-fullscreen with "Alt-Enter" instead of going through the menus. The other problem I had was slow down in some areas. I play my games on a laptop so I'm used to it not keeping up with games. The slow down was consistent when it did happened and not spiky so it felt fine.
Controls
I've only played the game with an xbox one controller. The controls can all be individually bound which I believe all games should do. I play with a 'claw' grip (right pointer finger over the main buttons while right thumb is on the joystick) and I modified the controls to feel comfortable to me. I believe it could be harder playing on mouse and keyboard if you don't have thumb buttons on your mouse. There are a few different modes the game can transition between including "side scroller" and "dual stick shooter", but the controls stay constant so the transitions feels pretty smooth. The problems I had with controls included locking on to specific targets, and lack of control explanations that I'll talk about later.
Difficulty
If you've played through games where you need to dodge attacks (Dark Souls, Devil May Cry, etc) you'll probably have an easy time with this game. The dodge timing is super lenient (on top of being able to extent it) and you can interrupt your own attacks to dodge. On top of this, you have a ranged attack and you can move faster than most enemies, so at the very least you can run in circles and shoot until your targets are dead. This makes 'clearing' the higher difficulties relatively easy, but if you want the game to stay fun I'd rather play a lower difficulty and use more melee.
The defensive options you can choose from chips (basically the game's version of gear) are pretty crazy, including up to 6 seconds invulnerability when you get hit. Couple this with no cooldown healing items and only one-shots will kill you. Personally I don't find difficulties that would regularly need to one-shot you to be a threat very fun.
Things I personally would have liked to know before/while playing
The game doesn't really explain how some things work. These are some things I would explained if I was a new player. This stuff might be irrelevant to other people.
-There is a sprint. To sprint, you dodge to reach max running speed, and then your character will accelerate to sprint speed. There's a visual effect behind your character when you are sprinting. Bushes and terrain can break you from your sprint.
-You can double jump followed by a pod jumping attack (pod attack and jump at the same time) followed by dodging to jump pretty far.
-Light attacks and Heavy attacks use your different weapon slots. You can't use the same weapon for both.
-The different weapon types have different attack patterns. Test light/heavy ground attacks, light/heavy air attacks, light/heavy dodge counter attacks, charged heavy ground attack, and rising heavy air attack (heavy when ascending with first jump) to see what you like.
-To evade then counterattack, you need to perfect evade (the animation with the shadows dodging) and then fire your pod, light attack, or heavy attack.
-Pods (the little floating robot that helps you) can be equipped with one progam at a time. If you get more pods you can equip different programs to switch on the fly.
-Each pod has a separate pod program cooldown.
-Pod programs can be charged up based on how many different pods you have. Every stage of charge uses the cooldown of another pod.
-Consider looking up Pod locations. One is fairly obscure, and they give a considerable boost to versatility. Also the locations don't spoiler much.
-If you hear a consistant on/off high pitched noise (the one many older people lose sensitivity to) it's a Pod distress beacon.
-Ignore chests with locks, it will be fairly obvious when you can open them.
-Work on the main story until you unlock the game's equivalent of fast travel. It makes side quests much less time consuming.
-Don't worry too much if you miss side quests. After you complete everything in the main story there is chapter select with numbers indicating finished quests.
-Side quests (the small red circles on the map) are not repeatable. They will reset their progress if you don't completely finish them while eligible.
-When there's a new vendor in the camp with your other vendors (takes a while), buy all of the special chips. Auo loot is a godsend and the item scanner shows chests on the map.
-The only thing you can 'miss' that would require a completely new game start is a minor bad ending. If you're worried about missing it, but you don't want to spoil other things, look it up after you upgrade 100% of the weapons to max level. (This probably wont happen until after you finish all of the main endings).
-Chips are the 'gear' of this game. In addition to strength (+0 to +8) there is a variance to how many slots they take. The black diamond indicates that the chip is perfect (the lowest) slot size. Fusing chips increases the + and slot size. Read a guide on fusion when you have a bunch of chips.
-The game isn't joking when it talks about deleting your save files

What a mess. What a shame. I was looking forward to this, incredibly so, only to be let down by laziness. I'm sure this game would have been a great play, sadly optimization issues and a complete lack of care taken in implementing this as a PC game rather than a shoddy port brings this game to what is essentially unplayable.
After battling with the in-game settings, eventually disabling all monitors but one, in an attempt to run this at 4K, the game decides that 4K is in fact some obscure resolution that is nowhere near 4K, then renders internally at even less, resulting in a blurry mess. Then at this blurry mess, it runs at a low 25-35fps on my system with an i7-6800K and an overclocked GTX 1070...
In fullscreen mode, 1920x1080 is in fact 1600x900 upscaled. Why they think this appropriate on PC I do not know, but I am deeply concerned for what I held as a highly respectable game studio churning out sub-standard crap like this.
The graphics in this game so far do not inspire, the textures are reminiscent of PS3 era games, with objects lacking any real definition. The first few minutes of gameplay were not anything enjoyable, and though I can imagine there is a grand story to be told here, the fact that I have to practically reconfigure my desktop, fiddle around with settings, to find no borderless window option is a complete shambles.
I should not have to mess around like this to then recieve a sub-optimal experience, there may be some third party mods to fix and correct these issues, but I should not have to do this when I am paying a fair price for it.
Shame on you Square Enix, shame on you.

Conclusion:
Overall an amazing game, with a few bug fixes to fix these issues the game would be exceptional, but because the game  has been out for several months and these bugs aren't fixed, it's annoying, but aside from that everything else about the game stands out and works well.
Recommended / Definitely try it out

It's a game with a good idea or concept in mind. However, it is poorly executed. While the devs did their best and got certain things right like the atmosphere, monster designs and particularly nice-looking (but stiff) female models, the actual gameplay is more an exercise in frustration.

Can't recommend.
- OK graphics
- Some enjoyable puzzles
- Main game mechanic is kind of a cheap gimmick
- Baffling control scheme
- No saving of room progress
- Very short (~1-2 hours)
The main mechanic of the game is that you see only basic shapes and outlines of objects. You have to try out all interactions with all objects, which raises your "awareness" level. At 50% you start to see the world in a bit more detail, and at 100% you see everything in full detail. This mechanic doesn't really add anything to the experience other than the tedious repetition of looking and interacting and using every object with everything.
The game is controlled with a keyboard, and there doesn't seem to be gamepad support. Arrow keys move the character around, but interaction is quite odd. You have four selectable actions: look, interact and the use of two different items. You select the action you want by pressing shift, which brings up a wheel of actions, and use the arrow keys to select the action you want. Some of the puzzles use specific buttons on the keyboard (QWER for example).
First, why can't looking and interacting have their own buttons? Second, why the two item limit when the last room has three items? Third, why the puzzle specific buttons? This control scheme is one of the least user friendly I've seen in quite a while.
Saving might not be a big deal when dealing with a game that is around an hour long, but you never know when the player has to shut down and leave the game. You may have unlocked 50% or more awareness, but if you have to shut the game down, you have to start the room all over again, which means you have to look and interact with everything yet again.
When you get to the main puzzles, they are OK for the most part. Some of the puzzles took some sideways thinking, but I don't think there was a single puzzle that was pure "guess-the-developer-logic" type puzzle. However, this is a short game that relies on doing lots of tedious ground work before getting to do the puzzles themselves, so there aren't that many puzzles.
Overall, Awareness Rooms is a short, lackluster and not a very player friendly game. There's an occational glimmer of a good puzzle, but the strain of the main mechanic and the unfriendly control scheme take away the enjoyment from solving the puzzles.

Resident Evil fans were dissapointed by Capcom because of their change of focus to more action-packed games instead of survival horror. For those fans Capcom made Resident Evil Revelations which originally came out for Nintendo DS and was later ported to all the main platforms. Does this version of Resident Evil really go back to its roots? And is this a good port from the Nintendo DS?
Well. Not only are there only very few "horror"-sections in this game (which were supposed to be the main part), but also these horror-sections arent horror at all. There isnt a single scary moment in this game, not even a creepy atmossphere like in Resident Evil 4 or the Leon Campaign in Resident Evil 6. The biggest design flaw of this game is that you have a coop partner with you (AI driven). This not only makes the game less scary than it already is, but also the AI is HORRIBLE and the game isnt even properly designed with coop in mind. The only thing your partner does is sometimes distract enemies and other times give you some additional fire power.
Let me makes this clear: This game is VERY far away from survival horror, but the problem is even as an action game it fails in many parts. The guns feel weak, have ugly sounds, ugly animations, clonky movement system, boring level design, boring weapons and also many unnessesary weapons. This game felt like a japanese MMO with tons of grinding most of the time, especially because it was so damn easy, probably because its a port from the nintendo DS where you have worse controls so it gets easier on PC just because of Mouse+KB.
The "puzzles", if you can even call them puzzles, were uninspired and boring. The worst parts of this game is when you are trapped in an area and you have to fight waves of enemies which is extremely dull.
But there is one thing which I want to give this game huge credits for and thats the creature design which is actually one of the best creature designs of all Resident Evil games, however for every cool enemy there is also a boring, uninspired enemy.
But especially the very first enemy you meet in the game is really cool, because their ugly look not only makes them look scary, but also because of their weird movement it makes headshots more challenging. If Capcom would capture the survival-horror atmossphere of the previous games in this game, these enemies would make you♥♥♥♥♥♥your pants.
The thing is, if you consider that this game was originally made for the nintendo DS you can understand why it cant be good. Not because the DS is a bad handheld, but survival horror simply doesnt work on DS and if you make an action game you have to make it very simple for the DS, which is way too simple if you port it to PC.
Thats why I am excited for Revelations 2, because that game is made primarily for PC and current-gen consoles, but there you also have Coop and multiple playable characters so we will see...
The narrative of this game is absolute garabage and functional at best. Not only is it full of annoying and cliche characters, it also is told in a very boring way, because it keeps jump from location to location. When you play some time with Jill and get used to the Queen Zenobia, suddenly the chapter ends and the next chapter starts at a completely different location with diferrent characters. I guess they wanted to introduce many characters (some from previous RE games) and make their storys connect later, but the ONLY reason they did this is because they needed filler and they wanted to have some action between the "horror" parts of the game (which arent horror as I explained).
Every character in this game is SO goddamn cliche, terribly written and annoying, even known characters like Jill and Chris are so bad in this game (what the ♥♥♥♥ happenend to Jill´s face and voice?). Chris is the only character which isnt annoying.
Also the game does take itself serious but at other times makes some stupid jokes and both of these dont fit at all, especially if you want to make survival horror (which this game isnt anyway).
Ugly. Only word I can describe this game is ugly. Character models, weapons models and the location, everything is ugly. Of course this is because of the technical limitations of the Nintendo DS, but they could still put some effort into the design of the places. Only thing which is designed really good are the enemies (but there are also many ugly enemies, and with ugly I mean bad).
Didnt even notice any kind of soundtrack, its just some random music in the background.
Oh my, the graphics of this game are worse than playstation 2 games even if it runs at 1080p60fps. I know its a DS port, but they could at least put SOME effort into and increase the quality of the textures and make better character models.

I don't have much play time on the PC version, but I did play through this entire game on my 3DS and played a large portion of the online before the HD version was released. Capcom, THIS is a Resident Evil game done right. To be fair though, I didn't mind RE6, or even ORC for that matter, but I'm probably in the minority here. Anyway, all the stuff that a fan of classic resident evil wants is here: excellent pacing, horrific tension, limited supplies (kind of) and all the cheesy dialogue the writers at Capcom could shove in here. I say kind of limited supplies, because you're given a scanner-gun very early on that allows you to scan enemies to create Green Herbs. The way it works though, is that if an enemy is already dead and you go to scan them, you'll get a minimal amount of points towards your herbage. If you scan a still-living enemy you'll get a load more points. You can also use the scanner to find handprints (RE games always have collectibles and, uh, this is it?) and secret pick-ups.
The gameplay is pretty much the same from RE4, but it's obviously a little bit more up to date. It feels familiar but fresh. The game also allows you to choose between aiming in first, or third person. I played with the first person aim and loved it. Give it a shot if you haven't, it's a whole different experience.
The story was pretty solid, for a fairly cheesy one. And I personally enjoyed all the nods/references to Dante Alighieri's Divina Comedia which I myself have read and very much enjoyed. However, that mission with the 2 random dudes that hold absolutely no weight whatsoever in the story? Kinda felt like padding, and it takes away from the almost perfect pacing of the game. I didn't mind switching between multiple protagonists, but those 2 goons were just, well, goons.
The game also has a co-op mode that I had put a handful of hours into. It's fun with strangers but even more fun with friends. It feels very different from the single player in the sense that enemies now have a health-bar, and power levels. If you've ever played Borderlands you'll get the grasp of it very quickly. There are tons of different guns to collect, including super rare/unique weapons. You can also modify your weapons with a plethora of different parts in single player and in Co-op.
Definitely pick up this game if you're an old fan of the series, but if you're new and looking for a solid entry point, go with RE4. And if you're interested in playing RE4 and aren't a graphics nazi, I highly recommend the Wii version. Best controls of all the versions I've played.

Even though this game is in early access I've played it for +20 hours and I'm not done with all the quests and only did one dungeon (there's 2 available and they are planning to add 3 more mini dungeons) and I must say I love the heck out of this game. I CANNOT wait until the full release. It basically takes an MMORPG and takes out all the bits I don't like (how it's basically aimless apart from leveling up). If you take up all the quests there is minimal grinding and once you upgrade your items in the next town and do some side quests (some of them which have a story while some are basically just collect x amount of y), you won't believe how easy you beat the enemies you were dying over and over to just a few levels ago, making it much easier to progress or collect items you will need for trading, quests and selling. The controls are incredibly tight and satisfying, the zelda-like jump is flawless and if you fall it's basically your fault.
The only thing frustrating about the game is that in one part of the game the platforms are sometimes too small and they are also "icy" (so slippery but sometimes also with ice growing out of them that you need to destroy...but it regrows very fast) so you basically jump onto them and slip right down into the abyss very easily, but I guess that's just platforming! The point is sometimes it's hard to get to where you want to go because of this, you need to be incredibly precise and quick. These places are also randomly placed, like basically you want to go through a door but in order to be able to do that you need to get on three little slidy platforms with ice growing out of them, you need to destroy each piece of ice after you jump on the prior platform and then destory the next, do a perfect jump and not slide off, and repeat this a few times and it's not even part of a puzzle.
Oh and there's a lot of puzzles....a lot of classic ice sliding puzzles too...which sort of got boring after the 3rd one even though they do mix it up with additional features.
Pros:
-Amazing soundtrack
-Quest system
-Feels like a real MMORPG
-Guilds! (I'm not sure if you will be able to select one other than the one selected for you)
-Trading

-Real time combat with special moves!

-So far great and interesting story (it's not done yet, I've read about 30-40 percent of the story is finished by now)
-Tight controls
-Minimal backtracking (mostly for quests, not frustrating as there is a teleport system)
-Very nice pixel art
-And seemingly hours and hours of fantastic gameplay!
Cons:
-Too many slidy puzzles
-Random annoyingly hard platforming which doesn't add anything to the game but frustration
-No multiplayer planned (which isn't a big con for me but might be for some)
-Game pauses when you open the menu to select an item but not while you consume the item to heal etc., you most likely end up taking more damage than you healed if enemy isn't focusing other party member as you are stationary while you use the item (for about a second or two), or if you didn't manage to go very far away from the enemy (most of them have a way of quickly getting back to you even if you run across the screen from them)
For the rest, play the game and see how you feel

Having played the online light version on Armor Games, I have decided to buy the full in house Steam version of this game. If you like solving tasks and shooting evil monsters for kicks. This game is great fun to play and I really enjoy playing through the levels at will and while the levels are quite easy at first. This is deliberate, so that you are settled into the game before moving onto the much more tougher levels.
The Objectives:
This can vary from level to level. But in order to successfully pass the level. It is imperitive that you keep your orb intact and to protect from banishment from the monsters because if the mana pool reaches zero or a lower number than the banishment cost from the monster and the monster touches the orb in this state. Its Game Over and you would need to start the level again. While this is not going to be an issue in the early levels as these levels have a lower waves of monsters, you will find this more challenging in the later levels that have tougher enemies and more waves of monsters that you must defeat in order to complete the level. Its doesn't stop there however because some levels have tome chambers that will have to opened by meeting certain criterias to unlock vital skills and also you will still need to survive all enemy waves to complete the level AND to gain the skill from the tome chamber.
Mana:
The Mana bar is your lifeline as it used to buy gems, build buildings and traps as well as to sustain banishment charges from those monsters that are successful in banishing your orb. Careful planning and conservative use of the mana in levels will gain you extra mana to use at the start of other levels. So its wise to conserve as much mana as you can muster in early levels. This is a method that I learned the hard way when I was playing the light version of this game online.
My thoughts:
If you are into tactical games like I am and want to challenge yourself. Give this game a try as you will need to use your tactical skills to conquer the more harder levels and you may need to replay some levels to give you more mana for the later levels so that you can buy more powerful gems at the start. Even things like the placement of a tower on the level to the strength of a gem can mean the difference of success or failure.
Verdict:
The key thing to have with this tactical game is PATIENCE and planning. If you rush through the early levels without giving much thought to points that I have mentioned. Then the later levels could be frustrating to some players if they do not plan their motives carefully. Patience and tactics are the road to completion of this game.
Overall Rating: 10/10.

An interesting hide-and-seek sci-fi horror taking place on a spaceship called Dispatcher. You basically are awoken and begin looking for an exit. This is an escape pod that is usually behind some mechanism e.g. a door you need to activate but you can only do so if the missing equipment is found and inserted into the relevant socket. So, some search is required instead of you just dashing straight toward freedom.
The problem is that there are only 3 levels or so-called blocks. Some are longer while some (Block C) are extremely small, therefore, the chase ends very soon. My issue, beside this, with the game is that as soon as the monster sees you there's no escape. There are no weapons just health packs (what is the point if 2 or 3 hits can easily kill you?) and batteries to recharge your flashlight. Beside these monsters (a zombie and a creature that looks like as if it was straight out of an H.P. Lovecraft short story)  there are traps such as a mine that is an insta-kill. You wonder why you are at such a disadvantage at all times.
It seems this is best played with your buddies so that you can use them as cannon fodder. There are some money items lying around that are essential if you wish to level up your character between rounds. The problem is that the RPG elements are minimalistic in the game. In fact, during the character creation process the creators even make fun by allowing you to create a drunkard or pornstar etc. characters that already start with a disadvantage. Essentially, of the many choices you'll find that one or two worth picking.
Money would come in handy for increasing your character's attributes (and eliminating the negative values) but this requires you to win. Which is very difficult in single player - as mentioned the best way is to sacrifice your friends. Multiplayer, however, is completely dead. I managed to join a host but as soon as both of us were killed we began the next round as monsters. Since there were no other players around we were just wandering aimlessly for minutes until I decided to quit. Also, while flipping off monsters seems like a funny thing to do later on you wish there was a gun in your right hand.
The game looks nice and there are some notes trying to provide some explanation of the background story. The problem with Dispatcher is that once you've played it for an hour or so you have pretty much seen everything that there is to see. With an active community, with means to fight back the monsters or make them stop for a while (flamethrower against the xenomorph in Alien Isolation, remember?) this would be pure fun. Hope CivilSavages executes their upcoming games much better.

The game is surprisingly fair, and very fun to boot. The only thing you can buy at all with real money, is cosmetic items, and 2x boosts for XP and Blutes. Blutes are used to unlock all the weapon parts, and while 2x would make you gain them faster, it doesn't matter much for a few reasons. For one, some of the best weapons in the game take no unlocks at all, or just a few parts to build. You can however level up parts over time with XP and by spending a large number of blutes, but even when maxed out, the difference in damage isn't substantial. It's useful to take a sniper, and upgrade the damage so that it does 50 to the body instead of 48-49, to ensure a 2 hit kill, but that's really about it. Upgrading the weapons takes TONS of the blutes and a lot of playtime with each part, so it really inst worth it, as opposed to the versatility of having all the items unlocked instead.
You can basically pay to get the tiny increases in damage twice as fast, but in the end, a better player will still beat you, and that's the only thing that really matters. In this case the base game is very fun and customization, but it could have all been ruined by greed. The character customization items are very expensive, BUT they are all completely optional of course, on top of the fact that they give out free items. The prize for playing once a day gives items sometimes, and they are less rare than you'd imagine. They have also given out shirts from Alienware and Razer, items for playing in the beta and on launch day, streaming the game on twitch, attending events, etc etc, and I'm sure more will come in the future. So really, even the free players get to have some individuality as well.
I can't recommend it enough. Support the game if you like what they have done, but just know that you aren't going to be treated unfairly if you don't/can't.

From Dust, a curious god game. In which you simply have to help your people to populate and vegitate the world.
Not too many levels to this one, some seem rather simple but with the constant effects of the world hindering your progress on occasion annoyingly seeming to undo you're every move.
Which while makes the game a challenge to complete, make also make for an infuriating time when you consider, are you really a god if you can't get this mountain to move?

On paper, the concept behind From Dust is filled with promises. A simulator where you can manipulate terrains on a whim? Groundbreaking! But despite its enormous potential, this title ends up offering too little.
From Dust is no more a simulator than it is a puzzle. In its (short) story mode, you are tasked with occupying totems scattered throughout several islands. Your opposition comes from the destructive forces of storms, tsunamis, and magma. Against these, you must utilize your godlike abilities to construct a safe haven.
Outside the campaign are dozens of challenge maps. Here, you are given a limited set of abilities with which you'll use to accomplish an objective, be it migrating tribes or saving them from extinction.
Once the campaign and challenges are completed, that's it. There is little to no reason to replay this game unless you really enjoyed it. The unreleased map editor would've gone a long way to making this a lasting title, but alas, it isn't one.
Grade: B-

The graphics are pretty sweet, especially for a downloadable game. It definitely has a nice style. The sounds are very well done as well.
All in all, it's a game I would recommend. There aren't that many 'God sim' games around these days, so From Dust is a great addition to anyone's collection.

It never stops.  The whole game is played by almost mindlessly repeating XXXY with the occaisional evade or potion drink.  It's initial offering of moderate fun evaporates very very quickly under the  heat of repetitive enemies, similar levels, and the awful, boring combat.  Double Dragon II for NES is more fun, has more moves, and requires more strategy and it only used two buttons!!  A modern beat/slash-em-up should have tons of different moves.  There's no reason a character couldn't have dozens of moves, akin to a fighting game.  Sorry I'm getting off topic.  Bottom line, this game gets boring very very quickly.  The combat has no substance.

So, what is there to say about this game that hasn't already been said (especially the review by Genoce)? Well, not that much. I mean, it's not a TD game for everyone, that I will admit. With 190 levels, a gazillion ways to tweak skills and difficulty settings, and the way to combine gems to create just what you want, it does have a higher treshold of entry than most such games. But if it does get its hooks in you, then wave goodbye to the next 100+ hours or so of your gaming schedule. And so this review should pretty much end.
However, I'd like to also respond to some of the negative criticisms in the game, which is going to take up a lot more space:
While it's technically true that these add an element of uncertainty, it's not that random (for one thing, you get warnings beforehand that it's about to happen), and it's therefore most certainly possible to plan for it. In fact, once you know how to deal with those things, then even if a shadow show up on wave 5, they'll never be a problem. And personally, the levels I've felt where randomness was more of an issue are the special Vision levels, because they're meant to be tight fights at all times. Sometimes they're so tight, that if your gems in the first wave tends to end up doing minimum damage shots, you've already lost. Then the next time you try said gems shoot maximum damage, and you survive and move on to clear the whole damn level.
Aside from that, I've hardly ever played any TD game that is -less- random than this game (maybe the previous games in the series, but they too had it, if in different forms)! For one thing, like I said, the difficulty setting is completely and utterly under your control, and never feels arbitrary. Take Kingdom Rush in comparison; the game's later mission levels on that game requires a lot of planning -and- early wave luck (i.e. good damage on the first few hits)... And that was on casual difficulty. Normal and Difficult requires nothing less than utter perfection in every single detail there. And Cursed Treasure 2 has levels entirely depending on early mana flask drops if you want three stars. This game, mana flow is forever something you can do something about, and you have a lot more freedom in placing your towers. There's nothing happening in this game that you cannot react to (except the aforementioned low-damage early shots in the vision fields).
Oh, and it seems like the amount of Shadows appearing has been severely downgraded compared to earlier versions of the game. I'm currently
Well... Yes. It's true. I mean, if you know what you're doing, you can sweep through the main levels doing them all only one time each, and the Vision levels are completely set in terms of what gems and spells you have, so obviously any amount of grinding won't help you beat them. But if you want a complete game, you'll have to replay levels, yes. And yes, the levels are pretty long too, because this game is about making a set-up.
...Which is something you do in every TD game that's worth a damn anyway. And at least if you want to grind here, you have to be clever about it, since it will always only be the highest score you get in any given level that counts. Also, don't forget Gemcraft Chapter 0. If you wanted a complete game there (i.e. each level completely shining), you had to replay every level 8 times. 8. Frickin'. Times. Here, you can get away with twice each (once on Looming and once on Haunting difficulty, ignoring Glaring), and if you unlock Haunting early, a fair few can be beaten with only one attempt.
Again, pretty much true. You don't spend that much time setting up walls to lead the monsters exactly where you want... And that is a bloody good thing too, because every TD I've played that's required excessive mazing on every level are immensely boring; with the fields usually being mainly empty except for a few ocstables that prevents you from optimal mazing every time. Who needs that crap? I sure don't.
Again true (I sense a pattern here)... And I'm not going to defend this per se, except saying that in the Gemcraft series as a whole, much of the point is about figuring out how to exploit everything. And I personally -like- games that gives you the option of doing that, provided they make sure that (barring going online and looking up other people's work) it's a challenge to find out how to exploit it. And this game's got that challenge. Way back when I first played this on AG, I thought I had a pretty good deal going on with the things I'd made up... and then I read about how other people had found stuff that put my strategies to utter shame (though they had the Magician's Pouch; I hadn't. I still wouldn't have figured out that other stuff in a million years, though).
Still, my non-Magician Pouch based strategy was good enough for me to then beat field O6 at Wizard Level 56. Others had problems with that field 30 or more wizard levels above mine, so that was nice. :D
Anyway, as you can see, I'm not always disagreeing with these criticisms, and you as a buyer should take them into consideration, as that this is a very, very specialised Tower Defense game. But I certainly like it, and since it is available to try out for free on several flash game websites, you'll have the opportunity to try it out for yourself. And I think you should. ;)

I had previously 100% this game on PS4. Automata is so good that I had to replay it, and i chose to do it on PC. This should be indicative of how amazing this game is. Everything about Nier Automata is superb; the gameplay is as satisfying as it gets for an action/slasher game. The controls are super tight and are both easy to learn but difficult to master. The story is also great, with deep characters and interesting and thought-provoking storylines (especially after the 1st playthrough).
Not everything is perfect, though. It must be said that the PC port definitely has some issues, especially noticeable during load times (i.e., cutscenes and entering a new location). However, the F.A.R. mod makes the game run much better. Overall, the PS4 version feels a little more stable, but that version suffers from terrible framerate drops at times, even in the PS4 Pro.
To wrap it up, this is probably my favorite game to come out in recent years and I cannot recommend it enough. The Steam version has some issues, but nothing game breaking in my experience. Some modding and fine-tunning might be required.

I bought RE Revelations because it was known as a revival/return to the original RE games from the 90s. Although it is still quite different from RE 1, 2, 3, as Revelations feels more like a hybrid of recent RE games (4-6) and older RE classics. Some of the returning elements such as  the weapon box, narrow spacial environment, limited ammo supplies,  as well as a stronger emphasis on exploration, work together to bring a sense of nostalgia and the longing to survive a bit longer. Particularly, the game-play in Infernal Mode feels a lot like playing original RE games. However, one down side of the game is that I found the puzzles too obvious or too simple.
Like many users have suggested, despite of its emphasis on shooting and actions, RE Revelations regains the atmosphere and chilliness which made Resident Evil an iconic survival horror franchise (which I personally think were lost in RE 5 and of course, RE 6).

I like it so far. I don't know why, but I like it. It scares me, even though I think it's just because of how god damn loud the monster is.
Pros:
+Spoops me pretty well.

+Decent replay value.
+Good atmoshpere.
+Seeing those things fly at you out of the shadows really does give me a good scare.
+Low price, especially when on sale.
Mixed
+/-Level design is ight.
+/-You spawn in one of a few predetermined spawn points every time at random, as does the monster(s). This means that you never know exactly what to expect. BUT, it also means that sometimes that son of a ♥♥♥♥♥ spawns within seemingly feet of you and you're dead in the first 15 seconds, though that's a rarity.
+/-Don't really know how I feel about the character creation stuff, it's interesting but feels unescessary.
+/-Giant boobs on headless corpses. You're always far more ashamed after you finish.
Cons:
-It is often too difficult to escape from the monster. Your character can't sprint for longer than a few seconds even though there's a hellbeast, mutant, thing, chasing him/her down a hall. Apparently not getting eaten alive just is not worth the extra effort to him/her. And there aren't many places to hide. Unless there is a shield wall or a closet to hide in, he'll hunt you to the end of the Earth. Simply springting around a corner and then hiding in an adjacent room, hoping he'll search the other one won't work like in other titles. It's clear that he knows exactly where you are, and his route isn't based on searching, it's purely coming for your booty UNLESS you get inside the closet at which point he just loses all sense of direction and wonders away like an idiot. Because of this, survival often depends on staying undetected which ties directly into the next flaw.
-The stealth sucks. The game wants you to hide from the monster, yet doesn't give you much capability to do that. It seems that if you're close to him and there isn't a wall, you're spotted even if he's looking the other way sometimes. Hiding in a doorless room in the corner as he passes in the hallway? You're done kiddo.
In conclusion, I can't really tell why I'm recommending this. I gave a great deal more negative feedback than I did positive, yet I still enjoy the game. Looking at it critically, it's not good, but it still scares me, so it's succeeding at its goal. Right now, it's on sale at $0.99. I'd say it's definitly worth a go at that. At the full $5, can't say either way. While deeply flawed, it's still scary and fun. Do with that information as you will.

It's a very interesting title... & it has a lot of promise. But there is almost no gameplay whatsoever. The game revolves entirely around you sneaking past an assortment of three different monsters depending on each playthrough. That's the entire game in a nut shell. Everything in the game serves as a tool to get past the monster & escape. Whether it be keys or whatever you need to find to unlock the doors barring your path, there is little here.
The character creation is not bad, & for a full blown game like System Shock or even Dead Space would be a great addition, but serves little to no use as there is not much depth to this game that would require it.
The RPG stats are are a nice addition, & in any other title would be fine, but once again... are rendered meaningless when the game is so shallow. You can defeat any of the levels with the standard setup with some skill & a little difficulty. I never once needed to upgrade anything on this screen to achieve a win.
Its stealth mechanic is the very core of the game as you can't fight any of the monsters. You can't even defend yourself other than finding a spot to hide in. Other than dark spots all over the maps, you can hide in the bathroom & shut the door behind you or turn on a shield wall temporarily for a few seconds. But there isn't much else other than waiting for the monsters patrol route to take them further away from your current goal.
The game consists of three maps (maybe four as I'm not entirely sure if the fourth funny mode uses a new map or reuses an old one). All of which are somewhat detailed but small. You will find yourself waiting in spots an awful lot for the right moment to move as this is the main length of the game. It feels like this game is entirely a demo as even with the three maps, it feels ridiculously short.
One thing to note is that I have not played any of the game in multiplayer at all as there wasn't anyone online at all. So there was no way to judge the online portion.
Even with all the nice visuals & effects, of which I had no real problems with, there is simply not enough here to warrant a purchase unless the other game in the bundle catches your eye. Because on it's own, this game simply isn't worth the purchase.

Full Review:
I can probably best sum up my opinion of this game with a mildly impressed “Yeah, it’s alright.” It’s not a bad game, just a game that didn’t really wow me. You start by selecting your character from a selection of 4 or 5 heroes. Throughout the game you can spend the experience you acquire in 4 areas: Attack, Defense, Agility, Magic. You mainly just run from left to right along the level killing whatever enemies are in your way. You can also acquire better gear from towns and defeated enemies as you progress throughout the story.
Speaking of the story, it’s about 3 hours long. That would be more understandable if it was a highly unique and rememberable story, but it is very cliché. It even makes a point to poke fun at the story when
.
The gameplay is decent, but rather repetitive. The game seems kind of lacking in ways to vary your combat style. It often feels like you’re just mashing buttons.
Even with all these complaints I found myself having fun with this game. Perhaps that was because I was playing with a friend. Either way, I got enjoyment out of the game and it never really felt like a bore to play.
Overall, if you think this game is something you might be interested in and can get at a good price it could be worth your time.

Well, it's another beatemup...Or is it a hack & slash?
I have this constant internal debate over whether certain games can be considered beatemups or hack&slashes. Both genres use the "belt-scroller" style of level design, both have the standard "move forward, kill enemies, repeat", but there are numerous subtle yet key differences that set them apart. Usually the simple answer is that everyone has weapons in hack & slashers (Konami's TMNT arcade games, Castle Crashers, etc), but uh...hmm. Capcom's Arcade D&D games feature characters with weapons, and I consider that a beatemup. On the other hand, t...
Uh...let's just get on with the review.
Sacred Citadel is a videogame. You kill things, acquire stuff, and complete challenges. I don't recommend this game, but it isn't bad. Out of 10 I'd give it a 4.1. By IGN's standards that might mean SC is a terrible, horrible, no good pile of etc, but eh I think it's ok. The plot is traditional fantasy fare. Big Momma is causing trouble, some mysterious person is seeking artifacts, and there's a bunch of monsters that need a good killin'. I imagine fans of the Sacred series will have a better understanding of what's going on. I played through Sacred 2 on the Xbox 360, but I lost track of the story in the middle of thousands of quests, billions of items, and hundreds of lands/dungeons/universes.
There are four classes to choose from (Warrior, Ranger, Shaman, Mage).
After deciding on your class (which IMO doesn't make a huge difference) you'll set out on a journey through 4 acts with 5 stages apiece. The level-designs are very traditional, but this game mixes it up a bit with mounts, falling objects, and even a little platforming.
The monsters typically consist of um...Grimmocs? Bedellers? Digestya? Covinters? I think I'm just making words up. There are "orcs" with spears, "mutant tribals" with swords, "robots" with shield-thingies, and you get the idea I hope. Whatever they're actually called is irrelevant, because they're mostly fodder for you to make disgusting paste out of. I play a lot of arcade beatemups (& hack & slashers). These tend to be really difficult. The odds aren't fair in the slightest, you get 2 or 3 lives, and enemies can do a lot of damage. Sacred Citadel is pretty much the exact opposite.
This isn't an easy game just because it has RPG elements. One of the standard tactics in a belt-scroller is "herding". You move around to manipulate the enemies, so that they crowd up together. When enemies separate, they tend to surround you, mess up your attacks, and generally ruin your day. It's like some awkward dance with occasional punching. It definitely pays off if you know what you're doing. With SC...all you have to do to herd enemies is X X X Y. This sends them flying to the corner of the screen. Aftwards you can just press X X X and X X X and X X X and you get where I'm going with this? Decisions in this game tend to consist of:
"Do I press X X X down Y and stun them?"
"Do I press X X up Y and juggle them?"
"Do I just press whatever because it doesn't really matter?"
It's nice having RPG elements, it's nice having many attack options, but there's no incentive to doing well because there's no challenge. Even if you choose a supposedly squishy class like the Shaman, you can still take lots of damage, healing items are prevalant, and you can even keep a few healing potions for emergencies. It's not uncommon to play through this game for the first time, and never die. The only aspect where you are liable to fail involves the stage rankings, book-keeper challenges, and certain "don't get hit by XXXX" achievements. All this other stuff really amounts to is a grind, since it requires playing through every stage a handful of times.
Still, while it eventually becomes a boredom-inducing ordeal, Sacred Citadel can be a satisfying in terms of leveling-up, acquiring loot, and gutting monsters by the dozen. If you expect anything more; like a challenge, or some truly compelling game-design, you're bound to be disappointed.

Medieval II is my favorite game of all time. The main campaign is fantastic and is always evolving. Between  technology shifting events like gunpowder and the three major endgame superfactions it makes the storytelling of newer total war titles feel downright tiny. It does not miss small details either its great to have a secretly female priest make her way up the collage of cardinals and become Pope or watch as that general who has been away from home for years picks up a mistress. Battles last a long time and units have a real weight to them, the AI isn't too great at sieges but it is still mostly competent. If that isn't enough this game has the largest variety of quality total overhaul mods of any game I've ever played. I have easily played more than 2000 hours between this and its expansion thanks to the sheer variety of worlds people have added to the game. It is not without its flaws and especially fans of newer Total Wars may have a hard time adapting to its building and replenishment systems but overall I can not recommend this game highly enough.

From Dust delivers excellent gameplay that's easy to learn yet amazingly addictive, making it one of the best simulators out there. Borderlands 2 was a hands-down upgrade over the original, and a great game with a few flaws that never quite were a dealbreaker. TPS fixes... ONE of the major issues B2 had, in that the B2 protagonists were less characters and more inventories full of guns attached to bodies. Outside of Dragon Keep and a couple of the Headhunters, the B2 Vault Hunters were interchangeable skillsets. The characters were simply bland.
TPS? These are actual, real characters. All of them have motivations that facilitate the story in their own vaguely different ways, even though the plot itself doesn't change. They talk, they react, they have personality. Even the Doppelganger, a literal body double of Handsome Jack, has a character besides that. It's quite fun and adds a nice touch, and their different reactions to aspects of the plot are fun.
With that comes a more colorful array of skills and active abilities as well, and the streamlining of skill trees allows for more build manipulation. The game just has more color and personality than B2 did... to a point. The NPCs take a hit - gone is the variety of B2 or the original, and instead you just kinda have a series of Aussie-accented random dudes with no real personality, aside from a gem or two here and there.
The problem is, the game otherwise is... quite literally less than a quarter the length of Borderlands or B2. The sidequests are dull outside the main storyline quests, and while there are new types of weapons, the gameplay itself just hasn't really changed. Zero-G is fun but doesn't really add that much more, half of the season pass is complete garbage, and the game is no longer being supported as halfway through the Season Pass the studio closed down.
In short, if you've finished 2 and still want More Borderlands, this is More Borderlands. The sheer shortness of the main game, however, means that this isn't worth a full price tag. If you find this on at least a half-off sale, I'd say grab it and the season pass... because while half of the pass it is garbage, the half worth getting (the DLC characters and Claptastic Voyage) are the total price of the season pass so you're getting some extra crap and a level cap increase for free on the side.
If it's not on sale, skip it until it is.

Oh well, your loss. Sucka!

Hi! This game takes all the best elements from the 16-bit era ARPG/JRPG and combines them into a 21st century package full of fun, challenge, charm, intrigue, and....balls. Great level design full of secrets, puzzles, and enemies. This game encourages backtracking, but in a good way. You don't even have to fight enemies if you don't want to. They are only aggro if you attack. Otherwise, explore to your hearts content, and  complete quests as you see fit. Then grind out some Flamin' Hillkats or Mad Bovines for items, exp and as a bonus... stress relief. It feels rewarding to use the many attacks and defensive mechanisms in the game. As a fan of Zelda, Secret of Mana, Chrono Trigger, this hits all the nostalgia spots with the fresh feel of a modern game. With a splash of tongue in cheek humor and really clever design choices it all adds up to a stellar game. If this tweaks your teats in the slightest then hurry up and buy this retro/modern masterpiece!

Fun little game that's basically a mixture of Smash Bros. and some flavour of Robot Wars.
There's an adventure mode and a tournament style fight mode.
The adventure mode is a bunch of platforming levels where you fight minor enemies and collect body parts that you can attach to your robot, steadily becoming more powerful as you play - a bit like in your standard loot based game, but with a much smaller amount of different loot available.
As your robot gains more powerful moves, you start to destroy the level by smashing enemies through walls, which gives you a really cool sense of might.
There's a bunch of ad hoc arena style fights in each level and each quest/set of levels ends with a boss fight; a robot with a special ability, which reminded me of Mega Man, but with a fighting mechanic very much like Smash Bros.
The tournament mode is basically a boss rush mode, where you fight strong enemies with special abilities just like your own 1 on 1 on a big stage.
It's not a perfect game, I wouldn't even call it great, but I want to recommend it because I know of no similar game on PC and I think there's potential.
I can't even exactly point out what bothered me about the game, but after playing for an hour or two I felt pretty burnt out and there doesn't seem to be much variety in the levels - just a huge maze like platforming area.
One last thing, a character in the game told me you can design your own stages; haven't looked into that, but that's a big plus I think, because if you really dig the game, building your own stages and sharing them with friends or other people in the community can be great fun.
If Smash Bros. x Custom Robot Battle Thing sounds interesting to you, give this one a try!
Super Smash Bros. combined with Custom Robo and Megaman. Worth every cent I put into it.

Megabyte Punch delivers a solid mix of fighting, platforming and character customization within a quirky mecha universe. I am perhaps a bit biased towards mecha games because I just love mechs in all shapes and sizes but I think most players will get a kick out of customizing their own character. Unlocking many different parts with their special abilities and looks in adventure mode and then playing around with different builds in splitscreen versus matches is a lot of fun. As mentioned in many other reviews there are a lot of similarities to Super Smash Bros. I think Megabyte Punch stands enough on it's own due to it's quirky polygon art style and the addition of character customization.
It's not a perfect game obviously, it is a bit on the short side (Considering current price: euro 13,99) and could in my opinion greatly benefit from an online multiplayer part to extend replayability. However, as a first in the series and considering I bought this within an indiegala game bundle incl. 8 other games for only 5 euros (roughly $7) I really am positively surprised. My hope is that the developers will create DLC or a sequel with even more parts, levels and more importantly more extensive multiplayer options incl online.
Conclusion: Get this game as soon as it is on sale! Current price is a bit steep but this really is a little gem of a game and offers lots of local multiplayer fun.

The ability to choose your own colour scheme (perhaps post-game?) would also be welcome. I disagree with people who complained the campaign was too short - it was about as long as it needed to be.
Oh, and online multiplayer. I know the developers said they can't patch it in now, but this game is begging for it.

The music was beyond amazing. ♥♥♥♥♥♥ for the ears. 1000/10. 'Nuff said.
The gameplay is very well polished. Never once did I get to a point where I would avoid enemies because I was bored of the fighting mechanics. This is because it switches between three types of perspectives (third-person, 2d, and top down) and two types of gameplay (hack and slash, bullet hell). But, the way it does it is smooth and streamlined, to the point that you would playing both game types at the same time and you wouldn't even notice it. This keeps the game fun.
Finally, let me just say I don't often get emotional over games. But this... THIS. Tears were shed my friends. The story is extremely well made and moving. Like its predecessors, there are multiple different endings, only 5 of which are 'Main' endings. Through these endings, I've been sent on the longest feels train ride of my life, from being amazed and happy, to being dragged through the deepest pits of despair and agony as Yoko Taro shreds my heart to pieces before dropping his pants and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥on the broken remains. And then the final choice at the end, just.... amazing.
So overall, I would recommend this game 1000 times, despite the issues that came from them porting it (FYI There is a temporary fix called Nier FAR that allows you to change the lighting down from the default Ultra to get better frames. Just Google it and it will be the first Github link).
TL;DR: It's ♥♥♥♥ing amazing. Throw your money at it.
Whelp, now that my normal run is done and I've experienced the full story, time to jump back on the feels train and get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥on by Yoko Taro again for my Very Hard run.

Right up until the final boss, Megabyte Punch is an
homage/mashup to both
and
in it's gameplay mechanics combined w/ parts-collecting and customizing your fighter including their special moves with those parts. The levels have oodles to see and lots to explode as you revisit things, with numerous valid builds and approaches for any given section of the game, and highly destructable worlds to boot.
The last boss, however, is a cheap cop-out by comparison - the core mechanic it uses is a very nice mix-up on the usual gameplay in the game, but you gain
benefit from any defensive or protective items against this final boss, and 'homing' effects don't work properly with regard to the core mechanic he introduces, so suddenly all that customization goes out the window.
the last boss has the abused schtick of at-will wide-area spamming projectiles that makes fighting it feel like flashbacks to Arcana Heart 3's Parace L'Sia.
This turns an otherwise near-flawless game into a massive let-down, due to just how sharp a slap in the face this sudden turn-around is. So, if you're buying this for single-player? Don't. And if you're buying this for multi-player? It doesn't have any except locally on a single computer. So, sadly, while it's such a well programmed game I simply can't recommend purchasing it to others.

Megabyte Punch is a low-poly robot brawler not unlike Super Smash Bros. and company. I can say with no doubt that this is worth every penny. The world is populated by Megacs, a race of robots that can change their parts. Of course you are one of them, and are tasked to protect your village from assorted robot bad-guys. There are six levels with three stages and a boss level apiece. Okay, I've gotten that out of the way.
It is freaking awesome. You get to dispatch tons of unique enemies that when killed, drop parts (out of many hundreds) that you can use to customize your fighter. There are also secret collectible colour capsules to change your colour scheme; and believe me, the customization is absolutely stunning. And it may just be me, but shooting the crap out of a robot and sending him flying across a room and exploding him against a wall is pretty cool. But the game can sometimes feel lacking in collectibles and stage length, but it may just be the low-poly art style that puts me off.
Aside from the main story, there is also a tournament that you can enter and win rare parts; and a local multiplayer versus mode, which can become amazingly fun and intense. This is definitely worth purchasing, but some people might not appreciate some simplified graphics and monotonous mechanics. All in all, the platforming, environment and gameplay feel amazingly fun and solid.
8.5/10
