This has become my go-to game for when I want to play a strategy game, but don't want to invest a dozen hours into it... which, as it turns out, describes the conditions under which I want to play a video game at all about half of the time these days.
OoB is challenging without being punishing: You can play it in a self-imposed ironman mode (i.e., no save-scumming!) and still just about manage to complete most (but usually not all) of the optional objectives across an entire campaign.  The campaigns consist of about a dozen well-varied scenarios that each take an hour or so to complete.  The campaigns themselves also sport an impressive variety for a game of this type, featuring theaters often ignored in WW2 strategy games.  What other game features campaigns focused on the Winter War in Finland, the "Forgotten War" in Burma, and the Battle of the Atlantic, in addition to the standard German/Japanese/American land conquest campaigns?  What's amazing is that most of these campaigns each have their own distinct flavor.
Mechanics-wise, the game is reminiscent of Panzer Corps and by extension, that game's inspiration, the venerable Panzer General (which happens to be my all-time favorite strategy game).  It's pretty standard tactical turn-based combat, to be sure, but what really makes it shine is that the same engine integrates land, sea and air combat seamlessly -- better so than any other turn-based game that I can think of.
Like its predecessors, OoB gives you a "core force" that you shepherd between the scenarios of a campaign.  You're constantly faced with the choice of whether to reinforce your existing units with veteran troops (thus making them more effective), upgrading them with the latest technology, or buying whole new units.  The fact that the choice is often agonizing is a pretty good indication that it's a well-balanced system.
I've now played through most of the campaigns at least half a dozen times.  As long as I keep having an hour or so to spare now and then, I'll probably be cycling through them many more times before I tire of it.

Regardless - RE:Revelations fringes the border between older RE games and RE:4 - you won't be desperately scrounging up bullets or solving intricate emblem-based puzzles, but the traditional RE cheese is all there. If you're an RE fan and you enjoyed RE:4 but understand the difference between RE0-3 and RE4, know very well that this is far closer to 4 than any of the others. Even then, it isn't without its challenges and I wholeheartedly recommend you give it a try anyways.

The game is pretty long, offers some challenge and extras to make you replay it, but it get's fairly repetitive at certain points of the story even on a single walkthrough. You get to play as multiple characters throught the game, although they mostly play the same. The story not too deep, yet difficult to understand at times (might be easier for people familiar with other Resi games), but the ending is fairly satisfying, even though it leaves an obvious lead-in for the Revelations 2. There are many returning characters from older RESI games, but there are some interesting new ones, too.
The game itself is rather a shooter than an actual (survival) horror and I doesn't contain usuall Resi-type zombies, but rather strange sea-animal hybrids. Most of the bosses lack charisma and boss fights generally are heavily based around finding a tactic and using it over and over again. The scenery lacks variety at times (a major part of the story takes place on a ship), but brings something new to the Resi series on the other hand.
There are multiple minigames / sub-mechanics to bring some variety into the gameplay. I'll mention scanning for fingerprints and hidden items, hacking mini-game, arcade-style railway shooter, weapon upgrades and augmentations. There ARE quick-time events in this game, but they're not too frequent or annoying in any way. The controls overall work faily well on PC with Mouse & Keyboard.
As far as I know, there is no co-op mode for the campaign, but there is a Raid Mode for multiplayer, with unlockable equipment and skillpoints.
After finishing the campaign, I can say I enjoyed the game, even though I've hated it at some points and wanted it to end already. There were some nice plot twists I liked, there were some plot twists I didn't really understand. Just don't expect a survival horror and rather expect an action shooter with long cutscenes.

This, this is a step in the right direction. I'm not sure if they could ever get to their glory days again. But this game was pretty good shot at it. There are some parts I groan at redoing when I replay it, but overall pretty damn good. There are even pretty creepy and unsettling parts.
Stuck on a ship, with small corridors, enemies in unknown places, and of course...doors that require emblem keys. Not for everyone but if you want something a bit different from the latest Resident Evils, then worth a go.
For the sake of Jill...

Take Resident Evil 4. Take away all the unique aspects of the shooting (shooting specific enemy parts, inventory management, etc.). Add some bad shooting and lots of walking and getting lost with pointless fetch quests. Call it a "return to horror roots" when actually it's a snorefest.
Congrats, you have RE Revelations. There's better shooters, better horror games, and better combinations of both. Play RE4 instead.

The shooting mechanics feel very, very bad. That's killer in a game where the only two things you can do are shoot enemies and do boring fetch quests. It might be to encourage you to skip unnecessary fights, but ammo is never scarce enough for that to matter. It's not scary or interesting to play.

(It may not show me having a lot of play time, but I played the 3DS version for 10+ hours, completing it and then some.)
If you like the older, more horror-oriented Resident Evil games, then you're going to enjoy this title.
If you like the newer, more actiony Resident Evil games, then you're going to enjoy this title.
Revelations is the perfect marriage between the gameplay styles found in Resident Evil 1 and Resident Evil 4. It meets in a great middle ground.
There's a tense atmosphere, a great story, and some chills to be had. The camera isn't fixed, but the ship is almost like a floating mansion. The puzzles aren't difficult, but there are a few here and there. You can actually aim your gun, but you won't find mountains of ammo sitting around.
The new enemy types are interesting and varied enough to carry through until the end.
The graphics are also pretty, but that's a secondary concern to me.
I'm not sure this release is worth $50, but I picked it up for $9 and I have no regrets. Wait for a sale.

I finally have enough hours to make a review on this game..
Medieval 2: Total War is an extremely entretaining game. This is one of the early total wars, dating back to 2005-2006. Unlike newer versions, such as Rome 2 and Warhammer, Medieval 2 has a different battle feeling, which is hard to describe, but if you ask me, is way better than these two newer versions. I myself prefer it to the newer versions.
The game offers you limited amount of factions in the beginning, but once you win with any of them, you will be able to choose any faction you wish, from Scotland to Egypt. Mongols and Timurids, which are invading armies aren't playable (for campaing), though. Maybe with mods.
As for the Kingdoms expansion, it has proven itself worth the money. Adds four new campaigns: Britannia, Americas, Teutonic and Crusades, each of it has it's own unique feeling. This expansion also adds new factors, such as the boiling oil siege defense, which is missing in the normal version and can be really helpful, especially in early game.
The tactics works a little different in here too. In Rome 2, for example, should you surround an enemy, they would break. In here, however, instead of breaking the surrounded unit will fight to death. Cavalry also has more use and diversity here.
Sadly, the naval battles here are fought automatically. General Bodyguards are more useful and are probably by far the best units in game, even though using them would put in risk the general himself. Well used, the general can eliminate even enemy spearmen(Generals are on horse) easily, with few losses. The campaign in general is very different, too. You need to pay refill a damaged unit.
The only lacking points would be the AI, which at times is just plain stupid both in battle and campaign, the pope and the diplomacy. I managed to use a damaged unit with three average heavy infanty soldiers to stand near towers close to the AI's army, and the towers killed over 30% of their army. The pope will annoy you at first, forcing you to make peace with your neighbours that attacked you, for example. As for diplomacy, wars are endless. It usually will only end if you get the lower hand in the dealings, and even if it does, the AI will just attack you after 10 turns max.
So that would be it, Medieval 2: Total War, nice game, with some flaws, but doubtlessly, a masterpiece considering the time it was made. A game enjoyable until this day and one of the best of the series.

Wurm is a game that appeals to a niche audience, and does a very good job of it. If you’re looking for a fast, flashy game that you can pick up and complete over the course of a couple of weeks, you will undoubtedly find it to be a slow and frustrating experience. If, on the other hand, you are the sort of player who enjoys sinking hundreds of hours into projects, working with others towards a common goal, and reflecting back weeks or months later about just how far you have come – you will find in Wurm a game of unique depth and complexity.
Yes, the graphics are unimpressive (although the excellent new render system is hopefully a portent of things to come!). Yes, the UI can at times feel a bit clunky – although the ability to bind hotkeys greatly alleviates this. I encourage you to look past this. This game, at its core, is mechanically extremely solid. It is feature-rich and nigh bug-free, which in my opinion thoroughly excuses its faults – especially given its tiny dev team.
Wurm rewards the time you invest in it. This is particularly true if you play on a 1x multiplier server, which I highly recommend. It’s “grindy”, sure, in the sense that you could very well be performing the same action thousands or tens of thousands of times. But from this “grind” comes a unique kind of emergent gameplay. As you specialize further in whichever skill or skills you pick (there are a multitude you can choose from, from carpentry, to baking, to exorcism), you will find that you can trade high-quality goods and skillfully performed services for the many things you can not make or do (very well) for yourself. Many of my (at present) 328 hours in this game have been spent mining. This has resulted in me being able to provide metals of particularly high quality, either for sale, or to supply the smiths of my village. The economy feels dynamic. Trade routes are plotted, ships and roads are constructed, to further this economy. It’s an incredibly immersive experience.
Combat is essentially turn-based, and reasonably deep. Martial stances, targeting, taunting, shield-bashing, special moves, a variety of weapons with meaningful tradeoffs, advantages from high ground and mounted combat, siege warfare… It’s not what I’ve focused on as a player, but I certainly see how others could.
It’s a deeply relaxing game, almost meditative. If you want, you can put it on your second monitor and check in occasionally as you watch some Netflix. Or you can chat with other players as you work on your latest project. As someone who often plays games as a way to destress after an exhausting day, I appreciate how it doesn’t demand 100% of my attention (obviously excepting things such as combat).
In short, this game hands-down does a better job of simulating a living, breathing world than any I have ever played (excepting Dwarf Fortress, but that should be implied). Don’t play singleplayer. This game is built heavily on interaction with other players, and the community is generally extremely friendly.

Domesticate and breed animals, sell them off to your neighbours, build a trading ship to transport all that grain you just harvested to the nearest marketplace, build shipping canals/community roads etc, become the local weaponsmith, make unfortunate new players your serfs by throwing them some iron in exchange for crafting you bricks etc. etc. Listing everything would take too much time.
That being said, it can be quite clunky and grindy at times. The grind is a lot better in Unlimited in comparison to the Wurm MMO (due to servers changing the action timers etc), but it can still be pretty bad if you're playing by yourself, so bring a friend (or a few). Combat system isn't the best either, it's more D&D than actually hitting stuff with your left mouse button. Another annoying thing is that you have to restart your game every time you wanna change settings, but it's not really game-breaking, just annoying.
So if you have ADHD or you're 12, or you just don't wanna dedicate a decent amount of time, you probably won't enjoy this game, Rust or something similar might be more up your alley. But if you´re an anarcho-primitivist, wanna larp as Saruman turning huge forests into firewood for your forges, or just wanna live in a peaceful comfy village - try it out.

Would be my favorite Total War game if just for the sheer mods alone, but sadly, it isn't, because of a few major problems.
1. AI pathfinding, the pathfinding in this game in sieges particularly is pants on head ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, as exhibited by this video
. Though playing on smaller unit sizes can help to alleviate this, the problem is still very prevalent, so prevalent that you have to consider yourself lucky to have the siege AI actually attack your fort.
2. Siege AI, the AI is beyond terrible, with a large chance of it just sitting there, allowing you to kill it's men with archers and ballistae while they sit idly, or shuffle between one command and another, never making up their mind, running in circles.
3. Clunky controls, this can be gotten used to, but it will always leave a bad taste in my mouth compared to the modern controls of the newer games.
Now, pros about this game are:
1. Good campaign AI, gone are the days (or yet to come) of diplomats threatening you with horse whippings for attempting to make a trade deal (Empire), gone are the days of AI sitting back and doing nothing all game until you walk over them (Rome II), if you choose very hard on this game you can actually expect a moderate challenge, which is an A+ compared to the pathetic show from Rome II.
2. Family trees, interesting character traits, and generals you actually give a damn about. In Rome II, Attilla, and all the games following Medieval II, there has been a severe lack of ♥♥♥♥s about your generals. In Rome II I remember using my general as a vanguard unit, if he happened to die I would just replace him, immediately, without consequence. In Medieval II choosing the right general can make or break a campaign, and losing him would be a big blow to your conquests. Generals/Family members in this game also gain experience based on actions taken in battle, such as if your general refrains from killing an enemy unit for some battles, he may develop cowardice, compared to Rome II which just gives a random trait based on RNG.
3. Better settlement improvement, are you tired of having to use an entire portion of your capital city to build a church in Rome II? Don't worry about that here son, because you can build whatever you want in your cities, provided it has the proper population, which is represented by actual ingame numbers. All the improvements will have a visible effect on the city. For example, if you build a blacksmith, it will show up in the battle for that settlement. Build a grand temple to God? It will show up in the battle. Have a wooden walled settlement and upgrade it to stone walls? You now have actual stone walls. The game is given life in this, so much that if you build up your capital it will look like a real ♥♥♥♥ing capital when it's sieged, unlike the newer games where all the cities are made by artists, so only Rome/Constantinople have that grand feel.
4. Mods mods mods, mods make this game shine over every other Total War game. Have you ever wanted to journey into the world of J. R.R. Tolkien? To fight against the Aldmeri Dominion as the Cyrodilic Empire? To fight for Skyrim's independence? To journey into the world of Warhammer? There are massive professional mods for each of these things, just waiting to be played. Mods a scope which can never be matched in future games, due to the Creative Assembly's blatant anti Modding policy (to support future games and DLC).
In the end, for all the flaws this game has, it is still one of, if not the best Total Wars around, so go ahead and give it a try.

7 hours may not be much, but it's enough  to make a review. Overall, this game deserves a 8/10. It's good, but has some flaws that Rebirth fixed, and even those flaws are pretty minor.
This game is about a boy named Isaac and his mother. Isaac liked to draw pictures and play, while his mother watched Christian television programs. One day, God calls from above, telling the mother that Isaac is corrupt and full of sin. So, she follows his orders and takes away all of his stuff, until one more time, God commands the mother to sacrifice Isaac so he can be saved. Isaac, in his room, sees his mom with a knife heading towards his room. He quickly tries to find a way to escape, but then, his mother bursts through the door. before she can do anything, however, Isaac finds a secret trap door hidden beneath the rug. He quickly jumps into the abyss, and the game starts, leaving the conclusion and his fate up to you.
The whole tone of this game is very... Biblical. There are multiple references to things in The Holy Bible. Hell, even most characters are named after significant people from The Bible. There's Eve, who defied god by eating the forbidden fruit bringing death upon everyone, Judas, one of Jesus' disciples who betrayed Jesus for money, and Cain, the first murderer. All of these characters have something in common. They're all sinners. The theme of sin is very prevalent in The Binding of Isaac. Some of the deadly sins are bosses, such as Lust, Gluttony, Greed, and wrath just to name a few. Satan is also the final boss of Sheol, along with a few other demons. In the game, you can also make devil deals, which you sacrifice a heart or two in exchange for an item. These devil rooms appear after a boss, but not every time.
Now that the plot's outta the way, I'll start the review.
-'s
1. There's a bit of lag. I have relatively nice computers which can run most games pretty decently, but the framerate can get a bit slow sometimes. It might just be the animation style, but either way you need a decent computer to run this.
2. The characters you have before you unlock anyone are limited. Isaac is an OK character, but it takes way too long to defeat some bosses and again, it's just unpleasant.  Combined with the "lag" and the overall feel for the controls are not so great.
Really, those were the only couple major ones I could think of. Onto the good.
+'s
1. A KICK♥♥♥♥♥SOUNDTRACK. Seriously, even if you don't like the game, buy it for the music. It's so good and it fits the mood perfectly and it gives you the feel solitude and despair. I highly reccomend getting some earbuds or headphones to play this.
2. The art style is very clean. It's unique in the fact that it was hand-drawn, so obviously it's going to look really nice. It looks like alot of care was put into it, and it's very smooth and it compliments the game so much.
3. The actual game is pretty damn fun. The layout is something akin to The Legend of Zelda. Now I haven't played this one too much, but I HAVE played The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth for about 40-something hours, and they're both pretty much the same but one has more content. On Rebirth, I found myself going through runs in about 30 or 40 minutes. They feel so short, and you'll be amazed when you look at how much time you spent and all that time you didn't realize that the game was sucking you in. It's absolutely fantastic. Not only is it a fun game to play on it's own, but it's also a really good time killer if you're waiting at the doctors office or maybe even a long car trip. I can't say much for it right now, but if this is anything like Rebirth, then I'll be playing this for a while.
COMPARISON TO REBIRTH-
Rebirth improved on a select few things that TBOI didn't do very well. However, select few is what I mean by select few. They tried to "improve" other aspects, but it didn't do very well doing that in my eyes.
1. The artstyle is ruined. I like retro games. They're fun. I'll play Zelda or Castlevania once in a while. One reason I like those games is because of the graphics. Yeah, they're not pretty compared to today's standards, but look at 'em. You can see that they're pretty detailed. Why? Because, developers at that time didn't have much to work with, so they tried to make the best graphics while dealing with some limitations, so it was hard to get sprites right. Today, however, pixel art is everywhere. It's easy to make Mario in sprite art. Or anything really. Just look at my avatar. My point is that today, there are no limitations or anything to stop, which can be sometimes a blessing and a curse. Blessing, because with an imagination you can make some really cool stuff. Curse, because you could just be lazy and make something in MS Paint, cut it so it has some edges, and call it "retro". This is what♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off. They tried going for that "WHOOA GUYS RETRO 90'S NINTENDO MARIO ZELDA WHOOOOA ITS SO RETRO" look but it really doesn't look like it. I'm also♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥because it's just a dumb fad. It's not retro, it's just a joke now because everyone tries to do it either because they want little kids to flock to it because it looks like Minecraft or they don't want to put in effort. It's not THAT bad, it's just not my thing I guess.
2. They didn't fix the music. You know the saying, "Dont fix it if it ain't broke" or something like that? Well, someone needs to put that on a letter and shove it up Ed Mcmillen's♥♥♥♥♥ because he didn't fix♥♥♥♥♥♥ The music is not bad but it ruined the feel of the whole game. It doesn't fit as well. It's like trying to put a square block into a circular hole. The soundtrack of TBOI was phenomenal.  The soundtrack of Rebirth is just mediocre compared to how good the original's was.
THE CONCLUSION-
This game gets an 8/10 because it look, sounds, and performs beautifully. Not only have I played alot, but you can get sucked in VERY fast and before you know it, you have 10 more hours on it. It's very addicting and easy to pick up, resulting in long play times and you never want to just quit, and that's not a bad thing. This game is perfect for when you don't know what to play. It's extremely easy to pick up and play, and you'll probably be doing that alot. I haven't played it much, but the times that I did play it, I did just what I typed above me. It's too good of a game to miss. If you're on the fence about this, pick it up. It's only 5 bucks and it will be the best 5 bucks you've spent in your life. I could not recommend this enough. This is one indie game that's worth the hype.

Sacred Citadel is a side scroll beat-em up that can be enjoyed with up to 2 other friends, and 4 characters to choice from. Though, is it worth spending your time and friend's time playing this game, let me break down the game for you.

The visuals are 3D models placed on a 2.5D plan, think of Double Dragons Neon. Actual they share similar style. I'm not a fan of the art-style, but I never judge a book by its cover.


The combat is sluggishly slow. You can't block every attack yet the game tries to encourage you to do so, you can roll but it too feels sluggish. I don't believe the game is polished. There were times that I got hit but was certain I was not within range. Later on my suspicion was correct, this game doesn't do an excellent job at detecting where the enemies' hitbox is from yours. At a particular boss fight, it was in the middle of the room and wouldn't jump onto my platform. I took advantage of this and started to range it. It did a bite attack in the middle of the room nowhere near me, and I received  damage.  I started to pay attention and noticed a lot of the enemies attacks were committing the same crime. This is a big deal! To be punished for not avoiding an attack that is nowhere near you is shameful, it should of been caught and polished during testing.


The story is dull, the dialog is dull, the soundtrack is dull*, the characters you play have no voice so they are husks, and the villains make Saturday morning cartoons look like awesome super villains. The characters play style don't really vary from one to another. Your "Power" attacks is the only difference but it isn't much of a difference, if that makes any sense. There is loot drop in this game but it feels like it was tacked on. If you were to remove it you wouldn't notice any change to the game. You also level up and can drop points into certain stats,  again this comes off as a tacked on feature.


I beat the game in about 4 hours, though I did leave the game on while I was eating. I can't really recommend this game. If you have $10 there are much better games to drop it on. If it goes on sale there must still be a much better game to get. The sluggish gameplay, the tacked on features, dull characters, unpolished hitboxs, and I have little want to replay this game. One of my favorite genres is mindless beat-em ups, but this takes the cake for being one of the lamest I played.


If you liked it that is fine, but my opinion is my opinion. I doubt it can be changed even if I got a friend to suffer through it with me one last time. If you are looking for a beat-em fix I recommend Castle Crashers, Dungeons & Dragons: Chronicles of Mystara, Guardian Heroes, ....
(The entire soundtrack sucks, if I am going to be smashing skulls I need something cool playing in the background. Look at Streets of Rage boss encounter music, awesome! Castle Crashers when things start to get heated, awesome!)

Version 0.7 at time of review.
The puzzles are some of the most creative and fun I've experienced, with fresh mechanics, intelligent solutions and no hand-holding.
In truth, not all the tracks are amazing, but even those that aren't are still quite good. The sound design is also above average.
Very likeable characters with lots of depth and personality. The interactions between characters feel very natural and not forced in any way. Fantastic humor as well.
I don't want to spoil anything, but you won't find any cheap tricks or quick time events here. Just fast bosses that take skill and strategy to defeat.
In its current form CrossCode has a suprisingly gripping story, with the potential to become something very special if they flesh it out. It truly feels like the first three chapters of an epic novel. My one worry is that, as we are already at version 0.7, the story will end up compressed and truncated.
It looks great, it's very fast and well thought out and it doesn't get in the way. I play using an Xbox 360 pad and I have no complaints about the controls.
This may not be a negative for many, but I feel the level grinding gets in the way of an otherwise well-paced game. This may be negated in the final version with greater enemy variety and more interesting quests which make leveling more interesting.
Many of the map areas have multiple elevations which are difficult to discern, meaning you will plunge into the water or fall to a lower elevation without meaning to. You will then have to backtrack, which in some cases takes a few minutes. Very frustrating and deters from exploration.
Overall a fantastic game that I will be watching very closely. If the devs give it the expansive story and scale it deserves, I am confident it will be among the best 2D RPGs around.

Tl; dr- It's a scary game. With puzzles to do as well! Basically, it's Amensia with a dash of Fallout in space. If you like being scared while trying to figure out puzzles, this is the game for you.
Without a doubt, Dispatcher is scary. Given its a horror game, that's a good start, but that's the thing done best so far about Dispatcher. It combines jump scares, with the shuffling sounds of the infected crew member to keep you on edge. You can't fight back, and all you can do is hope it never finds you.
Beyond the scare factor, Dispatcher is also part a puzzle game and part an RPG. You get to choose a class for your character, and then traits for it, which helps define your skills (and more importantly, how quiet you are!). The puzzle part comes in with the level design- you need to finish the level and escape, while avoiding the infected crew member/alien (not really sure what it is at this stage). So to do so, you've got to open locked doors, find key cards, etc.
Considering how early the game is right now, this game is looking pretty amazing. It looks brilliant, and the lack of lighting really creates that atmosphere needed for a decent scary game. When you combine the scare factor with the puzzle nature, and the RPG element, you've got the potential for a great game here.
The only issues you'll find with the game so far are the translations, which are mostly in Russian still, or in badly done English (you can still make out what they mean however, so its not an impediment), and the lack of a tutorial or help system (they offer a practice mode ingame, but it's another puzzle section that is more guided, without actually using any words. You've really got no idea what you're doing first up, so it'll take a few attempts to get going. It's an easy game to pick up though, so you'll be fine.
Right now, it's extremely early access. You'll get some fun out of the game right now, but not an infinite amount, so purchasing it now is more to support the developers so they can finish this game.

I had been looking forward to Atlantic Fleet, as it is a particular area of interest for me, and there is a paucity of entertaining games featuring the Kriegsmarine.
Now - as any serious wargamer knows - the Order of Battle series is hardly what one would call deep or accurate. It is stylized warfare - and has more in common with checkers, than - for example - Grigsby's Pacific War. So my expectations were not particularly high. I expected a "beer'n'pretzels" game, and that is exactly what I got.
But even for OoB, it was disappointing. I won't bother going into the nitty-gritty of flaws, which make the game somewhat less than enjoyable.
I will however, comment on the scenarios.
I had hoped to re-enact the pursuit of the Graf Spee, or the Scheer's cruise - during which she covered almost 50.000 miles in 161 days, and  sank 17 merchant vessels of over 110.000t  plus the armed merchant cruiser Jervis Bay.
Or perhaps the channel-dash of the Scharnhorst, Gneisenau, and Eugen.
Nada.
Instead I found myself blithely having to sail the fleet into Scapa Flow..........
I mean - seriously!?!!
I realise the Kriegsmarine was hopelessly outmatched, and it can't be easy to build a decent game around it, but I have to say the OoB KM DLC - is just plain lazy and pointless.

Order of Battle is a fun successor to the classic Panzer General wargames, with simple but exciting extensions to Panzer General's game mechanics.
Almost every mission that I've played (primarily from the US Pacific and Marines campaigns) has been enjoyable and varied.  Guadalcanal is a long battle where the initiative shifts back and forth.  The controlled retreat from the Phillipines is a tense exercise in bending without breaking. Meanwhile, the Marines campaign lets you storm the beaches with elile troops, and the Winter War campaign turns "General Winter" against the Russians.
You need to buy campaigns in order to play the game beyond the tutorial, but the free sample missions should help you decide which campaigns interest you.

It's a turn-based operation-level strategy games set on various theatres, some well-known, other less well-known.
It only requires 3 to 5 hours of play to learn the game mechanics, which allow some complex manoeuvers without being a hassle to understand.
In particular, the game features an excellent supply/frontline system. It's kinda reminiscent of the game of go, where you have to encircle the enemy without being encircled yourself. Too bad most scenarios don't play this at full, but if you're smart enough, you can try and flank the enemy anyway in most cases.
The UI is very responsive and after a few hours, any turn won't take you more than a few minutes, even when you have several dozens of units under your command.
The base-game has nothing for it and you must buy all the campaigns separately as DLCs. Each campaign is 20 to 30+ hours of play, making them worth of your money -- if you like the game. I heard some Panzer Corps fan didn't like this game, and I think it's partly because of scenario design, which is better in Panzer Corps than in Order of Battle. However, it would be a real shame for a wargamer to skip OOB, as it can potentially be a favorite of virtually anyone.
The game features a very complete level editor, and there are a good lot of mods available on the web.
All in all, this game truly deserves a better ranking on Steam -- "mixed" doesn't do it justice at all.

First off I got to say I loved this game, one of the best single-player experiences I've had in years. Unfortunately the PC-port has a few issues, which likely has turned a good few people away from the game.
On the PC-port you are locked at 30FPS, may experience lag spikes in cut scenes and you may also experience a resolution issue which puts you at a different resolution than what you selected and subsequently scales/stretches out the image to fit your monitor.
At the very least, these issues are easily fixable through installing the FAR mod and could be considered mandatory for some. Link:
Through the entirety of the game I had no technical issues after installing the FAR mod.
The visuals and lightning in this game fit the atmosphere of the game, although it does in my opinion look a little outdated as it seems like a direct console port.
Installing graphical-enhancing mods like reshaders, other post-processing effects or even improved textures can make the game look amazing, but may be taxing on your GPU and be a bit of an hassle to get to work with the FAR mod.
The characters look visually appealing though, especially parts of them. ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°)
The gameplay of the game is both fun and varied, the type of combat you will experience will vary a lot playing through the main story.
The foundation of the combat gameplay is a mix between a typical hack-n-slash and a 3rd person shooter mechanically, but depending on the scenario the game will switch to being a bullet hell arcade game, a sidescrolling platformer or a isometric hack n slash with some variations of these. A downside to the game however, is that content doesn't really scale that well level-wise, and except for the DLC content and a few specific things there's not much to do after you've completed the final ending.
As it is a RPG game, you have a basic level system, a weapon upgrade system and a customization system with "chips", which is the most interesting out of them. You are able to insert chips which grant you stat boots or even add new combat mechanics.
Through the chip system you can for example add an ability which slows time after a perfect dodge, get stat boosts that increase your HP or attack power or even add and remove hud elements like health bars. These chips are upgradable and there's a limit to how many you can equip, depending on their cost.
It's a fun system to play around with as it changes your gameplay experience rather than only adding raw power to your character, making a efficient setup with what you have avaible adds a layer of some complexity.
The story of the game takes place in the same universe as the original Nier game (you don't need to play the original game though), although quite far in a post-apocalyptic future.
For me this game has one of the best stories I've experienced in single-player games, but I don't want to go too much into detail as I want to avoid potential spoilers. :D
The story has an existential theme with a lot of philosophical elements and references. It's quite a thrilling emotional rollercoaster and it becomes better as you play more and learn more about the surrounding world, history and characters.
As the game has multiple endings, I highly recommend reaching ending "E" which is the games "true" ending that wraps up the complete experience nicely.
It's all accompanied by likely the most beautiful video game soundtrack that I've heard, and it all fits so well with the games atmosphere and the encounters down the road.
TLDR; JRPG hack n' slash with an existentialism-themed story, amazing music, butts and fun varied gameplay. Minus points for technical issues due to being a bad console port (at least fixable!)

One of the worst RPGs / MMOs I've ever played. I can't even describe it coherently because I literally cannot pass the outset of it. I have to just rant about random bits of it I've been able to actually experience in no particular order.
Why can't I pass the outset, you ask? Because this is the only game in the world that regularly loses connection to a locally-hosted server. As in, my computer doesn't need to access the Internet, the server is on the same computer, and yet it loses connection every few minutes and is unable to reconnect. That is baffling. It has never happened to me before. I guess I will have to play someone else's server and hope that 1. I don't lose connection to that too and 2. I don't lose my ♥♥♥♥ing♥♥♥♥♥♥over this horrible game and get banned for starting a flémewar.
Even if the connection was stable, everything about the game is implemented horribly to an unplayable level. It's one of those games where every single individual action has its own dedicated hotkey (?!), and otherwise you have to do them by clicking thru context menus. Is this Second ♥♥♥♥ing Life? Oh no no - in Second Life if you're too far away to interact with an item you'll move to it. Not in this game. You have to manually walk within arm's reach of something, "activate" the proper inventory item to enable the action you want if applicable, rotate your view up and down with the keyboard (no mouselook!) so you can right-click the item - by the way EVERYTHING is an interactive item including the borders between ground tiles so you need to pixel-hunt - and hunt through the menu for what you want to do. Basically, you play as a Mars rover remotely operated with a Guitar Hero controller played with your♥♥♥♥♥♥
In this game, you have health, stamina, water, food, nutrition level, calories, carbs, fats, and proteins. These are all actual recognized variables in the game measuring your character's health and they are completely unmanageable in a game where it's a seven-to-nine-click process to get a log from a tree.
Items in this game can have variable weight, becaue you can consume portions of an item to craft things, such as making wood items from logs. In addition to items of the same name being sublisted in the inventory tree (i.e. it says "Log" once and you click to see every Log you have), "mass items" can stack. For instance, if you cut several Kindlings off of a log, you can combine the Kindlings together into one Kindling. This is necessary because for some ♥♥♥♥ing reason this game will tell you that you don't have enough of an item to craft something when that something clearly takes less of the item than you have. For instance, about 0.5 of a Log's weight makes a Kindling, but a log with 1 Weight is apparently not enough to make a Kindling (?!?!) Logs, however, are not "mass items" and do not stack. Oh, and you have. To combine. Your first Kindling. With every other Kindling. One. At. A. Time.
Combat is a joke. Combat is done by standing close to a hostile and waiting. There's a nominal system with nine different directions to attack and defend from but I've not had the honor of fighting anything where this mattered. Hostiles will never stop chasing you, unless you pass something they can't such as a gate or a lake (if they can't swim) in which case they will abruptly stop and never move from the spot until they see you again. They will otherwise follow you to the other side of the world. You'll stop running before then, though, because you have stamina and doing absolutely anything (even leisurely walking) gradually lowers it. You move more slowly the lower your stamina is or the more injured you are. So basically the game is a slippery slope where the instant you encounter an enemy that's too strong you are already dead with no chance of escape or strategic victory.
NPCs try to act like players. They hold conversations with you and each other. They will use your character name like an item. Let's say your name is Bob. They'll randomly generate a conversation line such as "I can't say I am familiar with things like Bobs" or "If you have a Bob, I would like to see it".
Hostile sapient NPCs also send you private messages telling you they're coming to kill you. This is very creepy. (It is also the only thing about this game I like and that ♥♥♥♥ing works properly.)
I'm sure there are a lot more things to do in this game than it's actually allowing me to do. I know you can build housing and villages, and I think you can terraform like Minecraft. How to do those? Don't know, don't care. Even the basic controls of the game are a broken mess so I don't want to even try anything profound like that. The game feels like an experimental alpha. The only intuitively responsive things are gates & doors which authorized entities can just walk right through. As in noclip right through. You go through the actual physical door's wooden indie trash self.
Every time I sign in, I have to put up with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of tutorial dialogs popping up one after the other at odd times, including in the middle of fights. This applies even to a character who has already seen all of these tutorial popups. Idiotic.
All in all, bad game, bad.

Resident Evil Revelations is a Japanese game made by Capcom, that was first released on January 26, 2012 in Japan, initially for the Nintendo 3DS, and later on was ported over other platforms under the title of 'Unveiled Edition', first released on May 21, 2013 in North America.
The game is a return of the series in a classic survival horror style of gameplay, with returning characters and new ones.
But is the game is really that worth buying? Well, as a long-time fan of the series, this review is here to aid you on it.
The game takes place between Resident Evil 4 and 5 (2005), and it fits perfectly in my opinion. Kinda explains certain things that were not made so clear in RE5.
The plot can be a little cheesy at times, but it's great, and at the same time confusing. To help the player on certain plot elements, the game has this "TV series style" catch up everytime you start/load a chapter.
The game takes place on three core locations. The Queen Zenobia luxury cruiser ship, the Valkoinen Mökki Airport and it's surrounding mountains/caves, and the floating city of Terragrigia.
The main location of the game, where most of the gameplay takes place is truly amazing.
The
has this feeling into it that I haven't experienced for a long time in the series.
Since the ship's designs were based on blueprints left by George Trevor before he ended up disappearing, some areas of the ship are reminiscent to certain areas of the Spencer Mansion, the location where the events of the first game of the series, and it's remake, takes place.
It seems at first as a ghost ship. Where danger can be at every corner. For the first time ever in Resident Evil games, I've never been so scared of going into a particular room since RE2.
And since certain parts of the ship feel like the Mansion, it helps a lot.
The
and it's surrounding mountains/caves is quite interesting.
The snowy areas seems too similar to the ones found in RE6, but that's about it.
The floating city of
is just not that good.
But it serves it's point as a plot filling area.
For the first time ever in the Resident Evil series, the player will be likely taking control of multiple characters through the game's storyline.
Most of these characters are really cool, but a few of them are just plot filling. Each of them feel kinda unique when you play as them.
The game play-style is quite similar to that of RE4/RE5. Similar control scheme, but now you're able to walk while aiming/shooting/attacking.
But it's too limited sometimes. While playing the game I wish I could kick through the doors, or slowly open a door, not doing the "opening and going through the door" animation.
And there's no button used for running, instead it's all made with the analog stick, which is pretty bad.
The lack of having a laser-sight aiming for the guns also bothers me.
The crosshair isn't that much precise and reliable, since when you shoot a bullet in that style of game, the trajectory of it goes from where the gun is pointing at, not the crosshair.
The laser sight aiming from RE4/RE5 makes up for that, because at least you have a reliable way of showing where your bullets are going to hit.
And sadly, when making the port, Capcom removed both alternate versions of aiming in first person and laser sight, and kept only the crosshair.
The game also gives you lot of different guns to choose from, and an inventory menu that shows the files you find, area map, key items, etc is back.
But it's not perfect in my opinion.
There's little to no inventory management at all. You only get to change the weapon slots.
Key items do not take inventory space, neither does any ammo you find or herbs. But you do have a limit of how many ammo/herbs you can carry.
Any sorts of grenades also don't take place.
They also brought back the shop system of RE4/RE5. But only partially.
It's not that great overall. You get to find custom parts for the weapons and then place them on the guns you have.
You can remove the tuning parts any time you want, and place them back as well. Which is quite broken in my opinion.
Due this weird tuning system, the guns no longer have "realistic" ammo magazine size, unlike the classic games.
The shop is likely mostly made for Raid mode though.
Another broken aspect is the ability to save and continues.
You can't manually save your game, there's only auto-save checkpoints during the gameplay.
Only manual save that exists is when you are at the results screen of a chapter.
The were times I was playing, but I wanted to stop for a while and do something else, but the game wouldn't allow me to or "I'd lose my progress".
I really wish the typewriter system was brought back. Even if it was just like RE4, with no ink ribbon limit.
And the game has a continue option after you die. Which is pretty cheap and broken I might add, since this is a survival horror game.
The level design is amazing. And yes, backtracking from older RE games was brought back, which I love it.
But stills kinda bad in my opinion. The game always has a "mission objective" set all times during the pause menu, which kinda ruins the fun.
The game tells you what you gotta do, unlike classic games, where the game lets the player decide the order of things that needs to be done.
But there's barely no loading times, save for here and there, instead the whole are is accessible.
The doors really connect to the other room, which makes it a lot better than the classic games, since there's no loading times between them, you can't use an exploit to reset the enemy positions.
The enemies are amazing as well, so are the bosses. They're unpredictable in a way of attacks and movement.
Their designs are also creepy looking and the sort of thing you would totally shoot if you spot one of 'em.
Players can die pretty easily to the weakest enemies if they are not careful.
And enemy placement is randomized and/or dynamic, kinda like RE3.
The puzzles are quite meh, nothing really hard to it.
They're quite easy and time consuming most of time.
Item placement is quite scarce as well. If you get a herb, it never re-spawns.
But it's just meh as well, due the Genesis Scanner mechanic. You can get ammo most of the time by scanning an area, and always be able to get an herb by scanning enemies.
And unlike past games, there's only one type of herb. No combinations.
The game doesn't feature a life status as well.
Unlike past games where your life would show on HUD as a bar (RE4/RE5), or in the inventory menu as a status (Classic RE games), it's not shown at all.
You can tell how much health you have left by the screen showing blood splatters on the sides, and the colouring of the game going into a black-and-white sorta of filter.
And movement isn't affected by health status.
The game is divided by chapters just like RE4/RE5. But there's no chapter select screen like RE5.
Due that, the game has way too many cut-scenes sometimes (kinda like MGS games if you as me), which is pretty bad.
And there's the subtle changes of game location/player character through the story, where it turns into a big shoot-out through enemies.
It's kinda cool like, for taking a break of the survival horror thing, but it's done way too often.
Raid Mode is a really fun extra gamemode, it reminds me of the Extreme Battle mode of RE2.
But that's it. It's the only available extra gamemode, besides New Game+ for campaign.
No Mercenaries, no gamemodes that changes the story (i.e. Invisible Enemy mode), no co-op story, no alternate/side story (i.e. Separate Ways), no nothing.
It's a pretty decent game, but it can have it's flaws here and there.
My final score for this game is
It's worth buying if you want to play something different.
I can look past the graphics, but the controls are so bad and boring and the menus are terrible. Not worth the $1 I paid for it in a bundle, asking $30 for it is borderline a scam.

I rate this game a 10/10. Disclaimer: I don't care about the graphics. If you need good visual fidelity, this game is NOT for you.
If you don't, this game has a lot to offer.
I come from Wurm Online, which I played in the past but never really got into, due to subscription model and LONG grind time for literally everything.
This version fixes all of that. There's no sub fee. You buy once, you have access to everything forever.
Wurm Unlimited works with dedicated servers. There are TONS of good servers all over the world, and they're all customised differently. Default exp + crafting rates too slow? Go on a 5x server. Wanna play as a hermit? Plenty of near-empty servers, offering you lots of space to do your own thing undisturbed.
There's mods too, but I haven't really checked them out yet, apart from the custom maps which are VERY big and well-made.
All in all, it offers Wurm Online's features without any of the downsides. These are:
Complete freedom:
it's a sandbox, but for real. Go dig holes or build hills. The world is almost completely editable by players, it just takes a while.
Ridiculous depth:
From the combat system with all seperate limbs and different kinds of wounds, to the player nutrition with tons of different recipes with some effects, to some kind of religious system that will offer spells later on (I haven't gotten that far yet) it offers everything.
Survival:
Going into the wild is dangerous. Terrifying monsters roam the land, you have to take care not to suddenly become the hunted instead of the hunter. You have to use nature's resources to build up a shelter, start making tools and improve yourself.
Multiplayer:
The standalone version still supports all the typical MMO features. PVP/PVE servers, Arenas, "Kingdoms". The sandbox experience gets much better when working together, you can split tasks and work your way up to a functional village over time. There's settlement creation with hiring guards, managing access rights and more.
In my opinion, definitely worth getting, it improves so much over Wurm Online.

Keep in mind that this game was initially a Nintendo 3DS game that was ported to console and PC after the fact. The graphics and animations might seem a little dated because of this. That being said, this port is not bad at all, at least for PC. The graphic quality resembles Resident Evil 4.
Gameplay and controls are very well done. It's 3rd person over the shoulder. Campaign is singleplayer only but you will have an AI partner. Your partner... isn't the best or most helpful, but thankfully they won't cause a game over if they get hit too much and sometimes serve as a nice distraction, except on bosses. Difficulty ranges from easy early on and nicely becomes more challenging toward the end.
There is one glaring problem with the gameplay though. The dodge mechanic is incredibly shoddy. On a 360 controller, you're supposed to press A and a direction at the same time to avoid an attack at the right time, but it only ever seemed to work half the time I did it. Either it's broken or the timing needs to be perfect, but it's very frustrating. I also had an incredible amount of frustration with 2 of the Bosses in this game due to their rather odd mechanics, one of which isn't helped by the wonky dodging.
This game is a LITTLE short, but that's forgivable since it was initially a 3DS game. It's also broken up into 14 episodes, some of which are very short. It also makes the game feel disjointed, because you'll be flashing back to earlier events a lot. It's mostly non linear on the ship later on in the game once you progress, so you can go back and find different weapons, ammo, health, and weapon mods (the weapons and the different mods are a great aspect to this game).
The game's story is very interesting with a nice plot twist. You'll be playing and partnering with a bunch of very interesting new and returning characters, with Jill Valentine the one you'll be playing the most and the only one who can access the weapons and mods you find.
Side note: I had an issue with the cutscenes having audio desync issues, but I'm not sure if this is only my issue.
Overall, if you're a Resident Evil fan, you're gonna want to play this game, as the story alone is worth it and captures the mood from the earlier games in the series, with some new elements as well as other elements from later games in the series. Other than that I recommend waiting until it is on sale if you want to play it. But you'll be getting your money's worth.
I haven't tried Raid Mode, but that may add some replay value if you're interested.

The game itself plays like Zelda: Link to the Past or a Ys game, but with a little more in the melee combos/combat dodging department and a higher focus on physics base range combat. You can aim and ricochet shots to hit attack openings. This feature also is used a lot in the game's puzzles.

But of course their very special within the game world their playing. Overall the game has phenomenal 2D physics, inventive fast based melee combo combat with range puzzle elements. It also runs very smoothly on about any remotely current PC or laptop. "+ Great storytelling.
+ Its themes evolve as the story progresses in Afterstory.
+ Incredibly emotional.
+ Unique characters that all provide purpose to the story in some way or another.
+ Nagisa, Kotomi, Tomoyo, Ibuki, Kyou, and Sunohara are top tier best girls.
+ Akio and Sanae are the best parents I have ever had the pleasure of experiencing.
+ Exceptional humor.
+ Extremely replayable.
+ One of the most genuine MC's in Visual Novels (Tomoya Okazaki)
+ Unique story where you actually SEE the married life of a couple and the relationship they had prior.

I'd recommend this to anyone that wants to involve themselves in the "Visual Novel" medium as it is the best one I have ever played besides Steins;Gate. Sacred Citadel is aan old-school inspired beat 'em up with some RPG elements and a focus on Co-op, set, of course, in the Sacred Universe.
I have never played another Sacred game, so I couldn't really say how loyal it is to the franchise, regarding the setting and classes.
Going into this review, I've finished the game with a character in single player mode. I've also tried every other character. Unfortunately, there were no online games up for me to try it.
I haven't played many Beat 'em Up games, but I've played a few with unique twists and they're generally just pure fun!
Sacred Citadel started out that way, and I enjoyed my time with it, I'll give it that. Unfortunately, it's very limited, and despite having good foundations, it seems very rushed and shallow compared to what it could have been.
The game is structured with 4 Acts, each one with 5 different levels (including a Boss Level). Each act has a different set of enemies and takes place in a different place. You'll find occasional mini-bosses, which are essentially more powerful versions of normal enemies, and then a big boss fight that requires some pattern recognition.
Between each level, the player can go to the Town, where he can buy Weapons, Armor, Gems, Potions, or make bets to increase challenge.
Regarding
, I have very few criticisms.
The game was made in 2.5D, with a clean, cartoony artstyle, and I really like it. it's colourful and the backgrounds look really good, in my opinion. There's also a decent variety in the levels to keep things fresh.
The
is something that I have mixed feelings about. It sounds pretty good (perfect amount of organ - a lot!) and you can hear the old-school inspiration from it (more melody, less atmosphere), but it's very repetitive and gets easily lost in the background, unfortunately.
I had the music volume up, but it seems to miss the *humpf!* to complement the combat. I like it, but I don't think it's all that great to go along the game.
Still, it's not bad.
SoundEffects were serviceable, nothing noteworthy. They do the job well enough.
I'll talk about the features, and then go to the combat itself.
In this game, you have a few RPG elements, as mentioned. By killing enemies, you get some loot, and experience. When you earn enough experience, you level-up, restoring your health right away. You can then attribute some points to Attack, Defense, Dexterity or Power, after finishing a level. You get 2 points per level-up.
The loot is essentially Gold, Health and Potions, and then Weapons or Armour. You can use gold in the town to buy new equiment or bet. Potions can restore your health, have you do more damage, or restore your mana, which you use for special attacks.
One major criticism regarding equipment, is that everything is literally an upgrade. There is no real choice or change in playstyle by picking up certain weapons or armour. You can have Elemental Damage/Resistance, but it doesn't change anything, combat-wise. So, everytime a weapon or piece of armour is dropped, you can equip it if it's better, or just leave it. It has virtually no impact in the game, aside from scaling your damage and resistance to the enemies.
Unfortunately, this game has no difficulty modes. The one thing you can do, is bet in the town, accepting challenges for an upcoming level. I love the concept behind this. It could make for a much better experience, fit for very different players.
The downside is that it's not done right... at all.
There are
. Life, Time and Score (Health requires not dying. Time is well... finish a level within a time limit. And Score is to finish a level with a certain score, earned by combos and the like). Each costs from 100 to 400 gold (scales with the Act), and you can only have one active per level. I suppose this was a way to improve replayability, but these challenges barely change gameplay at all to justify replaying them a lot. Besides, not all of them scale well. If you're higher level for a level, Health and Time become very easy, but Score is essentially impossible, since you 1-hit everything and cannot combo.
Unfortunately, neither of them make the combat harder or anything, it only forces an artificial objective that helps absolutely nothing regarding replayability.
Lastly, there are 4 classes: Warrior, Ranger, Shaman and Mage (if I'm not mistaken). Each of them have a different special attack, but that's about it. And it serves as a segway to the combat.
Despite being a fairly fun game, there are barely any combos for the player to memorize, and you unlock them all within the first Act. That would be fine, if there were a lot of them. But it seemed to give you variety in combat for a while, and then it just stops, leaving you with barely anything to use.
This makes the combat very, very repetitive and simplified, which is a big problem in a game that encourages replayability.
You can not change classes as you want either. Each class as its progress saved, and you can get switch between them at will.
As a result, if you want to try out different classes, you need to play the same levels from the beginning.
Every character has personalized animations, and they're all fluid and look pretty good. But, every combo is essentially the same in every character, only with a different animation. Despite switching characters, there's no change in gameplay, rendering it all pointless. That's a shame, and it's the combat and its shallow systems that make me not recommend this game.
Level Design is also barely existent. It's mostly pressing forward, with the occasional vehicle/mounted combat. The downside of it is that it's far harder to combat when you're in a mount, since you're thrown down of it whenever you're attacked, and the mounts attack much slower, being more of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥than a good change of pace.
The game was way too easy, even with challenges. The Bosses were fairly enjoyable, but mostly too easy as well, with the exception of one of them.
Enemy Variety is pretty good, changing with each act, making for a more varied combat which is great. Flying enemies, however, were not very enjoyable to fight, due to their placing. Since there is a bit of a third direction in the game, flying enemies give a weird perspective, making them much harder to hit, and just clunky, really.
It could have been a very, very good game. Unfortunately, despite the idea being there, it just doesn't do much to execute their ideas well.
It's just the outer shell of a great game. I did get some enjoyment out of it, but it was a repetitive experience that tries to mask what it actually is by having some very artificial RPG elements.
It's not a very good beat 'em up, specially when compared to some other great games out there.
P.S.: I almost forgot. The voice acting in the game was really good! Despite being brief, it was really well done!
Also, I saw many people complaining about bugs, specially online. Since I saw no one online, I can not test it, but I didn't encounter any problem in singleplayer mode. Only BIG complain about the port is the lack of option, specially resolution and aspect ratio.

Deadly Premonition is a unique experience that every videogame enthusiast should play.
The game obviously looks a bit rough around the edges and surely doesn't have the tightest controls, but once you get used to it, it will suck you in and never let go until you get to the end.
Its setting is heavily inspired by David Lynch's Twin Peaks, which may be a plus (it is for me), however as the story progresses you realize that it stands on its own and it's actually pretty interesting.
Every character you'll meet has some peculiarity that makes him or her different from the others, and you will likely get attached to York, the protagonist, one of the best playable characters of the last gen, IMHO.
Things I didn't like are basically related to the bad PC port: long loading times even on an SSD, crashes and some problems with getting my gamepad to work.
It was worth the trouble anyway.
Buy this game, you won't get to play anything like this for some time.

As a fan of action RPGs, this isn't really a game I could ignore based on the reviews it was getting.
Story: A bit confusing at first. Because some things are simply not explained until later. There are multiple paths to take through the game, and you retread content a bit too much in the B path. Otherwise the alternate paths clear up a lot and are a refreshing because you play as a different character and see their perspective. The story does become more coherant and gripping as it goes on though.
Music: 5 stars, and really helps to give the game a unique identity. I am listening to some of the tracks even after beating the game.
Gameplay: The animation quality is top class, and the combat is fun. However the character growth curve isn't as gradual as it should be. On normal mode I found myself becoming immortal after obtaining decent healing chips. My recommendation is to switch to hard mode once you start encountering this issue. Some of the bosses become invincible once you deplete their health just for the sake of hearing their entire monologue or seeing a certain animation sequence, which just needlessly adds to the frustration of playing the harder difficulties. There are a large number of weapons, however their is little gameplay difference between them, because weapons of the same class play exactly the same. I never felt the need to use anything other than a one handed sword because it was so easy. I'm sure harder difficulties would push me to fight with more nuance, because the capacity for that is there. It was just unnecessary for me.
Graphics: About what you can expect from this generation. The art style however is what makes it stand out. Some areas of the game are drained of color and some are filled with glowing life, all which help to give the story more emphasis.
Replayability: Keeping spoilers out, you can expect your first playthrough to take 30-50 hours depending on how many side quests and exploring you do. Chapter select is unlocked upon game completion. Quest progress, chips, weapons, intel, and levels are shared between characters, which is awesome. There are hidden areas and weapons to find. Replaying the game entirely is a real possiblity for me. That's all I can really say. The ending does leave a lasting impact.
Score: 86/100

This is without a doubt my favorite video game of all time. It's one of the last great TW games. Without any expansions, it is a complete game with a large map, many factions, and a campaign that feels really open ended. The units are fairly diverse and the expansions each add an awesome, unique campaign with great factions. Moreover, it's really simple to mess around with some settings files and unlock all the factions (even the rebels) and mess around with other settings. The game is straight forward, but can be challenging and rewarding, it lacks all the unnecessary fluff added in later TW. It's obvious that this game was developed by people who really had a passion for history and fun historical-strategic gameplay, and not just a bunch of money hungry jerks who want you to pay up to 200 USD for a full, buggy TW game. Honestly, if you don't care about graphics, and just want a fun, engaging, historical strategic experiences, that you'll enjoy for hundreds of hours and numerous play throughs, get this game and the expansions. When I had the money to indulge in building a new PC for gaming, this game was my primary reason for taking the plunge.  I had seen friends play variants of Medieval, Rome, and Empire over the years, and after building my PC and taking advantage of a generous Humble Bundle, I acquired Medieval II along with all of the relevant expansions.
I could not anticipate how deeply this game would affect me.  This review is an emotional one for me to make, but I think that there is already enough information readily available to people to make an assessment of the game according to the technical specifications, and so I must speak to that which caused the game to enrapture me as well as what compels me to speak so highly of the experience.
This game elevated my enjoyment of historical strategy games to new heights, and the attention to detail on both the campaign and tactical theatres coupled with a fully immersive soundtrack and historically driven yet spontaneously occuring story-arc per campaign, makes for an endlessly engaging, glorious experience.
This game makes medieval warfare personal.  You will grow attached to your settlements, your castles, your generals, your armies, and you will grow to hate your enemies and the enemies of whichever cause you fight for.  You will construct grand cities, fortified outposts, and awe-inspiring tributes to your God.  You will weep in the depths of your losses and you will relish in the carnage of your triumphs.  You will take risks, you will be punished for your failures, and sometimes your only reward for victory will be in the knowledge of a battle well fought or a cause uncompromised.
You will sally forth from the imagined safety of your walls and meet the enemy horde in the field, often alone, and you will take the fight to them.  Your men and your enemies will fight and die on the walls, in the streets and courts, in the fields, and even at sea.  You will fight in desperation at each gate and breach in your walls, you will feel the thunder of hooves and the quake of war-machines and thousands of marching feet as war is brought across the Old and New worlds.  You will become a "Duke of Death", and your men and your enemies will mutually seek each other out for this death.
But in this death you will be reborn.  Reborn as a scion of war.  Total war.
If you are still reading this, then embrace your fate and pick up the sword.

I don't really know what to say about this. I mean it's a classic Total War where you basically have a map where you decide which direction your empire will take, where will your armies go, what buildings you will build in your cities, diplomacy and all that classic♥♥♥♥♥♥we see in all Total Wars. However it's not THAT great here compared to other Total Wars, it feels much more simpler compared to Shogun 2 or Empire for exemple, those are much more complicated (not as EU IV tho) and there are many things you have to take care of at each turn. There you feel like you really are on the top of an empire when on the other hand in Medieval II it feels like you could just take 1 minute before ending your turn and that wouldn't have any important consequences on your campaign if you made a bad decision. I wish there was a feudal system implemanted and all but hopefully one day we will see a Medieval III with that part being fixed.
Now of course there were bugs when it came out and they still are there, nothing really striking (usually thoses bugs are things like one soldier freezing or a unit not obeying directly to your order) actually it's just that they kill the immersion from time to time but it's okay, still better than Empire or Rome 2 if you ask me. But the biggest problem here is the AI. As always in those games, they really are not that clever, especially during siege battles where they almost don't react if you don't tease them in the first place. I recommend you to play on the highest difficulty to get a better experience out of this game.
By the way note that if you never played any Total War game or just any grand strantegy game then I believe M2TW is a great choice to start!
Well it's endless I'd say, you could play this for hundreds or even thousands of hours if you are a die-hard fan of the genre and the Medieval time period. There are tons of maps to play on, from the New World where you can play as the conquistadors to Lithuania where you, as a teutonic knight will burn some pagans in the name of the cross and then you may also take a ship to go to the Holy Land where you will deus vult and remove some filthy kebabs! There are tons of factions to play with, always new units and new aeras to discover and conquer etc... And I didn't even told you about the mods! Oh and of course if you are looking for some challenges there is still the multiplayer mode that allows you to play with real kings & queens from everywhere in the known world!
Just check it on YouTube, it's perfect, catches well the medieval vibe and you will feel invincible when the drums will beat during tough moments of a battle. I personally adore the soundtracks from the Crusades Campaign. Check it out and see (hear?) by yourself.
All in all Medieval 2 Total War is definitely a great game, probably one of the best, if not THE best Total War game (just check the amount of fans of this game that are dying for a Medieval III right now) out there. I have to say, this game is pretty good, though there are certainly problems with it.
Issue #1: combat, the combat is pretty lack luster, sure it looks cool with all the ships flying around and lasers/plasma, cannon fire, missiles, etc, but all it is really is that you send a fleet against another fleet, and hope yours is better.
Issue #2: boring diplomacy, all the diplomacy is, is asking another empire if they want to be an ally, trade, or declaring war on said empire, it's not that deep.
Issue #3: DLC, the DLC themselves aren't the problem, in fact they're all pretty great, the problem is, is that different forms of slavery (domestic, food) syncretic evolution, and hiveminds require you to buy DLC. Then there's the Plantoid DLC nothing is really wrong with it, just that it cost $7.99 (not on sale) at the time of this review, which is a bit more than what I think you should pay for what is mostly background stuff.
Other stuff: there's some balancing issues in there, and there's the increase in price that I've read about from the other reviews, I haven't really noticed an increase in price, so unless they lowered it to the original price before I looked at it again, then I'm just a bit confused.
Then there's stuff like how people think that any species should be able to live on continental worlds because of the variation in climate, and while I do sort of agree, I think it's for balancing, making it so that a rather very common world doesn't have the same habatibility as the gaian world.
What about good things? Well there are certainly good things such as...
#1: nonlinear technology, the game doesn't have a technology tree/web, rather you will have a random set of technologies you can research each time you pick one, any technology can appear aslong as you have the proper requirments.
#2: megastructures, this one is kind of mute unless you have the Utopia DLC which allows you to build megastructures, but even without it you can still find things like ringworlds, and repair damaged/destroyed ringworlds.
#3: graphics, not much to say here really, the game has some very good ship designs, artwork, species appearence, etc.
#4: Lore, most of the Lore lies with the anomolies that you'll find with exploring the galaxy, but you can find even more once you start getting the precursor events, the precursors being a certain long extinct species, or collective of species coming from anywhere from 600,000, to 6 million years depending on which precursor you get. Though the problem with this is that the precursor events are bugged, where sometimes you won't be able to find all of the artifacts from them that will allow you to find out what their fate was, and also allow you to find where their home system was.
In the end, do I recommend this game? yes I do, even at the base game I stilled enjoyed it, and that was all the way back when the government system was♥♥♥♥♥♥ but The game is even better with the DLCs, so if you have the money then I would recommend buying Stellaris, but if you think that all the bad stuff might out weigh the good things, then maybe you shouldn't, though I would recommend watching a play through just to make sure.

These games typically aren't my cup of tea, though I've always looked at them with a sort of envy. I tried GalCiv II after I read a fantastic piece by Tom Francis, but couldn't really get into it. Stellaris seemed to break the mold for me. The game appears overwhelming at first, but I found it really fun to create a society, shaping its ethics, its form of government, the species that comprised it. From expanding my pacifist, egalitarian fennec foxes out into the stars to dealing with angry, warlike neighbors by way of alleigance and strategic saber-rattling felt like the stakes were real. Because I'd made a society that I might actually want to live in, protecting it, and its people's way of life, felt worthwhile.
You also feel deeply involved in your society due to "Factions," representatives of your society's ethics that vie for influence over your populace. You keep these factions happy by pursuing goals related to those ethics. Some seem a little far-fetched: For example, my pacifist ethic got me an organization dedicated to accumulating wealth. I guess the creators never heard of the military-industrial complex. Nevertheless, keeping these factions happy made me feel active in my society's growth as it spanned the cosmos.
This game comes with surprisingly deep lore events, which you mostly discover through your 'science ships' which travel the cosmos and survey different star systems for useful materials. Occasionally they come up on something interesting--artifacts of another alien civilization, crystals that seem to be alive, space whales--in one instance, a religious icon representing gods of death and malice from deep in my species' past was found floating in a distant star system. I followed a trail of seemingly supernatural clues (in an otherwise science fiction setting) to find that the gods of that religion may have been aliens from the past. (Giorgio would be proud.) This lore event stood out to me, not just because of the change of setting, but because the tone felt grave in a cosmic sense, that I might find something horrible at the end of that road. In the end, I chose to cover-up their existence.
To give you an idea about how immersive this game can get: There's an option to increase your citizen's standard of living  and ergo, their happiness. My citizens are already pretty darn happy--they have planets that they're well-adjusted to, all their factions are satisfied, there's hardly any war, there's plenty of food to go around, the government's stable--but I keep at the very expensive "Utopian Abundance" option because I actually want these fox people, who I only see as pinpoints of light on a globe, to have the best lives they can possibly have.
