My personal relationship with the world-famous/infamous Resident Evil series has been a long and sometimes treacherous one.  The very first Resident Evil on the PlayStation 1 was nothing less than, well, a "revelation" to me when I first discovered it.  Having spent years prior basically disinterested in video games in favour of more "respectable" art/entertainment forms such as films, a funny thing happened on the way to the grave and I found myself no longer very "scared" by horror movies any more...a shame, since it has arguably been my single favourite of all genres since, well, at least my mid-teens or so.  Then I discovered that it was possible for a VIDEO GAME to have much the same effect, only perhaps more so...for in spite of the questionable graphics and clunky movement, it was officially now ME essaying the role of the lead protagonist in a horror story.  And that was a very scary proposition indeed!  The first time I discovered that giant shark in the mansion's basement...man, that was an epic moment...and the Resident Evil series was of course destined to become all the MORE epic, in time.  Though not necessarily in a GOOD way...

Resident Evil 2 took things to a SLIGHTLY more action-packed and, yes, "epic" level, but still managed to unquestionably maintain the horror credentials of its predecessor.  Resident Evil 3...well, it was still mostly favouring the fear over the fight, but with the first advent of a firearm-wielding monster, things were starting to veer just the teensiest, tiniest bit downhill.  Code Veronica thankfully steered things back toward a more staunchly horror-orientated direction shortly thereafter...but then of course came Resident Evil 4 (let's just ignore the Survivor/Dead Aim/Outbreak/etc games for the purposes of this review, since they honestly don't exist in the minds of most RE fans).  Yes, just when all seemed lost if the series were to indeed continue in the direction it was mostly heading in, RE4 managed to reinvigorate the waning faith of many a fan, not so much by taking the series in a less action-y direction, but by downright REINVENTING the gameplay in a way which better SUITED the increased amount of enemies and firepower and what-have-you.  And it managed to do so without compromising that all-important "horror factor" TOO much.

Which brings us to Resident Evil 5...sigh.  I mean, it wasn't that bad...at least until the utterly ridiculous rock-punching (!) climax set in a volcanic landscape, at which point those little hints of manga and anime which the series had harboured for so long took true hold and♥♥♥♥♥♥all over anything even vaguely resembling logic or atmosphere.  Its myriad sins seem pale in comparison, however, to part 6, which - from as much as I have been able to bear to play of it so far - appears to be a final declaration that the games which helped spawn a series of by-and-largely moronic MIlla Jovavich action movies were now SUBSERVIENT to said movie series, and it was officially a "horror" series no more.  Thankfully, however, the good people at Capcom saw fit shortly BEFORE this atrocity to give birth to a side-series which would better retain the "survival horror" flavour of the early games...

Resident Evil Revelations, please step forward for evaluation.

It's been described as "Resident Evil 4.5", and it can certainly lay claim to that title story-wise.  So what about...GAMEPLAY-wise?  Well...pretty much, yeah.  I'll admit I wasn't too impressed early on, finding myself essentially confused by all the episodic jumping back and forth between different characters in different places and what-not...which only served, incidentally, to compromise one of the single most important contributing factors to the tension generated in a successful "survival horror" game, namely that of ammo and/or healing conservation (that is to say, when you only have to make what few items you possess last until the end of one or two chapters, a good deal of this tension inevitably abates).  BUT...after a while the focus falls at least predominantly on the characters trapped out at sea, and it's in these segments that Revelations manages to capture some of that old-school "isolation horror" charm.
To some degree it's almost like the RE1 mansion set on a boat (well, three boats, but who's counting), with a bit of Tomb Raider-inspired swimming and butt-centric visuals - this is still aimed at young males, after all - to fill it all out.  But mostly, I gotta say...it's pretty good.  Not a TOTAL return to form - the AI is certainly about as♥♥♥♥♥♥as such things can get, including one bit where monsters were literally either walking or jumping straight past not ONE but TWO NPCs to get to my player-controlled character! - but it's about the best we can hope for for now, one suspects.  Though Revelations 2, horror of horrors, actually looks like a ♥♥♥♥ing SILENT HILL game in the screenshots!  So maybe there really is hope for this franchise after all.  It's pretty much like the film industry these days:  When in doubt, REBOOT.  It worked for the Batman movies, and it can work for the Resident Evil games.  We'll just have to wait and see, though, won't we?

Verdict: 9/10.

(And speaking of Batman...you know that a video game series has been going on just a LITTLE TOO LONG when an otherwise perfectly straight "rookie government agent" character is designed with hair which makes him look like THE JOKER.  What, Leon's hair in RE4 wasn't over-stylish or impractical ENOUGH for you people?!  Saints preserve us...)

CrossCode is a fantastic game. It reminds me of Golden Sun, one of my favorite games of all time. The graphics are simple but smooth. The story is engaging, and I enjoy a lot of the humour in the game. The soundtrack is very good, although like many RPGs, entire areas have one soundtrack that just loops, and some are better than others for listening to for a couple hours on end, but it can't really be helped.
The combat is good- and a big part of that is how you get punished for dying. You effectively don't- you get reloaded to your last save, which is the autosave that happened when you walked into that room. I think that's important, because the game is very skill based when it comes to more difficult fights. If you don't know the mechanics of a boss or a new room/enemy, you can get punished hard and quickly. And that's good that the game can challenge you like this and be fast paced in its combat, because it fits the style of it.
While it's difficult to judge, I think the puzzles overall are good. There are a lot of puzzles in the game- even just small ones like "How do I get a floor higher in this area so I can get the chest?", not just dungeon puzzles that encompass a whole room. It's difficult to judge because there were puzzles that I got stuck on when the solution, obviously, was right there on the screen. So I want to say the game has bad or frustrating or difficult to figure out puzzles, but at the same time, I have to weigh the fact that I'm an imperfect human. Of course there would be puzzles I would get stuck on! Some people found those puzzles easy, and other puzzles I figured out my first time stumped others. So I think overall it was mostly me not applying good problem solving techniques. The majority were enjoyable, or just challenging enough to where even if it took 5 minutes instead of 30 seconds like I might expect, it felt good to beat it, not frustrating to spend so much time on it.
Pro tip- always work backwards for puzzles.
Always.
The game is unique in a couple of ways. As of the most recent version, a lot of enemies in the game (I think all but two) are non-aggressive. So when you walk into an area with enemies, the health bars will be blue, and you can run right past them, or into them, and it doesn't matter. If you attack an enemy, you get it's "group" to attack you. In other words, an area's enemies are not all going to attack you if you attack one enemy. Enemies do respawn, but not instantly, and not when you leave and enter a new area. I believe it's time based. This is important for another way the game is unique- it's not just a combat driven or story driven RPG. Like mentioned when I wrote about the puzzles, the game has many, and many small ones outside of dungeons, for example. Not constantly getting attacked when switching between two areas trying to figure out a solution, or just having the enemies in the one area the puzzle is in respawn quickly and attack you is important to the game, because almost all areas in the game of some form of puzzle/parkour element to it. Again, it reminds me of Golden Sun.
The characters have a lot of character. They'll speak when they don't need to or it's not pertinent to the story, because in in the game world, they're regular human beings of course, not just cogs in the machine that is the protagonist's storyline. That's really cool. I feel like the writing is very good overall and mimics what a person might actually say relatively often. The story so far is good because of the characters. The story is interesting because of the characters. When you've watched hundreds of movies, play hundreds of games, or what have you, you realize that pretty much everything has been done when you generalize plots. What are most RPGs? Go find something that's long lost, go save a person you care about or a country or town or whatever, go stop the bad guy trying to awaken an evil power, etc. CrossCode is unique in that in CrossCode, you play a character who is playing a game called CrossWorlds, along with everyone else you meet, is in the CrossWorlds universe. That's new to me. What saves the parts of the story that is pretty generic- go grab the ancient thing no one has been able to before, is that the writing is good, the characters and expressions are good, the names for things and puzzles and actual gameplay is good. It makes the plot an acutal thing to enjoy and get invested in, instead of having it be this out of context, "Oh, it's another game where you go grab the ancient power. That's new..." story.
While currently short in story, (2-3 hours for me on my first playthrough to get through it), it did take me a healthy 17ish hours to get through the gameplay that there is so far. And for that matter, that's without story adding time to it. I've played games for less than 17 hours and thought they were good, so even though it's not finished, I'd still recommend it, it's still a great game, and the Developers are pretty interactive with the community and update about every 2-3 months- but the updates are big, for example, the last update brought about 6-8 hours of gameplay into the game, because it was the entire second dungeon and the surrounding area. One last note- there are two dungeons currently in the game, and there will probably only be 4-5. There are 4 elements you need to obtain in the game, and right now both dungeons contained one, so the game might be about halfway over gameplay wise. Although I wouldn't imagine you would just get the 4th element in the 4th dungeon and have the game end very quickly after that (which is why I said 4-5 dungeons), the game would still be about 35 hours with only 2-3 hours of story and the gameplay finished if it DOES end pretty much right after the 4th dungeon. And for that matter, if the 3rd and 4th dungeons and areas of the are about as long as the first two. Given the story will be carried throughout the whole game, I expect the game to be about 50 hours, but that's a total guess. Either way, 35 hours is pretty much the minimum, which is definitely worth the $15.99 I paid for it, and would have gladly paid $20.00 for it too. Also, keep in mind that that would be if you played through it once. I've played through it twice for a different build as it is an RPG with a skill/talent tree!
Okay, imagine the following scenario. A man you don't know at all (me) is sitting at his computer, playing CrossCode. Because it's $20.00 (though I got it for $15.99), and I've played it for 30 hours, that's about 66 cents an hour. When I played this game, I played it for about 5 hours straight through dinner and didn't even realize- that's how engulfed I was in the game. If I never played this game again, then I would have paid that 66 cents/hour for the game relative to how much entertainment time I got out of it. So imagine now that a man who isn't even aware he's played CrossCode for an hour is approached by another person. This person comes to the man at his computer and says, "You owe me 66 cents for the last hour you played."
While I would have been surprised a random person in my house was asking for 66 cents for the game I just played...
I would have undoubtedly payed it. I would have absolutely payed it to keep playing CrossCode.

Southend Interactive develops Sacred Citadel, a rather riveting game that can best be described as a side scroller beat’em up action adventure. This essentially falls in the same category as Castle Crashers; although, Sacred Citadel loses on the comedy it picks up on the graphics.
Sacred Citadel is about the far away land of Ancaria, which is under attack by the evil Ashen Empire. You play a random soldier (Warrior, Ranger, Mage, or Shaman) with each class uses different techniques in order to defeat the many enemies ahead. Mama Grimmoc, the evil orc mother, is attacking the civilizations which you have become accustomed to. As such you decide to take up your weapon to stop her. You eventually realize Mama Grimmoc is working for a mysterious man, The Merchant, who requires her to retrieve him two artifacts. Upon realizing their value you decide to take it upon yourself to obtain one of the artifacts in order to gain the huge reward The Merchant has promised you for them. The campaign involves fighting off hordes of orcs, bandits, soldiers, monsters and more. As your adventure goes on you must fight your way through four acts totaling twenty levels. Each act contains four levels and a boss fight. You must fight your way through each boss in order to progress to the next act each of the bosses require you to use different strategies. The bosses are Mossback, Mama Grimmoc, Queen Digestya, and Gatebreaker.
The There are only forty levels, which mean you cannot max a character out in every single attribute, but instead must divide them up appropriately. Luckily as you’ll quickly realize, you don’t need to put any points in defense in order to complete the campaign. The game itself is relatively easy and I believe I only died twice through the entire campaign, one time because I forgot to use my potion and the other time because I couldn’t figure out how to defeat the Gatebreaker. The game doesn’t get more difficult as you progress. The game just gets easier because you figure out how to play better. You don’t need to spend any of the games money; in fact I beat the entire game without spending a single coin.  But if you don’t mind playing easy games and just want to hack ‘n slash then this is a really good choice.
Most of the negative reviews focus on the server instability and glitches associated with the multiplayer. Well I never played the multiplayer, so I cannot tell you how that goes. If the other reviews are correct then I would highly recommend avoiding this game if you are looking for a multiplayer co-op experience. On the other hand, if you just want to play a fun little campaign that doesn’t pose much of a challenge then this is a great choice.
Act Five is added to the campaign and finally you can defeat the monsters that began the whole war. Mother Grimmoc has run the jungle and you must go in to retrieve the artifact she stole at the end of the original campaign. The campaign adds an additional five levels which push you to the metal as you fight off new, but similar enemies. They are all essentially stronger versions of past enemies, and in fact one boss is just a larger version of one of the orcs you fight. The game is intense and adds new weapons, but sadly doesn’t add a new village. This means you have to earn the weapons by playing the levels rather than just purchasing them.
If you enjoy hack and slack side scrollers then this is the game for you. I would recommend getting this game if you enjoy a single player campaign and don't really care to venture into multiplayer. In all honesty there seems no point to multiplayer as this campaign is so easy with one person adding three more would make the game a cakewalk. Although based on other reviews if you are looking for a four player co-op experience this may not be the game for you. Sacred Citadel offers fun combat, rather interesting enemies, and mixes hack 'n slash combat systems with platformer mechanics. The game is riviting to play by yourself and if you can get it for a good deal it's definitely worth the buy.
Pros:
+Easy to master combat with few combinations to memorize
+Lots of loot and weapons that can easily be obtained throughout the story mode.
+Interesting item add-ons that allow you to boost the power of your character beyond your maximum attribute points
+Easy, but fun campaign that allows for a single person to enjoy the adventure.
+Missions challenges that add replay value for already completed missions
+Easy to use controls
+They have added DLC to the game.
Cons:
-No mouse functionality (I set my mouse to preform keyboard functions so I could use my mouse and keyboard)
-Does not support 1080p resolution (I just played in windowed mode)
-Apparently the multiplayer did not function well (I have no experience on this)
-The campaign was relatively short
-There is no way to increase the difficulty

I don't usually bother with reviews, I guess because I'm just too lazy, but I felt it was worth the trouble to write a review for this game, because it's really amazing, and I want them to stay solvent and keep making new campaigns for many years to come. This game has gotten a very bad rap because of the way they chose to present the game (as a modular set of DLC that each cost money, with no central "main game" that also costs money). Originally, this game was called Order of Battle: Pacific. You paid $40 and got the U.S. Pacific and Rising Sun campaigns (which are now on sale as individual DLC's for #20 each), and the reviews for that iteration of the game were Overwhelmingly Positive. But then they changed it to the more open-ended Order of Battle: WWII, and decided that each campaign would just be its own DLC. The developers have talked about this on the discussion board, about how it's just the way Steam works that something like that is labeled "free to play," that wasn't their own choice. But because it is labeled that way, people come in expecting the free portion to be a fully-featured game that is self-contained and entertaining in itself, with no need to buy any DLC unless you just want some extra bonuses. That's not what this game is, and that's the main reason why it gets bad reviews, but it's just a problem of labeling and expectations. If they still had two campaigns as the core game and put a price tag on it, it would still be THE EXACT SAME GAME, but people wouldn't expect to be getting a full-fledged game for free. If you like turn-based strategy, or if like me, you're a fan of hex-and-counter wargames, then this is a fantastic entry in the genre. Just ignore the inaccurate labeling of "Free to Play," and let the game be what it is. If you like this genre of strategy game (especially if you're already a fan of the old Panzer General or the newer Panzer Corps), you will love Order of Battle.

This game is basically a rework/update and combination of a 20+ year-old series of (excellent) games, including "Allied General" and "Pacific General".  What they've done is take what were different games, update them, and offer them as packs of DLC content within a basic game framework. A lot of folks seem to be getting frustrated by the DLC pricing in a "free" game, but keep in mind the free part amounts to a basic demo.  All three of the original games this DLC content covers cost around $50 each when they came out, so you do get a lot for your money, especially on sale for $34.
I bought the DLC for the Pacific campaigns for $19 on sale, and compared to the originals, it's a great update in my opinion. Anyone familiar with the Panzer Corps or Panzer General series will be able to jump right in and play, and for new folks it comes with a  72 page manual, and by the end of the bootcamp tutorial you should be able to play any campaign with a good chance of winning.
The balance of the different units seems reasonable, as is the initial disadvantge the US has, especially in the Pacific, and the beach landing/shipboard supply system is a nice new addition. Combined unit tactics is essential, as is supply and reinforcement.  Overall, I really like it so far, and each scenario reveals a lot of fresh new content compared to the originals . . .one of my favorite hex/turn-based wargames.

Order of Battle: World War II is a very enjoyable turn based WWII strategy game. There is a wide variety of units (land, sea and air) and scenario's for you to battle across. Fighting as the US Marines and launching an assault on Japanese controlled islands is something new and fresh that you don't get the opportunity to do in many games. There is a lot of content in the form of dlc campaigns so you can pick and choose which interests you the most and what you'd like to buy. The details in the graphics are good and the sounds get the job done. Battles can become pretty intense when you think you have the numbers to win but you didn't consider the enemy has aircraft, or they snuck a couple units through the jungle behind you or you happened upon a more fortified position than you expected.
The game has a nice, fairly easy learning curve and a decent tutorial which should teach you all you need to know to jump in and fight,
The biggest issue people have in their reviews is the game is listed as free to play which allows you to try out the first battle from each campaign. As time goes on the developer releases new campaigns and sells them as dlc. People are putting negative reviews expecting the devs to work for free and give away all this content. That's not how any successful developer or business would operate. Having the game set to f2p isn't meant to mislead people, it's meant to offer a few levels for people to try, like a demo and then if people like those levels they can then buy which ever campaigns they want. Obviously they have to charge for all the extra work they've been putting in to make new content for the game. Ignore these reviews unless they actually offer up some critisim of the game.
If you have any interest in a turn based WWII game then this is worth checking out. It is one of, if not the best WWII turn based strategy games on steam. You can try a few battles for free and see if it's something you would enjoy, and if you do enjoy it then keep an eye out because the developer's are actively creating new campaigns.

A Diamond in the rough... just DO NOT play it on PC!  Play it on console!
I first encountered this game on PC. I had heard a lot about it, and gave it a try. I wanted to like it, but the PC version is a mess. Even with the DP Fix patch, this game just isn't stable. Bugs, crashes, compatibilty fixes that randomly quit working, random framrate drops requiring reboot of PC, terrible/broken controller support, etc. It was a miracle i made it chapter 8 on PC. I tried it on 2 PCs, and on both Windows 8.1 and Windows 7 on each PC. On 7, I can't even get the game to boot - on either PC. My main PC isn't weak either, my rig is more than capable of handling the game; so that's not an issue.  Last but not least : there is no hope for an official update in sight. Long ago the delvelopers heard the complaints and basically replied "Oh, we are sorry the Dev team the did the Director's cut butchered the game, it's embarrising. We apologize" .....and left it at that. It's quite unfortunate that such a unique game fell victim to this shady practice.
..So I picked up the Director's Cut on PS3. It runs much more stable, and was enjoyable. The reivews don't lie though: The PS3 version does suffer from a low framrate at times. Sometimes its fine, and sometimes it drops to as low as 20 FPS. But it's still playable, and I'd pick it over PC anyday, having also played the PS3 version to chapter 8 to compare.
Having decided I loved the game after playing the much more stable PS3 version, I found a mint copy of the Xbox 360 version (Original Release, not a Director's cut) for a 10 bucks, and decide to try it too. I was shocked at the difference!!! Hands down, the Xbox 360 verion of this game is the definitive version of Deadly Premonition! It runs best out of all 3 versions, and there are no framerate issues on xbox, you can really see just how badly the port was done after playing the original release.
The things people complained about in the XBox version I just can't agree with. First, people complained of the tank-like controls on the 360 - they are fine. The classic control gives the game the feel it needs, and I find to be much more sharp and responsive, better in battle after practice. The ability to side-step and do an instant 180 turn in classic controls are a must. Second, people complained about the color filters - they are great! If your TV can support XBox 360's Higher/Darker Color Reference/Black levels - the way the color is done in the original version looks brilliant. They give the environment and the character's faces the perfect flares of color right when they need them, giving the game a feel from some older horror movies. Even when the filter aren't running, like in the pause menu you will notice the color is much more vivid - making both PC and PS3 Director's cut verions look washed out. With the exception of the black/gray/white color themed HUD, the Xbox version looks better than the PC and the PS3 version in every way. And if you aren't a whiny spoiled brat, the controls are better suited too, once you learn them.
Play this game before you die; just don't play it on PC, you are just robbing yourself of a great game experience if you do. And if you have an Xbox 360 -  get that version ASAP - it's getting pretty expensive. At the time of this review, a mint copy is going between $40 to $99 USD on ebay (both used and new copies are in that range). So clearly, I can't be the only one that realizes why the 360 version has become so cherished as more people discover this game...

THIS GAME SHOWS MASSIVE POTENTIAL.  I say that a lot, especially about Early Access games, but rarely do I mean it as much as I mean it here.  The graphics are fantastic, the atmosphere is great, the sound is spooky, and the monsters are sufficiently gnarly.  Its "heart" is TOTALLY in the right spot.  But its "head" still needs a great deal of work!  My few attempts at play thus far have consisted of:  "Oh, here I am in a room.  I can pick up a few things - don't know what they do yet - but I can pick them up.  One way out of the room, I'll go that way I guess (though I'm not yet sure why...maybe I just feel like a quiet stroll).  Roam some more corridors.  Take a bit of radiation damage.  Work out that that's what the pills are for.  'Cause let's face it, they couldn't possibly be to counter any damage caused by the monsters, who within mere minutes seem to track me down and corner me at the end of a corridor and kill me more-or-less instantly.  GAME OVER."  Either this, or I step into some electricity...which zaps me for many seconds and maybe attracts monsters, but doesn't do any damage in and of itself...or failing all of that, I might step into some Alien-esque green gunk dripping from the ceiling and accumulating on the floor, which gets my foot stuck and promptly leads to me being killed by something unseen before my game unceremoniously crashes.

Let's see, what else?  Well, unlike the games I mentioned earlier- and Outlast, to name at least one other - you don't seem to be able to hide in lockers or under beds; indeed, I always seem to end up in situations where I'm not sure where to hide at all.  And considering that I don't even know WHY I'm walking around in corridors teeming with monstrous beasties in the first place, I can only conclude that my character has watched all their space-friends die horrible deaths, and is thusly resigned to SUICIDE.  I also don't know, for the life of me, how you actually "outrun" monsters, as they're always two steps behind and, like I say, you can't seem to properly "hide" anywhere even if you DID manage to outrun them for all of three seconds.  I'll also be dang-♥♥♥♥ed if I know what all the stats are for when you "create" a "character".  Though there is one small bonus for all the lonely male gamers out there:  If you play a female character, you can look down in first-person and see your own BOOBIES.  I guess that's what the devs meant by the sentence I quoted from the Store page up above.  After all, if you're gonna run around a spaceship with no purpose in mind other than to git yo'self kilt, you might as well do it with half yo' boobies hangin' outta yo' jumpsuit.  I know that's what I'D do, if was a sexy, big-boobied chick stuck on a spacecraft with rampaging aliens.  One, two, three, sing along wit' me:  "My milkshake brings all the monsters to tha yard..."
Look, with a bit of work - okay, a LOT of work - this game could end up being EASILY worth the ten dollar asking price.  But right now, unless you're like me and you just like wasting your money so that you can write reviews in which you whine about unfinished games with the words "Early Access" in the title, you may want to be SMART and wait to see if they actually knock this into some sort of shape.  All we have here, right now, is a quick run-around inside the corridors of a spooky spaceship before you get space-smushed.  If they manage to add a PLOT to all of this, well, we may just have a winner on our hands...
Verdict (for now):  6/10.

It's hard to review games like this. Idle games aren't so much games you sit down and play, but another task you do in the background that you click away from after you're done clicking 1-5 times. Adventure Capitalist is another incremental game that made the move from flash game, to phone game, to desktop. This means the game is not large, demanding, or very complex.
Gameplay: The gameplay is pretty straightforward. You click the lemonade stand a few times until you have enough money to purchase the next business or a manager. The manager will run the business for you. You have to keep buying more to make more money so you can buy more things to make you money. It's not something you do for fun, it's something you play out of curiosity and maybe you'll end up sticking with it. It's a formula that works well, but it's not something that you're going to claim is "fun"
Graphics/Visual Experience: The game is quite literally a series of menus.
Sound: There is a single track for each planet (well, the moon isn't a planet, but you catch my drift). This gets old after a very short period of time, but it's easy to mute.
Replayability: Pretty high, actually. As before, it's not particularly "fun," but you'll probably find yourself playing it for a few sessions more than you expected for some reason that neither you nor I understand.
How it Runs: If your computer can't run this game it probably can't read this review either.

From Dust is a very neat puzzle/simulation game where you manipulate earth, lava, and water to shape the land, making it livable for the tribe you're protecting.
The engine driving this game is really neat. As you tame the wilderness, rivers will change paths, hills will erode, and the lava shapes new land. It's definitely fun to play with, and it's very rewarding to see a ruthless wasteland turn into a peaceful grove once you correctly divert the hazards.
This game's weak point is everything else (except the game's mythos; that's cool too). The story is way too short (beat it 100% in <3 hrs) and rather easy. With such cool tools to use, I really wanted more of the sandbox-type story levels, to really show off what I could do. Huge disappointment. There's a challenge mode, which I beat in about another 3 hours.
I'd still recommend this game at $15, but be prepared for the short length. Also watch out for Ubisoft's wicked always-online DRM. Definitely get it if it's on sale.

GemCraft: Chasing Shadows is both a great tower defense game and time killer. It offers a lot of flexibility in how you want to tailor the challenge - make it easy as pie, or brutally difficult, with a set of unique constraints to pick and choose from (similar to Bastion's idols). And you have plenty of tools at your disposal - different types of spells, structures and skills so you can customize your defense to suit the situation best, as well as an upgrade system that rewards careful utilization. Later levels really make you think through your strategy and approach, and will punish careless players.
I've played dozens of hours of GemCraft chapters One and Zero, and feel that Chasing Shadows is an improvement on both games, so if you enjoyed the older titles and were considering this one, go for it.

Don't get me wrong, this game took forever and a day to come out. but the game is a well polished enhanced version of the AG version of the game.  In addition, it runs so much more smoothly than the Flash version does (assuming your computer can handle it), which is reason enough to purchase the game (even for a second time).  Well worth the money (and wait) the first time, well worth the money (and wait) the second time.

I will update this with a more in depth review a bit later, but for now, I am immeasurably surprised by this game. And that is pleasantly surprised. Gemcraft - Chasing Shadows has far more depth and strategy than your average tower defense game. Do not be fooled by the simple graphics - Gemcraft has a ton of game options and strong strategy content. HIGHLY RECOMMENDED.

Even though it's a really old game now, I believe it's still one of the strength of the game just like before. What I mean is that, not that it's a superbe game by the 2017 standards but it still looks very good! I mean you won't be like disgusted by watching your screen, they look really decent and they kind of have their own charm. The textures are okay, but most importantly the animations are sometimes better than some recent Total War games. For exemple when two units charge on each other there is really a clash happenning between them, you can feel it, I do not know how to explain it but it really does look like a real fight, you can see the swords swinging and clashing on the shields! In Empire Total War on the contrary when two unites charged, they were "sliding" on each other and it just looked broken and completely unfinished!
And you also don't have the problem of sprites that made look your units disgusting from a certain distance (a distance way too short in my opinion) in ETW or R2TW.
During sieges the cities look pretty good too, huge cities can be really impressive and they are a ton of fun to siege!
Overall it's more than decent. If you play it today I believe you won't feel like you're playing such an old game concerning the graphics.
I don't really know what to say about this. I mean it's a classic Total War where you basically have a map where you decide which direction your empire will take, where will your armies go, what buildings you will build in your cities, diplomacy and all that classic♥♥♥♥♥♥we see in all Total Wars. However it's not THAT great here compared to other Total Wars, it feels much more simpler compared to Shogun 2 or Empire for exemple, those are much more complicated (not as EU IV tho) and there are many things you have to take care of at each turn. There you feel like you really are on the top of an empire when on the other hand in Medieval II it feels like you could just take 1 minute before ending your turn and that wouldn't have any important consequences on your campaign if you made a bad decision. I wish there was a feudal system implemanted and all but hopefully one day we will see a Medieval III with that part being fixed.
Now of course there were bugs when it came out and they still are there, nothing really striking (usually thoses bugs are things like one soldier freezing or a unit not obeying directly to your order) actually it's just that they kill the immersion from time to time but it's okay, still better than Empire or Rome 2 if you ask me. But the biggest problem here is the AI. As always in those games, they really are not that clever, especially during siege battles where they almost don't react if you don't tease them in the first place. I recommend you to play on the highest difficulty to get a better experience out of this game.
By the way note that if you never played any Total War game or just any grand strantegy game then I believe M2TW is a great choice to start!
Well it's endless I'd say, you could play this for hundreds or even thousands of hours if you are a die-hard fan of the genre and the Medieval time period. There are tons of maps to play on, from the New World where you can play as the conquistadors to Lithuania where you, as a teutonic knight will burn some pagans in the name of the cross and then you may also take a ship to go to the Holy Land where you will deus vult and remove some filthy kebabs! There are tons of factions to play with, always new units and new aeras to discover and conquer etc... And I didn't even told you about the mods! Just play the Third Age mod and lead the orcs to the gates of Minas Tirith or choose the side of the light and beat Sauron in a real time battle... I'm telling you, you will never get bored of this.
Oh and of course if you are looking for some challenges there is still the multiplayer mode that allows you to play with real kings & queens from everywhere in the known world!
Just check it on YouTube, it's perfect, catches well the medieval vibe and you will feel invincible when the drums will beat during tough moments of a battle. I personally adore the soundtracks from the Crusades Campaign. Check it out and see (hear?) by yourself.
All in all Medieval 2 Total War is definitely a great game, probably one of the best, if not THE best Total War game (just check the amount of fans of this game that are dying for a Medieval III right now) out there. A must-have in your Steam library, especially for the price you can get it for during sales!

Well, I have played this game for a number of hours. And unlike many people who writes these reviews, I have the game beaten. The game is fun if you are looking for action topped off with some horror elements. What I will say is that this game is far from survival horror. Basically, this game is a spirtual sucessor to Resident Evil 4 as far as gameplay; however, the game has more survival horror elements than Resident Evil 4 but it has a long way to go before it goes back to the roots. Now on to the game itself.
The game basically takes place between Resident Evil 4 and Resident Evil 5 (prologue as well) making it in movie terms a interquel (a story that is set between the original and the sequel). As far as the story goes, the plot is basically revolved around Jill Valentine and her new partner Paker investigating a ship named the Queen's Zinoba (sorry if I spelled it wrong). There are many twists and turns through out the story so, I won't say any more.
On to the gameplay, I think the gameplay is smooth and responsive at 60 fps. The only issue I have is the game forcing you to have a partner 95% of the time. I know back during the Resident Evil trilogy that you had AI partners but I feel like getting rid of AI partners for the most part would make the game have more tension. Also, I didn't like the fact that there was a whole lot of ammo to be found. But the worst part is the scanner. I think this is a device for causals would can't seem to find items.
Overall, the game is a fun time for people who likes action with some survival horror elements mixed in. The old hardcore Resident Evil fans who want a game like the Resident Evil trilogy will not find what you are looking for here. So, let me summarize again. This game is a must buy for action fans while this game is a skip for surivival horror fans that want a challenge.

Resident Evil Revelations is the most recent RE game that, in my opinion, comes closest to the classic survival horror RE fans love.
I could do a massive in depth review, but I'll keep it short...I'll mention the atmosphere and the gameplay, though.
The atmosphere is done quite well in this game.
Most of this game is set on an abandoned cruise ship crawling with horrors. One of the strengths of RE is that they are able to bring any setting into the horror, and here it is no exception. I found myself genuinely creeped out by the many things on this haunted ship.
However I wish they didn't change settings during the course of the game. Because of flashbacks and attempts to advance the plot, the game sometimes changes its setting to a city on fire or a mountain range, which aren't quite as scary. But it's a fairly minor quibble, as this game still manages to overal creep the player out.
The gameplay is reminiscient of RE4 and RE5, with lots of shooting abound. Crosscode is a game that I decided not to back initially, because I thought the project had unrealistic goals.  Upon revisiting it in the demo and pre-purchasing, I think I can safely say that I was not only wrong, but that is the only project I even remotely regret not backing.  This is what I think an indie game should aspire to be: a passion project that has standout and unexpected production quality.
Describing Cross Code is difficult, because almost no one has played any of the games it most resembles.  Alundra, Terranigma, Secret of Mana, Shining Soul, Robotron, Gunman Clive... probably the closest well-known parallel is Zelda, and this ain't no Zelda.  In short, it's a top-down fast-paced action game with SNES era style graphics, "phantasy star" sort of character design, large puzzle sections and some quality of life improvements from modern games.  I'd say the closest new game in function is Hyper Light Drifter (which is quite similar), although the two games greatly differ in tone with Crosscode being much much lighter and transparent about its premise, but much less stylish and ambitious in that regard.
I don't want to just gush about this, so here's what's bad:  Flavor-wise the story and setting are busy and inane: People are playing an MMO as hard-light beings on a real-life alien planet, and you're injected into things as an outsider with likely special capabilities as well as amnesia and limited speech capabilities.  Some people are obstensibly people in the cities, so it's impossible to figure out what are questgiving ai characters and inhabitants of the cities which is fairly irresponsible given the MMO players are basically operating killing machines.  It's dumb, but it lets the game be a game and do whatever it really wants to.  In line with this, some of the characters are kind of annoying as well, in particular anyone who can't help but mix in words from other languages in nearly every single line of dialogue.
In addition, puzzle-and-action hybrids often have a lot of issues regarding their audience.  Although I for one love the mix, you force action lovers to do puzzles in order to play more of what they like and vice versa, and the game is linear.  In particular, the dungeons are very very puzzle heavy almost to the point of exhaustion, and the rest of the game is somewhat light on them (although the mix is worked in much better as of the latest overworld area).
Somewhere between bad and good is the music.  Most of the tracks are forgettable and a few are very unappealing short-loop midi-quality stuff.  On the other hand, the newest town theme and especially the boss theme are fantastic.  When you fight a tough opponent you will find no fault in the music for getting you psyched, and that's really what I'm looking for in this type of game.
Speaking of bosses, let's get into the good stuff.  The bosses themselves are pure pixel porn and must have been ages to animate given their size, and they are a joy to fight with their gimmicks and weaknesses- and ability to sometimes cover up their weakness or turn your exploitation of it back at you.  In particular, the duel against a foe of similar abilities is a blast because his AI is shockingly adept for this kind of game.  In addition, certain special encounters against regular enemies are made much more interesting with strange arenas or mixes of opponents.  Healing is tricky due to a delay but very helpful in some particularly deadly fights.  It's obvious that in most cases, these guys know encounter design inside and out.
Part of what makes bosses so fun to fight are the controls.  I cringed when I saw that the bumpers were going to be the main attack and dodge buttons, and that the right stick was used to aim shots, but actually it works very well on a 360 controller.  The bumpers depress pretty quick, allowing you to really tear into stuff- but it is tiring over a long play session.  Everything is fluid, from dodging to attacks to blocking to using special moves.  I didn't suffer any slowdown at all compared to Hyper Light Drifter, not that my computer is top of the line.  Pretty exceptional, really.
On the subject of slowdown, in the overworld areas it's pretty amazing just how much stuff is going on.  Despite the goofy setting, the illusions they use to convey a living world (mainly resting avatars and huge number of "travelling" players) are really good without interfering at all.  The towns feel populated, which is rare, and the trading mechanic supplements the cash shops really nicely in my opinion.  You can also jump all over the place, even if it's always going to be tricky figuring out elevation in a 2D game.  Still, you can jump on just about everything in a very golden-sun style of conspicuous parkour in order to find out-of-reach treasures, and for me that was just a joy.
Almost exclusively the puzzles are excellent.  They are unfortunately linear, but make up for it by teaching you constantly.  Each dungeon so far has two gimmicks that each engage differently with most or all of your abilities you'll have up to that point, and serve a purpose in fights.   Many puzzle rooms also contain additional goodies for going the extra mile as well.  A few of them, however, require fairly precise timing or aim (or both) and I can see some players getting stuck.
In short, I think this is a standout title and am greatly looking forward to its release- and would encourage anyone not disinterested due to the style or other negatives to do the same.

Unlike most Early Access games on Steam, this project is full of amazing gameplay mechanics and beautiful pixel art- all of which can be followed on their regular Twitch Dev livestream. This genuinely is one of the best "retro" games on Steam. If you enjoyed old 2D games action/RPGs like Secret of Mana and the like, then you'd get a kick out of CrossCode.
Brilliantly done pixel art animations that display the world and battles with great detail. Somewhere between classic SNES era sprites and modern "retro" popular releases. And with new content arriving semi-frequently, they often go over old art and revamp them with even higher quality- also giving a reason to go back through the game to appreciate its assets.
Moves like that of an SNES era action RPG, but more fluent with it's Controller Support, dodge/dash system and 8-way run freedom. Basically how you'd expect a 2D overhead Kingdom Hearts to perform.
What you'd expect of a fantasy sci-fi "retro" game, well performed music again like those of the SNES and Genesis era. The music fits each scenario well, and again like Kingdom Hearts, flows nicely in-and-out of Exploration and Battle to continuously give an action packed experience all 'round.
Continuously added content since the game is still in development but with plenty of material to enjoy already, from free-exploration secrets treasures and powerups hidden throughout the world, challenging quests from NPCs, and very well designed Dungeons that offer a great challenge for both battle and puzzle lovers- the kind that you'd expect in the great 2D Zelda releases.
With tons of content being added regularly, buying this game to support the progress of the immediately gripping sci-fi fantasy world story is one of the best things you can do- and you won't regret it.

This game has become my favorite game of all time after finishing the main story once. Now I played through the story three times, have about 200h of play time and I still want to play this game even more.
One thing that makes NieR:Automata this great, is the story with its characters.
The story is told in such a different way compared to most other games and it works so well and is such a fresh and unique experience. So I played every game, that was directed by Yoko Taro and I only found this kind of experience in games that were directed by him. While the other games of him had a great story, the gameplay always was kinda repetitive and boring, but I played them nonetheless.
So this time to make the gameplay better, they decided to team up with PlatinumGames. The result is a fluid, beautiful, stylish, thrilling and rewarding hack & slash gameplay with bullet hell elements that even after 200h never got boring and always felt exiting to play. The game has different weapon types with different combos, that can be combined in many different ways. The game also offers many enemy types in different variations, so you need to adapt your fighting style to each situation. After playing other games from PlatinumGames the combat is closest to Bayonetta but also reminds me of DMC, which is from Ninja Theory.
The soundtrack, thanks to Keiichi Okabe, is also phenomenal and so good implemented into the game that I instantly bought them. It also blends in perfectly with the beautiful open world, which seems a bit small, but is nearly perfectly designed and has many things to discover.
Throughout the story there are many different side quests, which are from a gameplay perspective not the most innovative, but each one flashes out the world and the characters a bit more.
Another thing that makes this game great is that everything makes sense in the games universe. From the skill system, to the saving and also the respawning. Other things like the pod and his programs or the red glow in the eyes of the enemies when they attack can't be explained by just playing NieR:Automata but are explained by digging deeper into the universe. I really appreciate how much fervor they put in every part of the game.
Also even if you haven't played the first Nier or the other "prequels", like me at first, you wont feel overwhelmed or like you were missing something from the story. This makes the game also perfect for newcomers to the franchise.
The only bad thing I can say about this game is that many people have experienced crashed and other bugs. At the time there is no official patch for this, but there is one in the steam community (named FAR), which fixes various resolution bugs.
For me the game only crashed a few times, which isn't nice, but wasn't a big problem for me, because the game lets you save quickly in many areas.
Another bug that I faced, was that the game didn't start in full screen mode and also only changed to full screen after many attempts.
The last thing I encountered was that the game didn't saved my custom control settings and every time I started the game I needed to change them again. I also didn't think this was a big problem because even navigating through the menus feels nice. Installing FAR helped to resolve the last two bugs.
Concluding I can only recommend this game to every player. Even if you don't end up liking the game after you played it, in my opinion everyone should have at least tried this game.
After playing this game I will at least give every game by Yoko Taro and PlatinumGames a try.

Great game, but I can't recommend it to the current teenage-generation.
Wurm Online / Unlimited was developed by Minecraft creator Markus Persson (Notch), back in 2003 and it was released in 2006. Back then, the indie game developer scene was almost non existent, let alone having an indie team creating an MMO.
Wurm Online was incredibly advanced for it's time, both, from the perspective of the technology as well as the concept of freedom it gives the players. There still isn't an MMO that gives you as much freedom as this game does.
Over the past 14 years, the gaming industry exploded, and the standards of games have increased drastically. New standards have been set in the gaming industry, not just graphic wise, but also user interface wise. Wurm Online is unfortunately part of the older generation games, that make use of a user interface which is no longer considered user friendly. That is why the current younger-generations of gamers, as in, anyone between the age of 8 to 20, will most likely struggle getting used to this game.
So, before you play this game, or even judge this game, realize that this game was developed back in 2003 by indie developers.

Wurm Unlimited - a game not made for modern Gaming community.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
About me:
There are times I just love realistic games who go far into detail.
Played wurm online since release, switched to Wurm ultimate back last year.
80 Hours on Wurm Ultimate - Thousands on the old game.
In this review I'll try and counter negative reviews for this game and add some arguments of my own, why you should or shouldnt play Wurm Unlimited. Why am I doing this? - Because i see hundreds of bad reviews for this game with a playtime of 2 or less hours and arguments about the game being bad, which could have been solved by just opening the game options or looking at the many Steam guides.
EDIT: 11.10.2017 WURM ULTIMATE IS Available at Humble Bundle right now (13 Days left) so if you are unsure you can get it there for a lower price!
Lets start:
Basics:
--------
Wurm is a server based Game and thus you have to play locally with friends ( via tunneling software or lan) on your own pc or you choose from the server list.
Either way you'll need some form of storing your progress. Also if you think of playing it casually you will find your progress is very slow. You WILL have do dedicate some time to it if you want to see fast progress.
That being said, you can, ofcourse play it casually but keep in mind, you will need a few hours to settle in.
WURM IS A HARD GAME WITH A STEEP LEARNING CURVE.
Every action in game requires thought and YOUR ACTUAL INPUT (like in real life)
(you cant bang 20 nails in a wall at once. You have to repeat the action 20 times!)
If you plan to master it on your own, tend to the wiki /steam guides often!
There are two game modes.
Survival: You start out with some basic equipment and all skills on twenty.
Creative: You start out with nothing and all skills on 1.
PVP is possible on both game modes!
Then there are Kingdoms, but only if you are on a server with multiple maps.
Kingdoms are like factions. Normally you can’t attack one of your own Kingdom, except you don’t care being an outlaw 😉
Graphics:
-----------
This is a game from 2006- Its sole purpose on being back is not to reel new players in (thats the job of us core players i guess) but to enable Players to play the game on a modern PC without any problems.
Wurm does NOT rely on graphics. Wurm relies on:
Wurm is made to last you a lifetime. Not to shortly arouse you with nice graphics. There are Texturepacks though.
Also, In my opinion you are a bad Gamer if a game is not for you just because graphics. I get graphics are important, but there is more to games ;)

True. But do you really need it?
Movement and Controls
--------------------------
You can set a ton of Keybinds! There is even a preset for mouselook (Spacebar). you can even bind custom actions to Keys via ingame Console! No need to drag with left click.
While Wurm does a bad job at explaining to you what it can do, with a little research it ALLOWS you to do literally ANYTHING Controls wise.
Wurm often gets compared to Minecraft (probably because notch was on the Team ;) ) But it is waaaay apart from left klick - destroy, right click - place. Which makes sense if you have a game being so detailed like Wurm.

The contextual menus are actually really helpful to not misclick somewhere else and show you clearly what you can do with the targeted entity UNDER INCLUSION which Items you have equipped. ( you will find that you can cut trees with a sword as well with an axe ;) )
Fighting
----------
Fighting in Wurm is as detailled and involved as everything else in this game.
Fighting has two modes, Automatic and Manual. Both have their benefits:
Automatic mode always tries to choose the best option for you.
Manual mode lets you choose the following: all in realtime
If you fight manually and your opponent adjusts its stance you have to counter act!
And still, if your "Knives" Skill is High but your "Fighting" Skill is low, you will most likely loose even against a boar.
I recommend crafting a training dummy first and using it quite some time before engaging any fights.
Crafting
---------
You have a detailed crafting menu with two slots.
You add a knife and a log -> You carve a stick -> you carve parts. -> you change the knife against a hammer -> you craft an axle it appears in your inventory.
All crafting can be done menu based with right clicks straight from the inventory! (The menu is more comfortable though 😉 )
Skills
---------
As stated before, there is a Skill for literally everything you can do. Supporting server communities allowing for jobs like butcher or blacksmith.
If your “Animal Husbandry” and Taming Skills are low, you can RIDE a horse, but the Horse still can have a mind of its own 😉
You have a Skill for swimming and an endurance bar to watch out for as well. In the beginning (and with a filled inventory) you wont swim very far without beginning to drown.
Drowning hurts you which in turn slows you.
Differences Wurm Online / Ultimate.
----------------------------------------------------
Wurm online was the classic title with online servers. Only a few of them remain.
Wurm unlimited lets you host your own server with your own server rules (if you want to) and is available at quite a few hosting agencies. (like citadel servers)
Conclusion:
----------------
If you are looking for a near realistic game which doesn’t take your hand like the modern AAA titles but really is demanding but rewarding,
If you are looking for a game with potentially hours of fun and enjoyment and a sense of proudness when you finally got your house finished after 20 in game hours,
If you are looking for a game with player involved crafting and building,
IF YOU KNOW SOMEONE WITH A SERVER OR DON’T MIND USING TUNGLE/HAMACHI,
YES definitely go for Wurm Ultimate! Youll probably die often until you get the hang of it (even with only passive mobs) But that’s part of the fun!
If you don’t like complexity, or a steep vast learning curve
If you don’t like that every action you want to do in game has to be actually ordered by you,
If you don’t like dealing with wikis and searching for info to learn about configuration and gameplay
NO don’t go for Wurm Ultimate yet. Look up some videos on Youtube and decide if its for you or not.

Hello Strategy Gamers:
If you love (or loved) Axis & Allies then you've found the perfect video game incarnation in Order of Battle by the good people (I assume) at Slitherine. I will return to the board game theme later in the review. But first....
Order of Battle is an extremely well-designed and satisfying strategy game with a tremendous attention to detail, and YET you can understand the rules and play a campaign in a short period of time. For me, strategy games like "Hearts of Iron IV" are slightly overwhelming in terms of deciphering the volume of information and rule sets. And, frankly, I like to see the small animated battles between tiny Marine divisons and tanks, or air and naval battles, or the amphibuous invasions which are a core part of the Pacific campaign. I'm a child at heart, what can I tell you...
I was also surprised this game still has "mixed reviews" and frankly the negative reviews start by complaining that the game is not "free."  Order of Battle is not free2play, but it does offer a solid demo of the "boot camp tutorial" and lets you sample the many diverse and unique campaigns. You'll have an excellent sense if the game appeals to you by trying the free content... After that, I spent $10.00 on the Marine campaign in the Pacific and realized how much this game satisfies that "Axis & Allies" itch, but without having to round up 2-3 friends and play straight for 6 hours and wonder if you hate one of your friends for being sneaky.
I have actively searched for (and played) many online versions of Axis & Allies for a long, long time. And Order of Battle is the closest approximation to that you'll find... I see a lot of the reviews are negative because 'it isn't a free game but a demo'. Hmm, semantics here I think. After all I doubt these people would give a negative review of a demo because 'I have to buy the whole game!' You get a lot more than a normal demo too. That said it would be good if the free part gave you limited access to the editor.
What you get for free is actually very good value for the time spent downloading with the bootcamp campaign (not just a 'move the mouse, click, well done mission over tutorial either) and the first level of every campaign that gets released. They all play differently and give a good idea of the mechanics.
It isn't a highly sophisticated operational level war sim but it gives a good account of itself and you have to use your troops well to avoid a sudden, sound, thrashing. The AI looks to exploit any potential opportunities to outflank and surround you or to target your weak link, though it is also has many dumb moments - usually when it outstretches itself.
The total cost is daunting, yes it is too high, but the quality is there and the four Pacific war campaigns (to date) do come in a bundle so the total DLC cost isn't what you see below (making further negative reviews invalid). Hopefully the European packs will get bundles in the future when further campaigns are released.
I've picked up the US Marines to see if I enjoy a whole campaign and get replayability from it (review incoming), I suspect I will get the rest of the Pacific bundle when I am done.

Magicite was a blast, I can't deny that, I could try to give it 1,000 thumbs downs, but I still won't deny that I had a ton of fun playing this game, alone or with friends. Despite this, I have a very good reason for giving this game the thumbs down. I see lots of other negitive reviews based around the game being difficult, unpolished, buggy, or hard to set up multiplayer, game was abandoned, and other similar complaints. These people are right... sort of.
First off, yes, game is hard. It was inspired by rougue-likes and was meant to be a challange, and frankly, was why I bought it in the first place. Many folks out there love a good challange, and Magicite I feel actually pulled it off fairly well. It was hard but most every death was my fault in some way or another. With practice came much fewer deaths and actually a consistant win rate.
Game is full of bugs. Yes, very much so. This is one of the reasons I can't recommend this game. Before the final update, there were bugs, however there were very few that actually broke the playthough, and singleplayer was even better. As a programmer myself, I almost found them to be entertaining and finding how to avoid some of the multiplayer bugs was like another obsticle. Then roles out the final update, and along with it, the reason I won't play this game anymore. I set up a LAN to play this game (and by the way, for people complaining about multiplayer, all you need is one friend who can port-forward and multiplayer sets up without an issue), and in two seperate multi-hour sessions (with not bad players mind you) we never even made it close to the end of this game. All due to crashes or something weird happening and our session just ending for no reason. With little hope that the dev would return and fix these issues, I stopped playing for good.
Dev abandoned the game. Yes and no. Technically the dev finished this game in his own mind, stating that this was the last patch and he was done. That does not make this game complete, as my complaint on multiplayer should have made clear. The dev did not leave, he quit. This is the other reason why I can't recommend this game. I bought this game in a playable state, the dev came in, broke it, and then said he was done for good, that he was moving to his other games. With a move like that, I'll never try his other games (though some of them I would really, truely love to play) because I don't want to, and will never, support a quitter. Who knows if he will do the same thing with his other games? I certainly don't want to be the sucker that finds out the hard way.
So tl,dr; Game gets a negative review because the dev came in, broke the game with a bad update, and said he was done for good.
Really have missed playing this one though, here's to hoping the dev comes back and fixes it. The day he does will be a happy day in my entire friend group.

GemCraft is a series that has been around since 2008, but this is my first experience with it. The tower defence genre is possibly me favourite genre beside RPG, so I was excited to see that the series is classed as one of the best in the genre. It works exactly like any other tower defence, the enemies have a set path to follow and you build your defense around said path. What I found to be very interested with GemCraft is, that your resource supply that you use to build your defences, is also actually your health pool of the crystal you are defending. As you kill the enemies, you gain mana, and in turn this increases your crystal's health, I found that to be an excellent feature and one that I had not seen before.
No, the graphics aren't anything to rave about, but you don't need anything fancy for this type of game, all of the enemy sprites are nicely drawn as well as the environments you play in.  Each stage has a different path layout, along with different features on each map, such as gate locks, which have to be destroyed by your towers in so many turns before they automatically wipe your crystal out, this along with plenty other different scenarios (not all negative ones, some actually help you) make it that little bit more interesting to play.
I found the difficulty/learning curve to be quite high here, the first two or three levels are really quite easy, but as soon as you start hitting level 4+, bearing in mind that there is 190 levels in this game, the difficulty really starts to pick up. I'm on about level 30 and each stage takes me a good four or five attempt before I manage to work out the best way to complete it.
Given the amount of levels, achievements and replayability in GemCraft, I can easily say that there is well over a hundred hours of content if you want to put the effort in. That is an amazing amount of gameplay for a game like this.
Tower defence lovers will almost certainly love GemCraft, and if this is a genre you always wanted to try, GemCraft is one of the classics that will keep you entertained for hours on end.

Dispatcher is a first person horror rpg by Civil Savages, where you are stuck on an abandoned spacecraft with an alien... sound familiar? Well, because it's the plot of 'Alien' and the recent title 'Alien Isolation'. Not that this is a bad thing, the idea of creating suspense with a secluded area and a few enemies creates magnificent tension. Which is done extremely well here.
Using the Unreal 4 Engine, Civil Savages creates a very immersive and beautiful looking game. The mechanics are fairly typical of this genre. First person control, pills to heal, batteries for your flashlight, and interactable objects. However, you don't come to a first person horror game for deep crazy mechanics. You come for the exploration, the jump scares, and the challenge of getting out alive. One thing that stands out as different for the gameplay is the rpg mechanics. Which are implemented in an almost roguelike way.
The first thing you do before playing is create a character and choose between 7 (5 available at start, one unlockable) careers. It's basically who are you on this ship. So you can be a scientist, signalman, engineer, etc. Each class has their own starting stats (Energy, Reaction, Stamina, Immunity, Quiet) that affect your character. After choosing your career, you then must choose from  12 different biographies. These are what you were before you were assigned to the ship. Each of these give you character a little flavor, but also change stats and add static effects in some cases. As you go through each playthrough you will earn money which can then be spent to increase each of the individual stats. Making the game have that roguelike feel.
Being in early access there are some bugs I ran into, like falling through the world in the practice area. So be prepared for optimization coming down the pipeline from Civil Savages. They are also planning to add a co-op mode to the game at some point this summer which I find to be an exciting take on the first person horror genre.
Overall, Dispatcher is on it's way to being a strong competitor in the horror market, with great graphics, atmosphere, and character, you'll be sure to have your share of scares.

I've played 11+ hours of this game so far. It has some problems, but it's held my attention for short, one hour bursts. This is a small-scale FPS (4x4, either PvP or PvBots) with zany™ design elements reminiscent of Team Fortress 2.
At its heart, it's a cartoonish, frenetic, gore-filled, FPS. You build some weapons and then shoot enemies. Over time, you accrue experience not just for your character, but also the parts of the weapons you've been using. That's right, your
and
goes up levels too. The catch: you have to spend Blutes (the in-game currency that you always earn alongside XP) in order to unlock that new level you've been working toward.
Currently, there aren't a lot of maps, and only standard playmodes. There are three character models available (to start) and a whole bunch of customizable bits of clothing in the Store. I'm an active SOE subscriber and have purchased station cash in the past. I'm not opposed to virtual purchases, but compared to every other game-purchase experience I've had, their costs feel high. I have no interest in either the virtual clothing options or the XP/Blute boosters, though that could change.
FPS fans that are accustomed to TF2-levels of variety may be disappointed. But problematic though it is, you can craft and evolve your weapons in a way that's quite new. There's some interesting promise in here, but games like these don't have very long to turn a profit.
All that said, I've had quite a blast so far and may yet drop some cash to show my support, even if I'm not enthused with their pricing structure. :)

This game is awesome. Stuck on a ship (great claustrophobic environment checked) after being misled, Jill Valentine and her partner Parker has to survive the horror that awaits them, and uncover a greater conspiracy.
The story is great with everyone's favourite Jill Valentine returning as the lead cast, comedic moments with the other supporting BSAA members, and a twist in the story. However, it is pretty straight forward, and gets boring by my 3rd play through, more notes could be left around to explain the backgrounds and motivations of the other characters.
Gameplay is not much different from Resident Evil 5 and 6, with the 3rd person shooting angles. However, no more confusing inventory system! Instead your weapons and upgrades will be stored in the classic storage box, and you can only take 3 weapons at a time. Key items does not take up inventory space, so there is no 'inventory puzzles' to solve.
The previous 2 Resident Evil games brough more action than horror to the storyline, which is expected as Chris and Leon are now part of anti-bioterriorism forces (who still expects them to be afraid of zombies?). However, the slower pace of RE: Revelations. limited ammo, narrow pathways filled with 'zombies' blocking your exit, and a 'stalker' type monster that refuse to die, managed to create the perfect creepy environment on board a ship. At times Jill will have to wander off alone and makes you wonder why her partner is such a wuss despite being a big man (not that he's of much use anyways). Decisions have to be made over fight or flight, especially on your first play through on normal or insane mode, although for those gamers who have to kill everything, the genesis scanner will help to uncover additional bullets. Do note that flash back and side missions which helps explain the story are more action oriented. Overall, i find the game having a good balance of horror and action done through great graphics, environmental sounds, back ground music, and dialogues. Afterall, as our favourite characters matures and become adapt at handling such situations, it is impossible for Resident Evil to have a pure horror storyline that makes logical sense.
Lastly, there is the raid mode which can be insanely difficult especially if you're an achievement hunter. This mode allows you to play RE: Revelations like a classic arcade shooter with weapons, trophies and high score to collect, and add on countless hours of fun for those up to the challenge.
In conclusion, RE: Revelations is worth spending time on. However, the steam sales ranging from 50-75% would be worth waiting for as the full retail price of S$62 is slightly costly. Whether you are a Resident Evil fan or not this game will surely not disappoint.

These games typically aren't my cup of tea, though I've always looked at them with a sort of envy. I tried GalCiv II after I read a fantastic piece by Tom Francis, but couldn't really get into it. Stellaris seemed to break the mold for me. The game appears overwhelming at first, but I found it really fun to create a society, shaping its ethics, its form of government, the species that comprised it. From expanding my pacifist, egalitarian fennec foxes out into the stars to dealing with angry, warlike neighbors by way of alleigance and strategic saber-rattling felt like the stakes were real. Because I'd made a society that I might actually want to live in, protecting it, and its people's way of life, felt worthwhile.
You also feel deeply involved in your society due to "Factions," representatives of your society's ethics that vie for influence over your populace. You keep these factions happy by pursuing goals related to those ethics. Some seem a little far-fetched: For example, my pacifist ethic got me an organization dedicated to accumulating wealth. I guess the creators never heard of the military-industrial complex. Nevertheless, keeping these factions happy made me feel active in my society's growth as it spanned the cosmos.
This game comes with surprisingly deep lore events, which you mostly discover through your 'science ships' which travel the cosmos and survey different star systems for useful materials. Occasionally they come up on something interesting--artifacts of another alien civilization, crystals that seem to be alive, space whales--in one instance, a religious icon representing gods of death and malice from deep in my species' past was found floating in a distant star system. I followed a trail of seemingly supernatural clues (in an otherwise science fiction setting) to find that the gods of that religion may have been aliens from the past. (Giorgio would be proud.) This lore event stood out to me, not just because of the change of setting, but because the tone felt grave in a cosmic sense, that I might find something horrible at the end of that road. In the end, I chose to cover-up their existence.
To give you an idea about how immersive this game can get: There's an option to increase your citizen's standard of living  and ergo, their happiness. My citizens are already pretty darn happy--they have planets that they're well-adjusted to, all their factions are satisfied, there's hardly any war, there's plenty of food to go around, the government's stable--but I keep at the very expensive "Utopian Abundance" option because I actually want these fox people, who I only see as pinpoints of light on a globe, to have the best lives they can possibly have. I think when a game is capable of getting you that invested, it's done something right.

Unlike most Early Access games on Steam, this project is full of amazing gameplay mechanics and beautiful pixel art- all of which can be followed on their regular Twitch Dev livestream. This genuinely is one of the best "retro" games on Steam. If you enjoyed old 2D games action/RPGs like Secret of Mana and the like, then you'd get a kick out of CrossCode.
Brilliantly done pixel art animations that display the world and battles with great detail. Somewhere between classic SNES era sprites and modern "retro" popular releases. And with new content arriving semi-frequently, they often go over old art and revamp them with even higher quality- also giving a reason to go back through the game to appreciate its assets.
Moves like that of an SNES era action RPG, but more fluent with it's Controller Support, dodge/dash system and 8-way run freedom. Basically how you'd expect a 2D overhead Kingdom Hearts to perform.
What you'd expect of a fantasy sci-fi "retro" game, well performed music again like those of the SNES and Genesis era. The music fits each scenario well, and again like Kingdom Hearts, flows nicely in-and-out of Exploration and Battle to continuously give an action packed experience all 'round.
Continuously added content since the game is still in development but with plenty of material to enjoy already, from free-exploration secrets treasures and powerups hidden throughout the world, challenging quests from NPCs, and very well designed Dungeons that offer a great challenge for both battle and puzzle lovers- the kind that you'd expect in the great 2D Zelda releases.
With tons of content being added regularly, buying this game to support the progress of the immediately gripping sci-fi fantasy world story is one of the best things you can do- and you won't regret it.

If the game continues to be developed and eventually finished it will be amazing. It could be best SNES game never released for SNES.
Edit: Well yeah, the game is far from being finished, so please be considerate with your money, because as of now, it's 20$/€ for 2 hours of story. Also gamepad recommended.
