This game caught me off guard. What at first glance may look like standard RPG Maker fare is actually something quite different, and very refreshing.
is probably best described as a mix of SEGA's classic
series of RPGs - including its groundbreaking MMO spinoff
(which very obviously informed
's scenario and design) - as well as HAL Laboratories' somewhat obscure Super Famicom hack 'n' slash title
, to which
bears likeness in its fast-paced combat and movement system. The look and feel is quite authentically that of an early 32-bit era game, still resorting to tile-based 2D graphics, but taking advantage of the "new hardware" for large sprites, zoom and lighting effects, and other shenanigans. All of that, combined with a so far very solid narrative and set of characters, makes for a game that is most definitely worth keeping an eye on. NOTE: I played a Humble Bundle copy given to me by a friend til I bought this. I've played it all up to the first PVP "boss battle".
This game reminds me of Legend of Zelda, Sword of Mana, and many old school ARPGs of the past. I would suggest exploring, grinding, and doing side quests for experience. I am only a lvl 5 at the moment, and am going to do more side quests and fight weaker enemies to grind up to lvl 10 or so.
I'd say it is worth the $19.99 price point as the devs of this game make sure an update is worth updating their game. I would say when I played it via Humble Bundle it took me around 2-3 hours to beat the "beta" of the game. I am sure now for me if I redid it, it'd be 4-5 hours if not more.
So, yes, I do recommend this game. The most fun I've had with any early access title in a looong time.

Despite being very much still a work in progress, I have put a bunch of time into this game. Exploring, doing quests (the fun kind), and just jamming to the wonderful music has been a ton of fun and certainly not something I regret spending money on. Do to the fact that the developers are mainly German (I believe), you will find a few typos and grammatical issues if you are looking and have a trained eye, but that kinda just adds to the fun as there is a built in text editor that sends suggestions to the devs. That way you sort of have a part in the making and fine tuning of the game!
tl;dr: If you like exploration and puzzly 2D action RPGs, I would highly recommend giving CrossCode a shot!

This game is incredible and I can't wait for it to be finished. I’m usually not a fan of the mystery genre, as there is a certain meaninglessness in turning a story into a guess-and-check puzzle. So believe me when I say that this is a whole lot more than a typical whodunit. It’s a psychological character study on top of a horrific murder mystery. Deadly Premonition is like playing through a TV show (particularly Twin Peaks).
This rollercoaster of a game blends psychological perspective and universal laws, the physical world and the supernatural, quirky humor and nauseating tragedy, all in one interactive experience. The framing of the piece creates plot holes, which upon contemplation leave an emptiness inside your ribcage. The personal interpretations and unanswerable questions are really the scariest part about this game.
It’s a shame this was given such a severely low budget, considering the remarkably high aspirations the development team had for the project. I suggest reading the English subtitles to avoid the characters’ poorly animated mouths. Save as often as possible to avoid losing progress from crashes. But don’t let the low production values fool you; if a bit of dialogue seems awkward and out of place, it’s supposed to be; if a character is acting strangely, don’t assume they have one-dimensional motivations. Even though it’s a bit shoddy, this game is carefully crafted.
The story and characters are weird and amazing.
You just have to play it.

Cross Code, while early in developement, is no doubt promising in all aspects.
The controls are fluid, making travel fairly quick and enabling fast-paced, challenging combat.
Special abilities that can be "Switched" out of combat allows you to decide what way is best to take on a group of enemies, before you attack them.
Elements (and shields/guards) allow for unique weaknesses in most enemies to be discovered, both in common enemies and in bosses.
The storyline (so far) is gripping and will leave you with question after question.
Stats, level, and equipment will only take you so far. Personal skill will be the deciding factor for higher level enemies, large groups of enemies, and bosses.
The artwork is absolutely fantastic. ABSOLUTELY. FANTASTIC.
Combat made fun by unique arsenal of powers where you develope your own style.
Combat made fun by smooth controls and fast-paced action.
Platforming is a large part of exploration and treasurehunting where a fall doesn't lead to a loading screen, but instead an instant nearby respawn.
Puzzles are unique and involved as they play on the game's combat and elements for different affects in some cases.
I cannot stress how much I like the combat in this game.
Seriously, buy it.
It's a great game, and some of the most fun I've ever had for 20 bucks. I'd happily pay more for it.
Even though it is early access, and it is lacking in story, and it is lacking in areas to explore, it's well worth your money and the wait.

Gemcraft is a multigame story about wizards, magic, and of course, gems. It is a tower defense game that is different from the "norm". It features towers that, on their own have no effect, but when you place gems in them they come to life with different effects. The game was meant to deviate from the average tower defense game by having bloodbound rather than gatling guns, and poison rather than archer towers and so on. This game is the fourth game in the story, which leads up to the biggest event in the game, but what that is, is for you to find out.
If you like tower defense, then this game is for you, with millions of different ways to solve levels, and all sorts of traits and monsters to juggle, plus with hours-lasting endurance, you will be sucked in for weeks.
10/10

For puzzle solvers who either have limited time or a limited attention span, GemCraft - Chasing Shadows provides both tremendous satisfaction and a lot of game play, for a very reasonable price.
Despite falling into the easily distracted category, I have managed to quickly rack up 35+ hours of play time.  Credit the highly episodic structure of the game.  Each of the many dozens of levels feels fast paced, and many can be completed in half an hour or so.
I have currently finished fewer than a third of the levels, have discovered fewer than a third of the Skill enhancements, and have acquired only 2 of 6 Spell enhancements.  Yet I feel a sense of accomplishment already, thanks to the amount of variation in the maps (levels) provided, the progressive difficulty of the challenges presented (which the developer has superbly balanced with progressive player ability enhancements), and the rich use that the game makes of Achievements.   Some of the levels are straightforward, while many are tricky and call for some lateral thinking to solve.  Occasionally a return visit after additional Spells or Skills have been collected is required.
Developer Game in a Bottle deserves a fistful of high level gems and a gold plated Giant monster for a job very well done.
I played the flash version last year and loved it.  This is very much improved over the flash game, and would recommend it to anyone that likes the genre or GemCraft in particular.

While Loadout is a decent enough attempt at a free-to-play shooter, and some have described the business model as "fair", preventing people from buying better guns with real cash, it suffers from one very large problem: pretty much everyone in the game already has better stuff than you.
There are a million ways to customise your weapon, or a billion. Maybe it's a trillion. Problem is, very few of these are very useful, and it's impossible to deal enough damage to kill another player who has been playing for more than a few days. Nearly every other player in the game has massively powerful one-hit-to-kill guns, so unless you can sneak up and inflict a lot of damage very quickly, you're out of luck.
The question really is: what's the incentive to play when you start at the bottom and you're outclassed at every stage of the game? The game makes no perceivable effort to matchmake you with others of similar progression, so almost every game involves dying repeatedly to players with much more powerful weapons, regardless of your own skill.
This is a real waste of potential in what could have been a rather enjoyable game. Perhaps with a fair matchmaking system or some kind of points-buy weapon system, newer players would have more of a chance, and might actually have some fun instead of being endlessly frustrated.

It looks like a Team Fortress 2 wannabe, but I assure you it isn't! It's like a classic arena shooter with very customizable weapons. It's actually a lot more like third-person Gun Bros, and is about as serious/comedic as such. Never fear, it's true: no items affecting your performance are premium-only. Additionally, it doesn't take too much gameplay to unlock any given part, as 'Blutonium' comes easy in comparison to currency in most pay-to-win Mobile crApps. I'm not even sure if you CAN shortcut the process with real cash, but if you did, you'd be really impatient. You won't be wasting months of play to unlock X item, not if you really want it; you'll probably take months getting everything else that's cheaper, because you can!
Granted, you can't REALLY design your own gun, as in, write code and special effects etc; you simply choose from many components to alter the performance of your weapon. But this isn't just adding a scope and a noob toob, these parts alter firerate and damage, reload speed, accuracy, etc. Just take your standard barrel off your assault rifle and add a sniper barrel, then your firerate drops but accuracy and damage go up. Add semi-auto trigger mechanism (or bolt-action!), and a manual loading clip like a shotgun, and your damage goes higher and higer, as your firerate drops. Scopes and stocks are also present, of course, but while there's no noob tube, you can choose ammo types, usually standard kinetic shots, electrified shots, healing shots, or even incendiary rounds. Healing shots not only heal your target, but you as well, enabling you to mend yourself if needed. And that's about as far as teamwork goes in this game; it isn't TF2, after all.
There are 4 basic weapon types as of right now, and if there are others to unlock or to be added in the future, I don't know of any. You get a bullet-weapon, which can be an assault rifle, shotty, heavy, sniper, or any mix in between; a 'pulse' weapon (plasma blaster), usually seen loaded with electric shots but not required; an eplosive launcher, which can fire rockets or nades or mines, with varying effects; and a beam weapon, which fires a constant stream of damage and overheats instead of reloading.
All weapons have infinite ammo, but require reloads (or cooling), so you don't need to worry about finding ammo pickups and get to rain rocket artillery all about, if you like. Special weapons like grenades, medkits, or even auto-turrets are available, and DO require pickups to re-stock, but all standard weapons are limitless.
Accesories are aquired by earning Blutonium (sounds like Xplodium!), and as said, it doesn't require too much effort to get enough to get any given item, but don't let that make you think you'll have them all in a week; there's a lot of accesories! Some features are unlocked after level up, like additional class loadouts, but more can be purchased if desired. This is as far as it gets to 'pay-to-win', but these extra slots are a mere conveinience, and are not required. Most of the stuff that requires real cash are simply cosmetic effects for your soldier. They really ment it when they said no 'pay-to-win'.
It runs well, smoth and clean on my laptop, and I am impressed to find this isn't another money-grubbing freemium piece-of-crApp. If it looks remotely interesting to you, give it a shot; you'll probably like it!

In no way is the game Pay 2 Win. There are two currencies in game:
and
.
Blute is primaray currency used to buy weapon/gadet upgrades for your weapons. You get it by playing matches and on daily prizes.
Spacebux is obtain with real money BUT can only be used for buying cosmetics for your characters.
So anything gameplay/mechanics related cannot be just skipped to. All gameplay content(maps, game modes, weapons) is available to free 2 play player.

Annihilation is also pretty nice (if im correct, this will be a part of competitive part of the game), its a combination of all game modes put on 1 map.
I saw quite a few people say "The game is a TF2 clone". I don't really see how, the only thing they have in common are the cartoonish graphics.
The game had some problems on launch with friend lists and matchmaking constantly being down but the developers fixed it quite fast and even gave out free in game cosmetics as an apology. They're really taking a part of the community and listen to people. Keep it up, you guys are awesome!
As for the cosmetics, if you're down on spending a few bucks you'll be amazed at how many items and taunts are available to buy(most of them really hilarious).

It was so refreshing to be back in the Resident Evil universe after a long break since the failure that was Resident Evil 5, and Revelations has done a magnificent job of reviving my faith in the franchise. Let me first state that I am, indeed, one of those purists that thinks RE1 was the pinacle of the franchise, and that the decision to move away from fixed camera angles really took something of the dread away from every corner and corridoor you couldn't quite see the end of. With that out of the way and taken as a given, Revelations is a good action game. Good, not great, good.
Let's get the bad stuff out of the way shall we? As an action game, the controls don't really cut it in comparison to other fast-paced action titles. Strafing is a little too slow, particularly for those of us who are used to using strafe to get around corners, and made me feel like I was driving a fire engine rather than an athlete in a cat suit. The bindings are an improvement on previous games, but I still found myself modifying them to match "the norm". There was a distinct lack of hoard activity, which is something I discovered while playing Revelations, that I have come to take for granted since RE2, and was a little confused in the end as to why they were not implemented. What they have done to Hunters also made me shed a tear, and I can only assume it was in order to make dodging have a reason to be included.
On to the good stuff! By an absolute country mile, the best thing about Revelations is the story, as you would expect from a long-running franchise. The plot twists and cut scenes were great, and were just as much part of the game as the gameplay itself. Playing as other characters to fill out the story didn't feel like a chore as it does in a lot of games, and I think the key to that is taking the RPG element out of it, and rather focussing on gun modification instead. Kitting said characters out in a somewhat OP fashion always helps though. I thought the inclusion of the "Last time on..." cut scenes after loading a save (and the ability to make them go away too - I'm looking at you AMC) was a great inclusion, especially if I hadn't played for a couple of days. Pretty much the only saving grace for Revelations, as an action game, were the boss fights. If anything, I wish there had have been more of them and against different BOW's, but the variation in what was there in terms of enemies was good.
I bought Revelations on sale, and having played it, I probably wouldn't pay the $40 or whatever they are asking for it at the moment, but for anything under $15 it's great value. There's an arena-style multiplayer element to it as well, but after playing Dead Island I'd had my fill of that, so didn't explore it too much. I'm keen to see how Capcom plans to put this series back in the Survival Horror genre, and really aplaud them on splitting Revelations from the other Resident Evil mainstream titles (which they plan to keep as action games), in order to give fans like me what they have been asking for repeatedly after Resident Evil: Nemesis.

Resident Evil Revelations is another step in the downward trend of the Resident Evil franchise. The fact that the HD version came out after the sixth installment is what makes it seem better than it actually is, because frankly anything is better than Resident Evil 6,
The setting is appropriate for a horror game, having been explored previously in the series with Resident Evil Gaiden and Resident Evil Dead Aim. One cannot criticize this story without doing so for the other games in the series because it's just as silly as the previous games, albeit without any of the charming character of Resident Evil 1 or 4 (both directed by Shinji Mikami, coincidentally).
It's a shame that they had to complicate such a simple story by going back and forth in time making the player control a variety of characters, most of them unecessary, a consequence of Capcom's decision to incorporate co-op or AI partner all the time. What ends up happening is that you have lots of names, throwaway characters and  a breaking of pace as a result of playing out irrelevant events in the story (playing as Chris in a boat to show him boarding the cruise ship for instance).
The gameplay is a step forward from Resident Evil 5, and a more sober affair than the mess that is Resident Evil 6's combat system. You move and shoot/stab and can occasionally stun an enemy to perform a high powered physical attack, which is satisfying. Less so are some of the enemies with instant death kills, which are a little cheap, but it's nothing new for the series. The gameplay does become tiring though, because the enemies are designed as bullet sponges and are very repetitive. That's not to say the zombies in the previous games are not, but they were shorter experiences as well.
Thankfully, the quick time events from RE4 and RE5 take a break in the game, being relegated to escaping an enemy's grasp and turning valves.
Being originally a 3DS game, some of the geometry and facial expressions do look a bit basic, and some of the textures are not up to PS3/360/PC standards, but it's not a bad looking game, it looks on par with early generation graphics. It's certainly well optimized and runs better than Resident Evil 4 Ultimate, which is mind boggling.
The difficulty of the game is balanced, but with some spikes that detract from the TV series approach and pace of it, namely in the boss battles that can be quite infuriating in the first tries. The Infernal difficulty mode is different from RE5's Professional mode but just as silly. Instead of overpowered attackers, the enemies become even bigger bullet sponges, turning the game into a brick wall, though it softens as one progresses and gets better gear. It's  a far cry from the challenging but fair Real Survival Mode of the 2002 remake, it's just pulling the bars to make it as unbalanced as it can be.
To add to the longevity is the Raid Mode, which is a worse time waster than Mercenaries because it features levelling and each level takes way longer to complete, and the difficulty ramps up to where you need to grind quite a bit through the ship you're already sick of traversing and the enemies you're already sick of fighting from the campaign.
It's a better game than what came after, and does many things better than Resident Evil 5, but it lacks character and importance in the overall series. For a game that's called Revelations, removing it from the story arch does no difference at all and makes it an entry that can fade to obscurity.

Resident Evil Revelations / Biohazard Revelations seems like a new game but it was released in 2012 on the Portable gaming platform that is the 3DS and then, a year later, on the XB360, PS3, Wii U and naturally, PC. The game itself was surprisingly decent. I had a whole lot of fun with it and a little piece of advice, the game plays way better with the Keyboard + Mouse scheme (a word of advice though, disable the mouse acceleration though!). With the XB360 gamepad, the aiming was all jerky and you end up missing so many shots.
As for the game itself, it was so much superior to the pathetic Resident Evil 6 which in my opinion was one of the worse RE game ever made. But this one, RE: Revelations, redeemed itself well enough in its atmosphere setting, the gameplay mechanics, voice acting and even the music department.
To make it short, this is the game RE6 should have been but wasn't unfortunately!
For a ported game, the only big noticeable CON would be the graphical and visual side of the game.
PROS:
+Ghost ship horror atmosphere.
+Decent campaign length.
+Neat characters models (well modelized, especialy Jill's Azz!).
+"Auto-sufficient" A.I. (partner manage itself so no need to run at him/her to heal).
+Nice soundtrack.
+Replay value with the Raid Mode or if you seek achievements completion.
CONS:
-Awful textures.
-Weak controls with XB360 gamepad.
-Messy story.
-Weak A.I. but helpful at times as it brings the enemies to itself.
-Limited enemy variety (same monsters that you see all game long).
-No chapter replay option in the main campaign.
-You cannot run... like, what the hell is that?
-No puzzles.
-This is no "survival horror" game like we used to play on the early RE games and keeps the game into the "action horror shooter" mode.
RECOMMENDATION:
Decent port to say the least! If you're a Resident Evil fan, you'll enjoy this game for sure! If you're a new comer, you may want to play earlier titles since you'll be really lost in this game, story speaking!
PS. The extra DLC doesn't add much to the gameplay. If you can skip it, do so! It is not really worth it in my opinion!

An HD Port of an early 3DS release, Resident Evil Revelations ended up being a much more faithful representation of the franchise as a whole than it's widely panned console brethren Resident Evil 6.
While RE: Revelations was originally advertised as a sort of prequel to Resident Evil 5, about all is shares with the previous title is it's main protagonists, Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield, and their current positions as field agents of the counter bioterrorism NGO BSAA.
Revelations brings subtle improvements to RE5's controls, in particular the oft requested ability to strafe, and includes new functionality such as equipment tuning.  Weapons are now socketed equipment able to hold a number of custom components that augment their performance, these components effects range from higher magazine capacity to greater damage output and faster firing rates, among other more unique effects I'll let you discover.
Revelations also features the Genesis system.  The Genesis is a handheld scanner not far off from Metroid Prime's scan visor, and quickly proves to be just as useful, allowing the player to locate easter eggs, hidden items, research dead enemies for healing items, and so forth.  The downside is you'll end up spending quite a bit of time behind the Genesis HUD, which can deflate the horror athmosphere for some.
The story of Revelations brings the series back to it's zany horror roots, this time mixed with a bit of old school Ace Combat crazy.  Some time after the fictional island utopia of Terragrigia is laid waste by solar sattelite weapons, Jill and Chris find themselves on opposite sides of the globe following the trail of a bioterrorism organization named Veltro, with Jill's search bringing her to an abandoned cruise liner named the Queen Zenobia.  In Resident Evil tradition things quickly go off the rails for both, and the story becomes a globetrotting race against time to unearth the plans of whomever, or whatever, has taken residence on the doomed ship.
The story also spends a significant amount of time fleshing out the BSAA and the people who work there,  and the game occasionally puts the player in control of a few of Jill and Chris' fellow agents following up on leads the former have discovered.  It provides an interesting look at an organization that has become the series sucessor to the ill fated S.T.A.R.S. unit of the first game.
Graphically the HD upgrade makes the game somewhat above average in visual polish, and a few bland environment textures notwithstanding it looks pretty good for an uprezzed 3DS game.  The character models can be slightly off, Jill's being the most noticable, it would have been nice if the character models and full motion video cutscenes had an upgrade pass as well.
Revelations has several other flaws, the transition to PC has led to some glaring omissions such as the lack of the laser sight present on it's handheld counterpart.  It would have also been nice if the PC upgrade could have had an increase in enemy variety, as most of the undead creatures you'll be facing on the Zeonbia share the same general design.  None of these issues are gamebreaking, however.  And while the game does feature on rails sequences, they're nowhere near the frequency and general unplayability found in those of Resident Evil 6.
Bottom line, this is an incredibly successful if somewhat flawed transition from handheld to PC.  And even for those who can't agree on whether Resident Evil 2 or Resident Evil 4 are the pinnacle of the series, there's something for everyone to enjoy.  So if you're a fan of Resident Evil or Survival Horror, you can't go wrong with Resident Evil Revelations.

"Free" this game is not.  The only free part of the game is the tutorial and the first mission of every campaign.  ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.  The seven campaigns that the game has are DLCs ranging in price from $9.99 to $14.99.  $104.93 is what Slitherine thinks is "Free".  ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.

The way they sell the DLCs is definitely not OK. The full game at this point costs £76.93 - waaaay more than a game should cost.
On the other hand, if one is lucky enough to buy it on sale, and also not interested in every campaign - there is a choice of what to buy exactly. Which is what I did.
Also, there is the Battle of Britain mod available for free with the basic game (which is basically a free demo, consisting of a mission per every campaign released). A free air-campaign with the free game - a good deal, IMO.
Now that we sorted out the pricing and all that - the game itself.
I hadn't played this particular style of turn based wargames since Panzer General in the 90s, and would not consider myself a connoisseur of the genre.
However, I'm a huge sucker for turn-based games in general, or any game that give me time to think and plan ahead - even require that to win, but not overly so. And this is exactly what we get here - thinking and planning, but nothing overwhelming.
Turns are limited, but on Veteran I rarely felt pressed for time, in fact most missions were over with in like 3/4 of allocated turns. But I did have to restart missions a few times, while trying to find the optimal force deployment etc - some missions really pressed that "all or nothing" high risk feeling to the extreme, fighting nail and tooth against overwhelming odds.
That is a good and a bad thing at the same time.
It feels awesome, when you manage to overpower those odds - but out of the two campaigns I've beaten so far there were like 3, may be 4 missions like this, and the rest were simple "slowly press your advantage, dismantling one defensive line after another" kind of deal. It feels that there are really only two ways the game (at least in the 2 Japanese campaigns) plays - either rather easy or damn hard. No middle-grounds.
Visuals... very good. The game looks good and feels good. And plays smoothly on most occasions - late missions AI-turns drop FPS considerably for 5-10 seconds, then get back to normal.
Sounds... Alright. Not annoying, not awesome, just enough not to distract form the game. Hadn't grown tired of hearing them either, which is a good thing for a turn-based game.
Scale... battles feel small(ish). There are no front lines or massive armies - the general feeling is that you are in charge of a division-sized force, with every unit representing a battalion or may be a regiment at most. That is for the big battles. The small ones feel like your entire force is one regiment and every unit is a company at most. I like it, but others may find this unsatisfying.
Land/Sea/Air... they feel balanced, and work rather well together. There are missions that involve only one of the 3 elements, two, or all three. They all feel quite satisfying to beat and I cannot say that either of the elements feels unfinished or like "just a feature". For me all three of them blend together well, and yet can be separate games on their own.
All in all, the money I'd spent - on sale - were well spent for me. I got more hours of enjoyment out of this game, than out of most AAA-titles released in the last couple of years.

This is a very fun and reasonably realistic game. Totally recommend. Perhaps the pricing model is a bit unfortunate, which seems responsible for the negative reviews. It is probably fair to say that the content per DLC is a bit thin for the full price, but definitely a good deal when half off. On the other hand, you get a better game than you do for other games that offer more content for less total cost.
The combined arms is very nicely done and most (not all) the scenarios are quite interesting. It "feels" right for the Pacific wars (I have not tried the Europe ones). I am a very old school hex boardgamer, and this definitely hits that spot. There are complaints in previous reviews about the naval combat, the number of units in one's core forces, and other things. I do not tend to agree -- I think those all strike the right balance between realism and optimizing the pure gaming experience.
As with and operational-level game that tries to do a lot, some things are unrealistic. One turn of movement is about an hour's worth, but a company-level unit starts to seriously lose cohesion if out of supply for just a couple of turns. Scenarios have surprise events that the commander would know were probably coming in advance (so you can play each scenario as pure "game" the first time and reply with the intel, though you will also then be aware of things that should genuinely have been a surprise). So, not a simulation. But still real enough to seem real.

If you enjoy slow-paced sandbox games and don't mind an outdated UI, then you will probably enjoy Wurm. If you enjoy games where building and community come before combat, but combat is still an option, you will probably enjoy Wurm. If you prefer games with instant gratification, quick combat, and the ability to jump and sprint, I do not suggest this game for you.
Even with nearly sixty hours in Wurm I am still very much a noob. There is a lot for me to learn, and I still don't have enough skill to build a stone floor or destroy a fence. I cannot kill a wolf without help from NPCs. I still don't entirely understand the ground flattening system. I can, however, load up the Wurmpedia on my phone, play some YouTube videos in the background, and spend an entire day building a storage tower next to my house that I spent a week on.
My advice for getting started is finding a good server. A server where you can ask other players questions and get help is a godsend, sometimes literally with certain deities prohibiting certain actions. I needed something that only drops off human guards, but the deity I follow prohibits butchering humans. I got help from another player whose deity demands butchering humans. In return, I buried her bodies since my god likes that and hers doesn't. It's a community game at its heart, and playing alone is very, very lonely.
TLDR; Sandbox, takes a while, find friends

CrossCode is a fast-paced 2D retro RPG game where you start playing as a 'jack of all trades' character in a MMORPG world and your main objective is to master all 4 elements and solve the mysteries. So, how well does the game runs in terms of its presentation, gameplay, story?
+Vivid and beautiful graphics with smooth 60 FPS animation
+Soothing and exhilarating soundtrack and perfectly syncronised audio
+Simple and easy-to-learn combat mechanics with many combos that can be freely executed
+Variety of puzzles you can solve that is not too challenging but not too easy as well
+Very well designed world environment that allows to traverse around easily
+Nicely written and interesting plot with a mix of futuristic sci-fi and dungeon crawler fantasy
Okay that's quite a lot of good sides there but what about the bad sides? Well, to be honest, I don't find any problem during gameplay and I actually enjoy it despite being early access but there are very few that I want to point out.
-Some battles can be frustrating at first and the first challenge starts very early
-You need a lot of info on the environment around you and it takes time in order to get from one point to a desired point
-Might experience lag in some points
-Game contents are still small right now
The game is written in HTML 5 instead of C++ or Python but it runs as .exe so I can't tell whether the game runs natively or still relies a lot on a default web browser.
So, is the game finally worth it to buy and play at this point? This game has many potentials here at its beta stage, but unless you're willing to support the developers, I'd say you have to wait until the game is finish developed, polished and ready to be publish as a full game.

Avoid this PC port, but play this game (on Xbox 360 or PS3)! It's a terrific, dramatic story, in a memorable, immersive, offbeat/surreal virtual town, PC porting issues aside.
If you do get the PC *port*, expect to put up with crashes every hour or so, long load times between zones and cutscenes (especially cutscenes), if you can even figure out the tricks to get it to run. Then, even when you're able to play, you still have to put up with broken vertical aiming that only shows up in the PC version.
If you still get the PC port, look at DPfix (and fiddle w/ resolution and windowing settings), and try setting compatibility to WinXP SP2, or better yet Win98 (but with Win98 you'll probably have to give up the built-in gamepad support and either use keyboard/mouse (mapped onto console/gamepad-first controls) or messing around w/ a third-party gamepad mapper).
I was on the fence "yes" or "no", but I'll leave it at "no" both to stand out in the reviews, and to stick w/ my opinion that this particular PC version should be avoided unless you really don't have a 360 or PS3. I would hate to have you sour on this game's story and world simply b/c the PC port sucks major suck (seriously, even if you could get around the keyboard/mouse, load times (with only a blank screen, no indication DP hasn't frozen--tip: unless it CTDs, it'll probably load, just give it a few more MINUTES) can be unbearable).

With that in mind, this game loves a good crash more than Nascar fans. If I could I would tell you it was worth it since the game is amazing when it is working, if you overlook the low budget that is.
Yet, you might not at the moment have any other choice but to play it on PC. If you choose to endure that path, get ready to fight for your right to play the game without problems. Now with the port aside, the game is far from perfect at times even seeming to be broken in places. Reasons why I like this more than Borderlands 2:
-Cryo > Slag (I really dislike the slag mechanic and cryo, while being fun, isn't necessary - which is a huge plus.)
-Your character talks/responds to quests (This is a huge one for me, oddly enough.)
-Anti Gravity (Hard to go back to normal gravity.)
-Story (Flow of the story makes more sense than B2, and has more emotion/depth.)
-Graphics/Music (Although I do miss the twangy country vibe the first two have.)
-Humor (Felt a little more varied, and not beating the same jokes over and over into the ground.)
-Laser weapons (Sorry Torgue.)
-Content
To expand on that last one further, I love the amount of content in this game. Sure, it's a little shorter than B2, but it's not short...and I feel like that's a false impression people will often leave you with in reviews. This game is still long and has a ton of content, but it's shorter than B2, which is a really good thing. B2 felt too long and I would always end up losing interest due to length (felt dragged on or quests made up just for added length). For me, it's a case of quality over quantity, with The Pre-Sequel winning out on this one. The Pre Sequel has a fantastic flow to it, the quests are very fun and the story is much more engaging. To state it again, this game, while being shorter than B2, is not short. I didn't feel like it was a glorified expansion to B2, as many others state, I feel like it holds it's own rather well.

There are a lot of negatives to this game, but the reason I am recommending it is due to the actual gameplay being challenging and fun. This game makes you pay for stupid mistakes and make those highlight reel plays feel well-deserved. Now on to the not so great stuff.
Price- I cannot recommend this title at $60. I'd say $20-$30 is a fair price. I recieved it as a gift from a friend who got it from his humble bundle subscription but I would not feel bad dropping $20-$30 on it.
Cut scenes- This is by far my biggest annoyance. As I said, the gameplay is quite fun and challenging, but every couple minutes you have a repetative cut scene. They are skippable, but usually it takes a few seconds before it will skip.
Performance demand- I admit I don't have the best rig, but this game requires more resources than most games out there.
I know I dwelled a bit on the negatives, but coming back around to the actual game play, this game is too fun to stay away from. Grinding out the My Player mode is almost worth the endless text messages, contract negotiations, practice sessions, and pointless "events" just to see your player finally hitting those shots and finishing at the rim. If you're a basketball fan who is in search of good gameplay mechanics, this game has my vote.

Out of all the Resident Evil games, 2 and 4 have always been my favorites (Leon bias?) with RE4 being at the top. But even so, RE4 still felt like a step in another direction; a more action-oriented direction, which would later turn out be true, because of RE5 and RE6. But, here comes Revelations, a game originally released between RE5 and RE6, that takes a step backwards for the better, back to the classic style of Resident Evil, when the series was more about survival horror and atmospheric settings. And I can wholeheartedly say, that
I was initially doubtful about playing Revelations, due to my general dislike of the direction the series had gone, and I thought that Revelations took the same direction as well. But boy was I wrong this whole time. Revelations takes the formula that made RE such a famous series within the horror genre, while at the same time improving the controls, making it far more accessible to newcomers, or people who hate the "tank controls" and/or the fixed camera angles. It drops having to manage your inventory and worrying about space (apart from selecting at maximum three weapons to take with you.) And an improvement over RE5 is that you don't have to take care of your AI partner anymore. And not to mention that it features a story that is kept seperate from the numbered games' plot, allowing it to stand more on its own, without relying too heavily on the other games - which is really interesting, since it's told in an Episodic nature, like a TV show, a first in the series.
If you've played the latest RE games and you've felt doubtful in that it'll ever return to its glory days, or if you've had a dislike of how the RE games controls, then look no further. I highly recommend you try this game, because it's
. Hell, I'd even recommend newcomers to start with this game, since it does not have the things that the majority of dislikers complain about.
Enemies are frightening again, ammo is limited again, darkness is back again, free-roaming is (partly) back again, jumpscares are back again, eerie atmospheres are back again, a secluded setting is back again, and most importantly:

CAMPAIGN REVIEW ONLY:
Resident Evil: Revelations (RE:R) is a spin-off from the numbered RE game, since numbered RE's have become more + more blockbuster-esque + action-esque. Revelations takes some steps to bring the RE series a bit closer to its survival-horror roots, which long-time fans of RE series are going to appreciate. Also, RE:R keeps some of the things that were found in RE5 (i.e. you will often have an AI companion with you + KB-mouse controls were drastically improved) + RE6 (the game will have you playing from different agents' perspective).
While RE's plot is typical RE stuff, if you've played any of the previous RE's, it's still enjoyable, ridiculous, quite over-the-top + hammy. Agents from different organizations are involved in a pair or so of ships that have a Virus on them - and the agents are here to clean-up the mess. With twists + turns in the story + plot, never is there a dull moment, even despite the dialogue + writing never ever really taking-off, staying quite serviceable.
RE:R delivers a much more solid gameplay experience than RE6, never feeling like you will be replaying the same exact levels + boss fights numerous times that you did on another campaign. RE6 had tons of major highs + some major lows, while RE:R never ever does that at all - from start-to-finish, RE:R is, for the most part, is excellent. Unlike RE5+6, expect to constantly run out of ammo and be switching weapons - often bringing back the survival-horror feel that had been dwindling since RE5. Controls feel very similar to RE5+6 PC, in terms of the actual controls - so, you're fine with how those controlled with the KB-mouse, expect more of that. For me, it was best to turn-off Mouse Acceleration in the Options - to make the mouse actually move more properly - otherwise, the mouse didn't control correctly.
When assets + backtracking get re-used, it is done in a way where something is twisted into a different way entirely - which was one of the biggest problems with RE6. RE:R's biggest problem is actually in its graphics quality, since its environments really show that this was a port from a mobile platform - with often some blurry environments, bland environments & not-detailed areas showing up on-screen. On the other hand - characters + enemy models look really good, showing that those are of a much higher + better quality.
The game rarely dropped belong 60 frames per seconds on its highest settings, playing smoothly most of the time. There were a few stutters and framerate drops - which, oddly enough, were when going from area-to-area in one of the hubs, when nothing of much was happening, when waiting to move to the next area. When it mattered, during combat - most of the time, 60 frames per second on my PC (i7 950; 1 GB of GeForce GTX 560 Ti; 8 GB RAM; Win 7 64-bit).
If you found RE6 disappointing for whatever reasons - and certainly many did, while I found it to be a gem, despite its numerous flaws - make sure to check out RE:R. RE:R is a return to the greatness that came from RE4 + also takes some of the elements of RE5+6 that were worthwhile. Certainly, RE:R is an improvement over in RE6 in terms of overall consistentcy + brings back some of the survival-horror elements that were missing in a majority of RE6. After 16 hours of playing, RE:R proves that graphics ain't always everything, when the overall gameplay is consistently fantastic.
Final Grade = B+.
ADDITIONAL NOTES On RE Series -> RE4,5,6 + Rev:
Keep in mind, I have yet to play RE1-3, believe it or not.
RE4 PC (Non-HD Edition) might've been the greatest RE game that I've played so far, despite it being a not-so-good PC port (in terms of PC controls for the KB-mouse).
RE5 was a really good game-experience + major improvement in making a great PC version for a RE game.
RE6 is just a flawed-gem of a game.
RE:R fits in as being the best actual RE game that I've played since actually RE4.

I will start my review with this: Wurm is NOT a game for everyone. It's the type of game that requires patience and willingness to learn and experiment. There is NO instant gratification in the world of Wurm; you will have to work and put time into everything you do in order to achieve results, but when you see those results, god is it satisfying.
You can do just about anything you'd expect from a sandbox/crafting/building game and then some, everything is wonderfully fleshed out. The best way I could describe this game is a combination between old school Runescape and Minecraft.
TL;DR Don't buy unless you're a patient person who's willing to learn.

Reasons why I like this more than Borderlands 2:
-Cryo > Slag (I really dislike the slag mechanic and cryo, while being fun, isn't necessary - which is a huge plus.)
-Your character talks/responds to quests (This is a huge one for me, oddly enough.)
-Anti Gravity (Hard to go back to normal gravity.)
-Story (Flow of the story makes more sense than B2, and has more emotion/depth.)
-Graphics/Music (Although I do miss the twangy country vibe the first two have.)
-Humor (Felt a little more varied, and not beating the same jokes over and over into the ground.)
-Laser weapons (Sorry Torgue.)
-Content
To expand on that last one further, I love the amount of content in this game. Sure, it's a little shorter than B2, but it's not short...and I feel like that's a false impression people will often leave you with in reviews. This game is still long and has a ton of content, but it's shorter than B2, which is a really good thing. B2 felt too long and I would always end up losing interest due to length (felt dragged on or quests made up just for added length). For me, it's a case of quality over quantity, with The Pre-Sequel winning out on this one. The Pre Sequel has a fantastic flow to it, the quests are very fun and the story is much more engaging. To state it again, this game, while being shorter than B2, is not short. I didn't feel like it was a glorified expansion to B2, as many others state, I feel like it holds it's own rather well.

This game has become my favorite game of all time after finishing the main story once. Now I played through the story three times, have about 200h of play time and I still want to play this game even more.
One thing that makes NieR:Automata this great, is the story with its characters.
The story is told in such a different way compared to most other games and it works so well and is such a fresh and unique experience. So I played every game, that was directed by Yoko Taro and I only found this kind of experience in games that were directed by him. While the other games of him had a great story, the gameplay always was kinda repetitive and boring, but I played them nonetheless.
So this time to make the gameplay better, they decided to team up with PlatinumGames. The result is a fluid, beautiful, stylish, thrilling and rewarding hack & slash gameplay with bullet hell elements that even after 200h never got boring and always felt exiting to play. The game has different weapon types with different combos, that can be combined in many different ways. The game also offers many enemy types in different variations, so you need to adapt your fighting style to each situation. After playing other games from PlatinumGames the combat is closest to Bayonetta but also reminds me of DMC, which is from Ninja Theory.
The soundtrack, thanks to Keiichi Okabe, is also phenomenal and so good implemented into the game that I instantly bought them. It also blends in perfectly with the beautiful open world, which seems a bit small, but is nearly perfectly designed and has many things to discover.
Throughout the story there are many different side quests, which are from a gameplay perspective not the most innovative, but each one flashes out the world and the characters a bit more.
Another thing that makes this game great is that everything makes sense in the games universe. From the skill system, to the saving and also the respawning. Other things like the pod and his programs or the red glow in the eyes of the enemies when they attack can't be explained by just playing NieR:Automata but are explained by digging deeper into the universe. I really appreciate how much fervor they put in every part of the game.
Also even if you haven't played the first Nier or the other "prequels", like me at first, you wont feel overwhelmed or like you were missing something from the story. This makes the game also perfect for newcomers to the franchise.
The only bad thing I can say about this game is that many people have experienced crashed and other bugs. At the time there is no official patch for this, but there is one in the steam community (named FAR), which fixes various resolution bugs.
For me the game only crashed a few times, which isn't nice, but wasn't a big problem for me, because the game lets you save quickly in many areas.
Another bug that I faced, was that the game didn't start in full screen mode and also only changed to full screen after many attempts.
The last thing I encountered was that the game didn't saved my custom control settings and every time I started the game I needed to change them again. I also didn't think this was a big problem because even navigating through the menus feels nice. Installing FAR helped to resolve the last two bugs.
Concluding I can only recommend this game to every player. Even if you don't end up liking the game after you played it, in my opinion everyone should have at least tried this game.
After playing this game I will at least give every game by Yoko Taro and PlatinumGames a try.

I have always loved Gemcraft, spent hours playing it on the flash version through the series and this one is fantastic.
Its a tower defense game with the ability to make it harder by sacrificing your own resources to make it harder. This gives you the ability to make the gamer harder and you can push yourself more then any other TD game I have played. Also the game gives you such a wide assortment of ways to make the game even harder if you want. Or you can just spend hours playing through the game without bothering with it.

This game, although it has a goal and story, is pretty much a sandbox Tower Defender. There are tons of ways to customize the level and difficulty, both before and during the level. It's kind of like an old arcade game, where you're trying to reach the high score and there is no defined ending.
Unfortunately, the game does suffer a bit because of it. There's never a need to stop and reconsider your strategy, you can always just go around grinding for exp until you can brute force through the game. The monsters are just walking numbers with hardly any relevant features. The bosses are nice, but you usually don't need any special strategies to beat them, just keep shooting with your strongest gem. The gem types aren't well balanced at all, you always need to go for highest damage output and ignore utility because monsters will get exponentially more healthy as the time goes, but they will not get significantly faster or regen more health or anything that would make you want to use utility gems.
This is very unlike games like Kingdom Rush where you have only 4 tower types (can be upgraded into some specialist towers later), huge variety of opponents and only few places to place your towers. In that game, you need build specific things to counter specific enemies. In Gemcraft? Nope, just combine yellow with red and upgrade whenever you can.
There are probably some techniques needed to beat endurance (1337 waves I think) or get grade 100 gems, but even then it's mostly about grinding enough experience to be able to do it.
The strong point of Gemcraft is all the customization. There's really a ton of ways you can play. But why would you? If you go too far with the difficulty buffs, you're not gonna beat it no matter what. If you go too low, you'll be bored to death. It's hard to find the sweet spot. It never feels like there's a challenge that needs strategy and wit because you can beat everything if you grind for more experience.
It's a good time waster when you're tired and just want to get instant gratification by doing nothing. But 10 bucks... Nah.  Don't. There are more entertaining games you can buy for that price.

A mixed bag of a game that will definitely rely on consistent updates from Paradox to continue to be fun.
My god, those first 20 hours playing this game are magic. Exploring the new procedurally-generated galaxy you find yourself in is incredible. Your customized race of people will meet strange civilizations of other races as planet after planet and star system after star system reveals mysterious secrets. The gameplay feels like it has some depth, the research is interesting and forces you to make choices, and the graphics are very pretty. I was addicted and played just about nothing else.
However, after those first 20 hours, the game's facade from earlier seems to fall apart. The addictive nature of discovery becomes Stellaris's downfall as events and discoveries become rote, repeated events. The gameplay seems to fall apart as well, as every mechanic feels a little shallow. Migration, tile building, fleet customization (just let the AI do it - I can't seem to figure war out and it defintely becomes a numbers game), and diplomacy all have the same couple of options. Tile building has the same problem as improvement building in late-game Civ - you just want to automate it. Luckily, the game does provide a Governor system that will do just that (along with a few in-game consequences, good and bad). Crusader Kings II suffers the same problems too, but the novelty of conquering the real world we live in and a procedurally-generated galaxy just are not the same. Not to mention, Crusader Kings sparks your imagination about character interaction and growing attached to your family, friends, and rivals. DLC and constant developer update are necessary to keep this game fresh. To Paradox's credit, they have done just that, but I worry what happens when the updates become less frequent.
Pick this game and its DLC up on sale. It has promise, but will need lots of updates to be competitive with other 4X (real time and turn based) Space games. Man, those first 20 hours though...

First thing first. The only real reason i would recommend this, is because i love the Resident evil universe. If you're not a fan of the series, don't even go there.
Starting off with the good parts. The story is rather decent. The characters are as lovely as ever and the not-completely-linier-except-it-is idea is a fun diversion from the regularity in most RE games.
I also liked the weapon upgrade system, gives a more changey feel and all choices are not permanent.
Now to the bad parts, the *WEAPON UPGRADE SYSTEM* is not permanent and feels weird for a RE game...
The *GRAPHICS* are sad, not as in bad but it gives a kindof dead feeling. The lighting is lighting up whole cupboards like it's a semi-budgettey game from the late 2000s. All textures who are about to move are semi-obvious to completely obvious.
The game suffers from *EXTREME CONSOLITIES*. The graphics is one of the clues, the other is the aiming. Even though we remove the aim-help, it's still jumpy, You can't aim properly when you're getting close to a monster couse even though it's turned off, the aim-help seems to kick and and prevents any fast or small movements of the aim.
THERE ARE NO REAL ZOMBIES! Just lots of weird blobby humanoids who are no fun trying to aim at with their wobbly heads and ♥♥♥♥ed up aiming.
There are *NO SCARY SCENES* where you know you're about to get ♥♥♥♥ed but still try to make it out with key-combinations, even though the rest of the game is console-oriented, this part which is usually the more fun, and mostly hated, part of the RE games IMHO, is left out.
*IT'S PRACTICALLY IMPOSSIBLE TO DODGE* it makes no sence that you have to time a turnabout to dodge, and you almost always dodge straight into whatever's trying to run into you.
But i still played through the whole campaign, and i actually enjoyed it. So the story is a pretty big plus, even though i am quite sure most people will not agree with me on that part. There are quite a few things that does not make sence, RE wise, but i suppose it's still legit. I want to believe.

I wanted to like this game. I seriously wanted to.
But it seems to do everything in it's power to stop me from having an enjoyable experience.
The game itself plays fine. Each champion feels unique to play, you get a great variety of cards and items to further customize your experience. There's an immense amount of satisfaction from finding that perfect loadout for your playstyle that just 'clicks'.
Paladins has a huge amount of character, with each champion practically oozing personality in everything they do. From their animations, to their voice-lines, to details about their character models, it's easy to tell that the designers in this game put a lot of love into what they crafted.
There's quite a bit of Pay to Win, with the whole experience being locked behind either a paywall, or a few hundred hours investment. This makes 'just picking up' the game into an exercise in tedium, as you'll need to play dozens of rounds to unlock a character, then another several rounds to get a decent loadout for them.
Of course, this is assuming you're able to finish an entire round.
Every few rounds, I get placed into a game where, because of lag, I can hardly do a thing. I don't mean 'my projectiles come out a few tenths of a second after I click', or 'the game occasionally hangs for a second or two'. I mean there's little connection between the buttons I am pressing on my keyboard and what I see on screen. My character teleports around aimlessly, and when I finally manage to get near the fighting, I find out that I had died 10 seconds ago and am treated to a killcam of me running into a wall. This is either horrid netcode, or matchmaking placing me on the other side of the world (considering my teammates rarely speak english, the latter is likely the case).
This is on top of the fact that, if you do manage to find a decent connection, you'll probably end up with a hacker on one of the teams. Despite an anti-cheat that makes you feel like you're in 1984, hackers still manage to run rampant through this game, meaning you give up quite a bit of privacy for no reason.
With problems like this, it's no wonder most rounds I play end up with at least one player AFK on either my team or the other team, making every round completely one-sided and killing any chance at an enjoyable game.
In about 60 hours of play-time, I think I can count the number of enjoyable rounds I've played on one hand. And it's a shame, since those few rounds were some of the best experiences I've had in any multiplayer videogame. They're just not worth putting up with all the other problems this game has.
Perhaps one day, we'll see Paladins come into it's own and separate itself from the pack to become a truly unique and incredible experience. For now, I'd steer clear of this game.

Oh boy, Crosscode, where to begin? :) This is a great game that i bought during a sale (25% off) and i don't regret a thing!
If anything, I'm just waiting, nay, drooling for more content.

First off, the Music. Ahh. Nice. The music is Beautiful, and reminds me of Snes classics like Chrono Trigger,
Secret of Mana, Secret of Evermore and Illusion of Gaia, and just a bit of Megaman and Xenogears as well :)

3- I love the music. No Really. I Love it. When it comes out as a soundtrack, or perhaps on bandcamp(you can check it out on soundcloud right now) i will definitely be buying it.
4- That story. Grahh. Want Moar!
Anyway, the long and short of it is, If Crosscode were complete right now, it would be more then worth that 20$ price
Right now, it might be a little hard to say(since i'm stingy) but honesty, I don't think you'll regret it.

A truly amazing hidden gem. I'm amazed that I didn't find out about this game last year, I absolutely love it! If you are interested in this game, I highly recommend playing the demo first. I thought of buying it based solely on the reviews. trailers and screenshots, but experiencing the demo is what sold it for me.
The graphics are in a wonderfully done 16-bit style that reminds me a lot of SNES RPGs like Breath of FIre II and Final Fantasy III/VI, and it honestly feels like true pixel art. Nothing ever moved or rotated such that the pixels rotated as well, which is what can hurt games in this style, in my opinion.
The sound design is really good, and everything feels like it has impact and right for the situation. The music is also very Kingdom Hearts-esque, which fits this game very well.
The gameplay is a very interesting mix of a twin-stick shooting, RPG elements, platforming and puzzles, but the game doesn't feel like a perverbial Frankenstein's monster. Everything is designed around the movement and the combat mechanics, and it introduces a lot of different puzzle mechanics around them, and it all works really well!
Even though it is only in early access, the RPG mechanics that are there are very easy to understand and use, and I'm very excited to see what new things are added in the future. As of version 0.5, the party system also has a lot of potential. The AI needs a little bit of fine tuning, in regards to the various command settings, but overall it works pretty well.
I also really enjoy the story and setting of this game. As I progressed, I became more interested in finding out about the world and the many different characters. All of the main characters so far have very unique and memorable personalities, and the conversations between these characters made me more interested in them. One of my favorite mechanics in regard to this was how the dialogue you can hear just passing by various people can sometimes hint at important information. During the window where these hints are up, you can begin a conversation with them and gain some new information which can either help you on a quest or find out more about the world. I am definitely excited to see how this plays into the rest of the game.
So, if you're looking for something new and unique, I highly recommend checking out this game. Although $20 might be a bit much for a game that is in early access, after playing the demo, I was totally willing to pay it if it meant I could support the developers of this amazing game!

Deadly Premonition is a notoriously polarising game, lauded for its similarities to David Lynch's Twin Peaks, and criticised for everything that it is on a technical level. It has a doom-laden yet sleepy atmosphere, it mixes the grotesque with the mundane to excellent effect, its characters are fascinating, its hero is a monotone FBI agent that follows his dreams and intuitions with deadpan seriousness, its musical themes expose and mock the manipulative nature of music in games/tv/movies (corporate training video jazz played in dramatic moments, dissonance when ordering a sandwich), and so on.
And yet when talking about its parts, the game is terrible. The horror sections of the game are awful because you can't walk and shoot at the same time. The map is unnecessarily large. It's sort of impossible to stumble into the wide range of side-missions available. The game has to be played with the its wiki open somewhere in the background and so the experience is never totally random or immersive. Accessing items and maps is difficult. Even then the map is impossible to use. Driving is awful. The animations look like The Sims c. 2004. And so on.
And so it's more than the sum of its parts, and this is why those in defense of Deadly Premonition have made the case for it as an example of 'games as art'. As a work of fiction, it's very good, and as a game, it is awful.
But so it is worth comparing to other games that favour things like atmosphere and narrative over technical game-ness. To the Moon and The Walking Dead, for example. These games are adored by critics and gamers alike, but on the level of gamerliness, don't really add up to much. The Walking Dead's parts can be described as a glorified point-and-click, To the Moon as sort of the same but with even less agency on the player's part. So why is Deadly Premonition hated when those others are loved?
Those other games knew what they were, and so they cut unnecessary 'game' parts out to streamline themselves as works of interactive fiction. But with Deadly Premonition, you're forced to play it. It makes the mistake of thinking that it could ever work as a conventional game.
You will drive for ♥♥♥♥ing hours, memorising directions from the map only accessible from the pause menu. You will yawn as York walks through doors but first checks what's behind them and this process somehow feels like it takes hours. You will yawn as you shoot ghosts from a stationary position. You will quit the game as you take a wrong turn somewhere and your car turns around really slowly and then hits a tree. You will wonder why the map is so large as you are driving for ♥♥♥♥ing hours and memorising directions. And these are all relevant criticisms because you're forced to do all of this and all of this will happen
And yet you will delight in York's schizophrenic monologues to his imaginary friend Zach. On tedious drives you get Patrick Bateman-esque descriptions of 80s films and film scores, both insightful and disturbingly relatable. You will want to check up on townsfolk as they're genuinely interesting. You will wince as York mentions cutting off peoples' heads, peeing in their skulls, and drinking it, over dinner. You will be seduced by the game's drowsy tone, and every now and then the shift into horror will genuinely disturb you because for an hour or so you were comfortable. You might even get scared of the Raincoat Killer, although encounters with him are Quick time events and so feel like minigames.
You might not care enough to solve the mystery at hand, but as with Twin Peaks, this is beside the point. If you're happy to settle in for the experience rather than the game, Deadly Premonition is well worth your time.

_A Missed Opportunity_
This game is essentially a modern day variant of the classic '90s 2.5D Arcade Action RPG Hack & Slashes (gee, that's a mouthful). If you ever cared for games like Golden Axe, Final Fight, Streets of Rage, or any Capcom brawler of the '90s, this game is right up your alley.
One feature that sets it apart from it's roots is that it introduces a town that you can go to between levels, an inventory and item system that lets you choose between weapons and spend the money you pick up.
In fact, with it's given set of features, you'd think this game would stand a chance at being a better-than-average entry, standing above peer games like the revamped Chronicles of Mystara games or the classic XBLA hit Castle Crashers.
It's a pity then that it has outstanding issues and has been dropped from support by the developers.
1. You must set resolutions higher than 1600x900 by entering them into the initialisation file.
2. You may or may not be one of the lucky ones who can play online co-op; I so far have found no success in either seeing a public game or in hosting one. All my attempts to do anything with the online co-op has resulted in failure and frustration. My friends also experienced this, with no obvious solution in sight. Yes, I had my ports open (80 for the record).
3. Other issues may be odd to the players that aren't apparent at first; no drop in/out functionality, 3 player party limit even tho there are 4 PCs to choose from. Unlike other ARPGs that use a merchants, you cannot sell old items, not even eventually like Dark Souls. This leaves your inventory full of old and useless weapons that just add the dross of simple inventory management, tho it is fortunately offset; the dross does end up ever towards the bottom of the list like a gravity well of irrelevance.
4. Some attacks can be spammed for maximum exploitive effect.
This game is only recommended (in it's current state) for those who are interested in finding more games that suit local co-op gaming, as ultimately, this game is a simple Brawler with some extra features tacked on... some of which may fail to work, ala the online element. That it fails to cut far enough away from the cloth that it comes from in other areas and the lack of followup support from the Devs within 2 months of release is a veritable early death for this game.
Resultingly, this game is fun but not deep enough to warrant much dedicated time.

There's a lot of depth in this game that has been absent from so many other space 4X games. In particular, I like how each unit of population ("pop") has its own identity including wants and stats. The universe really feels "alive" in that regard, and each update seems to add to the depth and richness of this. The only other game I've seen close to this detail is Endless Space 2, which is good in a very different way.
Games run good and long, but the real-time (pausable) format of the game keeps things moving pretty quickly. One thing that bothers me a bit when playing other games now, like Endless Space 2, is the turn button and just sitting for a moment. It's an odd feeling since I used to have so much patience for that, but now that I've been "spoiled" by Stellaris it's a bit of a distraction.
This may be Paradox's best, in my opinion, as each new game can be so radically different. You can be an egalitarian Terran confederation or human autoritarians, or galactic space turtles (my fave), and all the while have an awesome story grow from your experience. Great game.

This game is fun, but only when playing with a large amount of friends. The AI is extremely boring and basically boil down into an obstacle that needs to be purged every game. Most of the other problems  brought up by the negative reviews can be solved by the fantastic modding community, which is really what keeps this game afloat and playable.
The only reason why I have 1000+ hours is because of the mods the community has to offer, and makes the game far more enjoyable so long as you don't worry about the stupid AI and play with friends. Only get this game when it's on sale and absolutely raid the workshop until it's bone dry. (For instance, Alpha Mod, Stellaris+, and LEX Events are great mods/packs by great mod creators) Another thing about modding is that it's fairly easy to learn, so in my case I created a few personal mods for me and my friends to play without worrying about making it popular and whatnot.
The DLC of the game is also very good, especially when played with several friends. If you're short on money, you can pool your money into one friend's bank account and have that person buy all the DLC, and then have him host games in the future so everyone who's playing gets to use the DLC as well.
Overall: The game is not worth it unless you get a large number of friend, mods, and DLC which is what I fortunately have.
If you don't have these things, the game will become somewhat repetitive not because the game isn't extremely customizable and random, but because the AI are all predictable and have a general plan of action of dealing with each type.
Make sure to buy it a few days before it goes on sale like I did

After 366 hours of gametime I can honestly say Stellaris is a very good game well worth the time of serious strategy gamers. It is very hard to win (I am nearing my second victory today or tomorrow maybe, after all those hours of playing) Lots of reading and scouring the web for info is needed to understand the complex game mechanics. Strategically it compares more to chess where you have to think several moves in advance of your opponent and moving your pieces is trivial. You need to have a plan and know where you want to be years in advance (in game time)  and adapt to changing events. Like chess neither side has obvious clear advantages until something critical happens but unlike chess there is some element of good or bad luck as in real life. Individual games are very long ( I have played about 10 games, some unfinished yet, since I got the game on the last holiday Steam sale)
The game is not perfect, in the current Steam reviews <<Mack>> and <<Maethendias>> raise some valid points. There is a forum, there are different points of view expressed but to me the devs seem polite and respectful in their interactions with the community.
There are companies that just throw out a game after a big PR/advertizing blitz and just abandon it unfinished and buggy after cashing out. The early access scene on Steam is apalling.
This company is not one of those.
I never had a crash or game-breaking bug in all my play time which started in December 2016. It is stable and bug-free. An example of dev commitment to the game is font scaling for 2k monitors. Searching the web I found  old Steam forum comments that the fonts were too small... Well they fixed that. You can adjust that in video settings. Also I have seen patches for UI issues and bugs that I was not even aware of.
Do not let the current negative reviews scare you away: note that 85% of 13,400 reviews are positive and about 50% of 800 recent reviews are negative. Some negative reviews raise valid issues like the 2 I mentioned previously but others have an axe to grind and take advantage of the Steam sale to spew their venom.
As for price: If I pay about 20 bucks for 400 hours of gametime it works out to 5 cents an hour, 50 bucks/month for a cell phone@2 h/day is about 83 cents/hour ( seriously if you are on the phone more than 2h/day you are not getting enough work, gaming, fresh air or sex and you need to stop wasting your time on social media ) a 2 h movie works out to $10/h. If you need cheaper entertainment the only thing that comes to mind is playing with yourself.
Bottom line: even at regular price this game is good value for your money if you are a serious strategy gamer.

Behind the Memory is a short walking sim with an emotional story in the background. Set in a rather dystopian future we control Hector who is on his way home but not to find anybody but to remember. At various locations our job is to inspect items (mostly within households) that shed more light on what happened to Hector's family and what kind of relationship he had with its members.
The game looks quite nice considering the use of Unreal engine. It is unfortunate that graphics cannot really be tweaked and due to this vsync cannot be turned on, at all. Also, Victor walks at an extremely slow pace so your best bet is to hit run at all times. While some screenshots showcase daylight locales a major portion of the game takes place at night which is also in line with the atmosphere.
Such low budget walking sims usually don't have a professional voice acting like this game does, plus, I have found the ending rather emotional which is also unique to this genre. I recommend this game but would like to highlight that this is one of those walking sims that people can easily find boring; it's just one of those games that is either a hit or miss.

I had a blast with Revelations. It mixes really well vibe and pace from old REs with shooting moments from recent installments. Keep in mind this game was once a handheld.
I won't spoil anything, but don't expect to find an amazing story here. It will keep you're attention, but it will make you roll your eyes in its cheesiness. Aside from Jill and Chris, the rest of the characters seem to come from another game and are very uninspired stereotypes. The controls are similar to RE4, 5 and 6. Dodging is the worse mechanic in this game, it's hard to understand when to use it since there is not in prompt. The scanning mechanic, similar to Metroid Prime, is a nice addition that incentivizes exploration and rewards players with scarce ammo and other items.
Revelations mixes the methodical pacing from RE 1,2 and 3 using puzzles, backtracking, closed environments and the horror vibe while having the more precise controls from recent installments. You'll have the occasional shooting, but those are the minority. It's not as intense as the Remake, but it's better than 5 and 6.
If nothing else, at least Relevations is a step in the right direction.

Probably my favourite game of all time, and if not my favourite then definitely the most played.
But that's probably because it takes a day's playtime to accomplish anything significant in the game in the first place.
With regards to negative reviews about it being too slow, then that's just the way the game is. Like it or hate it, it's a fundamental part of the game, the fact that every single thing you do in the game you have to work for.
It takes a couple minutes to cut a tree down and chop it up
It takes 5 minutes to saw that tree into planks
It takes another 2 hours of doing this to get enough planks for a small shed
It takes another 2 hours of putting the shed together, and I've not even added the time taken to make a mine and find iron, smelt it then create the nails you'll need.
Oh, and you'll probably be fighting a few animals at the same time, so you'll be running around trying to lose their trail for a while too.
I don't see why the fact that the game takes time is worth a bad review, that's just how the game is.
Every review you see where people are complaining about bad devs, unbalanced pvp in the main game, low player counts, bad servers and cheating are all justified, so do be warned that this game, even a 100x faster progress server in WU is still quite a big timesink.
That all said, I absolutely ♥♥♥♥ing love this game. Going around the beautiful landscapes, carving roads through forests, digging through earth making canals or soaring across canyons on rickety rope bridges or just a flavour of what the game has to offer.
I've played since 2006 and well I've never played a game that game close to it.
The immersion you get from having the game fullscreen, I used to forget it was just a bloody game... Mind you, I was 10 years younger but even still, the first impressions did stick with me and i love it all the more even now.
I'd urge you to play for a few days with either a friend, or ask in global or find a recruitment board and go along with an existing village. The game is extremely hard to start out on your own, 2 players are faster than 1 and it really does show. It's a very cooperative, community based game, which unfortunately this Wurm unlimited loses as it's got a lower player base than Wurm Online (main MMO branch)
There's a good chance you won't like the game, most people don't and that's why the game's hardly more popular than it was 10 years ago.
But just give it a go, it might just be the best game you'll ever play.
