If you're a fan of Tower Defense games, you owe it to yourself to check out the GemCraft - Chasing Shadows. Great level design, player-driven progression, an unobtrusive gear system for hardcore min/max'ers, and an endgame that embraces overpowered combinations. I can't wait for the next installment.

I've taken a shining to very few tower defense games, but this one is a particularly impressive piece of work. Masses and masses of content and well thought out mechanics in an ever escalating cascade of insanity. It is NOT an easy game by any means, but it all feels quite well-balanced, and rewards you for challenging yourself. My only real gripe is that the primary way the game handles escalating difficulty is by throwing monsters with higher and higher health and armor values at you; which seems like a natural progression, but the armor values quickly escalate to the point where any defenses that aren't absolutely top-level for the part of the stage that you're at, won't even put a scratch on the enemies. This means that the optimal strategy for almost any stage is to have one, maybe two towers that you pump all your upgrades into (along with a few traps and amplifiers), because if you spread out your resources you'll be utterly ♥♥♥♥ed when the armored giants roll in. It's still tense as hell and requires constant management, but it seems like it could be more of a spectacle with encouragement to install a bigger spread of towers.
That being said, it is addictive as hell, well worth the asking price, and easily one of the most impressive TD games ever made.

The game is a fresh take on painting simulations, where you are actually the painter yourself.
It does not have a rotate option for the canvas, so all drawings have to be made in portrait.
Even so, the game works with most drawing tablets and should allow most budding artists to create masterpieces.
At the beginning of the game Passpartout only has access to a round painting tool which slaps 100% opaque paint onto the canvas.
While the size of this tool can be adjusted, it forces the artist to look more in the direction of pointilism than much else.
Resizing the drawing tool to the barest minimum allows for lines at the size of a mere pixel or two, which should be perfect for the more advanced artists among the game's playerbase.
The potential buyers have their own group-preferences although individuals among them may get pulled toward specific drawings if they appear tantalizing to them, sometimes against expected group-preferences.
You can slowly but surely adapt to their wishes, but they will abandon you if you repeat artstyles too much, and be very vocal about it.
Once you make a name for yourself, more painting tools are made available, but the demands upon poor Passpartout will rise.
The richer inhabitants of Paris leave little room for experimentation; they know what they like, and if you don't match their expectations they will complain to no end.
With all the flak Passpartout gets from those who look but don't buy, it's no wonder he's got an addiction to liquor. ;)

This feels like a student project, something a talented sixteen year old might make and show to his friends. While it looks nice on the surface, once you start playing it the first thing you'll notice is screen tearing, massive screen tearing. I don't have the fastest gaming rig, but with 16Gb of memory and a GTX 980 I can run games like Doom at ultra settings, 60 fps and no screen tearing. The story is okay, but very predictable. The tone is all over the place. The father goes from caring to psychopath in just seconds which makes the conclusion half hearted. And what sixteen year old girl would shout at her dad: "You can't tell me what to do, you're not my
!"? Yet that is exactly what she does, it doesn't make much sense. For a little while I thought the father might have had an "unhealthy relationship" with his daughter (especially since he mentions that his wife is dead). But it turns out that this is not the case.
The game is short, it took me less than an hour to finish and get all achievements. There is not a lot of story in the game and like I mentioned it's not very coherent. For instance in the beginning of the game the main character fondly remembers going to a cabin in the woods with his neighbours (though at first I thought Christian was his son, since you don't find out what their relation is until a later scene) and that nobody wanted to leave. Only to hear him say that he never liked them in the first place less than five minutes later. The voice acting is poor and clearly done by non English speakers trying to sound American. The characters in the cut scenes barely move and when they do they look like manequins. The developer clearly took effort to make the game look nice and it doesn't look like a cheap asset flip or a quick money grab. But the lack of proper set-up and the uneven story makes it hard to get emotionally involved. The writer obviously tries to paint the father as a horrible person while at the same time trying to make him sympathetic enough for the player to identify himself with him. That might have worked if we had spent more time with this character and if he didn't go from likeable to cruel in a matter of seconds. A game like "The Last of Us" uses a similar set up and in that game it works, because we get to spent a lot of time playing as the main character, working up a bond with the girl we've rescued and protecting her. In this game it just feels off. In order for the final choice to have the right emotional impact, we have to either actually care for the main character or really hate him. But with the minimal story and sloppy set up I just can't.

A really nice looking game, very short but with a nice atmosphere which varies well to fit the progression of the story, but let down a bit by the perspective of looking back at memories, where your character has been put in very difficult or impossible situations and made the worst/weakest choice each time. So we are left slowly recovering/retreading the events of the past, getting darker and darker - let's put it this way - almost all of humanity has been wiped out by an epidemic and that isn't really anything more than a MacGuffin to let the plot play out compared to the events that follow.
A particular problem with the plot is the most troubling decision our protagonist made in the past isn't even touched upon - we know the final act he did in the whole sorry episode (chronologically speaking, we learn a couple of scenes earlier what he did), but there is no elucidation of why or how events of that final confrontation transpired.
Overall it is interesting and atmospheric, if uneven in execution, and covers some very dark material that may be distressing to some,

Just found this gem. Don't know how I missed it before. Am an old-schooler who played Panzer General (Remember the old huge boxes games used to come in at Electronics Boutique, etc?) and later Panzer Corp. If you liked those then you'll like this one. All the moreso given the derth of these kinds of games these days...
It's turn-based. Thank God.
You play through a series of scenarios with some carry through based upon special objectives from previous scenarios (so you can improve your situation in the future if you did well in the past--like take out the other team's cruiser which will not be there to bother you in a later mission).
You can assign special commanders to units, Units can get experience over time which can be maintained or diluted depending upon how you replenish their depletions. You can even have your entire force improved with other strategic bonuses that are earned. It's all good stuff you'd expect.
Some new aspects over Panzer Corp and others of the like:
Red line showing your front moving and indicating what areas are in and not in supply.
Supply ships and supply depots which once captured take a little time to kick-in but once they do you can move up deployment points and get additional supply points for existing troops.
These are realistic additions that make it play more like a real war than a computer game. Very interesting.
Graphics are nice, but I'm not as needful in this regard as the kiddies today.
I only have two issues with it being about 7 1/2 hours in (which puts you in the midst of the final battle apparently of this free "bootcamp" demo):
1) They did a great job of including both 1 and 2 button mouse control schemes for the interface but I am still sending units to the wrong place every once and a while (something that can't be undone due to fog of war exposure). This may actually be MY issue stemming from my time playing some other game with a different scheme but maybe they can help fix this somehow. It's frustrating when it happens, and like I said it might just be my issue but I can't think I'm alone in doing this.
2) the DLC breakout is a clear monetization strategy and I think it will only hurt them. Make a discrete game and charge a fair price for it. For example: European theatre, Pacific theatre. Boom! Two games $39.99 apiece and put them on sale periodically. It's not rocket surgery. This DLC business is just making everyone cynical. We didn't have any of this back in the day. Wanna see someone who knows how to still do business who wants to incorporate DLC? Look to is it Triumph Studios? The Age of Wonders III people. They are the gold standard in Turn based. Follow their lead.
Recommended. This is a free demo. If you like turn-based you must try it out.
EDIT: I should add that I have not played this game enough to fully evaluate the AI.

To start out, Wurm Unlimited is probably not a game for the player who jumps around, playing half a dozen different games at once. It requires focus, and a significant time investment if you have large projects.
WU has some nice sandbox elements with full terraforming (dirt and stone layers) and many options for building and bridge construction. It goes indepth on skills: Combat, Farming, Carpentry, Masonry, Pottery, Animal Husbandry, Spell casting, etc, etc. This can add enjoyment or frustration, often both. It is a game that can be played solo, but was not intended as such; playing in a group allows for more specialization, no one player needs to master every skill.
WU Servers can be modded (often heavily) for increased skill multipliers, action timers, events and playability. Many of the different server maps are custom to that particular server. There is also a decent mod community, although this is often limited to the specific server the mods happen to be on. Often a particular idea, such as portals, may be implemented on different servers in completely different ways. There is also a decent client-side mod community with options for improving playability and the general function of the game.
While not a new game, the developers still release updates to it several times a year. They also publish monthly devblogs to keep their players apprised as to upcoming changes and additions.

I used to play Wurm Online a few years ago with some friends and it was free to play. It's a great game and I enjoyed it a lot. When I heard that Wurm Unlimited was releasing, I was pretty excited, and couldnt wait for the game. This may not be free, but for those who enjoy a hidden gem like Wurm Online, this is definitely worth the money. This game in my opinion is one of the best Sandbox games out there. It is very very niche though. Only a certain few will like this game, since it is slow and is a survival/sandbox, so if you are hesitant on buying it, watch some Youtube videos on it. Either way, I enjoy this game very much and although its a little dated, (Wurm Online was made in 2006 and this is the same, just with servers and a few other things), I love it a lot. It's not like any other Sandbox game I've ever played and it is very unique and love it for its niche style. The map is large and you can terraform ALL of it. It takes a very long time to make things in this game, but thats what makes it feel more real. I love how it is medieval/fantasy themed, and I really love the music too! Honestly this game is okay to play by yourself, but much better when playing with friends. I played this game for 20 hours in the past 2-3 days. Before it had a standalone (Wurm Online), I used to play the game on and off. Here are some things you should consider before buying the game:
This game takes time. LOTS, LOTS, LOTS of time. It took my friend and I 20 hours to FINALLY build a 1x1 shed. [to be fair he only anted a 1x1] (This was on a 2.5x skill gain server)
This is not a game where you can AFK, even though it has that theme of it. Macros are HIGHLY frowned upon and often bannable. The closest you can get to afk is opening console, and typing "bind <KEYHERE> <ACTION> (MINE_FORWARD for example)"
Leveling up skills in a server that isn't modded skill-gain wise will take forever, and ever. Even on skill-gain increased servers it will take a while. Especially since the game does not increment by just one digit. However, leveling up and learning new things is only available after a regular integer.
Instead, it's decimals. For example, Body control, an important skill for riding different animals, will increment by like 0.061, or even lower. (0.0051?)
This game is boring as all ♥♥♥♥ without playing with someone. Being alone is boring and slows down a lot of progress.
Again, TIME. This is probably what turns people off the most in this game, is the fact that you can't buiild a castle from the first day. Hell, you cant even build a house on your first night. (Not even close too unless 10x skill gain.. hehe).
This game will suck your hours in like a clingy girlfriend.
This game is targeted for specific audiences. A lot of people you will meet and play with are old. My main server's owner is a 64 year old.
Personally-- I think this game is built upon time and accomplishment. You spend a lot of time working on something and the accomplishment, the reward of building said object is what makes the game special.
You should take caution into buying this game- If you're willing to spend hours on this game, hours and hours of dedication into the game, BUY IT.
If you have a friend thats willing to play with you for hours, BUY IT.
If you're not going to spend at least 50-100 hours int othis game, DO NOT BUY IT. You will not enjoy it.
Impatient? DO NOT BUY IT. This game is all about time and patience.

okay, so now we have two dungeons, three functional towns, and a whole bunch of other space.
positives
-music is catchy and fits with the areas that they're assigned to! battle music could use some work, but the ambient music is spot on for the most part
-graphics are clear and crisp, making the fast gameplay easy to read, avoiding frustration from an abundance of effects and stuff like that
-puzzling is for the most part enjoyable. Personally, the ice temple was impressive to me, it offered a wide range of different puzzles from the standard "reflect the light" kinda puzzle to more complex movement based puzzles
-combat is fun for the most part, although some enemies are really annoying in the later parts of the game. Everything from the end of the ice temple and before (about 80% of the game at this point) was fun to fight and had dynamic systems which rewarded certain playstyles.
-movement, like combat, is fluid and responsive. The movement, in tandem with the ambient music and the graphics, make exploring the world a joy.
negatives
-enemies post ice temple are idiotic. Flying enemies that you can only hit once every 25 seconds completely ruin the pacing of the game and there needs to be either a way to ground them (that is more obvious if it's already in the game) or just be removed outright..
-the story really needs to be reexamined. Initially when crosscode came out it kinda seemed like it was going to be a cyberpunkesc gamem, but now i'm not so sure... the beta/alpha has next to no story exposition after the intro/first 3 hours, so honestly i can't tell if they just intend to leave it completely sparse or if they are going to fill it in.. I really hope they consider hiring a writer or actually putting a story in, because as is the "hehe we're an mmo aren't we so witty?" exposition is going to be unpalatable if there isn't a REALLY dark cyberpunk undertone to it with actual death and despair.. I understand that the dev team aren't writers by profession, but this game would be such a waste if they ruined it with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ story. also, we need cooler characters. stop with the cheese. cheese is only good when there are actual characters there to respond to it.. Like, the first mission of the game is in a traditional japanese style fortress, and it's AWESOME. Then it hits a really high note, aaaaaaaaand then exposition falls off the face of the (cross)world.
-the trading system is also kinda dumb.. it's kinda based on a component system (with a gold system on the side), so you can go out into the world and get components from the enviornment and mobs ala a real rpg, and then you can trade those up for better components at specific vendors to trade to OTHER vendors to get equipment. Functionally, what happens is you have to 1. find an item that you want to make, 2. memorize the components required, 3. find the vendor that will synthesize the higher componenets required, 4. memorize those requirements, 5. go out into the world and find all of the components.. it just takes a while and it's a huge pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ but i can see the potential for some hidden vendors/equipment creators that could potentially make it cool. Honestly, i wish they would add stuff to the map showing where vendors are and what they sell after you discover them. Then have a little intro to the system at the start of the game where you have to go through all the steps.
-some gear effects need to be explained in the synopsis section of the game
~~~
So in closing, it may sound like i have issues with this game, but honestly it's just because I love it. It has such potential, and I really do have a lot of faith in the developers because they seem like genuinely passionate people. The game itself is easily worth 20 dollars, so please give it a shot! i hope they fix the stuff that i brought up, because if they do crosscode could probably be up there with some of my favorite games! also, devs, please release an ost when the game "comes out!" please an thanks!

Re-reviewing the game as it nears release:
CrossCode has progressed a lot in the past years of its development and the developers have put love and care into every aspect of the game.  Pixelated graphics that don't sell the game short, fast-paced and engaging gameplay, large and rich world with amazing story-telling and lore, a soundtrack that is memorable and meaningful in both ambiance and emotion.  If you're looking for a fantastic indie RPG that's worth obsessing over, CrossCode is the one.
(I recommend picking up the game on release in early 2018, but there is nothing wrong with buying it early; a lot of content is available to enjoy today)

While somewhat unfinished, what it is currently is an entertaining and unique RPG combat and puzzle game.
+The combat mechanics are very fun and satisfying, and work very well with the lovely art style and movement system.
+Challenging & entertaining puzzles that fit into the world very well, & really wrack the brain.
+Plays very smoothly, and not really like any other top-down pixely RPG games out there.
+Interesting universe that brings me back to Spy Kids 2, where stuff happens in a videogames.
+The music is nice.
-It's still not quite finished, but is still being updated & has twice as much content than when I originally wrote the review.
-The isometric layers of the environment can get confusing and stressful at times. Trying to platform around to get secrets & sometimes even required items is a very stressful puzzle when you can't quite tell if you can make a jump, knowing that if you miss you will have to walk back three screens to try the jump again.
Overall it is quite a pleasant and promising game. Great gameplay, graphix, and sound. Even when I was grinding for money, loot, and xp I had fun. The only thing the devs really need to do is keep on finishing and adding things to the game, and fix the ocasional bugs and spelling errors. I felt that even in the games less than finished state, that it was a very entertaining and almost zen experience. This game is definitwely worth checking out if you enjoy Virtual Reality & Sci-Fi themes, & also enjoy pixely action RPG's that don't use boring old turn based combat.

Zach, have you heard of the 2010 video game Deadly Premonition, directed by Hidetaka Suehiro? It's about an FBI agent investigating a mysterious murder in a seemingly peaceful small town. On the surface it looks to be based on the 1990 television show Twin Peaks, but it really takes the idea in a new direction. It's a very unique experience!
I vividly recall the wonderfully awkward voice acting and sound design over all else. The song "Life is Beautiful" holds a particularly special place in my heart. Combined with the dated-yet-endearing graphics the game oozes an inimitable charm. Though Deadly Premonition mainly involves driving around Greenvale to investigate the murder and interrogate suspects, there are 3rd-person shooting sections where you fight paranormal monsters! Such scary fun! The controls were a little tough to work with at times, but nothing unmanageable.
Even though the game crashed on me several times I always came back to learn more about the strange residents of Greenvale and the bizarre story. Thankfully there are fans that love the game so much that they created their own patches to fix some of the problems! I highly recommend you look into them, Zach.

This is just about the Best Tower Defense game there is. Nothing special here. :D
It is maybe comparable in quality with Kingdom Rush, but (much) more complex, and way darker in style. I know no other relevant tower defense game to compare with.
You defend yourself on many stages (levels, maps) against waves of bug-like monsters coming through predefined (but not limited) path to your wizard core. Your defense consist of firing towers along the path you can equip with different types of gems. These gems define what kind of attack shot will tower use (for example slowing, poison, chain, mana steal), and gem types can be combined together. You buy towers and gems for mana that is slowly replenishing by itself, but mostly you gain it from killing monsters. Funny twist is that your wizard core can "banish" monsters reaching it in exchange for some of your mana burning up, if you have enough of it (and there are ways to decrease banishment cost). You usually lose a stage when your core is reached by a monster and you have no mana left for banishment at the same time. And this is just core mechanics.
But did you know, that on stages you can also: use gems as one shot bombs alone or to activate powerful shrines, build power amplifiers for gem towers, use several special skills and spells to curse monsters or enhance gem tower damage, collect special rewards from destructible buildings, boost your mana pool from harvesting mana shards, kill mysterious apparitions for more rewards?
And if it is not too much for you yet, there is campaign map, where you progress through stages and explore new areas, there are exp and levels that contribute to your skill points, and there are talismans you can equip for various bonuses ingame.
And surprisingly it is not complicated game to play. If you wish to play brutally simply you can. And if you feel like you are up for challenge, you can try to use all of your options at the same time.
To sum it up:
+ Solid but original and complex tower defense
+ Control over many aspects of game difficulty, before starting and during battle, so you can push your limits
+ Nine gem types to combine, several meaningful skills and spells, talisman system bonuses, over 400 achievements
+ Background storyline about wizards, forgotten evil and lost rituals
+ "Dark-themed" visual style and storyline are nice contrast to some "lightly" taken TD games
+- There are many, many stages to beat
+- You can reach ridiculous wizard levels if you are dedicated enough
- Lets face it, it gets repetitive after some time
- No gamma correction means less visible details, unless you brighten your display settings
- There are some disbalancing, yet not game breaking mechanics, especially on higher levels
Final conclusion:
Strongly recommend this game!

I usually don't play tower defense games alot, but Gemcraft is different.
Gemcraft is all about gems (as the name suggests), their special abilities and their combination. While a classic tower defense game requires you to build and upgrade static towers, in Gemcraft the only static part you will place, are sockets for gems (two entirely different socket types are available). And costs for sockets will become neglectable in the later game. The gem placed in a socket again does all the shooting and killing monsters. This gives the incredible advantage to combine and relocate shooting power at will.
Gemcraft - Chasing Shadows is part of the Gemcraft series, which can be found on Armor Games. I spent nights over nights and countless hours playing Gemcraft Labyrinth. I also dislike in-game purchases, so the Steam release, which delivers the full game (and more) for a one time purchase, is really awesome.
One interesting thing about Gemcraft is, that everything works exponentially. If you have a thing for numbers, you'll probably love this. For example a grade 2 gem features roughly twice the power of a grade 1 gem and a grade 3 gem twice the power of a grade 2 gem and so on. Costs also increase at the same rate and enemy strength does as well. So in lategame you will find yourself surrounded by very interesting looking numbers. :)
Besides the main tower defense action, Gemcraft features a variety to improve yourself like skill points, which will provide most advantage when precisely balanced between skills and unspent points, or talisman fragments, which feature a random loot and enhancing system. It's also possible to make the game harder. Alot harder. Just add your favourite battle traits to the battle.
Further than that there are also countless other features, like gem bombing, dwellings, monster nests, mana pool management, shrines, apparations, and more.
All together there is little I can not recommend in this game.

It’s the 90’s, I am bored and up way too late at night watching public access television. When a white guy with a huge afro appears on my screen with a white canvas and the voice of an angel. The Joy of Painting was my first example that art can be done beautifully, compared to my own art adventures where it looked like I was electrocuted holding a marker. We have been there though, looked at art and gone, “I can do that!” then quickly realized these people were talented and had years of practice. Still, sometimes I see myself in a fancy beret, pencil mustache, and talking about how ephemeral things are. Then I realize that sounds awful, and stick to games.
When a game comes along and gives me the chance to live out that painter fantasy, it has my attention. Passpartout is our canvas today and the games’ features are its paints and brushes. The beautiful thing about art is that it’s completely subjective and Passpartout captures this extensively. If you are like me and can only manage terrible stick figures, you can still play this game. If you are really, really good at using Microsoft paint and can make the Mona Lisa you can still play this game.
Passpartout is game you only get as much out of as much as you put in. While that sounds obvious, it’s something I felt needed to be stated. This is solely about painting nothing more. If you are looking for something with a tycoon aspect like Painter’s guild, you’re not going to find it. I found that you do become intimately familiar with the different forms and styles of painting. Despite that, I admit I myself, wanted more but that didn’t stop me from enjoying the game.
You might think there isn’t really much to talk about when it comes to how complex this game can be but you’re wrong. You start off with nothing but a canvas, one brush and your imagination. Go make some art. There is a way to lose the game in the form of bankruptcy. Every painting you make is sold for sweet cash. You use this cash for absolutely nothing beyond apparently baguettes and wine. I guess it’s hard to make good art without carbohydrates and being slightly tipsy. These fees come out every so often and if you don’t have the money in your register, game over. However, to really lose, you have to not try at all in the first level. In later levels, as long as you consistently produce the quality of art that got you there you will do fine.
The game has three acts, the first act you can pretty much get away with painting anything. I did in my first run of the game. What the game doesn’t tell you is that there are multiple paths to take in each act depending on the style of art you make. While you are free to make whatever you want, to see every possible ending you are going to explore many types of art. I started with hillsides, mountains, cabins, Bob Ross rip-offs basically. This led me to becoming the Donald Trump of painters. Not my favorite ending.
When I started over I went off the rails and just started painting lines. This surprisingly worked very well. Expressionism and minimalism are just some of the forms art explored in this path. Painting itself is simple, perhaps too simple. You play this game with your mouse and nothing else. You left click to apply paint/choose colors and brushes and roll your mouse-wheel to adjust the size. Aside from the brush you have only two other tools, a spray can and ink-pen. Some will find that rather limiting, but that hasn’t really stopped anyone from making awesome art. Check out the Steam screenshot section to see what I’m talking about.
Passpartout
When you are not making art, the rest of the game is simplistic. You can place where you sell your art, there are different galleries, aka levels. There are random news stories that occur throughout the game but this never felt like it affected the gameplay. Not in a way I noticed anyway. You can click and move around the levels and make certain things produce a sound for an achievement.
In all, the gameplay is pleasant. It’s painting, you can relax and take your time. The only gripe I had was with how things were judged. You could spend quite a while on one painting and making it just right and watch it sell quickly. Then you could screw around and draw a phallus and watch it sell faster for the same or higher amount of cash. I guess this represents how art in real life is very fickle and no one painting is better than another, subjectively. Lastly, there is a negotiating system for your paintings. While it’s implemented nicely the system feels slightly pointless as all you do with money is pay bills. So if you think you are being robbed you can try to get higher. Again this goes back to Passpartout not being a tycoon game despite there being hints of it at the surface.
There is all sorts of fun in the design of the game. It’s like a Neo-Paris with exaggerated colors and all sorts of weirdos everywhere. So I guess, Paris? The character design for me took front and center. Like Passpartout with his watermelon head, or the punks with pink spikey hair, all of the characters felt unique, except for the businessmen. They all looked the same but I think that’s the point.. There are all sorts of people to sell art to and identifying who likes what is key to getting all the endings.
If you take the time to smell the roses, you will also notice some nicely detailed levels. The backgrounds show the Paris backdrop and later levels have some really nice artwork for internal detailing. Not you will notice all of it, as most of your attention is focused on your canvas. It is there though and I did appreciate it.
Another art form makes a small but impactful appearance in Passpartout, the music!
While the music is hardly the focus here it is rather well done. Each level has its own theme to it with some levels being pop and loud. Others being more traditional instrumental. For me this felt important to the game, the graphics and music are the only thing giving this any kind of body and personality. Thankfully it doesn’t grate on the ears while painting and if it did at any point, I was too obsessed with my Snorlax painting to notice. Only gripe I had was with the sound effects, not much is really there. Then again the game doesn’t really need it either.
Replay and Repainting go hand in hand.
Passpartout has a high amount of replay value, much to my delight. The focus is on getting all the endings and mastering all the art styles. Which isn’t easy to say the least. Figuring out who likes what and the style is going to be a bulk of the games length. You could finish your first three acts in about two to four hours. If you add up all four endings, that is quite a bit of game time. This is all depending on your style of painting and how much you put into each painting.
Passpartout does have some rather fun Steam achievements and Steam cards. I actually chased a few of the achievements because I thought they were funny. There is no controller support and I believe no sketchpad support either, at this moment. Think that would be awesome and would certainly enhance the gameplay of Passpartout for those that did own that equipment.
Personally, I enjoyed my playthrough of the game but not being really all that talented at art, I found my eye wandering to other games. I think if you enjoy sketching or have any flair for art then this is a game for you. Anyone can enjoy Passpartout, but its definitely a niche type of game.
Passpartout is certainly distinctive.

After a hundred hours of this, unfortunatly, i had to give up. As I started, I had grand dreams of building a nice little house by the lake. Perhaps it's still there, but I doubt it's stood the test of time (things degrade if you don't take care of them). As I sat by my campfire and my tent, leveling the side of the hill next to the water, molding wet balls of dirt into bowls and pots for water, I developed a dream. I dreamed that I could make it big as a potter.
I would work and work and work, walking down the road to the nearest clay deposit, only a five minute walk away, dragging my massive cart behind me (I was waiting for the day I could afford to buy a horse). I would wet and mold the clay into beautiful earthenware, load all of that up on my cart, and drag it all the way down to the market, a half hour walk with the weight of my cart and lack of a horse.
By this time, my house was half way built. All I needed was to trade my pots for gold and that gold for nails. I was confident that, eventhough I was good yet, my pottery would be enough for a handful of nails with which to build my walls. This was when my dreams of being a simple potter were dashed.
The game is so poorly blanaced that the merchents never had any money or anything you need. Ever. It's a cold day in hell when youre the first one after a merchent get's a shipment of gold and then it's a cold day in hell again when they have anything you need. This means that trade is bogus and pottery is useless. You have to do eveything by your self.
The community is friendly. Friendlier than any other survival game you'll ever play, I'd bet my life on it. But there's not nearly enough of them. And without the merchents to give my useless pots meaning, all my dreams and all my work was for nothing. At least I got a pretty house out of it.
But without money, I can't pay the tax on owning land. And if I don't pay the tax, my house will fall apart right before me. And once I built my house, which was what took me a hundred hours, and it's a hundred hours I will alway fondly remember, there was nothing else for me to do.
My life became farming some crops, tending to some animals, all so that I could feed myself, though I don't think hunger can kill you, only slow your skill gain, but still. Monotany. All so I could farm and farm and farm, until I ran out of the small amount of gold I had managed to scroung, there was no way I could ever face a monster and live long enough to loot it's pockets. I was doomed to watch my pretty little house, and the dreams of my eathenware empire, fall apart around me.

As of this writing, Crosscode is still in Early Access; so many elements of the game are likely to change in the coming months.
What's there is amazing. The art is unbelievable. It's pixel-art by choice, not a needlessly restrictive throwback or cash-in. It's what I wanted the future of gaming to look like in 1994, before 3d and FMV came along and messed everything up.
The music doesn't quite hold up its end of the bargain, but there are great tunes scattered about and it's never a problem--it just doesn't quite match the perfect neo-16-bit splendor of the visuals.
Gameplay is reminiscent of underrated classics such as Terranigma, Beyond Oasis, and Landstalker; though with an interesting ricocheting ranged attack that changes things up a bit and provides for some cool puzzle-solving opportunities.
The writing and story are fun, though the tutorials are a bit wordy for my taste. Depending on the length of the finished game, this may not be an issue, but in an Early Access mode that only lasts a few hours, it's a bit of a drag.
Excellent groundwork has been laid, now let's see the follow-through.

Crosscode is raw, distilled RPG gameplay.
The game simply delivers. The art is gorgeous, the music...decent. The story is serviceable, the setting being a Virtual RPG world overlayed onto real life. This setting allows for great visuals, although the story itself isn't particularly fleshed out as of yet (early access).
Combat on its surface is an easy to grasp point and shoot/melee system, but the skill required is surprisingly high due to difficult mob attack patterns, and a hard to master dash and shield system. The combat is just fun. There's no reason it should be this fun given how it isn't something particularly new, but it manages to take something old and make it feel fresh. It's something you have to play with to understand. And when you do get the hang of it, the flow of combat is fantastic.
Turns out, there's nothing particularly unique about Crosscode. It's an RPG with puzzles, quests, some storyline, and pixel art. All of these have been done before. But somehow, Crosscode polishes these old tropes into an art. It's a game that doesn't look like it should be this good, but everything comes together to turn out to be a perfect RPG experience.
Edit: Still Good.
Very short story so far, but this game has the potential to be great. I'm excited to see what the final product brings.

The positives of Steel Ocean are of course the submarines, they have a decent gameplay loop and are pretty counterable by the destroyer/cruisers and in no way unbalanced like I thought it would be... (WoWS take notice that it can work!) dropping depth charges never gets old trying to flush them out! Then there are more detailed control options  on your ships like shooting your flak/AA guns compared to the automatic guns in WoWs.. also there are single torpedo shots compared to the all or nothing of the other game... though you can still select a spread if you wanted to. General Warship and Battleship gameplay with the main guns are more like I'm laser sighting with the projected target 'dots', where each dot on your target is where each shell will hit 100%... though you still have to lead targets! It's not a bad system just very different to WoWs which is more RNG with dispersion stats to effect the hit. The latter feels more realistic though and some may hate SO's system as it could feel abit futuristic and  too accurate. The Carrier/CV game play is also more in depth with planes requiring refueling and more skill based manual torpedo drops which are very tricky and fun to master. The planes do run out of fuel very quickly though, but I can see why they did this.. to probably stop people sniping enemy CV's by skirting the edges like in WoWs until a good time to strike.There is a crew based system here unlike the commander system in WoWs. It's like a trading card like mini game where you get people with good stats and special skills then assign them to your ship. Finally it also feels like less of a grind to get into certain classes of ships right at the beginning, unlike WoWS where you spend a good amount of time grinding just to get into a Carrier or Battleship which is a good thing for players wanting to jump right into their favorite class.
Ok on to my negatives. One is definately the outdated graphics.. though not terrible.. they pale in comparison to WoWS which looks like a modern AAA game, while SO's looks like a game from 10 years ago, making me feel like I'm playing with toys than with warships. All the ships also handle really arcadey and don't drift as I expected them to do on water... and finally the real issue that breaks everything... the LOW player base... no one talks/chats and matchmaking sucks. It can take up to 10 minutes (or more) just trying to find a mid tier game. I am sure it would take even longer the higher you go up in tiers, as there is less likely players who would stick around that long given the wait times. It's sad that this is the main reason that I can not reccommend this game. It doesn't matter how fun the game is when there is no one else to play, unless you want to stick to the low tiers forever and play with the noobs trying out the game. Not to also mention that support for this game is pretty dead... no promotions to get new people.. no patches... no news. At all. There was even rumors that the dev team all got layed off or just moved on to greener pastures...
So TL;DR:
A poor mans WoWs but with surprisingly fun submarine gameplay that works, but the lower player base with god awful queue times, and lack of support from the developers really kill this game and makes it not worth the effort to invest any time or money into. Best stick to WoWs.

If you've played Gemcraft Labyrinth on Armorgames, you know the general drill.
If you don't, it's a tower defense game.  You place gems in towers and let them shoot monsters -- different types of gems have different effects (slowing, poison, multiple hits, etc).  You try to kill all of them before they reach your orb.
Along the way, you accrue experience points in order to gain skill points that make you more effective.  As you progress through the game, you come across "traits" that you can use to make a battle harder in exchange for more xp.
Pros:
- Super addictive gameplay.
- There are a lot (a /lot/) of maps to play and things to do.
- Over four hundred achievements
- User-defined difficulty.  I like this.  Overall, each battle is pretty easy, but you're given many, many tools to make them harder (in exchange for more xp)...but it's all at your own discretion.
- The game progresses at a nice pace.  You can go back to a map that gave you trouble ten levels later and walk all over it, or try it again with more difficulty.
Cons:
- Can feel very grindy.  As stated, there are /a lot/ of levels.
- Enemy scaling (in terms of health or armor) isn't visually apparent -- if your towers are one-shotting monsters now, it is not apparent when that will stop until it happens.
- Optimizing the angering of waves still involves annoying mathematical calculations
Should you get this game?  You can play it for free on
(it has microtransactions there; the Steam version does not have any microtransactions) and test it out.

It's silly fun. I needed to test out some combinations till I found something I'm good with. Let me summarize you what it is. Third person shooter game. The different thing about this game is gun customization. As far as I can tell (I'm level 7 I think) there are no gun parts that can be bought with money. Only cosmetic stuff like outfits and different taunts, things like that are bought with money. You unlock gun parts as you play the game. You are given "Blutes" for each match you played through. Then you use those to unlock gun parts. There are daily rewards. They can be certain amounts of blutes or cosmetic stuff. Today I got hip-hop pants for my character :D
When you first get in, you choose a character model. I think there are 3 in total but customization is very nice if you are willing to pay money. Characters are white or black buff man (who looks like Mr. T) with chicken legs and Helga (who is a fat woman). Then you craft your gun. First you choose payload type: Rifle, Launcher, Beam and something I forgot its name of. Then you choose other parts for your gun. There are over 6 part categories for each gun iirc which in turn makes good variety in guns. You can immediately test your gun after crafting it against taunting AI. You should try different guns and find what you're comfortable with. Then you jump in a multiplayer game. There is nudity (cartoony) and lots of gore in the game both of which can be turned off if you like. There is some puerile humor going on in there too. Taunts have a use other than looking funny, stupid or taunting the opponents in Blitz matches where you capture the point faster if you taunt at a control point but it leaves you vulnerable for the duration of the taunt.
There are "Casual" and "Competitive" games. Under casual you can play with bots but I don't recommend that. For some reason it wasn't fun for me. Vs. Humans is pretty fun. The game claims to match you with people who are at your level but I saw people complaining about matchmaking. I guess it is very difficult to get this thing right. Always some people are unhappy about matchmaking in any multiplayer game.  If you do well in a match, you get extra blutes for that.
There are a bunch of different maps and game modes. In Blitz you and your team tries to dominate the enemy team in a given point in the map several times in a match in order to reach the required point to win the match. In Extraction, one of you tries to collect an ore called "blutonium" lying on the ground. The goal is to reach to required point to win before the enemy team does. In Jackhammer, you try to steal enemy team's hammer and take it to your base while the enemy is trying to do the same. Hammer is also a weapon with an AoE attack which is fun but harder to use for obvious reasons. Again you need to reach the required point. There is another mode called Kill Snatch where you have to confirm and deny kills. It works like this. When someone dies, they drop a glass container with blue liquid in it. If you killed enemy and pick that thing up or your team mate does, you score. If enemy picks their own blue thing, they deny your kill. When one of the teams reach enough points, they win. I think there is another mode called Annihilation but I don't think I've played that yet. I haven't played any on competitive yet, so I don't know how it's like.
There is another F2P shooter game on Steam. It's an FPS called Team Fortress 2. I had played that before. For some reason I didn't have fun with it as much as I did with this game. In Loadout there is also some platforming and parkour elements apart from gun crafting. If you are remotely interested in shooters (that's me), this game might provide you with some fun.

Alright now listen up you little scrubs! This here is one of them old timey Simulators. Ya know the kind that granddad or pep pep loves to play. But unlike the ones grandad plays, your pc wont be loaded with desktop stripper viruses from those seedy eastern European websites. Now I am a man of complex tastes like toast and white rice so this game fit my personality well. This game is about as exciting as watching paint dry, relaxing and rewarding.  I played this previously when it was in its mmo form and was a slave, then slowly worked my way up to peassant living in the woods being assaulted by cougars and spiders. But now that you can make your own servers I live like a king, being assaulted by cougars...and spiders.

There are a few setbacks to this game however, if your pc doesn't have dual monitors you are going to have a bad time; this game requires an absurd amount of researching at first. thankfully the fine developers had the hindsight to add a wiki of all the things you could ever need to know, it's best to keep said wiki open in a browser while playing. Another thing is you need to build your skills and depending on how much time you put into it this can take quite some time (server permitting). I know it may sound weird but don't expect to be digging on the face of a mountain within the first five minutes of playing.

Now with those things out of the way, this game can be rewarding. Considering the time you put into leveling up your skills  any accomplishment you do be it digging a small hole or completing a fortress you feel rewarded. I love this game because of its high failure chances, and slow grind.  But for some this may feel like watching grass grow. Not me though, I once spent 14 hours watching paint dry on a cement wall. Now granted i was on pain killers from a wisdom tooth extraction but I did it, and enjoyed it. Another thing to note is the servers, now i recommend spending the fifteen bucks a month to rent a server out. (Bluefang is a great provider if your looking for your standard server) you don't have to worry about becoming a slave or dealing with griefing and wars, but if your into that kind of thing public is the way to go.

The last thing id like to note is the absolute depth of the crafting in this game. the amount of crafting you do in this game still to this day astounds me. No joke, its down to putting tar on ships and pegs in barrels in depth. absolutely everything requires crafting. this game does not give handouts to you except for the standard starting gear. This is where when i was talking about it being rewarding really comes into play. Granted you might spend upwards to 30+ hours playing to start really crafting things that may matter to you.

In conclusion would i recommend this game?  Absolutely.

Before Minecraft was even a glimmer in Notch's eye (though it should be noted that Notch had a hand in this game as well). Another sandbox was flourishing as players created worlds and adventures together. That game was Wurm. Now more than a decade in development Wurm Online has re-released as Wurm Unlimited. Sharing all the same content and features as it's MMO counterpart. Wurm Unlimited allows players to host their own servers with modified settings such as skill rates and action timers as well as the ability to use mods and custom maps.
With 1000's of items to create and over 10,000 recipes to cook up, there is more sand in this sandbox than in any other on the market today. However there is a rather steep learning curve (almost a cliff to be honest) and the graphics are a decade old. So be aware of those things going in. For the patient there is a lot to discover here, but it's a niche game to be sure.
Try Wurm Online's free period if you want to get a feel for it first. Just bear in mind that in Wurm Unlimited you can (and most people do) increase the skill gain rate and action timer speed, so if the extremely slow pace of Wurm Online puts you off (as it does for some people), that can be changed in Wurm Unlimited.

Silverfall is one of those games I always wanted to buy at the game store but never pulled the trigger on.  It sat on the shelf with Divine Divinity, another game I always wanted to buy but something else had more of my attention.  Having now played the latter and just finished this game I can safely recommend that no one play this game and instead play Divine Divinity if you're looking for a hidden gem.  Silverfall isn't bad but it's terribly mundane, I only ever encountered one crash and following the Steam forum suggestions didn't have any issues installing it.  I played it to the end, though I'm not sure why, it's almost mind numbing enough combat like Diablo 2 to just parade through for loot but the loot isn't very exciting either.  Overall I think this game was just a bit too easy, and while it isn't terrible it just isn't worth recommending that any of my friends play.  It's one redeeming quality, if I had to choose one, would be that it's graphics engine plays quite nicely with the Nvidia Control Panel so I was able to easily add far more AA and AF than would have been possible at release.  Even tech that wasn't available then like FXAA played nicely, sadly the game doesn't offer a lot of thought through detail so while you have a nice smooth cartoony look after adjusting settings you still aren't left with much to look at.

This sounds good enough in theory, but... First of all the crafting system that was added to the expansion is just pathetic and completely useless since the items that drop from enemies are even of better quality, not even mentioning that to be able to craft you must use the skill points to improve it, which prevents you from acquiring good battle skills and ends by turning into a boring game since all the hard job is done by your companions due to your character not being able to inflict a decent damage. Secondly - this expansion looked verry short to me, but this may be just due to it being boring, thing that stimulated me in hurrying to finish it. The last reason why i hated it, but not the less important - bosses have a lot of HP but inflict almost no damage at all, it takes like 3-4 minutes to kill one of them, still you dont even need to heal yourself, you can just let your hero and his companions to auto attack and go make youself a coffee. I recommend playing the original Silverfall, but to skip this expansion since you may end up by being as disappointed in it as i am.

Be warned : Silverfall installation is broken as hell on Steam.
Original game contain Tagès system protection. It seem Steam version never corrected about that.
If you want to play bundle, always install game in that order :
1--> Silverfall (don't check files integrity 100% because installation is neverending looping)
2--> Silverfall Earth Awakening (SEA)
3--> after SEA install, check file integrity until you reach 100%

To play game, always run SEA instead of Silverfall. You'll get all content.
Never try to install SEA 1st because SEA is false standalone : it use files data shared for both original & standalone extension (like PhysX drivers). If Silverfall is already installed, SEA will only download few files to complete bundle.
Run SEA only when done, you'll get choice to play from level 1 Silverfall or level 45 SEA.

One of the best tower defense games I've had the pleasure to experience throughout my life.
I played them all, and all of them were masterpieces.  They are all free to play on various sites (Kongregate/Armorgames).  While this game may seem like a rather normal tower defense game, it's much more complex than others.
You build a tower which has nothing in it.  For the tower to do anything, you must place gems.  These gems start off weak, but can be combined with other similar gems or different gems to create very complex gems with a ton of various stats.  There's no "build bomb tower" or "build barracks tower".  You instead have gems like "Slow the enemy by x" and "Chain in X range".  They start off weak, but get much stronger as you invest into them.  You have to figure out which gems and gem combinations work best.   You can also place your specialized gems in other towers by just swapping them around, as well as traps and support towers(gives buffs depending on gem).  The player even has the ability to create a gem and THROW it at the enemies, doing damage/effects equal to the gem you used.
There are over 190 levels and each level can be customized (as you unlock the features by playing) to increase the difficulty, the wave amount, the amount of monsters, etc.  Each level feels different from the last, and it doesn't seem to ever get tiresome.  The game offers over 400 achievements, which while may not appealing to some, gives you skill points to spend on the various skills.   The skillpoints can be allocated in 25 various skills, all being able to be reset and toyed with at any time.  There is also an interesting "talisman" system which allows you to boost various things, sort of like rarer skill points.
Why buy it on steam and not play it for free?
The steam version comes with new levels, better graphics, full screen, steam cloud, and achievements.  While not much of a reason to buy it to some people, the game is easily one of the best tower defense games  and I'd recommend it to anyone who is a fan of genre.

Passpartout is one of those games with a really novel idea but the dev didn't take that idea and expand it enough. This is a 'not recommend' unless you've got a 75% off sale or so.
You know the premise: You draw stuff on a canvas with an MS Paint-like tool and AI characters buy it from you. The AI does a reasonably good job in identifying pictures. If you paint something that is similar to something you painted before, they'll pick up on it and call you unoriginal, for example.
But your MS Paint tools are extremely limited. You've got a spray can, a paintbrush, and a pen tool that is laggy as hell. You've got a palette of 24 different colors, and that's it. Your canvas only takes up a third of the screen and you can't zoom in, so putting detail in a painting is really time consuming - like drawing with zoom at 25% or something.
You can't save any painting. Once you sell one, it's lost forever.
Passpartout is also very short. You can play for all the different endings I guess, but do most players actually do that in games unless they're going for achievements? For me, not enough happens in this game that would make me want to replay it like that.
So this isn't an artist version of Rock Band or something like that, where you're encouraged to draw and practice and git gud. It's more like a decent mobile game with an interesting approach. It's not worth $10, more a 'decent mobile game ' price like $2.99.

STORY:
You are Passpartout, an up and coming artist that is selling his paintings on the streets to punks, creepy old guys and baguette boy. Then if you are good enough to a "master critic" you can move up the ranks and get a studio where new people come in, and the cycle is repeated. Paint and paint. Get enough popularity and make a good painting for the critic and move up the ranks again. Rinse and repeat
Here are the Pros and Cons;
PROS:
-Entertaining characters
-spastic npcs
-VOMIT TALKING!!!!
-You can make something childish and sell it for hundreds
CONS:
-Gets boring pretty fast
-You can go great fast, or wait days and go nowhere
-Amazing paintings don't sell
-You can have tons of color and someone says there's not enough
-You can use 1 color and someone says there's too MUCH color
Sure I listed more cons than pros, but this game is great. Its worth a bit less than $9.99, but maybe around the $7.49 range is better. Overall, this game is fun, its entertaining and takes time and patience. You should check it out on Youtube if you need confirmation

This is one of the few buggy games I would recommend to people, and there are very good reasons why. For starters, it's horrifying and unique. The story sticks in my mind the way that Walking Dead has, and may I say, even more so.
Did you like Twin Peaks? Do strange events picque your curiosity? Then this game could be for you. You play the role of a FBI agent with a split personality. The twist here is that you, the player, are treated like the secondary personality. York needs your help to solve a cross-country murder spree, which brings him to the town the game is set in.
Mr Francis York Morgan is thust into a stunningly creepy town that appears norma on the surface, but harbours secrets in almost every home. Help York to stop the Raincoat Killer, and oh so much more. Scratch away the surface and look deeper, take your time and explore the world, talk to people each day, and you'll experience the best this story can offer you.
Please, if you feel you can handle a few bugs, give this game a go if only for the plot. Save often lest it crashes (but I've had to do that with Saints Row 4 about the same number of times). This game isn't about combat - it's about everything else. Solve the puzzles, find rare items for townsfolk to help you in your mission, remember the past and recount the present.
If you fancy something strange, and you don't mind rough edges, *please* try this game. Wait for a sale if you're unsure, but don't let it pass by without trying it. Even a year after playing it, the 36 hours I spent in this world are still etched in my mind. Thumbs up all the way.

If you’re going to measure Deadly Premonition using traditional gaming yardsticks like graphical fidelity, gameplay challenge, and overall polish, then this Director’s Cut still comes up short of modern standards even with the fixes. Yet despite any obvious technical shortcomings, it succeeds on the strength of its story, its characters, and its countless WTF moments. It doesn’t feature enough new content to interest existing fans, but if you want to find out which side of the love-it-or-hate-it divide you're on, now’s the perfect time to play one of the most memorable and utterly insane survival-horror games ever made in its most accessible form.

The plot is bizarre, with odd twists and turns, though it does borrow heavily from Twin Peaks.  However, it actually comes together quite nicely in the end and is certainly one of the most memorable I've seen in years.  The gameplay reminds me of Majora's Mask, with the variety of side-quests that depend on the time of day.
Admittedly the gameplay can be cumbersome, and some of the side-quests are way more frustrating than they should be because of it.  Also, there are a number of technical difficulties (I've died a few times by falling through the floor).  However, if you can get past those annoyances, it's a game that is worth your time.

Everything Deadly Premonitions does is generally mediocre, but it doesn't feel like a knock off, it feels more like a self acknowledged B-Movie. And although it may not have had a large amount of fame, the game has gotten a cult fanbase and become a hit among its fans.
The gunplay is essentially Resident Evil 4 mixed with Silent Hill. The enemies aren't particularly tough, they don't generally evolve much, but they're creepy and they feel right at home with the silent hill like areas of the game. The driving portions control like a PS2 game, and not GTA quality either. The map also makes the driving a major pain as it can be frustrating to figure out where you wanted to get to without any waypoints or minimap GPS. And there's some simple detective work with generally easy side quests.
The game is open world during some portions, giving you anywhere from half an hour to several hours of real time to wander around, do minigames, simple sidequests, or gather collectables. There's a ton of optional content to keep you busy and it makes the game well worth the money as far as content goes. There's a few 'realistic' elements to the gameplay, such as a need to eat and sleep, these don't really ever detract from the main game though, and never feel like they're a problem. I constantly found myself with TOO much free time and slept in between missions.
The game really shines with how awkward it is. The dialogue at times doesn't even make sense, and is often thrown in front of hilariously inappropriate music. The animations during cutscenes are all fairly terrible and it adds to the charm. The game will jump from a serious sob story, to a completly out of place morbid joke in a heartbeat. And its fantastic. The community has uploaded several recordings of such scenes and it truly shows how surreal the developers are.
The game really requires a sense of humor and a bit of patience with some of its flaws, but if you can overlook them the game is a hidden gem. For an example of the humor see this
The game isn't for everyone, hell, IGN (US) gave the game 2/10 then the UK side gave it a 7.5. Give it a quick look and see if it grabs your interest. It's a great break from the usual stuff.

The are sandbox games and then there are sandbox games. And then there is Wurms Unlimited. Long before ‘Sandbox’ became a by-word, Rolf and Notch built Wurms Online, it was the one and only 100% sandbox game of its kind to ever exist. In fact it was/is so sandbox-ish you literally feel the sand in your boxer shorts, period!
A disagreement between Rolf and Notch, lead Notch to create a silly little 3D app called Mineshaft….Minedraft?...ummm, look it’s not important what that was called, but Rolf powered on, with the help of his games fan base and soon he popped out a stand alone version of Wurm Online and called it Unlimited!!
GAME PLAY
So here we are, Wurm Unlimited has absolutely nothing to do with what is used as fish bait (or that other stupid game ‘Worms’) and everything to do with Medieval life and how to die 1001 ways. With Unlimited you can build anything to your hearts content, from tools of any trade to houses or even to grand towns and cities. You can terraform the ground, mountains, rivers or even make island fortresses. You can also mine tunnels and in recent months you can now create dungeons and dwarven holds.
“But we can do that on (insert ‘something or other’ here) Engineer”, I hear you say! And true you can but Wurms Unlimited is a Mico-Building game, every step of building is done tediously as like real life building. For example, you want to make a simple hammer, you must chop down a tree, cut it into logs then carve these down to shafts then from the shafts you must make the head and handle and finally assemble them together. Every aspect of this game takes the same route, mining to smelting, to forging, it is all done in steps like real smithing. Making clothing, ships, cooking (yes, Unlimited and Online now have cooking recipes), houses, everything.
Did I mention there is 1001 ways to die! You can drown, starve, bash to death by Trolls, God Avatars, become a chew toy for Dragons, Fire Fiends or Daemon Hounds, break your neck/leg/arm climbing mountains, or simply pick a fight with players and tower guards from the opposing kingdoms, so much fun.
Although Unlimited is touted as a single player game it is more of a LAN game, so you create your own server and play with friends and family over the Net or Lan. With the choice of Adventure (with some npcs, starter towns and a limited amount of game quests) or Creative (completely clean slate to do as you please) modes straight out of the box you will have months of fun but with fan/community made mod tools you can create your own maps, re-textures and a lot of tutorials on creating your own quests. A great example of this is to check out Katspurr’s recreation of the Ultima Online map on Youtube.
THE CANDY
All is far in love and war, so Wurms is not going to compete graphicly with the likes of The Witcher or Skyrim and even a lot of MMO’s are more prettier but Wurm is still pleasing on the eye with everything looking like real trees, animals, buildings and people, not like other sandbox games emulating that annoying Lego block look (Mindbaft?), so not bad 3D for a Java game.
The music sound track is pleasing in the background with some authentic tunes and some modern pieces but you do have the ability to install you own in the appropriate folders (there are mods to help). The ambient environmental sounds make the world believable (just don’t go looking for those annoying f^%$&*g ducks, their not in game, yet!), there is a limited amount of animal noises, and a lot of animals have bellowing animations with no attached sound, which might brake your immersion.
THE BOTTOM LINE
If you love the Medieval life, love sandbox and love micro-building, Wurm Unlimited is the bees knees, hands down there is few games that can compete with it, not even that game by Notch, before he sold it to MicroSatan! Its name is just on the tip of my tongue, Minefall? no. And even though Rolf has since stepped away from the development side of both Wurm Online and Unlimited, both are constantly being upgraded and is only getting better with time.
Anyway Wurm Unlimited is just that, Unlimited and only your imagination is its upper limits.

Since the free-to-play tutorial is basically a four scenario mini-campaign, it's worth reviewing it in detail. Things may change later, once I get into the paid content.
follows in the footsteps of SSI's
, just like
did for
, and it too fails, albeit in a more original - not necessarily better - way.
Gameplay is basic hex turn-based strategy, player earns something like Prestige used for purchasing units, units gain experience and can be upgraded, larger emphasis is placed on naval battles, objectives hexes must be controlled in order to achieve a degree of victory and to provide supply. What could go wrong, right? A lot, it turns out.
There's a bad feeling right from the start. Units have a nice 3D look, but not the terrain (compare to
). Someone thought it would be cool to have the player reminded at all times that THIS IS A GAME, hence the map is shown in perspective with clear-cut borders on a black background. Hmm, maybe just display the map full-screen or throw in some fog/clouds to mask the edges? The strategic map is completely useless as it doesn't show which units have moved/fired; um, greyed-out icons anyone?
Full spider-sense kicks in by the time you start managing your core army. The units' stats don't include the spotting range. When upgrading, stats can't be compared because the highlight keeps switching to the newly selected unit. As for the enemy units, no way to check their stats except by memorizing them since selecting one switches your view to the terrain. During deploy, you have to click an unit in order to see if there's a commander attached to it; you can detach a commander from an unit but can't attach it to another one unless said unit is already deployed.
Odd gameplay options are all over the place. If an unit able to capture a victory hex passes through it, but doesn't stop there, that hex will be captured regardless. On the other hand, recon units - which only have two moves? - can't capture anything?!? There's no option of using a train (like in
), instead it's done automatically. In a particularly inspired idea, there's no Undo Move...
An unit can move and fire later, but if it fires first then it cannot move. If it forces a retreat, it can advance in the vacated hex, but only if it does so at once, otherwise it loses this option (called Advance Move). Very bizarre: exact same move is done automatically when clearing a minefield, which puts your unit right where you least want it. I thought clearing the mines was done in order to open a path for other units to move in, not to expose my engineers to enemy counter-attacks. O, forgot to mention that engineers are also pioneers now, which perhaps explains why they're virtually useless at laying bridges. Consider this:
Engineers: Turn 1 - move onto river, turn 2 - make bridge so that other units can cross the river.
Any other unit: Turn 1 - move onto river, turn 2 - cross river.
Spot the difference? Yea, me neither.
In the same brilliant vein, destroyers can use the sonar... if not moving; or move and not use sonar. As for the subs, they feature an useless command that says: "Surface to recharge the battery". Rather pointless, I daresay, in a game where naval battles feel and play exactly like land battles, with units chipping off one another hit points with no specificity whatsoever.
had different types of damage against ships, even including critical strikes that could sink a capital ship in one hit. I wonder how could they do it back in 1997 and not in 2015?
And with the naval units we've reached the true
of
: the Pacific campaign. When thinking of this theatre of war what first comes to mind is the idealized image of task forces, carriers surrounded by various warships, forging ahead through stormy... Er, scratch that: throughout a scenario, weather stays the same. This is a giant step backwards, as
had night battles and changing weather. Then you find out that planes on a carrier can be upgraded - wait, what? (In fact, units can be upgraded everywhere: one nice absurd touch occured when I found out that I could upgrade a Jeep on a road to a plane...). Or that, for no valid reason, only one plane per turn can be launched (and can't move after), while several can land in the same turn. A torpedo bomber needs - in flight - a three-turn wait before re-using its torpedoes (cooling time for torpedoes on subs/destroyers might be explained, but on planes?!?). Better use dive bombers then, but wait: there's an enemy plane right over the target. Fear not, it will conveniently move aside to let your bomber take its place. Once you're done bombing you get an extra one-hex move for your plane in order to let another one attack too, which is cute - but only if you don't move another unit between the attacks. Why can't planes be re-supplied at an airfield occupied by one of your units?!? One more extremely annoying feature (they even warn you about it during the tutorial): the more damage a plane takes, the harder it becomes to destroy. Even if there's a reason for it, it makes an already frustrating gameplay even more so.
Frustration was a harsh reality in the Pacific theatre, where land units were extremely difficult to assault, dislodge or destroy. That was the idea behind combining experience and overstrength in
, but here the latter is missing. As a result, scenarios usually 40 to 60 turns long feel a lot longer and become boring. Expect two or three turns of coordinated asssaults to luckily (and in
combat outcomes are much less prone to randomization) force a retreat. However, again there are some baffling options here, such as why support for an attack must come from units in non-adjacent hexes (it's called outflanking support, if you're wondering); or why artillery doesn't support defense, even when adjacent to the defending unit, while AA and AT do. Capturing hexes that supply your army is a nice idea, but poorly implemented, forcing the player to constant number juggling, thereby detracting from the game itself. Furthermore, it works in a rather counter-intuitive way (what hex would be better for that supply ship to move to?). Another nasty side effect is that units operating behind enemy lines are very nearly useless because they're constantly out of supply. You'd think that such a style of play is ill-suited, to say the least, for the much more fluid European battlefield, yet the designers saw fit to release a Blitzkrieg DLC instead of focusing on more elaborate Pacific campaigns.
's two campaigns offered bonus USA/Japan invasion scenarios and alternate paths. Here everything is railroaded, with the same predictable outcome.
Be warned: the AI cheats. In the third tutorial scenario, there's an enemy battleship that spots any subs in its range of fire (that is six hexes; a sub only moves three); in the fourth scenario, an infantry unit retreated two hexes. Still, a more accurate AI assessment can be delivered only after going through at least an entire long campaign.
About the editor (which is generously unlocked only if you buy a campaign): it's only accessed from within the game, on an i7 it loads in 15 seconds, it boasts a needlessly convoluted UI (you can't even browse from it) and no Help file. Just compare it to
' almost perfect editor.
Despite the recommandation, I strongly invite you to play
, since it's free and it offers a perfect experience upon which one can decide if it's worth spending money on the game itself. Plus most (if not all) the problems described above are something that one eventually learns to live with... probably. Definitely not worth full price though: same as with
, a 50% discount should be fair enough - for starters.

The gameplay is fun, the controls are very fluid and responsive, and the combat feels like a twin-stick shooter like Smash TV mixed with an old-school RPG. It also makes me unreasonably happy that the devs follow the "show, don't tell" way of introducing new mechanics. For example, in the newest dungeon, the Bergen Temple Mines, the entire area revolves around ice physics. In one room, you can't go anywhere because a pillar blocking one way, and there's a force field blocking the other. If you try shooting the pillar, you learn it can move around on the ice, until it hits a wall. Later, you find another room sealed off with a bomb near a rock with a pillar behind it. Here, you learn bombs can move pillars, and is key in progressing in the room. The only time the game outright tells you how to progress is at the very beginning when the girl giving the tutorial straight up says something like, "Okay, you can charge your shot, and when charged it ricochets." Beyond that, it feels like the devs put a lot of heart in to the game, the puzzles are interesting, the towns are fairly large and feel busy, and they put in a couple of fun references to other things, like the Giga Spiral Drill (said to be able to pierce through the heaven itself) and some other references I'm sure went over my head.
It's very nice visually, screenshots do it no justice, you really have to see the game in motion to have an appreciation for it. The music is very Kingdom Hearts-like, which is a plus in my book, and your shots make a very satisfying "thwack" when it hits something.
One thing I DON'T like about the game is some of the platforming. On one hand, it's nice that you don't have to keep mashing the jump button to get up on ledges, but on the other hand, one example I can think of is in the Bergen Temple MInes, where I fell off quite a number of times trying to do a simple jump because I couldn't control when I jumped, and jumping at angles generally feels weird to me. And even then, it was only the one time that really stuck out to me, and by and large it works fine, it's just a personal gripe.
Another thing I don't like is that the game is incomplete. Which is why I bought another copy to give to a friend who I showed it to, so he could also get hyped for future updates and so I could throw more money at Radical Fish Games.
Final verdict: "I'm throwing my money at the screen and nothing is happening!"/10 I highly recommend it, even in it's incomplete state, if only to support Radical Fish and get the word out of what I hope will be the next big name in Indie gaming.
