Mufin Mcflufin said exactly what we were all thinking... This game used to be a lot of fun. It was an interesting take on Rogue-like with various other recently trending aspects of games incorporated into it (procedural generation, crafting, and all-in-all mimicing the Minecraft aesthetic) while still keeping the core gameplay engaging without loading it down with unnecessary aspects. All-in-all, this was a great game that rightly deserved every dollar put towards it. Note this paragraph is all past-tense.
The final update to this game has ruined the entire game, made it in many senses unplayable (especially compared to the ways that players used to be encouraged to play it before), and has tainted my personal view of the developers themselves. The developers have abandoned this game in favor of making a new game, Roguelands, which is a side-scrolling Rogue-like with procedurally generated maps, with crafting, towns, bosses, weapons, classes, upgrades, unlockables, and many more things. If this seems a bit familiar, it's because Roguelands is almost a carbon copy of Magicite. The developers have (by all appearances) intentionally broken Magicite in favor of rebuilding the game and charging all the old players to play the same game again.
I won't list all the bugs the final update of this game adds (I don't have enough space nor time to do so), but there are plenty of old fansites that list the very numerous bugs that now make the game unplayable. To name just a few for examples, one death in multiplayer games now fails the entire run (players used to respawn at the beginning of each new level), cooking raw chicken locks up your game, many unlockable items fail to ever drop despite perfectly meeting the criteria for them to drop, interacting with some NPCs can cause all shops in the game to permanently shut down, and the game is literally unbeatable now. The game will freeze then crash on the victory screen, causing you to lose all progress made.
Some of these can be dismissed as bugs that were simply not noticed in development of the final update, but far too many of these bugs (and all the many other bugs all reported on old fansites) are bugs that would be almost impossible to not notice in testing the update, leading me to believe that the developers of this game intentionally put many of these bugs in to destroy all playability of their old game so they could focus efforts on making their new game that is almost exactly the same thing that Magicite used to be.
I would recomment this game 1 or 2 years ago, but as the game stands now, I would not recommend it or anything these developers will ever release

7/10 - A STEP IN THE RIGHT DIRECTION
The latest entries in the series have lost their way and stipped away the horror aspect of RE, and unfortunately Revelations doesn't do much better. So to answer your question "Is the game scary?", no it's not.
BUT it is certainly going the right way about things. It's trying to bring back the survival horror, with limited ammo, creepy atmospheres and puzzle solving. The start of the game is probably the creepiest with it's dark creaky corridors and a lot of atmosphere. About halfway through the game though the action sequences make their ugly appearance and the game turns into a running and swimming simulator. It progresses the story but kills the gameplay a bit. The game also gets a bit stale because of the similar environments throughout. You find yourself repeatedly walking through areas you've been before instead of progressing onto new and interesting environments.
What made RE:4 so great was the fact no chapter felt the same as the last. There was always something new and interesting that set them apart from each other, and i had standout events memrorised in each chapter after my first playthough. I didn't get that at all with this game, every chapter was very similar. The game also splits the story by using cutaways and flashbacks where you play as other characters doing things either in other locations or in the past. I found these sequences to be a nuisance. They were all action heavy and happened far too often.
The gameplay is great though. You can tell it's a handheld port because it's a little rough around the edges and the characters don't feel like they have any weight to them, but the game still looks and plays great. You unlock secret weapons liek the infinite launcher and alternate costumes. There's also weapon customisation, which is quite fun. Nothing better than adding a +80% damage mod, charge shot mod and burst fire mod to a pistol. Raid Mode is also a cool new addition that adds a lot of replayability. It's not like Mercenaries mode from previous games, in Raid Mode you run small segments from the campaign in a score attack fashion earning you points and leveling up your character. Points are spent on buying new weapons and mods. It's actually rather fun trying to S rank all the stages.
Overall though it's a good game, but it's still a trigger happy shooter. It's just not as "in your face" about it.

Deadly Premonition is hard to write anything for without giving away spoilers, so I will break this down into two sections: A simple spoiler-free "Pros & Cons" section with a summary of my review, followed by a spoiler-filled review.
Pros:
+ Lovable characters in a charming setting
+ Extremely relaxing atmosphere and gameplay pacing
+ Hilarious dialogue and (mostly) gripping plot
+ Tons of side quests and post-game content to explore
Cons:
- Frequent crashes (both random & reproducable)
- Terrible port that isn't optimized for modern PCs
- Clunky, unsatisfying combat with terrible SFX
- An overabundance of ammo, healing items, and other pointless pick-ups (food & sleep were almost never needed)
- Many boring, drawn-out travel sequences that are unskippable
- Terribly timed and overused QTEs
- Tons of muddy, low-rez textures
- Heavily compressed low-rez cutscenes
- A ridiculous ending that almost ruined the game
Overall, Deadly Premonition is a one-of-a-kind game. I would recommend you at least give it a chance because you might not experience a game like it again. It certainly has its ups and downs; the good parts are excellent and the bad parts are godawful, but in the end you have something really memorable here that is worth playing... if you can get it to work properly.
Spoilers below, you have been warned!
I went into Deadly Premonition expecting "Resident Evil with FBI Agents" and instead received "Shenmu with Zombies". While the town of Greenvale is very charming and cozy, I feel that more attention went into the production of this digital town than anything else. It's a great place to explore but I felt no reason to considering how literally overburdened I became with pickups (many times my extra storage also became full) just by playing the main story. Its a shame Greenvale's attention to detail wasn't put into the combat sequences of the game; the Resident Evil-esque generic horror music becomes very repetitive and the combat's SFX are weak, hollow stock effects that almost put me to sleep many times.
Although the game starts out believably enough, with you chasing a string of serial killer murders in a quiet town, the game started to introduce "supernatural" elements that I assumed were the main character hallucinating. In fact, the other world invasions seemed to all be in Zach's head up until you control Emily in the clock tower and she has to deal with them too. At this point I was really worried that the whole game was taking a literal approach to the events happening. I don't know if the game was rushed, or if there were massive re-writes, but things got really, really stupid during Episode 5 & 6 at the end of the game. I wish more time had been spent on fleshing out a proper psychological thriller rooted in reality rather than the supernatural DMC-style boss fights and plot changes that comprised the last two episodes of the game.
All this is assuming you can get the game to run (and keep it running) on your computer. Even with a fan-made patch (provided by Durante, the man behind DSfix for Dark Souls) that has been updated many times since launch, DP is plagued with random freezes, random crashes to desktop, and freezing at reproducable spots. Lots of other small issues caused me to replay tedious sections of the game (opening the browser in steam overlay crashed DP almost everytime, alt+tabbing WILL crash the game, etc.); even though I finished the game in about 17 hours, I have 24 hours clocked on Steam because of all the issues I had. There were many other small issues that detracted from the game, such as sound moving around seemingly randomly between speakers if you don't have Windows set to Stereo sound, that make me wonder if ANY QA went into this game.
While I wanted to love this game, the last two episodes were a jarring and ridiculously over-the-top change of pace that felt like jumping from watching an American TV series to watching the last two episodes of an anime. In fact, Deadly Premonition plays more like an episodic TV series, broken down into bite-sized chapters (with "Previously during the investigation..." segments) than an actual video game. Deadly Premonition is a very unique experience but definitely won't be appreciated by everyone. If this game worked properly, I would be more apt to recommend it. As it stands, it is a crash-riddled mess than is probably better experienced on a console.

And presumably this is the reason why it became a cult classic and a game of the year in 2010. The main character, F.B.I. Agent Francis York Morgan (And of course, Zach) is easily the most memorable game character ever was made, so as the Naomi Watts look-a-like, Sheriff Deputy Emily "I love to cook, but I can't" Wyatt, and all the other characters, be it secondary or even tertiary characters. It is a highly recommended game.

Like many people, I played the tutorial section of Deadly Premonition on the 360 and dismissed it as a cheap, ugly, unwieldy, cheesy afterthought.
It's not. Boy, is it not.
Imagine a game made by someone who watched Twin Peaks, loved Resident Evil 4 and doesn't have a cynical bone in their body. The jankiness of the PC port evaporated along with the essential widescreen patch (YMMV however) and what was left was something that was in equal parts charming, kooky and memorable. It's an action adventure that wears its influences with pride and revels in its clunkiness.
I get it now. Swery intended *everything*.
Can't recommend the game at full price though because although it chimed with me in a big way, there are going to be people who hate it (and I can't blame someone for having a different taste to mine).
With a large reduction, everyone should at least try Deadly Premonition - Just promise me you'll play past the prologue.

Before I begin I must advise that this review is based purely on the single player levels in the game. There are over 70 levels for single players to complete so on that basis alone there is more than a sufficient amount of content within the game that if you lack people to play to get your money’s worth.
Perfect Universe is a monochrome completely hand-drawn and crafted precision action game developed by Will Sykes Games. It may in fact prove to be one of the best packages of mini games that I’ve had the privilege of playing. The highlight of the game for me are the hand-drawn graphics. These are simply delightful and are very pleasing to the eye and demonstrates that black and white is still a very much viable color palette in 2016.
There are three primary game modes followed by a fourth. The first of these modes is titled ‘Perfect Moon.’ In this mode you need to run around objects and avoid obstacles while collecting all of the different gems on each level. This is probably my favorite mode of the game. Giving you the ability to glide as well as leap provides you with a significant range of strategies that you can utilize. Sometimes the strategy that you feel will be best ends in spectacular failure. The tutorial levels – and this holds true for each of the three primary modes – begins easily enough but by the third or fourth level the difficulty really begins to ramp up. By the time that the difficulty reaches super crazy levels I was having so much fun that rather than getting aggravated by my miscues I was quite happy to try and try again. Unlike some other games that make you wallow in your defeat starting a new round is exceedingly quick. The load times are minimal all throughout the game which was another advantage.
The second mode, ‘Moon Life,’ is one that I have seen before. It’s essentially a copy of the mechanics from QWOP only Sykes has taken the mechanics and taken the gameplay to the next level. You’re essentially tasked to do what you did in Perfect Moon – collect the gems on every level in the fastest possible time while using these mechanics. I’ve never been very good at QWOP and I wasn’t very good at Moon Life. However, don’t allow my inability to succeed at this mini game deter you. I can definitely seeing those who enjoyed QWOP falling in love with this mode.
In the third mode, ‘Star Light’ you control a rocket and again you’re tasked with completing each level in the quickest possible time. The rocket powers along on a well designed physics engine so you’ll have to bare in mind speed, thrust and gravity in order to succeed at being fast. At times this mode felt a little like breakout because of how zoomy the rocket actually is. But that’s not a negative in my book as the mode gave me the most laughs.
Sports Day features six multiplayer sports games based upon the core gameplay mechanics featured within the single player modes. Each of them can be played as a single player – there has been AI built into the game for all but the golf mode which can be played alone – but I am certain that the most fun in this mode will be had with local co-op couch party play. My favorite of the modes here was the mini golf. This is probably because I found that the AI in the other ones was almost flawless and without dedicating significant time into improving my game I just wasn’t skilled enough to challenge the tough AI.
In all, this is a wonderful collection of mini games. Other developers would have, and have in the past, dedicated entire games that feature less levels to just one of the modes featured in Perfect Universe and have not been criticized at all for it. That Sykes has developed them all himself as well as the graphics and decided to combine them into the one package for $9.99 is an absolute bargain that will present to you several hours of entertainment. An easy recommendation.
Steamified score: 8/10 – beautiful hand-drawn graphics, fantastic value for money and a purely relaxing experience. Something for everyone.

Non-spoiler review
The port has been known to have issues so do your research first, a mod called "Fix automata resolution" may help most of your issues though. I played the entirety of the "canon" endings on the ps4 when it was first released and have yet to get my steam play time to match as of the time of writing this. The game itself excels in gameplay, story, and uses literary devices to interesting effect (I'll explain later).
The gameplay is a hack and slash combined with a bullet hell for the majority of the game. Automata combines its crazy genre switching in a way that makes all the mechanics feel like they belong in the same place. I can't think of a time that "mini-game" was fair or appropiate as all mechanics are fleshed from my experience playing it. Platinum Games helped in the development of NieR: Automata and improved gameplay far above yoko taro's track record. Do note this is not a platinum game however, and the gameplay is NieR to its core, not platinum. This means it is accessible to less experienced players. Gameplay options are available to masochists who wish for that though.
The game consists of a collection of characters all with their own motives and egos that all befall the unfortunate realities of war. Automata had me always surprised with the story beats and did not have any inexcusable moments of downtime, which is impressive considering the game can last some players more than 40 hours. It does not end after the game first "ends". Endings are more like chapters in this game as completing one does not neccesarily mean you are finished with the game. Gameplay and story changes after completing an ending and as you proceed through the endings characters who previously felt unredeemable are possible to empathize with as you learn more about them. The game brings about questions of humanity and the nature of it through the lense of existentialist philosophy which leads me to my last point:
Although knowledge of many of this games allusions are unnecessary prior to playing, it does add to the experience of those who catch them. I am NOT saying go take a class on philosophy to play this game or do any research at all for that matter. The game itself could likely teach an individual about what existentialism is by itself, without feeling like a classroom setting. A player may not even know the game is about existentialism if they were not informed of its presence or what the philosophy is beforehand. Some characters borrow names of known existentialists and take humorous nods to their real life counterparts for those who are interested. You do NOT need to know these people as they don't change your understanding of the story so do not worry.
In short NieR: Automata is a game that trys its hardest to do new things through out the WHOLE game. It succeeded in it's attempts mostly. Individuals who dislike bullet hell may be turned off half way through the game. This game is one of my favorite video games period because of its density(how much one could disect it). Do not be deterred by the term "dense" the game merely asks for your attention and time to explain its events.
I would highly recommend picking this up for people who enjoy games and have the time for a over 40 hour game.
*Sidenote: Sidequests add to the story as well as keep you from being underleveled. Do them. If a quest is too hard, then maybe you shouldn't do it yet.
-A person that enjoys games that make you think

This game used to be a lot of fun. It was an interesting take on Rogue-like with various other recently trending aspects of games incorporated into it (procedural generation, crafting, and all-in-all mimicing the Minecraft aesthetic) while still keeping the core gameplay engaging without loading it down with unnecessary aspects. All-in-all, this was a great game that rightly deserved every dollar put towards it. Note this paragraph is all past-tense.
The final update to this game has ruined the entire game, made it in many senses unplayable (especially compared to the ways that players used to be encouraged to play it before), and has tainted my personal view of the developers themselves. The developers have abandoned this game in favor of making a new game, Roguelands, which is a side-scrolling Rogue-like with procedurally generated maps, with crafting, towns, bosses, weapons, classes, upgrades, unlockables, and many more things. If this seems a bit familiar, it's because Roguelands is almost a carbon copy of Magicite. The developers have (by all appearances) intentionally broken Magicite in favor of rebuilding the game and charging all the old players to play the same game again.
I won't list all the bugs the final update of this game adds (I don't have enough space nor time to do so), but there are plenty of old fansites that list the very numerous bugs that now make the game unplayable. To name just a few for examples, one death in multiplayer games now fails the entire run (players used to respawn at the beginning of each new level), cooking raw chicken locks up your game, many unlockable items fail to ever drop despite perfectly meeting the criteria for them to drop, interacting with some NPCs can cause all shops in the game to permanently shut down, and the game is literally unbeatable now. The game will freeze then crash on the victory screen, causing you to lose all progress made.
Some of these can be dismissed as bugs that were simply not noticed in development of the final update, but far too many of these bugs (and all the many other bugs all reported on old fansites) are bugs that would be almost impossible to not notice in testing the update, leading me to believe that the developers of this game intentionally put many of these bugs in to destroy all playability of their old game so they could focus efforts on making their new game that is almost exactly the same thing that Magicite used to be.
I would recomment this game 1 or 2 years ago, but as the game stands now, I would not recommend it or anything these developers will ever release.

Currently, with this review being written whilst it's in early access, it is definitely an odd one. I recommend this game to support it within it's current state, but honestly... it's just not worth playing, not yet anyway...
The foundation of a school simulator and that of a fun game really is there, as are most of the basic rooms and functionalities, but it's also about as early access as you can get...
You set up a school, simple. Build classrooms, bathrooms, a cafeteria, a faculty, an office, home room and that's basically it... so long as your students are healthy and happy, they go from year to year with a minimum of fuss. Sure, there are a few strange bugs and the AI gets a bit annoying in certain parts, but it's never really enough to get in your way or is game breaking
There's no fights, although there is bullying, but at the time this review was written, it's incredibly basic. There's no drama with students, no dropouts, no sport functions or buildings, no prestige, no head-start, no parents, no politics, no cheating, no strikes, and everything else you would normally see in a school. Honestly, play it for roughly two or three hours max and you've seen everything the game has to offer
It's incredibly bare bones but there is a lot of potential here, and I want to see this become as good as Prison Architect and I want this to be the next School Tycoon game, but as it is right now, think twice before purchasing it. If you want to support the developers, pay the full price but if you want to actually play it and have fun and explore what the game wants to offer to you, then wait for it either to add a few more updates first or when it completely leaves early access

This game is an incredible amount of fun. Surely a gem that game out under the shadow of WoW and never got a real shot. That is not to say it is a game that was a forgotten failure. It is anything but. This game has prospered in its own way.
More than any other game I feel that the immersion is one of the best. Whether you like to roleplay or just go out there and build some things, this game really delivers. The mechanics are deep, the expectations seem realistic, and there are still updates dropping for this game. When I am playing, I feel like I literally have been transported to another time in some fantasy dimension.
To back this up there is a fantastic community. Now I have not played on a lot of servers. In fact, I have only played on a single server, Mythmoor. The best way to sum it up is with a small chronicle of events. Within the first day I spawn in an elaborate temple settlement that is the starting area for noobs. This game differs from any other in the fact that noob does not seem to hold negative connotations. In fact, as soon as I said I was new I had a veteran of the server say hello to me and proceed to show me around the server. I was taken to many awesome places and offered many awesome devices, such as an endless buffet and a bed! The second day I meet a fellow player who seems slightly more experienced in the construction aspects, but I have been playing with combat more. He shows me how to get started on building and then I help him fight through a crazy seedy sewer dungeon. We become instant friends.
By the time the third day rolls around I have already been invited to join a village. I have been offered a way to quickly gain a deed for my own village if I desired and someone has just walked up to me and given me a strong weapon and solid armor simply because I was new and needed it. I decide to join the village and someone travels up by wagon that is not even from the settlement and takes me all the way south on a grand adventure. They show me all the local sights and drop me off with my rickety cart in the settlement I am now a part of. The cherry to top it off? There was a huge sailing competition being held in which all participants got a free boat just for trying! That was immediately followed by a fishing competition. I expected that on such an old game no one would show up, but I was wrong!
Now, this was just my experience and I can guarantee a similar experience to any who join Mythmoor. I am sure the other servers are great as well though so don’t feel like you must, it is just the only serve I have been on.
The crafting system is deep in this game as well. You might think making a bow is as easy as chopping down a tree, turning it into sticks and you are done. It is far from it. You must chop down a tree. Carve out a bow of your choice with a knife. Find hemp growing in the wild or get it from a player. Use a rope maker to turn the hemp into string. Then finally string the bow. Of course, you probably would need to make the rope tool as well which has all its components. The result if it is your first bow? Probably a piece of junk! But the crafting system relies on skills so repetition will get you there.
Cons expanded
The combat in this game, is kind of a joke. It doesn’t seem particularly deep. It is an auto attack based system. Things like your footing come into play. If you have a high ground advantage over your foe you get a small bonus in combat. Other things like being mounted come, type of weapon, and armor come into play. You can also choose where to hit your enemy. When it all boils down though, it is an auto attack combat system. Don’t play this game for the combat.
My next big gripe was the clipping. I don’t particularly enjoy it. You can clip through wagons and other moveable objects pretty much at will. There is a huge list of objects that the game lets you clip through. I think mostly this is a defense mechanism to keep griefers from like, locking you in your house by putting a wagon against the door or something. Might just be a limitation of the engine as well. Now, you can’t clip into someone else’s home or anything, but you can clip through a lot of things and it breaks immersion sometimes.
You will see a lot of reviews mention the learning curve. Yeah, it is drastic. I have played for 50+ hours and I am still learning and have a lot more to learn. I wouldn’t say I have even got through the tip of the iceberg and there is an iceberg of things to learn. The good note here is the community will always help you out and there is a decent wiki for this game as well.

After spending time and a small amount of cash on a few premium ships, I feel somewhat underwhelmed with this game, not because it's bad, It's arguably the greatest ship-based team game out there at the moment, but because of 1 failing in particular:
- A complete lack of ADVERTISING.
shocking I know, however it really lets the game down as there's hardly any playerbase at all. You'll be lucky to find 300 people online at a time...300! Matches should be 16v16, but the game struggles to find players to match with as there's none ingame, so you're stuck with 3v3.
So why the lack of population?
In short, no-one knows it exists! Everyone has heard of World of Warships [because they advertise] and yet this game makes that look like some sort of highschool design project.
How come the devs don't advertise?
The game is created by a team of Chinese Game Developers, and they have 2 servers for this game: 1 in China which is only accesible to Chinese citizens because of Chinese law, and the North American one you can access here on steam. The Chinese server has roughly 1 million individual gamers, with about 100000 logged in at any 1 time, so the devs feel that the game doesn't need any advertising, as they are already raking in the cash from their Chinese server.
Is there any chance of advertising in the future/something to increase the playerbase?
No. The devs have made it clear that they won't do anything new to market the game, and support dried up about 6 months ago leaving only server maintenance.
TL:DR
11/10 for gameplay
-1/10 for server population
Even War Thunders ♥♥♥♥♥♥ naval row boats would be better than this game, as you wouldn't have to wait 5 years for a match bigger than 3v3

I obsessed over my masterpiece for nearly an half an hour, selecting each color and placing each line just so, before deeming it ready for exhibition The first person to see it was an aristocrat wearing a powdered wig: she promptly decried it as unoriginal garbage, and left without even looking at anything else. I think she came into my gallery specifically to insult me. This is Passpartout, and possibly the art world it’s mocking, in a nutshell. You will pour your soul into a piece only for it to be misunderstood and mocked, and then be praised as a wunderkind for a painting that’s just the poop emoji on a rainbow background. I know because I sold that painting. I am not proud.
Passpartout is not deep game. I mostly stuck to abstract paintings not only because I lack talent, but also because the toolset the game offers (basically a few functions from MS Paint) makes it very hard to paint anything with any degree of precision. I took wild stabs in the dark when guessing what kind of paintings my patrons wanted, because they always seemed more interested in telling me what they didn’t like about a painting than what they did like. I tried painting a coffee cup for an older gentleman named George, because he always carried one with him; he loved it, and I was even able to bleed a few extra euros out of him for it. Though the guesswork and imprecision occasionally make the game feel directionless, they’re more features than they are flaws. That’s because Passpartout has very little interest in making you feel like a master of your craft or giving you the tools necessary to produce worthwhile art. It’s much more interested in watching you flail about wildly in an attempt to produce something passable, and then scam strangers into buying your misbegotten creations when you inevitably fail.
In the end, I attracted the attention of a wealthy patron who was more than happy to pay increasingly outrageous sums for whatever garbage I churned out. The art critics spurned me and called me a sellout, but it was hard to care when I didn’t have to worry about paying bills anymore. Was it a worthwhile journey? Yeah, probably, but more for the narrative I pieced together in my head than for any particularly outstanding mechanics. There’s the lack of direction I mentioned before, and pacing occasionally becomes an issue. There were times when no one wanted to buy my paintings and I wasn’t sure why, or extended periods when my work was flying off the shelf faster than I could produce it, and I was just waiting for the next act to trigger. Passpartout is generally good at hiding it’s technical shortcomings under a flurry of madcap nonsense, but in its quieter moments you begin to see its limitations and experience some of the drudgery that must come with being an actual real-life artist. Still, it’s to the game’s credit (or maybe just luck?) that even its failures can be hand-waved away as being part of the experience. Whether or not that experience will appeal to you ultimately comes to how willing you are to be carried away by its particular brand of comedy.

My favorite naval game.
The main reason behind it is the submarines. Because this game has them, the gameplay is less awkard than other games. It heavily relies on teamplay, and it's much more important to keep a balanced fleet composition alive than going for pure damage or whatever. And because of that, you are much more interested into playing your role well. Sinking a submarine as a destroyer probably won't give you the MVP, but it will save the Battleships in your team, who will sink the enemy destroyers in return. Which will in the long run give you the victory.
So why am I talking about submarines ? Because they have torps, which are rather slow compared to shells, their main targets in this game are capital ships. So you are going to need destroyers (fast and agile ships) to sink them. Destroyers that are essential for scouting (spotting without being spotted). Light cruisers will easily sink destroyers, while Heavy Cruisers will beat Light Cruisers. Finally Battleships take the role of artillery, but they will need scouts to find targets. Aircraft carriers will bring scouts, torps bombers, dive bombers and airfighters to the battlefield. In the end, it gives to the game a much more realistic tone than World of Warships, with absurdities like airfighters on light cruisers (because WoW doesn't have scouts). It gives much more variety in gameplay.
Also, the game is quite fast paced, with games lasting around 15 mins, which is not necessarily bad, given that I am talking about a video game.
The skill ceiling is much higher, for the simple fact that players are given a lot of things to control. Players have to train and pick your crew among a decent number of commanders, which have their own fixed traits. All the weapons, at the exception of 13mm AA guns, are under the control of the player. It's possible to configurate the load-out of your ship (ammo and consumables mostly), like removing dive bombers from an aircraft carrier and taking more airfighters instead (I wish your destroyer or sub never meets my japanese ramming sub ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°) ).
Some negative traits however: the graphisms are ok, but aren't up for 2017. The gold smoke is the only premium item that made me rage. It lasts twice as long as the default ones and you can take more of them. Ie you can take for 90 secs of smoke in your ships by default, but 5 mins with the golden smokes. And you will often meet them at higher tiers.
And no, it's not a copy of World of Warships.

I own 2 Total War games, This and Attila, and I only got Attila for The AOC DLC. Attila has some great features (manual aiming catapults for one), but Medieval 2 is definitely the better game out of the box. I had to mod the hell out of Attila before I started enjoying it (I still don't really like the Main Campaign). This game does have drawbacks though.
Pros:
-Medieval era, with eventual gunpowder/cannons development
-Runs well even on potatoes
-A few great mods like TATW,MOS,DAC (MOS is probably ~200 of my hours)
-Cavalry is actually useful in battle (rohirrim style charges)
-Spearmen can actually hold the line
-Cool battle maps
-You can actually pick out captains/generals from their units. They're the fancy looking ones (not a big deal, just neat, also very helpful for targeting them to break the enemy's morale)
-Can play as almost any faction without having to pay for them, unlike Attila
Cons:
-Diplomacy flat out sucks in my opinion. There's not really an "affinity" system like in Attila, so you don't really know where you stand with other factions. Also, allies you make may very well turn on you, or each other without warning. Trust no one. Especially the HRE.
-The game is from 2006, so graphics and animations are definitely not up to today's standards.
-No General's abilities apart from rallying horn. They're just heavy cavalry that are vital to morale.
-Artillery is very innacurate. No pinpoint shots like in Attila.
-The Pope is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥br>-DLC is actually worth paying for. 4 new campaigns for ~$1.50 (on sale)
I haven't played vanilla in a while, so I may not remember all that 100%, and I may have forgotten to mention a few things. But overall, It's a great game

This game is phonomenal! The campaign is absolutely survival-horror, it's actually the best survival-horror game I've ever played. You're outnumbered by creatures you've never even seen before, and trying to escape the Queen Zenobia (it's set on an abandoned ship) alive. This definetely gave me a good couple of scares, and some of the creatures you'll encounter will seriously creep you out (Rachel, anyone?). After you've finished the campaign, you can start a new game+, which allows you to replay the game with all your current gear, to relive the horror once more. There are 30 handprints to find throughout the campaign, which gives achievement hunters some satisfaction in searching. Once you're through the campaign, your fun has only begun; as there is also Raid Mode to accompany it. Raid Mode is a great multiplayer experience that allows you to go through sections of the game as stages, and each time you complete a stage you'll get new weapons and/or weapon parts, depending on how well you've done. There are a multitude of stages to do, as well as 3 difficulties to do them all in. If multiplayer isn't really your thing, you can do Raid Mode solo if you like. The price tag may be $50, but it is well worth it as you'll definetely clock in a considerable amount of hours. This is a great gmae to get if you're either looking to get into the Resident Evil series, find a good survival-horror game, or just want to have a really fun time. A must-buy :)

AdVenture Capitalist, the idle game that gives you a simple lemonade stand and turns you into the richest man alive. With so much to cover I will start with gameplay.
Gameplay: The gameplay is a simple style of gameplay that is suprisingly fun and addicting! You start off on Earth where you click a lemonade stand repetively to get money. With the money you can buy more shops or managers. Managers will run any shop for you so you don't have to keep clicking. More shops mean more money. The higher costing shops give you more money but take longer. As you buy more shops the game will reward you with faster money speed and multipliers. There are tons and tons of upgrades to help push you through the game. Also, there are Angel Investors. Once you have Angels you have to restart the game to obtain them. Don't worry, because the Angels help out a lot! They will give you more money. Soon, the first click on the lemonade stand will give you a million dollars! You can fund missions to Mars and the Moon where you basically repeat the same process with more upgrades, shops, and unlockables. The develepors are always updating, so expect more in the future. Also, they make events on holidays and such, which adds more stuff in the game.
Story: There is no story, so don't worry about it.
Sound: The music in this game is generally repetetive, but very catchy. Nothing much because there is a mute button. When you buy upgrades and get unlocks it makes a nice cha-ching sound. Very cheerful sounds for a cheerful game. It makes the game oddly brighter.
Graphics: It is a 2D game with a lot of text, cartoons, and buttons. Nothing too spectacular. The cartoons are usually silly and well drawn. Each planet and event has it's own theme and they all fit very well. Looks spectacular for what it is meant to be.
Genre: It is an idle game. You basically feel like you are doing something when you really aren't. You basically wait and do stuff on occasions.
Price: It is free! Even if this review doesn't convice you, you can still try it and not spend a dime, technically, you are making money.
My Opinions: To me, I love Idle games. They are very fun and addicting. I think this game is fantastic. With so many options and multiple updates. I never get bored. I think what they have done is amazing, and if you like idle games, so will you.
Tl;Dr: AdVenture Capitalist is an idle game that gives you many options and takes a while to complete. You gain money over time, buy♥♥♥♥♥♥ and make more. You repeat this on a majority of worlds until you are the richest ♥♥♥♥♥ alive. Also, the game is free, so just get it.

It is one of the best games which i played in my gaming history.
For me it should have at least a nomination for Game of the year, as it is just a fantastic and amazing game.
At first i wasn't really sure if i wanted to get it but after watching some videos and reading some stuff about it over internet, i decided to give it a go.
And it was worth every hour i spend playing it!
Story is just brilliant, it is one of the best stories i ever played.
It does have 26 endings but only 5 count as main ones.
Ending A - wasn't expecting that all stuff at end
Ending and route  B - can get a bit boring at some point but it is needed to play it to understand story even better
Ending C -  one word to describe it, amazing
Ending D - that ending is also amazing and make you think a bit...
Ending E - it is just one of the best endings i ever saw in games in many years... and you will want more after it... also after this ending there is something which is raerly seen in games and i was a bit surprised about it, but i wont tell what you need to find it by yourself ;)
It is required to play through all of main endings to fully understand this game.
Main characters of it are really nicely done;
2B is a main character and i liked her the most because of her "character".
9S is just a poor little boy who got himself into something big.
A2 when she appeared in the game she sounded a little bit same as 2B and it was also nice to play as her.
Because of that characters you can get a bit emotional at some missions (like i did) because as i said you can really get close to them and it dosen't really happen to often in games...
Soundtrack is one of the best game music i ever heard, especially Weight of the World.
Gameplay in overall is great too, main quest wast at start a bit confusing but later when you made it through few first missions it was just getting better and better.
Side quests were pretty ok and it wasn't necessary to do them, yet they were interesting despite that they were almost all same.
I really liked crafting system even when it was a little bit frustrating at some times to collect enough materials to upgrade weapons.
There is enough weapons for everyone to fit their game style :)
Graphic isn't the best in it but everything else compensate it or at least it did for me.
Voice acting is pretty nice too, on first playthrough i played it with Japanese voice and english text and now i'm planning to play it again with English voices to see how they sound :)
If you are a emotional person you might be "touched" by few moments in this game as i was left almost in tears at some points of it...
I guess that's enough of my mumbling.
Yes i do recommend this game fantastic game, it is a GOTY material for me, and i  give it full 10/10.
I might not cover everything or not say everything i want but last thing i will say is that after playing this game i was left in a shock how good it was, and it did touch something inside of me...

This isn't going to be a particularly long review, but I'm going to try to highlight the best things about this game that I've seen so far.
Gameplay: Gameplay is challenging, action oriented, and has a good deal of depth, with close combat and ranged attacks joined by powerful abilities, fluid and fun movement, dodging, and blocking to provide a robust game experience. A+
Art: Charming retro art that doesn't have the "Love me because of nostalgia" vibe. The developers are amazing at this kind of art, and the love and detail put into this game is clear. A
Sound: The music does get a bit repetitive at times, but is cheerful enough and in keeping with the graphics. The sound effects could use a bit of variety, but they serve well enough and are quite functional. While you'll be listening to a ton of the same stuff, it's solid, and my only complaint is the scarcity because I would love more (and I'd buy the soundtrack).  B
Story: Still in progress. The developers are putting content ahead of story in their priorities, so there's still quite a bit to play even though the story (more of a prologue at this point) only runs about an hour. The dialogue is tounge-in-cheek and often parodies videogame cliches, but does so without being too heavyhanded and I find it quite amusing. If the story is writen as well as the dialogue is, I forsee the outcome being quite good. ?????
Systems: I normally don't take note of a game's systems like UI because normally I just suffer through mediocre menus, only noticing when something is so painfully tedious that it requires extra effort. However, the UI of Crosscode is exquisite, with clear markers of what's happening when, items sorted neatly, and quick, easy to navigate menus. If every RPG had this menu system, I would not complain. It is wonderful. A++++
I have no complaints with this game in its current state. It is in early access (0.4 at the moment) and I expect there to be plenty of room to grow- and that's apparent. This will be one of those games that I check out every time a major update gets pushed out. I have no concerns for the future of the game because a wonderful foundation is in place, and as long as the developers manage to keep improving (the last time I played before Early Access was an early beta demo that only had the first few stages in, and I was hooked then) it will be great! The only danger I see is the chance of grind in the future; it's already a little bit grindy (since it's styled like an MMO, with MMO style quests and drop rates and leveling and all that entails) but if the gameplay is as solid as it is I will at least enjoy it.
Overall: Undecided. I am very optimistic, and would enthusiastically recommend it to anyone who enjoys action combat, RPGs, and puzzle platforming. There is a lot of potential here, and as long as it doesn't get botched I see it being a wonderful game. Likewise, my few complaints may be addressed in the future, so I don't want to leave any negative feedback that doesn't accurately reflect a later state of the game (since I'll probably forget to update this). Tentatively: A (9/10)

The gameplay feels responsive and is simple yet chalenging to play.  You have a dash or a block for defence, and a ranged "ball attack" or melee attack for offence.  This is the extent of gameplay at the begining of the game.  Their are upgrades which can give your character new skills and buffs.  Using all your characters abilities is essential to defeating enemies quickly and effectively.  Often I found I needed to learn the pattern of enemies and adapt how I played.

Your main character's ranged attack "ball" attack can bounce a few times when charged up.  This is great since dungeons so far mainly consist of puzzles, which utilize this mechanic very well.  This mechanic so far has not gone stale, since thier are many objects your ball can trigger, reflect, pass though, remove, and hopefully their will be more things your ball can do.  I hope the devs continue with this because bosses could be such a treat to defeat.  Their will be some more mechanics added later which look like you can change "elements" of your attack mid battle.

I own and have played every TW title from Medieval I to Warhammer. Of all these, although I do enjoy them all and play them frequently (except for Medieval I which frankly is too archaic and I can no longer stomach), my favorite is still Medieval II. Although the graphics are of course a bit outdated and it lacks some features we have come to take for granted in later games, such as tech trees, it still can be considered mainstream. You don't feel it to be that different from more modern TW games, which cannot be said about Rome I or Medieval I. On the other hand, Med II has some features that sometimes are missing in later games, such as family lines and royal marriages. Mods such as Stainless Steel further help to keep the game enjoyable and actual. Finally, it is the only TW game covering the Middle Ages period, which for many of us is paradigmatic for the type of warfare depicted in these games.
Overall I give it 4 stars; 5 stars if you dismiss the graphics factor.

Resident Evil: Revelations is a pretty decent Resident Evil game, following in the footsteps of Resident Evil 4 which changed how the series played.
+Campaign's an enjoyable ride of action and your run-of-the-mill zombie shooting.
+Gun customization allows you to utilize guns in both Raid and Campaign modes as you see fit.
+You see favorite characters returning followed by some new faces.
+Raid mode's a fun time killer with upgradable guns and rarities, but general experience grinding.
+Combat is standard RE4/RE5/RE6 fare.
-Story's kind of lacking and silly.
-The writing is pretty awkward at points ("Me and my sweet♥♥♥♥♥are coming to save you!")
-Boss fights (except the final) were repetitive "kite the boss around the arena and shoot the weak point" fights.
-Don't expect an active playerbase with the Raid mode. Haven't found a player match yet.
-On normal, the game seemed to give a LOT of ammo and health, much to the point it felt like the game was getting too easy. (This may be due to my experience with games, give or take.)
Overall: A general modern Resident Evil game with it's standard fare. Nothing amazingly new, but it's your usual zombie shooting game that's at least a bit more decent than Resident Evil 6, but not up to par with Resident Evil 4 and 5.

Twin Peaks gone Silent Hill, as realized by a Japanese dev team on LSD. There are plenty of flaws, even discounting the terrible porting job, but underneath it all is an awkwardly endearing and clearly ambitious hodgepodge of a game. The writing is occasionally quite clever and humorous, the characters grow on you and are surprisingly multidimensional. The story, while full of plot holes, is still interesting enough that it kept me going. And while it's usually easy to guess what happens next in the grand scheme of things, the details are usually completely unexpected. Especially when it comes to dialogue.
It's easy to see why everyone won't give this one a chance though. Production quality varies heavily. Many environments are incredibly detailed, characters are mostly well modeled, and voice acting is at least bearable and often genuinely decent. On the other hand character animations are often awful and level design is mostly uninspired and occasionally very annoying. This goes double for the corridors you end up traversing when the game switches to otherworld mode. There are occasional environmental puzzles that have no particular reason to be there. They're always easy but also almost always annoying.
Combat is trivial, at least when played with a mouse, so the Silent Hilly otherworld bits where you shoot your way through endless mobs turn into routine that you have to turn your brain off for to get to the story bit on the other side. It's not actively terrible but you get the feeling the otherworld fighting stuff was meant for some other game entirely. But then, that goes for many things in the game. There are also useless combat-related QTEs which range from irritating to really bloody annoying, depending on whether you see them coming and whether you remember which buttons you need to press in which order to avoid being instakilled by one of the baddies that haunt your persistently through the game.
The freeroam stuff, while novel, also doesn't work too well as there isn't much of interest to actually do. The things you can do are also usually pointless from a gameplay perspective. Unless you really like increasing your Agent Honor by driving over medals in forest corridors, that is. Driving in general is something you will spend a lot of time doing, and you will not enjoy it.
Thankfully the devs realized driving around is boring (unless you play with a keyboard and mouse, then it's a constant life and death struggle to just stay on the road) and recorded tons of monologues where the main character reminisces about pop culture with his invisible friend. These give the driving segments a lighter tone and also help deepen the player character. Unfortunately the devs didn't consider how aggravating it is to listen to one single repetitively terrible cop show theme whenever your character doesn't happen to be talking about 80s B-movie rentals. A car radio would have been an amazing addition, even just so you could turn it off.
The music in general deserves a few comments. The number of tracks is way too low and many scenes have incredibly ill fitting tunes. Some of it is probably intentional humor, but it's impossible to tell. However some of the tracks are genuinely very good. Everything gets repetitive real quick though. You always know what sort of scene is about to start when you hear the music start to play. Well, except for that one experimental jazzy tune which is used completely randomly.
Basically, if you can enjoy diamond-in-the-rough style games, and find amusement in weird things both intentional and unintentional, and enjoyed the general atmosphere of Twin Peaks, this may be a game for you. Or not. The divisive reputation is certainly well deserved as even though I've spent quite a number of hours in it, it's still hard to recommend the game to anyone that isn't me.

7/10 - This game - much like our main protagonist - is split into two halves.
On one side, it's a mechanical mess. Dialogue sometimes cuts off near the end of a sentence, music suddenly stopping while driving around, awful car controls, from the game randomly crashing, the impractical purchasing system which makes you buy one SINGLE item over and over instead of in bulk, its lengthy driving around town sequences (although teleportation makes this bearable later in the game), right down to some of its spoilerific achievements (seriously don't read them).
But on the other hand you've got a weird and wonderful world with a host of fascinating quirky and cooky characters you'll be talking to, in order to unravel a mysterious murder that has happened in this quaint little town as FBI detective Agent Francis York Morgan, who in and of himself is a very unusual man. In this, you will uncover an intriguing storyline of who-done-it that never gets stale or boring and makes the game very compelling. There's also a host of extra things to be done in Greenvale, with its numberous side quests, fishing and racing.
It is because of its story and characters that this game belongs in the upper echelons of "Weirdest game I've ever played", ranking up there with the likes of Gregory Horror Show.
If you can get past its technical faults, its definately one to experience. "Isn't that right, Zach?"

AdVenture Capitalist, the idle game that gives you a simple lemonade stand and turns you into the richest man alive. With so much to cover I will start with gameplay.
Gameplay: The gameplay is a simple style of gameplay that is suprisingly fun and addicting! You start off on Earth where you click a lemonade stand repetively to get money. With the money you can buy more shops or managers. Managers will run any shop for you so you don't have to keep clicking. More shops mean more money. The higher costing shops give you more money but take longer. As you buy more shops the game will reward you with faster money speed and multipliers. There are tons and tons of upgrades to help push you through the game. Also, there are Angel Investors. Once you have Angels you have to restart the game to obtain them. Don't worry, because the Angels help out a lot! They will give you more money. Soon, the first click on the lemonade stand will give you a million dollars! You can fund missions to Mars and the Moon where you basically repeat the same process with more upgrades, shops, and unlockables. The develepors are always updating, so expect more in the future. Also, they make events on holidays and such, which adds more stuff in the game.
Story: There is no story, so don't worry about it.
Sound: The music in this game is generally repetetive, but very catchy. Nothing much because there is a mute button. When you buy upgrades and get unlocks it makes a nice cha-ching sound. Very cheerful sounds for a cheerful game. It makes the game oddly brighter.
Graphics: It is a 2D game with a lot of text, cartoons, and buttons. Nothing too spectacular. The cartoons are usually silly and well drawn. Each planet and event has it's own theme and they all fit very well. Looks spectacular for what it is meant to be.
Genre: It is an idle game. You basically feel like you are doing something when you really aren't. You basically wait and do stuff on occasions.
Price: It is free! Even if this review doesn't convice you, you can still try it and not spend a dime, technically, you are making money.
My Opinions: To me, I love Idle games. They are very fun and addicting. I think this game is fantastic. With so many options and multiple updates. I never get bored. I think what they have done is amazing, and if you like idle games, so will you.
Tl;Dr: AdVenture Capitalist is an idle game that gives you many options and takes a while to complete. You gain money over time, buy♥♥♥♥♥♥ and make more. You repeat this on a majority of worlds until you are the richest ♥♥♥♥♥ alive. Also, the game is free, so just get it.

To all fans of "Prison Architect" who liked that game to the extent of wanting something akin, with similiar mechanics, basic game concepts and aesthetics but with something else than a prison to run (a highschool  in this case) - this is definitely a title you don't want to pass by.
At the time of this post, a title in early access, yes, but as other folks have pointed out by now this game has the makings of a great sim. The way I see it the tracks are set, and the developers seem quite eager to mold Academia into the game they invisioned, taking in account the recommendations of those who have experienced its alpha.
That being said, the game is still quite early in its development, and it shows: once you have reached "late game" (which for me was the freshmen's transition to sophomors) there is little to experience outside of grinding, expanding and taking in more transferees.
At this point I personally have the gall to propose to the developers to, for now, not bother with "fluff" like student/teacher character,bullies and additional zones and focus instead on making a balanced difficulty progression (things like challenges, crises and missions, as well as a more dynamic income/expenditure system).
But hey, that's just me.
All in all though, the potential is seeping with Academia, making it enjoyable enough in the early stages.
So if you're into PA and controlling a school instead of a prison in similiar fashion sounds like a fun concept to you, definitely support the devs.
Again, makings of great sim.

Suggestions for later additions:
- Senior Leadership, and other teaching staff: Schools have headteachers, leads for behaviour, SEND, and safeguarding all of which have a vital role to play in a school day. Also teaching assistants would be a valuable way to improve student attainment.
- Students out of class: punishment, detention!
- Parent-teacher conferences
- Gymnasium
- Sports field
- Outside playing area
- Students moving for different classes: rather than have each classroom a specific year group, why not have subject specific classrooms
- And finally a cosmetic change: all the menus for zoning/objects have everything in a completely different order. Can it be in some sort of order, or alphabetised?
On the whole, I believe this game has real potential - and you should definitely buy it!

This game is actually a hard sell for me. I got this off of Humble Bundle for 10 bucks and I can't really say I regret it, because it's cheap. But I have a lot of issues with this game as a Borderlands fan. But let's start off with the positives:
Using your Oz Kit to boost yourself added with the low gravity makes up for insane manuvering and some sick space combat. I find myself using this a lot (but mostly for a different reason), not even realizing that my Oz Kit is running out of oxygen.
I can't really distinguish them with snipers, shotguns, and rifles for their respective variants, but the beam laser is really fun to use.
No longer that you need to sell weapons anymore, you can just grind bad quality weapons for a good one. A feature that is missing from ALL the Borderlands games.
Replacing Eridium from BL2 because Eridium barely exists, we get moonstones that spawn more often but have a lot more utility than Eridium. You can open Moonstone crates for Luneshine loot, or put moonstones on the grinder to get the best possible loot
a chance to get the Luneshine version of that loot.
This is the first time where I actually give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about the story. BL1 had a generic story with a crappy ending. BL2 had a generic story with Handsome Jack. Nothing else to be said. But in BLTPS, we get to discover what Jack was and how he became one of the best villains of gaming history.
To be honest, the moon and space station settings are pretty boring (generic sci-fi crap), but the Eridian ship/cave/whatever setting is really mesmerizing.
They're WAY too big. I don't really mind if I can drive around most of them, but most of the time you'll spend in this game is
. I know that part of the game is exploration, but a balance between walking and gunplay is important here, and it's quite clear that BLTPS didn't achieve this quite well.
As much as I love the new additions of the grinder, laser weapons, and luneshine loot -- and make no mistakes, when I came back to BL2 it felt missing -- the game feels slower paced than BL2 and it really doesn't have anything much different than BL2.
It feels like BLTPS kind of underdelivered the content. Being a standalone game instead of treating it as a standalone DLC, I honestly expect more content from the start, without the DLCs. The main missions are pretty lacking, and the side missions are lacking as well. Again, most of the time you spend in this game is walking around in such a big map.
The gravity addition is nice but it feels like the maps are never designed to be for it. As such, you have collision derps and the similar.
Instead of offering 4 major DLCs, you get 2 character DLCs and 2 UVHM upgrades. It's quite lame to be honest. I haven't bought them yet, but it's clear that the offering isn't as impressive as previous Borderlands games.
Overall, it's a hard sell. Borderlands 1 was a decent start, but Borderlands 2 cranked it up to 11 and became one of the best games AND sequels of all time. BLTPS is just a repeat of Borderlands 2 and it didn't really change much, and it has a lot of silly design decisions that makes it worse than BL2 and a hard sell for me. I would respect it if it were a standalone DLC to BL2, or just have more, densely packed content.
So far: BL2 > BLTPS > BL1

This game seems neat on the cover but quickly becomes annoying with little progress to show for the time spent.
The crafting system is kludgy to control, unintuitive, lacks an in-game guide, makes inventory hard to manage, and heavily favors basic melee.
There are three 'classes' based on attributes, attack, dex, and mag. Dex requires limited use arrows that must be crafted from refined minerals and anything using magic is few and far between (I played for 4 hours and found nothing that used magic). Armor for the melee class requires refined minerals while armor for dex or mag requires both refined minerals and refined leather or refined cloth, both of which are much rarer.
The "random" nature of the game really just means replaying until you get lucky drops as all progress is locked behind a specific material upgrade tier system (must get wood before stone/bone, before iron, before gold, before diamond) and requires the first few resources found always be spent on crafting the next tier of pickaxe instead of armor or weapons, which in turn increases the grind. Or it requires that levels have any/enough enemies of a certain type to get access to any of the materials necessary.
The "random" stats can be rerolled until you get the stats you want so it doesn't really matter or impact anything other than forcing the player to click 'reroll' a bunch of times.
The "rogue" nature of the game and the very small health encourages going extremely slow, especially in single player games where you can't be revived by a friend, and encourage time played padding. Nothing carries over between plays, most unlocks require beating the game or of limited usage,

Magicite is a.. special game. It's sort of like that "special" kid by himself in the corner of the playground. Not the mentally disabled one, just the weird one who can't really decide what he wants to be - as a person or in the future.
Magicite is not at all what I initially expected. And compared to my initial expectations, it was garbage. But after I found myself with nothing else to play and stupid amounts of free time where I can hop on, do a fourty minute run in an attempt to gain some new items, and go do something else, I started enjoying it immensly. Yes, there are certainly bugs and a heck ton of quirks you have to get used to working around. I don't think calling it a finished game is fair nor do I think the pricetag is really fair, but I do enjoy it now that I have it quite a lot.
Addressing just a few of the bugs for anyone who does happen to get it and enjoy it-
NPC interaction is very buggy, however pressing TAB a few times (going in out of your inventory) and jumping around a bit before going up to the NPC again usually will let you interact with them again. It's annoying but you get used to it, and it's not gamebreaking when you know how to get around it.
Multiplayer is certainly buggy. I haven't used it in a year or so, so it may be better or worse than I remember (it wasn't very memorable to begin with), but it's alright if you want to put in the effort.
As for singleplayer, it appears very difficult at first and the wiki is crucial to get an understanding of what exactly you're supposed to do when it comes to character progression. But once you get a hang of the "classes" and stats and whatnot, the game is definitely beatable in singleplayer. Hard as hell, sure, but beatable.
This game is definitely an exclusive club of sorts and it took me over 50 hours to fully understand by trial and error how the different classes and systems work, how to combine races, hats and companions to get the most out of whatever fighting style you choose, etc. and it took 70 hours till I could beat it, But overall it was worth it.
I'd recommend if you have time, patience and appreciation for things that goes beyond basic, annoying but easy to work around bugs. If none of those apply to you, don't bother. You'll just end up angry.

I came about CrossCode as a web-based game, completely designed in HTML5, and therefore featured on Chrome Experiments. Back then, it wasn't even an RPG; it was basically a simulation of the aiming engine, a clone of the early tutorial now present in the current version of the game. As little of a resemblance that web-version has with the current state of the game, it did show the talent and ambition of the developers, and what has been added since is astonishing.
Astonishingly good. Although there are some loose ends in the story still, this is due to the fact the game is actually in Early Access as of writing this review. And already now, it's worth the $20.
Why? Well, first of all, the game looks extremely polished already. The pixelated sprites 'fit' each other, controls have been neatly arranged and the game mechanics up until now have been executed to near perfection.
These mechanics are quite plentifully present, actually. Every enemy has specific attacks and weaknesses, and even different 'evolutions' of itself. The attacking system is as elegant as it is challenging; WASD to move, left-click to hit, right-click to dodge/block. That's it. The maps have been built in such a way it is relatively easy to traverse through for a quick sweepthrough, but provides quite the challenge when going for the semi-hidden presents scattered all over the maps.
Now, of course, as it is still in development, the main plot of the story is finished in roughly half an hour. After that, you're kind of being released into the world, in order for you to explore on your own. Quests can be completed, ranging from collecting items to beating enemies. Because of the layout of the maps, some of those can take some time; not in an annoying way though, as you're mostly being busy trying to work out how to get to a certain ledge.
The only negative in this version is that the 'open-world' feeling of the game is somewhat limited. This is caused by the facts that certain buildings aren't visitable, some paths are blocked, and the world is consisting of only 5 maps (a city, 2 trails, the tutorial map and the main hub - these are rather extensive, though!). I'm not only expecting, but quite frankly plain confident the devs will be able to make that point go away.

This is an early access review, so the completed game may differ wildly from what I have seen.
First, the game serves as a massive homage to the 16-bit era of games. It has smooth controls, an easily intuitive UI, and doesn't burden you with massive complexity in terms of gameplay itself. While the current story is limited to the opening bits and one dungeon, it still gives you a great deal of room to explore and play with the game's mechanics.
In terms of the game environment and the bits of story seen, it takes influences from throughout the era, with a few from other eras to better flesh out the story. The world's details are reminiscient of the later 16-bit era games, with great attention to detail, colorful environments, and excellent pallete layering to give a perception of depth. This gives the game's aesthetics a very nostalgic feel without bringing up the era's limitations.
The music, of course, is and is not 16-bit. It is 16-bit as it uses the synthesized sound we remember, but isn't in the fact that it uses modern sound drivers which perfected the digital music compression started in the era. This isn't an insult to the 16-bit era of game music. Many of the best and most beloved video game musics were dome in the 16-bit era (anyone else remember Aria Di Mezzo Caraterre aka the song during the Opera Scene from Final Fantasy VI?).
The game is a complete homage to an era of gaming. An era where video games began to become more complex, an era where games came into their own, and an era which shaped the modern era of gaming.

Originally, this was a negative review. Paradox in May 2017 upped the prices in countries outside of the US and Eurozone to numbers bordering, or at, exorbitant levels, without any warning or communication with the community on this decision. It was both concerning and apparently greedy. However, as of 6/23/17 they've promised to revert the prices and released a very genuine apology, not one in the way of "lol sorry guys but that cash tho" so I will revert my review as such. This is how companies should conduct themselves and I respect that.

Their DLC policy is still rather idiotic but whatever, it's not mean-spirited or sleazy. Just out of touch.

Now for the actual game.

Stellaris is a pretty good strategy game. It's not amazing, nor is it terrible; it's just pretty good. What it is with certainty, though, is unique. It's in my experience both in playing and watching games the only thing close to its approach to strategy and I very much enjoy its approach. To put it simply, Stellaris is a combination of Spore's space stage (for those of you who even played that far into that game) and Sid Meier's Civilization style scale and strategy. You manage fleets, planets, diplomatic relations, technology research, and resources, which are food, cash, and minerals. There is only one win-con in the game right now though, and it's conquering 40% of habitable planets in the galaxy. There are two ways to acheive it, however; conquering them on your own, or having your federation own them collectively.

Here's the problems, and it's honestly quite a lot.

Stellaris is, fundamentally, broken. The game is horribly balanced to the point that it actually made me gasp out loud when I finally understood all the threads on the sub about "Corvette spam." The idea of this is to continuously build naked level 1 ships, and almost exclusively these, and constantly conquer empires by abusing the oversimplified war declaration system to take complete ownership of them nigh-instantly, and repeat ad nauseum. This could be okay, because playing mindlessly imperial is a totally valid playstyle and there's nothing wrong with that - EXCEPT - you ignore every single part of the game except for the combat. No diplomacy, no management of technology or ANY of the three resources or the content of your planets; just mash the planets into a sector, feed it minerals and cash, and let the AI handle the production of your planets. And you win, easily. You ♥♥♥♥ing STEAMROLL everybody else that isn't doing this, except to perhaps very late game when the overpowered end-game crises (unless you fight them with very, very specific meta-gamed ship builds) start to make the AI lose their ♥♥♥♥in minds and close their borders and get beaten into the dirt but 1 million fleet power extra-dimensional life.

You don't need to make food. If you have 0 food in your stores, nothing happens. That's great.

The AI is, in a word, infantile. They cannot manage planets for♥♥♥♥♥♥ They cannot speak to each other for♥♥♥♥♥♥ They have cookie-cutter, bland personalities that don't change or adapt to the universe. They have "ethics shifts" which don't really feel like they cause much change in how they approach the player. The diplomacy menu doesn't feel like interaction with an empire like Civilization does, it just feels like clicking on buttons - namely because of a lack of options. You only have treaties and trades and an insult. The only ways to make another empire like you if they don't immediately hate you because you're a hive mind or because they're xenophobic, which is about half the AI personalities. They cannot manage their empires at all; often tile resources are completely ignored (like the extremely valuable betharian stone) or the tile itself is ignored in the first place, which is patched over by absurd production buffs inaccesible to the player. The upcoming patch (1.7) promises to do some AI work and both introduce a new end-game crisis and completely rework the current AI (population, not opposing empire) uprising event. Here's hoping.
Unfortunately, this experience is apparently extremely inconsistent; plenty of people (at least on the subreddit where I lurk) say they have quite positive experiences with the AI and they do see the galaxy shifting as the game progresses. I can't vouch for that even slightly. For my friends and I, it consistently ends in defensive-pact stalemates that are frustrating to slave through. It doesn't even make for an interesting end to a story when I try to justify it by saying "oh hey when you put it in writing it's cool tho"
Stellaris has a pretty active modding community that I've yet to delve into, but there's plenty of people out there that try to fix these problems with mods and I hope I can find some mods that solve this for me.
Despite all this, the game is ♥♥♥♥in fun man. It's a great time. End game needs work, but the game as a whole is still enjoyable, especially with friends. I recommend it because I trust PDX and the community to be able to patch up these issues to bring it into the 4x titan it has so much potential to be. It's a good time in its current state and it looks to only improve over time.

If you are a fan of Tower Defense games, Gemcraft is an absolute must-try. I have spent a lot of hours on it on
(in case you were wondering: dude, already a review with barely any hours on it?), and I'm absolutely sold. What makes it so special compared with the enormous amount of other games available in the genre? Here are some key words (tl;dr: read only key words):
1.) Experimentation:
Most TD games are quite simple: you have a limited amount of towers types that can be upgraded, each with their strengths and weaknesses. Strategy is mainly finding the right combos and placement.
In gemcraft however, you build up defenses by forging gems and building defensive buildings separately, to then combine them. With 9 different gem types (all with their own colour) that have each a specific power and 3 different tower designs, you have a lot of freedom when creating your defenses against the demon hordes. Gems of different colours can be fused together to form powerfull combogems and can even be converted to gem bombs to rain death and destruction from above on a specific target.
2.) Create your own dungeon:
In most TD games you have 2 areas: the path that enemies follow to reach your base, and areas suitable to build your defenses. Sometimes it's a grid area that makes you puzzle for ideal placement, sometimes it is restricted to a few spots limiting the amount of towers you can build. Gemcraft has only one rule: There must be at least one route that enemies can follow to reach your base. As long as there is a path of one square wide with horizontal or vertical connections, you can build your towers on any surface that allows building. Aside from your towers, you also have the ability to build walls. Wide path? Make it narrow and windy by adding a lot of walls forcing enemies to follow a zigzag pattern! Multiple routes to your base? Block them untill there is one left! Create choke points with deadly traps waiting to turn unaware enemies into dust! Be carefull though, buildings and gems are build from the same recource pool (mana), so you are forced to be efficient.
3. From sandbox to nightmare with one click
Ever had that feeling during a mission when you were like: man, my defense is impenetrable, this is no longer a challenge, this is boring. Gemcraft allows you to suddenly turn the mission from an evil minion's deathwall to a tense fight for your live.  You can make the mission harder in various ways. First, like a lot of TD games, you have the option to early call waves. Only now you can decide to early call multiple waves at a time (if you are brave enough). All waves are displayed as 'wave stones' on the left of your screen, and they are all visible from the beginning. If you really want it, you can scroll down to the bottom, click the final round stone, and watch the fireworks (or your ultimate doom).Early calling a wave gives bonus mana and xp, so it's not just for fun. Another way is using gems. As I said earlier, gems can be turned into gem bombs to lay waste on the battlefield. However, when used on a wave stone, the targeted wave will be enraged: enemies become stronger, faster, more resistant, and more numerous. The stronger the gem bomb or the more gem bombs dropped, the stronger the wave becomes, and the higher the exp reward. Last but not least, you have the option to activate mission handicaps before starting the mission, such as less time between different waves, monsters receiving damage resistance on a direct hit, and much more. This can be very helpfull when you want to replay lower levels to rise enough in level to beat the harder fields.
My verdict: Gemcraft is a landmark in the TD genre: it is challenging, tactical, allows a lot of experimentation, and is not short at all (you WILL require a lot of hours of gameplay to even reach the hardest fields).
