This game is a masterpiece. Yes, it's imperfect, and has defaults, but if it reaches you, it goes deep, and you're not likely to forget it. Ever. On that somewhat random chance, I recommand this game.
Now, let's talk about perfection and imperfection. Starting by imperfection, to act as a fair warning :
- the technical aspect of the game seems not quite on par with what's expected nowadays, and by that, I mean that many people have reported technical issues going from annoying to making the game unplayable. Myself, I stumbled unto two main problems : white screen of death when starting the game, solved by updating my graphic drivers, and a couple random crashes. So I guess I was lucky to get into the "just annoyed" gang.
- the game is not accessible. Many people state that it can be played whitout having played the first NIER, and while it is kinda true, the world's background is awesome, and knowing at least the synopsis of the previous game increases the overall experience a LOT. In the same spirit, the game has no auto-save feature, but a hard and old savepoints system, that unlocks only after the first 45 minutes. Yes, it means that you have to sit and play 45 minutes non-stop before saving. The tutorial is minimal, and thus you can easily die during those 45 minutes before having the chance to learn how to control the game. However, this "questionnable" decision is in fact deeply rooted in the core design of the game. It's one clear exemple of "immersion over practicality". While I criticize it, I also encourage you to accept it and push through, as it is really worth it.
To sum it up : yes, this game will require some efforts from your side, perhaps more than what it should, and certainly not what we're accustomed to nowadays. Even so, it's worth it, because now I'll talk about maybe not perfection, but greatness.
- graphically, I always place art design and coherence above technical prowess. You can criticize the graphics all you want, but the art design is top-notch, and I'm not only talking about the fanservicy first look of the game, but about the quality of pretty much everything else, from character design to animations. The style is well-define and brings something special, an identity to the title.
- but that identity wouldn't be complete without the beautiful soundtrack, one of the best I've ever heard, one that will stick with you for a long time, akin to the legendary Ghost in the Shell theme, if you happen to know it. That's the kind of soundtrack you have here.
- after the look and the sound, we have the gameplay, and let me tell you that it's a stunning achievement. Nier Automata provides one of the most customizable experience I know, combined with thematic reflexions about the video game medium. Just that. Yes, you can over-level and make the game incredibly easy...but you can also just select a harder difficulty, and/or not use certain core interface element like showing your life bar. Platinium Games has a very good reputation for crafting action combat, and they do deliver here with a very satisfying amount of weapon and skills that you can combine in different playstyles, and just watching your character fight is a feast for the eyes. Now, just let me ramble a bit about people complaining about the difficulty,  at any point of the game. There is no difficulty achievement. With the amount of care this game has been made, it's not an oversight. It's just that you, the player, have to choose how you are playing. I'll admit, there is no in-game guide about it, it comes from tweaks you have to make. Will I go for all the side-quests? Will I farm the best items? Will I play in Very Hard? Only one answer : try it until you find your style, and if you're not happy, push through, and make your own rules. So rarely have you that amount of freedom over your experience.
- and finally, the story. While it may not be the best, the narration in itself is very well done, and is articulated around twists and revelations. And yes, it may seem artificial and even weak at times. But that's not even what's the most important about it. Because this story touches philosophy. Not the kind you find in books, but the kind you stumble on when you stop your everyday life to think a bit about your life and your place in the universe. Sure, there are references to known philosophers, but the philosophic and metaphysics thoughts and concepts presented are not dry and complex, they're intertwined in the narrative, making them much more accessible, and engaging. This, imho, is the biggest achievement of Nier Automata. It's showing that entertainment can be thought-provoking, that video games, and Games in general, ARE important, and have a rightful place alongside other forms of Arts, like literature or film-making.
So, yes, I genuinely think this is a masterpiece, and hope it will have a big impact on the gaming industry. Because there have already been incredible video games in the past, but never with that amount of self-awareness. This game is a weird case of fulfilled ambition without pretense, and one last time, I encourage you to look past the imperfections. Yes, it's worth it.

I really wanted to make this review, because it seems that people aren't actually playing the game enough and taking it at face value... When i first started the game, i spawned into a somewhat populated server. I wandered around wondering what the game was about and how to even begin to play. I was seriously considering refunding the game. But i didn't. And you know what? It's one of the best decisions I have ever made.
This game is incredibly deep and fun when you get the hang of it. Want to build a city with an npc trader and hire npc guards to defend it? You can do that. Want to Become a king and found your own kingdom while slaughtering your enemies? You can do that. Want to fight a dragon or a giant cyclops? You can do that. Want to sail the oceans and ascend to godhood? You can do that. There are over 50 different skills from which to base a profession on and perfect your craft, and nearly every skill has a couple or more sub-skills branching off from it.
There are so many things you can do in this game and I challenge ANYONE to show me a game that has more depth and variety than this one does. Yes it's old, yes it's clunky. It's a dated game but it has survived for over 10 years, surely there's a reason for that. It still recieves frequent updates as well. A new cooking update is even coming out that adds over 500 recipes!
If this game has piqued your curiosity at all, Please please please look past the graphics and join the community. There are servers with more than 50+ players. Or, if you're looking for a smaller server that will take the time to teach you the basics, please dont hesitate to ask me.

I came from Wurm Online so I had already undergone my learning curve for the game. If you are willing to play a game with its Wiki site Wurmpedia up on another monitor for reference the whole time, I would absolutely recommend Wurm Unlimited! It can be extremely addicting like you'd expect from anything which came out of a quality MMO. You can make the game as slow or as quick as you want now since you can choose a server with anywhere between the original almost gruelingly-slow pace with a 1x/1x server (skilling up speed multiplier/speed of completing common actions multiplier) up to almost instant pace for each action on a 10000x/instant server. There are PVE servers as well as PVP servers; however, don't expect to find a lot of people on all the time to play with in either case. You can host your own server as well as the server software is included with the game. I would not recommend trying to configure and run a local server if you're not comfortable searching their forums and following the various mods' installation instructions. If GitHub is a word you're familiar with, then you'll find it pretty easy to be honest.
Pros:
- It's like serious Minecraft from the maker of Minecraft, Notch; although he left the development team for the game some time ago now.
- If you get bored, you're doing something wrong. People have been playing the Wurm Online version of the game for years and have not reached the peak of their play yet.
Cons:
- Graphics and animations have not been upgraded much if at all from Wurm Online which by now is certainly showing its fair signs of age.
- Not really a casual game to pick and play for short bursts of time. If you build a house or a mineshaft and leave the game for a week, they could both be gone by the time you come back from decay/collapse, unless you host a local server which you can simply shutdown to essentially pause time from progressing.

While I like this game you will want to verify it is what you are looking for first.
What this game is
1. Large open world medieval sandbox
2. Faction based PVP
3. personal or private servers for an impressive number of people (based on hardware)
4. Very mature game with lots of options and features
5. Steep learning curve - (Game is not like most open world games out there)
6. Unforgiving (unless you modify server settings)
7. A game where you can eventually do everything
Whath this game is NOT
1. Graphically advanced - Game is over 10 years old and the graphics show it but they are not ugly
2. Modern UI - Interface is clunky and takes getting used to but it is functional
3. A game designed for solo play - It can be played solo but it's not what it's designed for
This is not the quick and easy fantasy game like WoW or Skyrim.  It's closer to ARK or Life is Feudal in concept but less contrained by skill trees (all skills are avalible and just need time to improve them).  This is also one of the slowest and grindy skill systems I have seen but since you can tweek the server to speed it up and often need to do the small stuff anyways it fits well.  You should look into server types and options to determin if this game does what you want.  If you are thinking of playing a more realistic Minecraft adventure game then look into Creative, if you want faction combat or a more story driven elements try out adventure.
This game is very mature and it's amazing the things you can do and how customized buildings and towns can be.  Compared to modern games like Life is Feudal it does have a lot more options and content but the clunky interface and minimal combat will likely turn off people.   There are no races or classes in this game and by default no magic.  There are ways to learn magic (Find tomes for mages or choose a god and become a priest) but this not something that you just level up and have happen. (You should read up on these heavily if you feel you need magic in your game before you buy)

Wurm is a survival game that is rich in detail yet easy to learn and play. It takes almost no time to figure out the basics of survival and the detail that you can get into with crafting and building is incredible. Fast becoming one of my all time favorite games.

I enjoyed Wurm had a neat private server to play on with no fee and some people to hang with.  Built a castle, killed some trolls, even sailed around the world for kicks.  Alas, I have had the "Duplicate Authorization" error for 6 months now and haven't been able to play.  I understand that the company is cash strapped but seriously it's hard to recommend a game that you literally cannot play.
Anyone thinking of buying this should recognize a few key "features"
1.  combat is very slow, at it's quickest you strike once every 4 seconds.
2.  advancement is very slow, grinding up the crafting skill to make anything vaguely useful, i.e. QL 50 takes many hours of click the same button 100's of times.  (more if you gather your materials rather than buying them off another player).
3.  ranged combat is very bad mostly because arrows have to be crafted individual and then improved individually.  Very long story short, each arrow takes just as much time to craft and improve as a sword or a huge axe, and at best each arrow is good for 5 shots.  So not only does it take a huge amount of time to do it in the first instance, but you are continually having to invest a similar amount of time almost every time you get into combat.
Basically this game reminds me of Eve Online, very slow progression, limited interaction combat and where the chief draws are fairly heavily based in the kinds of connections and friendships you make.  It's neat to make a castle or a ship, but unless there are a bunch of people who band together ultimately these things become meaningless.  I can't say for certain, but I think there are other games that can placate your crafting fix with better combat.

Steel Ocean is a World War 2 naval combat game. Compared to other strategy games, there are many gaps in the strategic gameplay. Diplomacy is frustratingly thin, especially for a Paradox grand strategy game. Combat basically boils down to spamming the same optimal ship template and throwing them into battle, with no sense of fleet tactics to be had. The AI is not very good either, which is extremely frustrating as you are forced to let the AI manage many of your planets in the mid-to-late stages of the game.
Speaking of the mid-to-late game, the biggest reason why the game feels unfinished is because the mid-to-late game is just a boring mess. While the early game is satisfying due to the randomly-generated worlds and events that pop up while you are in the explore and expansion phase, the late game is a dull grind with a dearth of events or choices to make things more interesting beyond slowly building up a doomstack and throwing it at a neighboring empire. This is disappointing as you would expect that a Paradox grand strategy game freed from the bounds of Earth and historical nations to be filled all sorts of creative events that make your space empire feel alien.

"CrossCode is a poster child for why independent games matter more than ever in a market where AAA relevance is dwindling. It's destined to become a cult phenomenon, reverently mentioned in the same company as Cave Story, Braid, or Fez. I'm highly looking forward to it and you should be too."
So I summarized the first (and currently only) review I ever thought worth writing over a year ago. 15 months on, it's truer than ever. In the intervening time, among plenty of other great independent games, we saw the absolute juggernaut that was Undertale blow up the internet. And at the risk of drawing parallels between two VERY different games ("indie" isn't a genre after all), CrossCode deserves that kind of recognition.
CrossCode is not the best game you'll ever play. Its story and characters are fun and infectiously endearing, but they won't redefine the way you think about narrative in games. Its art and music are lovingly crafted, but so are a dozen other great (and not-so-great) pixel-art games. The puzzles are smart and the fast-paced combat is insanely fun and suitably challenging, but it probably won't supplant your favorite ARPG. CrossCode is reminiscent of a lot of things, a synthesis of elements both nostalgic and modern that you've likely seen many times before.
What CrossCode likely IS though, is the best game you've never played. Because it's been fairly sparsely covered during its early access period, it's flown under the radar for a lot of people. And because that synthesis of elements is so well tuned, you'll wonder how you missed hearing about such a well-made game for so long. Almost every aspect of CrossCode feels really, really good to play, not just in an acceptably non-distracting sort of way, but dripping with love and care and attention to detail. The extreme ratio of positive reviews isn't a fluke or vote gaming by a hyper-devoted fanbase. Lately, it's people finding the game wondering if an early access game can really be THAT good, and discovering to their delight that yes, it really can be.
CrossCode is aiming for official release some time in the first half of 2017, and the amount of progress that the development team has made since the early access launch last year strongly suggests this is a realistic goal. Even if you don't want to spend money on an early access game right now, do yourself a favor and follow it, because you're probably going to want it when it's finished.

This is basically the Witcher 1. If the Witcher 1 would have been developed by another studio than CD Projekt. And if it was about Orcs. And lacked the freedom.
It's graphically meh, it's animations are either missing or clunky as hell, and the world is just visually boring and has no life in it. The gameplay has it's interesting touches, but just feels like they forgot to glue it all together.
Unfortunately. It's got some interesting ideas to begin with, it tries to develop a story that's different from the usual mainstream ideas. The idea of having two so unlikely characters go on a story together is not new, but good, and would work well, if there was some flow and enthusiasm in telling it. But this very much feels like a game in the kinds of "Yeah, we have the story and a gameplay prototype, let's mash it together in the next two weeks and then sell it."
If you're reading this, don't buy it. Go for it's spiritual successor "Styx - Master of Shadows". It's a way more polished and more enjoyable game than this is.

I purchased this game this weekend and just beat it with 13 hours of playtime (though a couple of those may have been AFK).
While it is a short game, every minute of it was enjoyable. The story was superb and the combat was fun once you got the hang of it.
Pros:
- I am actually amazed at how much story this game packed in. While the game is short, its full of very little wasted time, it keeps you moving at a brisk pace while developing Styx and Arkail, as well as the world and plot. I adore the characters I got to meet in this game. My only disappointments are that I don't think Arkail is featured in any of the other games set in this world, and that there is no sequel! There is a huge amount of room to keep this story going.
- Fun combat. It is not gimmicky, it is fair. Once you learn the terminology and how to have Styx and Arkail work together, combat falls into a comfortable cadence that keeps you reacting and thinking about the best way to pick your enemies apart. There are clear rules for the most effective way to take down any enemy.
- Landscapes and cities looked great for an older game - you can tell that a lot of time was spent on the details. I enjoyed going to all the different places the game took me to.
- Choices you make have an impact in the immediate story, though I am not sure yet what the end-game impacts are, if any, since I only played through it once. Does anyone know if there are multiple endings?
Cons:
- It is a short game, but I feel that its price tag is fair (especially at the time of this review at $2.99!)
- the voice acting for some characters was pretty awful, but Styx, Arkail, and some others were great.
- the dialogue/non comabt animations are shoddy and you see the same animations used over and over, especially for Styx. The lip sync animations are also not great. The combat animations are great, though.
- While there are no reused maps, the formula is pretty repetitive. play through map by getting form A to B, go to town, get new quest, go to new map and go from C to D.  There are side quests and items to find on every map if you are looking, but the system is kind of 'on rails'. The story does allow you to make choices though,I am just referring to how you play through the missions.

Order of Battle: World War II is honestly one of the better free to play strategy games I have played as of late. I feel like anyone interested in a free to play Strategy game should give Order of Battle: World War II a look. Turn based gameplay, multiplayer, a pretty large selection of units, all these things make for a game that could be pretty fun. I dont have that much time with the game yet, but I recommend anyone interested give it a try, especially now that the game is free to play.

Order of Battle: World War 2 is a turn-based strategy game developed by The Artistocrats and published by Slitherine Ltd. It was released in April 2015. It is set in World War 2 and there are multiple paid DLC campaigns that unlock new settings based on 'What Ifs' in the war. For instance, Winter War is a paid DLC that covers Finland. Order of Battle primarily is free to try, and this means that with the free version you can play the boot camp tutorial campaign and try the various paid campaigns. Furthermore, if you want to play more campaigns you need to buy them and if you want to play multiplayer you need to own at least one DLC.
Order of Battle incorporates fun strategic and realistic elements. Notably, there is an excellent supply system which alters the course of battle. For example, if your army controls one island and want to invade another island, you need supply ships so when you gain a foothold on that other island you can resupply and build units. But, Order of Battles' basic premise is turn-based hexagonal combat. This is very similar to the Civilisation V game in which you build units, capture territory, and move using a turn-based system. Each faction also has specialised units, which relates to the realistic aspect of history. These units, such as the M1 Stuart Tank, have special abilities and obviously are stronger or weaker than other units. For instance, tanks are stronger then infantry.
Tactics are essential to outsmarting your enemy and this is also apparent with the enemy AI, which can easily outsmart you and cut your troops off from support. Lastly, I adore the mission completion system. Specifically, in mission two I captured both island checkpoints, but did not complete the optional objective of destroying an enemy submarine. This resulted in the enemy submarine appearing in the following mission, providing a very realistic tone to the game because in war, if a unit retreats he will regroup with the rest for following missions. Overall, I really do like this fresh take on the strategy series through an alternate history turn-based style game. There are multiple consequences to think about, such as whether you complete all objectives, or where you should move onto the map. In other words, choices and tactical thinking matter.
Order of Battle features beautiful artwork. The artwork is cartoon-like, which I compare to the upcoming Civilisation VI. The idea of the artwork is that with a more friendly approach to characters and the UI, it allows for more information to be presented to the player in a simple and non-cluttered way. Furthermore, I believe the cartoon-like graphics showcase the brilliance in map design and elements within such as the terrain, the landscape, and even friendly or enemy units.
This is a very good game. I enjoy the gameplay and the alternate take on history through campaigns in various settings. I like the game mechanics in how balanced they are, but also how game mechanics affect the overall game. There are a large amount of units that differ with factions, meaning things are not repetitive, rather each faction feels fresh. The UI is user-friendly and the graphics fit the nature of the game. My only negative with the game is the lack of a free portion. I do not like I have to spend minimum USD$9.99 to play a major campaign or even just play multiplayer. Personally, it turns me off. In saying that, as a mild-loving strategy fan, I highly recommend this game to strategy fans. Furthermore, as I am not one to put hundreds of hours into strategy games nowadays, I do not see this as an everyday must play game, therefore, I recommend the DLCs on sale.
As a side-note, I understand I have only played this for about 100 minutes, but I was quick to grasp the game mechanics and overall strategic gameplay style.
7.5/10
- Turn-based gameplay that feels fresh and smooth.
- Beautiful graphics that balance land, units, and information on screen.
- Variety of units that separate factions.
- The lack of free content due to the dependency on paid DLC.

I must admit I was somewhat wary of trying OOB: WWII due to some of the negative reviews.  I have been playing strategy/hex games since Panzer General and Norm Kroger's Operational Art of War series, and I must say that playing this game did my heart a whole lot of good.  Modern graphics and animation breathe new life into the genre, as well as a supply system that makes sense and is easy to grasp. For those that play Panzer Corps (myself included) there are some features that will be familiar, but also many more that make the game more robust and realistic than Panzer Corps is at times.
The base game is free to download, and includes a bootcamp campaign and sample scenarios for some of the DLC campaigns which will cost you a few dollars.  This is by no means a bait and switch, as many people who have written reviews seem to think.  This is actually an extended demo with a generous amount of content which allows you to get a great feel for the game before deciding whether or not to purchase.  There are a couple of issues which need work on this otherwise fantastic game---
1) The game can become very choppy and slow even on machines which exceed the minimum requirements.  Hopefully in the near future the devs can work on optimizing the coding.
2) Artillery is quite weak, although in this game its stated purpose is to disrupt enemy efficiency rather than kill them.  Bumping up the killing power slightly would make artillery far more relevant in the game.  As of now, I do not deploy artillery at all unless I have extra command points.
9/10  All in all, it is a solid, fun, and addicting game that is well deserving of a try by any strategy fan.

Well, playing this game after Borderlands 1 & 2 brought nothing but disappointment. Let’s start with guns. They just.. don’t feel right. The same types of guns that were in B2 such as explosive, corrosive etc. feel like sh*t, while the two new types, especially laser, do way too much damage, so you will end up using just these most of the time.
Environments are quite dull, it’s pretty much just the same rocky moon surface with randomly scattered buildings and objects. Some large maps don’t have any catch-a-ride stations in them so you will often have to go on foot from one side of a large map to another and back again, only to have to do it again with another quest. Low gravity is fun the first few times, then it gets annoying as in some areas you can float outside the map and die if you aren’t paying attention.
Characters and storytelling in this game are nowhere close to the level of B2. After a few weeks I only remember Nina and that hilarious knight who wanted to lay claim to the Moon before somebody else did it. And, of course, Jack is as awesome as ever, this time he has far more room and his sarcastic monologues are on point.
Speaking of Jack, he is a playable class (you need to have the DLC though), as is Claptrap. Some other heroes resemble classes from B2 quite a lot (Wilhelm-Commando, Aurelia-Zero), while other (Athena, Nisha) are quite unique. I played Aurelia and must say she is by far the worst sniper class of the Borderlands games. Some of her talents don’t even make sense. Weird and overcomplicated talents seem to be a general issue among all classes in the Pre-Sequel.
As for the end-game content, there is only Claptrap’s Voyage DLC which is decent, but not as good as any B2 DLCs imo. Holodome is just a really mediocre arena with multiple, gradually stronger waves of enemies, somewhat similar to B1’s Underdome. Then there is of course TVHM and UVHM, but I don’t think the game is good enough to enjoy a second, let alone third playthrough.

I would argue that Medieval II is the best entry into the Total War series. While it's perhaps not as iconic as Rome I or Empire, and it certainly is not as flashy as newer entries like Warhammer, it is arguably the most varied.
On top of not having any faction restrictions (once you beat a campaign once), each faction feels distinct. Everyone starts out with roughly the same units and buildings, but once the mid-game is reached, the factions diverge considerably. Very few factions share castle-built units and the ones that are shared are early-game units.
The mechanics are all straightfoward and easy to learn. There aren't multiple towns in a province to manage, just the main settlement. Settlements only come in two varieties: towns and castle. Towns make money, castles make faction-specfic military units. Taxes are on a settlement-by-settlement basis, so you can tax London to death, but leave Edinbough lightly taxed.
Lastly, the game doesn't pull many punches. Even playing on normal, the AI will backstab you, refuse to cooperate, and handle you roughly.
As with all of the Total War games, you can see a bit of the next game in each preceeding title. Medieval II is a bit of Rome I and a bit of Empire. Plus, the DLC is actually worth getting, giving you new campaigns to play and not just a new faction that should probably have been playable from the start.
Medieval II is not without its flaws, however. The Senate missions from Rome I make a return in the form of Papal Decrees (if you're a Catholic nation) or the occasional Jihad (if you're Muslim nation). The UI isn't nearly as slick as Empire and beyond. Finally, obviously, the graphics show their age.
Overall, Medieval II is my favorite entry in the series, probably the best entry overall, and definitely the best value for money

A lot of Total War fans, mostly the old-fashioned ones, will tell you that the best Total War game by far was Medieval II or Rome I.
And if you're interested in this game, Medieval II is the more gritty, gloomy, up close and personal one of the two.
The goals on the campaign are simple: build up your cities and armies, find ways to make money, wage wars, conquer an empire.
And yes, multiplayer is also fun as well. Even after all these years there's still a sizable community online, you just have to be there at the right time of day.
The battles are awesome. In combat, soldiers fight each other in a more brutal fashion compared to Rome I. There's blood and some brutal finishing moves. And of course you'll be able to use a variety of tactics just like any other TW game, so whether you love cavalry, infantry, missiles, etc, you'll have a lot to do on here.
The campaign is also like Rome I, except that there are extra agents, you can recruit more than one unit per settlement (depending on how developed it is), and you can go on Jihads or Crusades.
Jihads and Crusades are basically military campaigns for Muslim or Catholic Christian factions. Depending on which one you are, you join the campaign, recruit soldiers, and try to complete it. Jihads and Crusades end when a targeted settlement has been conquered. Also, Orthodox Christian factions don't get crusades.
If you're a Catholic Christian faction, you get to participate in the biased, rigged bereaucracy (if that is spelled correctly) that is called the Papacy. I'll mention the details in the cons below.
Cons of the game:
1) The Total War games have always had a reputation for having bad pathfinding for armies. On Medieval 2, path finding is incredibly lousy. For example, when commanding infantry units, there are times when only a few soldiers at the front of the unit will charge the enemy when you have given them the order to attack. While this is happening, it takes a very, very long time for the soldiers at the back to move up. In reality, infantry units should be charging into battle as a whole, but sadly that is not the case.
Another problem? Cavalry seems slow and clunky at times, and it does an awful job at pursuing routing units.
Other problems include infantry units failing to reach their destinations in siege battles when they are stationed on walls or other areas of a city.
However, don't be repulsed at the pathfinding problems. While they can be very annoying, they don't make the game unplayable. It is still a very enjoyable game that works well.
2) If you're a Catholic faction, you will have to endure the biased, rigged political entity called the Papacy. The Papacy is headed by the Pope (obviously), represented by his College of Cardinals. Usually, the Pope makes everything bearable for the other Catholic factions except you. The Pope demands that all of the Catholic kingdoms build adequate churches and cathedrals, persecute heretics, and refrain from waging wars with each other.
The Pope is a very demanding jerk, to put it simply. Building churches and cathedrals cost lots of money. Persecuting heretics is easier said than done as well, because your priests need adequate experience to successfully get rid of them. But the worst one by far is how the Pope handles wars.
Expect every neighboring Catholic faction to stab you in the back and wage war on you. Obviously, you'll have to defend yourself, but asking for a ceasefire when you've successfully repelled the enemy from your lands usually won't work. Instead, you'll have to subdue the entire faction and conquer it just to end the war.
And while you're doing this, expect another Catholic faction to declare war on you, because they're just as manipulative as the last one you fought.
While all this happens, the Pope will try to interfere in the conflict. But no, he won't punish the scoundrels who started it. Instead he'd rather demand you to 'stop shedding the blood of your fello Christians.' If you ignore him, he'll threaten to excommunicate you.
Basically, the Pope is like a school faculty member who tries to make you look like a bad person for defending yourself against school bullies who tried to pick a fight with you.
However, not all hope is lost for you with the Papacy. If you finish a crusade, for example, relations with the Pope can improve greatly. You also have a chance to elect a pope from your own faction, who will hold you in very high regards, and you can use the rigged politics of the Papacy against your enemies!
Well, that's it for the review. Overall it's a great game with tons of other stuff for you to discover! If I decided to explain anymore about this game you'd end up having a novel.

Recommended, with a giant asterisk * There be bugs.
Overall – Campaign's okay, bugs, jumbled story, pop in texture issues.  And Raid Mode I've had a lot of fun with, and haven't notice any bugs in it yet.  Recommended for the Raid Mode, and the Campaign's is an alright time.
Extended ---
Bugs – The game only crashed two or three times, alt tabbing caused an additional crash or two, but the real problem was the graphical bugs.  Where certain textures in a room wouldn't load and I'd be left with blank black textures, sometimes including whole sections of wall, door, and enemies.  Finding either a door or an enemy, textured in all black, against an all black wall is difficult.  Other times the textures would pop with all white, and thrice with neon reds and blues.  Game immersion shattered.
Controls – A few small problems led away from the “classic” control scheme, like the camera determined to be set at an angle where I cannot see the character's feet or floor immediately in front of them, made it very difficult to pick up items when walking over to them and not being able to see them any longer.  Switched to Keyboard and Mouse and things were great other than mouse acceleration problems, where the game did not like to register small movements, worked much better with the acceleration turned off.
Game play – Campaign – An alright game, with some problems.  This is not old school Resident Evil, most battles are easier to fight than run, there's a three weapon carry limit, where in old RE a key can get you to three or more points of interest and new things, in this you get one new destination and maybe a pit stop on the way.
The story annoyingly likes to jump out of order, a few checkpoints lay between the beginning and end of chapters, which is also the only places the player can choose to save.  There's an odd ammo cap.  For each type of weapon you can hold so much ammo, until finding ammo packs to extend the number.  Once you've reached a full pocket of ammo for a weapon type you cannot pick up anymore, and you cannot store extra ammo in a box for latter, it's a bit annoying running out of handgun ammo later when earlier you walked past multiple handgun ammo packs you couldn't pick up.  Long loading times hurt as well.
Small note to enemies, who often refuse to attack your AI partners, walking past them, pushing through them, to get to the player.  Also of important note the map is awful.  The minimap on screen is fine, but the map found in the menu is bad, it does not match up with the actual game, you can only view it on an angle, and it's a jumbled mess at times trying to figure out what floor something, sometimes yourself, is on.
Raid Mode – Raid mode is fun.  You play through a slice of the map, sometimes with the objective to get from point A to B, sometimes to kill a Boss type enemy.  Before starting a location you choose your Character, your three weapons, can go to the store to buy ammo, weapon modifiers, new weapons, ect, then go to your mission and hop to it.  In Raid Mode enemies have visible health bars, enemies come in new sizes, from half sized to twice as tall, and in each map you have chances to pick up more gear.  One draw back to Raid Mode is Levels.  As you play you level up, and gain access to higher level weapons, this is just the same weapons but stronger, this then leads to higher level enemies, the same enemies as before but now with more health, which is a bit of a bore.  Also some of the character's are too much of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to unlock, one even going so far as to require you to complete every Raid Map with an S ranking, so, beat the absolute hell out of raid mode, complete everything in it, 100% the damn thing, and then you get your last character.

Updated 4/10/2016 to reflect the current state of the game.
Steam is saturated with early access sham games these days. They all release in some kind of beta sandbox state, with the dev house behind it promising the moon and the sun to the community within a year or so. Often enough these products stagnate and never realize any "potential" the hype train saw in the game. CrossCode is not another one of these games.
CrossCode is a wonderful action RPG that takes place in an alien world where gamers far away connect to avatar bodies and occassionally throw balls at hedgehogs, cows and similar kinds of dogs. Lea, the protagonist (so we're led to believe so far) is suffering a mad bout of amnesia. A floaty head guy tells Lea to play the game to kickstart her memory and following drama involving a giant enemy crab you begin your quest among the peasants to hopefully remember something about your past.
The developers have done a wonderful job pacing the release of the story along side the development of important gameplay features which has made every new release feel well rounded out and avoids spoiling the end before the game itself is complete. At the same time, they have been very responsive to input from the community which has thwarted any notions of stagnation (*cough* Starbound *cough*). The story is not yet complete so it would be ill-advised to buy the game expecting a full story right now.
Intertwined with the story are many side quests. Many of these are not required, but they help cement the impression of being in a living MMOG world and are justly incentivized to help you cut down the amount of grind time you have to spend to advance the actual plot. The standard quests are typically matters of item collection or monster slaying, and other kinds of quests are available if you seek them out. Those so far seem to entail more challenging monster battles or terrain puzzles.
The physics engine underneath everything is so smooth that you'll never feel like you're fighting your character or the environment. This lends itself well to the gratuitous ball throwing and parkour fun throughout the game and largely due to this you'll spend less time being frustrated by clunky gameplay and more time getting swole to beat a certain spikey haired rival into the ground.
Characters in this game have so far been very likeable with colorful (not in the derogatory sense) dialogue and unique personality. Additionally the game has an MMOG-like character party system which works and feels similar to any other MMOG analogue. This might seem minor, but considering the world of CrossCode is actually a pseudo-MMOG it adds realism to the experience and being able to bring other players into your party really makes any grinding stints much more fun.
Map design has so far been stellar. One thing that has been nice about the travel areas is they fairly open and built into the terrain are often parkour puzzles that hide not only collectables but also now players with quests to give you as well. There are still several that aren't done, but I expect it will be about the same level of quality.
There are only a few things I'd like to see improve, but does not deter my recommendation:
- It would be really nice to see gamepad controls improve. With a keyboard and mouse, if you need to aim for throwing a projectile you move the mouse cursor outwards in the direction of the target which allows smooth correction as you move or the target moves. With a gamepad (specifically, the Xbox One controller) you must use the right control stick to specify the direction of aim. This effectively moves your point of reference to over your characters head which makes it very difficult to aim with any precision. I feel like it would be reasonable if they added an aim assist for gamepad play to even out the gameplay experience between gamepad and keyboard control schemes.
- I still feel like the skill tree could use some expansion. But it is a minor point and the system as is works well enough given the amount of available play time available from the game.
Overall this game is a worthy purchase for early access. If you're looking to support development or just really like throwing balls its worth a buy. If you want a full story to play through right at this moment, however, I'd advise waiting to play the game until it is completed.

Wurm is one of the hidden gems of a game that you can escape into and forget the faces of your loved ones. It's less "sandbox" or "survival" and more of a Frontier. You have a pure world around you to sculpt as you see fit. Is that hill blocking your view outside your window? Grab a shovel and dig away. Want to love up someplace high? Grab a pickaxe and head up that mountain and carve out your terraced home. Think that river should curve east instead of going west? You get the idea.  The terrain is 3D (no blocks) and can be shaped as the player wishes. The crafting system is a huge seller for this game. You have to craft everything in the game, swords, bows, homes, nails, boats, wagons, shoes, ovens, boxes, kegs, keel beams, saddles, roads, walls, alters, etc. The game uses material type and weight in its crafting as well as a lot of different crafting/processing methods. You mostly build components to things, like hilts, nails, beams, chain links, shafts, then combine them in order to create items. You can then improve upon them by polishing, tempering, or other methods in order to improve its quality. While there is a small "tier" system to building materials (stone->iron-steel) for most thing the important thing is the Quality of the item. Quality will define an item's effectiveness while Material will alter is decay rate. There are a ton of skills in this game. Crafting wise you have Blacksmithing (tools), weapon smithing, armor smithing, fletching, jewelry smithing, smelting, leatherworking, cooking, boast building, house building, fences, roads, etc. Combat has, but is not limited to swords, maces, archery, polearms, greatswords, shields, scythes, etc. There is also a Religion system that can offer you bonuses and even unlocks the ability to become a Priest, giving you Magic at the cost of voluntary restrictions on what you can do. Food is very important in this game, you not only need to keep yourself feed and watered you must ensure you are eating nutritional food. To help with this you can farm, fish, keep herds of animals, all you help you cook, make cheese, cakes, wine, stews, etc. All in all Wurm has about the most robust crafting and freedom of any game you're going to fine. If you happen find something else feel free to drop me a line.

This game has a lot of potential, but as is, it's definitely in the very early stages of early access.  Since a lot of people have mentioned Prison Architect, I will agree it has a very similar vibe but is very, very simplified even from fairly early stages of Prison Architect's Alpha phases.  I don't think the game is so complex that a tutorial is in any way neccessary right now.  If you're familiar with other sim games, you'll figure out how to get started and going fairly easy, and like Prison Architect Alpha it has a to-do list as the basis of some guidance.  The only thing that was less than intuitive with the GUI was how to set boys and girls bathrooms.  If you go to edit zone for the most part the only option is to remove the zone rather than actually make any changes to it, but it also gives you the option to change the bathroom gender and grade level for classes.  Other than that, the game is pretty simple and intuitive for those familiar with the genre.
That said, I'm only recommending it if you're interested in supporting the developers.  If you're hoping for a game as enjoyable as mid to late stages of Prison Architect alpha testing, you're going to want to wait a while.  Currently, there is absolutely no problems to manage in the game.  You start with ample funds to have students in small class sizes with the best teachers no problems.  There is no conflict that arises aside from frequently sick students due to a dirty school, but I'm not 100% sure why that's happening aside from my janitors being slackers, and there are no consequences for it.
Long term, things that would likely improve the game are adding objectives/failure clauses such as ways to measure the student body as a whole's learning (though that might be a result of trauma from the American Education system, aha), more effort in attracting parents to transfer students to your school through meeting academic or musical/athletic goals with your students such as competitions you send specific students to and making more money possible only after reaching certain objectives.  The introduction of delinquents is a start on making the game more whole, but there's a long way to go to add depth.
Also, A+ for using the Prison Architect artist.  His/Her art is so cute <3

Well, playing this game after Borderlands 1 & 2 brought nothing but disappointment. Let’s start with guns. They just.. don’t feel right. The same types of guns that were in B2 such as explosive, corrosive etc. feel like sh*t, while the two new types, especially laser, do way too much damage, so you will end up using just these most of the time.
Environments are quite dull, it’s pretty much just the same rocky moon surface with randomly scattered buildings and objects. Some large maps don’t have any catch-a-ride stations in them so you will often have to go on foot from one side of a large map to another and back again, only to have to do it again with another quest. Low gravity is fun the first few times, then it gets annoying as in some areas you can float outside the map and die if you aren’t paying attention.
Characters and storytelling in this game are nowhere close to the level of B2. After a few weeks I only remember Nina and that hilarious knight who wanted to lay claim to the Moon before somebody else did it. And, of course, Jack is as awesome as ever, this time he has far more room and his sarcastic monologues are on point.
Speaking of Jack, he is a playable class (you need to have the DLC though), as is Claptrap. Some other heroes resemble classes from B2 quite a lot (Wilhelm-Commando, Aurelia-Zero), while other (Athena, Nisha) are quite unique. I played Aurelia and must say she is by far the worst sniper class of the Borderlands games. Some of her talents don’t even make sense. Weird and overcomplicated talents seem to be a general issue among all classes in the Pre-Sequel.
As for the end-game content, there is only Claptrap’s Voyage DLC which is decent, but not as good as any B2 DLCs imo. Holodome is just a really mediocre arena with multiple, gradually stronger waves of enemies, somewhat similar to B1’s Underdome. Then there is of course TVHM and UVHM, but I don’t think the game is good enough to enjoy a second, let alone third playthrough.

I haven't played many strategy games, but I got this one because of the Winter War DLC (few games have this interesting theater). I'm completely hooked now.
Without DLC, there's about 10 hours (probably less for hardcore strategy enthusiasts) of gameplay in the Bootcamp campaign, plus the first mission of every DLC campaign, plus an entire Battle of Britain free DLC campaign. It's certainly not lacking for free content.
I played through the Boot Camp campaign first and had a great time. I hadn't wanted to buy the DLC in case I didn't like strategy games, but the Boot Camp campaign convinced me I'd love it.
I'm now playing through the Winter War DLC and, at this rate, will be getting the other DLC later too. I'll wait to leave a review for them until I've finished them, but I consider it well worth the $15 I paid already.
The units are interesting and feel different from each other and other nations, it doesn't seem like a "puzzle" like the few other stategy games I've played (it feels like there's a lot of ways to win, rather than finding the exact combination that will win), the sound and visual design is great, and the game is very fun for me.
I'd elaborate more on what I like, but really, you've got 10 hours of free content (ignoring the free DLC and first campaign levels) to figure out if you like this game or not. If you're interested, give it a try.

Over a decade on, and this game is still excellent fun. The depth of the overall grand strategy combined with the satisfaction of the tactical battlefield really make this one of the all-time greats.
A campain will take you a long time (40hrs+) to complete with a single faction. There are 5 factions to start with (English, French, Holy Roman Empire, Spanish and Venetian), and once you have defeated another faction within the game (such as Denmark, Moors, Russia, Byzantines, Egypt etc.), you get to play as them. Each faction has individual units, with distinctive strengths and weaknesses and different play styles.
The depth and detail of this game really is something to behold. I've had bloodthirsty, paranoid kings who assassinate anyone foreign within their borders, beautiful princesses with secret boyfriends, honourable chivalric knights getting killed by stray cannonballs, and I had one of my bishops elected Pope even though he was secretly a woman.
The newer TW games might have better graphics and more polished animations & pathfinding, but you'll find it hard having as much fun as playing this game and building your own Medieval dynasty.

Resident Evil Revelations isn't the answer to the series problems but it's certainly a small step in the right direction.
The gameplay still similar to that which you'll find in RE4, 5 and 6 and once the get past the first few episodes the game will return to the third person shooter trend the past few games have set.
You certainly won't find horror or survival here, infact the episodes are so short it's hard to feel any kind of atmosphere.
However I would still recommend this game. While the story's throwaway and the epsiodes are too short, the gameplay can be fun at times. The setting also get's close to what Resident Evil should be about, an abandoned cruise ship, sounds perfect and for the most part looks great, but you will find some low res textures due to the game being a port of a 3DS game.
I however, feel the real meat of the game lies with the Raid mode, if you can find a friend to play it with it can be a real blast. Now and again you'll be able to connect with someone via the search filters but I wouldn't cross your fingers. The Raid mode is basically co-op, running through parts of the single player levels with different enemy layouts and strengths as well as being tested in things like speed, damage took and accuracy.
This game's fun in it's own right and the Raid mode adds just enough to recommend it, but if you're looking for a Resident Evil expierence that's like the originals, you won't find it here.

This game is awesome, even with so much content under development.  Despite that it is in early release, it is really well polished.
The short part of the story story included is good, graphics and animations are 16-bit eye-candy, and the music fits well.
The best part in my opinion is the combat system.  It is very intuitive, fluid, and simple to learn, but it is hard to master.  The basics are moving, dashing, cutting, throwing energy balls/spheres, and blocking.  There are other aspects like attack elements you can easily switch between while attacking, and other special abilities and upgrades you can unlock.  There is also a simple,efficient, "no-nonsense" equipment system, which isn't tedious or time consuming like in many games.
The game is polished well enough to be a final product (minus content wise, being still in early release), and that nothing feels tedious; I've played hours and haven't gotten tired of combat (which is saying a lot for me, I end up avoiding combat half the time in many games because it can get annoying/tedious).  Plus, you can just walk/run away when you don't want to fight (except boss battles.)

CrossCode -  a retro action-RPG, promising exciting fast-paced combat, serious puzzle-solving and on top of that a meaty story. So far so good!
Making these kinds of promises as a new development team certainly takes a lot of... courage, but how does CrossCode hold up so far? Thankfully, the current Early Access version is split into three parts, each of which is focused on one of these things:
- Exploration Mode puts you into a large open area populated by monsters. It allows you to get a feel for the game's controls as well as the extensive systems for skills (think FFX's sphere grid, but designed by a sober person) and equipment. Trying to find a large number of hidden chests you get the chance to freely jump and battle your way through the area, all the while learning new techniques and improving the stats of your character. This mode makes up the bulk of the game's current playing time and is I have had a blast playing it. Running and jumping around is just a ton of fun! While it took me a while to get comfortable with the controls during fighting, the feeling you have when you start improve and manage to defeat large mobs of enemies (that just minutes earlier were vanquishing you mercilessly) is incredibly rewarding. The game it reminded me most of is Bastion, which was one of my favorite Indie action games of the last few years, but with the beautifully animated SNES-era graphics it of course also recalls classics such as Terranigma.
- Puzzle Mode shows you an example of what the dungeons of the finished game might look like. It is only a short part of the current version, but it complements the action-y parts very well and gazing into my crystal.. eh... sphere I foresee a lot of fun once these puzzles get properly integrated into the main narrative. Think Alundra, but with a feeling that you have actually solved the puzzle instead of exploiting the game's jump physics (nah, I'm just breaking your.. stones here, Alundra, you're a great game)
- Story mode mostly works as a tutorial for the controls and an introduction to some of the game's main characters as well as a teaser as the game's larger world and plot. So if you're hoping to get deep into the world of CrossCode already, this might leave you with a severe case of blue testes, but that's not a bad thing in my book. Well I guess it is... should have rephrased that. Anyway, I'd rather have the chance to enjoy the game's style and mechanics now instead of delving into the plot too deeply - that's best left for when the game is actually finished.
SO GET TO THE POINT, SHOULD I BUY CROSSCODE NOW?
Well, maybe! ("Ooh, such decisiveness," the crowd murmured approvingly.)
See, part of me wants to go and make everybody buy this now, but I think that would do the game a disservice. CrossCode is certainly not a finished game at this point, even if the controls, animation and soundtrack already have a very high level of polish. And the current price is certainly at the level (or likely even above) where the finished product will be sold next year. So I would suggest this: if this sounds like your kind of game and you're curious to experience a game as it goes from its early stages to a fully fleshed out product - get it now! If you're interested but already don't have the time to play half the fully-finished games in your backlog? Then put it on your wishlist, follow their regularly updated and very detailed development blog and come back in a year or so. This is not a game that will always be expanded or be significantly cheaper during Early Access.
In short, CrossCode is already a ton of fun, and if the devs keep their eyes on the .. prize then this should turn out to be a great game once it's done.
Full disclosure: I backed this game during the Indiegogo campaign and I'm friends with some of the devs, so I might not be entirely trustworthy. But for what it's worth, I promise you that I wouldn't have written any of this if I didn't enjoy the game and thought it deserved a wider exposure. AND I DIDN'T EVEN SAY BALLS ONCE. EXCEPT FOR NOW. Like the other Focus games I've played, this game goes from too easy to too hard in a short span of play -- it is unbalanced, leaving it unchallenging (sort of causal) for much of the play and frustrating the other. Also very much on rails -- point to point, down narrow paths, following the story.  There are side quests but they are the same.  It does have some fun aspects, especially if you like to experiment, but overall I do not recommend.

About the only real fun I had was stealth killing with Styxx.

This is not a hack-and-slash, fast-paced combat game. So anyone looking for that type of action or enemies that drop pools of loot, I suggest looking elsewhere. It is a game that involves a mild amount of strategy with a good enough story to play through once. The combat is fairly simple, I highly recommend assigning all of your skills to hotkeys, so you don't have to pause the game every five seconds to add a new attack to each character. If  you do this, the game goes by much faster and feels more organic. Personally, I found Styx to be the much more interesting character to play as (go figure, he's the one with the series after the game). Styx adds another dimension to the game with a simple stealth dynamic that makes the actual combat easier.
This game does what it aims to do well. However, this is the style of game that is very easy to just find one strategy and use it the whole game (e.g. using Ark as a meat shield, and Styx picks everyone else off on at a time and revives him when necessary). The game is very linear, so don't expect open-world, but it is easy to find the objective and complete it without getting lost or wasting time traveling. The choices in the game are interesting enough to make you contemplate them for a short while. But, once more, the take-home is the story and the development of the characters. Which was the sole reason I continued the game.
Overall: 6/10
Worth a single play through for fans of the genre only

I would like to start this review off with a fact that may lead me to a biased review of this game:
- I loved Nier
Set in a distopian future you play as one of three androids. Each with a distinct personality; however, only one (9S) has a unique combat system. A game that is beautiful and marvelous in it's own rite, Nier: Automata has: vivid landscapes, epic quests, and amazing overtures. If you loved the first game you will love this one. If you are a newcomer to the franchise then this game may (or may not) be for you. Let's get to the Pros and Cons.
Pros:
+ breathtaking landscapes
+ unique quests and plot
+ great soundtrack
+ replayability
+ combat is fluid
+ vast amount of customization
Cons:
- no special edition for pc or xbox
- almost too much customization
- it can be slow to get going at first
- the game involves item farming (which is not really explained well in the tutorial)
- gold disappears after a short time, leaving you to decide whether to get money or finish a battle
Ultimately, the Pros outweigh the Cons and I would highly recommend this title because all of the cons can be fixed and/or worked around.
* I hope they make a special edition for pc and xbox.
* A better built in guide (maybe an in-game strategy guide you can buy to install on your pods?) would fix a lot of the cons.
* Making gold last as long as items would be great.

Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel is a step forwards for the Borderlands franchise in terms of game mechanics but two steps backwards in all other components. The game introduces ice and laser weapon types, which are welcome additions, yet are ultimately not as enjoyable to use due to the bland and uninteresting environment and enemy designs. Most of the game takes place on the moon, where the Australians seem to have been cast off to. The environment is thus overwhelmed by the darkness of space and colourless world design. The boring colours create a feeling of emptiness, which plays a surprisingly large role in making the story less engaging. The new O2 mechanic is enjoyable at first — extended jumping and attention to oxygen levels both enhance gameplay — but quickly become tedious. The Australian humour is different from previous entries in the franchise, and though there are still some funny moments, they fail to recreate past entries’ comedic charm. Even being able to play as Athena, one of my favourite Borderlands characters, can't save this game from its distant and disengaging feel. [5.5/10 - 22.05.17]

I don't think you should judge a paradox game until it's been out for a year and they have had time to add additional DLC and fix bugs. Unfortunately Stellaris has now been out for a year and its still a buggy mess with incredibly shallow gameplay. It's a strategy game where the economy (if it can even be called that) requires constant user interaction but offers no meanigful choices. You are constantly manually building the same thing over and over. This is not only tedious, but because humans are better at it than the AI, you have an enormous economic advantage that makes the game less challenging.
In addition to the broken economy combat is boring and repetitive. There is no terrain, garrisons, or supply limits like in other PDX games. So you mass all your ships into one ball, they do the same, and you chase each other around for a long time until finally you fight. In addition to being completely unablanced some aspects of combat (like missiles) just don't work.
Add to this a tech system that offers so few benefits that the dominant multiplayer strategy is just to spam the ship you get at the beginning of the game and take over the first player inexperienced enough to actually try to colonize.
The only good thing is the writing. The little things the AI says at diplomacy screens are clever and amusing, and so are the events you get when making your initial scientific exploration of the galaxy. Your first 20 hours with this game will be quite fun, but once you come to actually understand how all the mechanics work you will understand how shallow and repetitive this game is.
If you like pressing the same buttons over and over to make a number get higher like a rat in a skinner box, buy this game. If you like PDX grand strategy games, don't.

I have been playing the Resident Evil games ever since the first original one came out on PS1 so I have had a long history with the series which has had its ups and downs. Resident Evil 4 was amazing, 5 was so-so, 6 was much better than 5 but, still could of used more of the old RE horror survival flair that was very much missing in 5. Now with the release of Revelations I didnt know what to expect but, once i began playing the game I was extremley pleased to see that it felt like the old RE games but, had the gameplay style of RE 4 which to me is an amazing combo. Theres a lot of good in this game and a few bad things.
PROS:
.Amazing storyline that is one of the best written
.The story all blends together over episodes which each episode works off the previous to have a seamless addicting campaign
. Ressurection of VECTRO & the search for understanding the virus as well as revealing hidden secrects
. Gameplay is well developed
. Nice smooth shooting mechanics as well as dodging the enemy and CQB Knife attacks work well also
. Sound design is as always good
. Lots of different characters are being involved in the story which really makes things interesting
. You go back and forth between playing with Jill & her partner to playing as Chris & his partner which each on there own mission but, both all working towards the same goal
. A good length to the SP campaign that isnt short and at same time isnt super long to where it drags; its perfect length to where your hooked till the end
. Great enemies and intense moments of surviving
. Some awesome locals as well as very well made enviroments that are creepy and well designed.
CONS:
. Camera can get in the way at times but, its not a major issue
. Graphics are good but, they def could be better
. Co-Op is okay but, goodluck trying to find someone to play with
. Replay value isnt to high
. Enemies can be sluggish even for being infected zombie mutated monsters
Overall all the things that I list that are bad are so minor and really pointless dumb things that there really isnt too many actual bad things in this game. I really love this addition to the RE series and am super hooked in playing more and more because of how awesome and well written the story is which just is one of those story/plots in a game that gets you hooked and super curious to know whats gonna happen next to where you dont wanna stop playing. I'm a sucker for the whole Resident Evil franchise. If you have any reservations about the Revelations title, don't. The campaign is certainly not the meat of this game, but is well worth the entry fee. Raid online play is not a highly populated arena, but there are lots of community players who would be more than happy to oblige.

Resident Evil Revelations is a great game for fans of the series or just survival horror fans in general. The game is a perfect mix of new RE gameplay mechanics (third-person perspective, moving while aiming, and instant switch between items without having to enter the inventory menu) and classic RE structure (dark scary atmosphere, puzzles, and limited ammo and health items). The new scanner equipment allows the player to search areas for hidden items and rewards the player with health once 100% scanning requirement of enemies is met. This is a welcomed and smart addition to the series. The enemy designs are really great and creepy as well. They are reminescent of original RE designs and Silent Hill monsters.  Aside from some weak dialog and a couple of just downright terrible side characters, this game is fantasic and will hopefully set a standard for future Resudent Evil titles.

Remember the cult 90's show Twin Peaks? Fantastic series, and this game holds up well as "companion media" to the show. You are put in the role of Francis York Morgan, an FBI Special Agent who is dispatched to the small country town of Greenvale to work on a homicide case. As the game progresses York becomes involved in the town's sinister affairs and realises that things are not as they seem.
The game plays a lot like an actual investigation. You will go to gather evidence, interrogate suspects and follow leads. The game world is open to you with no time limit, so there's nothing stopping you from enjoying what Greenvale has to offer!
The game's story is its true strength. The characters, locations and subplots adds to everything that makes the game "so bad it's good". A terrific game to play if you're interested in Twin Peaks or The X-Files.

I was going to say something bad about this game since the PC version of Deadly Premonition has one of the worse ports I have ever encountered (It's really bad on the PC & the devs won't even bother fixing the PC version so Durante had to do their work for them) but I played the Xbox version of Deadly Premonition so I have something different to say (I know the xbox version doesn't include the Director's Cut but I had to play this game to see why it was in the cult section of videogames).
Deadly Premonition Review:
I usually have an average experience on most modern horror games like Outlast for example (I'm a very picky person on what I think is a good horror game) but this game gave me the best experience in the psychological, mystery horror genre & I'm going to try to explain why.
Well for starters this game has one of the most interesting main characters in the world of horror. His name is Francis Morgan a.k.a York who has a split personality named Zach who helps him in his cases, every time he takes a sip of coffee he gets a random fortune or a message from it (I wish my coffee could do that) & he has a unique talent of collecting clues then automatically getting his "Profiling" skills running in his brain (The way he already knows what's going on is amazing, Sherlock Holmes would be proud). The game's strengths are the story, characters, the open world of Greenvale, the amount of side missions you can do (There are also trading cards that you can collect) & the strong plot twists but there are downsides to this game like the combat for example but I'm not going to mention them because the game forgives it's flaws by having cheesy charm (It's hard to explain).
One of my friends gave a perfect word for this game which is "Bat♥♥♥♥♥♥crazy" (I played a lot of disturbing games to the point of being desensitized) & I have to agree because the game has one of the weirdest characters in gaming history like Sigourney for example who is obsessed with warming her pot (Not the drug you idiot) & I can't forget the transformation that Thomas had with a red dress later on in the game (Thomas get the ♥♥♥♥ off drugs). The story to this game is your typical who murdered this person scenario but the way the game feeds you the character's backstories & the amount of thinking is brilliant, this game forces you to not trust everyone but it slowly weeds out your guesses (Me, my friend & my family were having fun trying to guess the murderer & we were all talking about theories on who the murderer is). The fact that the game is a combination of Resident Evil's combat (Resident Evil 4 mostly) & the open world sandbox of Grand Theft Auto is a nice combination from the game director SWERY a.k.a Hidetaka Suehiro so I hope future game devs use an open world sandbox in future horror games.
Overall this game is a good example on how to make a good horror game without overusing cheap scares like jumpscares when the main thing you should be afraid of is the unknown & to be aware of who you trust (If I missed anything then be sure to leave feedback so I can edit my review & I forgot that shaving your beard gives you money).

: Radical Fish Games

: A key for this game was provided by the developer for the purpose of writing an informative review. No other compensation was given.
==========
CrossCode is the perfect example of why Early Access exists. It gives us an idea of the game the developers have in mind, while allowing us to support them and help them to finish their game. CrossCode is an action RPG, and a shiny pearl in the sea of  trash that's currently swimming in Early Access. There are a lot of systems and features in place and ready to go, such as melee/ranged attacks, dodging, guarding, skill trees, elemental attacks, interacting with the terrain, trading, puzzle-filled dungeons, story scripting, enemy AI and attack patterns, bosses, and more! CrossCode draws heavily from the 16-bit era, and if you've played Secret of Mana or Zelda: A Link to the Past for the SNES, then you'll see the influence easily. The gameplay is very similar to those two games, and it's simply amazing. The current version of CrossCode is a set of demos, one for each mode: Story, Puzzle, and Exploration. I'll go over each one in turn.
==========
First, let's go over Story Mode. In Story Mode, you are introduced to a cast of characters and the game world. I'm not going to spoil anything here, but let's just say it's a premise that's been done before but with a few twists. You begin in a sort of tutorial area, which has you running a character through a small forested area towards a building. Along the way, you are taught the basic controls and basic combat abilities.  Once you reach the building a short dialogue occurs, then the game transitions to a cargo ship where we meet the main player character and the supporting cast. More tutorials occur, such as ranged and melee combat, switches, dodging, and later guarding. You have a melee slashing attack, and a ranged attack that has you shooting spheres. The spheres are able to bounce off walls when charged. The Story Mode demo wraps up after a boss battle that introduces an antagonist who tries to abduct the main character. She is saved by the supporting cast and makes an escape.
Next, we have Puzzle Mode. Puzzle Mode takes you through a typical dungeon that will be implemented into the finished game. This has you hitting switches to open doors, moving boxes to press switches, navigating large rooms to solve puzzles scattered throughout, and ultimately ending up at a boss battle that introduces you to Boss AI scripting. It has 3 phases, the first being the melee phase. It'll be within your melee range, so just attack it normally. Next with Phase 2 it'll move away out of your melee range, so start using your ranged attacks. In the combat area are 2 switches which raise 2 pillars. When the boss starts charging up it super attack, hit one of the switches and hide behind a pillar that pops up. The boss will finish his attack, then hit the switch itself and lower the pillar and resume it's attacks. In phase 3 it gains a shield, which you need to solve a small puzzle to figure out how to bring it down. It involves bouncing your ranged attacks off of bumpers to hit it from behind, shorting out it's shield. Defeating it gives you the option to take on the "Final Challenge", which is a short Survival Mode, that has you fighting waves of enemies. The Puzzle Mode Demo wraps up afterwards.
Last, we have Exploration Mode. This starts you in an area called Autumn's Rise, where you are introduced to even more features, like Elemental Attacks, Skills, Items, Equipment, and Combat Arts. In this mode you are free to explore the map, defeat enemies, and buy equipment and items from the few shops that are present. There are even a few trading booths where you can trade items you find for other items.  Exploration Mode ends when you find all of the hidden treasure chests in the area and open up the last challenge.
==========
CrossCode is a very colorful, vivid game, with detailed character sprites. Remember how the SNES did sprites? Take those, and make them 100 times better. CrossCode uses very crisp sprites with fluid animations for all aspects of gameplay. Attacks, movement, dodging, etc...all look extremely detailed and very well done. No complaints from me in the graphcis department. I grew up with classics like Super Mario World, Secret of Mana, Final Fantasy III (VI), Chrono Trigger, Earthbound, and Lufia, so I'm no stranger to sprite-based games. CrossCode features some of the best sprites I've ever seen in a video game. Even the character portraits are sprites!
==========
Great sound effects and cacthy tunes that fit any given situation. The music sounds like it would have been right at home on the SNES, and sounds very Secret of Mana or Star Ocean-esque; this fits the theme of the game extremely well. When combat starts the music changes to a more fitting tone, and transistions back to normal when combat is concluded. Being a big fan of video game music, I can't go on enough about how much I like the music in this game.
==========
I ran into absolutely no issues while playing CrossCode. Everything was crisp and smooth, no framerate issues or crashing. The game seems very well optimized for a game in what looks liek an alpha stage. This makes it very easy to recommend this game to all players who are fans of this genre, as they will have very little issues getting the game to run so they can enjoy it!
==========
This game has everything you could possibly want from an action RPG. Combat, exploration, puzzles, dungeons...the concept is here and it's amazing. Please buy this to support the developers and help them get this gem finished! I'd hate to see such potential shut down, and this game has a ton of potential. It could be the next big indie title. It just needs a helping hand. And with Steam's Early Access program, that could very well happen. Even with it's early alpha/demo state, it still offers several hours of fun gameplay.
==========
This demo covers all of Puzzle Mode and a nice portion of Exploration Mode.
