This one impressed me from the very start. The music, colors, and animation I was greeted with on the title screen alone were all of fantastic quality. Upon entering the game, Crosscode treats you to a wonderful color palette, and a basic mysterious introductory story scene, that gives you a brief briefing of the combat system you'll be working with.
Crosscode, from what I can tell, is a game about an AR MMO where the players are hooked into avatars made from instant matter. There is a physical location in the world starting with Rhombus Square where they can play the game. Their attacks, it seems, effect the physical world, although they can only be seen with AR glasses. It also seems that they are not necessarily prohibited from leaving their designated game zone.
The tutoral will cover all of this and a bit more, as you take on the role of the protagonist Lea, who has amnesia and is going to be playing the game to attempt to recover her memories. The story may be starting to become familiar territory, but aside from a few grammatical mistakes, is excellently written. Likewise, the gameplay is as smooth as can be, with many options for you.
In combat, you can fight with ranged or melee, even to some extent simaltaneously, and both will be needed, but often times you are allowed to use either as you see fit. There will be many RPG features like equipment, a sprawling skill tree reminiscent of Path of Exile, inventory management, levels and experience, etc. The gameplay I've experienced so far reminds me a lot of Golden Sun, in that it's an action-puzzler RPG with excellent graphics, world design, and puzzle elements flawlessly integrated into said world design.
The UI is also flawless, and the developers have made it very easy to navigate. It's stylish but also very functional. The game has full keyboard/mouse and controller support, but goes the extra mile to make keyboard navigation easy. The camera transitions, dialogue, and everything else are smooth and refreshingly simple.
After playing this demo I could not be more excited about the final product-which I will now commence eagerly awaiting. Even more importantly, this demo has made me feel like I have a high degree of assurance this will be a game of the utmost quality.

I have played this game for nearly 700 hours as unlimited, and before that several hundred as Online.  This is a true sandbox.  There is no 'end game'.  You find things to do, projects, friends. You want to play a game with no pressure to have follow a certain path?  Maybe you grow weary of killing mobs for hours on end just so some NPC can have his mob bits. Breed animals for food or crafting materials or pets or to sell.  Build a cabin in the woods, a castle, a bridge, a kingdom.  Become the baddest♥♥♥♥♥fighter on your server, big game hunter, magic user, even become a deity.  The list goes on.  Of course you could choose to do all of these, or none.  That's the beauty of a true sand box game.  Play how you want.  There are even mods out there that can alter game mechanics or add or change items, abilities etc.

I played the free campaign (Boot Camp) through its entirety and it was indeed enjoyable.  It is a more simplistic style of the typical turn based strategy of the WWII era, yet it has enough depth to keep it interesting. In fact, I actually find it more enjoyable than some of my more involved TBS war games as the older I get, the less time I want to spend hashing out a single turn through a campaign made up of 50 or more turns.
The strategy aspects of it were pretty well done in my opinion. I've seen other reviewers complain about the AI cheating, but I saw no indication of that. What I saw was having to plan out each attack, ensuring you had better odds by unit placement and proximity to friendly units, softening up enemy units with artillary shock treatments, and attacking with flanking support. The AI knows how to do this as well, so it made for somewhat realistic battles and forced you to strategize to be successful.
All in all the game itself is a worthy one. So why the thumbs down?  For one simple reason: The monitization of this game seems like a terrible one from a customer perspective. Many WWII TBS games exist out there and come with several campaigns built in. A slew of these can already be found on Steam for sub $20 / $30. Some even sub $10, yet all come with several campaigns. Slitherine has taken the "pay for each single campaign" method, where each campaign is $20 (with the exception of a $15 and $10 campaign). So to get 4 campaigns (where most others come with 3 - 6 campaigns or more in the product for their $20/30 pricetags) you pay $65.
So using the strategy where each campaign is a DLC you buy, Slitherine has found a way to make more money than other games having many more campaigns for the price, and where others have more value as well. If these 4 campaigns all came in at $25, I feel the product would be a commensurate value to its quality at its release date. So by now, it should be sub $20 due to time, not $65.
Long story short: Play the free "Boot Camp" (tutorial), it was fun and I certainly recommend that. If you feel the product is worth its cost afterwards, then by all means get it. I would not recommend it at its current pricing, but if it goes on sale where you can get the entire current DLC for sub $20 then I would absolutely recommend.

As someone who plays both the "absurdly complex" hardcore strategy games you need to spend 10 hours reading the manual to even start playing and seemingly-simple-but-actually-deep, colorful strategy games like Advance Wars, I can say this fits into a comfortable middle-ground that is approachable, yet not quite as goofy and gamey as Advance Wars. (So no, you can't block a panzer division by keeping a plane on the one bridge to your base since air and land/sea units are on different layers.)
This game has definite "I'm tired, but just one more turn an- oh, God, does the clock say 4 AM?!" potential.
The game really does lean more the "Advance Wars" route, with the clear-cut unit types and one-unit-per-tile (excepting air units flying over land or sea units) that generally have rock-paper-scissors vulnerabilities to one another.  Battleships cost only a few times as much as destroyers, which are on par with infantry units in cost.  Expensive tanks are countered by cheap AT guns that can interrupt attacks against neighboring units while on the defense, but are severly vulnerable on offense and generally just eaten by infantry.  Unlike Advance Wars, where Infantry was just there to capture towns, infantry are totally viable and actually a highly deadly unit since they are more generally flexible and don't have a whole class of units designed specifically as their counter.  More than Advance Wars, the game also has an "efficiency" score that really serves as a combined/abstracted organization/morale/supply meter.  Artillery, strategic bomber, and naval bombardment all deal less direct damage than they disorganize/demoralize the enemy for your infantry to storm in.
One thing that the game does very well in comparison to many other "serious" hex-based historical strategy games is incorporate land and sea forces into the same battles fairly well.  Land units can spawn their own transports at ports, and sail to beaches to land and invade new islands, a somewhat gamey, but highly strategically interesting prospect.  Along the way, they're at the mercy of naval units, which are also capable of heavily bombarding coastal emplacements when not fighting for naval supremacy.
This game also features "core units", which are units you keep from scenario to scenario in a campaign, gaining experience.  You can even rename them, which I highly recommend doing, as having your favorite tanks and ships (named after your dog or friends or favorite fictional characters) pull through the war with elite status makes it more enjoyable. It also makes moments where the unit is in real trouble far more tense, and keeps you far more invested in the well-being of your troops in a game that otherwise tends to prioritize speed of advance over keeping your troops in a cohesive state.
With all that said, there are some weaknesses; The AI doesn't rely upon a single general strategic script that is rather sophisticated like they do in Advance Wars, instead, units are assigned to individual scripts that tend to be extremely single-minded.  On scenarios where you are on offense, the AI often just sits in place and waits for you to come and swarm them, with the exception of the units that really need to sit in place, the AT and AA guns that bizarrely are super-aggressive and break out of their entrenched positions so your infantry can obliterate them more easily.
Likewise, the game relies upon giving you very limited units, but letting you repair them with absurd ease, provided you have the cash.  Since you have a super-low unit cap, however, once you've deployed your units, there's literally nothing else to spend that money upon, anyway.
The naval combat in particular feels like it needs a rebalance; There's almost no role for cruisers at all.  Battleships are just clearly better at ranged surface gun battles, and cruisers aren't significantly less expensive enough in comparison to battleships (especially in the ever-so-crucial unit cap department) while they are significantly less effective in combat.  Destroyers redeem themselves with sub-hunting, torpedoes, torpedo-blocking, and cheap repairs to justify themselves, but cruisers are left in the cold.  And when I say "cruisers", I mean "heavy cruisers".  Light cruisers aren't even available for purchase!  Too bad if you're an Atlanta or Agano fan, they aren't there.
Likewise, if you're a naval buff, you'll find that many units become "obsolete" and removed from the lists of purchasable units when they really shouldn't be.  Having the air force phase out the A5Ms for A6M (zeros) makes sense, as does making new infantry units come equipped with the year's latest model of panzerfaust.  Ships, however, weren't so easily replaced.  If you want a Fubuki, you better buy one in the first mission, even if you can't really use it there, because it goes obsolete by the second mission!
Logistics exists, although I'm not entirely sure why. It is nearly always a non-factor since you have a super-low unit cap and essentially always start out with more supply than you need for your whole army, and then are sent out to capture more cities that expand your supply more.  It would only matter if you used paratroopers or landing craft to outflank the enemy by taking towns and using supply ships and destroyers to supply the troops as they became established... which the game's scenarios basically never allow to be a sane option.  It feels like a totally wasted oportunity, since this game does combined forces combat so well, but fails to capitalize upon it with true land/sea/air combined scenarios, instead splitting them into a "naval battle before the landing" scenario and then a "land battle after the landing" scenario, and skipping the landing portion entirely. Intro:
So far so good! I absolutely love this game! If it keeps going well, this will be one of my top favorite of all time games. I subscribed to the subreddit, email, twitter and the youtube channel so I don’t miss a single thing. If you liked or loved Prison Architect, you will feel the same way or stronger about Academia. It takes on a very similar gameplay and artwork to that game. I messaged the Dev on Twitter and sure enough, the artist from PA is on this game and he is working in a small group to make Academia. This is his own project and he is passionate about it. I expect great things from this game and I bought 2 copies right when I could on launch day.
Summary so far:
You start out with a blank slate in an open canvas as you prepare to make your school. You have 3 zones already that you can of course change. You have deliveries, garbage, and an area for your workers. At this point, there are no scenarios or tutorials implemented yet but that should change over time. To get a sort of tutorial now, you can just take on a grant, finish the grant, then move to the next. In this way, you will get the idea and progress. I haven’t played until end game or anything yet but I can see how it will progress based on what I’ve done so far. The gameplay is similar enough to PA to know what to do intuitively but it is a different game still. You can hire at this point: janitors; teachers; workers; cooks and nurses. This game is based on a high school so there is freshman through senior classroom zones to make. There is even the ability to have a bathroom for men or women. This game looks, feels, and sounds great. It’s a very positive experience so far. I would definitely recommend this game to add to your collection.
Pros:
•	Great art
•	Great music
•	Great UI experience
•	Intuitive menus for building and management tasks
•	Sandbox mode for just playing around or experimenting
•	Great communication with players and perspective players
•	A team that can be trusted in early access to deliver and not abandon the project
•	Tasks don’t take too long to get done by workers
•	Being able to vote on the next game project for the devs
Cons:
•	Some editing tasks can be tedious such as having to bulldoze grass if you lay down grass and want to change it to something else like concrete tiles
•	Not enough tile and wall pieces yet
•	Lack of campaign so far
•	Lack of proper tutorial so far
•	Slow loading to start the game
Verdict:
I won’t give a game that released practically a second ago a numerical value or something of the like. I can say that the issues with the game so far will most likely be fixed over time. I don’t see my cons as permanent problems. I simply added them because they are there. If I were to recommend the game or not, I would always recommend it. This is a great start to what will become a great game. I say go for it!
Still not sure:
I can blame you if you don’t know if you should get it or not. I recommend checking out the dev logs and gameplay videos on Youtube. I would also check out the site. That should help you decide for sure. Some games in early access are simply not worth getting yet until they fix and add more content. I think this is one game worth getting and enjoying the journey over time.

Academia: School Simulator, is a very fun idea and the simplistic but awesome art style that is similar to Prison Architect is awesome. It's extremely fun to play, as it's a "Prison Architect" meets high school, which is again a lot of fun.
However the game is EXTREMELY lacking in content, and even basic things like zones are too buggy right now.
Want an L shaped kitchen? Can't. Once you make a zone by clicking and dragging and letting go, that's the zone. Adding another zone to it won't make it one zone. You can build everything within 10 minutes, not even using sandbox mode.
Pro's:
- Loveable art style
- Groundwork is there
- Make a school emblem, motto and name.
- You can give classrooms names
- Big map, so you can build a huge campus
Cons:
- No dorms/beds. Students simply go home (not even using a school bus)
- Very limited amount of zone types and things to do
- In current state, absolutely not worth the pice.
- Can't rename students/teachers or staff.
- Can't buy land to make an even bigger school
- Everything can be built in 5-10 minutes, leaving you with nothing to look forward to.
- High graphical settings can bug out your game, huge amount of memory also used
- No missions/challenges or anything really to make it more interesting
- No tutorial, you are thrown in and you have to figure it out all by yourself
Final thoughts:
I will update this when updates come to add new zones/items etc ofcourse.
If you want to support the devs, and believe they won't abandon this project, then I'd say buy it.
If you want a prison architect game that is about schools, do not buy this yet.
Is it right now worth 16 euros? ABSOLUTELY NOT!

I don't think you should judge a paradox game until it's been out for a year and they have had time to add additional DLC and fix bugs. Unfortunately Stellaris has now been out for a year and its still a buggy mess with incredibly shallow gameplay. It's a strategy game where the economy (if it can even be called that) requires constant user interaction but offers no meanigful choices. You are constantly manually building the same thing over and over. This is not only tedious, but because humans are better at it than the AI, you have an enormous economic advantage that makes the game less challenging.
In addition to the broken economy combat is boring and repetitive. There is no terrain, garrisons, or supply limits like in other PDX games. So you mass all your ships into one ball, they do the same, and you chase each other around for a long time until finally you fight. In addition to being completely unablanced some aspects of combat (like missiles) just don't work.
Add to this a tech system that offers so few benefits that the dominant multiplayer strategy is just to spam the ship you get at the beginning of the game and take over the first player inexperienced enough to actually try to colonize.
The only good thing is the writing. The little things the AI says at diplomacy screens are clever and amusing, and so are the events you get when making your initial scientific exploration of the galaxy. Your first 20 hours with this game will be quite fun, but once you come to actually understand how all the mechanics work you will understand how shallow and repetitive this game is.
If you like pressing the same buttons over and over to make a number get higher like a rat in a skinner box, buy this game. If you like PDX grand strategy games, don't.

NBA 2k17 has very great visuals. The game looks and sounds like you were watching a broadcast of a nba game. Modes have improved with more features. However the actual gameplay is sorely lacking for things that make it feel arcadish and at times straight broken. I'm going to mention the 10 biggest ones and all of them are a HUGE problem not just moderate that you can live with.
1) Celebrations online can be hazardous. If you are playing MyCareer it isn't a problem because you can trigger the celebration animation by pressing a button. But in other modes online that the animations trigger anytime you score it becomes horrible as your player(s) go off celebrating while the other team goes down the court passing your celebrating player(s)
2) Defense AI is really buggy. After scored possessions some defenders do not go to meet their assigned player. This is a huge problem as it happens a lot and can lead to open shots.
3)Pick and roll seems to be forced in this game. The roller 90% of the time can absorb the defender into them even if the defender is trying to avoid or even go in the opposite direction. It almost feels like a magnet
4)This game is fast paced. Not a bad thing. Especially if you like to play up and down the court. However, the rest of the game doesn't match that speed. Pass animations, dunk animations, and layup animations seem to go 3 times as slow as the overall speed of the game.
5)Speed thresholds don't seem to make sense this 2k. They have speed and speen with ball ratings. However, even with these ratings the game seems to break its own logic. Players will significantly slower speed can sometimes keep up with players on a fast break. It doesn't happen all the time however. It reminds me of a racing game when you have a car behind another car and the car behind gets a speed boost due to slipstreaming.
6) (Traditional) Big men are unappreciated in this game. You can get a rebound and immediately one tap on the steal button or just a stumbling animation can make them drop the ball. Some people may not have a problem with this but for me a big man shouldn't have a problem holding a ball if they aren't dribbling.
7) Because of what I stated earlier about the defense being bad in this game I honestly believe the developers at 2k knew this and their way of "even" it out was the steal animations. Steals isn't much as a problem as the animations that they create. Players sometimes lose the ball and just flop to the ground on their own. Others completely pick up their dribble after stumbling backwards 2 or 3 steps. These animations also create a huge delay. You could be performing a dribble move, a post move, or a passing move and these steal animations will make you do the move but gather your dribble as well preventing you from finishing your action. And your player has to come to a complete stop in the animation before you are able to press a button and for it to respond to it. That's just unacceptable.
8) Doesn't happen a lot. In fact it may never happen to you. But with the 800+ hours I have played I have had this happen to me once and did it twice. Sometimes a contested shot can look as though it will be an airball and then all of a sudden the ball does a Super Mario Jump in mid air going into the basket. I don't believe this is lag because one of the times I did this it was offline. I believe that it is a glitch for if you hold the shot all the way allowing the meter to come back to empty.
9) Players on offense tend to go out of bounds for no reason (especially on fast breaks). This is really annoying when you are trying to kick it out and your player is standing out of bounds and makes little attempt to even get back in sometimes.
10) NBA 2k17 really makes you want to look into player's tendencies and IQs. Because some of them don't seem to ever be active or in effect. For example a player can be wide open on the wing and a good 3 point shooter. You pass it to him but as you pass he decides to cut into traffic. Sometimes big men who can't shoot hang around the 3 pt line for a long time. You can call plays or pick and rolls to have them move but if you have to do that then it means that tendencies and IQ mean nothing. And no playbooks are not the reason. I've played with multiple playbooks and players just don't seem to recognize what's happening on the court.
Now there is a lot more problems for the gameplay. And some game modes have issues as well that I could speak of. But honestly these are the biggest gameplay problems. Gameplay efffects every mode essentially so if the gameplay is too broken it doesn't matter how good the visuals or the modes are. The game does have some good things. Shooting has been improved (almost to a fault). Stamina actually seems to be accurate this year as fatique in past 2ks were either way too punishing or hardly even there. Post moves got some attention this game (mostly just the post spin). But even with all these improvements they aren't huge enough to overcome the faults that certain gameplay moments come with. This game offers more frustration then it does excitement. This is mostly because some things feel out of your control and you are left trying to play to the rules of 2k and not the rules of the modern nba which ironically it should be simulating. You will experience this when you win and when you lose. Yes the halftimeshows, pregame shows, cutscense, postgameshows, interviews, stat tracking all feel realistic. But once the ball is horribly jumped for at mid court all realism is thrown out the window.

Ah, the classic indie smash hit that is The Binding of Isaac.
Now before I start the review I wanna say something, I enjoy playing this game, but I suck at it. Like a lot.
The biggest problem I have with the Binding of Isaac is how harsh it treats you when you die, because its back to square one for you, (almost) literally. But this reinforces good gameplay habits, meaning that you need to try harder and harder just to get to the games last dungeon. Also, I haven't even beat the game, haven't even gotten close, that's how much I suck at this game. Yet, its still a blast to play.
Storywise, picture it like Margaret White from Carrie, but Carrie is Isaac and also naked, doesn't have psychic powers, and experiences Zelda-styled dungeons with lotsa crap in them. Metaphorically and literally.
The best part about this game is the basic gameplay alone. If you've ever played Zelda: Link to the Past, then you'll have a great understanding of how the game's mechanics and controls behave. The Binding of Isaac is like a hybrid between the original Legend of Zelda on the NES and Link to the Past on the SNES, while still being original and creative. Also, the controls feel very slippery, kind of like Super Meat Boy (if you know where I'm going).
Overall, if you are a fan of games similar to the classic, top-view Legend of Zelda games, and are up to a fun but vigorous challenge I reccomend this game, as well as ReBirth (considering they're more or less the same). Its a cheap game, especially when on sale, and is just a nice time killer.

Deadly Premonition is one of the most unusual and strangest games I've played for a long time. That is true, not only because of its progressively more mystic story and the many weird citizens of Greenvale but also because of the peculiar mix of gameplay and technical elements. Many parts of the game are great, others are so bad they're good again, some are truely (ragequit inducingly) bad. Deadly Premonition is a very rough gem; it's seriously flawed but the game has real character.
While I had a lot of fun with the game, playing it was quite frustrating sometimes. After the ending credits rolled I was left unsure whether I should be sad it ended, or glad that I won't have to experience any more of it. All in all the positives outweigh the negatives for me but I only recommend the game to people with patience in combination with high tolerance for bugs and broken gameplay.
For a little bit more detailed impression of some aspects I start with the technical side as this is where the most frustrating flaws of the game lie: The PC version of Deadly Premonition is a terrible console port. From what I read on various websites the game was already quite buggy on consoles; on PC most if not all of these bugs are still there but others were introduced on top of that as well.
For starters I experienced a half a minute up to 5 minutes long blackscreen before any cutscene would play. Because an intro cutscene would play before the start screen everytime the game starts and another one - summarising what had happened in the game before - everytime a game is loaded, this issue already made just starting the game an annoyance. Now add periodic crashes into the mix and the annoyance level is upped to eleven. The game crashed about two dozen times in the course of the game, mostly in the worst situations possible ("Oh, you just beat a sidequest in which you have to refight stronger versions of all bosses in a row without being able to save inbetween and you're just two steps away from a savepoint? Why don't you do it again? TROLOLOLO!").
Deadly Premonitions allows you to replay already finished chapters in order to pick up missed collectables or do sidequests, however during such replays saving is disabled until the chapter is finished, making crashes even worse than in the regular playthrough where often enough a savepoint is closeby.
Usually the crashes appeared somewhat randomly but then the game crashed everytime on the transition from chapter 8 to 9. Setting the compability mode to Windows 98 eventually got me through that part, though.
Additionally to long loading times and crashes there are some bugs with quests: After replaying earlier chapters quest items (especially temporary ones like keys for locked doors) are sometimes deleted from the inventory and can not be retrieved in normal ways. This happened to me once with an item needed for a side quest before I could finish said quest; in the end I had to change my savefile with an hex editor to get it back.
Before playing I got the recommendation to play the game with a gamepad because, like many console games, it's supposed to play better that way. Turns out my gamepad (an old BigBen pad) isn't supported and because of the way gamepad integration is done in this port programs like x360ce or xpadder don't work with it rendering it impossible to use my gamepad. Still I found that keyboard + mouse controls worked well enough most of the time, only the handling of additional cars that can be bought later in the game is horrible.
Gameplay: Deadly Premonition's gameplay comes pretty close to what I wished Alan Wake, another game inspired by Twin Peaks, would be like: Almost at any time the player can choose to ignore the mainquest for a while and freely roam around the town of Greenvale, learning more about its citizen by questioning people, starting sidequests and searching for collectables.
At some points the game throws a puzzle at the player. The puzzles are few and they're really easy but it's still more than Alan Wake had to offer, which was mostly composed of cutscenes and filler combat. Speaking of which, a flaw Deadly Premonition shares with AW is boring, repetitive and clunky combat. Reducing the amount of combat or even removing it completely would have been an improvement in my opinion. In order to make up for less/no combat I would have loved to see the "Profiling" feature expanded.
Profiling, for me, is the #1 area where the game left a lot of unused potential. From the role profiling plays in the story one could assume it's a core part of the game but in the end it's pretty dull: At a crime scene the player sees a couple of noisy pictures showing the circumstances of the crime recreated by Agent Francis York Morgan, the game's protagonist, and now has to search for clues. Each found clue makes some of the pictures now appear clearly visible. And that's all.
Turning these profiling sessions into puzzles, maybe even letting the players make their own deductions, leading to a branched-out (to some degree at least) storyline, would have vastly improved the whole game and further increased the incentive to replay finished chapters.
So I didn't really like combat and the lackluster profiling that much but still both is 'okay' and far from gamebreaking. The one thing I hated about the gameplay are Quick Time Events. I hate QTEs in general but Deadly Premonition has some of the worst QTEs I've ever seen. An especially annoying QTE in the game makes you press buttons, apparently randomly chosen from four possibilities, in rather short time; be too slow or press a wrong button first and it's instant "gameover, try again!" (including going through several black screens). Fortunately QTEs aren't that abundant but they were closer to making me quit the game for good than any of the technical issues.
Deadly Premonition plays a bit like a Japanes horror shooter (think Resident Evil or Silent Hill) combined with an adventure game and a little bit of open-world.
Story/characters/music:
The thing I enjoyed the most about the game are the wonderfully eccentric characters. It's full of well written, funny dialogues that are made even funnier by the often completely inappropriate background music. Or rather "foreground" music, sometimes and seemingly random the music gets louder than the speech (like in a couple of other cases, the overall oddness of the game makes me unsure whether this is a bug or if it was than on purpose). Deadly Premonition can be very surreal sometimes. Still there are many scenes with a more serious tone (it's all about a murder case after all) and those work very well, too.
Setting, characters and story are heavily inspired by the TV series Twin Peaks, therefore the aforementioned absurd dialogues are not surprising. Twin Peaks is among my favourite TV shows, so I highly enjoyed Deadly Premonition's setting.
However from time to time the game draws a bit too heavily from its inspiration: some details about characters' backstories that get revealed through side quests are no big surprise if you've seen Twin Peaks.
The main story line is, several parallels aside, mostly original, though. For the most parts it's well written and interesting but, especially towards the end, it gets cheesy and loses some of its charme. Biggest problem I had with the story was that, without need, the game gives an extremely obvious clue regarding the solution of the case very early on and no character, not even the alleged super-profiler Agent York, considers it during the investigation. Of course, from a meta perspective the game can't just end before it even really started but why bring a thing like that up at all then?
Again I can't rule out that it wasn't done on purpose, though; maybe in order to lampshade B-movies from the 80s which are a recurring theme throughout the game and plotholes like that are not exactly a rare occurence in those movies.

On paper, this game has everything. It's a horror adventure game with an elaborate Twin Peaks-inspired story that takes roughly 20 hours to complete depending on how much time you spend doing sidequests. It's got an open world for you to explore, there's a bunch of ranged and melee weapons, puzzle sequences, hunger mechanic, you name it. The problem is that this game plays and looks like a Playstation 2 game. The graphics are outdated, which wouldn't be too bad if the design wasn't also outdated: it basically plays like a poor man's Silent Hill, and it is full of tedious missions and easy combat encounters.
This PC port is also a mess that is locked to 720p, lacks color filters that the console version apparently had and crashes regularly. You can fix all of this by installing three easy fixes that you can find on the forums, but still. If you want a game that works right out of the digital box and plays like a modern survival horror game, it's hard to recommend this.
Yet, I absolutely loved this game, and it is all thanks to the story and characters. You play as Francis York Morgan, an FBI agent who comes to the small town of Greenvale to solve the murder of a young woman. Sounds familiar? Yes, the game's story is basically a funnier Twin Peaks, and I loved it. It is at times super weird, super funny and super interesting, so it was easy for me to overlook all the shortcomings of the game. The dialogue, story beats and even the cheesy comic relief made this game so easy to enjoy. I just wish this "Director's Cut" had more stuff to it than extra costumes and some cutscenes, and also made the game look and play a bit better.

There is something about Nier: Automata, it’s an unforgettable experience, a unique journey, and some of the best definition of humanity－both inside and outside the game.
Story
10/10, unquestionable. Yoko Taro’s idea of unpredictable gameplay and amazing skill of “backwards scriptwriting”, combine with his understanding of human, give Nier: Automata, as well as Nier and Drakengard their soul. There are many moment we as player feels what the character feels, thanks to decision of force the player to spend as many time as possible with the character, to build up relationships, bonds, and memories. And then, destroy all of them, one by one, not just in front of the character, as well as in front of you. The linear story structure is also perfect for a hopeless, meaningless story like this. You think you can do something by making some decision, but in fact, you can’t. You are a doll who is play by the story, just like the characters are an automata who is play by their fate. After all, “Director: Yoko Taro” properly is a quality insurance for story whatsoever.
Gameplay
Well, there aren’t much I can talk about, I didn’t play a lot of ACT or ARPG, but there are one thing for sure. The gameplay mechanic is simple, it’s easy enough that pretty much everyone can play and enjoy the story, as well as making the well done camera changing possible.
Music
I don’t think there are much need to be say about music, everyone know how good it is.
Graphic, Performance, PC Port, and Asian Zone price
This game can be a masterpiece without this sh/itty PC port, Square Enix. I hat to mention this, but what Square Enix had done to the PC community is disappointed. How many god/damn people had being complain about performance on PC? How many god/damn “Not Recommended” did this game get because the suddenly rise of price of Asian Zone without any explanation or announcement? This is the worst marketing I had seen for past years.

First, to get this out of the way. Some people say this game crashes a lot. Fortunately, I had no problems with that whatsoever and it ran rock-solid with a good framerate.
Now to the content itself.
I consider this easily to be in my all time top 10 games. The direction, story, and art style are consistent throughout the whole experience, and I loved the way it strings you along and keeps you guessing.
There is a lot to explore here in an open world with a few distinct areas (desert, forest, city ruins, ...), a lot of sidequests to do, many telling their own little story. It really doesn't feel padded out with lots of busywork at all, everything is worth doing.
The story is very emotional at times, and you really get attached to the characters' fate. Heartstrings. There are 5 main endings, but the game doesn't take itself completely seriously and offers a lot of "joke endings" as well, like, when you just wander off in the opposite direction of a boss fight and abandon your mission and get teased for being a coward.
The gameplay is very dynamic, the dodge mechanics are quite easy to get used to and there are different weapon styles to choose from depending what suits you best. There is enough variety in there to keep it interesting, but button-mashing works for the easier fights as well. For really casual players, there are even a few built-in helps  called auto-chips, that can automate most of the combat actions for you.
Throughout the game, you get to play with different characters, e.g. 2B and 9S, who you meet very early on in the story. 9S can 'hack' machines, take control of them or make them explode. Personally, I didn't see a great reason for this feature in the game and much preferred 2B's playstyle.
The background music is probably the most sophisticated I have heard in a game before, with each track having several versions that change depending on the situation. All songs are great and underpin the mood of the scene.
I have played this game with a Dualshock 4, and would recommend a controller for it as that seems much superior.
Finally, the Arena DLC. It's a nice bit of distraction with a few extra costumes to obtain from previous Nier games. Not sure about the value really, but didn't hesitate to buy it given what a masterpiece this game is.

This game. THIS GAME. THIS GAME...IS AWESOME!!!!!!! Looking for a good shooter to play? Play Loadout. Looking for a game
where you can craft your own weapons? Play Loadout. Feeling bored or overpowered on Call of Duty? PLAY FREAKING LOADOUT. This is a game where you start off with one gun slot. You have four types of Guns. Beam, Rocket, Pulse and Rifle. Each one has it's own way of playing with. Then you got the Loadouts, aka the gun slots. And the Payload (gun Payload), Tesla Gun, Healing, Pyro, The Juice, then you got the Stock. And the Scope. And the Barrel. And WAAAY more. There's lots to customize in your weapons. You got the Tech Tree, the place where you upgrade the weapon parts. And we got the Outfitter (in case you don't already look badass enough). And, of course, the "Fight" tab. There you can play against other humans, or against the Bots. The game is 100% online, so if you don't have a decent Internet connection (at least 50 KB/s download or upload) you can expect some lag. There are loads of game modes, there is Blitz (where you have to stand in "Activation Points" to get points), Death Snatch (sorta like Death Match, but once you kill someone, you have to capture their flask of 'Blutonium'), and the Jackhammer (Get the 'flag', which is actually a hammer, which you can use as a weapon, and get it over to your own team. Be warned! You can't get the points until your own flag is back, if it was stolen by the other team) game mode. And is that it? NOPE. You can level up, you can add friends (Also, the game runs on own accounts, not on your Steam account), you can murder people and even better, THE GAME IS 100% FREE TO PLAY!
What I think is even better than it being free to play, is that it's not PAY TO WIN! It is PLAY TO WIN! No weapon parts or weapon themselves can be bought for real world money.
This game has partial Xbox 360 controller support. That means that your Xbox 360 controller (together with your Xbox 360 Controller Adapter) can be used to play the game. Be aware that it is PARTIAL controller support, so you can't use your controller to navigate the menus, only to play. You can also buy "Spacebux" (with real world money) to buy unescessary, but cool stuff to your character, or to get Blutonium Boosters (the currency of the game) and XP Boosters.
There are options in the Game Settings to turn off Gore, Nudity (even though I've never seen any with the option on) and Profanity (Profanity in the chat, doesn't affect the game itself).

I've played both Borderlands and Borderlands 2. Borderlands was love at first play back when I was 14, it's what got me into FPS, felt nostalgic playing it for a second time last year. I still get the chills listening to the sountrack and feel like sniping a Skag while it's roaring at me. Borderlands 2 came in as an even better game with great improvement in graphics and mechanics, naturally. I have probably 300 hours or more on BL2. Challenged myself to beat both Normal and TVH mode, even dipped a bit in the UVHM. Collected so many legendaries. Had memorable moments of laughing and just feeling good. Enjoyed it thoroughly as a little more than just some shooter to faff around as time passes by.
...And then there's THIS. I don't even know where to begin with. BL2 Strayan, high budget DLfloppingC (wait, isn't this a DLC?) in space. I'll list here as many pros and cons as I can think of. I'm really mixed about it.
BASE GAME:
PROS:
+Overall environmental ambient on this is amazing. Does feel like a lunar wasteland to me.
+Sountack is enjoyable. Very athmospheric, even though there's not much athmosphere in there. ;3
+Graphics are beautiful. Still maintaining the typical comic book style, but even better.
+Weapons are interesting. Really loving the lasers and cryo elemental.
+I thoroughly enjoyed the vertical approach to battles and movement in general.
+Butt slams. No other details needed.
+Comeback of several characters from the previous games (or related to them).
+Australian accent!
+Creepy details along the story.
+Playable characters interract with the world around them and with each other more by commenting on the current situations.
+The Grinder - love-hate relationship with this device. I love how you can dump your rubbish away and get potentially better stuff.
CONS:
-The shortness of this game made it feels more like a DLC and less than an actual game.
-I can't stress how overly politically correct this game is. You know, there's a difference between randomly dropping a line about being gay like a real, mentally sane person who happens to be gay (see BL2) and having 90% of your quotes about how gay you are just to prove the world that you're special. It's cringeworthy. Also, they completely cucked down Torgue. From the badass macho man to a completely dumb white knight. Doesn't feel like a wasteland with tough scavengers anymore when they all censor down their language. It's a game for grown ups for a reason. Don't get me wrong, I'm not the type to swear, but if it's part of the character, don't censor it. Also, only 2 male chatacters (1 DLC. Clappy is a robot, doesn't really count) when the majority of gamers are men? Way to distance most of your audience, good job.
-Way too expensive for such a short game. Expected much more out of this.
-Characters are uni-dimensional with very few exceptions. The only character that received a noticeable level of depth was Jack.
-Most of the missions felt like a chore. Long and boring.
-A little bit too many fetch missions for my taste.
-Lack of diversity among enemies. Borderlands 2 offered you a much wider range of heads to shoot.
-Incredibly annoying dialogue. And not just any dialogue. LONG, NEVERENDING DIALOGUE.
-Really buggy. It crashed a lot.
-The Grinder - love-hate relationship with this device. I hate how strict mixing recipes can be.
-Moonstone drop is really low for how demanded it is.
-Enemies lacked funny lines compared to the previous games.
-Maps were too large for how scarce saving points were. Walking was a pain in the bum until I unlocked vehicles.
CLAPTASTIC VOYAGE DLC:
PROS:
+Gave Claptrap some real depth in here.
+Feels trip.
+Ambient is stunning.
+I advise you not to eat during this DLC. You'll thank me later.
+Music has some Borderlands 1 vibes. Especially to Traversing the Deep.
+You get to see some places and people you might've missed. Or not.
+Glitch weapons were really cool.
+Did I mention the trip down the memory lane?
CONS:
-Way too short.
-Mostly the same defects as the base game.
-Honestly I think it's a bit flawed how easily you can lose good items by having your enemy fly way outside the map borders while taking DoT and dying there, making loot impossible to pick up.
-You know it's awful when a DLC is better than the base game.
IN CONCLUSION:
Don't buy this unless it's on sale for really low to give it a try. It's not utter rubbish but at least 60% of it is. RIP Borderlands, you were a beautiful series, ruined by Anthony Burch.

I've seen a lot of articles comparing this to WoWs, but I can safely say that I've had more fun playing this than any of the dreck Wargaming has churned out. First of all, it's not nearly as frustrating an experience. As far as I know, there are no one hit kills. If you died, it wasn't because RNG demanded it so. It's because you got hit by torpedoes (which are excessively lethal), you thought you could take on those 3 battleships by yourself (you can't), or you just weren't as accurate as the other guy. The ships are all very lovingly rendered, more than enough to appease any history nerd, and the art for the various commanders is FANTASTIC, all of whom are historical characters. You want that guy who came up with the idea of the U-boat wolfpack as your sub captain? You got it, buddy.
Every class of ship has its own shtick and advantage and plays in a unique way. Destroyers are fast little spitfires that can't take much damage but can churn out a great wall of torpedoes. Cruisers have great anti-aircraft power and do not fall short in any particular way. Battleships have the longest range, and sight capability of the classes, and can shoot targets halfway across the map (and they will, so don't move in a straight predictable line), aircraft carriers are delightful fun and will act as the eyes and glass cannony muscle in an engagement, and submarines are my particular favorite. Especially the sniping of carriers while they busy themselves with things happening miles away.
Lastly, the business model. Obviously, the game is done through steam, and has the security and reliability you'd expect from such a service. Their prices are indeed cheaper than wargaming, and they often throw gold and VIP time at you for achievements you make in the game. There IS ammo that can be bought with real money, but the advantage it affords is so minute that its hardly worth the investment, even if it is cents on the dollar. Bottom line, I would recommend this to anyone who likes naval history, military technology, or is just looking for a good ship game.

I must say I was pleasantly surprised by this game. It offers relatively fresh adaptation of the popular "noble savage" trope, with interesting setting, well written dialogues (although the poor translation hinders it somewhat), ambitious scale and immersive atmosphere.
On the other hand, everything else is very crude as if the game was programmed by orcs themselves. The combat is absolute unintuitive mess, the equipment system confusing, the stats are hard to work with, sometimes you don't know what to upgrade before you spend resources to see the resulting stats, and if you build your characters wrong, you can face difficult to unplayable battles later in the game.
I recommend the game for the obvious ambition of its creators, for their effort to break the monotony of the standard gaming loop with new elements, and for their attempt to create a memorable gaming experience. They succeeded only partially, but not for the lack of effort.

While I've been trying to shy away from early access games due to getting burned a couple times (I'm looking at you, Spacebase DF-9) I made an exception for this one.  I've been following this game since it was very early in development.  I took an extended break from playing to allow the game to grow some more and now that the game is more complete (in fact it's nearly finished at the time of this writing) I feel I can talk more about the gameplay.
Crosscode is an action RPG with a strong retro flair, recalling classic 16-bit-era games like Zelda: Link to the Past, Phantasy Star IV and others.  You play as a girl named Lea. Lea has unfortunately lost her memories, and it's been decided playing the futuristic MMO "Crossworlds" is the best way for her to get her memory back. Players control hard-light constructs in a real physical world via some kind of remote interface. Lea is somewhat of a silent protagonist (something went wrong with her speech controller, so she can only say a few words at first).  Along your path you'll meet party members, explore huge dungeons filled with complex puzzles, and kill lots and lots of critters (including some very impressive bosses) The death penalty is fairly minimal in this game (you lose whatever you gained in that room) so there's no harm in trying and trying again until you get past whatever obstacle you're working on.
Combat is fluid and slick.  You have a close-range melee strike that deals heavy damage, and a long-range projectile weapon. Both of these can be upgraded over time, and you'll quickly unlock special attacks to make you even more powerful. Later on in the game you'll get elemental powers that will not only amplify your ability, but allow you to take advantage of certain enemy's weaknesses. And it's in your benefit to dispatch enemies quickly. The faster you move, the higher your combat rank goes, which allows you to collect better loot from the enemies you slay.
You won't lack for stuff to do either. NPCs all over the map have various sidequests for you to take on, that give XP and loot of all kinds. There's also tons of merchants and traders for you to swap all the useless junk you find scattered around for new and better gear.
The game's audio is somewhat simple, but the tunes are catchy and even after multiple repeats they don't seem to get annoying.
Overall I still really like this game. It's a wonderful throwback to the old 16 bit RPGs I used to love, but it's new enough to be a standout in its own right.

Wurm Unlimited, At first glance, it can be incredibly overwhelming. The game features a few hundred skills that each branch out into their own area of the game. Every skill seems to be connected via a characteristic or a sub skill, and this makes leveling up a very rewarding and exciting part of the game.
I only sunk in about 100 hours total into the stand alone version before I moved on to the Online paid version of the game, populated by players from all around the world.
I'll be referring to Wurm Online/Unlimited as solely Wurm, due to both games being the same, with a few changes.
I've played Wurm for about 2200 hours since the day I logged in almost a year ago...
Wurm has truly changed my expectations of open world/sandbox at least what most games consider they are today... they really are not at all... by miles. Wurm will show you the true meaning of Open World.
Having the ability to truly modify the land around you, build on it until your hearts content, sail off into the night... and maybe touch land a day or two later... or go for a stroll on your horse, into the deep forest maybe looking for that one special place to call home.
Wurm will let you do just that, the means of transportation are quite limited, boats, walking, horses/cows/bears and wagon/large cart, will be your only means of transportation in the game.
A lot of people seem to get upset when a video game requires that you out source to a wiki of some sort to gather information on how to play the game... Wurm is too big, there is so much you can do, so many things you can change that you’re going to have to do this if you want to get a lot of things done. The game does not spoon feed you information like some other more mainstream games do, where they fit every use of an item into the description of it. Although wurm has it’s methods of feeding you information from outsource without making you leave the game, there is a feature that allows you to search items directly in game from their main wiki page giving you a wealth of information, and this applies to everything in the game. From that wood scrap you got from turning a log into planks to the hide of a dragon!
If you’re truly looking to dwell into a real open world, full of adventures then this is probably the game you’d want to try, as long as you can overlook the dated graphics of course.
Wurm Unlimited is a great game; even better with a second monitor!

This is a tough thing for me to do, given that Deadly Premonition is one of my favorite games I've ever played, but I can't honestly recommend playing this version of the game. I first played Deadly Premonition on the Xbox 360, and that version had its issues, of course, but it at least functioned out of the box. I installed the latest version of DPfix (0.9.5 as of this writing), and that helped, but it didn't fix the constant runtime errors that would pop up during gameplay, causing the game to stop functioning. Usually they'd pop up after an hour or so of gameplay, but sometimes later (if I was lucky), or sometimes much sooner (if I was unlucky).
Even if this version wasn`t completely unstable, I still wouldn't recommend playing this over the 360 version. While this is the "Director's Cut", the story by and large is exactly the same, with the exception of a few added cutscenes at the beginning/end of each episode. The storyline is perfectly capable of standing on its own without these added scenes, so playing this version of the game just for them (especially if you've played the original game before) is not worth it. If one really wanted to see them, I'd recommend viewing them on a video site, rather than playing through this version for the sake of seeing them.
There are some other things regarding the game design that have been changed; most notably the controls. The original game featured Resident Evil 4-style movement, in that moving up or down would move your character forward or backward, while moving left or right would turn your character in those directions; camera remaining behind your shoulder the whole time. There were also some parts of the game (very few; only a small handful) where the normally over-the-shoulder camera would switch to a completely different angle, again reminiscent of Resident Evil (in this case, the classic horror-style games). One complaint the original game did receive had to do with these controls, so in the Director's Cut you can instead move in any direction, while moving the camera completely independently of your character. As far as basic maneuverability is concerned, this is an improvement, though I would argue it's not really necessary, as the original game's movement controls were just fine, if not entirely self-explanatory. The aiming and shooting mechanics are virtually untouched in the Director's Cut, aside from moving aiming control to the right analog stick (if you're playing with a controller). You still have to stand in place to aim and shoot, so this aspect of the controls remains faithful to the original. Whether you consider that a drawback or not will depend on your preferences.
While general movement is improved by the new controls, I think keeping full control of the camera during every moment of gameplay was a bad change to make. This is most apparent in one of the side quests, in which you push boxes around a maze. This puzzle-like gameplay was shown from an overhead view in the original game, but here in the Director's Cut, the camera is moved closer to your character, as if you were in a normal area. This makes trying to solve this block puzzle unnecessarily much harder to do, as you can no longer see the entire playing field; thus making it much more likely that one will make a mistake, and thus have to restart the block puzzle from the beginning. This was much less of a hassle to complete in the original game. There are also some other scenes which originally had fixed-camera perspectives, yet now don't. These other scenes' original perspectives aren't nearly as important as the block puzzle's, but this was still a change that added nothing to the game.
This is a relatively minor change, but the green tint the original game had was removed in this version. This doesn't really affect the game that much; the graphics are mostly identical otherwise, and if you've never played the original game, you won't find yourself missing it. I personally miss the green tint, as I felt it helped add to the atmosphere, but I wouldn't consider its removal a deal-breaker on its own.
The only other significant addition to the game is some bonus features, such as alternate outfits for certain characters to wear, as well as a house in town for the main character to rest at. This, again, is unnecessary, and the fact that time and effort was spent on frivolous things such as this, as opposed to fixing any of the graphical deficiencies in the game, or refining the level and quest designs, or even fixing some translation errors in the text or bugs that the original game had, is disappointing. The original Deadly Premonition was a pretty unpolished, buggy game, and this retains all of the bugs that version had, while introducing several new ones of its own. Over three years passed between the release of the original game, and the release of the Director's Cut on the PS3, followed soon after by this PC port. Were the developers really not able to fix any of these problems during all this time; not even the grammatical/spelling errors that are prevalent throughout the game's text?
It hurts me to write this, because at its core Deadly Premonition is a game I truly care about. Its story (which I won't go into detail about at all, as it's one that should ideally be experienced with as few spoilers as possible) is incredibly compelling and well-written, managing to mix multiple themes and moods in a way that fits well together; after my first time beating the original game, I found myself reflecting on the game's events and characters time and time again. Every character in this game is incredibly memorable, and the majority of the work by the game's voice actors is very well done. The actual gameplay itself... has its ups and downs. The game's world is very interesting and has a number of secrets to be found, as well as multiple unique characters who maintain their own schedules and lives as the game progresses, somewhat similar to The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask. The sidequests are mostly good, and stand out from each other pretty well, while at times giving essential rewards for completing them.
The game's combat is often derided, which is understandable. Most of the combat areas in the game are terribly designed, being repetitive, dull, and often way too long for their own good. It's as if the developers spent most of their time on the main storyline and sidequests, and rushed to include some combat areas at the last minute, having absolutely no time to playtest them. As with many other things, none of this is changed in the Director's Cut; if you hated the combat in the original game, that's still an issue here. All I can recommend to deal with it is doing certain sidequests as soon as possible, and using their rewards to help make the combat less tedious.
To sum things up, Deadly Premonition is a very unique, memorable experience; one that as of now, I feel is best had on the Xbox 360. If Deadly Premonition seems like a game you really want to experience, and you have a 360, I recommend searching out a used copy of that version instead, and afterward (if you feel like it) watching the extra cutscenes online. If you have a PS3... I haven't played that version myself, but from what I have read online it at least doesn't crash after every hour of play. If neither of these platforms are available to you, and you absolutely have to play this game, well... then you might want to take a chance on this PC version; preferably during a sale. Remember to download the latest version of Durante's DPfix prior to playing, and make sure to save as much as possible, lest you lose your recent progress due to a crash. Also back up your saves often; fortunately they're easily accessible in their own folder inside the game's files. While it didn't happen to me, thankfully, I have read about instances where other players' save data was corrupted, forcing them to start over. With that in mind, enjoy at your own risk.

Deadly Premonition is a very mixed bag. If you enjoy a good narrative, like I do, this game certainly delivers. The story is very reminiscent of Twin Peaks, but not so much that it seems unoriginal. The narrative is engaging, and the voice acting is good, but the graphics do sometimes create unwanted comedy. The graphics are strong PS2 quality, so they are perfectly acceptable. The real problems with this game arise from the mechanics. While the mechanics on foot are similar to the mechanics used in Resident Evil, and Silent Hill games, the driving mechanics can make the game a chore to play. While there are some nice immersive elements in the cars, like wipers, the driving can get very irritating due to the floaty controls. The cars feel like they have no mass, and fly across the road very easily, with the exception of the police cruiser which has the best controls out of all the vehicles I have tested, and in case of collision the cars stop with no momentum.
Deadly premonition delivers a great story with good voice acting, and it clocked in at 16 hours on my first playthrough on the ps3. If you can deal with the shortcomings of the mechanics, I heartily recommend this game for all fans of mystery and horror.

This game can be fun, but it's unpolished and has tons of issues.. I haven't found a proper balance- Rookie is so damn easy that you can easily drop 60+ points 10+ rebs, asts, and steals (per game),  and WIN almost every single game. The AI of your team also seems to be fairly on point. Pro is basically the same- it's slightly more difficult, but it's still really easy. Then, All-Star is more reasonable, but it's still not easy. Actually being able to steal the basketball, being able to pass it without getting a turnover, and making shots more than missing becomes a rare occurence.  Your team AI becomes worse, and the opposing team's AI improves. Superstar is more of the same, however making shots becomes even more difficult, and your team AI becomes garbage, whilst the opposing team plays top-notch. Attempting to steal the ball will most of the time lead to a reach-in foul. Turnovers become extremely prevalent in this difficulty, as it seems the opposing team intercepts 50 percent of your passes. But, although I have bashed these difficulties, it still is very possible to win, it's just most games will be a nail-biter.  Also, it will likely be not very fun, as you will miss shots way more often, get fouls way more easily, and accumulate turnovers at a ridiculous rate. But, the Hall of Fame difficulty is the real problem with this game. Shots simply don't go in for you or your team anymore; you'll be lucky to make 20 percent of your threes. Steals simply won't happen for you (be prepared to get fouled out), or your team anymore (probably for the other team though). Turnovers will make up a big part of your stats....and you simply will not have fun at this point. It's very unlikely you will win at this difficulty unless you are very skilled. You essentially have to do everything yourself, as your team becomes useless, while the opposing team excels.

While I've been trying to shy away from early access games due to getting burned a couple times (I'm looking at you, Spacebase DF-9) I made an exception for this one.  I've been following this game since it was very early in development.  I took an extended break from playing to allow the game to grow some more and now that the game is more complete (in fact it's nearly finished at the time of this writing) I feel I can talk more about the gameplay.
Crosscode is an action RPG with a strong retro flair, recalling classic 16-bit-era games like Zelda: Link to the Past, Phantasy Star IV and others.  You play as a girl named Lea. Lea has unfortunately lost her memories, and it's been decided playing the futuristic MMO "Crossworlds" is the best way for her to get her memory back. Players control hard-light constructs in a real physical world via some kind of remote interface. Lea is somewhat of a silent protagonist (something went wrong with her speech controller, so she can only say a few words at first).  Along your path you'll meet party members, explore huge dungeons filled with complex puzzles, and kill lots and lots of critters (including some very impressive bosses) The death penalty is fairly minimal in this game (you lose whatever you gained in that room) so there's no harm in trying and trying again until you get past whatever obstacle you're working on.
Combat is fluid and slick.  You have a close-range melee strike that deals heavy damage, and a long-range projectile weapon. Both of these can be upgraded over time, and you'll quickly unlock special attacks to make you even more powerful. Later on in the game you'll get elemental powers that will not only amplify your ability, but allow you to take advantage of certain enemy's weaknesses. And it's in your benefit to dispatch enemies quickly. The faster you move, the higher your combat rank goes, which allows you to collect better loot from the enemies you slay.
You won't lack for stuff to do either. NPCs all over the map have various sidequests for you to take on, that give XP and loot of all kinds. There's also tons of merchants and traders for you to swap all the useless junk you find scattered around for new and better gear.
The game's audio is somewhat simple, but the tunes are catchy and even after multiple repeats they don't seem to get annoying.
Overall I still really like this game. It's a wonderful throwback to the old 16 bit RPGs I used to love, but it's new enough to be a standout in its own right.

I've already played and loved the demo, so I just had to back this.
For now, the Early Access pretty much resembles the demo, but I am definitely looking forward to the updates.
All I can say is, that you can play this on pretty much everything (maybe even Potato-GlaDOS).
I tried it on my Acer Switch 11 and the game itself runs amazingly fluid.
There's little lag in the cutscenes and rather long loadingtimes, but I noticed no influence on the actual gameplay.
Specs of my Acer:
Intel Atom Z3745 with 1,3GHz, 2GB RAM,  Intel HD Graphics.
About the gameplay:
I haven't tried it with a gamepad yet, but playing with mouse and keyboard works absolutely great.
For some it might be a bit unusual to play a retro oriented game which reminds of the SNES era with mouse and keyboard, but it definitely pays off. The aiming works well plus it doesn't have any influence on the melee attacks like pointing in the wrong direction. The combination of shield and dashing as defensive moves also gives the game more variety since you have to decide on how to defend yourself against the enemy in front of you.
This next to typical elements of RPGs like stats, resistances etc. offers a lot of possibilities for enemies and obstacles which the player has to understand to be able to beat them and therefor is a great opportunity for challenge.
Also it seems some accuracy improvements were made in comparison to when I last played the demo.
The jumps and platforms feel easier to to access and I generally think that it's responding more playerfriendly.
Obstacles and riddles with the ballshooting mechanism are fun and I hope they find plenty of use further in the game.
Also I like how the game switches between melee and range attacks. It's a lot more fluid than manually changing the attack type and helps keeping the fights focused on the actual battle.
Generally I'm having a lot of fun with the other two game modes, which are pretty promising and give a good hint at what might be added to the game in the future. In my opinion it was a really good idea to show different aspects of a game by presenting short bits of each of them instead of just delivering a fraction of the actual gameplay and doing the rest by teasers and promises of how awesome it will be.
CrossCode definitely gets my recommendation and if you're not sure whether the game suits you: Play the demo, it's free on the games website.

This game was one of my personal gaming highlights of last month.
It was on my radar since it's realease back in 2012. I finally tried it out and oh boi did i enjoy my time with it.
You play two characters, the honorable and hulking orc berserker Arkail. He's on a suicide mission to kill the human emperor to free all orcs from human occupation/enslavement. And Styx, a sly and foul mouthed cutthroat goblin mercenary. He's following a contract to help the green one-man-army Arkail for cash.
One of the game's absolute strong points is it's story, playing with perspectives, tropes and the causality of evil with some pretty neat world building and a nice twist. I also fell in love with it's soundtrack.
In my opinion, the game shows some similarities to the game Summoner (2001) in it's presentation, playstyle, thick and somewhat mystical atmosphere, different landscapes and beautyful soundtrack.
The game contains of some bad language (a lot of f*cks, to be percise) some ppl complained about. Personally, i quite like the cursing little Styx. It adds to some trash factor and gives him some character.
The stories beginning dragged a little bit. But it gets more involving the longer you play. And the story as a whole paints a nice gesamtkunstwerk.
It's somewhat like a raw diamond. The combat system let's you pause at every moment to give your 2 characters commands (several different attacks with unique effects like debuffs, DoTs etc. - Dragon Age comes to mind) and if you want to optimize your potential you have to pause the game a lot.
Unfortunately, some encounters feel a little bit... unbalanced. But testing out several different strategies got me to victory every time (at least playing on normal difficulty).
Recommended to ppl who like unconventional fantasy stories.
Edit for a tipp: If you want to get this game for cheap, try to look for the "Focus Selection Pack" from 2015 on the usual trading sites. It includes Of Orcs and Men, Styx: Master of Shadows (a hardcore stealth game and the prequel to Styx' story) and 19 other games for around 27-30€!

Tried this game for a little while. Ended up getting a refund.
The interface, is extremely detailed. Every item has a huge selection of different options. That's great because it means that there really is a lot of depth to everything in-game, but at the same time, it also means you're going to invest a considerable amount of time just learning how to play and how to do things. Was it easy to navigate? Eh, it wasn't terribly difficult for me. Interacting with things takes a bit of getting used to. You have to right click on EVERYTHING, even NPC's.
Inventory management was pretty straightforward. The small interface text didn't help though.
Combat seemed clunky and little more than click on this, select attack, follow the target around. Not much depth there, but then again, I didn't exactly get terribly far in to the game.
Visually, the game does have its moments where it looks good, but it also reminds me of the original everquest. Some people would call it outdated, but ignore them. Those same people still enjoyed minecraft..  Suffice it to say, Despite having a 6800K and a GTX1070, and all the detail settings maxed, the game ran just fine. I just don't think visually it had the same quality that the demo videos did for some reason.
Core Gameplay wise, If you have a good amount of time to devote to this game, you may find it enjoyable once you get past the steep learning curve. It's like passing a kidney stone. Be prepared to sink a lot of time into a game that's on it's way out though. If you're really interested in this type of game, I think I'd suggest Life is Feudal, and hope to god that they put in hostile NPC's to raid at some point.
I'd strongly advise playing any game like this with friends, or multiplayer. While it is playable solo, it still feels empty.

Positive: game is somehow unique in some way (like Braid, Limbo, Alan Wake and etc.). I love those "unique" games which you can't see every day.. So I try to play them all.. This game is based on Twin Peaks (main plot almost the same, some characters are very similar in some details) so if you're a fan of TP you must play. However, before buying please read negative side. I bought it for 7 euro and still think price for this poorly optimized game is still too big. If you played Dark Souls (which is titled as one of the worst ports) and thought that DS is worst port try this game…. DS only problem was locked frame rates and resolution although no other problems I noticed...
Negative: ou boy... where do I even begin from..? Well, I guess I’ll write about everything what I didn’t had positive opinion…
Sound: music and other sounds is nothing awesome. Problem is that it may stuck and loop again and again at some point (had a car brake sound loop). Problem is that IF you save (stupid that I did it) when this problem is occurring you're stuck with it even after PC reboot. Strangely enough it fixed itself after I progressed 2-3 chapters. Thank god... Unless you want to hear everywhere stopping car sound (even through cutscenes!).
Ragdolls/textures: during my gameplay I noticed few graphical issues (main character's tie was sticking from his belly to the back, sometimes his jacket mysteriously disappeared). It's nothing major although it annoys a little.
Graphical look: this game looks like 2005 game.  Well at least it is at acceptable levels.
Enemies: during the whole game you encounter only 4 types of enemies (sure they have different appearance or carry different weapons, but the fact is that it is SAME enemies only they carry or looks differently): shadow, climbing shadow, birds, dogs. Not to mention that 2 types of these enemies you can even not to notice (I barely noticed them myself and never killed or had to kill one of those 2).
Boses: during the whole game you encounter X (I won’t spoil exact number but it’s only a few) bosses and they all are a joke once you know their weak point.
Cutscenes: although it occurred to very few people but the cutscenes may be shown to you upside down. I was one of those unlucky people. How do you like that? I browsed internet and some other games had this issue. It’s related to codec problems. Tried to install CCCP and K-Lite mega pack codecs but the problem persisted. (Good side is that there aren’t a lot of them + subtitles are displayed correctly so if you’re as am I more interest in a story it won’t bother you a lot).
Dungeons: once you’ll play your 4th or 5th dungeon you’ll realize that there is no benefit to kill enemies (except few times when they drop not ammo or medkits) because money is not an issue in this game. So you begin just run through them. These “dungeons” are boring and annoys a lot when you have to repeat them (if you want to collect all trading cards).
Loading times: I store all my games on Samsung 840 PRO 500GB SSD drive (which is one of the fastest in SSD at the moment) and believe me when I say that you have to wait a LONG time to load this game different parts. I have to wait around 1 minute till it loads “Press Start button” (if I had simple HDD I probably would think that game is crashed), for every cutscene to load (if the game won’t crash) I’ll have to wait around 2 minutes before cutscene and around 1 minute after cutscene, if I enter somewhere (i. e. house) I’ll have to wait around 1 minute too (this is especially annoying because for example in L4D2 I have to wait around 10-20 seconds to load next map and graphics there are at least twice better, hell… I can even compare this games loading to  Windows 7 booting time… AGAIN 10-20 seconds…).
Optimization (crashes): why I said that 7 euros is a lot for this you ask? Well everything above I mentioned is forgivable if not the OPTIMIZATION problem (yeah I wanted to type in the uppercase letters). This game crashes whenever it wants: it crashes during the loading screen, during the driving, when you try to open your inventory, on really rare occasion’s game crashes right when you launch it, hell it crashes before or even after the cutscenes (I really enjoyed this when I finish chapter and there are a few cutscenes… It crashed 5 times till I got to the words: “Do you want to save?” I saved the game and it crashed AGAIN. Good thing that I could continue from the save). So… In summary it crashes whenever it likes… Don’t forget that this game starts to lag after 30 minutes of gameplay. During constant crash you even can’t replay some chapters (I couldn’t replay chapter 7 even after 20th try…).  Not sure… Maybe crashes related to AMD card I have…
For those who gonna BUY THIS: use ALL available and possible fixes:
Increase game launch exe file max RAM memory access to more than 2GB (yes, the game has memory leaks due a bad coding i. e. after 30 minutes of playing it increases ram usage from 200MB to more than +2100MB and starts to lag a lot). Note: this “increase” method works only on 64-bit systems
Use DPFix for desirable resolution (yes same story as Dark Souls… Devs couldn’t add support for high resolutions).
SET DP.EXE and/or (I used same on both files) DPLAUNCHER.exe files to use Compatibility with Windows 98/ME and check mark “Run as an Admin”.
Shutdown your antivirus (at least for me it helped and crashes decreased even though whole Steam folder is added to antivirus exclusion list…).
And yeah… Never do anything to stress your computer during this games’ gameplay or you risking with crash (for me even once occurred a crash while I tried to make a screenshot with steam integrated feature).
For those who doing all side quests: do them as soon as possible unless you want to experience more crashes (during chapter replay you cannot save) and to lose all your progress..
So if you still want to try your luck with this super SLOW and constantly CRASHING game be my guest. Just make sure that you apply all (or at least as much as possible) my suggestions… That way your game may become almost playable (you minimize crashing number as much as possible).
And yeah although it annoyed me a lot I still liked game mainly due to it's story and gameplay :)
