Deadly Premonition is a game unlike any other that has came out in recent years. The way in which the story grips you, the way you relate to the protagonist, the way the small town the game is set in is always alive, the... Well, just everything about this game sets it apart from the rest of the market today.
The story of Deadly Premonition centres around FBI agent Francis York Morgan who is sent to the small rural town of Greenvale to investigate the tragic and mysterious death of a young girl, Anna Graham. Upon nearing Greenvale, however, he is swerved off the road and comes to in a strange place known as the “other world”. Whilst attempting to make his way out of here, York catches a glimpse of an enigmatic axe-wielding man. Eventually you escape and make your way back towards the town, it is here that the first of the colourful cast are introduced. The sherriff of Greenvale, George Woodman, and his deputy, Emily Wyatt, greet York just outside of town and provide an escort to the hotel, where work on solving this case can finally begin.
It is here where the character of Zach is firmly introduced into the game, and the way in which it is done, will grip you for the entirety of the games 26 chapters. The player takes on the eponym of Zach throughout the game and is consistently addressed by York when left alone. When driving, or wandering through town, York gleefully strikes up a discussion about one of many different topics. From childhood memories and music to sharing his encyclopeadic knowledge of the film industry, there is no shortage of dialog in these moments of solitude.
As mentioned earlier, however, there is quite a large and colourful cast of characters within Greenvale, each with their own story to tell and each possibly implicated in the murder of Anna Graham. From the effiminate policeman, Thomas MacLain; the potato-chip enthusiast and local doctor, Ushah Johnson or; the travelling sapling salesman, Forrest Kaysen. Each and every resident of Greenvale is memorable for their own reason, and further pulls you into the game and into the role of York.
Encounters with these residents are not isolated incidents, as the world of Deadly Premonition is constantly alive. Each person lives out their lives with their own daily routine, oftentimes they can be seen passing you on the streets or hanging out at the local bar, the SWERY '65 (a nod to the developer of the game Hidetaka Suehiro, SWERY for short). As such, every moment in Greenvale feels unique, a feeling that hasn't been represented in gaming since Yu Suzuki's Shenmue for the SEGA Dreamcast in 1992. Most of the residents have their own sidequests attached to them, and the rewards for these greatly assist in completing the game, with new weapons and discount cards being just an example. These sidequests can be creative as well, from assisting Emily in bettering her abilities as a chef; helping Anna's mother deal with her loss or reorganising the store room of the convenience store. Everywhere you go, there will always be something to do or something to see, and there is almost always a benefit to exploring Greenvale.
Unfortunately, this is where some of the problems of Deadly Premonition rear their head. The map provided to you can be difficult to use as it faces in the direction that York is facing when you open it. This means that if you were to check the map to see where you are going, then check again to see if you were still on the right track, the map can look completely different. The map can't be rotated once it's open and also can't be zoomed out to a comfortable level, always feeling a little too zoomed in, forcing you to learn the town's layout rather than rely too heavily on the in-game map.
The layout of Greenvale isn't the only that you need to keep in the back of your mind, however. Firstly, there is a stamina meter in the game, meaning that running for too long or attacking too many times in succession can cause York to stumble around blindly for a moment whilst he catches his breath. Hunger and tiredness also play a role in the game and can be checked at any point by accessing the pause menu. Food is littered throughout town and the various “other world” levels that you venture through, and therefore isn't much of a problem. Even if you are out of food for whatever reason, there are many places in Greenvale where you can get a meal at a price. As for tiredness, this is replenished through either sleeping at various beds scattered through Greenvale, or by consuming coffee. Lastly, the game has a 24 hour timing system where certain places and events become inaccessible late in the day. You can sleep to fast forward up to 12 hours at a time, however sleeping for too long will cause you to gain hunger and also cause your clothes to need washing (yes, you read that right).
The little things that you have the ability to do in the game is a small but interesting detail. Clothes can be washed, your beard can be shaved and we haven't even gotten to the driving yet. Deadly Premonition is a free roam game, but not in the same vein as, say, Saints Row. You have the ability to explore Greenvale freely and it is encouraged to do so, as such York is provided a Master Key to all the police cars in town soon after arriving (though several more cars can be unlocked later into the game). If driving at night, you can use your headlight; rain, use the wipers; need to turn, then indicate. All of these little nuances, on top of everything else mentioned earlier, cements you into the game and makes you feel as though you are York, as though you are the protagonist. A feat which is not easily achieved and one that SWERY should be commended for accomplishing.
Though not all is well in Greenvale, and it is still your job to uncover what is going on. Upon progressing through the game, you learn the folklore of the Raincoat Killer. A mysterious figure who, in the 1950's, went on a murderous rampage through Greenvale; a legend that instills fear into even the youngest of its residents, resulting in a town that stands still when it rains. These are the times when York often ends up in the “other world”.
These sections are filled with enemies and puzzles that must be overcome before you can return to the normal Greenvale. Hidden within these words are often vital clues to uncovering Anna's tragic death. Often the word “PROFILING” fills the screens whilst York nonchalantly lights a cigarette. This is followed by many  static images that flash before your eyes as you try and piece together what is happening in this small town. As you progress through the “other world”, these images will slowly clear up, allowing York to slowly piece together the events that occurred.
Progression through these sections is slowed by a number of zombie-esque enemies known as “Shadows”. These enemies move slowly and are unarmed at first, but soon they will be wielding pitchforks and eventually shotguns. Though they aren't difficult to kill, they often respawn and, as a result, become more of a threat as a mob, rather than when taken individually. To bring them down, York can arm himself with a variety of weapons, including shovels, axes, shotguns and rifles. The combat takes the over-the-shoulder format that was popularised by Resident Evil 4, meaning that you are frozen in place whilst ever you are lining up a shot. This serves to intensify the action sequences, limiting the shots to only those that are essential so as to keep moving and outrun the shadows hunting you down.
To further hinder progress, several puzzles lye in the way to solving this case. Though, unfortunately, these are never too tricky, as they are mostly explained upfront and serve more as a motivation to explore these levels rather than to test your ability.

To be honest, the Pre-sequel has to be my favorite Borderlands game to date.  This is mostly due to the improvements that were implemented over the first game.  I'll go ahead and list the pros:
1. Characters aren't cardboard figures and actually TALK.  Yeah, this always sorta bugged me that the characters you were playing as had absolutely nothing to say, even if someone in a quest asked you a question.  Though everyone has their own opinions about the character dialogue, it does make it at least replayable for me to go through with each character to hear their dialogue.  Oh yes, and I cannot forget that in cooperative play, your characters will comment on others using their skills.  The party will hate Claptrap for anything he does, people will comment on the awesomeness of Wilhelm's drones, and they will also shout at the enemies to shoot at Athena's shield because it makes a great target.
2.  Low Gravity + Butt Slams.  This adds quite a bit of variety to your combat options when in low gravity, and variety in combat is great.  Plus it's also fun to butt slam an enemy and watch their corpse fly off 100 feet in the air from your slam.
3.  Lasers and Ice.  The lasers are a great weapon category to be added, both for their cool factor and how they're basically just elemental damage spam.  Ice is also an amazing element, and probably the best one to date.  Freeze an enemy and throw an explosive at them (or, if you're wilhelm with the explosive punch, just do that.  Instant obliteration of ANY enemy.)  However, I'd assume they had to make a great element for how bad fire is when you're in a vacuum...
4.  More interesting classes + more co-op skills that are still useful in solo.  Not only are there more skills that affect teammates, but with how the Baroness character also has her own portable Ice generator makes for great cooperative experience.  I'd like to see more of these skills that are good in solo but great in co-op.  (Though a whole tree of the Baroness being locked behind co-op is definitely something that should not be done again, even though it is fun.)
5.  Better balanced UVHM.  Oh boy, this one's a big one in my opinion.  Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode being as ridiculous as it was in Borderlands 2, with insane health regen and every common enemy being able to tear you a new one even with great shields was definitely not the best feeling ever.  However, when you come to the Pre-sequel's UVHM, you'll find that the health regen is not nearly as fast as it was in 2, along with common enemies being just like how they always felt in the first two playthroughs; easy to kill and easy triggers for skills.  I don't mind a challenge, but when I want to play a game where every common enemy can kill you in a blink of an eye, I'd play a game where that's the norm rather than the exception.
6.  Pacing of the Intro.  This one's a bit of a yes and a no, but mostly a good point.  The intro sequence starts off a lot more action-packed, and gets you into the story a lot quicker.  You also get your skill point earlier than in the other Borderlands games (at level 3 as compared to level 5).  However, the intro does drag on a bit too long since it's slowly introducing you to the moon's environment as well as low gravity and Oz kits.  You also take a very long time to unlock your 3rd weapon slot too.
7.  The moon's atmosphere and Oz kits.  This was actually one of my favorite things about the pre-sequel; you actually feel like you're on the moon of Pandora.  You have Oz kits to provide you with oxygen along with helping to extend jumps and butt-slam, and you also have atmospheric generators as well.  Fire cannot be procced on enemies who aren't in atmosphere for obvious reasons, though this does make fire feel like a weak element when you're fighting on the moon's surface without atmosphere, but fire's extra damage to flesh still applies.  And then there's Oz kits to replace the Eridian Artifact slot.  This is hit or miss, but with how much oxygen gets scattered around, it's not really going to be a major problem unless if you're walking around a cleared area and refuse to turn on atmosphere generators or walk over oxygen cracks.  Not to mention, running out of oxygen doesn't really do anything horrible; you can't use your Oz kit to extend your jump (or butt-slam, I think), and you lose health VERY slowly.  However, the health you lose from running out of oxygen is replenished immediately upon grabbing any source of oxygen.
The DLC for the Pre-sequel isn't very numerous, but I'd still recommend getting it.  The two characters are great classes to play as, especially if you have a friend for a Baroness.  The claptastic voyage is a very, very good DLC considering the story as well as the things it adds.  (Namely glitched weapons)
Now for the cons:
1.  Voice acting is a bit of a hit-or-miss.  I love the hilariousness of the autralian accent on most of the characters, but sometimes the voice acting when it comes to the quests are quite hit or miss.  Sometimes they don't really sound like it's an urgent matter when it really is.
2.  Slow pace of the game and amount of walking.  This one's a bit of a "Let's make the player take as long as possible to complete the game", mostly because the Pre-sequel is a bit shorter than Borderlands 2 in the story department.  However, even with as short of a story it has, it's still great for that period of time.
3.  Not many changes to the formula, as Borderlands 1 to 2 had.  It's not really bad that the Pre-sequel didn't try to change up as much of the formula as the 2nd borderlands did, but because it didn't change much, it does indeed just feel like a Borderlands 2.5 rather than a whole new game.  It's just more borderlands, basically, but with a few new mechanics.
I'd highly recommend the Pre-sequel, *especially* if you have friends to play with.  It's a much more polished cooperative experience when compared to borderlands 2, and the story is good to experience if you're solo.

This game has two layers. The interior is a basketball game that's too complicated for me to play and it's wrapped with some of the most awful fake drama that has ever had the misforune of gracing a computer screen. I'm not sure there's anything worth saving here and frankly I'm not spending any more time trying to figure it out.
To start, the controls are far, far too complicated. I'm sure there are some people who have played the series for years who understand all of the nuiances of the controls but I simply can't perform the same move twice even though I'm doing the same thing with the controller (which works fine). There's a tutorial mode but it never bothers to see if you can actually perform the move that you're trying to make. So my gameplay consists of wildly flailing with the controller to see if something happens. I'm sure if I spent months on end trying to figure it out I might actually become competent. But the last game I had to spend doing that was Falcon 4.0. I shouldn't have to do it with a basketball game. This game screams for a simple controls mode for those of us who might have hit puberty before Lebron James was a teen sensation.
I tried the MyCareer thing. The servers are offline but I was able to save locally. My supposed #1 recruit is slow, can't hit a shot to save his life and pretty much performs nothing like a top recruit. It's a terrible system. I know that 2K wants to give you the feeling of progression but how about letting ME make that choice? Perhaps I'd like to start like Durant or Lebron - built for the NBA from High School and see how much fun that is. Instead, I'm stuck taking a 55 rated player into the NBA because of this awful system. Then it's just a grind to become somewhat proficient. Oh, but you can pay to make your player better! What the heck does it say about a game when they're asking you to pay to skip their content? How bad must it be?
Then there's the problem of the AI being absolutely brain dead. I could be all alone in the lane and it would take a searchlight, signal flairs and a bullhorn to get them to pass the ball to me. And if I call for a pass because I'm open and the AI chooses to ball-hog (and God do they!), I get penalized. Great system, 2K. The AI guards over-dribble more than Rajon Rondo. Maybe I can call plays - I dunno - but I'm not the coach or PG so I shouldn't be doing so in this mode and I never saw that in the tutorial anyway. Needless to say, I'm not sure that the developers have watched a basketball game in their lives. If they have, they don't know how to put it in a game because the AI doesn't understand the first thing about the fluidity of the game.
Then there are the long, incredibly dull cutscenes that you can't skip. Yes 2K, when I'm looking to play a game of basketball what I really mean is I'd like to watch the court intro scene for 3 minutes. My time isn't important at all...take it up with awful cutscenes that belong on a bad Brazilian Soap Opera. It's bad content made worse by the fact that you have to sit through it. I can't really describe how bad these are but let me try. Find an old episode of Days of Our Lives. Put it on repeat. Repeatedly slam a basketball into your ballsack and repeat "there's no place like the D-League, there's no place like the D-League". That might approximate how painful watching these truly is.
I never bothered with anything else. I'd rather do the aforementioned ballsack thing.
/uninstalled - it ain't even worth the hard drive space.

Got this game on release, didn't really know what to expect with it, but let me summarise my positive points about this:
Storyline is great, lots of twists, with plenty of sidequests to distract from the main story, breaking the game down and making it more enjoyable overall, however there are some tedious side quests that spoil the bunch, especially if you're looking for 100%, there are quests based at certain times of the story, miss them and you'll have to grab them the next spin around.
Graphics are alright, not the best and not the worst, I do love the aesthetic of the game though, clean HUDs alongside nicely designed areas with multiple environments to go to, there's a place for everybody in this.
Controls seem fine on controller, but can't give my input for keyboard and mouse as I haven't played it with these, but from what I played, I'd say steer away from keyboard if you can, I feel the twin stick sections would be better suited to controllers.
The port overall is probably below average however, some decent options but a game like this shouldn't run as bad as it does at times, stuttering and frame drops galore, aside from this I personally haven't been hit by the bugs reported by others (crashing, white / black screens), I'm running a 290X with an FX 8350 for comparison of your machine, if you feel like you're unsure if you'll suffer the same fate as the others.
to summarise:
+ good story, plenty of side quests to disengage and break apart.
+ nice environments, well varied.
+ solid controls on controller, unsure about keyboard but from playing I'd say stick with controller.
- graphics look dated in parts
- some quests are tedious
- reported port issues that haven't been addressed
Overall, I'd recommend this, but only if you can guarantee it'll work on your system from the information you can find, and only if you like typical RPG settings alongside twin-stick segments and bullet hell segments.

I give this a recommendation only with heavy qualifiers:
This game is a mess through and through- it's gone through many developers through over a decade.  The graphics are dated, the animations are choppy or nonexistent for some actions.  Combat is fairly passive and random, with the outcome having very little dependence on player skill.  The interface is clunky and difficult to navigate.  The 'NPCs' are terribly scripted to the point of just being annoying distractions.
That being said, there is no game like it to my knowledge.  I'd be lying if I said it has never irritated me.  It's had me rage-quit more times than I'd like to admit.  It can be very frustrating at times, and difficult to troubleshoot if it's not working right or crashing.
But if you want a game where you can find a secret valley in a mysterious, whimsical, and dangerous land and start a homestead from nothing with your friends, yet don't mind a pretty steep learning curve and having to go to external websites(
), or the kindness of strangers to figure out how to do many things, this may be of interest to you.
Wurm players are an odd bunch and you won't often find their likeness anywhere else.  They may squat on your land and try to steal your stuff. They may frighten you, become extremely paranoid at you- -They may try and roleplay an 8th century Byzantine akrites at you.  But they will probably, most likely try and help you the best they can.  I've met some really great and interesting people in Wurm, and hope to meet more even if the golden years have passed.
If you're not sure, you can always try Wurm Online on a free trial account to get the gist.

An Extremely Deep Game.
I have been playing this game for the past few months and I have enjoyed every hour of Gameplay. Compared to many MMO Games Wurm is made by the Players who play it. In the server I play on we have countless tales of events which happen day to day. The World is completely interactive where the average farmer can influence the War of the Gods in the Sky to the Combat of the Great Powers. You grow attached to that special horse you have had for months or that hardy sword that has kept you alive for countless battles. On whatever server you play you will have rememberable moments and make new friends.
I can think of very few downsides I see of this game. You do have to put considerate time into the game depending on the server and must always be ready to accept the loss of something you spent so long working on whether it be the murder of that special horse or the stealing of that hardy sword.
Your Overall Experience will be defined by the server you play on, not every server is the same. Some servers are fast paced, others slow paced. I encourage you if you are in need of a game to spend countless hours on, a game to become part of a living real time world, pick up Wurm. You will enjoy every moment of it.

While having minor technical issues this game provides a good story with two interesting main characters. Styx was used in later titles of the developer and this game gives a bit more background of him.

I will start the review with by quoting Styx, "Oh, f*ck me sideways".This is what you get by the battle system in this game. A bit broken ein the end, but fortunately its doable with the right skills and attributes. Onward to the review, I am going to list a short pro cons because this game doesnt have much to offer.
Pros:
- Story might be the only strong point in this game (depends on your taste and perspective of a good game)
- One of the interesting part of this game is you play as an orc.
- Every equips you wear on your body is visible and changes Arkail appearance.
Neutral:
- Grahic is OK at best. The graphic option is simplistic with SSAO, FXAA, shadows, texture, particles, and resolution
- OK soundtrack and music, nothing memorable in this part.
Cons:
- Battle system is similar to Dragon Age where you can pause and plan your attack, what skills you will use, who is attacking which enemies, but its not as polished as in Dragon Age, you cant change tactic for your team, so everything is manual, and there no usable item in this game, which makes it a bit hard sometimes. There are two types of attacks for each character, Attack & Def for Arkail, Melee & Ranged for Styx, each has its own upgrades. Overall, the battle system isnt that bad, but it isnt easy to master, and there are some battles which has difficulty spike, especially the final boss battle when the boss summoned the super berserker orcs with unreasonable damage.
- No loot, equipments come from killig enemies (a bit rare to get) and from somewhat lacking chests. In the course of the game from start to finish, there is only 1 chest in 1 dungeon and there is an additional loot sack you can get in each dungeon (this one is not 100%, I have only encountered 4,5 loot sacks in the game maybe its randomized or something)
Conclusion, I dont recommend this game, if you want it get it on sale and if you're not a fan of Styx, dont bother. If you wan to delve deeper into the Styx's world, definitely get it.

Magicite is a challenging Rogue-like RPG platformer. The entire game is based off of a hardcore-like structure, which is definitely a good thing. It is nowhere near impossible, just quite difficult to stay alive until the end of the game. It's one of those games that will take quite a few tries until you complete it - there's no story, just lots of action.
Learning the game is relatively easy from the offset, and it shares a similar crafting system with games such as Terraria. Each "district" - levels, if you will - are randomly generated, however they are not very diverse. At the end of each you can choose one of three doors which lead to unique biomes, which in turn have different creatures and loot within.
Magicite is a great game to use when you're waiting on friends ending their turn on Civilization V - it runs perfectly over any modern game. I'll definitely be back to this game in the future.

Man, as a fan of real time strategy games that mix in management mechanics here and there, this game really comes off as a masterclass to me. I would argue Rome Total War has a few more loving touches (I guess holdovers of a bygone era in CA) than this game, but Medieval 2 has captivated way more than RTW ever did. It's kinda hard to describe what makes this game so killer. Every good non linear game has a loop. Some cycle that the game follows that constantly delivers the player conflict and resolution in satisfying and diverse ways. This game's cycle is, condensed; raising an empire from a few territories that can muster only a few useless peasants, making mates with some blokes or raiding their settlements for personal gain (you can't argue the game doesn't provide some riveting player choice), accruing a few key settlements you have been eyeing for turns and can now use to turn the tide in a war you have been embroiled in for ages, completely swallowing that once huge empire, and then turning to THEIR former neighbours for potential land. It's...it's not subtle. It's quite blunt, it's silly, and it is goddamn satisfiying as all hell.
Now, a breif note: as a historian this game is conflicting at best. It does a good job at tossing in events, at getting some level of accuracy on the outfits and architecture, and properly representing more than just the standard lot of European countries. I'm pretty tired of Eurocentrism in the field and it's always refreshing to see Creative Assembly putting equal effort into capturing the Ottomans as they do the Germans. However....oh heavens. Does it get some stuff wrong. I mean what on earth are those strategies? And why on earth does Russia have so many archers? What is with that? Basically, if you have an eye for historical accuracy and are also familar with CA's other stuff, you know your lot. You'll raise your eyebrow, indignantly show off how much "smarter you are than those fools at CA and Sega", and then sink tens of hours into it.

This is a "Not Recommended" because I shall responsible for PC community, however I will recommended it for PS4 version.
There is something about Nier: Automata, it’s an unforgettable experience, a unique journey, and some of the best definition of humanity－both inside and outside the game.
Story
10/10, unquestionable. Yoko Taro’s idea of unpredictable gameplay and amazing skill of “backwards scriptwriting”, combine with his understanding of human, give Nier: Automata, as well as Nier and Drakengard their soul. There are many moment we as player feels what the character feels, thanks to decision of force the player to spend as many time as possible with the character, to build up relationships, bonds, and memories. And then, destroy all of them, one by one, not just in front of the character, as well as in front of you. The linear story structure is also perfect for a hopeless, meaningless story like this. You think you can do something by making some decision, but in fact, you can’t. You are a doll who is play by the story, just like the characters are an automata who is play by their fate. After all, “Director: Yoko Taro” properly is a quality insurance for story whatsoever.
Gameplay
Well, there aren’t much I can talk about, I didn’t play a lot of ACT or ARPG, but there are one thing for sure. The gameplay mechanic is simple, it’s easy enough that pretty much everyone can play and enjoy the story, as well as making the well done camera changing possible.
Music
I don’t think there are much need to be say about music, everyone know how good it is.
Graphic, Performance, PC Port, and Asian Zone price
This game can be a masterpiece without this sh/itty PC port, Square Enix. I hat to mention this, but what Square Enix had done to the PC community is disappointed. How many god/damn people had being complain about performance on PC? How many god/damn “Not Recommended” did this game get because the suddenly rise of price of Asian Zone without any explanation or announcement? This is the worst marketing I had seen for past years.

With all the BS marketing: 7.5/10

For the first time in my 33 years of life; I took the time to get a refund for this mistake I made.  The trailers may be spot on, but in the 28 minutes I played; I found the game to be repetitive, tedious, and clunky to the max.  Started the game with my usual settings of 1920-1080, started playing and realized that there is no way at all to change the GUI scale or even lower the resolution while playing.  So all my interface text and chats were super tiny.  That's a little thing (pun intended) and I could have restarted to fix it, no real challenge there.  So I kept playing for a bit, the game tells you you're gonna need food and water, and that I can forage for food in the wild, and fill water at fountains in pots and such.  Tried to do just that with a pot they start you with, couldn't figure out how. (Been playing MMO's for 15 years BTW)  Everything you want to interact with, you have to right click, open a menu, select your section, select your subsection of what you want to do, then do it.  While foraging for food in only 5 little plots of grass, I realized that this was gonna get old fast.
So, aside from the annoying, I pressed on for a tad longer; I started playing with the GUI elements, character screen, crafting menu, etc.  found them to be outright overwhelming to a beginner of this particular game, couldn't find anything to show me MY stats (the STATS menu at the top shows useless info like distance walked and framerate crap only).  So, when I picked up two random logs that I might need for crafting something later, my movement speed slowed down, but I have no idea why, or how much, because I didn't see any sort of carrying capacity or encumbrance level.  As I continued to play around with GUI stuff, I saw one of of the menu tabs that said GUI; so I was a little excited for a bit, until I clicked it.  When I did, all of my interface components disappeared for the purposes of screenshots or immersive play I imagine; but when I tried to hit escape, or every other key on my keyboard, it never came back.  I am sure there is a way, but it would have been great to know what it was before being allowed to turn it off.
So, as I said, it's clunky.  I am sure it has it's good points, but it sure wasn't the game for me.  I had hoped this might be a good stopgap until Chronicles of Elyria was released; but it seems I shall look elsewhere.  Happy gaming to all, and kudos if you have the willpower to play this one.

Most of the reviews will tell you that the game mechanics suck, and for the most part I understand why they say that it is. The game is very reminiscent of Dragon Age (1). It uses a real time strategy combat system that you can pause and interrupt to issue more “complex” actions. You literally micromanage your team’s position every step of the way so that you can better tackle every encounter. Given that the game is very challenging on Extreme. You really do have to get familiar with gameplay.
So where does this game go wrong? Well, in Dragon Age, you can pause mid-fight and use your mouse to reposition your character in the battle field, having complete control and awareness of your full team location. Enabling you to manage agro, employ better kiting, making use of choke points for better tanking, etc;
In Of Orcs and Men, the strategical play behaves a lot like a game console. Instead of using your mouse to direct your team’s position you basically move them in real-time. The consequence of that is you lose sight of your other character’s position only leaving you to decide by looking at his life bar. I’m not sure if the design was intentional or if it was because this game was originally for consoles and was just later ported to PC, but the general feel of the gameplay is clunky and unnatural. The game does not make use of the capabilities of a PC, and as a result, majority of the difficulty in playing the game stems from this. Personally, I could have finished Extreme, 4-5 hours less the time it took me if the controls worked similarly to DA.
Barely makes the cut. Of Orcs and Men is like how F13 is to me. Hate the gameplay, but love it for its story and characters. If you are a “story-guy” like me, I highly recommend the game for you.
The combat can be clunky at first but if you let yourself get immersed the story really pulls you in, and it has some great characterization of the two main heroes

Every once in awhile I give a game the benefit of the doubt and give it a go even if I'm on the fence over whether it appears to be worth my time or not.  Often, my gut feeling is correct and the game turns out to be a mediocre experience at best.  However, Of Orcs and Men is one of the exceptions and ended up being a great game.
Of Orcs and Men has one of the best narrative experiences that I've played in a linear RPG.  You play through the tale of a Bloodjaw, an elite orcish warrior, who is on a mission to kill the human emperor who has been eradicating and enslaving his people.  The reversal of roles very much helps push the narrative as you see it from the eyes of an orc, instead of the humans, elves, and dwarves that are against him.  Shortly after leaving for his quest, the orc is approached by a goblin with a completely lack of morals who acts as the personality counterbalance to the honorable and straightforward orc that the game begins with.  The adventure that follows is full of twists and turns that will keep you on the edge of your seat as you are absorbed into the atmosphere of the world,
The combat mechanics of the game are not anywhere near as impressive as the narrative, though I found them to be adequate.  You control both the orc (Arkail) and the goblin (Styx) in a real-time with pause combat system that reminds me of Dragon Age to an extent.  Character building was entertaining as there are a number of ways to build your characters so that they perform like a well-oiled machine.  There are several stats and two skills trees that are unique to the characters, and both of these mechanics are there for you to customize your playstyle.  An additional perk to add to the mix is that at a cerain part in the story each of your characters makes a choice regarding their own story arc that upgrades them to one of two classes narratively tied to it.
Of Orcs and Men is a game that you should get to playing right away if you are a fan of games with a good narrative and can let yourself be pulled into the world.  If you are a heavily mechanical player, you may not enjoy this title as much but I would still recommend giving it a chance as I found the game in its entirety to be a memorable experience.  Overall, Of Orcs and Men is a solid entry into the RPG genre and one that I am very happy that I gave a chance even if I am several years late.

So if not plot is to your satisfaction, some gameplay may make up for it.
Raid mode i have to say is one of the most interesting concepts in the game that i've seen. Usually in the modes of resident evil franchise referred to as The Mercenaries, this game mode introduces the concept of seeing the life of the enemies and a level based on exp almost like an RPG. Strangely enough, its satisfying to beat these modes as the monsters are now on a harder level, can be made more powerful in ways of either speed or/and strength, and the bosses of the game whether Mini or true, now become quite harder. That isn't half the difficulty either, as your invetory from campaign and raid mode are completely seperate meaning you now have to conserve your ammunition as it isn't as readily available AND your weapons are weaker until you find new ones! As your progress though and beat the stages... you unlock bigger, harder difficulties which i'll admit i have not unlocked yet, BUT i can probably say are alot harder than the beginning difficulty.
So to simplify all this for people who don't like to read, It's a good game to play if you want the challenges of resident evil, just not the usual plot or characters. Raid mode is fun and challenging, though you will have to play the campaign to unlock some levels, and the system of graphics and gameplay remain at least on par with Resident Evil 5.
Hope this helped everyone. peace.

Silent Hill meets Twin Peaks. Sounds freaking AWESOME, don't it? But let's take a closer look...
Your character is an FBI agent, who has frequent conversations with some imaginary (?) person in his head. This would be a fascinating enough idea...except that he does it RIGHT IN FRONT OF EVERYONE ELSE, and no one flinches an inch. He drinks cup of coffee after cup of coffee just to read the tea leaves at the bottom; in fact, one of the main, recurring "side-quests" of the game seems to be the eternal quest for a cup of coffee. And when he does find a cup of coffee, or a tin of pickles (branded "The Pickles" on the label), we get a spooky little tune to, er, remind us that this is supposed to be a spooky-arsed game even if nothing particularly spooky has happened for the last half-hour of gameplay.
WEIRD, maybe...there is weirdness aplenty, no doubt...but the spookiness is a little more on the sparing side. At least as far in as I have played this game. Maybe I'll try and play it again some other time, but for now I need a break 'cause, quite frankly, MY ♥♥♥♥ING HEAD HURTS. Seriously.
Here's some of the other madness you'll encounter, should you be brave enough:
There's wooden crates, in various public places. You can "push" them. But instead of pushing them aside to reveal something, you just push AGAINST them until they shatter under the sheer Herculian strength of your besuited character, sometimes revealing cash. Cash you can use to buy live worms and a fishing rod from the strange old lady who runs the huge hotel in which absolutely no one else is staying, so you can nip out to the back of the hotel and catch yourself some fish. To eat, I presume (I didn't quite muster up the courage and/or patience to test this theory, though).
Next, there's a couple of bars in town which you can apparently visit, one of which is called...wait for it...The Galaxy Of Terror. Which appears to be an oddball reference to the semi-obscure 80s horror movie of the same name, which I guess is meant to tie in with the recurring theme of quirky low-budget 80s horror films which is fleshed out further in the conversations our protagonist has with himself / his split personality whilst joy-riding around in a police car which he has freely been given the keys to (along with the apparent permission to blare sirens, beep horns, and run into other cars with absolutely no repercussions whatsoever).
I mean, c'mon...I love 1983's The Deadly Spawn as much as the next guy, but I'm not sure I need to hear the name of its director and fascinating little tidbits about it having a completely different crew to its sequel, while I'm in the process of driving to a police station to find out some information about a real-life murder victim. Whose file has been lost by the nerdy, quite possibly homosexual deputy who then spends hours looking for it while you can pop downstairs for a quick nap in the cells (to replenish your "tiredness" meter, of course; there's a "hunger" one too, hence the aforementioned coffee and pickles and fish and whatnot).
Next thing I know, it's 5pm and the police station decides it's closing time - "come back tomorrow" - and while I'm driving back to the hotel after an amazingly productive day of stealing freshly-made cups of coffee from unoccupied hotel rooms and completely failing to find out ANYTHING whatsoever about the ONLY murder case the sleepy little town has had in eons from none less than the police department itself, I decide to stop by and investigate a completely random letterbox outside someone's house and lo and behold, find some pistol ammo in it. As you do. Oh, and there's at least five or six cops in the police station at any one time, but if you try to talk to the majority of them your character decides that "This person probably has nothing to do with the investigation". I guess they must need all those surplus cops to do traffic duty in a town with absolutely no bloody people in it, and couldn't possibly spare the manpower to contribute to the solving of a perplexing and incredibly rare MURDER case...
What...waitaminute. You're STILL reading this review? Okay, should I mention some of the technical problems then, like the fact that the mouse is INSANELY oversensitive to the point where your character spins almost 180 degrees with the faintest movement of one's hand - running around is a particularly enjoyable chore herein - even once you reduce the mouse sensitivity to its absolute minimum, which you can only do in the game's launcher, meaning you have to exit the game to perform such a privileged function? And don't even get me started on the -
No, look...seriously...I'm done. I don't even want to think about this any more. Like I said, I HAVE A HEADACHE. I wanted this game to be good. It looked so much like my cup of tea...er, coffee...er, t-tin of pickles...
Oh man, I'm gonna have nightmares tonight. And not the type which I WANT games like this to give me. I'll probably be wandering around an endlessly huge and empty hotel searching for warm beverages and canned food all night. I swear to God, if I develop yet another bloody psychological quirk from this game, like never being able to look a tin of pickles in the face again without suffering a nervous breakdown, I am going to SUE THE DEVELOPERS. I just wanna go to bed, and maybe cry myself to sleep. I can't take it any more. I'm sorry. I just can't...I just can't...
Verdict: 4/10.

There are only two types of humans that roam this earth.  Those that don't like this game and those that were birthed by the divine womb of Deadly Premonition to rise on high during endtimes and sit in judgement of those that are unworthy in both earth below and heaven above.
I count myself as the latter.  Are you mortal or are you divine?

The actual game itself gets a wholehearted recommendation. Though the gameplay is certainly rough around the edges--to say the least--there's an immense amount of charm, humor, and Lynch-esque eccentricities found in the fictional town of Greenvale. Deadly Premonition was never a "so bad it's good" game, but rather a genuinely good experience saddled with a low budget and a couple of design pitfalls. The main issues lie in the combat. The game's director SWERY65 has been on the record stating that the "shooting bits" were not actually a part of the game's original concept. The combat was the last part of the game developed in what seems to be an effort to give the game a broader audience appeal. And it shows. Killing enemies in this game is by no means a dreadful or broken experience, it's just a very barebones and arguably pointless affair--some shallow padding until you reach the next chunk of entertaining story exposition and exploration of the game's quirky world. I'd argue that most people played the Dreamcast classic Shenmue for the exploration, character interaction and investigation segments rather than the just-OK fighting-game showpieces sprinkled throughout. As it follows in Shenmue's footsteps in many ways, Deadly Premonition should be treated in the same regard. Do enjoy the warmth that Greenvale has to offer.
If you can.
The lack of resolutions higher than 720p in this PC port have already been discussed and criticized--and then fixed, by the same dude who made the Dark Souls PC fix. DPFix, however, does not fix the lackluster native controller support and constant crashing. You can go find additional third-party mapping software of course, but as this is originally a console game and advertises controller support on the Steam store page, the exclusion is a bit disappointing. The crashing, on the other hand, is not as immediately remedied. It seems very temperamental and varies from system to system, but across my two Windows 7 and XP machines I've had nothing but instability. I have tried putting the .exe in Windows 98 compatability, numerous restarts, and other tweaks found from various discussion threads. But the game still crashes at the worst, most pivotal moments (like before I can get to a save point) or slows down to an unplayable framerate. The framerate is momentarily fixed by a full system reboot, but the sluggishness and screeching halts always return again and again. I've never seen this kind of thing happen in any other game.
So in a bit of frustration and resignation, I've uninstalled this game and returned to finish the original, Xbox 360 version. But I feel like I'm missing out on the definitive experience. The Director's Cut provides some nice touch-ups, like a better map system, less washed-out graphics, marginally improved driving controls, some extra cutscenes, and an easier default difficulty setting, which basically lowers the sometimes ridiculously high health bars on the various enemies throughout the game. Though there's much talk these days about the dumbing down of modern games--that they're too easy--I can assure you that toning down the frustration in this game is definitely a good thing. Anyone who has spent 30 minutes killing one of the "wall-crawler" enemies in the 360 version should be able to attest. It's attrition, a hurdle, not a fair and invigorating challenge by any means.
Some people have been able to play this port to completion, sidequests and all. Maybe you're one of them, maybe not. Maybe in a year (or more), the game will be patched up and as nice as the Dark Souls port. Until then, I consider this game an Xbox 360 exclusive (the Playstation 3 Director's Cut port is even worse than the PC version, don't touch it please!).
Buy this port if you like a gamble, Zach.

This is the type of game that will only excite people who get into the characters and story. In concept the game itself is fantastic, but technical flaws narrows the overall appeal to an already niche title. I loved the game, but I feel it's only fair to recommend it with some caveats.
It's a murder mystery with quirky characters. They give the game a lot of heart and fans of the TV show Twin Peaks and 80s pop culture should find some things to love. The juxtaposition of horror and comedy is something special.
Basically this is an open world survival horror game where you drive around and look for clue to further the story. If I remember correctly there are 50 side quests as well. I really liked that many prizes for completing side quests were useful (unlike many open world games). You normally travel by car which is a jarring, experience. The car controls very poorly and has a blind spot where the frame of the windshield is. Opening the large map takes up half the screen and does not display all of the information that the menu map does. As bad as it all sounds, you do get used to it, and fast travel options open up with the right side quest completion. I would say the driving was my biggest peeve.
The combat is familiar to anyone who has played Resident Evil 4 or Dead Space. The controls are a stiffer than expected in the previously mentioned games and aiming is not as easy. There is some required melee combat and all weapons break after a few uses. I was ok with this considering that it's a survival horror game. I never was weaponless during my playthrough. there is not a lot of enemy variation though so be ready to hear "noooo i dooon't want to dieeee!" about over 9000 times.
Though Deadly Premonition still contains a fair amount of jank, it only adds to the wealth of charm within. The end result is a ridiculously original masterpiece that hearkens back to an era where the gaming landscape had more room for wildly imaginative budget games, a far cry from the abundance of focus tested blockbusters that are prevalent today.

I sadly did not enjoy the game since its humour did not get a kick out of me. And if you won't find this game funny, unfortunately there is nothing much else in here, its humour is the main selling feature, and unfortunately I did not find the style of humour that is used here funny.
Let it be known that not at one point I was offended or any of the sort, my feelings were never hurt, the game just simply didn't make me laugh and annoyed me sadly more than anything else, I never found the "every sound effect even soundtrack is made by mouth" thing. It gets annoying quite quickly, at least to me. Enemies repeat a lot of the same lines and over and over again when you kill them, and some have the same death lines every time they die, if they come in groups this can become particularly annoying (Especially the ghosts).
I also encountered some technical issues, at the "park" level, after the world war level that is. The mini-games crashed my game after they ended (Mini-game where you shoot kids for example) so I started avoiding these since they crashed my game and forced me to start a level from the beginning.
So, what kind of humour is the game going for? I hear it is a parody of Call of Duty, that is its intention. Yet the way it's done does not seem to be such, there are some♥♥♥♥♥♥takes at how Call of Duty potrays certain situations and comments there and there, but some of the jokes are almost completely unrelated to the game it claims to parody. Most of the jokes don't really play off Call of Duty and seem to rely more on being as random as possible and throwing the player into random goofy situations, sadlly soon the player can start epxecting what will come next.
The game is very loud and constantly spams player with various voice lines, from enemies to various characters in the game, there isn't much moment of silence, if any, which eventually makes the experience tiring
The charm of the humour to me weared off around the time the tutorial ended. Like most parodies it's hit and miss, sadly to me it was mostly a miss, as the game spams the player with a lot of noise and silly voices, one could get a PTSD flashback to the "Scary Movies" (It never gets THAT bad) which get annoying quickly and stop being funny. Some gags go on for too long yet never go quite anywhere, for example there is a comrade on your squad that is introduced in the beginning that is needed in the team because he opens doors, this is obviously a reference to the COD's scripted sequences where AI would constantly open the door for the player rather than player himself, yet it never goes quite anywhere and the gag never develops into anything. It just suddenly vanishes without giving a proper punch.
(I could be wrong, maybe the gag will return with its punch like at the end or something?)
The gameplay sadly is even worse, there are some interesting ideas there and there, but tehre are parts that are quite lazy, like when you were told to destroy "Salties" which essentially are huge "salt" vehicles shooting rockets at you, you are given a rocket launcher and are told to, well, obviously kill them. This part of the game goes on for far too long to the point it stops being fun and you wish to move on to something else, the enemies that are presented here are not even slightly fun to battle. It doesn't help that the trails of smoke behind the rockets obsecure the rockets themselves pretty well, and you have to dodge these rockets, which can be pretty annoying since the before mentioned smoke makes them very hard to see.
What's even worse is that after you die, the smoke these rockets left behind them don't dissapear, this means that the screen is covered in even more and more smoke from these rockets and it becomes a huge cluster ♥♥♥♥. This is another example of the game having certain technical issues, another one comes to mind with snipping nuns, where the player is tasked to kill them, sometimes they would dissapear out of the windows and re-appear, I am not sure if this was intentional, if this meant they are "hiding" or if this is some kind of error, I honestly could not tell.
The weapons are unsatisfying and not fun to use, you might argue that I am going towards the gameplay too much and excuse it as a "parody" I do not believe that you can excuse flaws in a game play just because it is a parody.
Parody should not excuse poor quality of anything. And the gun play here is anything but fun, it's slow, some weapons are almost worthl-ess, the weapons the nuns drop are essentially one hit kill, I believe. The problem is that the projectile is slow, VERY slow. Taking forever to reach its target, I am not sure if that is the joke.
So should you get this game? Well, watch the trailers, watch some gameplay videos, if the humour seems appealing to you, I guess go for it. I am not sure even a person wh o would genuinelly like the humour wouldn't get tired of it after a while as the game goes along.
Nevertheless, I wish the developers who made this game a good luck in their next projects, as this is a big improvement from NotGTAV. Even if I don't find it funny, I find it quite charming. And in the end.
TL:DR: You have to find the humour here funny to like the game as the gameplay cannot hold it alone, sound design is annoying, there are some technical issues which will probably be fixed as time goes on..

NotCoD™
2D Action Parody
NotGames
NotGames
is a 2D action parody game of
developed and published by NotGames. Your enjoyment of the game purely relies on how much you find its premise funny.
Set in Britain, you play as Private Suds Sudzington Jr and you find yourself dropped♥♥♥♥♥♥firstwards into this Hell. You will murder WWII reenactors, priests, nuns, children, and even animals.
The script is very funny, and most jokes hit right home, making fun of not only CoD, but also other games, religion, and much more without feeling disrespectful, which is something really hard to achieve.
The hand-drawn graphics are quite ugly at first, but the more you play the more you get used to them, and they are quite charming in the end. But still, they are not all that good (even though it is part of the joke).
The game smartly uses a 2D perspective, with really smooth controls for both k/m and gamepad. You can carry two weapons at a time, 4 frag grenades, and 4 smoke grenades. A good achievment of the developers was making this a constantly enjoyable game that has good variety: gunfights, turret sections, on-rail sequences, and even puzzle keep changing the pace of your playthrough. There are many different weapons and enemies to fight, each requiring a different strategy to dispatch them as efficiently as possible.
I enjoyed playing through the game, and it felt pretty good. I can't deny, however, that in the long run it got a bit tiring, even with the different gameplay sequences.
You have a health bar, and you need to find medikits to regain health. Gunfights are mostly doable, but some sequences tend to get really hard, delivering some decent challenge.
The british voice acting is a joy to listen to, and the soundtrack is darn fun to listen to. Props to the composer!
Multiple episodes will be released in the future, and when you finish the game you can play it again to find more secrets, or you can play a Zombie mode with a friend in split-screen coop. And don't forget the 73 achievements to unlock!
Overall, this is a funny and competent shooter that delivers good jokes and decent variety. Easily one of the best satire games available right now. Highly recommended on sale, and on full price for lovers of parodies.

Just started OOB: Pacific.  Tried a fan-created scenario first and it was "ok."  Then, I thought, I'd try out my 1st campaign as the Imperial Japanese.   I can't believe how puny and undramatic the opening battle of WWII for the U.S. vs. Japan was portrayed here.  Seriously.  I had about 6 planes TOTAL, plus 1 I bought.  The U.S. Navy had 3 battleships and 3-4 smaller vessels in port in this scenario.  Sorry, but I expected something more historical, along the lines of what inflamed the fires of American patriotism that day.  TONS of enemy planes sinking/damaging TONS of unprepared/ill-equipped US vessels and property.  This scenario was a BIG disappointment.
MAJOR HISTORICAL ERROR:  Surely by now, someone else has noticed how the 40's-era commercial announcer says, "Once a Marine, Always a Marine.  Semper "feeee."  That made me puke just a little bit.  It's FI/pronounced "FYE," as in Semper Fidelis, "Ever/Always Faithful!"  Semper "feeeeee"?  Almost a deal-breaker, folks.
The opening panel artwork is atrocious as well.  I saw what I believe was intended to be a Colt 1911 .45 U.S. military-issue side arm with some rounds to the side of it?  The artist's conception made it look more like a cross between a Browning High-Power 9mm (especially the anaemic bullets to the side of it) and an emaciated Desert Eagle.
I'm guessing that most players will be comparing this to the offerings in the Panzer Corps line and/or Battle Academy.  Of the 3, this comes in dead last so far.  It reminds me of WWI type games where it takes way too many moves to accomplish anything.
Only one real game into a "campaign" that cost $40 and I'm having doubts about what kind of military research was done other than to feature true battles that actually occurred in history.
I DO appreciate the fact that SOMEONE has taken on the conflict in the Pacific over the European theatre for a change, though.  5 Stars for that!  Sadly, STEAM will only allow you to +/- this game with no wiggle room so I must say that, at this point in time, I would not recommend this game....unless you willing to take the only offering of WWII Pacific Theatre action out there.
Hopefully, I'll be revising this review in a more positive light soon.  I just wish you would have asked me some questions before this went to market.  I've not been involved in Beta testing but I have to wonder if it's limited to playability alone or are testers allowed to comment/suggest ideas.  Hmmmm....

Negative aspects are some stability and performance issues. As to stability, I've had some crashes, although few and far between. Performance wise, the AI turn can be very slow, particularly with older PCs and in large scenarios.
All in all, this is IMHO the definitive PG-alike game that falls short of perfection due to the stability and performance issues.

Hmmm... What to say what to say.
I've played this game for a few weeks now, both by myself and with a friend. Look, I'm going to be honest here. I have seen/noticed a few bugs in the game, primarily with multiplayer, but they really, really don't happen often. I read over a few negative reviews, and I'm thinking to myself...I don't think these individuals TRULY gave the game a chance.
______________________________________________________________
______________________________________________________________
Crafting - The crafting system is pretty fun, when you take a rogue-like dungeon crawler game like this, and add in a loot system with simple crafting, it makes it so you have something to look forward to.
Unlocks - What I mean by this is, as you progress through the game you unlock characters, followers, and masks, you get these typically by progressing through levels, or beating certain bosses, etc.
Visuals - The game honestly is pretty cute, the visuals are really well done and nothing seems out of place, it really has done a good job of keeping me engaged with the different colors and effects.
Gear - To be honest I didn't expect such a decent variety of gear, once you progress further you can come across some pretty cool and rare items.
Perks - When you first build you character you can pick 2 perks that enhance your gameplay, either by boosting stats or by giving nice little bonuses for harvesting or making gear/equipment
Skill Paths - I think it's pretty cool that the Dev made it so you can progress either as a melee hero, an archer, or a mage; by rolling your stats right and picking your perks the right way, you can really enhance the way you play your character, it isn't a linear skillset either, and for me it seems like you can really build your character to match the way you play.
Character Builder - I mentioned little tidbits about this above throughout all of my pros, but I think this deserves a segment of it's own. I like that you can select followers, and unlock masks that give you certain augments, for example there's one that gives you a 50% chance to get a +1 to attack when you level up. You also unlock followers as you progress that will follow you around, they usually enhance you in some way or give you some form of augment.
Permanent Death - Some people may hate this, I hated it at first, but as I died more and more, I gradually learned how to do more things in the game, the combat became more exciting and engaging as I was able to overcome my enemies. Honestly, I almost stopped playing because of it, I was getting pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ but, I stayed patient with it, and I think having to start over gave me more adventures to look forward to.
Tutorial - There is not a tutorial, if you want a game that just throws you right into the mix and actually forces you to learn the content, then this is the game for you. There are guides available online, but that just ruins the excitement you get when you learn how to craft a new item. For me it was a pain at first, but after awhile it really added to the adventure aspect. I really was just immersed into all of this content and all of it was for me to discover; I think that games have lost that luster, it's how it used to be, and nowadays there's just way too much hand holding. I hate to admit it, but even I have become accustomed to 20 minute long tutorials, and then all I'm left with is the grind.
I think that's about it for my Pro's. There's quite a good bit of content in this game for $10, most of what I've stated above is most of the content you'll experience. I've left a few end-game things out and other pieces of information so I don't really ruin the game for you, but these are the key mechanics/visuals that I enjoyed.
______________________________________________________________
______________________________________________________________
Bugs - Like I said initially, I personally haven't experienced many bugs, but I played with a friend, who encountered a few, but they were intermittent and didn't really hinder/ruin the experience of this game for us. Typically when he 'bugged out' we were actually able to duplicate some items, and the bugs typically went away by completing a level. We didn't abuse the duplicating too much, but we had some laughs from it. My recommendation to the Dev (assuming you even read this) would be to take a look into fixing these, because for some people it really could be a major annoyance, me and my friend are patient but some people may not want to take the time; plus, if I hadn't been there to finish levels when my friend glitched out, the game would end for someone playing by themselves at that point. I digress.
Content - After so many hours of gameplay (About 13 hours) I feel at this point I've crafted mostly everything you can craft, and found or seen most of the items available. I would really, really love a DLC, or SOMETHING to give this game just a little more substance. I would love to be able to progress further, for there to be more bosses, more gear, etc. I still haven't unlocked all the characters and stuff, so there's still things for me to do. But I'd really like to have more to choose from, you know.
Tutorial - At first this was a huge no-no for me. I literally had no clue how to craft the most basic things, there's guides and stuff online but I decided to tough it out and did it the hard way. For new players this could serve as a huge deterrent. Now that I've played the game, I think I understand WHY the Dev didn't add one. It adds to the discovery aspect of the game, there isn't any hand holding. This is why I also added the tutorial to the Pros section, because some people want a game that just throws you right into battle with a stick and says "Here, take this stick and build an empire." because for me, that's how I felt when I first started. I had absolutely no clue what I was doing, it was awful, but once I got the hang of it, I see why it was done that way.
Lack of Support - Personally, I haven't seen any response from the Dev, since I bought it a couple weeks ago there haven't really been any updates, and I'm hoping I didn't just buy my way into a game that has no further progression (Given that it has been out for 2.5 years already)
______________________________________________________________
______________________________________________________________
Honestly, bugs and content aside, I'm still going to recommend it. For the laughs and entertainment it has given me so far, and the future entertainment I think it'll provide, the 10$ is a really fair price tag. Really, I've enjoyed the game, and I think that you should give it a chance, too. There's plenty of things to do, and I don't think I've learned everything just yet. I seem to discover a few new things each time I play.

I played Wurm Online for a good 9 solid years. I was genuinely hitched on it.
Ultimately I burned out and after a good year hiatus I got Wurm Unlimited.
If you've ever played Wurm Online, that's the gameplay you're going to get, but with some changes you can make like the rate you gain skills, the amount of creatures, speed of crops.
Unfortunately, there really isn't much more than that.
This is probably one of the messiest pieces of software on the Steam store from a functional standpoint. You're given barely any maps to use in your servers, and if you want more you'll need to use programs that aren't packaged nor even mentioned in Wurm Unlimited to get them.
The actual launcher client for picking servers is pointless in its design, as it just shuts itself down once you're in and if you don't like a server you're going to get really annoyed when you have to keep relaunching the full thing to just pick a new one.
As for customization, this was clearly an extremely quick job when they decided to let Wurm be privatized. The UI is extremely annoying to navigate, it has search options when trying to spawn items that can't even search for things when you type them exactly right or only partially, you have to get the amount it wants to search for just right.
You want to customize something on your client? That means restarting of course. If you are hosting your own server (As many will likely do), you need to shut your entire server down because it won't let you open the game client on its own, another example of it's poor usability.
Wurm itself is a very *VERY* dated game and it's been suffering from that for a long time. It's received no quality-of-life improvements in the last few years, and for its age and graphical fidelity, it still has pretty horrendous performance on the CPU side of things.
As I've recently said in the comments, the only reason I can see why you should buy this is if you've enjoyed Wurm Online itself in the past, have been able to handle all its problems, but just don't want to be paying 8 euros every month for it.
It's a shame there's no really good modern alternative to Wurm, but it is time to admit this is just too old to work these days. The performance is horrendous even on CPUs like an i7 6700k, the UI is extremely dysfunctional and tough to use (nor can it even scale properly). They keep stacking features on overtime but it's just devolving into a mess that's struggling to still be called a program that can run.

Well I've played this game for just over 10 hours now, and I can certainly recommend it to any mmorpg fan. Sure, the game has a low population, but there are a number of active guilds which organize events and keep the game alive for you - the veterans are all very friendly! Anyway, here's a list of pros and cons for this game that I can think of, with the knowledge I have of the game by this point.
Pros:
-Amazing combat system - its actually fun to kill mobs.
-Friendly community - unlike most mmos.
-Player housing - very customisable and fun. Makes a nice break from questing.
-All voice acted in depth storyline to follow
-'Path' system gives you something different do whilst leveling.
-Ability customisation and Talents (AMPS) - easily customisable for different builds. Fun to play about with.
-Nice optimisation (Im playing on a pretty awful laptop at 50-60fps :D)
-Nice enviroments
-Endgame raiding looks pretty intense and fun.
Cons-
-Some quests require 2 or more people - unfortunately it's hard to find them!
-Low level dungeons are steamrolled - Give lots of exp and loot but not so much fun as the bosses still die without really following mechanics.
-The default UI (imo) is a cluster♥♥♥♥ - I suggest you download ForgeUi off Curse.
-Lack of players - Sometimes the zones feel quite empty, and dungeon queueing is almost not worth doing. (You're better off asking the Nexus chat or joining an active guild!
Overall, I would highly recommend this game to any MMORPG fan.
-Side note:
I haven't reached max level, but from what I can tell, their seems to be a lot of challenging content at max level such as raiding, prime dungeons and pvp quests.
-I also havent done any pvp yet - I haven't really heard anything about it either, lol. That being said, I'm sure it would be good fun with the active combat system in this game.

Let me just start out by explaining some of the bad reviews which come from Square Enix not releasing a patch since release. I installed the FAR mod before even playing the game, which allows you to run the game in native resolution, 60 FPS and adds much needed improvements, and have had little to no problems while playing the game. Now let's go on with the review.
This game is AMAZING, I don't usually write reviews but I feel this game deserves the praise. The comedy is hilarious when it needs to be, whether it be the ability to remove the Operation System of your character or accusing one of the protagonists of "wanting to $#@%" the female lead, it had me laughing. The combat feels smooth, and refined with swaps between sword play, and classic bullet hell, and there's varying amounts of weapons, upgrades and abilities to change it to how you like. The characters I absolutely loved, even ones that seem like they were made to be disliked I grew onto after finding out their stories,
As for the story, I absolutely loved it, it pulled at my heart on several occasions making me care about and feel for machines, and anytime I thought I fully understood the world and what was happening, something new would happen, leaving me craving for the more information, you'd think you figured it all out and them BAM, your whole world get rocked. The atmospheres are captured perfectly with a post-apocalyptic, post-war, nature has reclaimed with world, type setting which can look beautiful, but feel eerie and mysterious, leaving me wanting to learn what had happened. But it isn’t all perfect.
I have a only a few complaints about this awesome game such as the hacking minigame, which you used A LOT get boring very quickly, as you repeat the same thing over and over it feels more and more like a chore. The story goes a bit stale after the first "Act" as I'll put it,
but then it quickly ramps up. The environments can feel dull as the colors almost feel washed out and some of the building and terrain can look odd at times (buildings that look incredible square). And obviously, the lack of patching which requires you to download the FAR mod to enjoy the game in 1920/1080 res with 60 FPS.

Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel was a highly anticipated game, especially after the massive success of its gargantuan predecessor. Without DLC's, you play one of four in the band of misfits—most of whom show up as antagonists in Borderlands 2. Each person has their own motive for working as a group; some want to be heroes while others just live for the thrill of it. There's better mobility, new weapon types, money is actually useful to get loot, women who love women, Claptrap, and your excessive collection of guns can actually be used in a vending machine called "The Grinder" to rely on RNG to make a better gun. There are some intuitive changes and upgrades to the game. Skill trees have changed, giving you new abilities such as double jump and the skill to be like Kirby and do a butt slam in order to make a quick descent. Everything I loved about Borderlands 2 mechanics were built into the game—from higher tier modes with great loot drops to fun easter eggs.
However, there was a lot wrong too. The writing suffered with the different team, opting for censoring profanity that broke immersion from the coarse world of Borderlands. Some jokes were more cringe-y than funny. The progression is significantly slower because it was padded with boring fetch quests. The new terrain was beautiful but seriously lacking in save points; someone else said it's like the game wanted us to die and restart from the beginning. They hit the nail on the head. Raid bosses were one of the highlights of Borderlands 2—and there was only 1 in TPS that was on a predictable respawn timer. As with any Borderlands game, I also strongly recommend playing this with friends. Otherwise, it will get boring really fast.
So did it live up to the hype? Yes and no. It answered a lot of questions but it also left a lot of questions unanswered. If anything, the game is more worthy as an expansion to Borderlands 2 than a standalone game. I'm recommending it if you love Borderlands 2 lore and have a really strong desire for more Borderlands content. I also recommend playing this first if you want to appreciate
more; many characters show up from this game and Borderlands 2.
7/10

So many reviews and so many positive. I honestly doubt this will even be read. I would rather have a 1-5 rating system than a black and white yes/no. As of this writing the approval rate is 80% and in my opinion, the game doesn't deserve that. So I'm going to say no. Here's why.
Except for the playable characters the voice acting was notably inferior to BL1 and BL2. It lacked motivation, inspiration, emotion and believability. I felt as if the voice actor asked the producer "what is my motivation?", and there was either no producer or the producer didn't know or didn't care. I'm sure the actors are skilled but a clueless actor results in mediocre acting.
Making a dialog comment about not being able to understand the Aussie accent and dumbing it down ya'll, was clearly targeting the American market and annoying. It wasn't funny. I understand the dialog just fine. It is however, difficult to follow
dialog of speed-talkers, which occurred once.
I did appreciate the how the BL1 vault hunters inserted dialog into the story as it developed. That being said...
2K Australia's design for this game focused on high spawn rates and repetitive mobs over story development. The story became progressively confusing and disjointed, senseless. It is incredibly disappointing and lacking. If you want to witness what happened to Jack that made him the psychopath that he was in BL2 then you will be disappointed as well. Evidently all you have to do is lie to him, end of story.
Jack is surprisingly capable of taking care of himself. He never acted like a code-monkey. He was rarely timid. There was no story development as to what he was doing on the station or why Hyperion was even building it. The few details regarding this in BL2 were not elaborated upon in the Pre-Sequel.
So Moxxi sabotaged Jack's precious laser. Roland and Lilith did nothing but assist Jack. Except in the final scene where Lilith...
So if Jack is mad at anyone it should be Moxxi... at least according to the 2K Australia story.
The game is fun but not worth paying the full price. I enjoyed the insight into the new vault hunters, as these are characters that the BL2 vault hunters will encounter. I didn't care for Nisha and Wilhelm (didn't play Claptrap). And while I could relate to Athena, I do not feel any desire to replay the Pre-Sequel for any character, even in True Vault Hunter mode.
Don't buy this game for the story. Don't expect any fan recommended engine improvements to be addressed.
