So, normally I write my reviews with a rhyme theme, but I couldn't do it this time because I'd never get my point across if I tried to do it that way.
So look as a platinum overwatch player, I should say how I wound up in this game, I lost a bet to a friend and had to install this game to try it,  mainly because I got sick of overwatch and how it felt more like an RNG based game system compard to a team based game. Look you know how this dance works, games with team orientated gameplay usually revolve around LUCK half the time or self reliance in the end. Paladins was nice because I actually felt like I was doing something, maybe it's because of the 1 less player making things somehow more tense because each death is one more person you're down for a few seconds with. Maybe it's because supports can heal more than 1 person at a time faster than 25hp every half hour. Maybe it's because when someone HITS you it HURTS.
Paladins stands out so well on its own that I've kind've brushed off my past belief of how it was an overwatch clone. It's different enough and original in its own regards but still shares a lot of similarities. But the loadout/customization moba like aspect changes it a million different ways so no two matches are the same, and you can't change characters once you pick one so that's a lot more alleviating to know that what I'm going in against or as is what I will be stuck dealing with and don't have to stress over how to deal with each different situation that MIGHT arise as in overwatch.
I love this game, I want that to be clear, I feel like teamwork is important... The problem is, the classes, the main one being flankers. AKA the things that are simply too fast to even have a remote possibility to keep up with, without the use of a root or a turret. And this seems to be a renown issue in the entire game because if I don't focus on these people my teammates never do. And every time I point out that we should stay on top of the ones behind us constantly I get called a toxic user and told to go sod myself with a power sander glued to an augger.
Skye was never an issue for me, apparently to most she is but I usually wind up accidentally killing her when she's cloaked so I can't tell if I've just been lucky or more skilled.
But then there is Maeve, the one who can fly around basically and throw very VERY high damage knives from afar. Most people can't seem to register where they're being nailed from annoyingly enough, so when she's on the enemy team (As she is 80% of my games which is another issue.) I have to simply hit my head on the desk and pray I canstop her on my own because no one else will notice. Y'know whatever a hard to keep up with character is one thing one that can blind you basiaclly and gurantee escape as well as do enough damage to rival a terrorist in a washing machine.
Then there is Ying, the one who can place multiple clones but each one can heal teammates which doesn't sound like much but when you have 8 targets to focus on instead of 5 and the fact that support can hit like a concrete truck with a long range rifle/mirror thing, and you can't ignore these targets because if you do they heal that up fast.
Yes obviously I'm over exaggerating a lot of things from both MY personal experience and from what I'VE read.
I really enjoy this game a lot, I really do. But these two characters alone, were so so so bad, that I don't think anyone will want to try this out simply due to the fact of how busted they are. The constant radio silence from the game devs (Aside from the robotic alert to a teeny update) makes things more hopeless too. Their support isn't too responsive either so if you need something like your account recovered, then you're in a bad spot.
TL;DR I love this game and probably will keep playing it, I've had more fun with this game and felt like it's been more fair in every game of it than any game I ever played in overwatch, it's evolved enough on its own to no longer be in the ripoff or duplicate category and can be called simply inspired from instead. Order of Battle: Pacific (OoB:P) has one advantage and one advantage alone over competing titles like Panzer Corps, Panzer General and all the other hex strategy games: The revolutionary supply system. The hex field where a unit is or moves through belongs to the player of that unit. That way you can establish areas that are under your control. If a supply source (a town or a supply ship) is within that area, then the units are in supply and can fight at their full strength. When you cut enemy units of from their supply source by moving one or more of your units through the area, that connects their area with the area of their supply source, then their effective combat strength drops radically. This gives tanks e.g. their realistic operational combat value to cut off enemy units and start a battle of encirclement and annihilation. This is great. This is what I had been waiting for in a game for decades. It opens a completely new dimension of strategy.
Sadly, this is the only advantage OoB:P has to offer and there are so many disadvantages that wear this great feature down.
The waiting time during the enemy's turn:
My PC is using an OC i5, 8 GB RAM and an SSD, along with a pretty good graphics card. The waiting time during some turns can be up to 7 minutes. Attention: I'm not talking about a situation where the enemy has 20 units in close combat with mine and needs to figure out a good tactic. I'm talking about where I can see ONE enemy unit on the map and the AI takes 7 minutes for hidden movement in the fog of war. I've read about other player's who claim to have waiting times of 20 to 30 minutes during each turn. A typical battle lasts about 25 turns, but 50 turns and more is not uncommon. To be fair, 7 minutes is, in my case, the absolute maximum. Most times the AI needs maybe a minute. But when these spikes happen, then they come in a row.
Predefined tactics:
This is - by far - the worst. It's what made me uninstall the game. The developers obviously don't trust the players. They have a very narrow idea of how a battle should be played, e.g. in which order strategic objects should be captured, where a player should send his units and where he MUST NOT send them (or else he will be punished by, and I♥♥♥♥♥♥you not, SPAWNING huge amount of enemy troops right before his troops to bash them back where the developers think they belong). Other means how this is enforced are, that the player may not bring specifc CORE units into battle or that he's limited to a very small force until he captures a specific location. There are very often AI controlled units in battles, that fight on your side, but which move at scripted events or times to directions that you can't influence, e.g. they wait for 15 turns and do nothing and then move to attack a small island on the map even though you've already cleared that one out. Result: You've waisted time to clear that island (which was supposed to be attacked by the AI controlled allied units - without telling you before) and now you don't have enough time left to complete the rest of the (secondary) objectives, so you have to restart the battle. Because of this, I had to restart about 3/4 of the battles that I've played. It's extremely frustrating.
Stupid and cheating AI:
I could put up with the extremely long waiting times during the AI's turn if the AI was smart. But it isn't. I had moments like "Oh no, if this unit moves two hex to the southeast, then it will cut of my units." But no. Never have I witnessed one single smart move of the AI but A LOT stupid ones. The AI does two things: A) Attack the weakest unit or the one that has already taken the most damage and B) move to the closest victory location. That's it. A higher difficulty level doesn't mean a smarter AI, it just means better combat multipliers for the enemy (more damage to your units, less damage to theirs). The AI also cheats like hell, e.g. an enemy planes uses its maximum range to fly right next to one of your planes, which is at a location where it's guaranteed that the enemy has had no vision, to attack said plane. Fog of war exists only for the player.
Exit points on battle maps:
This is really the last straw. At some border locations of the map are "exit points" where you or the enemy can move units to and remove them from battle. That may sound like a good idea at first, when you have spend all your supply points but realise that you actually don't need a certain unit, so you move it to an exit point and then bring in a better unit from the reserves that helps you more in this situation. But in the campaign, these exit points are exclusively used by the AI to remove - without any need or warning - units from battle that are part of secondary objectives. Like "Shoot down 5 air plane squadrons" and after 15 turns or so, all enemy planes are suddenly "gone". The most absurd situation was when an enemy carrier literally vanished at open sea in front of three of my torpedo bomber squadrons. Secondary objective: failed. WTF??
Ammunition resupply:
The resupply system that I've mention in the beginning is good, but it's very, very oversimplified. Your units are either in supply, or they're not. This decides whether they can fight at full strength. You don't need to supply your troops with ammunition, like in Panzer Corps or - heaven forbid! - like in Battle Isle, where you had to control supply units to bring ammo and fuel to the front. The only exception are torpedo bombers and submarines that work in a very strange way: Their torpedos simply "respawn" after a few turns. I adore the feature that let's you cut off enemy units from supply, but the rest of the supply system is oversimplified.
Bugs:
I had no crashes, but several very serious bugs that forced me to reload a scenario up to eight times. I've read that other players encountered even more bugs and had several crashes.
Bad modability:
It was promoted that the game would be open to modders, but as far as I've read this isn't true. Several critical game files are only editable with unusual special software and there isn't any interface to activate mods in the game except for mods that are distributed directly by the developers.
All in all OoB:P was a huge letdown. Some problems may be fixable but the humiliating spoon-feeding regarding "what should the player do and how can we force him to do exactly that"-attitude of the developers seems to be something that can't be fixed with a patch.

UPDATE:
Just tried the new patch. Huge improvement. Now the AI turns typically take 2-3 mins. Nice job! Now I definitely recommend this game.
============================================
ORIGINAL REVIEW:
I have never written any reviews before, because I feel most things I want to say have already been said in existing reviews. But this time I think I really need to write something about this game: I simply can't stand watching a game with such outraging performance getting so many positive reviews.
To be honest, this game can be fun sometimes. The wide variety of units, the supply management system, the unique specilization feature, and some more subtle designs provide the game great promise to be one the best in its genre (I particularly like the design that when a ship maneuvers closer to or farther away from its target, damage output from its artillery will drastically reduce, because in real life in order to fire a full broadside a ship has to move parellel to its target).
All the good sides, however, are irreparably ruined by its abysmal performance (ironically, all the pros of the game make the cons all the more aggravating). Specifically, the AI turns usually take way too long during large scale engagements, which, making matters worse, actually constitutes most part of the campaign. While it typically takes me 3-5 mins to finish my turn, it can take the AI 10-30 mins, making the game virtually unplayable. I'm simply tired of the gaming experience-play for one turn, wait for a long time, play for another turn, decide to get something to eat, play for one more turn, read some news, play for another turn, take a nap, and wake up furious because the AI still hasn't finished its ridiculous turn.
I don't think its my computer's problem, since when I play Civilization V or the Total War series things are always velvety smooth, and since I have seen many people in the forum complaining even the most high-end computers cannot stop the AI turn from taking forever.
I understand that the developers were on a tight budget (that's why I'm not very critical of the game's lack of voice acting or its hideous music), but I think the AI problem is due not so much to insufficient budget as to downright irresponsiblity. The developers are obviously not as concerned with making the game more playable as with making more money: instead of fixing the problem, they devoted their limited resource into making one DLC after another and shamelessly ask you to pay more cash.
Therefore, the verdict is simple: DON'T BUY. The developers do not deserve your money.

TL:DR
Want to mess around on Wurm with higher rates, but with absolutely no value or safety in your player, world or data? Or use it to learn modding and Java? Get Wurm Unlimited.
Want to play around on Wurm and compete with other players at a lower exp rate with all Wurm has to offer, knowing that years later your footprint is still on the world? Get Wurm Online which can be played entirely free as you can purchase premium in-game with coin you can earn from other players or game mechanics.
------------------------
Wurm Unlimited is just a dodgy version of Wurm Online, we get less features, less recipes and apparently less attention to detail.
I run a (100% no profit) server for 2 years, I've put almost 4000 hours into the game (though, probably half of that is due to the application not actually closing properly when the 'Exit' button in-game is pushed - Definitely an impact on the Steam played charts), only to have chaos descend on update day repeatedly.
The latest funsies; all the traders suddenly start dying, the merchants are laying dead on the floor, there are corpses of new players all over the 'safe zone', we are noticing things decaying much faster than normal in certain areas etc.
Sure I have a backup, but I can't use it till this behaviour stops and the last time I had a niggle with the software, I had to delve into the server.jar and fix it myself by changing one very small line of code (it was fixed 6 months after I posted my findings on the forum) - FYI I'm not a programmer, I had to spend weeks learning the basics on how to debug this mess, I don't fancy doing it again, especially for a game that is not 'beta', 'alpha', 'dev' or 'early access' - This is technically a well established game that has been running for many years and at a guess, a badly made clone of WO (to protect the online version?), stripped of a few features, a little code update here and there, prepped for Steam and thrown to the general public.
I honestly can't imagine WO's server side looks like this, if it does... Cheesus, don't tell me it does or not, I honestly don't want to know.
-I have to login every day to see if any profiles are 'stuck' and these players aren't always people who ALT+F4 on character creation, sometimes its a friend who has disconnected, sometimes it because the player crashed and can't log back in to finish creeation (happening ALOT lately). The server leaves their player in the world (invisible) and sometimes they 'might' eventually leave the world, but more than often... -*logs into the GM character and sighs*-.
- The server needs rebooting when someone tries to drive a cart off the edge of an unfinished bridge (resulting in said bridge being removed).
- Some players can't dig randomly, because if they dig a corner or dig whilst touching a tile border, they crash.
- Dismounting from vehicles results in random kick sometimes or more commonly, client camera locks in place and refuses to budge and more zoning errors in the logs.
- LOD Far+ is still ugly as ~
- How is -Dglass.accessible.force=false to prevent crashing when using dropdown boxes, not a default configuration still? The games tutorial should include this, as I have to instruct EVERY newbie wurmian I meet how to fix this.
Thats just the main niggles that are still an issue after 2 years.
I'm done, I'm sick of apologising to my small playerbase for these stupid mistakes that are wholly out of my control, I was proud of the players accomplishments, the server in general etc.. Now I'm just annoyed I've wasted soo much time on what I should have seen as an inevitable data-loss.
It's very likely my server will shut down permanently this month and I'll be on WO (Indy), bring on the old memories!
I used to love Wurm, I had nothing but good things to say about it, it's a bit of a love-hate relationship... I'm certainly not fond of the direction thats being taken, it's suspicious-as-f and I can't stand suspicious-as-f things, as it usually turns out to be true.

The longer you play this game the more obvious that the lack of depth, and the poor AI and events are exposed.
I played 400 hours.. is that a lot? Yeah. Is it a huge amount for a 4x game? Not really. Plus, a lot of that time was wasted doing stuff that was boring or resulted in getting killed because it didn't work. And now this review gets the benefit of those hours.
* Combat is doomstack vs doomstack.
* Tech is irrelevant. In fact, the higher tiers get less efficient and the fleet cap penalty isn't high enough.
* This means you cannot win unless you have a bigger economy.
* The only way to get a bigger economy is to colonise as many planets as possible to get pops to work the handful of relevant resource buildings.
Playing diplomatically is boring.
Most games the galaxy splits into 2 or 3 giant federations of alliances.
The mid-game is stagnant and boring, and human players will snowball beyond the ability of anything but the end-game fallen empires (not the empires that develop alongside you) to stop.
The vaunted end-game crises are little more than giant doomstacks that get boring to fight over and over again.
Sectors have been broken since day one, yet the game expects you to hand over planets to this inadequate sector AI that WILL ruin the planets if you let them.
If Paradox ever read this, STOP releasing games & patches without adequate testing. This game and HOI4 have been ruined by a lack of QA testing. You are not an indie developer, you are a full publishing studio with multiple development teams. It is inexcusable to have QA this poor.

I recommend not spending money on Wildstar, but I do recommend playing it for free. Ultimately, the game suffers from poor game design, and I think this makes it a great game for people who love gaming (especially MMOs) to study.
1. First, the game's audio design is just awful. They went to a lot of trouble making quests nice and short - which would make this game inexpensive to completely voice and players could get voice-work whenever they select a quest from their log (so long as they had not already heard it that play-session - like in Borderlands), but someone put this at such a low priority or it came last in the development cycle such that it was not completed prior to launch and they've never gone back to fix it. This is huge as I found that I didn't know why I was doing things most of the time and while the game world's audio effects are good and the sound track is often excellent, the narrative is completely let down by the insane low production value of having mute NPCs. Sure, that works in WoW because the game launched 13 years ago and it is too large a game for them to reasonably voice now, but someone spending money on making a AAA MMO being cheap about something that would have made the game's narrative come to life is insane. I wonder what happened because this omission is huge.
2. Lack of scalability in design - when the game launched, many quests (particularly for professions) were unplayable because there were so many people that you could not find the materials needed to complete them. Now, there aren't enough people for the various game queues to populate and they do not have design to deal with that like having queues for wider level ranges, bonuses for random queuing, etc. (basically look at how FF XIV handles queues for the gold-star rating of this).
3. The game designers went for a hybrid of different styles and sometimes this works and sometimes it doesn't. The Eldan stuff is meant to be high-tech, but it is still sort of cutesy-cartoon-ish and the music and sound effects aren't as different as they should be. . .  but the real important bit about this is that they don't establish mood well. I am in the magical forest tree home of an Aurin Matria and it doesn't feel solemn or wonderous. I am in an ancient civilization's advanced technological outpost and it doesn't awe-inspire or frighten.
4. It isn't just world design either. Some of the characters should not have been chosen because NPCs, by their nature, are passibe while the hero does things. For example, Deadeye gets upset that his pregnant wife dies and, despite being a badass cowboy, he stands around to give quests to players to go avenge her death for him. He also presumes her dead instantly after the crash even though there isn't an explosion and the lift only falls about 50 feet out of the air. . .  which could be deadly but is more likely to simply be bruising and/or break bones, but that is just one bad cut-scene failing to really blow up his preggers wife. Writing isn't easy, but I have to think that there must have been at least one good one and that he or she should have been able to say that Deadeye should be a no go.
5. Finally, I am not yet at the endgame but I can tell from the people who spam the world-chat for groups that the dungeon finder must not be working or it is so difficult at the highest tiers that you must create pre-made groups of a certain item-level to be successful. This is further proof that they have not scaled their game down for the smaller audiences who are far less likely to be able to put groups together for content and/or that they have not given people the proper tools to make that happen with less fuss.
Having said all that, this was the AAA MMO that was aimed at becoming another WoW, so there is a good amount of production value here - especially in the art where it is super time-consuming and expensive. There is also a reasonably good combat system and player-housing for people who are interested in that.
By all means, play this and form your own opinions but to me this game highlights the importance of sound design, narrative, and having an inclusive endgame/scalability.

Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel was a highly anticipated game, especially after the massive success of its gargantuan predecessor. Without DLC's, you play one of four in the band of misfits—most of whom show up as antagonists in Borderlands 2. Each person has their own motive for working as a group; some want to be heroes while others just live for the thrill of it. There's better mobility, new weapon types, money is actually useful to get loot, women who love women, Claptrap, and your excessive collection of guns can actually be used in a vending machine called "The Grinder" to rely on RNG to make a better gun. There are some intuitive changes and upgrades to the game. Skill trees have changed, giving you new abilities such as double jump and the skill to be like Kirby and do a butt slam in order to make a quick descent. Everything I loved about Borderlands 2 mechanics were built into the game—from higher tier modes with great loot drops to fun easter eggs.
However, there was a lot wrong too. The writing suffered with the different team, opting for censoring profanity that broke immersion from the coarse world of Borderlands. Some jokes were more cringe-y than funny. The progression is significantly slower because it was padded with boring fetch quests. The new terrain was beautiful but seriously lacking in save points; someone else said it's like the game wanted us to die and restart from the beginning. They hit the nail on the head. Raid bosses were one of the highlights of Borderlands 2—and there was only 1 in TPS that was on a predictable respawn timer. As with any Borderlands game, I also strongly recommend playing this with friends. Otherwise, it will get boring really fast.
So did it live up to the hype? Yes and no. It answered a lot of questions but it also left a lot of questions unanswered. If anything, the game is more worthy as an expansion to Borderlands 2 than a standalone game. I'm recommending it if you love Borderlands 2 lore and have a really strong desire for more Borderlands content. I also recommend playing this first if you want to appreciate
more; many characters show up from this game and Borderlands 2.
7/10

So many reviews and so many positive. I honestly doubt this will even be read. I would rather have a 1-5 rating system than a black and white yes/no. As of this writing the approval rate is 80% and in my opinion, the game doesn't deserve that. So I'm going to say no. Here's why.
Except for the playable characters the voice acting was notably inferior to BL1 and BL2. It lacked motivation, inspiration, emotion and believability. I felt as if the voice actor asked the producer "what is my motivation?", and there was either no producer or the producer didn't know or didn't care. I'm sure the actors are skilled but a clueless actor results in mediocre acting.
Making a dialog comment about not being able to understand the Aussie accent and dumbing it down ya'll, was clearly targeting the American market and annoying. It wasn't funny. I understand the dialog just fine. It is however, difficult to follow
dialog of speed-talkers, which occurred once.
I did appreciate the how the BL1 vault hunters inserted dialog into the story as it developed. That being said...
2K Australia's design for this game focused on high spawn rates and repetitive mobs over story development. The story became progressively confusing and disjointed, senseless. It is incredibly disappointing and lacking. If you want to witness what happened to Jack that made him the psychopath that he was in BL2 then you will be disappointed as well. Evidently all you have to do is lie to him, end of story.
Jack is surprisingly capable of taking care of himself. He never acted like a code-monkey. He was rarely timid. There was no story development as to what he was doing on the station or why Hyperion was even building it. The few details regarding this in BL2 were not elaborated upon in the Pre-Sequel.
So Moxxi sabotaged Jack's precious laser. Roland and Lilith did nothing but assist Jack. Except in the final scene where Lilith...
So if Jack is mad at anyone it should be Moxxi... at least according to the 2K Australia story.
The game is fun but not worth paying the full price. I enjoyed the insight into the new vault hunters, as these are characters that the BL2 vault hunters will encounter. I didn't care for Nisha and Wilhelm (didn't play Claptrap). And while I could relate to Athena, I do not feel any desire to replay the Pre-Sequel for any character, even in True Vault Hunter mode.
Don't buy this game for the story. Don't expect any fan recommended engine improvements to be addressed.

Before I get into the game: Ignore my hours played. I got a physical copy of the game many years ago and played around 300 or 400 hours on the physical version before I figured out I could redeem the game's CD Key on Steam.
This is simply one of the greatest strategy games ever made. What really makes the Total War series as a whole special is the combination of turn based strategy in the vein of games like Civ with amazingly detailed and cinematic real time battles. Medieval II in my opinion just does it better than any other game in the series. The battles feature thousands of individually rendered soldiers at your command, combat animations that still look decent today, and an incredible soundtrack. It really is amazing how well this game has aged over the years. The depth of the campaigns allow you to manage your empire any way you want. You can conduct espionage, attempt to influcence the Papacy as a Christian faction, and manage your own royal family among many other things. What other game lets you assassinate the Pope? The game will also remind you of the day when DLC actually meant something thanks to the Kingdoms expansion pack. It alone gives you 4 new campaigns and over 20 new factions to play as, all for five bucks on Steam. I am not joking when I tell you you could play this game for thousands of hours with Kingdoms before running out of challenges and I haven't even mentioned the incredible modding community this game has. The Gold edition for 25 bucks is an absolute steal and this game is a must for any strategy fan.
Improves on Rome in every way except with battle Announcers and soundtrack. A wonderful gem of a game that I am glad I picked up.

Evopollution has a simple pixelated art-style, somewhat similar to that of the 16-bit era of consoles (the way the game looks actually reminds me the typical SNES action/adventure game, minus all the characters & creatures). It's a simple, but not a bad look. Some things are animated, and the animations are simple, but do the job well enough.
The background music in this game gets annoying fast. It should have been more low-key and soothing, that would have fit this game a lot better.
The idea behind Evopollution is that you're supposed to generate profit without destroying the world around you. This is done through building some different buildings. Some generate more profit, but more pollution, some less profit and less pollution, and some does not generate pollution at all. Trees take money, but remove pollution. If pollution gets to high, then disasters starts happening.
If you just build low-pollution buildings (solar powerplants & windfarms), put some trees between them, and then build some power storage (pollution-free profit based on the number of solar plants and windfarms you have), you can't lose. It might not be the absolutely most effective way of winning, but you can't lose. If you would really want to make things as effective as possible, I guess there's some room for staying with the game, but there is an optimal mix, and it's not going to be very hard to at least get near it.
Evopollution is a terrible game. It's simplistic, repetitive, and it's very easy to put yourself in a state where you can't lose, and all you need to do is wait for the game to say that you've won.
I get the message the game tries to convey, we need to find a sustainable way of living, producing things, and generating power. The issue here is that the way the game portrays this is just flat out wrong. To the developer: Please look up what a lifecycle analysis is. Because if you intend to make another game about sustainability, then having a basic understanding of that is needed (and time to get political, because the internet loves that ;) Politicians, please also look up these concepts, because otherwise you end up making misguided efforts that cause more harm than good).

Evopollution is a great idea, a great concept, and even because of the mostly bad reviews, I bought this game. But even if the idea is good - it was badly executed. There is no fun goals to aim for, no replay value, and after 30 minutes you are already sick of the game. But the graphics are well made - and with more objectives, more gameplay value, and other additions made, this came could become actually better. Consider making changes to boost the game's fun, and I will consider turning this into a positive review.

I finally got this game on sale after being intrigued by it several years ago, and looked forward to an interesting plot, unusual characters (I like the idea of playing through an atypical perspective), and what seemed engaging gameplay, using the strengths and compensating for the weaknesses of your two protagonists.
Unfortunately, it was bad.
The game is obviously dated, and hasn't aged well. The graphics aren't terrible, but they're nothing to write home about. The environments (at least in the first hour I forced myself to slog through) are completely static, and the game runs on rails without even the illusion of choice.
Combat is slow and frustrating, with inexplicably lengthy animations and minimal control. You can slow combat to select actions (up to 4 in a row), and watch as your character stands there, taking hits from multiple enemies, to agonizingly raise a sword... and miss... then fall to the next barrage of attacks.
The worst, though, is the writing/dialog. In other reviews, I'd read others commenting on the ridiculous amount of vulgarity, and I thought to myself that it's probably just someone too sensitive to realistic conversations between hardened characters in awful situations. I was wrong. It's written more like a 13 year old trying to sound tough. It's out of place and awkward, and it's sprinkled throughout often corny and disjointed dialog. After coming back from games like Witcher 3 and Sunless Sea (brilliantly written), I tried not to hold this game to those standards, but it's awful.

Writing this review a long time after actually playing the game, but here goes. The game had♥♥♥♥♥♥poor marketing, so I feel it my duty to give it a voice, however small.
It's a flawed little gem of grim-bright fantasy that explores some interesting concepts that you'll find most RPG's don't play with like:
A soundtrack that isn't identical to LoTR (and is trully one of a kind)
A dialog system that allows you to control both party members and who talks in an encounter
-(God I wish there was another RPG that let this happen)
A story told from the perspective of "the bad guys", the Orcs!
-the characters are good, some are more unique than others
-The setting looks high fantasy but it has some pretty grim dialogue/story (slavery, genocide, racism)
--Magic in this setting is more subtle (akin to Gandalf in LoTR, rather than your avg WoW fireball slinging-mage) which has its own charm
A combat system that has unique features and doesn't feel canned
-the mechanics behind your main brawler is HILARIOUS, he can go ape♥♥♥♥♥♥crazy and start to pick ♥♥♥♥ers up and breaking their spine. Including your goblin buddy! (This mechanic actually makes the combat refreshing, the loss of control isn't bad if you just know how to use it to your advantage.)
-You'll feel massive changes when fighting heavily armored knights vs your average guard
So what are the flaws?
The game has a short run-time, for an RPG. You can blast through it fairly quick and feel satisfied.
The combat system has quite a bit of jargon, sometimes you'll resort to just queueing up attacks and hope for the best
-Eventually you master it and it becomes pretty easy
The gear choices are sparse, and often won't feel like they make significant changes to your character
The stealth is ham handed and is much less satisfying than the combat. The branch-off to this game (Styx: Master of Shadows) does the stealth much better.
Its likely going to be priced very low so you should give it a chance. Trust me, there's things to love in the game.

Ok, to be honest, this game can be a lot of fun and will take you ages to accomplish anything so if you want something to pass time, this is a perfect choice.  If you hate frustration and irritation, then you better just walk away now because I have never encountered a game that lives to make playing it as difficult as possible.
- extensive crafting system allows you to create everything in the game and there are thousands of things to make.  Every type os skill is used so to make a tool you will likely use blacksmithing and both carpentry and fine carpentry.  If any of those skills are low, then you will make junk.  So to be really good at making things, you need to become very good at a lot of skills.  Oh, yeah, no npc vendors so you must make anything and everything you need.
- extensive breeding system to make your pets better
- Huge world to explore that mainly consists of unpassable mountains next to uncrossable water leaving you to wander a tiny strip between the two and spend hours getting nowhere near where you want to go.
- tamed animals get sick....and only a priest can cure the illness...and you need to get to the shrine to make a priest...which means trying to follow the coastlines.
- snail slow skill increases but you can change the default rates.
- snail slow combat increases mean you will spend more time running from monsters than actually fighting.
- some crafting skills are stupid difficult such as weapon and armorsmithing.  It can literally take an hour of failing, repairing and repeating to get a 1.0 increase on the quality of a weapon or armor since you get .02-.04 per success on those skills and the success rate looks to be about 1 in 15.
-the interface is dated but once you get the hang of it, it's workable.
- the graphics are also dated but saying that, it doesn't take long to load and with one pc being used as the host server and also as a player computer, it doesn't seem to have lag issues when other players connect and travelling is seemless over hours of exploration *along coastlines so straight line distance probably was only couple hundred tiles.

Overall though, it's fun if you like to create things and don't mind working for the rewards.  I can say that I probably spend around 99% of my time within the limits of our settlement and never lack for something that needs doing.  If you hate crafting, then you won't like this unless you find a server where you can get everything you need supplied to you because this game is really more "crafting unlimited" than anything else.
Now for the major negatives -although the mmo version has been out for years now, this game still feels lacking in development.  The latest update shows how far behind this game really is.  They just now get around to adding a comprehensive cooking system.  To date mines are 2d in a 3d world, so you can't layer them.  The tunnels must align or they won't let you connect them.  You can't dig out of a cave so no digging a tunnel through that ridiculously long cliff that cuts your island in half.  Animals can't be carried on boats, even though the primary map is an archipeligo with small shore areas bordered by unpassable water or unpassable cliffs. How is it reasonable that you create an island infested map, then make it impossible to transport animals to your island?

I recently started playing wildstar roughly 2 to 3 days ago so I'm not very far into the game. This game does not disappoint, I've been looking and trying other MMORPGS for a long time, trying to find something that could match OR at least be on par with World of Warcraft. Some good ones I consider worth playing are ArcheAge and SWOTOR, both games unique in there own ways with in-depth story and loads of voice acted scenes to get you in the mood. Like those two games WILDSTAR is probably by far the closest MMORPG To WoW I've come across yet still separating itself as it's own game. One mechanic I absolutely love is the combat system. You don't just tab target an enemy and spam ur keys, your required to pay attention to the enemy and move around, which makes you feel completely engaged into the fight. Other games such as Neverwinter does this as well but for some reason with the clear indicators marking the enemies attack and the dodging mechanic adds a fun I haven't experienced in such a long time. Healing is similar to fighting, rather then just selecting an allie  and clicking a button You have to focus ur ability towards the person ur healing! That's a really cool way to heal cause as a tank i have to stay in the indicators be it a frontal heal or an AOE heal. Which means I have alot to pay attention to, and something I find that makes an MMO not work well is feeling  un engaged while grinding. I've played a good chunk of the starting area and so far I have yet to be bored with my quests even if they are silly ones. Wildstar always finds ways to change things and make quests interesting as you play through. The art style Wildstar chose isn't far off of WoW and I actually prefure it. The world is huge and so full of life with beautiful lands scapes and colors to enjoy. Gear even at low levels looks really cool which pushes me further into wanting that end game look. Taking pride in a character is something I havent experienced in a long time playing these kinds of games. The world isn't just nice to look at, the story and characters in it are interesting and full of life as well. I found my self laughing alot at some of the NPCs comments as well. Characters are voice acted with perfection, and the cut scenes are so well executed, it really keeps the momentum moving forward. Every time you level you get a kick♥♥♥♥♥metal theme with a funny comment thrown in. You be like he'll ya, and find urself super pumped to see what things you've unlocked. Another big benefit is changing ur class and abilities on the fly. I lost a tank in a dungeon I did so I switched to tank to fill the roll. Speaking of dungeons my biggest pet peeve in an MMORPG is when it caters to making the game easier for the player. I HATE THAT, I really enjoy that Wildstar doesn't cater to that kind of game play. My group managed to play through each boss np up to the last mind you with one team mate short. We died 4 times on the last guy because we had to pay attention to the boss mechanics, dodge when we had to dodge, kite when we had to kite and most important interrupt the big guy at the right moments otherwise he'll smash the ground causing an AOE effect that will wipe the group. There are loads of amazing things this game does right and I find the Pros far out weigh the Cons. The music is amazing the combat is fantastic and the game itself left me exhilarated and wanting to play more. I can say that this game is highly under rated and feel it can compete with the big boys. This is my first review and I felt like this game deserved it. Top marks in my books only thing I could say that needs improvement is sometimes the quest boxes stay on the screen alittle to long. Also forgot to mention the looting in the game is great. Games a solid 9/10

Passpartout: The Starving Artist,
During my time playing this game I did enjoy myself quite a bit, If you are looking for a relaxing game to chill out and play by yourself this is a great game to do so with. There are countless paintings and ideas that you can make in the game to see how much they would sell for. I really felt as if the game catered to my needs in being a relaxing game as well.
Pros:
The game is very well made, during my time playing I did not experience any frame rate drops or technical issues with teh game.
The art style is great, its almost as if your shop or place where you are painting is the centre stage, everywhere else is irrelevant and you can focus on the wonders that you can paint.
The game aids relationships with the NPC's, believe it or not, it does. The game adds this wonderful sense of relationships to the game by making you cater to the needs of the NPC's that like your things that you know you can count on to buy a piece. I found my self commenting and getting excited when NPC's such as George or Don came to visit the shop and annoyed when NPC's such as the Hipsters or the Ladies came to visit.
You don't have to be good at drawing, allthough it does help. I found myself actually improving on painting as I painted on, the countless ideas that I had in my head made me go though periods of churning out paintings that weren't good quality, I quickly realised this was not a good way to go about this and tried my hardest to produce painings that were being bought by the likes of George and Don. The main point is that you don't actually have to be good, the game still recognises when you have out effort into something and rewards you for that.
Cons:
It does get a bit repetitive, at times I felt myself running out of ideas in my head which is when your paintings don't sell. Its definutely a game you can't play for hours on end but rather play once a day or week for about an hour, I think that coming into the game with a headfull of ideas is a good way to go about it.
From what I see, there isn't much in the way of progress during the game, Yes you do get different venues or 'levels' and you do get some new tools, but there isn't much in the way of really progressing, the new level is just a reprint of the last with the oppurtunity to get more money for the same type of paintings. If it weren't for the fact that different areas bring different NPC's and new artwork ideas, I think I would have got really bored really quick.
It doesn't quite get there. The idea of this game is really really good, but it can be so much more, if they had more mechanics and features such as talking to the NPC's or engaging in this such as auctions or even asking the NPC's what kind of paintings they liked to get a better idea of what to paint would be great. Things like a store would be perfect, I don't know if I have reached far enough to spend the money I have accumulated and I shall definutely play more but I feel if there was a shop where you could buy items and customise the areas you were in, this would aid the game a lot by adding this depth to it.
Final Verdict:
For the price it's at now, I would say buy it. it's a new experience not really seen in other games that is generally fun. For £6 (Price at Purchase) I have enjoyed this game and look forward to coming at it in the coming days with new fresh ideas. If however you are looking for a game to sink hours into, i wouldn't say this is the one, it's not that type of game and I can see some people getting really bored really quick.
Feel free to add me and message me on steam for anymore questions about the game.
Updates:

If the Devs can manage to continue and update the game with added levels I would be appreciated and needed to be worth the full price. At the moment it seems a bit lackluster and is more of a demo than a full game.

Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel is the "third" installment in the Borderlands series, and personally has to be my favorite. As someone that has completed Borderlands 1 about 14 times on the PS3, completed Borderlands 2 on the PS3 PS4 and PC for a total of about 20 times, and completed Pre-Sequel on the PS4 first, I've become exahusted with the series. It's why I didn't bother trying to 100% the achievements for this game. But why do I say this is my favorite one of the series? I'll explain.
Pre-Sequel takes place after the first game and before the second game, and Athena is re-telling the events of the Pre-Sequel. (So it kind of is after the second game...) It shows the events up to how Handsome Jack and how everything came to happening for Borderlands 2, and frankly I think the story is just as good, if not a little better than BL2s story. I will say though that it does take awhile for it to pick up. I find the first hour to be pretty boring and very hard to get interested in the game, but once it starts to pick it I found it easy to play through it and have a blast. What is even better is having what ever character(s) you are currently playing chime in with unique dialog during certain parts of the story. That little feature alone made this story more interesting and enjoyable compared to BL1 and BL2. Even playing on True Vault Hunter the "Re-telling" dialog is slightly different, with different characters chiming in about the events. It gives another reason to play through the story again.
Characters
The Vault Hunters this time around are previous bosses from BL2 and characters from 1&2.
You have Athena the Gladiator which first appeared in BL1 DLC. She wields a shield that absorbs damage, then thrown to hit/kill her enemies.
Then you have Wilhelm the Enforcer, who was a first major boss in BL2, summons drones to help fight/defend him. Cool fact about Wilhelm, any major upgrades you take on his skills, will actually change how he looks/sounds, which is a cool little feature!
Next you have Nisha the Lawbringer, who was a minor boss in BL2, who plays as a cowgirl/weastern shooter and duel wields pistols... and stuff...
Last but not least, and by far the best character to play as, you play as Claptrap, but is now trained in combat, so hes now called Fragtrap. Claptraps ability is "VaultHunter.exe" and is the most entertaining out of the other powers, because it's semi-random on what you can get, based on your surroundings and what is going on. You can get a super useful boost like increase damage/speed/rate of fire, or cause a lazer disco inferno, or you can cause the whole party to start bouncing around. And to top it all off, Claptrap also has some of the best dialog in the entire game. Nuff said!
*DLC Characters
The Handsome Jack Doppelganger is by far the second best character to play as. Also has some of the best dialog in the game. The skills are also tons of fun. You can get frickin lazers on your arms!
Lady Hammerlock the Baroness... I absolutly hate. I hate her more than Nisha, so I'm not gonna talk about her.
Combat/Weapons
The new addition for combat in Pre-Sequal is the introduction of Low Gravity and Butt Slams. This makes the combat so much better compared to BL2. This adds in some verticallity and more range of movement to the combat, making it more enjoyable and feel more fast paced and action packed. Now being a Borderlands game, it has the trope of "It has a bazzilion weapons!" and frankly, I hate it. Why? Because 98% of the weapons is just useless trash! Just like BL1 and 2, yes it has lots of weapons, but in terms of any "unique" or fun weapons, are very limited. This was always a feature that I hate, cause I'd rather have more interesting and fun weapons, instead of being dumped a bazzilion useless trash guns/items. Still there is some great weapons that have special effects or abilities to them that can make things more interesting. With the new addition of lazers there is even more fun weapons to use.
I will say though, the Moon Buggie has the WORST driving mechanics I've ever seen. The slightest bump on the road can send you flipping off a cliff to your death. The second I was able to get a hover bike, I never used that pos buggie ever again.
PROS:
- You play as Claptrap. BEST DAY EVER!
- Story is slow to start, but gets great.
- Low gravity is really fun.
- BUTT SLAMS!
- New lazer weapons are fun.
- Season Pass does NOT give you "Shock Drop Slaughter Pit" (It's not worth it, it's garbage.)
- Claptastic Voyage is a GREAT DLC!
- Jack Clone is too sexy.
- Achievements.
- Steam Trading Cards.
CONS:
- Athena, Nisha, Wilhelm, Lady Hammerlock all have boring dialog.
- Jack Clone is too sexy.
- Not lots of DLC.
- Holodome Onslaught DLC is boring and super short. Only thing worth out of it is the Upgrade pack.
If you're a fan of the Borderlands series and wanted something thats the same, but a little bit different, it's a great pick up and is really fun. The Claptrap DLC adds on for even more fun and makes things even more interesting. I highly recommened it!

Medieval 2 Total War is another game in the total war series. I consider this game and rome 1 to be in "Gen 2" of the series. This game allows you to take control of many nations during the middle ages.
Your objective is simple: Build up an economy, use that economy to build powerful armies, and conquer (Or slaughter) your neighbors.
Of course, every game in the series has a unique trait that makes this objective harder to reach. In Rome, it was rome being split into 4 different factions. In Empire, historical alliances, muskets and artillery, and a tech tree. And in Medieval 2: The Pope, political and religous strife, The Pope, very poor cities for most factions, and did I mention The Pope? Like in Rome, if you are a certain faction or group of factions you will be given missions to complete within a turn limit. But in Rome, you can only get rome to be angry at you, in Med 2, half the world joins a crusade against you. These missions range from something as simple as building a church in a certain town, conquering a nearby town, sending a diplomat to another nation, or joining a crusade.
Onto the basic gameplay.
You manage your cities on the main map. You build new structures and upgrades to previous structures to be able to train new or better units, improve your economy, or please the people. This is all to become strong enough to build up an army to attack someone with.
Once you begin the attack, you are taken to a 3D battle map where you control your army. If you're new, you probably are tempted to mass your troops and charge in, and this can work on some scenarios. However, most of the time, you must use a wide variety of unit types to win. You fight off the weaknesses of the enemy force. Sometimes you and the enemy are evenly matched and a large battle where both armies are forced to slug it out without any tactical advantages. Other times you put spearmen against the enemy cavalry, cavalry against archers, and seige equipment against walls and large groups of infantry.
However, there are some problems. The economy can be unpredictable. The pope doesn't like it when you attack another catholic nation, so you have to spend extra time and money on getting the pope to really like you. Archers default to skirmish mode, so they move around too much when they should be standing still and constantly firing.
Overall, this is a great grand strategy game that any fan of the genre should like.
You owe it to yourself to play this, rome, and empire (Just add darthmod to empire).

Evopollution tasks you with gaining one million dollars by setting up polluting and/ or clean energy sources: you'll have to keep your pollution levels under control or disasters such as lightning, comets and a big worm will destroy your assets.
Too bad the actual game is sadly marred by technical problems, weird design decisions and a truly dull gameplay, thus failing to live up to its interesting Store description.
-had an intriguing premise
-seeing pollution interact with the environment (with bushes and trees getting bare, then growing again if you purify the zone)  was interesting
-soundtrack gets grating fast
-save game doesn't work, I tried several times on all levels but I'd never save my progress, forcing me to restart each time
-unbalanced gameplay, a polluting asset will damage its surrounding area in seconds, summoning all disasters in a quite wide area: you'll have to spend 3x the asset's cost in trees to balance it out and hope a random disaster doesn't destroy what you've built right away. The various energy sources also have skewed price/ profit values, with some being quite useless
-even when it works, the gameplay is simply dull and boils down to building a few assets then wait for a LONG time until you get enough cash to build more. There's no way to speed up time so your best bet is running it windowed and do something else
-weird controls, you can close certain menus with a click while others only react to you pressing Esc, the map only scrolls with the mouse etc..
-incomprehensible design choices, beginner mode is actually harder than normal mode due to the fact that you have to unlock assets yourself, certain buildings do nothing at all and only cost money and waste space on the small map
Evopollution's biggest sin is the fact it turns into a waiting game in a matter of minutes as you start up a game, spend your starting money and are then supposed to wait 10 to 30 minutes to get enough funds to build something else while starting blankly at the screen. This simply isn't fun and makes the game feel like one of those mobile apps you run in the background and check a few times a day.
Add to this its skewed pollution model, where most assets require you to waste several times their purchase price and land space to counteract their environmental damage, unrealistic objectives (one million $ will take ages), extremely low production values and a broken save feature: you'll quickly realize why Evopollution feels like a badly programmed flash game at best, one that'd not be worth playing even if it was free.
The only reason you'd start up the game is to get its cards if, like me, you got it on a bundle: everyone else can safely skip this one.

is a two person party dungeon crawler for most intents and purposes. You control both the Orc-- Arkail and the goblin-- Styx. So from the onset you have very established characters both in terms of personality and style of play. The holy trinity of RPG tropes of Tank, DPS and Healer now are taken by only two which can be problematic.
Styx is the tiny DPS stealth based rogue character and Arkail is the brooding angry Orc with a heart even the most honorable warrior doesn't posses. I have heard many complaints that the combat is why they put the game down as it was not direct enough for them. I suppose if you draw from the archetype of what an Orc is you might expect a sort of “Push button to smash face” setup. But I bet you wont see those same people complain about identical combat in a game like Knights of the Old Republic. It's queued actions with active pause and it works just fine, not to mention if you use Styx stealth stance you are granted the ability to sneak into enemy territory and assassinate enemies that don't know you are there.. except dogs.
The gameplay loop is basically start in a HUB wherein you can shop for new gear or upgrade existing gear. Talk to some people and then start a mission. The maps are very linear and almost behave like an a solo instance in an MMO. You basically must traverse a hallway towards the X. There is almost no loot to be had in the environment making exploration trivial and almost discouraged. The few things that are found in the environment are emblazoned with a glowing effect that stick out like an oasis in a desert. Additionally, upon picking up the gear it auto-magically goes into the appropriate persons inventory.
The game almost feels a bit dumbed down. As there is no real currency. You can't sell old gear for money to buy potions for instance; there isn't a need to. Both Arkail and Styx regen health very quickly out of battle. However you get “trade points” to be used in order to buy potentially better gear or to upgrade your current gear. There isn't even a system to have extra money to say persuade a guard or something which seems like something Styx would be quite akin to.
I really enjoyed the gameplay loop. I enjoyed and like the characters; they are well voice acted and have roles and personalities. But the game is totally unbalanced. There where fights that really seemed like boss fights that I breezed through without even establishing a strategy while other fights, fights of attrition if you will that seemed borderline impossible and I couldn't overcome without micro managing  every single hit and action.

This might be my longest review yet so here's a TL;DR: Alright game that probably could've been amazing if it had more development.
Of Orcs And Men is an Action-RPG type game where you get 3 sets of different moves you can use for 2 characters and you can input 4 at a time and they will initiate automatically when you choose who you want to attack. While the gameplay is somewhat unique I can't help but feel most of it is flawed in some way.
Gameplay: One of the biggest problems I had with the game was that you get about 30 different skills that you can choose to unlock as you please, and also assign skill points when you level up, but a good portion of the skills seem to be near useless or have barely noticable results. Throughout most of the game you rely on the goblin, Styx, for the majority of the fights whether you're using the extremely OP stealth mode to take out as many enemies before you have to initiate a fight or having to almost ALWAYS use the "Armor-piercing" skill since a majority of the enemies get tons of armor that you need to break down. Area of Effect skills also seem to have a bigger priority over every other type of skill. Arkail, the orc, compared to Styx is almost completely useless in most cases if not only to be a hit-sponge distraction to ensure Styx never gets attacked. He can also build up enough rage to go into Berserker mode yet that is entirely useless and often does more harm than good. You also can't see the amount of Dodge/Deflection an enemy has until you're attacking them and you notice they constantly Dodge/Deflect your attacks. In the end the gameplay wasn't horrible but it definitely left a bit of a sour aftertaste with me.
Story(probably spoilers): The story was honestly pretty good. You play from the perspective of an exiled orc who's people are being hunted down and enslaved for the glory of the human empire and you are tasked with killing the Emperor. You're accompanied by the only intelligent Goblin in the world, Styx, who helps you get over the Wall and decides to stay with you for the entire journey. Arkhail has a strong racial bias against Styx in the beginning and Styx is just looking to get paid, but eventually they become good pals after they witness the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ conditions that orc slaves must endure and even witness each other's troubling pasts. They even gain some human allies along the way showing that not everyone supports the orc's enslavement and befriend some mages too. In the end you kill the Emperor, but it was just a trap to turn the elves and dwarves against the orcs as well as make some♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥the new Emperor. Then you kill the Emperor again and you kill the super evil, super strong wizard leader of the Inquisition. The last boss was pretty disappointing since it was very easy compared to a lot of other tough fights and the game ends with Arkhail and Styx being happy but now everyone, except the few mages left, is waging war on the dwindling orc race. The voice acting wasn't terrible but it has some very amateur moments and could've used some work. One thing that really surprised me as well was that nearly all the orcs and goblin talked exactly like a human compared to having an odd accent or speaking in strange tones.
Everything else: For a 2012 game the graphics are slightly underwhelming, but it wasn't a big enough problem to make me stop playing. Some areas randomly drop frames quite a bit but the majority of the game was stable. The AI was a bit shoddy at times as well ranging from enemies or even my partner getting stuck on other people or objects in the environment. The music was quite good at some parts, but it wasn't anything special.
Why did I make such a long review for this game? It's not everyday you get a fantasy game where you play as orcs who are on the morally good side and the world is quite different from the typical Tolkien/Warhammer fantasy. Like I said in the beginning, the game had a very promising start but it seems as though there was a major lack of development that set it to be just "alright" even though the game was published by Focus Home Interactive who has supported a large amount of other games(some being Warhammer based). Of Orcs And Men is definitely worth at least one playthrough and at most ~$10 on sale, but don't go into it expecting anything amazing.

I wrote a previous review which I realized is very unhelpful, and im going to try and make this next one simple and more on point. Stellaris has a good base game, and depending on who you are there might be some DLC that you like and some that you don't. Like most people, I've noticed that there is a lot of DLC being added on to this game. Wall the DLC doesn't subtract from the base game (for example, if utopia had never been concieved, nor the features for it, there wouldn't be so much buzz.), it does suck to have a lot of DLC, almost as much content as the base game (though not as neccessary). I would guess that paradox does this because they want to make more money off of a smaller part of the fanbase then smaller amount over a bigger part of the fanbase. This isn't economically wise since it limits the growth of the fanbase and it is better to make (this is just an example) 40$ off of 1,000 people than 80$ off of 100 people. I understand that programing is hard, and that the DLC are worth the money (at least individually), but I think that more people would be happy with not as costly (to the programmers) additions to the base game, even though its less content. To simplfy, the base game is good, but I think paradox is focusing too much on DLC. This doesn't make the base game worse, it just makes the game focus on a smaller portion of a fanbase than a bigger portion.

Let me just start out by explaining some of the bad reviews which come from Square Enix not releasing a patch since release. I installed the FAR mod before even playing the game, which allows you to run the game in native resolution, 60 FPS and adds much needed improvements, and have had little to no problems while playing the game. Now let's go on with the review.
This game is AMAZING, I don't usually write reviews but I feel this game deserves the praise. The comedy is hilarious when it needs to be, whether it be the ability to remove the Operation System of your character or accusing one of the protagonists of "wanting to $#@%" the female lead, it had me laughing. The combat feels smooth, and refined with swaps between sword play, and classic bullet hell, and there's varying amounts of weapons, upgrades and abilities to change it to how you like. The characters I absolutely loved, even ones that seem like they were made to be disliked I grew onto after finding out their stories,
As for the story, I absolutely loved it, it pulled at my heart on several occasions making me care about and feel for machines, and anytime I thought I fully understood the world and what was happening, something new would happen, leaving me craving for the more information, you'd think you figured it all out and them BAM, your whole world get rocked. The atmospheres are captured perfectly with a post-apocalyptic, post-war, nature has reclaimed with world, type setting which can look beautiful, but feel eerie and mysterious, leaving me wanting to learn what had happened. But it isn’t all perfect.
I have a only a few complaints about this awesome game such as the hacking minigame, which you used A LOT get boring very quickly, as you repeat the same thing over and over it feels more and more like a chore. The story goes a bit stale after the first "Act" as I'll put it,
but then it quickly ramps up. The environments can feel dull as the colors almost feel washed out and some of the building and terrain can look odd at times (buildings that look incredible square). And obviously, the lack of patching which requires you to download the FAR mod to enjoy the game in 1920/1080 res with 60 FPS.

For 12.50$, this game is golden. Remember those B-script action-drama shows that would pop up on TV now and then? This game is exactly that. For those who are just getting into it, the story will♥♥♥♥♥♥its-self after the first 'episode'. Then it just gets whackier from there.
Yeah, towards the end, the story wraps its self up (and even has a short-clip+text-card sequence explaining what happened to all the characters), but I still can't get over how rediculous it all was.
Remember back in the 90s when we had the technology to make a solar powered floating utopia city? Or when the RE universe made use of the orbital sunlight cannon? I can't help but feel that this game was going to be written as a sort of "Own-universe" type of game, but since it ties into RE5, that's not the case. So now we just have to accept that while RE1 was just happening, some philanthropists were making a giant floating city.
Anyway, the game is fun, not much in the way of puzzles, but the ship has a strong RE1 vibe to it that I enjoyed. Also there are quite a few hidden things for those who want to explore. Overall, it's probably the most fun I had in a RE for a while.
However, your AI partner is even more of a turd this time around. All he/she will do is just stand still and shoot at enemies on occasion. Also all enemies will aggro you, your partner just stands and looks pretty.
Enemy designs are brilliant when it comes to the sea-creatures, quite a few looking like they could fit at home in Dark Souls (especially some of the later ones). While for the enemies found in the mountain/flashback segments, you just get your standard Hunter-α (plus a new variant), as well as the return of the zombie dog.
Voice acting is on-par with the standard RE-terrible, with some lines like "Jill, where are you?" "I don't know, a room I think. On the boat."
For a 3DS port, the game doesn't look that bad. As a PC game; it's passable, but is on par with late-PS2 graphics. Won't find a RE5 level of detail here. Or even RE6.
This game also has a comedy duo who have hip-hop in the background whenever they have a scene. I don't really have much else to say.

Evopollution is a neat idea. You come across those games every so often; the premise is sound, it's presented well and gameplay seems solid, but in this game's case, it was very poorly executed.
Evopollution is not just another piece of shovelware bs, so I'm giving it a reccommendation, but don't spend more than 50 cents on it.
The basic premise is to make a million dollars. This is poorly explained by the game so just trust me on this. You're given multiple different ways to generate power to sell, including green options and more damaging options. Oil, gas and nuclear make money faster, but generate pollution, which you have to keep in check with trees (or random disasters will destroy your buildings. The faster you make your million the higher of a score you get. Good premise, right? Well yeah, there is a really good game hidden in here somewhere. Unfortunately the game is either a very poorly executed propaganda project or the developers had no idea how to balance a game, because filling your map with wind turbines is literally the only way to win. All polluting power plants have hilarious side effects which make the game harder, and kill everything around them with just immediacy. They also will almost never give you any return before being struck by lightning or a meteor or eaten by a sarlacc or whatever.
Evopollution is cute and well designed, and worth a quick play, but there is very little game here. I find it hard to believe that a developer would present a project so well only to fail at balancing its gameplay styles, so the only conclusion here is that they are trying to convey a message though a tissue-thin veil. Unfortunately for them, they didn't make me feel anything, all they did was make me strive to win with the most polluting build I could manage, and that's a scary accurate representation of real-world pollution policies if I ever saw one.

I really wish I could recommend this game.  I really do.  The premise of it sounds really interesting, and I'm glad I got it when it was on sale (though after playing probably 90% would be more worth it instead of my 75%).  The only real good thing was a 5 card badge.  Yay badges?
The premise is simple.  You have a land map.  You are to earn lots of money (1,000,000 for each map).  You can adjust difficulty and starting money.  And it seems that each one is somewhat randomized.  To get your money you have to balance the buildings you make with the pollution they create (and add trees to counteract it).  Sounds like a good start, no?
However, from there it gets...awkward.  The map control is really funky (move mouse to edge of screen to pan, hold mouse wheel for faster pan, no zoom).  The difficulties don't make a lot of sense to me.  There's Beginner and Normal...but I feel like they should be switched as Beginner makes you build through the 'tech tree' (not much of one) and Normal has it all unlocked.  I've seen in other reviews a harder difficulty but not sure how to unlock it.
The pollution balancing is...interesting.  You have large trees and small trees both with different upkeep (like you're paying to maintain them) which balances on your profit (other buildings) and the pollution offset.  There's no real clear indicator how much it's acting...but you can eventually get a feeling of the radius like coverage.  Easiest way I noticed was on the final area where you need to start with trees...and you see a clearer look of its effect before you can start to build.
The sound/music is...attempting at a sense of ambience but it gets a little old.  The graphics are fine for cost.  They're actually kinda cute in a way.
Basically, you have a Simcity without the Sims and all the pollution...and some natural disasters.  Well, somewhat natural-ish anyways: meteors, lightning...and a giant worm like from Dune?
I've got no idea how the grading scale works for when you complete a map and get the 1,000,000 dollars.  Best I've done as of this review is...a D+ (lowest was an E+).  Ouch...
If you get for cheap, it's an ok way to pass the time and get cards for a badge.  However, there REALLY isn't much to the game and like others have said the science is...biased, extremely biased.  I'm sorta tempted to see what the "Hard" is like if I can figure out how to unlock it...but I'm really not expecting much more.

As a big fan of city-builders and goals in games besides 'kill this' and 'destroy that,' I wish I could like Evopollution. But I can't recommend a game on its concept alone. There's not much content or gameplay; it mostly involves just sitting and waiting for your money to pile up enough to advance, with very little planning or strategy involved. I feel Evopollution would work much better as a free social media game.

Have you ever heard of "propaganda games?" Hopefully not.
Evopollution may not be a full-on propaganda game, but it's the closest thing I've seen in awhile.
In evopollution, your aim is to earn a million dollars, and you accomplish this by building structures on your little island.
Of course, as the name suggests, most structures also generate pollution.
If the environment gets even a little bit tainted around your structures, the environment will rise up against you, in the form of comets raining from the sky and giant worms coming up from the earth to devour your structures.
Once you play for a bit, you'll find the only solution to this madness is just to set up the strucutres that generate no pollution, and just leave your computer on until the game proclaims that you have won. It's that thrilling.
Building anything else results in swift and terrible punishment at the hands of...giant worms.
Oh, and can we talk about the fact that the "nuclear power plant" creates more pollution than any other structures in the game? No...just no...if you're going to have a little propaganda-fest, at least DO IT RIGHT.
I mean, short of blowing up a reactor, nuclear power plants have very little impact on the environment.
Not that it matters. Those giant worms will eat any nuclear power plant you place within moments.
So yeah, Evopollution is basically saying, "GO GREEN, OR DIE!"
They should show kids this game in schools, instead of "The Unfortunate Truth."
I mean, global flooding has NOTHING on giant worms!

Aside from Warhammer 40,000: Armageddon, I was quite unfamiliar with the Order of Battle games. It wasn't until I saw the Morning Sun expansion, which involves the Japanese invasion of the Chinese Mainland, that I realized I need to play these games. I have not regretted one, single hour. Order of Battle is a wargame in the same vein as the Panzer Corps games so veterans will feel right at home reqqing in troops and trying to overcome superior AI to complete objectives that vary from Defend these Points, Wipe out this many units or simply take these cities. You have control of an absolutely ludicrous amount of units for each faction which allows you to customize your force, from battle to battle, in whatever way you choose. Are you more of an Air General who likes to command squadrons of aircraft to bomb enemy positions and maintain air superiority or are you a more aggressive general who focuses on overwhelming tank assaults to capture objectives? I'm personally the latter. In all seriousness, the unit variation between each playable faction is downright impressive. If you've played WH40k: Arma, you're probably familiar with what I'm talking about and it should be said, the unit variation is one of this game's best features. I also love the focus of the expansion being in the rather ignored Japanese Invasion of China before and during WW2. This allows the devs to really bring a more unique view to WW2, especially since you play as the Japanese.
Order of Battle: Pacific also features a completely new and updated graphics engine that is full of great animations, burning tank/plane carcasses as battles drag on. This is a huge improvement for me over Armageddon because the animations really bring the battles to life. What's better, if you're not a fan of it, you can even switch to a more classic 2D mode through the options menu. There is also a campaign in the game which is were you'll be spending a majority of your time. The campaign doesn't really allow you to choose where to fight except in a few rare occasions, it's more of a mission to mission set up. However, units are persistent and units depleted at the end of the last mission will be depleted at the start of the new mission but will also be more effective than just requisitioning inexperienced units.
I only have two complaints in regards to the game. The first being, some of the missions feel like they drag on for far too long. For example, the first mission in the American campaign was kind of drag and it might be because Pearl Harbor isn't exactly untread territory. It also feels like that the AI calculations can eat up large portions of time inbetween turns and this feels like it lengthens a missions required completion time to double. Some may find that to be a negligible complaint but for me, it's a really nagging one.
In summary, this is a blast of game and I'm glad I got the chance to experience it! I truly cannot wait to see what other expansions are released for it. I wouldn't mind seeing some more "What-if?" scenarios either.
