Long Review, you have been warned!!!
For those that prefer to watch a video explaining stuff, here you go :-
So, this game looked pretty unique. We haven't come across many "business" management games that have a emphasis on the impact on the environment. The retro graphics style caught my eye, as did the fact It was also nice to see a game on steam that wasn't in early access or shovelware from the 1990s.
The game itself seems solid in theory, try to make money whilst maintaining the environment. If the land gets heavily polluted then weird stuff starts to happen, like meteors falling from the sky, or giant worms trying to destroy your precious buildings. The fact that there is random generation in the 5 maps you can choose from adds to the replayability (although the only thing I really noticed this have an impact on is the number and location of Oil Nodes).
First thing I noticed, there is no tutorial to explain how to actually play the game. There is a small "?" in the top left which you would assume would give you some kind of help or options, but instead it just tells you that you need to accumilate 1 million dollars to win.
The UI feels clunky, you can only scroll the screen with the mouse at a painfully slow speed. Good Luck finding the scroll speed on the options menu, all you get is music and sound sliders (oh sorry and full screen, can't forget that).
Perhaps my main gripe with the game at the moment is the lack of display information on the buildings and such. OK, yes you can see how much a building costs, how much weekly profit you get and it's (very vague by the way) pollution output, but how much does it cost to maintain? Is there maintenance costs? The system feels very basic.
It would also be nice to see some graphs of some sort. I'd like to see what my monthly profit (and expenditure) is, or how polluted the land is on average. This is the only business management game that I've come across that doesn't even have that basic functionality.
Considering the game is centered around the idea of keeping a clean enviroment why can't we upgrade our buildings to produce less pollution via installing (costly) filters and such?
Edit: So after playing for alittle bit longer I've found the game to mainly reward the playstyle of building nothing but buildings that cause no pollution. Apart from the fact that it takes alittle longer to reach the money goal there is no downsides to it. This seems flawed as it then gets extremely repetitive to just do the same set-up over and over again. That's rather disappointing.
Most of these problems could be patched. "If" it does, I'll happily re-review it, until then though I won't recommend it.

Right now, this game is not in a good state. (TL;DR at the end)
The aim of the game is to reach 1,000,000 credits, starting with a custom amount of credits, up to 25,000.
You can affect your weekly income by building different kind of power sources, including polluting types (oil, gas, etc) and pollution-free types (solar panels, wind turbines, etc) which all generate credits. Pollution shall be the main difficulty of the game:
If you build too many oil drills for example, your randomly generated world will suffer from pollution, causing e.g. lightning strikes that destroy your buildings. In order to fight pollution, you may chose to plant trees. Two types of them.
This balance system is however not transparent at all. You don't get to see, how much you pollute and how much your trees help, making it hard to find a proper distribution. The only feedback you get is when catastrophes are happening, nothing else.
The plantable trees are the only units that cost credits. And once again, you have no indicator showing how much you earn and how much you lose per week.
The biggest downside though is how damn easy it is to win this game, even on hard mode (not the expert mode, have not tried that one). If you don't want to be spoilered, don't read the following passage.
Basically, what this game needs is a downside to the pollution-free ressources, so that the difficulty lies in finding the correct balance between fossile fuels, 'green' ressources and vegetation, instead of just.... waiting.
Moreover, the whole game (featuring music, menu, interface) needs more love. It all seems
minimalistic. In the end, this game is, without further work, no fun.
I really hope that the creators will rework the game, i love the graphics and the general concept and idea of the game. There is potential. Unfortunately, it's still sleeping.

[For the lazy ones: Skip the text for pros and cons.]
Well, this game really looked interesting to me so I bought it. Unfortunately it's not quite as good as it looks. Why? Let's see.
You are thrown onto that map with a chosen ammount of money and you buy stuff to produce energy and earn money for you. Nice start.
Some of the buildings affect the pollution of the map, like gas plants or oil refineries and some don't, like solar panels. But clean energy takes forever to produce money. Does it even produce money? I get a little "3" on my oil drills to tell my something happens, but my clean energy just keeps looking fine... however.
If you earned too much pollution accidents start to happen, like lightning, meteors or a giant worm randomly popping out of the ground destroying everything in range. When any of these desasters destroy your building the pollution stops and... yes, that's it. You rebuild it, pollution starts again, and hello Mr. Worm!
You are able to clean the pollution by planting trees, but I was not able to see any difference so far. So I'm not sure how or whether these trees affect the pollution...
So in fact you could just build a lot of solar panels and hope you reach the goal. Oh, "what's the goal?" you might ask. Well, there's a little "?" in the top left corner to tell you: "To win you must make 1.000.000 Dollars". Oh my. And all that with a solar plant that... I don't know, does it work at all!?
Besides that the interface is minimalistic. Building menu, money and that nice little "?" top left. It would be great at least to know how much pollution my buildings produce just to plan how many trees I need to plant. But nope.
Next thing very annoying is the lacking possibility of erasing the enviroment. There are trees everywhere on the map, mostly in positions that block nice building grounds. And you have a wonderfull bulldozer-tool. But guess what? You cannot erase trees you did not plant by yourself. That's somehow nature-friendly, but come on... Don't cut my choices where I want my trees! At least they got different colors for map-trees and self-made-trees. Makes it easier to remember which ones to cut down...
What else? Graphics itself are really nice, I like this retro-Pokémon-look. On the other hand the music sucks. It's like a cat walking across a keyboard. With a lot of reverberation. And a bit of rhythm. Annoying to me. Well, at least you can turn the volume down from the options. That's one of three things you can do there. Sound and music volume and fullscreen-toggle. Wish there were at least some more graphics options. Or the scroll speed toggle. It's sooooo slow, jesus!
The last thing is the lack of progress in the game. Yes, you can unlock new buildings, but the world itself doesn't change (except when you have problems with leaking oil... :s ). Also it would be great if you could upgrade your buildings with better filters to produce less pollution, but that simply isn't possible. In fact you can't do much more than build things. This game is called EVOPOLLUTION, but all I get is POLLUTION, where's the EVO?
Guess that's it so far.
Pro:
- great idea
- many building possibilities
- making money. Who doesn't like making money?
- cute worm-monster
- nice retro graphics
Cons:
- repetitive
- hard on every setting
- no feedback on what you do (how does that tree affect my world?)
- no instructions
- always the same goal (reach 1.000.000 Dollars)
- cannot bulldoze any map enviroment (like trees, seriously?)
- annoying music
- no growth (besides the new buildings you unlock)
- would be somehow catchy, if it wasn't that hard ("Yai, I build a gas plant! ... Oh, the worm destroyed it..." YOU JUST CAN'T STOP THAT THING!)
- lack of options (sound and music volume and full screen on/off)
- incredibly slow scrolling
Conclusion:
I gave it a chance and it just didn't convince me. All in all it's a nice idea, but not much more than that. This game needs a lot more work to make it an enjoyable game you would play and also re-play. So far it's mostly frustrating. But maybe we get an update, that would be great!
Until now it's a no, I do not recommend that.

Wurm Unlimited is one of those gems that's not for everybody.  I had mixed feelings about giving this game a thumbs up or down, but only because of it's price tag.  I'll get to that a bit later though.
First thing's first.  Going into this game I knew to expect a few things.  This game is from the early 2000's, which means the graphics were going to be severly dated by todays standards.  It also started out as an MMO, which means that running it single-player might not be a very good experience.  I also knew this game wasn't for the faint of heart.  It's not your typical survival game, and it doesn't pull it's punches.  This was quite evident when I first entered the world, spawning almost direcly on top of a spider which proceeded to slaughter me without remorse and then camp my corpse.
Ok, so I mentioned a bit about graphics.  This game is pretty dated as far as the graphics go.  If you can't look past that then you really won't enjoy what this gem of a game truly has to offer.  Being an all-around gamer I found this to be not so bad.  In fact, there are many aspects of the graphics that I actually really like.  Little details, like fish swimming in the water, are very nicely done.
The interface of this game will frustrate the hell out of a lot of the newer generation of gamers.  Most of your actions are done via right-click menus and require you to have certain items or tools "activated" before the right-click menu will give you the options your looking for.  For example, having a hand saw activated and right-clicking a log in your inventory will give you completely different crafting options than if you had a knife activated.  That said, once you get the hang of the interface you can actually see it's really well designed for the level of detail and openness this game offers.
It's hard to judge the world of this game, having not seen all of it yet myself and also knowing that you can use custom worlds with a little tweaking.  It seemed very "real", as if the map was created naturally rather than by a person at a computer.  The jist of it is that there are 3 kingoms on opposing sides of the map and they expand their territories as much as they can, eventually meeting each other and then... Well, that's open to whatever the players want do at that point.  They can be diplomatic and trade lands for other lands, they can war and attempt to take land from the other kingdoms, or they can just live peacefully with their current borders.  There are goals to the game, with "winning" being an option, but depending on what style of server you play on those goals can either be important or not.
Now we get to crafting.  This is where this game REALLY gets some major points.  The crafting system is incredibly indepth, as mentioned earlier.  It's so indepth that you can't actually craft a lump of metal, which you have already smelted, unless it's reheated to a "glowing" state.  In addition, the more indepth a crafted object is the more resources and crafting stages it requires.  Example, to build a guard tower you have to first build the base of the tower, which is easy.  Then you have to add 500 stone blocks (a crafted item), 500 clay, and 100 planks (a crafted item) before the tower is finished.   This is a HUGE task!  Another example would be a knife.  You can't simply place a lump of ore on a stick and call it a knife (lookin at you Minecraft).  You have to craft the knife blade out of metal, and then a handle from wood, and put the two together to finally make the knife.  Crafting materials and requirements seemed very logical, almost "real".  That seems to be the theme of this game, bring as much reality to it as you can, while not loosing the fact that it's a fantasy game.
In addition to crafting, the materials of the world didn't come in numbered items.  For example, if you picked up a rock you didn't have 1 rock.  You had so many kg of rock.  Each time you crafted something it took a portion of that rock to craft it.  You could also have many rocks, of various weights.  Some might be too small to craft an item with, some might be big enough to have leftover.  They could also be combined to merge their individual portions into one larger portion.  So you could have one rock that is 10kg and another that is 20kg, merge them together and get a 30kg rock.  The weight of items was very important to monitor, as your movement speed didn't just go from 100% to encumbered.  There were actually multiple stages to walking speed.  So carrying 40% of your maximum weight would actually have an impact on the speed you walked, again very realistic.
So getting down to the nitty gritty.  What is Wurm Unlimited?  Well, it's a very good MMO, in a fantasy setting, including a high detail of realism, that's been converted to home use.  If it's just you playing it you'll find the world very empty and a lot of things will be a very difficult challenge.  If it's you and a few friends there is quite a bit of enjoyment to be found, although the 3 kingdom aspect of the game will probably never be used.  If it's you and a dedicated server of 30+ players you might be able to experience all this game has to offer.
So do I recommend it?  This is where the difficulty is.  For a player such as myself, who loves a challenge and doesn't mind tedious grunt work to get a task done, this game is absolutely awesome.  For the newer generation of (spoiled) players who like to press one key and click one button to get stuff done this game will come across as boring and very hard to play.  Personally though I absolutely love this game for it's mix of realistic crafting, true sandbox environent, and RPG aspects.
So again, do I recommend it?  Oy...  It's extremely hard to decide.  If I was to look at this game 10 years ago, at it's current price, I'd think it was a hell of a deal.  Today, not so sure.  Personally I think $32 is fairly overpriced.  That said, I got it on the Steam Sale for $16 which is a much more reasonable cost.  So?
Yes... Yes, I recommend it.   ---- BUT ----  Only if you can get it on sale at 50% off it's $32 price tag.

I played this game years ago, and to this day if someone asked me to name the craziest game I've ever played, or the most annoying game, or most surprising game, OR even one of the best games E-VER - you guessed it. This one right here.
I've always been a survival horror fan, so it was pretty natural for me to pick this up on the 360 back then. I did not quite get what I was expecting. Deadly Premonition is Twin Peaks meets Silent Hill with many other influences thrown in and brewed into a cup of joe that, well, might be best left to interpretation. The game is not perfect. It's awkward at times, annoying at others, sometimes makes no sense and sometimes makes ALL the sense! (yeah) But in the end, I don't think I've forgotten a single thing about it. That is how it stuck with me.
I admit, at times I sincerely hated this game and thought it was the worse piece of crap ever thrown together - a game that tried to be everything and yet couldn't find its place in a proper, comfortable gaming category. I ranted and raved about it to anyone who would listen - but this game was always on my mind. Did I stop playing? No. I HAD to keep going! And I did.
I remember the day I finally finished it. I told myself "I will beat this game tonight! I will finish it and then I will never have to touch it again!!!" I believed it was doable. I thought I was near the end... And so I played. And played. And just when I thought it would be over... I was mentally exhausted but I couldn't stop! By the time I reached the end it was at least 3 in the morning, and I just sank down in my chair and looked at the screen to see the credits roll by. But even then I was still thinking about it.
It was a gaming experience I have never forgotten. And now I'm ready to do it again!
Thank you, Deadly Premonition, for scaring me and driving me crazy (and also thank you for letting me figure out who the killer was a little ahead of time because of my own clue hunting effort. OVERALL 8/10 (as of June 2015)
One just cannot resist the temptation and compare Order of Battle: Pacific to Panzer Corps even if that would not be entirely fair as "Pacific" is a beast on its own and should not be seen as a mere expansion of its illustrious predecessor.
It is a "simple" wargame as Panzer Corps and uses pretty much the similar approach in terms of movement, core force build up, and, obviously, combat. So, if you enjoyed Panzer Corps, you will like this one as well.
PROS:
There are some serious improvements over "that" game:
+ Experienced units have advantages, yes, but nothing too overboard, so forget about killing off a horde of enemies with a single 5 stars Tiger tank.
+ Supply! oh yes, supply is very well done in this game, almost its finest point. You don't just need a clear line to be in supply, but also enough supply to keep your units up and running.
+ Air and Naval combat is vastly improved (yet still very simplified).
+ Units have several distinct abilities that make all of them useful at some point (not just limited to engineers building bridges, but also commandos not needing supply, some tanks hunkering down and so on).
+ The AI does a decent job at hunting down weakened units and is not an utter fool when on the attack.
+ Maps are detailed and terrain is critical to plan ahead
+ Some unique events happen during scenarios that force the player to change its strategy along the way, making it for a more dynamic experience.
CONS
- The hypotetical scenarios (like, invading Tokio by sea) are a bit too unrealistic.
- Unit balance is not there yet: Japan built 300 tanks during the entire war, mainly deployed in mainland China. Considering each tank "unit" represent a number of tanks (how many, we don't know) I'm positive I've destroyed three times the entire Japanese WW2 tank production in 12 battles.
- Some units are in dire need of an overhaul: you just cannot reload torpedoes on torpedo bombers while flying (plus Devastators were a total disaster, as Midway showed).
- The nice "dynamic path" (one scenario outcome changing the next scenario that was so critical in Panzer Corps) is gone, now everything is very linear.
- Commanders are far and few in between, allowing for little diversification.
The potential is there for a great platform to be used for pretty much any scenario from 1940 to 1977, some game mechanics are really nice, and most of the things that need ironing (an "undo" button, unit balance, a way to get rid of the animation, magically reloading torpedo bombers in the middle of the ocean, AI constantly attacking infantry entranched in the jungle and so on) COULD be easily fixed (if there's a will to do so).
All in all this could become a standard for simple wargames with very minor changes.
I would not suggest the DLC way to expand it as everything important about WW2 in the Pacific is already here, but I could definitely see the same platform used to cover the Mediterrean in WW2 (pretty much absent in the 200 scenarios of Panzer Corps), Korea, 'Nam.
Simply brilliant.

EDITED: December 21, 2016
After playing for countless hours, I'd like to make some clear points.
PROs:
-Excellent strategy game - Different unit types(planes, tanks, infantry, etc.) all bring different play styles. Prefer storming the enemy? Deploy tanks to overwhelm the enemy. Prefer a slower war of attrition? Deploy artillery units that slowly chop down the enemy.
-Good dev response - Many issues that were common in the beginning stages of the game development(I have been there) have been fixed speedily.
-Opportunities are limitless. If you prefer to stick to the tropical warfare of WW2, try the US Marine Campaign or the imperial Japanese takeover of the Pacific.
CONs:
-Yes, some of the campaigns in the game require you to pay for DLCs in order to play them. But when I first got the game, know that you had to pay $50 just to play the US and Japanese campaigns. At least now you actually get to try it for free(the tutorial).
-Multiplayer support is little to none at times. Sometimes, finding a game is impossible.
-Gameplay does get indeed, repetitive. Or if you just prefer clicking on enemy units over and over again, then that's your deal.
Overall, it's a great game that I really do enjoy playing. I own all the DLCs except the most recent(Blitzkrieg) and I plan to purchase it in the near future. Once again, yes you do need to buy DLCs in order to play the campaigns, but remember that the game originally was $50 just to play the American and Japanese campaigns. Lastly, if this game seems boring or dull to you, don't bother playing these types of games. It's just not your style.

Alright, Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel. This game receives a ton of, for the most part, unwarranted hate. Yes, when it was first released the game was a major fail. Key elements in the game were executed poorly or missing entirely which made the initial opinions on the game very negative. Have these issues been fixed? Of course. The Pre-Sequel is officially a polished and complete game that will reward its players with an absurd amount of enjoyable content for a very small price.
Steam often provides sales for the Borderlands series and within these sales are bundles that allow you to pick up the series for dirt cheap. Due to the fact I already own Borderlands and Borderlands 2, I was able to pick up Pre-Sequel in one of these bundles for as little as $3.50 (ultimately, I chose a bundle to get Tales From The Borderlands AND Pre-Sequel for 11$, however). Sadly, that beautiful price does not include the DLC. Luckily, however, you can find the DLC for VERY cheap on "IsThereAnyDeal" to complete the entire game. The story DLC, Claptastic Voyage, is, in my opinion, better than the first three story DLCs in Borderlands 2 and the main game in Pre-Sequel BY FAR. If it weren't for the insanely difficult final boss that was designed by a sadistic prick, it would easily contest for the #1 spot as well. The arena DLC should be avoided like the plague unless you truly love torturing yourself (see: masochists), but the two character DLCs are well worth the money if you have already finished the game as the other four characters or have a special interest in playing as either Jack or Aurelia.
Each playthrough (Level 1-30 or 30-50) can take anywhere from 8 hours to 25 hours. Obviously, that is an enormous leap in playtime. Your first playthrough can take a very long time to complete if you try to enjoy the gameplay, scenery, and side missions to their fullest; however, upon beginning subsequent playthroughs, you will begin ditching some of the more tedious side missions with little rewards and eventually strip down the game so you can complete it as efficiently as possible.
Achieving 87 hours in this game was only made possible because of the unique and fun variety of classes you get to choose from. In my opinion, Pre-Sequel has way better classes than Borderlands 2. None of the characters are
(ahem, Gunzerker) and all of them feel unique and enjoyable, while also containing much more satisfying skill trees and perks to strive for. I have played (and reached level 50) as Nisha, Athena, Wilhelm, and Jack. Athena is my favorite.
The story is nothing to jerk off to and the characters make me want to pull a glock out and splatter my brains across the wall. Pickle and Springs are the worst characters I have encountered in a video game EVER. PERIOD. The dialogue is stripped down or unfunny and the bosses are either way too idiotic to be taken seriously or just boring/annoying just like the supporting characters. The characters and story just dont FEEL like Borderlands 2 and that is what puts many players off, including myself. Luckily, there IS a solution. After slogging through the narrative and the rage-inducing characters one or two times, you can mute the dialogue/music and replace it with your favorite songs from iTunes, Spotify, Pandora, etc. Listening to music that pumps you up or makes you feel happy fits perfectly with Pre-Sequel's gameplay and even fits in if you want to imagine Athena wearing a pair of music-blasting headphones while she soars through the sky mowing down enemies with a submachine gun and slamming down on them causing them to explode into a puddle of blood, organs, and sadness.
...but.....the key thing that drives the Borderlands series is not its characters or story. They were more like extra benefits to Borderlands 2 that successfully supported the real powerhouse: GAMEPLAY. Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel maintains the chaotic and exciting gameplay you will find in the previous games and even EXPANDS on it through the use of gliding, slamming, and the 10/10 addition of lasers. The action skills are very fun and the skilltrees, like I said before, were much, much better than the ones found in Borderlands 2. You will always feel excited when you reach a new skill to unlock because you KNOW it is going to make your methods of electrocuting, melting, and tearing enemies in half much more efficient.
And that's what leads me to my final point and the most important thing in a video game: fun. Pre-Sequel. Is. FUN! Yes, it will begin to lose its sense of awe and intensity when you start pushing yourself through your sixth playthrough in two weeks but seriously, what game wouldn't? Besides the unskippable dialogue and boring filler you have to sit through  once in a while, you are always doing something entertaining. The varied settings, enemies, guns, characters, and skills always keep it fresh and FUN. YES, IT IS FUN. BUY IT.

The graphics/models/textures all looked pretty good. Not amazing but it’s 4 years old now. The setting/story is interesting. It puts you in the shoes of what is often thought of as the evil mindless villains. You get to see that they have their own motivations and are only mad because of the racism, slavery and cruelty they have suffered at the hands of man. This game is very story driven and one of the things I didn’t like about it is that you play for a couple minutes and then interrupted by a cut-scene sort of thing with dialogue and whatnot. Occasionally you have a little bit of choice on what you want to say, but rarely. Matt asked me at one point how I was liking it as I was about 25 minutes in and I said I had hardly played any yet because it’s all cut-scene. That doesn’t always bother me if it’s the right type of game, but I thought this was more action oriented. Oh well.
Being a story driven game it should be really well written, and this one, I would say is okay. Not great. It has some jokes, some of which are REALLY crude!
But at the same time it’s littered with modern language, particularly swearing, that just seems so jarring to me. I don’t need middle English thee and thou but it sure doesn’t feel like fantasy talk to me, when the language would fit today. So that is a bit of an annoyance. And it is constant, so, if you hate that then I’d avoid this game. Otherwise, the story as a whole is pretty decent, I think. You are on a quest to kill the “evil” [in your mind] emperor. You hire styx the goblin as a guide. Greenskins in general are persecuted, sometimes without reason.

But you still deal with humans plenty. Sometimes to do jobs, sometimes to get help, sometimes they are on your side from the start. You learn stories of other orcs and whatnot. I think styx is the only sentient goblin though.
Voice acting is ok. Sometimes it’s pretty good, sometimes it can be bad. I think it kind of depends on the writing. Apparently this was made from a French studio, so some of it might be translation issues.
The combat is where it really gets…iffy. Instead of, more or less, a hack and slash, you have a hack and slash via commands. When you enter combat, you hit space bar to go into super slow-mo, select a target and assign 4 actions to move through. The Orc is like a tank, kinda, except not a very good one. He can have an offensive stance or a defensive stance, though I haven’t really figured out if there is a difference. Then each stance has different things, like punch to stun, fast basic attack, powerful attack, round swinging attack that hits more than one enemy, etc. Enemies can parry and defend, but it just never seems to work all that well in general. Styx has melee attacks and ranged attacks. I usually stick to ranged if I can, but he usually gets surrounded anyway, and he’s pretty weak. With both guys I try go with a combo of stun and then smash, but it’s never totally clear what does what exactly. Combat is definitely the weakest part of this game. It’s interesting, it just doesn’t seem to be handled really well.
Styx can also hide and do silent takedowns from behind, which is useful until you are spotted.
So, TL:DR – decent game with some issues. Recommended in general, but it’s not for every one.

Ending (The ending dialogue is cringy and dumb. Words flash on the screen and it just ends. You don't get to see the art you've made. No gallery. Nothing. You can close the game, or play the same 3 similar stages over again.)

It's a great idea, but this game is weakly developed. Quickly developed for some sort of cash grab.
I loooove the concept and bought right away, which I really regret. So buyers beware. I really hope some other devs pick up this idea and make a better game, so I can be a starving artist in RL and in-game.

I don't usually write reviews like this, but for Passpartout that's the best I can come up with I think.
In my sophomore year, I took American Contemporary Art. At the end of the semester it required me to do a presentation and I was left with Mark Rothko.
During the presentation something went wrong with my slides, or the projector. Anyway it went pitch black. Darker than my lungs. And for a moment I was so embarrassed. People sat in silence as if they enjoyed every second of the incident.
Then I came up with something. I told them this was titled
. Done in the year 1968. And I elaborated the social circumstances and my assumption of its purpose, so on and so forth. True story.
Anyway I improvised and nailed it. I think the professor didn't fall for that (but he must have enjoyed it) but the class totally did. And that's how I lost faith in modern art.
Of course I am not saying Mark Rothko is bad. If the presentation slides were able to reproduce the subtlety of his paintings I couldn't have pulled the stunt smoothly.
And playing through Passpartout reminds me of that experience. For me the game is hilariously realistic and painfully true.

For a game about machines, they could have given the PC port a little more care. Despite the issues, of which I had plenty, the game itself is quite the ride. My enthusiasm tapered off a bit towards the end as various video bugs presented themselves, but the experience was solid, overall. I love the story, overarching lore, setting, characters, music and art direction. The gameplay is what I remain somewhat torn on, oddly enough. The use of the camera to dictate playstyle is a very interesting mechanic. I feel it helps the game more so than not, but it certainly gave me my fair share of headaches during the last couple of boss encounters. (Though that could be due to the fact that I am bad at video games.) As for the structure of the game, it's rather perplexing. One moment, it feels like an open-world sandbox, then the next, a linear narrative-driven adventure game. Not entirely sure of how I feel about that, but I appreciate the creative freedom on display, nonetheless.
My biggest hopes for NieR going forward are fixes that alleviate the multitude of issues Automata's PC port suffers from, as well as well-done PC ports of NieR and Drakengard games.

Stellaris continues to frustrate me, yet I recommend it heartily if you enjoy 4X games...and I continue playing it despite my frustrations. The AI seems to have perfect information and cheats to compete. Example: you build a large empire with your home planet in the middle. You build up a large fleet and invade a neighbor in your quest for galactic domination. Jusssssst when your fleet is at it's most distant from your main assets, a different and rather potent neighbor declares war on you, sends in massive fleets and takes most all of your planets. Oh, and they bring all their allies who proceed to destroy your entire fleet. So, yeah, once this happens, there is no coming back into the game.
This travesty happened a number of times until I figured out how to "game" the AI a little better, but one of my own primary tricks is to play a ring-shaped galaxy and make hyperlane travel the only option. With these features enabled, I was able to make it to the late game. But then, after I had vassalized 70% of the galaxy and built an incredibly mighty empire, an Awakened Empire asked me to join their alliance. At the time, my fleet capacity and naval power were greater than this nation, though they still had a huge tech advantage on me. I thought, "Oh, sure, I'll join their alliance." Next thing I know, I lose ALL my vassals, I in turn AM a vassal to this nation, AND this other nation INSTANTLY has a huge fleet power advantage over me?!? WTF? There was zero warning that this would be the consequence of joining their alliance. Since I play on Ironman mode, I can't rewind. Then, exactly at this time, some creepy interdimensional race appears in the galaxy, all around my home planet....no one else's, and proceeds to crush me with a fleet about 8x larger. Game over.
The point of all this: there are clearly still some serious balance problems. And yet, for each time I find myself at a point of no return, I come back to the game. So many things are well done. The level of detail and balance of different races, technologies, and governments are excellent. I enjoy the Unity system with its various perks and I think the tech trees are incredibly fun. The graphics are great, there are exciting and interesting events, the level of planetary micro-management is just right (not too little, not too much), customizing and upgrading ships is fun, the music, etc.
Stellaris was very easy to learn as well, and I was able to get right into the game. It continues to madden me that the AI empires have perfect information and seem to be able to "cheat" in a variety of ways. I know that the developers have to balance their AI and find a way to make the game competitive. Cake walks aren't any fun either. But man it's frustrating at times...probably enough that some players will rage-quit. I also think it's an oversight that, when you go to war, there is NO OPTION to just destroy everything on an enemy planet. If you win, you have to take the planet, along with its disenfranchised populace. In Stellaris, this is a problem, as you have a limited capacity for planets in your empire.
Despite my frustrations, I have found that Stellaris scratches that Master of Magic/Master of Orion itch. It's extremely engaging and I hope it will continue to receive the polish it needs to become exemplary in every way. Give it a try!

Stellaris is getting there. Slowly. But it's getting there. It's a leap into something very different for Paradox and, a year in, some of the niggles still remain.
The good stuff is in the customisation options for your Empire. It really does allow you to play in a number of different ways. It's a game which plays well if you're interested in creating a story. The soundtrack is excellent, and the game is very easy on the eye. The game also supports epic campaigns of 30 empires and 10,000 stars within a galaxy. You're never short of exploration and elimnation options.
The niggles remain with space combat turning into just one battle involving every ship of each side. The absence of a trade system is also notable. One can see work is ongoing with some game systems and mechanics - recently improved was the system granting the AI control of areas of your empire, It sounds good for reducing the micromanagement workload but also can lead to frustration with what the AI decides to build on your planets.
Overall I'd recommend Stellaris. Paradox games typically got a lot of patching and DLC so I've confidence some of the niggles will, eventually, get worked out as new ideas get implemented into Stellaris.

Community: Very friendly, people construct towns together with complete strangers and form bonds just like in real life.
Gameplay: Dated, but very solid and compelling, deep. Turn-based combat mixed with realtime movement
Visuals: While not as highly detailed as newer games on the market, Wurm's forests and mountains feel very real and get many things right that other games never will.
Excellent game for those who desire a greater sense of depth, adventure, and progression from their survival sandbox type experience. Wurm Online (Unlimited is basically a player-hosted version of WO) is a very old game, and you will not find a game that plays quite like wurm to date... a very specific niche in gamefeel that makes this a hard game to recommend without one first trying out Wurm Online for free. Creation in wurm arises from necessity, players construct the very crucial highways and sideroads that span across the world, everything seems to have a purpose. This is because everything that isn't natural landscape is player-made, giving every server and every world on the server a very real, breathing sense of life and wonder. For those who admire an abundant amount of roles to fill and an elegant (if hard to get used to at first) style of crafting, where things can be constructed based on what makes physical sense and not just what the developers want you to put together, Wurm is possibly the perfect game.
Bottom Line: It's great for the people that find joy in living peacefully instead of constant looting and pillaging (although there are places for that in wurm), it's great for people who enjoy turn-based games like classic roguelikes who want a compelling multiplayer experience that is a bit more up their alley. Wurm is a great game for many people but it is certainly a very unique experience, which is not very easy to break into without a bit of effort.
~Join a server with multiplied timers and skillgain, and find your place in the world of Wurm~

This is a very good game.  Plays much like the Panzer General/Panzer Corps series, but with much thought and improvements to naval and air power.  Anyone familiar with Slitherine's Afrika Korps expansion to Panzer Corps will see similarities in the linear campaign pathing and mid-scenario events.
Gameplay is tactical in an operational environment, meaning your units do not represent combined arms brigades, rather pure all-tank, all-infantry, or all-artillery type units.  This is for fun and has a "beer and pretzels" aspect to the gaming.  On the macro picture (strategically), the game is pretty realistic, however.
The player must strike a balance between caution and deadlines to reach objectives.  Move in too fast and you will encounter ambushes.  Too methodical and you will run out of time.  This is not the cakewalk of the Panzer General series, and every scenario can be lost if the player is reckless.
Also, scenarios are long, as in epic.  Some are 60 turns, I think one may have been 100 turns.  100 turns!
Overall, a great game with solid replay value.

This game does for Pacific General what Panzer Corps did for Panzer General. It  updates a classic game to a more robust and rounded game. There are a few things that seem odd at 1st but once you learn the system it works well.
Units are different with different capabilities. Engineers can  place mines, remove mines, demo bridges, repair bridges. These may seem like trivial things but in some games they are vital to your success.
Different air units are capable of different things . IE there are 3 types of fighters, each excels at one thing  but can do all 3 just not as well as the unit that is made for doing it.
Units gain experience and can be upgraded as new equipment is usable. You may add a  Heavy cruiser to your force pool in 1942,  and then as the game progresses upgrade it to a retrofitted model. This is very historical as the TOE  changed drastically as the War went on. At the start of the war the main AT gun for the US is the 37mm  by the end of the war that gun was far outdated.
Leaders. These are gained by doing certain things in a mission. They may be  for naval, land  or air units. Some are for just the unit they are attached to, and some for units  in an area.
Supply is vital. Units are effected by being out of supply or under supplied. Learning to use your supply ships in an invasion is vital.  you cannot just run all your units ashore and have them functioning as normal. As you capture ports and  cities  it allows you more supply, but it takes a few turns to  be full effect. Some units are Supply resistant   or  ignore supply (recon)
Reinforcements are triggered by completing certain things in the game.
No undo button. Yes this is true BUT. The game auto saves at the start  and the end of each turn. So if you really goof up you can always reload the game and do it over. ( I know a lot may not like that but it is an option)
Game needs more content. There is the training tutorial which is 4 missions. And 2 campaign games  Allied and Japan, each with 12 missions that must be played in a set order.
Game has some flaws, but the Developers are very active and respond to posts in the Steam Forums. They just did a patch  on the 15th that fixed a lot of the flaws.

Overall I agree that the game is well worth the price. I have war gamed since about 1970. This game has a lot to offer.
I have played Panzer General, Pacific General and Panzer Corps. This game is the best of them.

[+337 hours gameplay from beta & pre-steam versions]
Two factions, the dominion and the exiles are at war.  Choosing one side or the other you follow a fascinating world story which slowly reveals information about the long forgotten race, The Elden. Gameplay involves levelling, level 50 exclusive gameplay, raids, PvP, adventures and dungeons (offered at two levels; normal and veteran)
Graphics are crisp and vivid.  The UI is pleasing and supports a multitude of add-ons.  The music score by Jeff Kurtenacker is simply stunning - I actually listen to the Farside theme whilst offline.
This MMORPG was made by the same team behind World of Warcraft. Often this shows, in the funky world graphics and levelling tasks, but this is altogether a far more polished game. The largest difference with WoW is housing. With the arrival on Steam, the housing plots became bigger and the new expansion 'Homecoming' has 100's more objects and colours to choose from. Another difference is the humour - I get the feeling WoW takes itself a bit too seriously.  Meanwhile, from lore entries, to sarcastic holographic rez points and sexy level up messages, Wildstar always seems to be poking fun or just being tongue in cheek. Despite all those hours of gameplay I'm still laughing out loud whilst playing.  Finally, in WoW, it is difficult to play with others if you happen to have accounts in different regions. I joined the US west coast server, as did my husband (who is level-capped in Europe), only to find that we couldn't play together in the free edition.  We would both have to buy the game in order to play together.  No such barriers from Wildstar - and realm switching is free too!
With six races in each faction to choose from, six classes and four paths, this game offers plenty of versatility and replayability. Throw in crafting, resource gathering, rune modifications and an extensive wardrobe and we have a game that simply has it all.

This game takes what people consider in a typical RPG and makes something new and more exciting about it. There are many different ways to play this game, and they all involve a lot more action on your end instead of the typical "Press number, do attack" system that LOTRO and SWTOR are somehow popular with.

Really wish I could recommend this game as it has one of the best combat systems I've ever seen in an mmo, the combat is fluid and heavily telegraphed, rewarding the player for utilizing dodges and positioning, especially for raid combat.
The raids encounters are extremly complex and brutally unforgiving, some of the best I've ever encountered (pun intended)
The story is decent, and there is a fair amount of lore of you're into that sort of thing, character design is exaggerated and cartoonish, take that how you will, I personally see it as a positive rather than a negetive, the housing system gives alot of room for creativity, I've seen crazy stuff built by people.
Unfortunately the negatives are alot more apparent and glaring, the HUD and UI is beyond saving, working off of a system akin to modding, which could of been a high point, but it's extremly unstable most of the time, even with all the defaults applied, the crafting system is completly useless except for extreme endgame and a few other niches.
With only 8 ability slots, you'll aquire alot of abilites that you will never use, as each class has a core set that it needs to run to be viable, the default stat acquisition on leveling is entirely passive, no room for customization at all, and the endgame stat tree is a grind fest locked behind daily/weekly timewalls, the classes themselves albiet unique, are almost completly interchangable for most raid fights, except for slight class specific combat buffs.
Moving onto the elephent in the room, the playerbase is extremly low and continues dwindling, increasing que times (2h+ for some content) for everything, doubly so for raids, as cross faction raiding has still not been implemented.
All in all, I'd recommend trying it during a double xp event, seeing things for yourself, and joining up with an active clan.
I dont want to discourage people from giving it a try, but see this as a fair warning.

I've played this game for just over 100 hours, and I've played it almost since it was released in beta.
I have enjoyed playing this game many times, despite the early glitches, bugs and various other issues. The game got better as time went on - it's in beta so it's expected that problems will occur.
However, it's been in beta for around a year now and recently they've started adding randow new components to the game rather than fixing the existing issues. For example there are 4 different currencies in the game which you use to buy various different things. It's incredibly confusing!
New Champions are ridiculously OP when they get released and often they haven't been nerfed so early champions are weaker to play.
There is also something else that's incredibly irritating about the game, that has existed since it was first made. When you pick a champion, you have an amount of time to pick and customise. However, you can change the selected champion at any time, and often people will change from say a tank or healer to something else in the last second, which completely ruins the team as you now don't have one of these positions filled. If you quit out of these games so that you can play with a decent team, you get a deserter penalty - all from someone else messing up the game. It used to be a few minutes but they've made it ridiculous now. I'm now on a 30 minute deserter penalty because I quit a game when someone changed at last second - it happens every other game. Why they haven't used the league of legends lock in system is beyond me.
If you don't got as a tank or healer you're screwed because 4/5 times no one else on your team will go as one so you're stuck playing a really boring role and champion just so you don't lose.
Gameplay wise is fine, there's not much to say. If you have a good team you win, if you don't you lose. There's no close call or "almost won" game, you either do amazing or awful, and there's no inbetween.
For those reason, I don't currently reccomend the game, as it seems like they just want to squeeze the players for money.

This game is widely considered the best basketball video game franchise. However, the PC version of this game seems to get more hate than the console versions. While some of it may be deserved, I will dive into what you can expect from buying the PC version of this game.
In short: If you want to play online, no. Get the console versions. If you want to play offline or don't care about online, YES.
First of all, this is a huge upgrade over the previous versions of 2k. The gameplay is redesigned in many ways, including the shot meter. The most significant new features are found within the offline modes. In MyGM/MyLeague, you can now expand your league to up to 36 teams. In 2k16, you could only relocate teams. Within this mode there is also league meetings in which you can change the rules, and, one of my personal favorites, jersey retirements for good players.
The MyCareer mode has also changed for the better. There is still a story mode and college, like in 2k16, but it is fresh and allows you the freedom to play every game in your NBA rookie season. There are a ton of other improvements with this mode as well. The graphics improvements are not very noticeable, but the graphics remain incredible.
Now, you may ask, "What's wrong with online?" The problem with the PC version lies in the fact that it is much easier to cheat and hack the game. When you play online, you will occasionally run into these people. The other problem is that the PC online doesn't have nearly the same playerbase as the console versions, making it very difficult to find games sometimes.
As a pure basketball simulation, there isn't a better game out there. I enjoyed Draft Day Sports Pro Basketball 4 as a basketball sim, but this game is far more realistic and much deeper. It will be very hard for any competitor to dethrone the NBA 2k franchise as the best basketball video game franchise in the world.

I don't usually write reviews like this, but for Passpartout that's the best I can come up with I think.
In my sophomore year, I took American Contemporary Art. At the end of the semester it required me to do a presentation and I was left with Mark Rothko.
During the presentation something went wrong with my slides, or the projector. Anyway it went pitch black. Darker than my lungs. And for a moment I was so embarrassed. People sat in silence as if they enjoyed every second of the incident.
Then I came up with something. I told them this was titled
. Done in the year 1968. And I elaborated the social circumstances and my assumption of its purpose, so on and so forth. True story.
Anyway I improvised and nailed it. I think the professor didn't fall for that (but he must have enjoyed it) but the class totally did. And that's how I lost faith in modern art.
Of course I am not saying Mark Rothko is bad. If the presentation slides were able to reproduce the subtlety of his paintings I couldn't have pulled the stunt smoothly.
And playing through Passpartout reminds me of that experience. For me the game is hilariously realistic and painfully true.

jackson pollock simulator

Ever dreamed of being an inspiring artist selling your work in a public place? Sell physical paintings to customers as they walk through your wares? Look no further than Passpartout: The Starving Artist! Don’t worry about the starving part.
Set in France, you have a few levels to sell your paintings. But...you don’t start at the top. You start around the bottom, not so much where you are sitting on the sidewalk but at your storage space. Unknown by the public, work your way up so you can make an impact in the art world. Or just go bankrupt.
And man, will it not be easy at all. You can, technically, draw whatever you want and still progress but it has no guarantee of selling. You will have three different brushes, the regular paint brush, the spray can, and a guided pen (the last 2 being earned after a certain amount of sold paintings) to make what you desire or what the customers desire. Everyone has different tastes to what they like, and you are not marketing to yourself. Even more frustrating, they will be cryptic to what they want. When they are not insulting your work, you can get something like “I hate these colors” or “I want something fresh”. And even when it’s as simple as wanting more detail, the question remains on how much detail and at what point do they deem it as not having any meaning. This can help you go through the end of each level, where an art critic will show up to comment on one of your current paintings (as I never had an empty showcase, I’m sure they wait till you have at least one up for sale). When a customer actually likes a painting and buys it, nothing is more satisfying than seeing their little dance they do.
As you work through the level, notifications will show up on the top left of the screen. It can be a notification of your bills, a bidding on a painting you have for sale, a critique/harsh comment on a painting, or newspaper headings. The newspaper headings are missable, but they do hold humor in them. Once you gain enough publicity, special  notifications will show up, such as Passpartout gaining popularity in the first level, someone “special” coming to visit, or a group of customers deciding not to come anymore. Though, I did get the same customers that said would not buy my paintings buy them. Knowing your customers will help you in the long run.
You can specifically save a painting you worked on and loved as a screenshot, which opens up the screenshot area of the community forums toa nice area to share your in-game artwork. Though I do wish the paintings you already had out for sale followed you to your new place. I know that it may not exactly work out as you lose display spots as you rank up in popularity, but nothing is worse than working hard on a painting just for you to lose it as you continue to the next level. Especially when you just made it.
I love the style they decided to take. It is very much like you are on a stage controlling a puppet. The music starts up, curtains opens, pleasant music greet you as customers enter and exit stage left or right. Than when you gain the ability to go to the next level, you hear disembodied clapping and muttering. You and the customers look like puppets as joints are ball joints and have a wood like texture for skin. Every different type of customer is dressed differently depending on what they like to buy. Fancy dressed women love detailed art while someone with a spiked mohawk love art with spirit and action. The sets you are given are also great to look at. You can always see the backdrop as the stage is decorated accordingly to where you are.
There are multiple endings for you to explore, which I believe is decided to which style you leaned towards. If you favored drawing something simplistic, you will progress to a level where they mostly come in. This may be the easiest route considering they are easier to decipher, and is one of the routes I first received. With bills constantly incoming, I can’t imagine how hard it may be to keep detail up for the fancy dressed ladies.
+ Soundtrack
+ Friendly to all levels of art skill
+ Can save artwork
+ The little dance customers do when they buy a painting
+/- I do wish the paintings for sale transfered with you, but I get why they don't
- Can be cryptic to what the different types of people want
- Ouch, that was harsh mister (Can go a long time getting insulted before someone buys)
Passpartout: The Starving Artist is a one of a kind game. Encouraging drawings to be made by those who have no talent in art and those who do. This could've easily been a game where the more simplistic, the less it will sell. But instead added customers with a wide variety of tastes to ensure that anyone can complete the game. While it may be hard to decipher what the customer wants, it sure gives us a taste on how cryptic people can be in real life.

Fans who disliked Resident Evil 5 and 6 will find much more to like in Revelations, though it's still not the return to survival horror that many have been hoping for.   The game plays like a hybrid between Resident Evil 5 and the original Resident Evil, pairing the modern combat system with the cramped, atmospheric indoor settings of the older games; think of what the GameCube remake of RE1 would feel like with an over-the-shoulder camera and you're halfway there.
The combination works so well that it makes one wonder why Resident Evil 4 abandoned so much of the classic gameplay in the first place.   The Queen Zenobia and its enemies are actually frightening (even if there aren't many of them) and the game often manages to build up genuine dread about the scenarios the player is in, something newer titles sorely lacked.  Ammo and health are also more limited, but not to the point of making Revelations a true survival horror game.   Unfortunately, the exploration still feels watered down compared to the older games with less backtracking and fewer puzzles to solve, but it's still far less linear than 4, 5, or 6.
Capcom can't seem to let go of action and Revelations is packed with a few over the top sequences, most of them occuring in chapters that jump to other characters outside of the Queen Zenobia.    These chapters break the immersion in the ship setting and feel like obligatory diversions from Jill's more interesting campaign, but they're brief enough to be excusable.   In general, the game feels like a broken up collection of moments from all across the series history, in both a good way and bad way- the dumbed down action rears its head once again, but the horror of the older games resurfaces to counter it, sometimes within the same chapter.
The campaign can be beaten in about 5-8 hours, a far cry from RE6's 40 hour duration.  Unlike most entries, Revelations does not include the Mercenaries mode to fill out the package, instead offering a new take called Raid mode.  Raid mode has much more in common with the original RE3 incarnation of Mercenaries in which the player would travel across a large, linear stretch of the single player game rather than fighting enemies in a closed arena.  It's generally fun and serves as a welcome break from tradition, but there are many odd choices that hinder the experience.
For one, each weapon has its own level.  As the player collects xp from matches, they will be able to purchase higher and higher level weapons, which forces one to keep purchasing the same guns over and over each time they level up while simply discarding their old weapons (they can't be sold back).
This is already tedious, but the fact that the store randomly displays only a few guns at a time makes the process that much worse.  Trying to do something as simple as upgrade your pistol from a level 41 to 42 may require opening the shop 4 or 5 times until your handgun is displayed, and even then it may actually be a
level than your current gun or it may inexplicably lack any item slots to equip perks to, forcing you to repeat the process until you find one that does.
Why in god's name they didn't use the system from RE4 and 5, letting the player keep and upgrade
over time, is beyond me.
Online play is also tedious in that a level 50 player will have guns capable of killing enemies in single shot while a level 5 player will have to empty several clips to get the same effect.  To avoid a wild mismatch of power, high level players have to lower their level manually.   Considering that this must be done every time you play with a lower level player, it's hard to miss the straightforward simplicity of dropping into a Mercenaries match.
In terms of what's different from the 3DS release, there's not much worth mentioning- it's 95% the same and the few alterations are meaningless.  Even when maxed out, the game doesn't look good enough to make the 3DS version any less impressive, and the loss of 3D may even give the original  the advantage.  To put it bluntly, it's absolutely not worth upgrading if one already has the 3DS version.
Revelations isn't perfect, but it's hard to complain when the game gets so much closer to the classic RE gameplay than the newer installments.  It's certainly worth picking up, but don't expect it to solve all of the series' problems and don't forget it's origins as a more limited handheld game.

Per Wikipedia, Wurm Online started beta back in 2003 and went gold in 2006. In 2015, the developer completed a standalone version of Wurm Online and packaged it as Wurm Unlimited.
Pros
- I like the soundtrack and find it soothing. There's something soothing about mindlessly mining ore and listening to the audio that keeps you in a trance.
- Lots of parameters can be altered to generate the experience.
Pro and Con - depending on your perception:
- In depth crafting system. A large amount of resource gathering is required to build end products. Building ships, buildings, etc. involve quite a bit of resource gathering and give a sense of accomplishment when you finally build the finished product.
- Age of game. You get a product that has been around for quite a while. This means that people have worked on it for quite a while to develop the systems (Pro). It also means that you're not likely to get a "fresh interface" or the latest graphics (con)
Cons:
- Declining population:
Steam charts -

Steam charts -
Per the above, you can see that there's never been more than 2000 players online playing this game at one time. The population and number of servers continue to decline.
- Cost:
As of June 2016, the regular price for this game is $30 ($29.99 for those worried about a penny).
As far as would I recommend it to others... Overall, I enjoyed playing this game, but I would have to give it a no based on the current price tag and current decline of the population. Truthfully, this game is not for everyone. If you can find the game on sale at a significant discount, then it's worth picking up, but only if you like games that involve an extensive resource collecting experience where you don't mind finding yourself spending a considerable amount of time playing solo.

Filled with a patent strangeness not unlike that of Twin Peaks, Deadly Premonition provides an incredibly memorable cast of characters and an excellent story that will keep you guessing until the end. The game is thrilling, suspenseful, intense, cheesy, and ridiculous, with the right balance of each. It has relatively low production values, but it's almost endearing, feeling akin to cult B movies. This game has solidified itself as one of my favourites. I have no doubt I will come back and play this game again many times in the years to come, reliving the story and getting to know the citizens of Greenvale all over again. Right, Zach?
A quick disclaimer: This game is a relatively poorly done console port, so at the time of writing, there are some technical issues. I found the experience was greatly enhanced by using DPFix and JoyToKey to play with a controller with better looking visuals. Crashes were rare for me, and I was able to play the game without too many problems, but some others have had trouble running the game. The developers have expressed intent to fix these issues, though, so we will hopefully see an improvement soon.

It's really hard to rate Deadly Premonition. In one hand it's utterly broken, buggy and sometimes even outdated, but it's also very clever, atmospheric and unique. Basically DP is an open-world investigating taking place in a little town, just like Twin Peaks. But this description just doesn't cut it. It's also extremely bizarre, weird and often creepy. The "side quests" are also very  different from what you're used to, they mostly revolve around getting to know the people of Greenvale, and actually this is how I spent around 3/4 of my almost 40 hour playthrough... just getting to know this town and the people living in it. York (and Zach) the 2 in 1 detective, George the king of the town, Harry the weird millionaire who always wears a mask for some reason... and even though you get to know the characters very well, they still managed to keep the thing that are important well hidden, lurking in the background, just so they can surprise you with it later. The story and the narrative are just perfect. Same could be said for the soundtrack and the voice actors, all top-notch.
All in all Deadly Premonition is a terribly broken, ugly (and despite these) amazing game, which I'd wholeheartedly recommend to all my friends :) This is probably as close as we'll ever gonna get to a Twin Peaks game folks!

Disappointing.  Let me start by staying, I love the concept, to play as  an orc fighting humans for once, and the developers have created a rich & detailed world with interesting lore, as well as two well-written & interesting main characters. I'll happily read novels set in this world.  And the graphics are pretty good.
But everything else about this game is painfully uninspired.  Every level is a corridor, and some have long stretches with neither enemies nor points of interest.  Loot is rare and frequently boring, the skill-trees are uninteresting, and while combat has a novel design allowing you to switch between the characters & queue up actions, the result delivers neither interesting tactical challenges, or good action sequences.  Hard fights often find you leading your enemies in circles while trying to revive your other character - and this is not helped by comically bad hit detection that can see you killed by a swordstrike from 20 feet away.

Rating 7/10
Overview: Third Person Tactical RPG
The Good:
+ Artistically and technically I thought the graphics were good. Every chapter has a unique atmosphere so the setting never gets repetitive.
+ I like playing as an orc and a goblin, it provides a unique twist to an otherwise standard formula seen in so many other fantasy RPGs. Both characters are well written and excellently voice. The relationship between the two is what holds the entire game together.
+ Each character has two main skill trees to choose from to fit your play style. Although it becomes pretty apparent that certain skill trees/skills are more powerful and practical than others.
The Average:
The story is decent but never really evolves into anything. The entire premise is explained in the first hour of the game and never deviates. Other than the main characters, no other character is given a lot of dialogue so it becomes hard to care about the villains or side characters.
The first two chapters take a while to complete, both of these chapters have side quests. The other remaining chapters are much shorter making the game have a very uneven pace.
Un-skippable cut scenes. Normally I would consider this very bad, however this game has very little cut scenes and are not very long.
The Bad:
The levels are REALLY linear with the occasional off beaten path that usually leads to a chest. Thus, every level plays out almost exactly the same. Run through a corridor beat down some enemies, rinse and repeat until the end.
The combat is identical to that of Knights of the Old Republic. I hated it back then and I hate it now. You give a series of commands and sit back and watch as the character executes them, keep doing this until all the enemies are dead. The combat is not engaging, gets very repetitive and once you have your favorite skills unlocked gets even more boring.
Conclusion:

Eh, it's ok.  Not great, but maybe see if you can get it on sale for cheap.
This is an adventure RPG.  You follow a linear set path, deal with enemies a few at a time, find some hidden treasures, change and upgrade your armor and weapons, and gain experience points from combat to level up your skills.  The world is a "fantasy" setting where the humans have come together and formed an empire after a long war against the Orcs.  Now the emperor is running a campaign of genocide against anything with green skin.  The dwarves and elves have joined him, mostly out of fear for their own people.
In this game, you play as two characters.  You can switch control from one to the other on the fly, but whichever one you are NOT controlling will be active with AI control.  The AI is stupid as a bag of rocks, by the way.  The big orc is loud and likes to hit people in the face.  He has a mission:  to save his species from genocide by assassinating the human emperor.  The little goblin is tasked with helping the orc get through the city so he can do the deed.  The little goblin is very sneaky; if he enters stealth mode then the big guy will stop following you and wait until you exit stealth mode before he runs to catch up.  While in stealth mode, many times you can make a fight easier - or avoid a fight completely - by sneaking behind the enemy and assassinating them one at a time.  If a fight does break out because you are witnessed killing a soldier, then you will be alternating control between the two.  You can set a chain of commands for each of them, but they can only remember four commands at once.  Each character has his own upgrade tree, for which you gain points when you level-up.  There is one area that has SHARED commands for both of them, and each character has two fighting styles to upgrade.  The goblin has a path for ranged attacks (dagger toss) and another path for up-close fighting.  The orc has a path for strong but slow attacks, and another for attacks that allow him to also block or parry incoming blows.
The graphics are pretty well done.  The music isn't awful, but also not great.  The story is interesting because it is rare that you get to play as a "bad guy" but still have it feel like you're doing the right thing.  The combat, in my opinion, is pretty terrible though.  And the path you are allowed to follow is extremely limited.  That does detract from the fun story aspects a bit, so I only give this one a rating of "Eh, it's ok" whereas if the combat system had been done a little better I might actually call it a good game.
Story:  good stuff.
Combat:  terrible, though the stealth assassination style is amusing for a little while.
Still worth playing?  Sure, if you can get it for just a few bucks.  Don't shell out big money for this one though.
If you try this one and enjoy it, consider another game in the series:  "Styx: Master of Shadows" which as of writing this I still have not played.

Of Orcs and Men is a game with some interesting ideas but ultimatly fails in a whole lot more areas than it actually succeeds, which seems to be a common theme with this developer as I'm playing through their games... Anyways let's get to it shall we?
I've had to rewrite this section actually because originally I had a big rant about the combat here but it took way too many characters and didn't leave much room for the other stuff in this review, you can still
, anyways here's the short and to the point version
The combat is pretty bad, and playing on harder difficulties only makes it worse, you control 2 characters, a big warrior orc and a small rogue goblin, they both have unique abilites that you select from a weird wheel which slows time when it pops up as you press the space key, suffice to say it's quite clunky because the game doesn't know if it wants to be turn based or real time and it's just this really weird "strategic" combat as a result
It's a very clunky system that feels unpolished, you can't dodge / block damage in a straightforward way, it's all up to some stats and RNG, same for your enemies blocking / countering / dodging and the stupid rage mechanic for your big orc character (I go into more detail about that on the longer version) and you're always overwhelmed in numbers which limit a lot your options since only a few skills can be upgraded to be uninterruptable because the enemies interrupt most of your other attacks by hitting you
A lot of encounters devolved into me using the goblin character running around in circles to avoid enemies to revive the big orc, getting 1-2 hits with him, dying and getting revived again over and over again until everyone was dead, sometimes they got hits on the goblin aswell and if he died it got even worse by the two characters reviving each other all the time and barely getting any hits in to kill the enemies, but you have to play as only 1 character in some sections which can make things even more frustrating
You can also use stealth to 1 hit K.O dudes with your goblin before you get spotted and it's a very useful way of thinning the enemies ranks before you inevitably have to face them in "real" combat, but there are a lot of fights triggered by cutscenes or with enemy placement which you can't stealth your way out of so there's that

So yeah, safe to say I'm not really happy with the combat at all, it's pure ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t a lot of times and I haven't been frustrated like this with a game in a long time, the real kicker is that you know what you do for like 90% of the whole game? Just go through straight corridors walking very slowly as a big fat orc (or a small goblin) until you get into slightly bigger rooms with a bunch of dudes in them, kill them all, go through another corridor, get to another slightly bigger room, rinse and repeat until you get to the objective at the end of the map, for the whole game, it seriously takes its toll upon you and the first time I played this game was for around 1-2 hours, but I really thought I've been playing for the whole day, serisouly it felt like an eternity, this game's combat really grinds upon your very soul and the only real exploration is that there's maybe a slightly shorter branching corridor which leads to another big room with lots of dudes in it and some loot, or you get a sidequest from an NPC in one of the hub areas and you go through the exact same formula of going through corridors and then big rooms again
The story while it may seem interesting at times, but it's pretty meh, there's nothing really all that special about it, I think the main thing here is that it's different in a way not many other games explore because you play as Orcs and Goblins which usually are the evil bad guys and all that, but yeah this time around the humans are evil and conquered almost all the orcs and enslaved them, you're in control of an orc named Arkail, a strong elite warrior which is part of the Bloodjaws clan on a crazy suicide mission to kill the human emperor and hopefully make things better for his kin, and also Styx, a goblin rogue type character helping him along the way
The voice acting is a mixed bag as usual with this developer and the same can be said about the characters, some can be pretty likeable like Styx which is probably one of the reasons he's got his own game which maybe I'll try at some point and then there are your generic villains or the twist which you could see from a mile away near the end
But ultimatly the story is just that, it has a nice / different coat of paint with it's setting, I'll have to admit that's what kept me going but it's pretty average and I didn't feel any real sense of satisfaction after completing it (aside from being free from the horrifying combat maybe) and at no point I really felt invested or cared for any of the characters, the only real fun one is Styx to be quite honest, the others vary on the spectrum from fine to stereotypical trope "x" or "y" character
You have some choices but few actually matter, a lot of it it the same whatever you choose with some differences only being like a line of dialogue, the bigger changes / minor consequences are a result of sidequests if you wish to go for those
All in all I'd have to say that while it's different it's a pretty mediocre game, you're doing the same thing for pretty much all of it i.e the "Exploration" section from this review and sadly that same thing is just not all that fun to do, maybe the story might intrigue you in some way but I wouldn't hold by breath on it, it's sad to say this because this game did have some cool potential but it just didn't come to fruition, honestly don't bother with this one, but if you REALLY want to give it a go for whatever reason at least do yoruself a favor and wait to pick it up on sale

Wildstar in my opinion deserves more respect than it gets. But also could have used a team of quality assurance people to make sure their new ideas launch without a hitch.
This game FEELS like the kind of game that the devs had fun making. It feels like they poured in good, bad, and sometimes ugly ideas and their criteria was 'That sounds fun'.
If you give this game a chance, you'll find it flawed, but coming in you'll also have fun.
That's why I nomitated it for 'The No Apologies' award.
