(I would first like to preface this review by saying that despite any technical troubles this game may currently suffer from, you would be doing yourself a disservice by not giving this game a shot.  I don't condone the fact that Square Enix seems content with leaving the game as is for those with problems, and I feel bad for Platinum having to shoulder the blame, but I personally didn't have any big problems playing it and getting good performance, and you can always refund it if you have major problems.)
Nier: Automata is a breakthrough moment in gaming.  I can only recall one other game that married its gameplay, soundtrack, and story so effectively together to deliver such a masterclass gaming experience, and that would be Undertale.  This is high praise considering how Undertale shook the gaming world, but comparing this game to it is far from unreasonable.  Yoko Taro will go down in gaming history as one of the greatest directors of his time, alongside titans such as Hideo Kojima and Shigeru Miyamoto.  Nier's balance of fluid and effortlessly stylish combat, haunting and evocative musical accompaniment, and brutally resonating, emotional storytelling is a recipe for one of the most compelling experiences in all of gaming.
Controlling your character feels responsive and tight, and combat never feels like a chore thanks to its diversity.  The game delights in surprising the player with its variety, as one moment you could be hacking and slashing away at enemies in a ballet of swords, then participating in a twin-stick shooter the next moment, and finally a bullet-hell style hacking minigame.  Yet, these changes in style, both bold and sometimes subtle (like forcing the camera to shift to a new perspective to nudge you into playing differently) never feel like they don't fit in the flow of the game.  Every part of the game strives to make sense of the mad mixture of styles by making each style contribute to the other, and tying them all very closely to a story context.  Never will you be doing an action in Nier that does not have some impact or relevance to the lore or story, which you will eventually care about deeply.  In this way, many of the quests are given more weight and pertinence to the player's actions, making the fun gameplay its own kind of rudimentary reward beside the payoff of learning some new piece of information about the fascinating world of Nier and its characters.
Its characters as well, really are the stars of the show.  It's been hundreds of years since an alien-led invasion of Earth left the planet inhospitable, forcing mankind to flee to the moon.  The aliens employed machines to fight for them, and humanity in turn, made androids to fight this proxy war and hopefully regain their former home.  The war is not going well for humanity, and it has been raging longer than anyone can remember.  Androids in a central stronghold called the Bunker, as well as those left on Earth as part of a resistance movement, try to eek out some sort of life amidst the neverending conflict.  Likewise, the machines they fight against, while initially simplistic and seemingly mindless, begin to take on human characteristics such as seeing eachother as family, getting angry over the death of a friend, or pondering existence itself; blurring the lines between the machines and more emotive androids.
In no time at all, making you care about the fates of friend and foe alike becomes the game's bread and butter, and lends an added weight to all of the tragic conflict unfolding on-screen.  Nier Is a sad tale, steeped in melancholic moments of humanity for characters that are, by all accounts, not human.  The world is an endless war, and both sides feel the fatigue and sorrow of waging it.  It's compelling and heartbreaking in a way few games dare to be, and it will leave you thinking and feeling long after the credits roll.  Nier has a lot of story to tell though, and even after the initial cedits, the game will drastically change things up as you progress to each "New Game+".  It paces itself so that the story, the stakes, and all of the beautiful moments are continually raised to greater heights as you progress.  The game also finds ways to radically shake your expectations the further you delve into it, and masterfully prevents you from getting too comfortable with any currently established gameplay pattern or story breakthrough.
All of these moments are brought to life by a musical score that is ever-changing and consistently enthralling.  Nearly every piece of music is unique and has multiple versions of itself, with vocals ranging from French to English to Spanish, played at exactly the right moment to help reinforce the emotions or scenery on display.  Not enough can be said about Nier's masterful use of audio and music to make its world believable and so unforgettable.  While in the middle of a discussion with an NPC, if the tone in the conversation shifts to a more sad or ponderous one from the initial harmless small-talk, the background music will shift from a cheery melody into a slow acoustic guitar accompanied by wistful French vocals.  At all moments, Nier knows exactly what it wants to convey and make you feel, and its audio design perfectly accompanies its multifaceted world every step of the way.
Truly, Nier: Automata makes such a lasting and deep impression that it can be hard to let go even once you've finished all that it offers.  After it has left you emotionally devastated and absolutely captivated, with its subject matter so fascinating and endearing, you will only wish you could forget it all so you could experience it once again from fresh eyes.  Nier: Automata, despite what you may preconceive about it as a game, will absolutely astonish you and take your breath away in unexpected ways.  You will let down your guard while playing this game, and it will plant itself in your mind like a seed waiting to sprout into something utterly ineffable, and you won't ever be able to forget it.

A game that understands the player, and uses its entire design to promote both its understanding of player experience and atmosphere. Contests with The Stanley Parable in making player choice contextualized in a way that matters and acknowledges the player's motivation without compromising it, unlike many Triple-A titles that garner more praise. A truly amazing game, and one worth playing at any cost. If more games were like Deadly Premonition, the world would be a better place.
Unlike almost any game before it (with the exceptions of The Stanley Parable and Demon's Souls), Deadly Premonition understands the unique and powerful triad of Player, Character, and Narrator. At no point in the game is any of these functions invalidated.
Many users comment on how "weird" the game is, or how the graphics are outdated or the controls clunky, and this is important. The game's major aesthetic is that exact cognitive function: It means to play like a PS2 game, look like a PS2 game, and even ape PS2 games. Secretly, though It does all of these things the best way possible: By actually constructing and improving upon the foundation it attempts to make fun of. Deadly Premonition is the unique and rare game that actually constructs on, as opposed to strictly deconstructs, what came before. You may hate the controls, and you may think the graphics are outdated, but if any of these things were changed its own aesthetic would clash with itself. These choices were deliberate, intelligent mirrors for the game's internal design and direction.
Deadly Premonition is surprisingly one of the most intelligent games I've ever played. No matter how strange, unexpected, or uncomfortable it might be it is a game that understands what games can do. It fully utilizes the medium, and for that, it deserves a perfect score.

Quite simply a better version of the Panzer Corps system. If you liked that, you'll very likely enjoy Order of Battle: Pacific. The inclusion of air and sea units really mixes up your tactical options and makes it feel like a whole new game. You can soften up land units with your ships before doing a beach landing. The addition of supply also adds another new layer and something to be considered. You can't just charge ahead into enemy territory without risking being cut off. So, a bit more of everything without tipping over into being bogged down by too much detail or too many dry and unnecessary mechanics.
I'd say this is very much a game for those who like the idea of wargames but are put off by the larger scope of the more traditional and more 'serious' type of wargame. When you get right down to it, it really is just a medium weight puzzle game with a military coat of paint.
While I like Panzer Corps, I always felt a little intimated by it. Strangely, while being slightly more complex, OABP feels much more accessible, more varied and more immediately fun. Strongly recommended to those who like the idea of wargames but don't want to cross over into the deep and serious territory. Easily worth its full asking price.

Great panzer-general-like (or pacific-general-like, both apply :p) tactical wargame. After 9 hours, I just finished the tutorial campaign, taking my time to achieve all secondary objectives, it's a long time since I had some much fun playing a wargame :)
A little more in details :
+ solid gameplay, a bit generic/usual for this kind of games, but with a few nice innovations/twists (flanking, officers, engagement distance at sea and so on)
+ supply "management"
+ a tutorial campaign (but see below)
+ upgradable core units which follow you through the campaign
+ secondary objectives can have some impacts on the following missions
+ nice graphics and animations, good sounds
+ good manual, clear and precise
- the tutorial is a bit on the short side regarding explanations (reading the manual is thus strongly recommended), and on the long side regarding the length (as I said, it took me 9 hours to complete it, even if it was by taking my time, so to speak)
- music does the job, but remains very  generic
- frequent slowdowns when it's computer turn
- I wish there was some cohesion bonuses (keeping formations at sea, keeping infantry "groups" together), but nope (probably a bit tough to simulate at this level)
- I think the supply system could have been better
- no move undo : on a couple of times, I messed up (clicking too fast) what I wanted to do ... in such a case, you need to reload the last save : an undo would have been nice as long as you did not bump into an enemy.
Overall, the cons are very minor, and it's a very pleasant wargame to play, definitely recommended !

Should you buy this game?  It looks good, right?  Nice graphics, interesting Steampunk setting, turn based strategy with a sense of polish and big-budget production.  What could possibly go wrong?
Sadly, you need to turn round and walk away.  This game isn't just bad, its a tragedy.  Angels cry black, bloody tears at the state of this hot mess.  Keep your money in your pocket and remind yourself 'all that glitters is not gold.'
Ladies and Gentlemen, this game is a STINKER.
But you don't believe me.  Of course not.  I'm just some scrub on the internet, so why should you?  You're going to need some convincing.  So here goes.
First off, this game has  a great setting, a great game engine with interesting game mechanics.  The story is polished and reasonably well written (for a computer game.)  In short, it has a lot going for it.  Clearly a lot of time and effort was spent getting the look, feel and mechanics of the game right.  This is the heart of the tragedy, because it should have been a tremendous game and a runaway success.  But some very, very stupid mistakes in the process of development have utterly ruined the experience for the player.
The two biggest mistakes were these:  the game was made to be played as a multiplayer game, and the initial price of the game was staggeringly high (about twice the price of a full-price game.)  I don't understand these decisions.
First off, no one ever, ever, EVER plays strategy games in multiplayer.  They don't because each match is a huge investment in time and effort and no one wants an opponent to rage quit on them just as they've put forty minutes into beating them.  Strategy games do not lend themselves to competitive multiplayer.  Put it another way, unless you are Blizzard and make Starcraft, you have no chance of marketing your strategy game as a multiplayer product.  Everyone knows this.  Just ask your marketing dept. to run the numbers.  Its a law as old as the Ten Commandments.  No one ever plays strategy games online.
Second, if you absolutely must make a strategy game online, to stand any chance of it being played you have to make it free-to-play.  Get as many people into your user base as early as possible, then do microtransactions.  It still won't work, but its the only way to gain a modicum of success.  Instead, Warmachine Tactics had a phenomenal, eye-watering price tag on it when released that basically guaranteed the user base would be tiny.  Sure, the price has dropped now, but the damage was done.  People saw the price and balked.  No momenturm, no user-base.  End of story.
But wait - there's a single-player component, right?  There are missions and everything.  So what's all this about being multiplayer only?
This is the most baffling thing.  Having hired phenomenally talented artists and developed an expensive, clever game engine with good story development, the developers went cheap on level-design.  Having decided the game was multiplayer, why bother hiring talented level designers for single player?  Instead they've farmed it out to hacks that have produced some of the most inept, incompetent, lazy level development I've ever seen in a game with this budget.  The single player game isn't just bad.  Its gone down in history as a legend of 'how not to do it,'
The tutorial level is comically bad.  The game is years old, is still being developed in fact, and yet no one has bothered to fix the tutorial mission.  It cannot be completed.  Its broken.  The most important level of this game - the level that introduces new players into the game, develops its concepts and is supposed to show the promise of what the game holds - does not work.   What's more, the developers know it doesn't work.  They've known for years it doesn't work.  But they've never fixed it - because its part of the single-player campaign, so why should they care?  New players have to muddle-through and work around it.
Some of the level design is so bad its laughable.  Clearly the level designer was having a lot of fun when he made these levels.  He clearly assumed no one would be playing the game single-player, so why not just mess around with the format a little?  The result is a weird Curate's Egg of level design.  The levels are never straightforward, having weird twists in them that are impossible to follow and lead to massive confusion.  Weird arbitrary things happen.  A level fails when your armies morale is broken in some levels, but not on others.  There is no measure of unit morale for the player to see - it just happens apparently randomly.  That's strange.  But its comparatively acceptable compared to some level design decisions.
My favorite one is offering multiple exits to a level, but only one of them works.  The one that works is hidden behind terrain so the player can't see it.  Cue a confused mess with the player running around in all directions trying to find the way out, being slaughtered along the way like a blood-soaked Benny Hill chase.
You'll need an internet connection to play this game.  Not because the game needs the internet, but because you'll need to be constantly logged into the discussion forums to find out what the Hell you have to do to complete each level.  Where is the exit?  What is the end-level condition?  What machines am I supposed to destroy?  The weird thing is, its not meant to be difficult - the level designer just never considered that someone would actually be playing his levels so he didn't bother testing them to see if they were at all playable.  They're just carbuncles stuck on to what was meant to be a multiplayer game.
Except no one plays it in multiplayer.  The game is dead.  Even stranger, the developers have doubled down on the multiplayer side.  Even though no one plays it as a multiplayer game, all the DLC is multiplayer only.  The broken single player levels are never fixed.  Its total madness.
I've said enough.  Either you've got the gist by now, or you never will.  This game does not deserve your money.  From the moment of its inception it was destined to fail.  In a universe where Starcraft II exists, there is no place for this game.
Save your money and mourn its passing.

This is my first Borderlands game, and to be honest, I think it's awesome. Now, some people might think that starting right in the middle of something can be confusing, and I agree (I did have to do some reading about some of the characters), but even then, the game does a great job at storytelling, since you get to know the characters and all. While I wasn't too familiar with the Borderlands universe, I did know about Handsome Jack, and it's nice to see how a person with noble goals descends into villainy; and it isn't just a "he's a good guy who becomes crazy with power", there's different events throughout the storyline that start showing his true nature.
Like I mentioned above, the storytelling is pretty good. The main story seems somewhat short when you think about it, with a few missions that feel like filler; mostly because of all the walking around, not so much the writing, which is great, with lots of hilarious dialogues, and some serious ones when the situation demands it. If there's something I enjoyed about the writing is that; it can easily go from the characters making jokes and such, to a really dark moment, and it still feels natural. The game also has tons of side missions, which unlock as you progress through the storyline, and offer some more gameplay (as well as some great rewards, depending on the mission).
The level design is mostly good, with great open areas, and some really cool visuals. Still, there's a few sections (mostly during main story missions) that feel like they were designed in order to extend the game time, as there's lots of going back and forth in order to open a few doors. Also, while most of the large maps have vehicles for you to use, there's one near the end of the game that's really big as well, but doesn't have any vehicle station, which means you must walk around.
Now let's talk weapons. From what I know of Borderlands, this game is practically Diablo with guns, or a shoot 'n' loot, as the game says. That means that a great deal of the gameplay involves killing enemies, finding better weapons and gear, and so on, until you can defeat stronger enemies, to get even better loot, all the way up until you finally get a broken♥♥♥♥♥combination of loot, which you'll then proceed to show off on the Internet. It's a good system, I'd say, especially when you defeat some tough boss and see all that sweet, sweet loot dropping from them. And the variety is impressive: from pistols and submachine gus, to laser weapons with different elemental effects, not to mention the legendaries and uniques, which have their own quirks (I love Miss Moxxi's Vibra-Pulse, for example).
The soundtrack is mostly ambient sound, which changes depending on the situation (combat or exploration), it's good enough, but it's not something you'll pay a lot of attention to.
As far as playable characters go, there's four of them, at least in the vanilla game: Athena, Wilhelm, Nisha and Claptrap. I haven't played Wilhelm and Nisha that much, but their skill trees seem interesting. When it comes to Athena, she's easily my favourite character, her Aspis shield is great for soaking up damage and throwing it back at the enemies, and one of her skill trees greatly improves elemental damage. And Claptrap, well, he's fun to play, but the randomness of his action skill can sometimes be frustrating.
Well, I think I've written a fair bit about Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel. There's a lot more I could write, but this review looks long enough. To sum everything up: get this game, because it's awesome.
It's not much more than a big expansion pack for Borderlands 2. It feels lackluster and empty in comparison and should only be played if you want more Borderlands.

in the end it was a coin toss, literally, head said 'not recommended'. shame steam doesnt have a neutral recommendation.
for me, it was a slightly enjoyable experience with a lot of frustration. mind you, not exactly my genre - i like rpgs and can enjoy action titles with some kind of character development but i was on the edge with this one the whole time.
so i will enumerate my laments (he-he) but keep in mind that the game has some nice features too, but you should read about them in the 'recommended' reviews. i will not even try to seem objective, not my, heh, objective (i know, goal, aim etc).
-well its more or less hack 'n slash, im not much for it, but it cant be helped, i wasnt the target audience. but for me it seemed that at least the half of the many attacks/abilities were only to fill the place. in a good game there should be purpose or at least a niche for every one. balance?
-the maps were very linear, also a bane of the genre so i shouldnt criticize the game for it but i do, and even more so when i just run through half of the map for nothing, no loot, no enemies.
-maybe the creators were so proud of their product that they wanted to show off the scenery but although there were some eye catching design elements the graphics were not very convincing for a 2012 game.
-the voice acting was superb most of the time but there were a few clear miscasts eg raven. also if you have to wait for your mate every 2 minutes, there should have been a greater variety of clips reminding you, i was both annoyed by the fact that my buddy was too back for the games taste and also by the message telling me so.
-btw, if i want to explore the (not too big) map with styx slahing throats here and there maybe i shouldnt have have to wait for ark at the door of every second room. hey, some freedom? some immersion or something?
-music was nice, atmospheric but forgettable. nothing to criticize here and nothing to remember, did its job.
-i dont see why almost all good items were placed in the first act. after that i picked up a few here and there but very few really more useful, i mostly did it for variety. balance?
-i still cant understand why developers think that its a good idea to make those who ultimately pay their salaries watch their logos every time the game is started. its an old grievance of mine and im certain im not alone with this. remember dawn of war (the first one)? you had to watch the intros for the first time (and it was sooo cool), after that, you could skip it. if you cant achieve that, let me skip it the first time. i didnt pay to suffer, thanks.
-ah, you say, why dont you just alttab from the game instead of quitting? that way you can minimize your watching them again. and again. and again. 1. sometimes after alttabbing the music stays on, so you have to mute it and then unmute it, doable of course but inconvinient; 2. once i couldnt manually save after coming back from desktop. but of course i didnt know that was the reason, i thought the game is screwing with me not letting me save (in a way it did), and that was the first time i almost uninstalled it as i had to fight through some hard battles and when i died i had to start anew from much further. alttabbing btw: they still did much better job than bethesda - they cant solve this conundrum (among others) since morrowind (2002!)...
-ah, battles? you have a map where you p1ss blood to survive (and i dont mean bosses) and the next five is cakewalk. again, balance?
-i felt i spent too much time watching cutscenes. dont misunderstand me, i like meself a good story but it seemed to me sometimes that i have to watch 5 minutes of cutscenes to play the same amout of time. maybe i just wanted to get over with this game to start another with better entertainment/frustration ratio, i dont know, i generally like these story elements.
-you cannot skip all cutscenes. im at the endgame where i failed twice miserably and i have to watch half of the damned talking to try again, and of course no saves between battles. thanks, devs. im not sure im willing to do it more than 1 or 2 times more and however i hate to leave a game unfinished, especially so close to its ending theres a good chance that i will in this case.
all in all with some polishing and playtesting, balancing the powers/items/battles this could have been a much better title.

now, despite all the criticism above, dont be (completely) disheartened: this game have some nice features and might be much more entertaining for you than it was for me. if you love the genre and you feel you can forgive the problems above, go give it a try. i almost gave it a 'slightly recommended' but the coin thought otherwise.

Deadly Premonition is my favorite game of the entire generation.
It's plot, characters and setting are just that engaging every time you come back you still have a great time.
The story may sound familiar if you have watched twin peaks in that a girl is murdered in a small town out in the boondocks of america and its up to FBI Special Agent Francis York Morgan to solve the crime (Call him york by the way, everyone does) but as he arrives in the small town of Greenvale things are not what they seem
with strange phenomenon involving red seeds and a legend of a killer in a red raincoat that only appears on rainy nights.
The game bursts and ozzs with personality and charm from the music that plays in the opening menu to the way that York interacts with Zach (his special friend) about b-movies.
The directors cut that was originally released on PS3 boasts a new scenes that expand the games ending and also tell the story in a different way.
The PC version however brings very little to the table by only offering halloween themed suits for York, Emily, The Raincoat Killer and a car skin and even though the game now runs past 30FPS it just doesn't feel right at that speed as it feels to fast...
Another issue is that since the directors cut features reworked movement it feels clunky on the pc without a controller while if it used the original versions tank style controls (which I actually liked) then maybe it wouldn't feel so wierd on PC.
The last issue that I have that wasn't addressed in the directors cut is the timing of certain music I will give you an example You're examing a dead body and this forboding unerving music is playing then suddenly it changes to light hearted jazz I will admit I got a laugh out of it the first time around and this is the only time I can really remember this happening.
All complaints aside
Deadly Premonition: The Director's Cut is a game that you have to own
Everything about it feels right and it was the game to renew my faith that games can exceed the bar in many aspects without needing multiplayer, graphics with volumetric lighting (otherwise known as WANK)
You are a fool to dismiss such a fine game and even more of a fool to insult it

I've played this game for just over 100 hours, and I've played it almost since it was released in beta.
I have enjoyed playing this game many times, despite the early glitches, bugs and various other issues. The game got better as time went on - it's in beta so it's expected that problems will occur.
However, it's been in beta for around a year now and recently they've started adding randow new components to the game rather than fixing the existing issues. For example there are 4 different currencies in the game which you use to buy various different things. It's incredibly confusing!
New Champions are ridiculously OP when they get released and often they haven't been nerfed so early champions are weaker to play.
There is also something else that's incredibly irritating about the game, that has existed since it was first made. When you pick a champion, you have an amount of time to pick and customise. However, you can change the selected champion at any time, and often people will change from say a tank or healer to something else in the last second, which completely ruins the team as you now don't have one of these positions filled. If you quit out of these games so that you can play with a decent team, you get a deserter penalty - all from someone else messing up the game. It used to be a few minutes but they've made it ridiculous now. I'm now on a 30 minute deserter penalty because I quit a game when someone changed at last second - it happens every other game. Why they haven't used the league of legends lock in system is beyond me.
If you don't got as a tank or healer you're screwed because 4/5 times no one else on your team will go as one so you're stuck playing a really boring role and champion just so you don't lose.
Gameplay wise is fine, there's not much to say. If you have a good team you win, if you don't you lose. There's no close call or "almost won" game, you either do amazing or awful, and there's no inbetween.
For those reason, I don't currently reccomend the game, as it seems like they just want to squeeze the players for money.
September Patch Edit: The game got worse... they nerfed Torvald and other decent champions, they added ridiculously op new champions with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ artwork and unimaginative abilities, they changed the style of onslaught to add a pointless overtime which makes absolutely no sense and drags out the games until everyone gets so bored they just want it to be over.

The first Borderlands was a surprise for myself. I typically don't like dungeon crawlers but, combined with FPS mechanics and a unique personality, I thoroughly enjoyed Borderlands. When the sequel came out, I thought it addressed most of my complaints with the first game and is still one of the funniest games I have ever played; I played and loved the crap out of it.
With the first 2 games, I didn't want them to end. With this game, I couldn't wait for it to be over.
This game bothered the hell out of me. I would say it actually tarnished my enjoyment of the series itself. It was such a shadow of its predecessors. It really felt like 2K Australia had no idea what made the first 2 games special. Everything felt like a ripoff of itself – from the vault hunters to the supporting cast to the humor.
And it bears repeating: this game is not funny. Some of the lines – as they were written – COULD have MAYBE been funny, but the voice acting (and direction, most likely) was terrible. This has nothing to do with the accents – I think non-American accents are a good change of pace. The problem was that there was no personality in the characters or the delivery; they never felt like characters – just people reading a script. It was like the writers collected a list of funny things from the other games and said, “Lets just do that again! Super funny, right?!” Super disappointing.
The gravity mechanics were okay at best. What they did, more than anything, was turn Borderlands into a slow, imprecise platformer. I rarely found the slam damage helpful versus weapons (you can't jump ON people for damage, just next to them?!). I died more from jumping where I shouldn't than I ever did from enemies. Not my idea of a good time.
There were so many once-thought-extinct annoyances like invisible walls, tiny inclines that you couldn't walk over, floors that aren't actually solid, and see-though spaces that you can't shoot through. Apparently, this game was designed in 1996. I kept saying/screaming to myself, “Did ANYONE playtest this thing?!?!”
While I can't definitively say that all Borderlands fans wouldn't like this game – it's obviously got its supporters – coming from this Borderlands fan, I just can't recommend it. Maybe it's more palatable with 3 other people; I've primarily played solo. If you're a crazy-mega-fan (I'm a fan, but didn't really dabble much in any UVHM/post-game content), you'll likely find things to enjoy here. It's more Borderlands, but mostly in name only. Temper your expectations.
A bit wild with the story, and more of what the second game had, expect a little more than a smidge of fun.

If it wasn't clear at first, this game is a bridge between Borderlands 1 and Borderlands 2. In a sense, the whole game itself is just a huge DLC to fill in some plot holes. It's much shorter than Borderlands 2 and... well, less Borderlands-y, I guess? The main source of negative feedback from this game, I think, stems from the fact that it was released after Borderlands 2. If this game was released in chronological order, it would've made the series a lot stronger as a whole, since I believe it's stronger than Borderlands 1 but weaker than 2. Most of the negative reviews are by players who loved Borderlands 2, so it makes sense this game's a bit of a disappointment for them. Looking past that tinted lens, though, the game IS really fun. If you're new to the Borderlands series, definitely play them in their chonological order, 1, Pre-Sequel, then 2. You'll get the most fun out of all 3 that way.
On it's own, it's a pretty solid game. It's really only bad when compared to Borderlands 2, but compared to other Shooters and RPGs, it's definitely a great pick. And even if you loved Borderlands 2 and have doubts about this one, just trust me that it's more than worth buying if you're even a low-key fan of the Borderlands series. If you ask me, the game is perfect, as in, no flaws or anything missing, however so was Borderlands 2, and it just happened to have way more content. The DLC is... okay... 2K got shut down for some reason soon after this game's release, so they didn't get to add much, so only buy the Season Pass if it's on sale if you want to try it out. But it's still fun without it. It has a New Game+ feature which does a little bit more than just make the enemies harder, and lets you continue leveling up your characters... Sadly you can only do a Plus run with a character you've already beaten the normal mode with, which is fair I suppose.
Tl;Dr the game is extremely well-made and fun on its own, the only way anyone makes it look bad or gives it negative reviews is by comparing it to Borderlands 2. If you're a fan of the series, definitely get it, and if you're new, get it and then play through the series in chronological order.

Let me start with the cons:
- The game has just rudimentary systems and gameplay. The stats don't matter for the most part and only few skills open up new combat strategies. Most numbers and stats are not important (+5% dodge or +10% dodge? +2 Mind or +2 Stamina? Doesn't really matter).
- The level design is very linear, there is nothing to explore. Regardless of whether you are in the catacombs, the forest or the monastery, all levels are just corridors.
- The quest design is similarly simplistic. There are only a few sidequests and they don't really matter. There are almost no choices and consequences. In the middle of the game there is one interesting series of choices but there is no sign later whether it changes anything. The game plays more like a linear adventure with stat-based combat than an RPG.
Despite that I recommend the game. Why?
- The main characters are what drew me forward. Arkail and Styx are superbly written and voiced. As you play on, their relationship develops and they both confront their past. Styx especially is wonderfully sarcastic and misanthropic and it never grows stale, even until the final cutscene.
- The music is wonderful.
- The environment styles are also nice (apart from the catacombs, those were boring). Especially in the later parts of the game.
I found the gameplay in Bound By Flame, Mars: War Logs and Of Orcs And Men similarly repetitive. But this was the most compelling game of the three for me, mostly because of the two protagonists, whose story I wanted to see till the end.

After years of playing repeating MMOs (grind grind grind) My friends and I finally found a game that put the adventure back. This game gives you nothing, you will have to earn it. It's not that hard to figure out and you will love the rewards x10 compared to the other games that are now days making it to easy. No you wont get to power level. You cant buy your way in. Your gonna get dropped into a world face first with a compass and a few supplies to get you by. Its getting dark outside so you better run to a city. But wait, you hear a wolf growl from the bushes, you start to run but you are bitten in the leg. Turning your back WU gives the wolf a advantage since you turned. Secondly it not just , you took 23 damage please heal, oh no its WAY more detailed. Your gonna need to find some cotton and bandage that wound. But it also depends on where the wound is and what type. You see your right leg is bleeding out and infection is sure to come. This game is ok on graphics and fighting, but the hidden treasure is in the details. Theres a skill for everything you can think of, sometimes  branches of 2 to 3 skills for one thing. Anytime you make something, your skill effects the quality. You got to get to know people and trade, because you dont have npc shops that sell stuff, only venders owned by players. I'll have to say I am alittle spooked sometimes, the game seems to have some witchcraft in it. It has gods to choose from, altars, animal sacrificing,ect. You can also breed animals, groom them, tame them, sell them, eat them, ride them. Any trade you can think of is in the game and broken down into many parts and it wont be easy. But after you put in the time to be the best at that niche people start coming to you and buying. I went from rock bottom to having a nice little town in about 3 weeks. But in that time I dug dug and dug and my friends dug and we sold the dirt to some rich guy down the street. He needs the dirt for building. We started out with a little hand cart that carried 40 dirt a trip. After becoming friends with the guy, he built us a large cart and then a wagon capable of hauling 3600 dirt. We bought some land and hired some guards that now run around and kill those wolfs. I'd have to call it more of a simulator then a game. It could use some work on the graphics end, but im thinking thats why I dont have hardly any lag issues. I also don't see alot of bugs. Yeah there must be a few, but for all the stuff thats going on in this game they have really put alot of work into making it solid.

The Bad:
- Second playthrough repetitive, yet required to proceed to third playthrough that completes the story.
- Repetitive hacking mini-game played a large part in the game after the first playthrough.
- Mediocre writing. While I enjoyed some of the narrative ideas, I found much of the dialogues unnatural and emotions unbelievable. And I just could not warm up to all the biblical nonsense.
- You could easily complete the game using the starting default weapons (with a few upgrades). While there are many hidden weapons throughout the game, they offer no significant benefit.
The Ugly:
- MMO style fetch quests everywhere. Lots of running around for a few lines of semi-witty writing as reward. My recommendation is to skip the side quests altogether.

I'll let IGN explain it ...
"Imagine if you took the complete script from David Lynch’s Twin Peaks television series, translated it into Japanese, then translated it back into English, then had a drunk friend read it to you from the passenger seat of your car while they clumsily flicked between obscure jazz radio stations that intermittently fluctuated in volume."

I've never played Panzer Corps, so I can't review the game from that angle.  As a computer war game, I'd say this is an enjoyable, somewhat light offering that does a good job with what SPI used to call chrome back in the days of paper and cardboard gaming.
There are quite a few elements that make the game feel almost like an arcade offering, such as having torpedo planes "reload" in flight, and getting rewards in the way of upgrade/reinforcement points for capturing objectives.  To my eye, the simple 1 through 10 step ratings of units seems un-grog,
To balance this, traditional concepts like zones of control, bonuses for supported attacks, and supply considerations are present.  It's an odd balance, but with the relatively pleasing graphical presentation that does a good job of imparting the right PTO flavor, it works.  It feels enough like a serious war game to give it a little heft, despite some of the lighter elements.  No one is going to mistake this game for a Grigsby monster, but it's not a History Channel offering, either.
Replayablilty seems a little suspect, but there are secondary objectives that will allow for slightly different outcomes.  It could be argued that between the boot camp, US and Japanese campaign and multiplayer options even a once through would give enough game for the asking price, but without knowing how moddable the basic package is I can't say it's going to give endless hours of service without growing stale, but that's asking a lot of any game.
I'm having fun with it, the learning curve isn't too steep for the casual wargamer, and it's substantial enough to make you feel like you are playing a "real" wargam while being light enough to keep things moving right along.
Reccomended  as good casual fun for the serious grognard, or as a dip into deeper waters for those who think of Risk as being pretty complicated.

Deadly Premonition can be best described with the old adage, "Don't judge a book by its cover". At first glance it’s a clunky RE4 clone with bland combat  that looks more at home in 1999 on the Dreamcast than a modern console or PC. But if you play past the first area you’d start to see what makes the game truly great and why its become such a beloved cult classic, its writing. DP’s cast is a gaggle of lovable goofballs with all their own weird quirks, most prominent of all being the protagonist, York, who loves spending time shooting the♥♥♥♥♥♥with his imaginary friend named Zach about John Hughes movies and The Ramones, divining the future through  the morning coffee, or going around town staring into people‘s windows.  It’s no secret that DP is practically Twin Peaks: The Game and it wears it love for that show and all kind of 80‘s pop culture on  its sleeve. The plot is actually rather good too considering and it actually gets pretty damn dark but it somehow all works because the game’s characters are likable enough for you to care. DP is just a game full of enthusiastic charm and it has a creativity that most AAA games lack. If you can look past the dated graphics and  sloggy combat you’ll find an endearing game in all its honest B-movie cheese.
Be warned though that this port isn’t all that great, but the same dude that patched Dark Souls is on the case and it looks like with his help this will be the definitive version of the game. So if you’re a bit on the fence wait until that comes out before buying it which shouldn’t be too long.

Hell, I would probably end up writing a sequel. There is just so much going on in this game that one book simply couldn't content everything that needs to be said about Deadly Premonition.
There are lot of great games out there, but in my view there is only about 3 games that have ever gone far and beyond and pushed what a game really is capable of being. A game that changes the way you will look at games. A game that makes you realize what a fantastic medium games can be, if it's utilized for more than simply being another entertainment form to ultimately make you pass time. A game that ruins gaming.

The Resident Evil series has had its ups and its downs from the greats of  the franchise like 2,3 Code Veronica and 4 to the worst entries (survivor,0,5 Raccoon city and 6) but this game is definately a decent entry and probably the only entry since darkside chronicles that is actually fun to play.
The story of the game is basically that Jill Valentine is trying to find her partner Chris "steroid junkie" Redfield who has mysteriously gone missing. This game also takes place before 5 although some things like Jills older look (though I guess that you could put that down to the fact that the game was originally done on a Nintendo console) and some of the technology available like the fact of a city built on the water are hard to believe because of the timeline.
The gameplay is a lot like that of 6 in the fact that you can move whie aiming but with the restraints of 4 in terms of melee combat. There is also a dodge feature that Jill originally had in 3 but it isn't as reliable as that one as you can never be too sure if it is going to register properly and this can be a problem as some of the enemies and bosses play out that you can damage them by dodging them when they go to charge at you whic will leave them open to attack.
You can only carry a total of three guns at one time and ammo is actually scarce if you play on normal and if you feel up to the challenge, infernal. The upgrade system for guns is also back but you can never really upgrade them enough to think that you can kill everything and still complete the game with loads of ammo for every gun. The upgrades are also interchangeable so you can change what your guns atributes are if you want to tr using it to stun enemies more of veen give one of them a burst ability.
The order in which you get weapon types is a bit weird in the whole fact that you can end up getting the stronger version of a weapon type before you get the weaker versions and some of the weaker versions can only be gotten by doing things like playing he game on infernal as that is the only mode that they appear on.
Overall if you are a fan of the series of old, mainly 4, and want to play a decent modern Resi game then you should definately give this game a try

So let me preface this by saying I am very much a Warmachine fan and love the fact that I have the opportunity to play, in multiplayer/skirmish at least, both of my favorite factions. I mean, one of them gets the campaigns (yes you do, Cygnar), but the fact that Ret is DLC is fine, because I am willing to pay for them.
However, these facts aside, I can't help but feel this game has so many rough edges that require polishing it's not even funny. Like the fact that I thought I got stuck on the tutorial for the campaign, because I couldn't for the life of me figure out how to get that blasted charger up and running because I thought that there was supposed to be a highlighted action button. They even said there was a highlighted action button. There was not. It took me a few tries to figure out that "Oh. Hey. The button that is supposed to be highlighted blue is highlighted by being the exact same color and style as the buttons that aren't functional. How novel!" Or the fact that the grids will only sometimes show up, for things like control area. Not a big deal, right? Except it is, because you didn't realize that your warjack, that you were hoping to get off two shots with with it's cannon no longer is able to because he was one or two squares out of radius during the focus phase.
Now, the game does feel like a slightly tweaked version of the Prime 2.0 version of Warmachine, which is great. It's faithful to the game, which I like. But I wish that the rough edges had recieved more polish. As it stands, I can only really recommend the game for players who A) Love Warmachine, B) are willing to put up with the lack of polish and C) are able to get it on sale. In my case, I got it through a Humble Bundle deal, and bought the DLC deeply on sale, and didn't feel cheated by the price tag I payed for it.
Poor UI, broken tutorial, buggy and crashes.  Thought this must be early access but apparently is not.  Only own because I got it in some bundle.

Get this game is you are a fan of Warmachine, and want to play a desktop version of the game, however dont have your hopes too high.

FIRST IMPRESSIONS
PROS:
GRAPHICS: Gorgeous. It is the right balance, everything goes together and nothing really "sticks out." It's dark and secretive befitting the setting.
STORY: Interestingly attractive. At first, because we are all human, we think we get to play the anti-hero; but then, we realize we are actually playing the role of legitamate heroes, attempting to kill the man enslaving your people (though killing inocents still make you evil lol).
CONS:
LANGUAGE: Quite honestly the languae is immediatly offputting and breaks immersion. Having served in the military I am mainly desensitized to foul language and I understand and agree in some games colorful dialouge can inhance the tension or emotion of the scene. But this is basically a twelve year old trying to sound edgy by dropping the F-bomb every other sentence. It doesn't even flow with the characters themselves. It even happens in casual conversations between characters who seem to be friends. It's as if the voice actors who were hire are so stuck on their automatic swearing they couldn't turn it off just to make a game. Where are the antequated euphamisms, or the fantasy twinge on standard words (Frak anyone?), or even just making it more appropriate to the story? When he refered to Styx as vermin in the Orcish tounge that was great, but this school yard "look at me I give the game a mature rating" edgespeak is just a joke. It isn't offensive, it is annoying.
MECHANICS: As mentioned in several reviews the mechanics are a bit "meh." The near time-stop action que is a great idea, but you feel like your character is always 3 actions behind everyone else. Not to mention there is no command for movement when in this menu.
6/10 Get it on sale.

Excellent.  What I hoped out of this title was exactly what I got.
Pro:
- Story
- Music (Kind of like Apocalyptica's Master of Puppets cover)
- Visuals
Con:
- Combat
- Odd Lipsync and some strange character acting
- Choices?  In a linear rpg?  Whatever gets me more EXP and loot
Details:
The story is the number one reason to check this game out.  Like it says, the game is told through the perspective of the orcs.  While they are shown to be victims in the war the orcs are far from peace loving nature folk.  Humanity has broken a lot of the orcs but they are still a threat.  As many have said, Styx steals the show with his dark humor and interesting past.  There is an unnaturally large amount of swearing that feels very offputting.  Hearing an honorable orc discuss his nature themed religon only to drop the F-bomb midsentence is pretty jarring.
Opposite of the great story is the rough combat.  By the end of the game combat will come easy (although if you're like me you'll have to drop the difficulty a notch for a few major battles).  With some work I think this could have gone over easier for players.
Combat:
I figured it out around the time where you "challenge" Fox.  Both characters have three "stances".  Red (left) for all offense and little defense.  Green (middle) for utilities like steath and throwing Styx.  Blue (right) for defending and range.  As you level up you can put skill points into new attacks from the three stances as well as upgrade them once (choose wisely!).  Typically for me I used Ark's roar that provokes the crowd to him (getting them off of Styx) followed up with his defense buff and then a series of arcing swipes (since he is taking on the group).  Styx buffs his knives with poison, then throws an amber bomb, followed up with his area of effect knife throw.
That is the beauty of this system is that you can set up a series of attacks for one character and then switch to the other to create another form of punishment.  During the late, late battles I had Styx target the pesky range and weaken enemies while Ark took on the rain of blows from the crowd.
Long and the short, if you can look past the indie roughness of certain elements and stick with the combat you will have a great time.  Now if you'll excuse me I'm going to start installing Styx: Master of Shadows.

-useless crafting system
-basic sounds
-poor graphics, several untextured parts, horrible water and fire effects: it still manages to stutter though

Unsurprisingly Once Bitten, Twice Dead has no redeeming qualities whatsoever. Preface: This has been my first experience playing a " sandbox/MMO " game - ever! So, steep learning curve-you betcha. This will be more for the novices like me. If I can do it anyone can. This may not be for everyone. It's NOT x-box or PS4 it's much more. If you notice, the negative reviews came after only playing 2 or even .5 hrs. In all fairness, you can't get a true feel of a game of this complexity in such a short time.
Likes:  This is an awsome game. I think the graphics are very good-again not ps4 but wait till you see your first baby lamb or foal you breed, they're sooo cute. From the realistic clouds,thunderstorms w/lightning bolts to the snow flakes in winter, it's all good. Some say the game play is to slow, I disagree. Working to improve your skills so that you can build say, a row boat (which is invaluable by the way) gives you a greater appreciation for where you started and where you are now. It also addes to the angst when going up against a nasty old bear, knowing you might loose the tools you worked so hard to make and improve and some of your skill gain if the bear kills you. I even feel my heartbeat quicken with the uncertainty of the outcome - now that's game immersion. I'm just now getting into the community aspect of the game, pretty sure I'll like that. I caught an 11.02 kg catfish yesterday and wanted to compare notes w/my fellow wurmians on their biggest fish.
Nuts & Bolts: as I understand them.  1st, Wurm Online-has existed 10+ yrs. Has official deticated servers that will probably never be shut down or wiped to play on-this is a plus.  It has deed costs and upkeep costs payable with "in game" money (silver coins) which you purchase at the "wurm online store" or earn selling goods or services to other wurmians. Please bare w/me. You also must purchse "premium time" if you want to raise your skill level above 20.
2cd,  Wurm Unlimited - basicly plays the same as wurm online but w/these differences.  You purchase the game upfront. Once installed you have 3 ways to access a server/severs to play on,                                                                            1 - the game comes with the ability to manage yout own lan server. This is fairly easy to set up, although I had to go to a link with step by step instructions (remember NOVICE) and it connects thru steam so you have to have an internet connection. Does'nt have to be great, I'm playing on DSL.  You can password this server so only your friends can join you or open it to the public. You can adjust certain aspects of game play like - up to 10 x skill gain. This is simply-you will get 10x the skill gain for the action you are performing as oposed to the original wurm online. Lastly I believe there is a spirit templer (deed guards) mantainence cost according to how many you have. Again not sure but my settlement info says there is.                                                                                                                                                                                          2- You can manage your server offline. This is harder to set up - I don't know how but there are no costs and you will be the only one in this world.
3- You can play on someone elses server if it's open to the pubic or you have the password, It may or may not have upkeep costs, it's up to the host of the server.

Dislikes:  Not much in the way of clear and concise information on what the game is or how to set up it's different capabilities or the true costs. I just bought Wurm and i've only put about 5 hours into it, and I gotta say, i'm not impressed.

-The user interface is a painfully illdesigned and antiquated one where you have to interract with several windows clicking and dragging things just to get the most basic things done. The gaming world has evolved past this sort of idea to a much more friendly hotkey/drag-and-drop system.
-Just trying to chop a tree down involves having to open the inventory (which is list based), double click the axe, then open your character sheet, then drag the currently equipped sword into your inventory, then drag the axe into your right hand, then right click on the tree, then slect a series of options on the popup menu, then repeat until the tree falls down.
It's just bulky and combersome, and for no reason.
-The actual play is slow, and painful. I mean, moving around the world is slow, the reaction to items you have to interface with is slow, and the general gameplay is slow.
I will NOT be recommending this game to any of my friends.
I just wish I could get my money back.

Today, we are more than seven billions of people, each with our own life, our own friends, and our own worries. But everything is irrelevant, only a small fraction of those 7 billions will care if you die, and your actions will be meaningless to most of them too. everything you've done is either futile, or will become futile. By the first thirty minutes of the game, it has become clear that the game is filled with anime tropes : teenagers, cute girls, giant mechs,and it has only been thirty minutes ! By the end of the first playthrough, it seems like there is only that, with the addition of moe girls, and cool-looking dudes.

BUT oh god are you missing a huge part of the game !
After starting again with 9s, the title finally appears (yeah, just now) and you embark in a magnificent tale of upbeat existential crisis, coupled with amazing combat system, quality characterization (even for... unexpected people), well-paced story, amazing (and two awful) side quests, an ASTONISHING climax and a top-tier waifu who is NOT 2b (she's nice too but a2 still best girl). In all seriousness, most of her reactions are PRICELESS and if you fell in love with this game's humor (which is, as expected from the writers of Drakengard 3, pretty good) then you'll fall in love for A2.
With all that in mind, there's nothing better I can do for you than recommanding this game, and that's exactly what I'll do. !

This is the funnest strategy game I have ever played.. for the first 50% of a play-through. Unfortunately, the game is mostly CPU bound so even with a 4.5ghz overclock on my i5 the game drops to 7-20 fps after nations have the ability to get 500k+ fleets. For reference I have a NVidia 970 and it utilizes 30-35% of the GPU regardless of the overclock, infact the GPU does not even go to full 3D overclocks. This is irrelevant as even forced overclocked clocks speeds the result is the same. To put it in perspective for anyone who has not played this game, expect to only play on a small size map for a complete playthrough.
The game has the ability to speed up time from slowest > slow > normal > fast > fastest. Expect to have 60 fps on normal speed at endgame. Now you're possibly thinking normal speed is fine for me.. no, no it is not. Maybe on your first 2-3 games getting used to the game mechanics normal is fine but after you get used to the game you are sitting staring at the screen for minutes on end with no input. Researches take many years to complete so you will want to speed up the game. As soon as you go from normal > fast you halve your frame rate and then again from fast to fastest.
TLDR: This game looks great and it's features are. The game is severely dlc money gouged. It is unenjoyable to play once you learn it simply due to the frame rate. The whole game slows down based on your frame rate. If you don't have a pc that is 6months~ of bleeding edge then the only thing you can do is /sigh.. enjoy or buyer beware, your choice.
To any responds posters: I will not take down or change this review unless the aforementioned issues are fixed. This game will crash, it will.

I genuinely like some of the core mechanics in this 4X game, but I think it fails at a lot of them and overall ruins the experience.
There's some interesting mechanics. You can customize your empire's ethics-- Want to make a dictatorship that uses slave labor? Want to make space democracy that loves aliens? Want to make a spiritual technocracy that forbids AI? Go for it. Empire leaders then give objectives: build 4 mining stations, build 4 science stations (these are the only ones I actually received weirdly enough) that keep you slightly on task. Along with the ethics, political factions are established seemingly from how you play the game: have a lot of wars with aliens? Build a lot of mining structures? Factions as guiding goals and effect your populations happiness, dependent on your gameplay style. Hire leaders who essentially act as buffs with life expenctancies that can be placed in charge of fleets, science vessels, or as governors for sectors and planets. Establish sectors for mid-to-late game, placing the AI in charge of micromanaging systems with behavior focuses, set your cut of their minerals. Raise up a primitive culture. Use science to give non-sapients freewill, and subjegate them, and watch as they migrate to your other colonies. Or set your policies to disallow migration, and keep those aliens off your worlds. Late game crisis happen--events that threaten the universe that takes a coordinated effort from all. Stop other empires from committing atrocities, or take worlds and force the xenos from your new planet. Old stellar empires are out there, rich with technology and, most likely, wanting nothing to do with you. Send out science vessels to find and research-flavor text and resource boosts await.
But there's core flaws that ruin the game. The AI isn't very competant and you have very little say in diplomacy or coordination for war efforts. Formed a huge federation? Get war declared on one empire, and watch as your compatriots jump their fleets back-and-forth, confused, between two systems while a fleet four-times what you can muster bears down on your homeworld, unable to even request assistance. Agreed to a research agreement? Too bad you can only choose a few research options at a time. Oh, and those "unresearched" techs include tech from an entirely different part of the tech tree. Wondering why your 5 other federation empires voted yes to go to war? Too bad. Don't understand the warscore system, where you declare your empire's demands? Me neither. Curious how your set rally points for shipyards? Seemed like it would be useful. Combat essentially boils down to numbers--two fleets banging into each other with no input from you.
Overall, it's not terrible, there's some absolutely great ideas in here. The AI interaction just kills it though.

Revelations is a rather interesting part of the Resident Evil series. On one hand, it does feel like a side-story, not part of the main series. On the other, it often plays more like what Resident Evil used to be, than the newest entries. It feels like a more focused and better put together game, than Resident Evil 6 (released same year). But at the same time, doesn't evoke the same feelings, RE6 does, feels like designers lacked confidence and built the game by the checklist, not by their inner desires.
Basic gameplay and the main parts of the game are really well done. Controls and some of the principles feel almost a perfect fit for a potential remake of the classic RE games, both in a more survival horror auto-aim style, and survival action over the shoulder more action style. Stuff no longer falls from enemies (escept for rare cases of mini-boss encounters, most of which can be skipped), ammo is rather scarce, running away is very often a very viable and even preferable option. Many locations are very narrow, but there is a rather well implemented dodge move, which is quite important to master. There's more freedom of exploration and good old "hey I found a key, let's open the door from before" moments, than even in Resident Evil 4. Although, it never quite truly tries to go full RE0-CV in terms of allowing you to roam free, since game is divided into chapters and quite a lot of them limit your options by some story reasons.
However, there's a bigger issue with chapters. Sadly, despite the main part of the game being good and very classic RE-like most of the time, developers constantly shoehorn boring, repetitive and action heavy chapters from other characters perspectives into the flow of the game. Those tend to reuse areas from before, don't use the same weapon/herb/weapon upgrade setup as the main game and are, ultimately, completely disposable except for several key moment, which could've been done as non interactive cutscenes and nothing of value would've been lost. Part of the reason behind their existance is probably due to Capcom's fear, that game will sell less if there's not enough action in it.
And another part is due to the silly story the game has. Now, Resident Evil games always had silly stories, but they tend to be awesomely silly, when you know that events you're watching unfold are dumb, all the characters are quite over the top, but it's so awesome you can't help but love it. And, besides, there was always a layer of seriousness in the story, which made for a good contrast with all the silliness. RE6 is that. Revalations is not. It's just plain stupid, always trying to look smart with all the plot twists and out of order side-chapter releals. But at the end of the day, it's just all dumb, full of new characters with crazy outfits and hairstyles, whom we will never ever see again, most likely, apart from the main duo of Chris and Jill and one small character, who had minor appearence in RE5. Also, Parker is quite clearly the result of developers wanting to have Barry Burton but not being able to for story reasons. And also, Jill is rather weirdly redesigned and looks a bit creepy.
Creepy mostly due to the fact, that this game wasn't vastly visually improved over the 3DS version, so facial animations are crap, and many models and textures are rather "meh". Game still looks quite good, but there's a huge difference between it and RE6 even in how dynamic enemies' reactions to being shot are in RE6, and how boring shooting enemies in Revelations is. It doesn't detract much enjoyment from the game, but is rather noticeable.
There's also an interesting bonus mode, called Raid mode. Unlike RE4-style Mercenaries (which I could never get into, to be honest), it plays much more like Mercenaries: Operation Mad Jackal from RE3 or The 4th Survivor from RE2. There's no time limit (but time affects your rating), you don't *have* to kill every enemy, and the main point is getting to a specific place on the map. But along the way you can (and sometimes have to) kill enemies, potentially find ammo, upgrades and new weapons. It's a really fun mode that can be played solo or co-op. It has one big issue, though, which ties with the fact, that the game was designed to be portable. In a "gotta catch 'em all" way, there's a lot of stuff to get, get leveled up and such, but it's very grindy in nature, meant to be played in short bursts and gets quite repetitive fast otherwise. Hence, on a portable device it's a definitely more fun mode to play, than on a PC or console.
Overall, a really solid game, with nice return to the oldschool ideals for most of the time, and disposable annoying sequences inserted inbetween the enjoyable main game.

Overall, I have to say that this was a really good game, despite my contempt for the combat system.
Pro's:
- Storyline is well done
- Good voiceovers (I'm usually not a huge fan of profanity as it shows a lack of creativity but the way it was done completely fit the context)
- Great graphics with immersive environments
- Good skill customization where decisions can make a pretty big difference but also fit differing playstyles
- Awesome soundtrack, very fitting to the atmosphere and environments
- Likable characters that are easy to connect with
Con's:
- Horrible combat system for an action based game (similar to Dragon Age Origins)
<disclaimer> I completely understand I am a bit bias in this regard but I really don't care for this type of combat system and believe it really held this game back from being excellent
- Itemization lacks depth, not a whole lot in the way of gear and weapons
In the end, I would definitely recommend this game, especially as it's usually on sale for under $10 and undoubtedly a worthy value for roughly 25 hours of entertainment (1 time through on medium settings). Even though I am not a fan of the combat system whatsoever, I still own Styx and am excited to delve into that game simply for the positive reasons mentioned above.

As someone who hasn't played a NBA game before and doesn't know all of the NBA rules. As well as someone who comes from a country that isn't interested in Basketball, I'll share my thoughts on the game. Although I'll only talk about the single player elements, since I didn't want to make an account for online mulitplayer.
Career mode
For me the career mode was sort of a mixed experience. When you don't really know the controls, you are put on the back foot through the start of the career mode, which is your college basketball experience which takes place over 5/6 games. Since how well you do during the college games changes where you are likely to get drafted during the NBA draft. My 1st time experience I got my college to win the championship but the game deemed me as not doing that good (I'll explain why later) so I got put as a late 1st round draft. Which turned out to be the 24th pick by the 76ers.
I've had a 2nd go through the college stage again with a different save when I knew more on how to do things. I believe the game focuses too much on the points you score, compared to other stats like steals, assits etc. Which affects where you get drafted. 1st time through had a lot of assits and steals but hardly any points, with the 2nd time through had a lot of points but nothing with rebounds, assits etc but got drafted 6th overall.
Anyway post college experience and into the actual NBA season, I feel like there is a good story to your journey with other players that get drafted along with you into your team (you always get Justice and Denver drafted into whatever team you are in). The team practise sessions are basically the only sort of tutorials you'll get in the game where you can learn new things, if the game chooses the right practise things to show you. Your character's skills pretty much start at a very low point, which you can upgrade via getting points through how you play within games and endosement contracts. The Endosement contracts are very basic where you just have to make sure to go to the event. Once you get enough points you can spend them in different areas like 3 point shooting, defending etc. Making your character better, more accurate etc etc.
Now I have 2 problems with the career. Number 1 is the cutscenes. There is too many cutscenes for my liking, but that isn't my main problem with them. My main problem is that the game sometimes freezes during the cutscenes, which happened the most during the college basketball stage. The freezing became less frequent after that stage in the career and has pretty much gone by about 25% through the season and hasn't happen in any other part of the game.
My 2nd problem is that the career mode seems to be too easy from my experience. With my save where I got drafted with the 76ers, we only lost 6 games during the normal season. 4 of them happened during the first 10 games when I didn't fully know how to play the game with the other 2 happening when I decided to sim the games (because we already quailified for play-offs and didn't want to spend hours going through the rest of the season). Now the play-offs also seem to be too easy having gone 4-0 in the first 2 rounds. This has put me off from finishing the play-offs because it just felt far too easy and I moved onto MyGM mode instead. Maybe, I got lucky by being picked by the 76ers and had a very good/dominating team, whereas this may not have happened if I got drafted elsewhere. Also as a side note once my player hit around 70-75 overall mark, then it felt very comfortable in dealing with other teams and players who are much more skilled when comparing overall levels (me being 72 and someone else being in the high 80's/low 90's for exmaple).
MyGM mode
I like the GM mode as you control a franchise (team) into becoming a dominating powerhouse. You can play with just the 30 original teams, have an expansion by adding in 6 custom teams (there are about 10 pre-made ones like Kansas City Knights, or you can completely make your own), or have a custom league with a mix of current, expansion and historic teams. Personally, I like going for the expansion setting.
In the GM mode you basically try to balance the team owner's wishes, players egos, morales, money, trades, draft picks etc with your own goals for the team while trying not to get fired. Well I say try not to get fired, I don't know if its possible since I haven't been fired yet across about 10 seasons worth of MyGM. The fun of MyGM is trying to do what you want while trying to keep everyone else happy. If you want to get a load of young players with a lot of potential but are awful when you sign them. You can do that. Want to get a superstar player? You can do that. Want to win the NBA year after year? You can do that as well.
You can be as hands on as you want from playing every game to simulating every game, from messing around with the training, relocating the team etc. Personally, I simulate every game and a season usually takes around 90 mins not including the off-season. The off-season is usually where I spend most of my time in the MyGM. Seeing who I want to draft, which NBA rules to try and deny/approve, which players I want to keep, which staff to hire, which training camps to use etc.
However, my problem with this MyGM is that with a patience team owner its too easy. I've won the NBA play-offs with the Timberwolves in the 2nd season and in a different save won with an expansion team (Pittsburgh Force) in 3 seasons. Even though I wasn't planning on challenging to win the NBA play-offs both times.
Other game modes
There are other modes but there isn't much to say about them. MyLeague seems to be a more simple version of MyGM. Season is where you play with a team of your choice over a season instead of just being a player like the career, or do the play-offs only. There is an online version of MyLeague so you can play with friends as well but you need an account to use it.
Overall
I like the game, and I would recommend it to people who don't own an NBA game, or have one that is 2/3 years behind the most recent title since I can't imagine that much has changed between titles except for roster updates and the career story being slightly different to be worth buying every year. There is a bit of a learning curve for new people to the NBA games but after a while you'll learn everything quite fast. I would only buy the basic version of the game (on sale), since the items from the legend edition don't seem to be worth buying (unless you are really into those items) and the VC points aren't worth it.

So where to begin with this game?
I think it's all been said. This game is, in my humble opinion, the best game in the total war franchise, which is saying something.
It features both a turn-based campaign and a real-time battle system.
In the campaign you play a faction of your choice, be that the kingdom of England, the the Moors, Hungary, or one of so many others. The goal of the campaign is simple: conquer the old world. Do this with somewhat boring methods like espionage, religion, trade and diplomacy or the one you always end up using: pure military might.
Which brings us to the main attraction of the game: the amazing real-time battles, where you can command armies numbering in the thousands to glory.
The battles are incredibly fun and, espicially in multiplayer, can get very challenging. The game allows you to kill your enemies in a large variety of ways. Let your heavily armoured infantry slaughter them in brutal melee combat, have your crossbowmen tear through them with focussed fire, launch burning projectiles from your artillery to watch them die in agony, or, my personal favourite, hit them in the back with a cavalry charge so powerful it would seem like God himself has smitten your enemies.
Do all of this and more to one of the most epic soundtracks in gaming history. (Seriously, go check out "War of Kings" by Jeff van Dyck on youtube if you don't believe me)

The Good:
- Beautiful graphics and music.
- Innovative perspective switches that kept battle varied and fresh.
- Fast-paced battle with beautiful animation.
- Epic boss fights with huge "goliath" machines.
- Some interesting stories with robot kingdoms, extinct aliens etc.
The Bad:
- Second playthrough repetitive, yet required to proceed to third playthrough that completes the story.
- Repetitive hacking mini-game played a large part in the game after the first playthrough.

This game has a great core and graphics but is horrendously implemented, rendering it sometimes unplayable by my standards. My complaints are as follows:
The matchmaking system is horrible. Sometimes it works well, but usually, it just matches you up with people of vastly higher rank than you, making gameplay almost never fun.
The “hiding factor” is an overpowered gimmick that makes gameplay less fun and more aggravating. I understand that it is supposed to represent camo and anti-radar gear, but still.
The game selection system is non-existent. I do not prefer to play the game modes where you are out once you die, because while it is more realistic, it sometimes is not what I want to play, but instead I would want to play the “Competition Mode” that allow for perpetual respawns. There is no way in the game to select what game mode you want to play.
I also do not like the fact that the game often creates small games when it does not need to. Often, when the game has enough players to make a full 15v15 or whatever match, it only creates a 3v3 or alike. Smaller games are often less fun because of the way they are set up. What gives?
I really wish this game was better, because I really like what it represents and is trying to be, but it lacks some of the components that make a great game good.
