An enjoyable Naval Combat game, quickly paced to give it a more World of Tanks feel than World of Warships does. Includes submarines, including the famous Japanese I-400 carrier. However, the iconic Yamato is reduced to it's pre-upgrade state unless you pay real money, and every one of the Japanese Battle Carriers require real money as well. Battle Cruisers are often relegated to "weak battleship" in ship classification. How ships are tiered is strange as well.
Despite these short comings, the game's quick pace, daily rewards which keep loyal players playing, and wide variety of play styles, including the German "pocket Battleships," makes it a heck of a lot of fun! It also rewards a player for performing team support roles. Actions which routinely provide pathetic experience gains in other games, such as spotting, damaging, shooting down enemy planes, etc, all reward handsomely, so while Battle Ships are still the predominant choice by players, if you wish to play something else, you don't feel like the game is holding you back. Ships which are unlikely to get the kill shot but still are extraordinarily helpful in other ways have reduced experience requirements, even if they rival their BB cousins in tonnage, like the carriers. These factors make moving along in the game and progressing to the "fun" ships a brisk experience that only really dragged when I tried out the Emden.
So, does it have some faults? Yeah, and they are definitely annoying, but after my initial disappointment I decided to step past that and try out the game for what it does offer and see how much fun it is at what it does excel at and really, I had a ball. It does very well what it wants to do, even if it doesn't do everything that I personally want.
My verdict? It's got a thumbs up from me! 4/5.

Unfortunately, the game is mostly CPU bound so even with a 4.5ghz overclock on my i5 the game drops to 7-20 fps after nations have the ability to get 500k+ fleets. For reference I have a NVidia 970 and it utilizes 30-35% of the GPU regardless of the overclock, infact the GPU does not even go to full 3D overclocks. This is irrelevant as even forced overclocked clocks speeds the result is the same. To put it in perspective for anyone who has not played this game, expect to only play on a small size map for a complete playthrough.
The game has the ability to speed up time from slowest > slow > normal > fast > fastest. Expect to have 60 fps on normal speed at endgame. Now you're possibly thinking normal speed is fine for me.. no, no it is not. Maybe on your first 2-3 games getting used to the game mechanics normal is fine but after you get used to the game you are sitting staring at the screen for minutes on end with no input. Researches take many years to complete so you will want to speed up the game. As soon as you go from normal > fast you halve your frame rate and then again from fast to fastest.
TLDR: This game looks great and it's features are. The game is severely dlc money gouged. It is unenjoyable to play once you learn it simply due to the frame rate. The whole game slows down based on your frame rate. If you don't have a pc that is 6months~ of bleeding edge then the only thing you can do is /sigh.. enjoy or buyer beware, your choice.

I genuinely like some of the core mechanics in this 4X game, but I think it fails at a lot of them and overall ruins the experience.
There's some interesting mechanics. You can customize your empire's ethics-- Want to make a dictatorship that uses slave labor? Want to make space democracy that loves aliens? Want to make a spiritual technocracy that forbids AI? Go for it. Empire leaders then give objectives: build 4 mining stations, build 4 science stations (these are the only ones I actually received weirdly enough) that keep you slightly on task. Along with the ethics, political factions are established seemingly from how you play the game: have a lot of wars with aliens? Build a lot of mining structures? Factions as guiding goals and effect your populations happiness, dependent on your gameplay style. Hire leaders who essentially act as buffs with life expenctancies that can be placed in charge of fleets, science vessels, or as governors for sectors and planets. Establish sectors for mid-to-late game, placing the AI in charge of micromanaging systems with behavior focuses, set your cut of their minerals. Raise up a primitive culture. Use science to give non-sapients freewill, and subjegate them, and watch as they migrate to your other colonies. Or set your policies to disallow migration, and keep those aliens off your worlds. Late game crisis happen--events that threaten the universe that takes a coordinated effort from all. Stop other empires from committing atrocities, or take worlds and force the xenos from your new planet. Old stellar empires are out there, rich with technology and, most likely, wanting nothing to do with you. Send out science vessels to find and research-flavor text and resource boosts await.
But there's core flaws that ruin the game. The AI isn't very competant and you have very little say in diplomacy or coordination for war efforts. Formed a huge federation? Get war declared on one empire, and watch as your compatriots jump their fleets back-and-forth, confused, between two systems while a fleet four-times what you can muster bears down on your homeworld, unable to even request assistance. Agreed to a research agreement? Too bad you can only choose a few research options at a time. Oh, and those "unresearched" techs include tech from an entirely different part of the tech tree. Wondering why your 5 other federation empires voted yes to go to war? Too bad. Don't understand the warscore system, where you declare your empire's demands? Me neither. Curious how your set rally points for shipyards? Seemed like it would be useful. Combat essentially boils down to numbers--two fleets banging into each other with no input from you.
Overall, it's not terrible, there's some absolutely great ideas in here. The AI interaction just kills it though.

I've tried and tried to give this game a chance, but after 3 hours all I can conclude is that this is a prime example of a great idea gone wrong. Thanks to misguided game-tags this is being sold to players as an "Action, RPG, Story Rich" title. I'll tell you right now it is none of these things.
First of all, the combat is clunky, even fans of this terrible game will tell you that's true. The combat is slow and strategy based, NOT an action game. Action games are free-flowing with non-stop "action" like Space Marine, Tomb Raider 2013, and Dragonball Xenoverse. Those are action games, this is not.
And regarding the RPG elements, it's very easy to completely screw yourself if you don't spend your skill points in the right way. If that happens, you'll find yourself at the end of the game unable to finish, forcing you to start all over again, because there's no way to undo your skill points. This completely defeats the purpose of customization, which is the core element of an RPG.
Secondly, the dialog feels like it was writen by a 13 year old trying to sound cool by swearing all the time. Honestly, there's no need for that much cursing. I'm by no means offended by it, it just doesn't feel appropriate to what's going on in the story. And the rest of the dialog is just, well, awful. Nothing about it is immersive.
Story Rich? Really? Who tagged this game with that? Because it's not. The story is nothing more than your basic "Orcs VS Humans" genre. The original Warcraft had a better story to it than this. Either the developers didn't have a big enough budget to afford decent writers or they just didn't care. However, the end result is the same. A lack-luster experience that left me feeling cheated out of my money. There's no way in hell this game is worth $30. Maybe $9. Maybe. But it would still be awful.

This is a really nice looking game, with an interesting story, and a unique angle. I like the characters, and the voice acting is pretty good. The concept is excellent. What a shame, then, that the mechanics are complete crapola.
Did you play KOTOR and think, "Wow, this combat is too much fun. I don't think I can handle having this much fun. If only someone could do something similar, but make it boring and terrible."? If you did, then congrats, I've found the perfect game for you. Everyone else should stay away. This game would be better served by simple hack and slash combat, or Final Fantasy style turn based combat, or even a freaking DDR pad for me to stomp on to complete combat. Hell, it would have been better with no actual combat and just cutscenes showing combat. That's how bad the combat is - it would have been better if they had done nothing at all, because this combat is less than nothing.
The other mechanics aren't exactly brilliantly done either. The camera zooms in on an orc's massive back, and you can't zoom it out, so his shoulders take up about half of your screen width. The parts of the scenery I could see past his massive back looked nice, though.
This was a major disappointment. So much potential thrown directly into the trash.

After seeing this on sale this weekend, I'm gonna have to give this game a hefty..."No."
I'm a fan of the series, and got into it around the time the first game came out, and played through both 1 and 2. I then saw pre-release gameplay and trailers and pre-ordered the game (this was the time when this was still acceptable), and thought it looked like BL2 was stacking up to be. Turns out its just what Saints Row 4 was to Saints Row The Third:
You are sent to the Hyperion Space Station to help Jack and Hyperion, and defeat Dahl Corperation's "Lost Legion". You then select from 4 characters: Wilhem The Enforcer, Athena The Gladiator, Nisha the Law Bringer, and Claptrap...the Fragtrap (there was DLC characters released later on: Jack The Doppelganger, from Opportunity in BL2, and Aurella the Baronness). You go through what I like to call "Moon-stralia", and help Jack essentially topple Hyperion and become who he is in BL2.
Overall, the story isn't that interesting. It tries to be what Borderlands 2 was in terms of story, where you go from area to area killing and looting all the enemies, with quirky characters and bosses to interact with, just at a slower pace then the original games.
It's the same as Borderlands 2. The only thing thats different is the characters, their skills and abilities. Along with new characters to mess around with, comes new weapons and elements. When I mean this, I mean literally copied from BL2 line for line, with changed around "manufacturers" such as "Bandit" being "Scav", and the weapon element "Slag" (introduced in BL2, causes an increased take in damage when coated) being "Cyro" (introduced in this game, literally an overglorified Slag.)
Same play style, different game.

You want interesting, well designed areas? Yeah? Well you're looking in the wrong place. It's waaay too open for a Borderlands game. Yes, in BL2  there were open areas, but they were filled with
Whether it was buildings, props, or enemies. This game? Wide open areas far as the eye can see. It just feels so...empty. You would think moon colonies would be more populated.
Guess not.
A lot of the songs in this game are very slow, more sci-fi-ish. The problem is, the WHOLE game has this as a soundtrack. It's like if DOOM (2016) had Michael Jackson for it's soundtrack, where "Beat It" plays as you tear off a demon's head, it just doesn't feel right. With a game thats all about killing, looting, etc on the damned Moon of all things, the music doesn't fit that much into rest of the game.
It fits with the theme, not the game.
Story: 7/10 - While trying to stick to the regular formula, it just seems way too slow compared to other games.
Gameplay: 8/10 - Just your old regular Borderlands gameplay with the same ups and downs.
Atmosphere: 5/10 - Too open. Please add more here Alan.
Soundtrack: 6/10: While it may be good for offline listening, it doesn't fit the game style.
OVERALL RATING: 6.5/10 - While this is still considered a "Borderlands" game, it doesn't feel like an actual Borderlands game instead. If this game was given a different title and removed the Borderlands lore related to it, it might work. But Saints Row 4 tried this and what did we get?

This game gets a lot of hate.  Depending on how you play Borderlands, it might be justified.  Since it's impossible to talk about this one without comparing it to the other games in the series I'm going to assume if you're reading this, you've played the other ones.  If you don't already like Borderlands, I see little reason why you'd like this one over the others.
While there were minor graphical and engine improvedments between BL1 and BL2, this one had made effectively no improvements over BL2 from a technical perspective.  The main draw here is the different environments and characters.
As far as characters go, TPS offers easily the best skill trees in the series yet -- very few skills do something boring like "x% less recoil", or those that do offer it as an additional effect on top of something else.  Skills synergize together to create different ways of playing the same character.  Each action ability feels functional right away, whereas in BL1 or 2 it often felt as though you needed to spent points in certain things before they felt worth using.  Similar to later DLCs in BL2, the characters will talk to quest givers and other NPCs, giving them some badly needed personality aside from "likes to shoot guns."
The moon makes for a fantastic change of pace.  The low gravity makes for much higher (and floatier) jumping, and you can spend your oxygen to give yourself a boost.  And you'll notice I said oxygen -- unless you're in air bubble or other enclosed area, there is an air meter.  This sounds tedious, but it's not.  You'll usually have somewhere around 2 minutes of air, enemies drop oxygen canisters and there's a lot of interiors, air bubbles, or air vents.  You have to go out of your way for it to become an issue.  Low grav also gives you a slam attack as well.  All in all, the lowered gravity makes for a higher emphasis on movement and active play.
The game falters when it comes to end game.  BL2 sported multiple DLCs, high end bosses, and multiple playthroughs with different mechanics.  While TPS has a Playthrough 2, it's not too different from the first playthrough, and there's very few high level bosses.  There's not a whole lot of DLC either, and one of them is arena style and is completely forgettable.
Ultimately what this comes down to is what is the draw of the series to you?  If it's the character building, the humor, and wacky guns, it's all here, in an admittedly smaller but more focused campaign.  If it's the raiding and brutal difficulty of a third playthrough, you're not going to find that in the Pre-Sequel.

So I am a huge fan of all things RE, but I am sad to say this is starting to be a dying plot and style of game. If you have played all or any of the RE titles you will, if you are like me, want to play this just to satisfy that OCD "I need to play all the RE titles" itch. If you are new to RE, I have to say this one certainly seems to harken back to RE1 in many ways, so you can get that first time "like a virgin" RE experience.  Unfortuantely, the graphics also harken back to RE1.
The Cons:
They took out typewriters and went to autosave with this title, and I believe 4-5 (but I don't remeber). I miss being able to run back and save whenever I had the typewriter ribbons to do so.
The developers are still relying on graphics from ten years ago, complete with hair that doesn't move and looks like it is being held frozen in space and time with a whole vat of hair gel.
Fans of shooters of any sort are going to be extremely frustrated with this game because the hit boxes are just flat out off in some sequences. More than a few times I have been shooting point black at something and not hitting, or the real annoyance is when you go through a door fully prepraed to fire at the creature behind it and it lags for no apparent reason.
This game was clearly designed for cotnrollers and the lack of kb commands is a little annoying.
I swear these are the slowest running characters in any RE game to date. There is no sprint, and dodge is about as clunky as it has always been in RE games.
I don't like the TV show aspect of this game and especially the "Previously on RE Revelations" cut scenes. I also don't like the fact that it takes you out of the atmospheric settings to do flashback sequences to "previous episodes."
The Pros:
Very cool atmosphere when you are on the ship. Kind of hard to believe they haven't done a ghost ship setting for RE till this one.
Despite what some other reviewers have commented on, this game hasn't been about zombies since RE4 and frankly I like that. Zombies were great back in Raccoon City, but the story has well evolved past the zombie genre over the last several years and this game carries on with the whole mutant flesh creature scenarios.
Once again we are dealign with two of the classic characters near and dear to all RE fans, Chris Redfield and Jill Valentine. I kind of feel like they are old friends, and it is nice to see some consistency in their return.
This game actually does fill in some of the evolving storyline, and so far has not gone off the rails like RE3 and 4 did. So many RE titles seem to lose something in translation from Asian culture to English, but this one is relatively clear in plot and story. Even the voice acting is superior to some other RE tiltles "looking at you RE 1-3."
Conclusion:
If you are an RE fan get this game for the simple fact that it is a different setting. I liked RE 4 and 5 for the same reasons, and this one is supposed to take place between those two titles. This game is not, however, worth the list price of $50. That is way too much to spend on something that will more than likely be a trivial moment in passing in your gaming career. I caught it on sale for $12.50 on Steam and I was certainly happy enough with it for that price. I might even go as high as $25 for this game, but no more than that. You'll have some fun with it, cuss at it a lot, and you will remember what it was like when this series first emerged on the PS1 back in the 1990s. Those who are looking for graphics and pinpoint accuracy in shooting should probably look elsewhere as this game is not really a shooter, despite what some of the game propaganda says. I bought it and enjoy it simply for the fact that it is one of those game series I have been playing for about 20 years now, and the fact that RE pretty much set the bar for survival horror. Now, if someone would just bring back Dino Crisis I would feel like a kid again.

The short of it: Not as good as RE4
The main gripe I have with this game compared to RE4 is that RE4 had a great combat system, everything was very deliberate and it was very clear what the enemies attacks were, as well as what your capabilities were, and RE4 also had an amazing locational damage system, enemies reacted in heaps of different ways depending on where you shot. In this one, however, all these slimy-looking piranha people all react pretty much the same way when shot; they don't (with the exception of looking like they're tired for a bit so you can go up and kick them in the face, but triggering that is unreliable). There are positives though, the movement system is much more fluid and the weapon upgrade system (in my opinion) is better, in RE4 you had to spend money to upgrade your weapons but in this you find weapon parts and can swap them out.
Raid mode is pretty fun, however having to play through the story by yourself to unlock the stages for raid mode so you can play them with a partner is a bit stupid. Overall, it's worth playing, but not worth paying $50 for.

This is easily one of, if not the BEST story experience I have ever had the joy of witnessing inside a video game.
There are so many things that Nier: Automata makes you think about. SO many things that it makes you FEEL.
It’s rich with subtle, but brilliant philosophical narrative, heartbreaking stories, interesting and deeply troubled characters, and overall just fantastic game design and writing. This game does an incredible job of subverting your expectations, and taking advantage of the unique video game medium to tell a story in one of the most creative, genius, and beautiful ways that I have ever seen.
JUST MAKE SURE THAT YOU DON’T STOP AT JUST ONE PLAYTHROUGH. Trust me, after the first ending, you’ve only experienced maybe 35% of what the game has to offer.
The “final” ending is just a thing of a beauty. The most beautiful thing I’ve ever experienced in a game.
The ideas and the writing swept me off my feet, and made me more emotional that I’ve ever been with any game ever.
This, coupled with a smooth, responsive and fun combat system, and one of the greatest video game soundtracks of all time, make Nier: Automata a masterpiece in my opinion.
Sure, it has very obvious flaws that I could spend quite a while talking about.
But the feeling that you’re left with after fully finishing the incredible journey that is this game just overshadows ALL of that.

I originally got this game because I loved the art work you see on the games store page and the backgrounds that they did are all very good I think and done by a very tallented artist.
Having said that nice art work and backgrounds for my Steam profile, is not enough and while I also honestly hate to give negative reviews mostly cause I like to give developers a chance, plus the assets they licensed are really nice ones, but after playing the game for four (4) hours now I can say with certainty that its not worth the $5 and I can't say that I recommend it either to anyone.
One thing to watch out for is that number of things stated on the store page, that were available in the early alpha demo and that you see in the video are not in the game. For example right now you can play the police officer and the fireman, but not the other characters that you see playing in the video. Also, other than the jeep, you can't drive the other vehicles, like the van that you see being driven in the video, you can't drive it. Which is a bit of a disappointment and I hope they add back the stuff they remove as soon as possible or at least change the video to reflect the game that they do have.
Also, the game needs a lot of work, right now its just shell of a game and little more than money grab and a whole bunch of pie in the sky promises...
For example, the game presently does not do many of the things that are said on the store page, which is very misleading. The game does not appear to support 100 players, only 32 players as with UnitZ. The game does not let you pick from one of 15 different characters, so far only 2 characters can you play. The game does not have 50 different zombie types, it has 10 different zombie models from Simple Zombies asset pack and different skins that comes with it, but all of them like using the same UnitZ zombie logic. Also, the game does not appear to have 50 weapons, only around dozen from UnitZ. Nor does the game have 100 craft-able items, only the half dozen from UnitZ. Also as far as I could tell the game does not do split screen, at all. I think much of what we read from the store page comes from the original KickStarter / Greenlight description and appears to be in need of editing to reflect what we actually are getting.
Worse the thing looks to have been shoddily done in a  short period of time by hurriedly throwing a handful of packages from unity asset store together and little else.
$50 UnitZ game demo from HardWorker Studio (that is what you really getting and doing the game logic) and around $100 worth of models from Synty Studio (and those are the models your playing with) and one of those cheap $10-$20 cartoony GUI skin.
So there you have it, not much else to it...
Worse the GUI is horribly integrated and not fully functional. I actually can't figure how they thought it better than the one that UnitZ came with, at least in my opinion that one looked and worked better.
Also it does not look like they made a single change to UnitZ game template and have left all the bugs, including using its horrible network code. So I dont see how they can say it will ever support 100 players because it does not support a dedicated server, does not do any caching/pooling of game objects to keep the garbage collector at bay and the game logic is all running basically on a single native thread.
Worse is the fact that nobody is playing this game and playing solo becomes boring really quickly. Even worse is the fact that UnitZ demo is available completely for free and lots of people are playing it.
So I cannot recommend this game or give it a thumbs up until the time that they make major improvements to the original UnitZ code and add missing functionality like they show in the video trailer and like they had in the original early alpha demo, but for whatever reason do not include in the release that they give to us. Like being able to drive the vehicles we see in the game video being driven and them giving us more than just the single jeep that comes with the UnitZ demo and until they add the ability to play all the characters that they have which we see them playing in the video on the Steam store, and that were again in the original early alpha demo, but we are not able to play in the release that we get. And not until there are more people to play it since it's really not worth playing by yourself. Basically I want the game that is shown in the Steam store in the video and in the feature list, not the release I was given. I'm actually not sure why they removed stuff like driving the van which looks like it was working well enough in the video and the ability to play other characters which might have been removed cause the GUI they sort of kludged is unfinished, but who knows...

Warmachine: Tactics would have been a great game about 10 years ago. I'm a fan of the tabletop game and really wanted to like the PC version, but the interface seems to willfully ignore the advances in usability that the industry has made in the lase 20 years. There are no keyboard shortcuts for common commands, and everything you need to do is buried in at least two layers of the interface, often in non-intuitive places that you have to scroll through to find. I actually had to restart the tutorial 4 times to make it through - not because I wasn't payting attention or making good choices, but because I couldn't find how to do the things it wanted me to do. The critical command to activate your warjack was actually mislabeled with a placeholder. Controlling your units feels like a poorly written choose-your-own-adventure book, where there appears to be any number of valid choices, but only one leads to success.
I only made it two missions in before I quit struggling with the interface and moved on to a game I would enjoy more.

At it's core Warmachine Tactics feels like a game that was designed to fail. By slavishly forcing the developers to recreate the tabletop version of the game in digital format, they completely miss out of the wide variety of advantages that the format has over in person physical tabletop gaming. This is honestly a shame, as the setting and general concept for  the universe are perfectly suited for a fantastic video game. It's really too bad that Privateer continues to throttle the life out of their own franchise rather than letting it grow organically. They completely missed their shot at accessing a new market, new players and new customers for their delightfully creative and captivating world.
Additional Notes:
The visuals are competent but dated. They fail to capture the promise of the concept art for the characters, soldiers and mechs, but it's also clear that there were a lot of constraints on the developer, so it's hard to really fault them for it. Likely they did the best with what they had available.

Paradox Review:
It is in extremely poor taste for a company to raise their prices for the Summer Sale. While i had considered purchasing additional content during the sale, I have chosen not to due to Paradox's recent bad pricing practices.
Game Review:
This game is unlike any other that I've played. Stellarsis is realistic, slow-paced, and challenging. You will not conquer the game on your first playthrough, but you will learn from your mistakes and put the strategy back in strategy games.
The game is absolutely beautiful, and the soundtrack is great mashup of what sounds like a combination of Mass Effect and Blade Runner. Combat is extremely challenging, and resources are not easy to acquire.  Research occurs slowly.  Once again, this is a game for patient people.
With all of that said, I highly recommend the game to anyone who loves space strategy, because it's exactly what you've been looking for in the genre.
Like most Paradox games this does not disappoint. You could spend hours upon hours doing dozens of different play styles. Difficulty wise it is kinda like Civ in a way with its own uniqueness.

Tactics is a historical phenomenon that should be referenced in game design for the next twenty years.  There's only a few games out there where you can demonstrate so easily the Do's and Don'ts of Game Design, and Warmachine Tactics has the entire Don't side all in one place for your convenience.
In case this shows up on a Steam Sale somewhere and you don't realize the origins of this game, let me help you out.  Warmachine: Tactics is a PC Turn-Based realization of the Warmachine Tabletop Miniatures game, except it failed to realize the game at all outside of the artwork.
Don't: Kickstart a game that's supposed to be a PC conversion of your kickstarter audience's favorite miniatures game, and then make sure it's just enough like the tabletop and a PC game to have it fail miserably at both.
Don't: Blow your budget on graphics that aren't going to run on the computers of people that typically play boardgames and miniature games.
Don't: Make the game so mind-numbingly glitchy that Vassal becomes an option again.
Don't: attempt to explain me why it's ok that my giant robot has to hit that little infantry guy six times to kill him. (minus the 2 he misses completely because your random "dice" mechanics are miserable)
Don't: attempt to marry the best of a PC game design company with a Tabletop Minis company without a successful model in mind, and a clear goal of how to get there.  E.G. Dawn of War I, even II.  Not Xcom, but run through a digestive system with laxatives and crapped out the other side in the most rapid manner possible, yet highly detailed specular graphics and PhysX requirements that cause my actually decent computer to crash on a regular basis.

Don't: Buy this game.  Ever.

The MMO otherwise known as "What could've been". I love this game for everything it is and hate it for all it could be. It's been buggy since the first release (some of which still persist 2 years later), and it's -still- not optimized and runs like crap depending on your CPU (If you don't run Intel, good luck). The gameplay is burdened by too-complex character trees (which has been made only worse by the most recent updates), and storylines that never seem to come to any conclusion and leave you infinitely hanging. The major characters aren't really all that memorable, and PvP is non existent outside of a set number of hours per night (and even that's up in the air). The dev team has absolutely given up on this game; You can hear it in their voices and their PR-riddled messages to the community.
Upsides include a fair cash shop that will allow you to gain anything within it without spending a dime, several hours of entertainment, raiding guilds that will take just about anybody and difficult content that takes time to master. If you're looking for RP or PvP, look elsewhere. If you're looking for PvE, you're in luck.
I enjoyed Wildstar while it lasted, but I can't recommend it to anyone. There are better MMOs that provide a more stable, friendly experience. This game has left me with very little else but disappointment.
Edit: Ignore the hours played, I've clocked well over several hundred over the last few years I've played through the original launcher.

This game is a 7.99/10. Worth around $22-25. Got 14 hours out of it, 75/80% off all achievments, could get I guess around 20 if I tried to beat the game on highest difficulty.
Story: The world was interesting, and the main characters were too. Their personalities played off each other well, and had me in stiches the whole time. Unfortunatly, the side characters and villians were pretty much 1-dimension. It was hard to be attached to them, or be even interested in them.
World:
Interesting, but nothing special or awestrucking. Seems to be semi-linear, but if you look at all the maps carfeully, there's like 8 versions of linear paths, just angled differently or starting in different areas, thus making it really really liner. If you don't analyze maps alot, then it's semi linear for you. Occasionally some invisble walls in the enviroment, that were probably accidently left in the game, because they're as thin as a pencil. Annoying in combat, but rare. Occured 5 times.
User Interface:
Basic, which first seemed worrysome. Later on, I realized this made the gameplay easier, as meant less time spent on micromanaging, and nothing to slowdown the game speed. Helped by making only one, basic currency. Trade points. Ex: 2 points for a sword at most, 1 point to upgrade, one point gained to sell it back.
Graphics:
Mostly good, for a 2012 game. Occasionly some hiccups, nothing to worry.
Audio:
Usually the most underrated part of a game. The voices sounded crisp, no hiccups. They put alot of effort in the quality of music. Some of it is memorable, and fitted well with the enviroment/combat. Lip synce issues were annoying at first, but you eventually ignored it. Later on in the game, it smoothes itself out.
Combat:
A basic version of Dragon Age 1's combat system. Some options of equipment, but not much. The main characters combat roles play off each other well, with the Orc being a tank/bezerker and the Goblin being a rogue/assassin. Whenever you only had the chance to play one in a combat setting, you're made to realize that they need each other, and can't function well alone. Most be a good message hidden there.
This games need a sequel. Actually, would be okay with a properly done trilogy.

All of those things being said... It is one of the best crafting RPGs I've ever played, hands down. EARLY ACCESS REVIEW:
Please note that this review is based on an incomplete build of the game, so it may become outdated as improvements continue to be implemented.
Sentinels plays unlike any tower defence game I have played previously.  Where as the majority of them I played from the start of the genre involved waiting for the cash to roll in to add new weapons/upgrade them, they felt somewhat passive.  Alternative FPS/TPS games such as Sanctum and the Orcs Must Die games provide a more active gameplay mode, which I prefer, although at times it could get frustrating when a wave starts on the opposite side of the map and you have to rush to get there to set up traps/towers etc.
Sentinels provides a unique compromise where you can jump to any tower on the map to provide extra firepower, but you do need to be strategic in where you place them, otherwise you might have a wave get past and you do not have the funds to build a tower to take them out.  You need to watch your ammo usage along with reload/targeting to ensure you take advantage of your extra fire power effectively.  Additionally, towers can be upgraded in the traditional TD 3 level manner along with out of session upgrades to customize your play.  This is done through money/upgrades through waves by clearing waves successfully, leveling up, as well as shooting loot crates that drop through gameplay.  This provides as lot of variety to gameplay along with goals to continue playing.  It is possible to play solely by building towers, however the gameplay feels much more engaging jumping in and out of towers while toggling specialty towers to slow, deal AoE damage, or activate mines.
There are 3 groups of units that I have encountered so far in the game: land-based units, which follow the road, air based units, which follow a specified route through the air OR over the road, and "roaming" units, which weave a path between the ground obstacles.  Among the different groups are several unit types with varying HP and abilities.
The current things that need improvement are mainly streamlining gameplay through UI improvements and clearer explaination of how the mods/upgrades work.  While you can equip different weapons based on character/attack type, the descriptions do not clearly help explain how one would compare to another.  And while a power upgrade gives a percentage-based damage increase, you do not have values to determine how much damage it currently does and if it means you need 1 less or 5 less attacks on a given unit.  This can easily be remedied by improving the UI to allow you to compare currently equipped weapons to another or to show how much a given mod/upgrade will improve.  I find having the numbers helps to best determine what would fit my play style, given the multitude of options.
Pros:
- more proactive gameplay than traditional TD games
- RPG elements with additional tower types, out of game upgrades/mods to suit gameplay to your style
- unique elements on a per-map basis that add variety to gameplay (explosive crystals/mines/cloaking enemy units, etc)
- story elements that delve into the world
- easter eggs to the One Must Fall franchise (previous series developed by Rob Elam) (*I think ??!)
Cons:
- UI needs improvements to help clarify exactly how mods/upgrades/weapons compare
- adding ability to look up enemies to know their abilites/weaknesses would help with determining loadout
- add wave indicators so you can easily determine what unit types are following what attack route
I'm overall pleased with the gameplay so far but tightening up the UI and general readability will greatly improve the quality-of-life for new players to get up the speed due to the added complexity of the RPG elements.

The game is already polished at this early stage of development, and the developers are open and responsive to community feedback. I can easily recommend this to tower defense fans, and fans of horde based shooters like Serious Sam or Earth Defense Force will find a lot to like here as well.
I could easily see myself sinking many hours into this game, and would recommend to anyone who enjoys tower defense or strategy first person shooters because this is not a shoot 'em up game.

Sentinels is an action/strategy hybrid that encourages you to fight in the trenches as well as in the command room. You can take control of the stationary turrets that make up your defense at any time in the battle. Your shooting skills are just as important as your tower placement. Mechanics like the critical hits on weakpoints add depth to the fast paced battles, and make you feel like an ace when you line up a perfect shot at the last moment.
Sentinels avoids the rigidity of its tower defense genre peers and offers a far more replayable, free flowing action experience. The game design is much more flexible than the rock, paper, scissors you usually see. I never felt like I lost because I used the wrong tower at the wrong time. The sheer chaos is something to behold, and the gorgeous graphical engine has no problem handling all the mayhem.
The game is already polished at this early stage of development, and the developers are open and responsive to community feedback. I can easily recommend this to tower defense fans, and fans of horde based shooters like Serious Sam or Earth Defense Force will find a lot to like here as well.

I highly recommend this strategy game as a military geek interested in Imperial Japan, their weapons, and "what ifs".
This game allows for exploration of those what-ifs by land, sea, and air. It's a great package with depth but not crazy in-depth cryptic detail that requires you micro-manage mundane details. It has enough "stats" under the skin of an easy to approach GUI that make it a good wargame as well. No ugly or abstract counters to represent your units, either. The graphics here are quite pretty for the scale. Think of 6mm scale wargaming. It's a huge step up in terms of scope, polish, and feel from other Pacific-focused turn-based wargames I've tried over the years. I feel a bit sorry for the competition. It's also approachable even for players of RTS titles - and not just grizzled grognards (who may find this game a bit TOO pretty and approachable!).
It includes a scenario editor which I am sure I will use for Japan v. Commonwealth scenarios, though DLC is promised by the developer, we'll see. I think they made a solid game to start here, though. The campaign I've played for the Japanese so far is great, though I did dial up the difficulty one notch after the 3rd map.
1. The turn-based system/engine is engaging and fun, the graphics up to par for a game of today (which is not always the case for turn-based wargames), and the sound effects are great.
2. This is one of the very few games you will find that let you play Imperial Japan with actual ground invasion scenarios, not just Japan on its heels after it lost crucial battles. The perk system makes playing them unique as well - and there isn't an exact match for every vehicle in-game for the other side, keeping things realistic.
3. The Japanese troops are well done, as well as US troops and stay true to the era, allowing you to upgrade equipment as years go by. The initial US forces look much like they did after the US was pulled into the war.
4. The variety of vehicles is great, and the pace at which they are introduced by year avoids vehicle overload. They have a very good representation in the game, and several that may be new to people who think Japan is only about Ha-Go's and "Zeros." There is a cool one - the Type 91 Sumida armored car, that can convert for rail or road use just as the vehicle did historically.
5. The scenarios and objectives are what makes this game shine, along with the "doctrinal abilities" or perks and "special events". A turn-based game where you have no time-based objectives can be a real slog and a bore as you slowly grind it out -- but add in "you must capture bridge X in 10 turns" then add a reward for achieving that objective? Great stuff and adds tension. Also, since units go from campaign to campaign and gain experience, you will want to keep them alive and keep them from losing too many men (replacing with greens). One more thing - while you can deploy many vehicles, you need to watch how you use your money - you can't just keep pumping out troops like Company of Heroes or something.
6. Another VERY cool feature is that your enemy's vehicles - like Battleships - that were not taken out in a prior scenario will come back to haunt you. So the scenarios are dynamic like that.
Nitpicks:
Some of the controls are not intuitive at first - a few buttons for the 'next active unit' and how to purchase untis for deployment - but once you get the hang of the menu / UI those things are really all that's not immediately obvious. Again, this is not Hearts of Iron!
Airplanes need a place to land - so don't blindly buy non-carrier aircraft before you are certain you can take an airfield.
Summary:
All in all this is what I wanted when I envisioned a game that let me play and change history as Imperial Japan - or as the US to try things from a very different angle. Playing pre-determined maps of Guadalcanal is not my bag, but you could also play as historically accurate as possible as the US or Japan and see if things work out the same!
I do recommend turning the difficulty up one notch as I mentioned above -- I found it a bit too easy in the defaullt setting, but it can be changed between scenarios in the campaign. Will be interesting to see how many optional objectives I can hit with it dialed up a bit.
As a light wargame, this has enough stuff going on under the hood to model a lot of the intricacies of the PTO without being overly complicated in its systems. It's really... really good.

There was miscommunication between the developers and the playerbase in terms of moddability and cooperative multiplayer, which I'm personally frustrated with.
Modding - All of the graphics/sounds/values are packed into non-openable resource files. It would require a 3rd party tool to open any of them. The developers have said that they wanted the game to be easily moddable - that is not the case. Panzer Corps and Panzer General have survived the time due to mods - I dont see this game lasting very long without mod support.
Cooperative Multiplayer - The developers have pushed this one hard, but the reaility is that there are only two cooperative multiplayer scenarios. The developers have claimed that producing cooperative multiplayer scenarios is easy - but there is no way to distribute player-produced scenarios. Additionally, relying on the player-base to produce content is always risky. I dont anticipate that we'll see much from the community.
The campaigns / scenarios are extremely EASY, with the only challenge being in secondary objectives. Even on the hardest difficulty, primary objectives are relatively easy to accomplish - and require little to no strategy.

After seeing this on sale this weekend, I'm gonna have to give this game a hefty..."No."
I'm a fan of the series, and got into it around the time the first game came out, and played through both 1 and 2. I then saw pre-release gameplay and trailers and pre-ordered the game (this was the time when this was still acceptable), and thought it looked like BL2 was stacking up to be. Turns out its just what Saints Row 4 was to Saints Row The Third:
You are sent to the Hyperion Space Station to help Jack and Hyperion, and defeat Dahl Corperation's "Lost Legion". You then select from 4 characters: Wilhem The Enforcer, Athena The Gladiator, Nisha the Law Bringer, and Claptrap...the Fragtrap (there was DLC characters released later on: Jack The Doppelganger, from Opportunity in BL2, and Aurella the Baronness). You go through what I like to call "Moon-stralia", and help Jack essentially topple Hyperion and become who he is in BL2.
Overall, the story isn't that interesting. It tries to be what Borderlands 2 was in terms of story, where you go from area to area killing and looting all the enemies, with quirky characters and bosses to interact with, just at a slower pace then the original games.
It's the same as Borderlands 2. The only thing thats different is the characters, their skills and abilities. Along with new characters to mess around with, comes new weapons and elements. When I mean this, I mean literally copied from BL2 line for line, with changed around "manufacturers" such as "Bandit" being "Scav", and the weapon element "Slag" (introduced in BL2, causes an increased take in damage when coated) being "Cyro" (introduced in this game, literally an overglorified Slag.)
Same play style, different game.

You want interesting, well designed areas? Yeah? Well you're looking in the wrong place. It's waaay too open for a Borderlands game. Yes, in BL2  there were open areas, but they were filled with
Whether it was buildings, props, or enemies. This game? Wide open areas far as the eye can see. It just feels so...empty. You would think moon colonies would be more populated.
Guess not.
A lot of the songs in this game are very slow, more sci-fi-ish. The problem is, the WHOLE game has this as a soundtrack. It's like if DOOM (2016) had Michael Jackson for it's soundtrack, where "Beat It" plays as you tear off a demon's head, it just doesn't feel right. With a game thats all about killing, looting, etc on the damned Moon of all things, the music doesn't fit that much into rest of the game.
It fits with the theme, not the game.
Story: 7/10 - While trying to stick to the regular formula, it just seems way too slow compared to other games.
Gameplay: 8/10 - Just your old regular Borderlands gameplay with the same ups and downs.
Atmosphere: 5/10 - Too open. Please add more here Alan.
Soundtrack: 6/10: While it may be good for offline listening, it doesn't fit the game style.
OVERALL RATING: 6.5/10 - While this is still considered a "Borderlands" game, it doesn't feel like an actual Borderlands game instead. If this game was given a different title and removed the Borderlands lore related to it, it might work. But Saints Row 4 tried this and what did we get?

This is an action rpg with many cool ideas and multiple endings that encourage you to replay the game from different view points. While there are 26 endings (one for each letter of the alphabet) only A-E are actual endings, with the rest of them mostly joke endings such as when you uninstall your OS or die in the prologue. Not every idea it has is a winner in its execution, but the general execution of the game along with the height of its best ideas raise the game up to be a memorable one.
Notably the game tries to channel the player non-interaction of Dark Souls in the guise of the corpses of where your fellow players died which you can use for minor temporary bonuses. But after 5-10 hours you can just ignore them. Yet this player non-interaction does eventually play out in a rather impressive way by the end.
The game starts out challenging, including the prologue itself to a certain degree, but mostly because there is no way to save until you complete the prologue. If you die, you even have to reach your corpse to collect all your equipment and items since your last save. Yet once you get the right equipment, death becomes neigh impossible through the use of auto-healing unless you want to crank up the difficulty.
I feel like I spent 10 hours more than I would had liked with this game as I tried to complete the side quests, farm for upgrades, and extract all the enjoyment I could from the game. While the side quests can sometimes be annoying to complete, they often have a nuget of a cool story bit with each of them. Regardless, whatever self-inflicted bad taste I had in my mouth was washed away by the final ending.
One thing to note about attempting side quests and farming early is that the game offers more and more quality of life options as the game progresses. It starts with teleporting between every save point, the ability to open locked chests, unlocking a ride-able animal at each save point, and finally a chip that lets you auto collect all those items in a decent radius that you had to walk up and push a button to collect. And if you hate being a completionist, well you'll eventually unlock a merchant who will flat out just sell you the game's achievements.
Sometimes complaining points to genuine problems with the game, other times when a game is so good, the few problems it has seem more glaring. With Nier, it is squarely in the latter. The game becomes more depressing with each play through and I enjoyed seeing it through to the very end. Notably I found the start of route C and the final ending E to be the standout moments of this that I will remember for quite some time.
Despite this, my one legitimate complaint is the poor quality of the PC port. I had a number of crashes when I played in full screen mode (which had an ugly black box around the screen). Until I played in Windowed mode for the rest of the game. I feel like it could had used a little more time and polish on this end.
Never the less, I enjoyed my time with Nier and would recommend it to anyone.

This game gets a lot of hate.  Depending on how you play Borderlands, it might be justified.  Since it's impossible to talk about this one without comparing it to the other games in the series I'm going to assume if you're reading this, you've played the other ones.  If you don't already like Borderlands, I see little reason why you'd like this one over the others.
While there were minor graphical and engine improvedments between BL1 and BL2, this one had made effectively no improvements over BL2 from a technical perspective.  The main draw here is the different environments and characters.
As far as characters go, TPS offers easily the best skill trees in the series yet -- very few skills do something boring like "x% less recoil", or those that do offer it as an additional effect on top of something else.  Skills synergize together to create different ways of playing the same character.  Each action ability feels functional right away, whereas in BL1 or 2 it often felt as though you needed to spent points in certain things before they felt worth using.  Similar to later DLCs in BL2, the characters will talk to quest givers and other NPCs, giving them some badly needed personality aside from "likes to shoot guns."
The moon makes for a fantastic change of pace.  The low gravity makes for much higher (and floatier) jumping, and you can spend your oxygen to give yourself a boost.  And you'll notice I said oxygen -- unless you're in air bubble or other enclosed area, there is an air meter.  This sounds tedious, but it's not.  You'll usually have somewhere around 2 minutes of air, enemies drop oxygen canisters and there's a lot of interiors, air bubbles, or air vents.  You have to go out of your way for it to become an issue.  Low grav also gives you a slam attack as well.  All in all, the lowered gravity makes for a higher emphasis on movement and active play.
The game falters when it comes to end game.  BL2 sported multiple DLCs, high end bosses, and multiple playthroughs with different mechanics.  While TPS has a Playthrough 2, it's not too different from the first playthrough, and there's very few high level bosses.  There's not a whole lot of DLC either, and one of them is arena style and is completely forgettable.
Ultimately what this comes down to is what is the draw of the series to you?  If it's the character building, the humor, and wacky guns, it's all here, in an admittedly smaller but more focused campaign.  If it's the raiding and brutal difficulty of a third playthrough, you're not going to find that in the Pre-Sequel.

After playing this and completing all but the final mission I read up on the rules of the tabletop game this is based off. I was not a fan of the way units activated to completion and that it doesn’t offer complete freedom in the strategies you use. That being said, it’s not terrible, though I prefer the way movement and shooting goes in 40K. So, I will not discuss how I believe this limits your options, as it is true to the tabletop and therefore a non-issue, but this version has a serious issue that involves this.
If you move a unit but you forgot or just noticed another unit that you’re curious if they can get into range. Just forget about it. As soon as you click the other unit, the previously selected one has now ended its turn. In the tabletop that’s fine as you could look over and measure something without actually activating that unit. In this, that is impossible. Plan your entire turn out to surgical precision and then start doing stuff, only then will this not punish you.
That would be fine if the AI wasn’t so dreadful. It’s bad, and I don’t care what anyone tries to say. The enemy units will simply banzai charge your heavily fortified lines on all difficulties once you come into range. So just form a neatly comprised firing line, then perform a classic contact retreat, ambush tactic. It’s literally the oldest strategy comprised. Oh, you need to move up, just move the firing squad forward, wash, rinse, repeat. I’m assuming this wouldn’t happen on multiplayer, but with my dislike for the rules and the host of other problems I wasn’t interested at all.
The easiest thing to criticize is the camera, well maybe besides for the user interface. There is no vertical panning option. Meaning you can pan side to side, but the only way to look further into the battlefield is to zoom into your units. This will not help you at all. Most of your time playing this will be about trying to get a good look at the battlefield. You will move your units and shoot at the enemy about a quarter of the time you’re playing this. That’s how bad the camera and UI is.
The UI, hahahahahahahahahahahahahahahaha. Pretty sure elementary school kids thought of this one and it was then implemented by paid professionals who must not have played a game like this in their lives. The amount of information you’ll want to look at, and what you’re given are polar opposites. They give you a unit list, but don’t mark which ones have moved or not? Why give me a menu with all the unit’s stats… That’s all the menu is, like seriously… why? Then have another menu that has the exact same thing just on the other side of the screen. Like I’m too lazy to shift my eyes over to the other side?
Storylines are just terrible. I would bet that if you’ve played the tabletop then you could predict 100% of what was going to happen. I don’t play it and I knew what was going to happen every step of the way. There aren’t any original ideas in this, everything is incredibly contrived. As stated before I haven’t completed the final mission, simply because I was so unmoved with the relationship between Allison and the last boss that I wanted the human race to go extinct. I didn’t care about protecting the people, or the other NPC’s around me. I just wanted them to die, hopefully then I could get a decent protagonist.
Fans of this tabletop need to demand better. This is a terrible excuse for a game. Even if you fix all the problems, it would still be mediocre at best. You’ll have done and been through everything this game will put you through. Even with my minor dislike for the rules, I might still have been persuaded to check this tabletop out, but after this experience I’d rather not hear about Warmachine ever again.

Thanks to Steam, WS was brought to my attention. Now I play and I like what I've played so far. I'm a level 21 Mechari Engineer. 20 hours logged total.
As a new player, Wildstar may be intimidating to approach. However, the "cluttered UI" is really not that far off from World of Warcraft's UI. It functions much the same. 3rd party add-ons can remedy this, much like WoW. The quest log is a little bit garbled up, but I'm getting it down.
Combat is a breath of fresh air from over a decade of WoW. I've always been wanting a telegraph style system where you actually have to direct your attacks toward your enemy, rather than clicking and locking on a single target. Much of the combat in WS is aoe pack based, but there are plenty of single mob battles. There's been a lot of criticism on this system because you end up watching the telegraphs more so than you end up playing the game, so to speak. So far, I haven't had any issues. I feel like I'm more engaged in an MMO than I've ever been. Once again, I am a new player and I haven't gotten to end-game content yet. Levelling feels like it should: it's not a breeze, but it's not a chore. I can probably gain 1 level per day of gaming sesh. Just like the old WoW days. I actually feel like I'm working for my levels, rather than leveling being arbitrary. But then again, max level in WS is 50, whereas in WoW it's 110, so you can gain more levels in a day in WoW, mostly just spamming dungeons.
The graphic style is quite visually appealing. The soundtrack is awesome, too. The music seems to dynamically change based on what's going on in the game. It's generally enjoyable to listen to. The in-game housing feature is quite insane and much talked about. You get a whole plot of land that you can build whatever you want on. It's quite easy to use and in-depth.
What don't I like about Wildstar? Well, for one, the somewhat cheesy voice-overs when you level up. This may be something that will grow on me in a good way. But for a new player, it's a little jarring when you level up and the typical radio DJ voice over is like, "Holy F@$%! You just blew my mind!" I kid you not, they bleep out words and all. Or, "You just leveled the F@*# up!" This is one thing that is totally out of place in this game.
I get rather low frame rate in some areas. I hear the game isn't as optimized as it could be.
I'm afraid that there won't be any addition of new max level content based on what I've been reading about the game. I'm hoping the devs will do something about this.
As a vanilla WoW player, I really like Wildstar, and for the first time in a looong time, I really feel like I'm enjoying an MMO. I played WoW pretty brainlessly for years, just because it was easy to pick up and populated. I just recently tried Guild Wars 2, and while I dig the art and music, the gameplay just didn't have it for me. There didn't seem to be any incentive to complete objectives. The gear was...meh. Level was more or less not a factor. I looked into other popular MMOs like Aion and BDO, and I'm just not into that weeaboo style. BDO doesn't have end game content apparently? So what do you even do? I stopped playing WoW months ago because I feel like the content they are adding is just vapid and shallow. It's an active game, but the updates just don't stimulate me anymore. Tired of fighting the Burning Legion; they seem to be the only real antagonist in the game.
Anyway. If you're looking for a pretty solid improvement to the vanilla WoW days, Wildstar is a safe bet. It costs nothing to try this game, so you can't lose. If you're looking for difficult and excellent PvE content, try Wildstar. If you're looking for a very unique storyline and loads of lore, Wildstar. If you're looking for an interesting universe with funny/lovable characters, Wildstar. If you're looking for solid and challenging PvE content (while limited), Wildstar.

I've been through several MMO RPG games and Wildstar is still my favorite. It has a sense of personality that I don't get from many others and has my favorite combat system so far. Another big reason I prefer this game is because it doesn't bottleneck you to make a purchase. The in game store is almost entirely cosmetic and even the majority of those can be bought with an in game currency obtained through virtually every form of game play. No level or content is blocked behind a pay wall. Payments such as signature member ship are worth getting if you're really dedicated, but it's there to speed things along.
The only downsides about the game seem to be your typical RPG issues shared through out the genre. Missions can get dull at times as you are mostly killing enemies or collecting items. The character creator could use some additions but it's pretty solid as it is.
I strongly recommend the game to anyone interested. The combat system is very satisfying to use with tons of options to individualize your fighting style. The races are also creative and, thought some of them resemble those from World of Warcraft, I like Wildstar's quite a bit better.

This is my first review here in Steam. I probably saved it until today because WildStar is a game that really grew up into me real fast.
First of all I gotta tell you that the way I pick games is based on customization options, the Roleplaying factor and the art and believe me if you are a person that also enjoys this then WildStar is a game that truly deserves a chance.
As a guy who's always looking for MMORPGs this one is the best F2P I have ever played.
As soon as you start you can see that every class is amazing, I mean it's so unique the way you can play them.
You got your faction archetype, good and bad. I love this one because for me it's a lot of Empire vs Rebels in Star Wars and here you got Dominion and Exiles so, that's something that I truly loved from the beginning.
Classes, again, are so amazing, every single one has its way to be played and all of them can be built the way you want.
The art is amazing. From mobs, to places, to housing, every single piece in the game is awesome.
The gameplay, god, it's so fast-paced that you won't get bored at all. It's not only click and wait to beat a mob, not at all, you gotta dodge, jump and plan your scape or your charge into an enemy, everything in this game's combat system is awesome.
The Lore, I still got a lot to go and invest time into it but as far as I've seen it is pretty amazing. The history of the Nexus is one you should really look into and I truly hope we get a lot more of Lore.
Housing, dear Housing. Let me tell you that for me this is something basic in any MMORPG, a place where you can leave your footprint. Make it public and have people see your creation or just invite your friends. Either way your small plot is something that will grow into you for a long time.
Now, the Roleplaying factor for those of you interested. I love, I seriously love it. The setting has a lot of chances to develope a character. My favorite class is the Stalker because all the gadgets and weapons just make a lot of room for that space bandit that runs inside me.
Content? It's rich in my opinion. I never get bored. Even if there aren't a lot of players online you can enjoy a lot of stuff. There are always people around in some areas, yeah, some more than other, but you can always count on people roaming around killing stuff and completing missions. Plus Paths and Housing truly make solo time awesome.
Is it truly F2P? For me it is. My main goal was always creating all characters and you got your currency that will allow you to buy the slots. Really, you can buy anything with in game currency so for me it's all accessible.
Are there any cons? For me it might only be that is a graphical demanding game and my laptop suffers at times but it doesn't matter to me, I'm faithful to this game and I would truly wish that more people would give it a go.
It's an amazing F2P MMORPG and I hope this review really helps people to try it out. About playerbase, well, it's growing again, it has its ups and downs but I know Devs are keeping it up to make people come back and for me that's the main thing that speaks highly of a game, even if playerbase drops, Devs are always here to ensure that some of us come back.
So dive into the Nexus, you won't regret it!

Resident Evil Revelations is Capcom's attempt at a modern 'survival-horror' game, and makes claims to go back to the series roots. This isn't completely true, but that also does not mean this game isn't worth your time.
Resident Evil Revelations primarily focuses on Jill Valentine before the events of Resident Evil 5. Chris has gone missing (which if Claire has anything to say on the matter, is not an uncommon thing), and a distress signal has been sounded off on a cruise ship left out on a stormy sea. Jill, and new-comer Parker, go in to investigate. And what commences is probably one of the cheesiest plots to exist in the whole series. Resident Evil being cheesy isn't anything new, but this is usually a result of voice acting or nonsensical doors. The plot of the game is just ridiculous, with over-the-top plot twists, extravagant characters even by the series standards, and almost feels like it's convoluted for the sake of being convoluted. But that's not to say it's bad. In a B-Horror sense it's actually rather entertaining, but I suggest you don't come to this game for some deep drama or serious tale and take it for the off-the-rails ridiculous story that it is.
The game is split into 12 episodes, which in part have two parts each. Typically in each episode, you'll play one part of it as Jill in the 'present', exploring the ship and its horrors. The other half changes chapter-per-chapter of what it contains, but typically it stars some other character, either in the present or at some other time, doing something somewhere else that's somehow important to the story. These chapters are usually notably more action-packed than Jill's chapters, and honestly they're usually not quite as good as Jill's chapters either, but they're not terrible. And as the game has an episodic structure, episodes usually end off with a cliff-hanger, and when you start the next episode, it starts amusingly off with a, "Previously, on Resident Evil Revelations..." recap.
The game plays sort of like Resident Evil 4 or 5, but there are differences to the system here. Firstly, the first big difference you may notice are the enemies. The Oozes, are what they're called, and they don't just look different, they chug along, waving their bodies all over the place making them a bit hard to hit. On top of this, they respond different to being shot than, say, Ganado or Majinni. And this takes a bit of adjusting too. Basically, the Oozes are hurt most in the head, but shooting them in the head doesn't actually stun them (and they won't explode in this game, either). It's actually sometimes far more worth your time to shoot their arms or legs. Oozes can lose use of their limbs temporarily, and can be noted when their limbs are damaged and unusable as they dangle around once damaged enough. If you shoot the legs of an Ooze, it'll start crawling around. Shoot an arm off, and it won't be able to use attacks with that arm for a time. Shoot both arms off, and the enemy will be stun-locked, letting you run-in and melee the enemy. Unlike RE4 or 5, you can hold-down the melee button to charge it up for a more powerful melee strike.
There's other changes too that lead to the game feeling different. There's no red herbs, or first-aid sprays, only green herbs in this game, and they're full heals in the title so its often worth holding onto them until you're almost dead. The game has some swimming sections, where you can't shoot your gun but just swim around the flooded areas and make sure to get air every once in a while. You have an item scanner, which you mainly use to find hidden items or scan enemies to fill a percentage (as when it reaches 100%, it gives you a free green herb and resets itself back to 0%).  All of these changes lead to this feeling like a very different sort of game.
The ship is atmospheric and moody, and while linear, does contain the sort of back-tracking and key-collecting you'd expect. Puzzles are underplayed unfortunately, but the game does throw some interesting twists and turns your way through the course of the game to keep things interesting.
The enemies are also fairly varied. The main force being a selection of different types of Oozes, as mentioned earlier, but there's other types about, one returning BOW from the older series, and the game does a pretty good job at introducing new enemies up until the end of the game. There's also a few bosses, who work well for being intimidating, but also fun to fight.
Music is actually rather fantastic. Some excellent songs help the mood and keep the cold ocean feel and melodic charm going. There are several stand-out tracks, but the entirety of it is pretty good.
And let me get this out of the way. It's an excellent PC port. The game shows its handheld nature in many ways, but the graphics have been updated substantially since its original 3DS release. Lots of options to customize, and it runs rather well. Honestly the only issue I've really had at all with the port is sometimes when in windowed mode if you click out a lot, the game will on the rare occasion crash, but its a very minor thing, both as its fairly rare and the game saves progression automatically quite regularly.
The only other thing to touch base on is Raid Mode, which is the replacement in this game to Mercenaries Mode. To best describe it would be to basically say imagine Mercenaries had a child with Monster Hunter, as in this mode you go through locations from the game (either alone, or with a co-op partner online) and hunt and kill monsters, get a ranking, and earn loot. Guns, mods, and the like. You can unlock a rather large variety of characters from the game, each who have their own unique skills (some better use certain weapons, some recover health over time, each has a different knifing style and melee attack, etc.), and a unique level. The level system is like an RPG, where you gain experience and gaining a level increases things like your defense and attack power. However, in a neat addition, you can select your level when selecting your character up to the point you've unlocked, so let's say I had a level 20 Jill but wanted to play with someone who was level 2, I could lower my level down to 2 to play with them a bit more fairly, and then raise it back up whenever I wanted, but not past the level I've unlocked, which is 20.
Raid Mode is absolutely addicting, and probably what will keep you coming back to this title most if you take the delve into it. There's 21 levels, and each one gets longer, more extravagant, and as they go along, start throwing in things like multiple explorable areas and even boss monsters from the campaign. On-top of this, each level has four different difficulties, and these don't just make them harder, but change the layout of each where enemies spawn, where items are, and more. But you need to finish all the stages on one difficulty to unlock the next difficulty. That is, except the 21st level, which is kind of a bonus level that's only recommended if you're maxed out. The last level is a treat in itself that you have to work hard to tackle. It's basically the entire ship from the main game turned into an open-world, enemy-infested obstacle course, with multiple ending points, multiple paths through the ship, and lots of goodies to collect, including a hidden boss exclusive to this stage. It's a lot of fun and very challenging.
Revelations may have a convoluted story, cheesy dialogue, key collecting, back-tracking, and interesting inhuman enemies... But it also feels more like a mash-up of new with the old, and not a true overall callback to the classic survival-horror of the series. But that doesn't mean it's a bad game, and completely worth your time if you either enjoy the series or enjoy these sort of action or horror type of games. It's a lot of fun, and has a good amount of replay value. It may not be the best in its series, but it's a fun, ridiculous ride while it lasts.
