is problematic & at times unimpressive, but still something I'd recommend to single player fantasy action & RPG aficionados.  The game is saved by engaging story & characters as well as the unusual combat mechanics.
First of all, combat.  Of the two player characters, Arkhail is a natural tank with taunts, stuns, area of effect & heavy hitting attacks.  Styx deals big damage & has useful debuffs at both melee & ranged distance.  There are a few "shared" utility skills requiring both characters.  The skills eventually make combat a little tedious, even though you can bind skills to number keys.  Pause feature is nifty, giving you time to think about which opponent to eliminate next.
A quick word on the RPG progression elements: You'll level up, distribute attribute points into statistics like strength, agility, etcetera.  You'll also find, buy, sell, & upgrade equipment with varying stats.  I tended towards Agility for Styx & Stamina or Defense for Arkhail.  This mostly worked well.  Bear in mind however that there will be times when you're forced to rely on one or the other alone, so try to keep them a bit more self sufficient than I did!
As for strategy, I tend to travel using Styx, open combat from stealth, then switch to Arkhail and hold aggro.  Certain units are strong against either Styx or Arkhail; be sure to learn & exploit enemy weaknesses (it's not obvious).  Be mindful of patrols & time your assassinations to cull a group as much as possible before open combat.
Friendly AI isn't always helpful; absent your input, the non-controlled player character will default to the basic attack or even at times delay before doing anything.  In these cases you have to switch back & forth manually giving orders to both.  Targeting is another issue: it doesn't always stick, so you have to retarget the desired enemy; particularly annoying is that your movement is locked at times due to the AI carrying out your orders, which means you can't quickly move Styx out of harm's way without pausing, clearing his action queue, and re-engaging.
Stealth mechanics also leave something to be desired, and even at times feel immersion breaking although that's arguably nitpicking.  While in stealth, Styx has a maximum range of movement away from Arkhail (can't leave the big guy behind!) so be sure to park Arkhail as close as you can without being detected, especially working a large area.  Stealth doesn't require disposal of slain enemies.  Enemy AI doesn't notice bodies at all; patrols walk right by bodies you just backstabbed without pause.  They also have impossibly narrow vision range & poor hearing, allowing you to kill baddies close by their friends (especially if you upgrade Styx for stealth).
On difficulty settings & boss encounters: There are Easy, Medium, Hard & Extreme.  I went with Medium, & the antiheroic duo felt very powerful on this difficulty.  On the other hand, combat difficulty soars from low to very high transitioning from Medium to Hard or Extreme.  In my opinion it simply isn't fun or rewarding above Medium.  Frustratingly, two of the late/final combat encounters are absurdly difficult until you figure out the right tactics.  Making this worse is that choosing the wrong stats & skills can & will sabotage your ability to complete those fights as well as you could; like I said before, gear & upgrade your characters carefully.
What really tops that cake and renders the entire thing a bit ridiculous is the poorly placed save points.  Coupled with your inability to save manually while in combat, this means for those tough fights you'll have to either redo most of an area to reach the boss combat, sit through a mountain of unskippable cutscene & dialogue before actually getting to play, or both.  I'm fine with having to retry a fight until I've learned how to succeed, but nobody wants to sit through the same content like that only to die in a poorly tuned combat encounter.
The aforementioned design & balancing issues were enough to sour the experience for me a bit, in spite of my appreciation for the unique combat mechanics & my enjoyment of the story/characterization.  I know lots of players will be better than I and get through the game on Hard or Extreme but I can't imagine bothering with it.  I was ready to be done by the time I beat the game.
I was underwhelmed by other aspects of
.  Level design is a bit simple, doesn't take much advantage of vertical space besides placing ranged enemies in unreachable perches.  You can use Styx's ranged stance to eliminate them, or the Goblin Toss ability.  Pathing and physics felt jumbled in certain areas.  Visuals were okay by 2012 standards when the game released.  Audio was acceptable, but unmemorable.  Thankfully there were no discernible bugs or technical issues.  The game ran well with settings maxed @ 1920/1080p.
Story & characterization were clever.  It is solidly entertaining fantasy fiction fare with colorful main characters & a unique angle, showing the plight and perspective of orcs & goblins rather than humans, elves & dwarves.  Even this had pros & cons though.  Writing for much of the dialogue & cutscenes (there is a lot of both in the game) felt at times heavy handed, cheesy or just too drawn out.  Voice acting was passably good.
All said & done, the reason I'm giving this a thumbs up recommendation is the creative treatment plus the modest amount of fun the combat offers.  I'm glad I played & learned the tale of Styx & Arkhail.  I would only recommend
if you've already tapped other, better fantasy fare & are interested in a slightly different take on the genre.  I'll eventually be trying out the 2014 sequel,
(which is apparently the prequel in terms of story).

You may of heard that the Resident Evil Series is dead. In some degree that is true but after playing this game I have a different opinion. Resident Evil Revalations was actually my first 3DS game and I was hooked. The Graphics were mind blowing, the action was fun and the game was actually pretty damn scary. When I had beaten the game I gave an applause to Capcom for making this astounding game. The problems I had with this game was the lack of character development and horrible controls. Because I didn't have the dual stick attachment for my 3DS, my rules of engagment was to stop and shoot. Even though all Resident Evil games before Resident Evil 6 had this sort of control scheme, the game was sometimes really hard because you were surrounded by fast moving enemies.
However thanks to this port I can now play the game with modern controls with very little trouble. While the port is a bit buggy (much like every other Japenese ports) Capcom really gave it their best with more content, a well done reskin and of course new and improved controls.
While game could still be better in a lot ways in terms of its horror mechanics, you can tell that Capcom has started to listen to their true fans and are on the right path to resurect the series to its undead roots.

Ok, I'm rewriting this review.
WARNING / TLDR - This game is not for everyone, it is tedious and does not hold your hand, you must be willing to learn, experiment and grind. This is not a new user friendly game, you will have to use your brain - an alien concept to some.
Right, first off the bat, graphics are a complaint I see a lot. If you NEED a game to look pretty to enjoy it, fine, bit shallow in my opinion, but fine, go play Black Desert Online or some newer "sandbox" game. But please, don't let it push you away from Wurm, if you're unsure of how you feel from the screenshots and / or youtube video content check out Wurm Online, you can make a free account which will allow you to see if you can "put up with" the graphics and level all the skills to 20 - which may not seem much, but is usually enough to give you a feel for what you may enjoy, my personal favourite is Carpentry and Weapon / Armour smithing.
The solo player is effectively one huge grind with only self satisfaction at it's end, I'll admit to be a tad gluttonous in that respect (I forged up a 100 quality sword just for the ♥♥♥♥♥ and giggles).
But multiplayer, particularly as part of a dedicated community is incredibly rewarding, with each person fulfilling a specific role through which they rely on each other and can continously train up their skills to be of even more help to their comrades.
The controls are a little dated, but can be rebound to suit your needs, even using macros to do specific actions is a thing - search the wurm forums for suggestions or even just a quick google search to help make the games controls more welcoming.
All in all for me, Wurm has and still is a joy to play, I find it has this odd beauty to it, like a relic of an era when sandbox meant sandbox and not just some adventure game with some procedural generation and limited crafting abilities, but when you taste the upper rungs of the skill caps you struggle to re adjust to the lower levels as the crafting at low levels will usually either fail completly or be of extremely low quality and nigh on worthless for work or crafting uses.
Wurm is a great game. Im sure they improving alot after WU launched here. If you like sandbox games this is the best we have.

I've been following this game for over a year and am happy with my purchase. It's basically Panzer General in the Pacific with better graphics AND:
-Generals with abilities that affect the unit it is attached to and those around him. You can switch which unit he is attached to at the beginning of each scenario.
-Specializations that you can unlock
-More random events
-choose which objectives to pursue from a predetermined list at the start of each scenario. You can gain cool abilities from some of them and cripple the opposing army, but   you won't always be able to complete them all. You will have to make tough choices as to which objectives you want to (or can) complete.
-Much needed supply line mechanic
-More strategic air and sea battles. I'm just diving in, but can tell you that there are slight variations in the mechanics of different units and situations that add to the strategy.
I was initially concerned about the length of the game, but can happily report that I'm only into the third mission of the training campaign and already have enjoyed several hours of play time.
It really is a nice game and right up my, "point and click/ strategy" alley. It keeps to a successful formula and builds on it. Like Panzer General and Panzer Commander before it, you can:
-carry over units from one mission to the next (including their damage/kill stats).
-gain veterency and upgrade units
-attach generals with special abilities (in Panzer General you gained a random hero, which would attach himself to a unit who gained veterency. But the hero would be stuck to that unit. You couldn't reassign him like you can a general/captain/ace in this game).
The only downside is the price for a game like this. While other Indie houses are charging around 20 bucks for similar titles, The Artistocrats are partnered with Slitherine. This means a chunk of the profits have to be split with another party; thus the higher price point. Unfortunately, this means that this really solid game won't reach as many people who haven't played this type of game before...at least anytime soon. They will all wait until this dips to about 20 bucks.  By then, development on a new game will be underway and the funds needed for future updates and dlc won't be as great. I really hope I'm wrong about this because it's a fun game and I'm looking forward to additional content!

It's a fairly good game. It is not as good as it's tabletop counterpart and several key stats and rules have been changed, but it still retains the feel of Warmachine. My biggest complaint is the AI. It has mainly one rule it follows. Run and engage in melee combat as fast as possible. If the unit is a melee unit, then fine, but units with ranged weaponry that close too fast. C'mon, it's headscratching and irritating.
So my recommendation is this:
If you like miniatures wargames but due to space, time or disabilities and can't play much, then this game could easily be for you.
If you are a Warmachines fan and can handle the rules being off a bit and grunts having health and your warjacks missing easy hits, then you'll enjoy yourself.
If you are a wargaming or Warmachine purist. Please don't play it. It won't live up to your expectations and you'll never enjoy the game for what it is.
If you have no interest in miniatures wargaming, then stay away. The game is not for you. It is not fast paced, it requires (some) thought, not as much as against a real person, of course, and you have to understand the rules of the game to play it effectively.

6) Hilarious and stylish in every way - from text, dialogue, voice overs. Even just leveling up!
7) Massive raids - bringing back the good old days of 40+ players and tactics you have to learn
8) Crafting, customization, and your own personal home - there's so much you can do I simply don't have enough room to mention it all. There's pages upon pages for each of those topics.
9) Competitive PvP - if that's your thing, this game's skill cap is incredibly high in terms of PvP
10) Variety of load outs for each class. Want to be a Rogue tank? You can do that. Want to shoot people full of healing with literal guns? That's a thing in wildstar. Every class has at least two or three roles you can specialise in.
Cons (Only one I can think of)
1) This game is suffering from a vicious cycle:
People play and enjoy the game -> There's not enough people playing the game to queue for dungeons or PvP -> Although they enjoy it, since a few of the things are literally impossible to do solo, they end up quitting -> More people try the game -> repeat.
Sadly, this game can feel like a single-player game in many zones. You'll see a few people starting out, then some more in the starting zones, then you can go a long stretch without seeing much of anyone. When you get to big cities, you'll see quite a few people, but not not nearly enough at your level to do early instances or otherwise and many of the party quests you'll find along the way... well... I hope you're good enough to solo most of them.
It's quite the dilemma. Should anyone from the Wildstar team trip across my review, or anyone else who loves this game and wants to encourage more players, here's my suggestion:
Casualize it a little bit more. I truly hate suggesting that, but until the game is back to a big and healthy player-base, make it so groups of 10 or 20 players can do those 40+ player instances. The second thing would be to encourage or even reach out to and/or pay youtubers and the like to play the game for an honest review.
And to those currently playing - I say the same, encourage friends to give it a shot at any chance you get. Hop on forums and combat the naysayers who are stuck in 2014.

I'll first say this game is quite nice. The art is good, the characters too (playing an orc and a goblin in an RPG with humans as enemies is really refreshing), the story is average but the characters are interesting. However, this game has one serious flaw : frustration.
First, all map are linear. More linear than Skyrim's dungeons. More linear than FFXIII's. And all optionnal quests' maps are designed the same way : a linear corridor with 3 battles. Ok, optionnal quests are, you guessed it, optionnal. But in difficulty 3 out of 4, you have to do thoses quests to level up.
The battle system is really frustrating. At least in difficulty 3 out of 4 (thus, 4 too, and maybe 2). Especially for those who want a little RP and want a badass orc without hacking through the levels in a too easy difficulty.
First, your orc is weak. Well, he's stronger than the average enemy, but I was shocked how quickly he can fall, even in defensive mod. For most battles, you want him in full tank/defensive mode while the little goblin does all the dps...
So much epicness is lost here. It would have been better to have the goblin in full status inflicting/assassin role. But no, he will often deal most of the dps...
The rage thing is probably the most frustrating for RP players like me. IF Arkain becomes enrage too early, the battle is probably lost. The only moment when the rage is handy, is when there are only one or two enemies left with little HP, and Arkain can benefit from the extra health he gains when he becomes enraged.
So, basically, either the rate comes too early and you lose, either it comes too late and you lack the epicness, either it comes in a stupidly easy fight you would have won without touching your controller/keyboard anyway...
Why play an orc if you can't go full berserk more often ? Why can't they be a little more useful ?
For the battles, the orc is slow. Ok, it's an orc. The muscular beast who hits hard but is slow. However, his attacks can be cancelled by the enemies a bit too easily. And by "a bit", I mean "a lot". In the early game, trying to stun an opponent fails 3 times out of 4. And the stun time is so short you'll regret trying to stun them. Other skills are so long (because the orc hits multiple times in the same skill), you lose time because he hits the ground after he killed his target... while other enemies are still hitting him in melee range.
Those may seems like little details for you. If it is, well, buy the game. I think I said the main problems I encountered with this game. But for those who wanted to play a badass orc, either don't buy it or play in easy difficulty (with all the boredom it may imply).

This is a great game. Read the other positive reviews, I'm sure they've nailed down the good stuff.
I'm writing this review for a very specific reason, which shouldn't detract from your decision to get this game.
I'm wrecking face in my current game! It's great. I came across a hive-mind empire, and they specifically have a trait that makes it so they literally care about nothing but consuming all other living beings. So they're bad guys. I go to town, take over like ten of their planets in a single war, then begin purging their population from the planets so my guys can live there as their species isn't really compatible with mine or any others.
Purging happens on a timeline. It tells me when it's gonna be done. Great!
Meanwhile, I'm setting up research stations all over the place in my new area, sending ships of settlers to wait above ten or so different planets while I research Gaia terraforming. Future's looking pretty awesome!
Then the purge finishes. All the enemy lifeforms in my new planets are destroyed.
... And now they are no longer my planets.
Instantly, I lost almost all of the territory I'd won in the hard-fought war I just finished. This is obviously weird, so I head to google, and obviously I'm not the only person this has happened to. Others ask the same question I have: "Why did I just lose all my territory after killing off the native population?"
The answer is, apparently, that if there's no pops on the planet, you lose it. And of course people are just like, "Yeah, duh, nobody's there so you can't claim it." Meaning that the species I was systematically murdering for the past month was, in fact, the only reason I could hold a claim on those planets. How kind of them to do that for me while I committed genocide against them!
My obvious followup question is this: WHY IS THIS A THING THAT CAN HAPPEN?!
If the game is just going to up and decide that in doing something it's going to lose me my territory, why the hell doesn't it give me a warning about it? Why doesn't it require me to send a representative citizen to head up the death squads and then begin the colonizing process after the native population is dead?
Why doesn't literally *anything else* happen other than what the game just did?
And here's the kicker: All that territory didn't just vanish, no borders, up for grabs by anybody. IT WENT BACK TO THE EMPIRE I JUST TOOK IT FROM. I look at the population map and there is NOBODY there. There's no pops at all. Because I murdered them. But the thing that just took those planets away from me - there not being anyone on them - also just gave it back to the previous empire... even though there's STILL NOT ANYONE ON THEM. Why the hell do the rules apply differently to me than to the other empires?
This is driving me insane. It's incomprehensible. The game is so well-done - except for this nonsense right here. If I have one wish to come true as a result of me having written this review, it's that the devs will see this and at the very least understand how infuriating this has made the game for me. You know what? I'm gonna tweet the dev team. It's gonna get lost in a sea of♥♥♥♥♥♥that actually matters and I 100% don't expect to get a response, but I need to know that I at least tried.

I can think of a few times where the story was coming to an awesome climax, but just before then, in order to get a special gun, you had to do a fetch quest on the other side of the planet (or something similar). The side quests are especially forgetable as well, which is a shame.
So... BRILLIANT GAME, weighed down with lengthy side quests that do little to add to the plot. In the main story line, all the great Borderlands magic is there, and I'd say, if you ignore the side weight, the best entry in the series.

When I first got onto the game, I was expecting it to be just like world of warships (though this is older than that I beleive According to this post
) however I was pleasantly surprised to see that it was not- despite its similarities. The game is very well balanced compared to War Gaming games, and it is very player friendly and most certainly not pay to win (though the only way it would be is if you spent thousands of dollars a month). The biggest difference between it and its western counterpart is that there is a gamemode with respawns for those looking for something like wows but not as hardcore. The playerbase may be small, but if you are like me, and are tired of alll the headaches and hardcore grinding of WoWS, then give this game a shot. IT HAS SUBS! Also, you are not limited to just American and Japanese ships, you can also do German, English, and they seem to be adding 2 other countries- France and Italy.
First thing I want to clear up though, is tha tthe sonar is automatic, and you need to read its stats in the research tab by hovering over it. Secondly, you may accaisonally play with high teir ships, but thats only because the community is small, and I have personally sunk a T7 in a T3 ship. Also if the enemy has a t7, your team will also have a T7 normally.
I have seen a few players struggle to get used to the games mechanics, and giving up on day 1.  I would like to say that if you are expecting this game to be like CoD where you can just run in, and go guns ablazing, or camp in a section of the map and not die, then get your head out of the frickin gutter dude, this is a NAVAL COMBAT game! Not your 12 year old go to when your mommy refuses to give you twinkies in your lunchbox.  Take time, learn how to use torpedos (ACTUALLY DO THE TUTORIALS), lead your shots, and use your head more than your left mouse button.
EDIT: This game is increadibly underrated with what I can assume to be a very friendly dev team. I strongly reccomend playing this game at least for 3 hours of combat time before judging it. Furthermore, the ingame consumables dont seem to be worth it from experience. You get some crates every now and then and they give you consumables for free, though it is random along with the daily logins. The system for gold coins in the game is surprisingly friendly, however i dont see much use for it. The game gave me some free gold an I used it only to convert XP from one ship to global XP for others when i had maxed it out. One thing i would like to add to this review is that the player base seems to be dropping, which is really sad in my opinion. It is one of the only games I've played where playing as a submarine is fun. Those reviews saying its pay to win probably are all of the type who are unwilling to GRIND!*Caugh* well, not everone wants to obviously, but Im already at T4 and I didnt spend any money on it so far, and im about to unlock T5. So I strongly reccomend trying this game for yourself as its probably the hit or miss types.
Over all a great game with some minor issues they may or may not fix.  Its been a blast, dare a i say a ship tonne of fun. :)  8 out of 10 for solidity.

Nier: Automata
When the game first released, I avoided it like crazy. Reasons? Bullet hell. I absolutely hated bullet hell games. Long story short, while NieR didn't change my views on bullet hell games, it certainly surpassed my expectations.
Overall: 9.5/10
NieR: Automata is an immersive 3rd-person hack-n-slash RPG that incorporates multiple mini-games like bullet hell, maze puzzels, tell-tale, etc. Multiple playthroughs with multiple joke endings brought about by your decisions makes the game enjoyable on multiple levels. I was able to achieve 100% achievements within 48 hours of gameplay, but this game could definitely last longer than that.
Basically, NieR: Automata = Kingdom Hearts + Geometry Wars + Metal Slug
Spoiler Alert for the reviews ahead. Read at your own risk.
Gameplay: 8/10
NieR: Automata gets a little getting used to. As a veteran Souls series player, the control scheme was a little difficult to get used to. Good thing it's very customizable. The gameplay itself was a little strange at first as well, balancing bullet hell with hack-n-slash was weird at first, but soon to learn that basically you just have to find a rubber band and tie it around the fire button and you're good to go (don't do this lol, just that firing constantly provides benefit over harm 99.99% of the time, save for those few times where you don't want to attack friendly NPC). The combo system isn't exactly polished, but a hell of fun to work through them. Each typees of weapons have their own attack style and length of combos, you have 2 weapons on at all times, so mixing those combo and lengths together allows you to dish out some cool stuff all the while blasting them with your pods. The only thing that really brings gameplay down is playing as 9S. His ability to hack seems cool at first, but quickly became repetitive and tiring and just a drag to do. Part of the DLC emphasizes on the hacking mechanic and makes it a pain to complete. Hacking is basically Geometry wars but worse, althought there are multiple variations, the basic gameplay of the hacking is the same.
Story: 8/10
As a newcomer to the Drakengard and its spinoff series, I known nothing coming into NieR: Automata. Good thing its story is standalone. The story revolves around the YoRHa androids engaging in eternal battle against the machines and their alien masters. Or so that's what the game should've been. Instead, the plot progressed into 9S being obsessed with 2B and trying to get revenge by killing 2A. While this is the main plot driving point for endning C, D, and E, this felt lackluster and a drag to advance. 9S became really annoying almost immediately, but i'll get to that later. The main endings, on the other hand, was really fun to achieve, saved for D (but that's just because 9S is a little ♥♥♥♥♥). The endings are ambiguious, mysterious, and almost open ended as to what happens afterwards. Personally, I really enjoy these kind of endings that doesn't close the series, almost allowing a sequel to occur in the future.
Characters: 9/10
We following the main characters 2B, 9S, 2A through the game.
2B: The first character we're introduced to, cool, calm, collected, and hot. Very hot. Anyone who has self-destructed knows that sacraficing all but 1hp of your life is totally worth it, and not just for the damage. 2B is a strong female protagonist that knows her♥♥♥♥♥♥ Her personality, paired with NieR: Automata's setting makes the first playthrough of the game extremely fun. Plus, her secret achievement? 10/10 would achieve again. Sadly, 2B doesn't get much love outside of the first playthrough, or else she might be my favorite.
9S: Oh boy this little ♥♥♥♥er. During the first playthrough, 9S was tolerable at most. More emotional, headstrong, and sassy than 2B, 9S is your buddy for most of the first playthrough and protagonist of the second and part of third. 9S has his moments, especially those conversation with Operator 21O that really brings his quirky personalty out and makes him likeable. But other than that, 9S was a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ He was overly obsessive, attatched, and felt like a teenager during puberty.
A2: Hmmm A2, basically take all the good traits of 2B, raise it to the powerlevel that's above 9000, and you get A2. Stronger in terms of stats, more appealing in terms of character traits. A2 is an older, in terms of production, and more mature, in terms of personality, version of 2B, that is playable in the third playthrough. Juxtaposed to 9S, she was a more fun character to play. A2 represents the old school Android views that all machines are bad, yet you witness her changes as she meets Pascal and others.
Music: 99999999999999999999999999999/10
The music for this game is too good for my lowly ears to listen to. Each area in the game has its own theme song and all are absolutely beautiful. Within the first 3 hours of gameplay, I was compelled to buy the soundtrack and boy was it worth it. I can't really describe it so either play the game, or buy the soundtrack. Its the best part of this game.
Bonus: Bullet Hell; 1/10 - 10/10
Like i said in the overall, I hated bullet hell style gameplay. This is actually a core mechanic in the game, ranging from top down to 3rd personal bullet hell. From geometry wars to just projectiles during your hack-n-slash, and the hacking. While this wasn't fun to play, it certainly wasn't that bad. However, SPOILER ALERT, the final true ending consist of a bullet hell through the game's credits. While 99.99999999% impossible to beat on your own, the game allows you to receive help for all other players who has finished the game and sacraficed their save files. Their save files then tags along you and makes the bullet hell extremely easy to finish. After the difficulty decrease, you are left with a breath taking bullet hell sequence that has beautiful effects, AMAZING theme song (again, get the soundtrack) and reminds you that you were able to get here with the help of other players.
Conclusion: NieR: Automata wasn't on my list of games that i want to play, but it ended up being one of my favorite games of all time. Give it a try despite the negative reviews that you might read.

Really wanted to like this game, as I'm a fan of both Warmachine and TBS games; but there are too many bugs in it at this time to get any kind of enjoyment out of it.  The most annoying is that multiple units will frequently lose activation status in the middle of a turn before all units have acted.  Trying to end turn gets a message that some units still have actions to perform, but none of those units can be selected to act.  Worse, the turn cannot be ended, so once that happens, the only thing that can be done is to reload from the most recent save point.  Some turns have taken three or four tries to get through because of that bug.
Optimization is poor, as I'm constantly dealing with performance issues with a system that is over the recommended specs on processor and memory, and roughly equivalent to the  recommended speds on video (dual Nvidia GTX460s in SLI config).
The controls are also rather clunky for a TBS game; particularly the camera.  Character focus is particularly annoying, since the game will auto-center on whichever character is activated, which can shift camera position wildly and slow things down as focus changes.
Ranged targetting also has some significant flaws.  It's also not always clear who is within a particular unit's field of fire; and targeting is extremely clumsy.  Cover appears to exist, similar to X-Com Enemy Unknown, but it's very hard to tell if it actually has any effect on the actual gameplay, since the RNG seems to overrule any such effects.
One of the weird things is that there is no character amination in the cut scenes.  None.  There is dialog, but the characters just stand there like figurines, not even any lip movement, and it's often hard to tell who is speaking without the voices.  Dawn of War 2 handled this much better.
Even more annoying, the official website does not appear to have any community forum, and no mechaism for submitting bug reports.  It's like the producers simply don't care about making it work.
I got the base game and all DLC for less than $20 on sale, and it was still overpriced; as the game is almost entirely unplayable at this time.  I would strongly recommend against purchasing this, even at a discount, until they get these bugs fixed (something that the development team seems to be making no effort to do at this time).

TL;DR: This game is rad.
Let me begin by stating I've never written a review online for anything -- at all. I've tried almost every MMO out there looking for a new home after having a tumultuous, multi-year relationship with World of Warcraft.  My hope by writing this review is to spur some community growth because I believe so strongly in the potential of this game.
I've tried almost every significant MMO out there like WoW, Tera, Archeage, GW2, Aion, BDO, ESO and a few others not worth mentioning.   Not only is this game extremely charming and reminiscent of what Vanilla WoW was to me years ago, but it’s relevant in such a way that motivates me to continue playing it instead of trudging through earlier content just to get to how endgame feels, which is what is had been doing trying to find a WoW replacement.  It’s funny, the music is great, the combat is snappy and impactful, and I LOVE the graphical style.

After around 4 years, after of its console release, Under Night In-Birth Exe:Late or UNIEL for short, is finally here.......only for Under Night In-Birth Exe: Late[st] to announced for this holiday season for the PS4, and with no word on a PC port anytime soon. Classic Arc Sys. However, don't let that discourage you from buying the game because there's still enough to at least carry you over or prepare for UNIST's release!
I'm doing to divide this into several major topics: story, art-style & graphics, casual content, mechanics, accesibility, and netcode.
Story:
This section is going to be short because it's not something I prioritize in fighting games. Simply put, the story is a over the place. The gist is that Hyde was just a ordinary high school dude, but everything changed when
some beings of darkness attacked him and awakened his ability to use a strange energy called exs after being saved by a young girl named Linne. Did I say young girl? I meant 500 year-old soul of a princess that takes control over new bodies every time she dies thus making her immortal. After seeing hyde's potential she teaches him swordsmanship and gives him the Danretsu no Menzaifu. Together, they try to kill Hilda the ringmaster of the void.
The game doesn't really do a good job filling us in what kind of past each character had or where each relationship comes from. At the very least, they could have told us how other characters discovered their ability to use exs. Whatever, it's not an anime fighter without a convuluded story.
Art Style:
This is one the games major selling points. It took me bit to realize this game uses sprites. The characters have good designs with Merkava and Carmine probably being the best ones. Some are good but a bit generic with Hyde being the biggest offender. The anime opening before the title screen looks fantastic and the song is catchy too! Kinda makes you feel like you're standing in front of cabinet in Mikido, Japan. The characters animate well, stages are colorful but not distracting, the special moves are flashy as hell. The game looks damn good. Moving on.
Casual Content:
Aside from story mode there's a few modes to keep you playing. Time attack has you defeating fighters as fast as you can, arcade mode is your traditional 10 stages of fighters but no cheap boss at the end (Can't really tell if that's good or bad), survival mode is where you only have one round and your health is only slightly restored after each fight and your goal is to beat as many fighters you can until you die. You earn in game currency (no microtransactions) to get more colors for characters and customization for your title block but title blocks don't really matter if you're not doing netplay which in most cases, casual players stay away from. In short, there's really nothing to write home about. Just ok.
Mechanics:
Oh boy, my favorite part of any fighting game. The core mechanics. UNIEL is a four button fighter A, B, C, D which are light medium heavy and concetraition respectively. The first thing you'll notice is the Grd system in the bottom middle of the screen. When the circle fills up the fighter with more diamonds will get a buff called Vorpal. While in Vorpal, you get 10% bonus damage and the ability to use chain shift, which converts whatever diamonds you have on the grd, into meter. The grd circle is a timer so whoever has vorpal has the ability to lose it if their opponent has more grd. On a side note, you can mash A to do an auto combo which is perfect for casual play. It looks flashy and it's easy to do. There's more to this game but this is all you need to know to start with. Which leads to the games' major flaw.
Acessibility:
The combos are not too difficult, but not really easy either you want the big boy damage and setups. If you've played arc sys fighter, you'll feel right at home. Some characters are more difficult than others, with Seth being the most unforgiving. Training mode is solid with recording functions and the ability to set you input delay by the frame. Perfect for practicing for offline tournaments as the Ps4 has a native 3f input delay. So what's the big flaw?
There's no tutorial mode.
This is a HUGE turnoff for most players (Although a minor inconvience for me because I usually do outside research on fighting games anyway). There's a good amount mechanics I didn't mention that are imparitive in order to be good at the game. So you want to learn the game and character, you're going have to consult some outside sources.
Although a tutorial mode is added in UNIST along with character combo trials to fix this issue, It still should have been in there initially.
Netcode:
The most important part of any fighting game and I'm happy to say that the netcode is great. It can handle coast to coast connection pretty well, and on average I only get 2-4F max when playing online. The lobby system is where most players reside (which the player base is really small, but it's up to you if that's good or bad. Personally I like it) and like most anime fighters, ranked mode is dead because nobody plays it so don't bother with it.
Conclusion:
The balancing of the cast is pretty solid, but not perfect. Despite that, all the characters are unqiue in terms of playstyle and their personal mechanics. However, if you want to git gud, you gotta put some effort outside the game, but then again, what fighting game doesn't?
If you like anime fighters or a fan of Blazblue & Guilty Gear, I'd highly recommend you pick this game up. If you're on the fence about it, wait until UNIST is released on Ps4 this feburary since it will have a tutorial mode and 4 new characters.
Hopefully, a PC port of UNIST will be developed shortly after the ps4 release, but until then have fun with UNIEL!

I find this game to be a fun and relaxing way to spend a few hours.  Well 175 hours as I write this review.
It does take a bit of time to figure out how to achieve things but after a while you soon get it and find yourself enjoying the experience.
I find that treating this as a game where you spend time initially surviving and then finding yourself thriving as you build your home / village up and spend time making various items and improving the quality of them as high as you can so you can sell them to the traders scattered around.
The silver you make will then be enough money to pay for your deed and guards, if you have any, and then to keep paying the upkeep costs of the deed as, if you fail to do this, your village will eventually disband and decay away if you dont manage to keep up with the payments.  This wont happen too quickly though if you do find youself away for a while.
There is combat as well, both against the animals and other various creatures in the environment as well as other people if you venture onto the pvp lands.  Its a bit you hit them then they hit you but your clothing / armour / weapons and elevation etc all help to decide the result of these battles.   You can normally get to pvp enabled lands via a boat from the pve lands so whatever your prefered gamestyle there is something here to suit you.  Having said that the pve area's tend to have the most people playing .  I think f you approach this in the right way through then pvp its a fun diversion and a good use for all that armour and weaponry you will have built for yourself.
I guess this wont be for everyone, but if you are unsure then trying out wurm online itself is free up to level 20 on your skills.  If you want to get those skills to 99 though you will either need to buy this version for a one time fee and play on the free servers (or create your own) - Unlimited tends to be a slightly speeded up version of the game as your skills can increase more rapidly and other actions like growing crops can be speeded up.
Or if you want the full experience then subscribe to wurm online itself.  Its been going over 10 years and has a loyal following.
Overall I find this to be good fun.  I am going to log in again myself now and work on improving the cloth puppet toys I am making.  I find they normally sell quite well if they are high enough quality.... then I guess the pigs will need tending.... I also need more iron.... see ya!

I am writting this review now that I am near the ending of playthrough no.2 (ending B) so I can keep an happy mind to write this review without tears. This japanese story writer is famous on having happy endings but when it goes to true story route it became some wild emotional rollercoaster.
I been following this game serie from drakkengard. It's very interesting to see a serie from dragon rider that fight flower into a post alien invasion world that inhabited by machine and rebot while humanity escaped to the moon. The story is very loosely connected to drakkengard but it's quite tightly connected to first Nier. I never played first Nier but to prepare myself for this game I spent many hours on Utube to watch an entire playthough of it. I Personnaly recommend your guys to do the same before playing this game IF you never played Nier. A lot of important and interesting reference from the old nier are in this game and this game is the after effect many years later from the first Nier.
Plot itself is very interesting but the most interesting part of it are at the very begin of the game when fighting boss the size of the building for the first time. That's probablly one of the most interesting boss fight I had in this last few years. The other boss are also very interesting but it doesn't have the chill quite like that first target.
Graphics and control are smooth with fantastical combat sequences. The CG quality of this game is nothing short of epic. Regular graphics of background and object are not exactly the best I ever seen but it does give this game a feel of digitized realism.
Very interesting Chip skill system and there are a lot quests that give you some much needed items resources and exp.
Overall difficulty is quite easy. I recommend player start on normal but as soon as you get use to it change the difficulty to hard as the game difficulty would be too easy without it. At least on hard you will need to use all your buff items and restore items until you gain those good recovery skill chips.
What tops all the good things that I said so far?? Music and Sound effect is legendary for this game. I can listen to some of the metalic songs for this game for hours and hours. (This cannot continue is my favorite and can put me into a trance).
24 endings with 1 dlc endings are mostly silly but A-E are the important ones that will only be awarded if you finish a playthough. Make sure you at least playthough the game 3 times as the third playthough will be vastly different then the A and B.
I will deduct 0.5 point to my review score from low difficulty and some of those silly fletch quests to give this game a solid 9.5/10
Time to play on and finish the rest of the game.
PS: Like many japanese port this game is not very good on game optimization so it does require high spec pc to run effectivly so if you low end spec pc run this game on low spec I wouldn't recommend it.

This is a great game. Read the other positive reviews, I'm sure they've nailed down the good stuff.
I'm writing this review for a very specific reason, which shouldn't detract from your decision to get this game.
I'm wrecking face in my current game! It's great. I came across a hive-mind empire, and they specifically have a trait that makes it so they literally care about nothing but consuming all other living beings. So they're bad guys. I go to town, take over like ten of their planets in a single war, then begin purging their population from the planets so my guys can live there as their species isn't really compatible with mine or any others.
Purging happens on a timeline. It tells me when it's gonna be done. Great!
Meanwhile, I'm setting up research stations all over the place in my new area, sending ships of settlers to wait above ten or so different planets while I research Gaia terraforming. Future's looking pretty awesome!
Then the purge finishes. All the enemy lifeforms in my new planets are destroyed.
... And now they are no longer my planets.
Instantly, I lost almost all of the territory I'd won in the hard-fought war I just finished. This is obviously weird, so I head to google, and obviously I'm not the only person this has happened to. Others ask the same question I have: "Why did I just lose all my territory after killing off the native population?"
The answer is, apparently, that if there's no pops on the planet, you lose it. And of course people are just like, "Yeah, duh, nobody's there so you can't claim it." Meaning that the species I was systematically murdering for the past month was, in fact, the only reason I could hold a claim on those planets. How kind of them to do that for me while I committed genocide against them!
My obvious followup question is this: WHY IS THIS A THING THAT CAN HAPPEN?!
If the game is just going to up and decide that in doing something it's going to lose me my territory, why the hell doesn't it give me a warning about it? Why doesn't it require me to send a representative citizen to head up the death squads and then begin the colonizing process after the native population is dead?
Why doesn't literally *anything else* happen other than what the game just did?
And here's the kicker: All that territory didn't just vanish, no borders, up for grabs by anybody. IT WENT BACK TO THE EMPIRE I JUST TOOK IT FROM. I look at the population map and there is NOBODY there. There's no pops at all. Because I murdered them. But the thing that just took those planets away from me - there not being anyone on them - also just gave it back to the previous empire... even though there's STILL NOT ANYONE ON THEM. Why the hell do the rules apply differently to me than to the other empires?
This is driving me insane. It's incomprehensible. The game is so well-done - except for this nonsense right here. If I have one wish to come true as a result of me having written this review, it's that the devs will see this and at the very least understand how infuriating this has made the game for me. You know what? I'm gonna tweet the dev team. It's gonna get lost in a sea of♥♥♥♥♥♥that actually matters and I 100% don't expect to get a response, but I need to know that I at least tried.

I'm playing it since two months and I'll say some words about it.
Basically is a WoWs clone but with some significant differences (at least for me).
We have 6 ship classes.
. Battleships. Damage dealers. You sit back and shot whatever your team is spotting. Equivalent with arty in WoT.
. Destroyers. Backbone of the game. They are spotters equipped with torps/depth charges. A good DD can win a game. Equivalent with scouts in WoT.
. Light cruisers. Almost the same role as DD's.
. Armored/heavy cruisers. Now that's a curious class. They are not BB's (lacks firepower/armor) but also they're not CL/DD (lacks agility/view-range). :confused: Looks like mediums in WoT
. Submarines. Very interesting class and nice implementation. They are TD's from WoT.
. Carrier. Hard to master but fun when you succeed. Can be arty from WoT or scout.
Big plus for me is lack of aim-assist/auto-aim whatsoever. Landing shots on moving targets is all about your skill.
Second plus is separate control for all your armament. Primary guns, secondary guns, torpedoes, depth charges, launching planes, AAA, smoke bombs, all is managed by you. A lot of micro-management in the heat of the battle but is fun.
RNG is fine. Both for accuracy and damage. Nothing frustrating here.
Different battle modes. Deathmatch/respawn. Event/fleet battles but I'm not here yet.
Gold ammo/premium consumables. They exist but I can handle the game with standard ones.
Maps are fine. You have big open maps but also small and filled with islands. There are nigh battles, very interesting game mode too.
Matchmaker. Perfect fine as long as it has players to choose. Wacky if lack players.
Grind. Nothing new here. If you have played WoT/WoWs/WT/AW you know the drill. As a side note I'm playing for two months and I have a Tier 8 ship and a lot of Tier 5-6-7 (all equipped with equipment/consumables) and I still have 36 mil. in bank.
Rewards looks fine too. It happened to finish a battle as MVP (best player from both teams) even I lose the battle (so I received more XP than the first guy in winning team). Also if you have a bad game you receive almost nothing even if your team wins.
You have a lot of rewards. Daily login/daily reward, weekly reward, monthly reward and even season reward (each season is reset at 3 months). Usually the rewards are consumables, premium battles, premium days, equipment but also gold or qualification points for commanders or merit points.
New players are helped too. Reaching Tier 2 in each class unlocks a commander. Reaching Tier 5 and you'll have merit points. You also receive a premium Tier 2 ship if you login for 20 days (it doesn't need to be consecutive) and a premium Tier 4 ship for 30 days login.
Also you have some gold packages and buying one you receive same gold value as a bonus and a nice Growth plan where you invest 10k gold and you'll receive 22k gold and a lot of free XP when you'll unlock ships from Tier 4 to Tier 8.
Otherwise 1$=500 gold. A month of premium is 4500 gold so you pay $9 for it.
Another interesting option is to pay for premium battles (not time). So let's say you don't have time to play every day. You play 10 battles today, nothing tomorrow, 5 battles day after tomorrow and so on. You can buy exactly how many battles you want to play on premium account. Nice idea.
Ships classes are well defined too. Play well and know your boat/role and you're important for team. There are some Premium ships that look like P2W (yes Laforay I'm looking at you) but they're not game breaking.
We have subs as a new thing compared to WoWs. And they are interesting to say at least.
Game mechanics is OK. Scouts are essential. A well played scout can win a game without doubts. A bad scout usually means a defeat. Physics is arcade. Arcade. Ships doesn't feel like real ships but I can pass this.
Overall the game looks playable and fun.
Now the bad parts.
The biggest bad thing is lack of players. Basically the game is for China and Steam part is forgotten. No advertising whatsoever and they even don't want to make press accounts for youtubers to promote the game. Now you spend a lot of time in queue waiting for a battle and when you finally have it it's a 3 vs. 3. Bummer.
is the chart of player population. 400 average players with a peak of 600. Not exactly a multi-player game...
Graphics. They don't look too bad but they are far away from 2016.
Ping. On the high side (170 for me) but because they have only US servers and nothing for us from Europe. Is not too bad I still can land shots where I want.
Sealclubbing. It's connected to lack of players (at least this is what I want to believe) but when veteran players are playing in low tiers is not exactly an encouragement for new players to be slaughtered by elite ships with fully trained commanders (even if commanders skills are crippled until Tier 5).
Another thing that I really don't like is commanders. In fact how they implement them. Right commander on right station on right ship can make a difference. Bad thing is that those commanders are draw with merit points lottery. You have no control of what you get, just pure luck.
Yes you can buy some commanders in shop, yes you receive some commanders reaching Tier 2 but the "real" commanders (I talk about 4* commanders) are received via lottery.
And the icing on the cake is qualification for commanders. They can be qualified on 2 levels:
- first level is playing them until they reach Level 10. Some skills are unlocked just by this level of qualification. This is fine, more you play faster you get to level 10. As a side note all my DD/BB commanders are level 10 because you use same commander for same class of ships (even more, you can use on some of them on different classes, first in mind is Arashi with his spotting range skill).
- second level is promoting them in rank. Those damn stars. And the only way to promote them in stars is with Qualification Points. Those QP's are only obtained from commanders lottery. When you receive a commander that you already have you'll receive QP instead. 10 QP for one star commander, 20 for 2*, 50 for 3*. But promoting a 3* commander to 4* costs 1000 QP and from 4* to 5* 2500 QP. You have 5 commanders/ship and 6 ship classes. Just imagine how long it takes to have them 5*...
So for me this commanders mechanic is BS. It has nothing to do with player skill but only with luck.
As a side note I don't have any 4* commander until now. And I did some lottery draws until now...
Bottom line, the game is playable and looks fine. It gives me some fun but only in peak hours when games are not only 3vs.3.

I really, really, want to give this game a positive review.  Unfortunately, in its current state I cannot.  I love Warmachine, both the fiction and the table top game and this game could be among what makes this setting enjoyable if only the game mechanics weren’t such a wreck.  What makes this game so bad isn’t that it is an actually bad game; it is that there is a layer of greatness under all the bugs, poor optimization, needed quality of life improvements and just plainly lazy game creation.
Many of the issues have been present since the games pre-release for KickStarter Backers.  The game is poorly optimized, sometimes needing you to be on the bare minimum due to some asset that is continuously renderings in the background and other levels you can crank it up to maximum.    The graphical bugs are many, from ‘dancing’ corpses to clip in issues.  One of the most annoying parts is the cut-scenes (if you can call them that).  They are literally just the characters on the battle map freeze framed.  Looks more like a picture than a scene, which would be fine if they worked with that as a basis but the implementation looks like a bug or at least accidental.  Some very well done RPGs use just character portraits and text to tell story and do it just fine.  But, it has been checked, this is intended.  What is even more frustrating is the tools used to help measure and draw lines bleed into these scenes making it even more frustrating.  The ultimate annoyance is that some scenes actual have animation and you see what could be…
From a Turn-Based Strategy point of view this game needs a lot of help, tooltips are incorrect and many useful functions are hidden under layers of tutorials that the game never prompts and lacks any form of toggle options for things like range measurements, grid form or markers (common in all TBS).  To be fair, some of these things do exist but they are implemented more like a tech tool than a game function.  They are launched by shortcut control keys and their functionality is lacking.  Their appearance even looks like a tech tool or else something in beta.  Even worse is that these tools were not implemented with the terrain in mind, there are maps where you can’t see the effects or they are so poorly done (smoke clouds) they become invisibile.  This was later 'fixed' by creating colored grids... again this comes off as a tech tool or a placeholder but have been present for months.  Even when properly visible it becomes a glorified marker, again looking like a tech tool used for game creation and less like an awesome effect (the biggest violator of this is warjack debris).
From a setting point of view the game is NOT Warmachine Table top in video game format, and I’m okay with that, I’d be able to go as far as saying I prefer it.   If I wanted that I’d go play warmachine.  They make some really good changes to make the game flow but it comes back to a screeching halt on some of the other decisions, infantry seemingly designed to kill other infantry struggle but suddenly become wolverine when in melee with a ‘Jack.  The developers appeared to understand that things had to change to make the game feel more epic but it was just too easy to manipulate, sending Jakes into a heavy warjack knowing I could heal through it or positioning my army knowing the AI would just run into melee with me.  I am left with a feeling that the AI is either poorly designed or intentionally neutered.
If you are reading this and you are struggling with the single player all you need is:  Defender, Bandit (the Charger), and take stormblades and gun mages.  And you win, not because it is super effective but because the way the AI plays.  You shoot them until they ultimately run into range, your melee kills what is left and any real threat is just kept at arms length with your gunmages.
Ultimately, if you love turn based strategy games stay away from this title, if you love the warmachine table top, again, stay away from this title.  I really wish this wasn’t the case, I trogged through the entire single player campaign and will play the expansion but so much needs to be done to make this game worth playing outside of just die hard fans.

TL:DR This is a really good game.
So, Under Night In-Birth Exe:Late (hereafter referred to as UNIEL because that's what everyone calls it) is a fighting game made by Arc System Works, also known as The Guilty Gear People or alternatively The BlazBlue People, which says a lot about what you can expect. Unlike other ASW fighting games, though, UNIEL is much more accessible, and thus much easier to recommend, and its dark/gothic anime aesthetic is much different than their other works.
PROS:
*Simplified fighting systems that still have great depth, making the game good for all skill levels
*Grind Vorpal system rewards agressive play, naturally making matches fast and action-packed
*Fluid combat with combos that string together easily and look cool while doing so
*Strong character diversity with really fun characters
*Multiple singleplayer game modes to keep you occupied with a variety of challenges
*Soundtrack is a nonstop list of epic music
CONS:
*The newest version of the game, UNIST, comes out in February on Steam, so you may just want to wait for that
*No tutorial or combo challenges, so you have to learn and test everything with no ingame guidance
*Online scene is very quiet since ArcSys didn't do much to tell people the game existed
*Only 16 characters, making for a comparably small character pool compared to other games
*Not much content to unlock, just some artworks, extra colors, and profile decorations that can all be unlocked decently quickly, leaving you with nothing to spend your ingame currency on
Ultimately, even if you only play the singleplayer content, this game is still great, and when you fight against your friends it becomes basically magical. Unless you want to wait for UNIST to come out, I strongly recommend getting this game and then playing as Gordeau for a good time.

Of Orcs and Men is without a doubt the worst RPG game I ever played (and finished). It has serious issues. The pacing of the the storyline, the overall cut short game length, the corridor level design, the lack of enemy variety (there are only 5 types of character models in the whole game), shallow strategy, obstructive unadjustable camera, overly long cutscenes and the worst controlled in game target acquisition i have ever experienced. Sometimes my characters just deliberately ignored the appointed enemy and attacked what they felt like.
I dont even know why i continued to play this game. The combat handling is unlike anything i have ever played before. This game does not know weather if it is a real time strategy game or a turn based RPG. The tutorial sequence is very short and taught me next to nothing at all. You get told pretty much nothing and have to inch yourself forward by trial and error. In fact the first 2 hours in this game were so bad i wanted to drop this game right on the floor.
The character management is not very noteworthy. You have few items slots that can be filled with pretty much few identical items. If you ever go for a defensive stance you are pretty much ♥♥♥♥ed. You can never respecc your Status or Skill Tree Points. If you made a poor decision once, your are stuck with it until the end of the game. The fact that some of the enemy encounters are just outrageous and you need to kite them around obstacles just to not ♥♥♥♥ing die in the blink of an eye is just ridiculous. I'm looking at you, Dog Trainer. What the ♥♥♥♥ was Cyanide even thinking.
I give this game credit. Cyanide made a bold move daring to create their own dark fantasy themed franchise in this overly bloated market. As i was able to experience in the later Installment of Styx: Master of Shadows the team has a vision. I would compare it the closest to Warhammer. Dont get me wrong, i am very glad they do something independent and different and as much as i wish i could like the game just for that, i can simply not.
The graphic design of this game is acceptable to impressive. The main characters and the scenery stand out. They are nice examples of how to properly do greenskin characters. The sound design is acceptable. Fighting sounds and scenery music are good, though with 5 tracks a little short. Some of the characters have poor voice actors, while others have excellent ones. Styx ones is Excellent.
This game back in the day when it was released was overhyped. I don't know where the problem was, that the team was too much occupied with the foundation build of a new engine and a new fantasy brand, but it really hurt the overall game. It did not age well. Its just too short and the levels string badly together. The first and second chapter are so long that you will spend approximately 75% of your playtime there. The 3 last sections are so short that i was confused to the point where I wondered if I have accidently skipped some missions. It doesnt help either that they cut out crucial parts of the story with drawn cut scenes where you could be there out in the field making the way with actual gameplay.
It really is a regrettable waste of effort. If this game would have gotten a slightly bigger development team and about 6-12 months additional time, this may would have turned out to be an excellent game. Maybe even game of the year material 2013. But as it stands, Of Orcs and Goblins is a game only a RPG fan or a Ork enthusiast with a strong stomach can digest. I give it a 4 our of 10. Still , i hope Cyanide will just do the same as they Did with the stealth game in this series and deliver a new title that will surpass this one. The few times when the game was not teabagging me i was enjoying it. Remembered me of Metal Gear Rising a little. It has long elaborate cutscenes, which sadly can annoy or stress you at times. Some scenes were implemented poorly right in front of a difficult encounter and end up unskippable.
The current asking price of 30 euros is a little high. I recommend you wait for a sale and get it when it is under 10. Playing warning is adviced. Play on own risk.

There are plenty of stories out there that put you in control of Orcs, but few do the fearsome race justice. 'Of Orcs and Men' does what other titles in the genre fail to achieve: it makes you see what it's like to be a hulking beast of rage and muscle. As the warrior Arkail, one of the main gameplay mechanics is to manage your bloodlust - if you let it get the better of you, Arkail will go on a blind, murderous rampage. While he amps up his damage this way, you can only watch on helplessly as he makes poor tactical decisions, exposes himself needlessly to enemy fire, and even turns on his constant Goblin ally (who you also control). Built around this unique idea is a rich story adhering to a fitting theme - that of Orcs being enslaved as beasts of burden by human masters.
The combat is handled by queueing up your next attacks, reminiscent of the system from Knights of the Old Republic. This may push the patience of those wanting more immediate and visceral action, but it works well enough to get you through the entire adventure. With sharp writing and characters you grow attached to, this is a unique experience that deserves a lot more attention than it received. Unleash your inner berserker and give this revolution a shot - whatever happens, at least you know you'll go down fighting.

Having only recently played through it, I don't regret taking so long to do so.  It's just... bland. The bosses and legendaries were also sort of forgotten about, bugging one of my friends much more than myself.
Nearly the entire game was just fluff to provide a game around 2 major events concerning Jack.  Really, anything that didn't involve him or Fragtrap was just kind of null and dumb.  I didn't find many other characters memorable or really cool, just one-off gags and/or tools to progress the plot.  Plenty of forgettable and annoying landscapes, characters being pushed along by a forced "you're working for me" and "we have to save the world" theme instead of their own motivation, and no new mechanics since Borderlands 2  (except Ice and oxygen) didn't help.
The oxygen system is beyond unnecessary.  Like... there's no way to put it other than it's dumb and useless.  It takes forever to drain, and when it does drain you just have to find some bubble or geyser to refill it, and if it does run out you don't even die that fast.  Imagine, while playing (for example) Far Cry, you just have to hit the Page Up button on your keyboard every 5 minutes or you start to lose health slowly.  That's not interesting or fun, it's just annoying and a waste of time.
There's 3 major plot points that I found to be the only reason to care about this as a Borderlands installation.  MAJOR SPOILERS AND MY OPINION ON THEM :
Aside from that, there were only a few other small events that were really interesting and fun(ny).  It was just recycled Borderlands 2 stuff but not as exciting.  It's not an awful game in itself, but definitely a letdown compared to its predecessors.

Having read some negative reviews concerning this game, I did not put too much hope into it. Everybody who has played Borderlands 2 knows exactly what will come, and everybody who did not play Borderlands 2 should do so first.
The gameplay is better than in Borderlands 2:
- Cryo weapons are much more funny than slag weapons. You WANT to use them and are not FORCED to use them.
- Laser weapons are a much better ETech replacement. Versatile, strong and good to use. Best addon to the Borderlands line of games.
- The levels are much more diversified... Low gravity, standard gravity. Atmosphere or vacuum. Running across a moon surface or hopping along across the outer hull of a space station using jump pads.
- The Grinder is a good way to improve your gear in the endgame; an alternative to boss farming.
- Vault hunters actually talking to NPCs and each other ingame gives them more personality.
Worse than Borderlands 2 is the story and the NPCs. Except from Springs (because she is first new one you meet) and Pickle (because he is so annoying) I don't remember any one of them. Most of the time, I did not really care why I was doing this mission or that. OK, I get it, Elpis is Space Australia. I understood the joke half an hour into the game, but they keep re-telling it during the whole following rest of it. You need to get the Claptrap DLC to get a good round story ending that fits nicely into Borderlands 2. The biggest story con: there are four original vault hunters, but the story is only told from the perspective of one of them, Athena. The rest don't seem to matter much.
So overall: if you can buy the complete package with all DLC for about 25 €: get it, you'll get your share of fun. But I wouldn't pay full price... the "it should have been the last Borderlands 2 DLC" feeling did not leave me during playing this game.

I'll just make this review quick.
Story is dry, not very appealing.
Quests can be a bit tedious at times.
Game is a bit slow off the bat.
Gameplay is nice, the laser weapons are definitely fun.
Bouncyness of the moon can get a bit annoying, but once you learn how to treat your double jump as extra mobility you soon get used to it.
The characters talk more often and have a bit more depth than the more or less silent protaganists in the previous games who occasionally remark about critical kills or their action skills.
Cryo seems like an acceptable replacement to slag, and I like its function, it can feel a little overpowered at times though.
If you're a fan of the other games, this one does absolutely no justice, its story is lackluster besides the fact you're teetering between being the bad guy and the good guy.
Play as Nisha if you want to just plow through the game without really thinking or have someone with no experience to the other games, her skill is just an aimbot with increased damage, and is generally very lax to play as.
Wilhelm is there for the sake of filling in the backstory of a bossfight that wasn't really that hard in Borderlands 2, and just fits the support class with the obigatory turrets, good for mobbing.
Claptrap is the support basically, if you're not healing the team, you're living by the skin of your teeth with the fragtrap tree, or constantly switching weapons "cuz subroutines r fun."
Athena is the melee character, and generally good all around I'd say.
Jack (The doppleganger) is meant to buff himself based upon the misfortune of others or yet again switching weapons over and over.
Au-Ar-The ice woman, sniper based gameplay, and almost entirely based around the concept of constantly debuffing your enemies, sniping them, and incorporating cryo in to pretty much everything you do, has an entire tree dedicated to co-op if you're into that.
Huh, this review wasn't exactly short, now that I think about it.
I say its good, story is about as indepth as a puddle, but the gameplay is very nice, playing with a friend is heavily recommended as some skills entirely depend on co-op or just have one because friends are nice.
Get it on sale, and try and tell yourself that most of the story isn't canon.

FIRST OFF, THIS GAME ISN'T BAD. I only picked 'no' because Steam hasn't given us a "Depends" button yet and I like to think this might encourage a little more critical thinking.
I would reccomend this game to a specific group of people: namely the long time Warmachine fans. The devs did a great job of recreating the game and it's rules- it's about as close as you can get to playing the actual tabletop wargame. The graphics are rock solid and the battlefields well suited to the skirmish style gameplay.
Pros:
-Plays almost exactly as the original game
- Models are faithful to the original designs, and even improve in some areas.
-Good maps
-Fair range of units
But...the cons:
-UI and menu layouts/designs. They're servicable, but inelegant. If you're new to Warmachine, you are going to struggle to make sense of what might come naturally to someone who plays the tabletop.
- Sound design is limited. The music isn't bad, it's just that the same song loops continously while you play. I eventually turned it off and had a playlist going in the background. Voices are sporadic and mediocre.
-Unit selection is fair, but  getting nickled and dimed for the  additional units is some BS.  I bought the video game to get away from this in the tabletop game, man.
-And most damnably, the AI. My word, the AI is breathtakingly stupid to the point of most matches feeling anti-climatic. You'll feel like you're bullying a ret,arded kid. This AI could be decent for practice if you're new to WM as a whole, but is mediocre for anything beyond that. If you get this game, be sure you've got some buddies to play with. Because after the 6th time your AI opponent just walks it's warcaster right into the melee range of your juggernaut, the novelty wears off.
In short: If you've played the tabletop and are an existing fan of WM- go for it. Just be sure you have some friends to play with. Beyond that though, I can't reccomend it. It's a good adaptation for a niche game. You just have to be into that niche to get your money's worth.

Okay, to start with, I'll point out that there was a very small review (archived at the bottom of this one) that was essentially a complaint about how the game lacks a save system. Well, less than a week later the Dev's implimented a save function to single player. Clearly they read the old review and terrified by the thought of annoying me as they had, they fixed it as soon as they could. (I don't actually mean that. That was a joke.)
Oh, and I'll also mention I've never tried the multiplayer mode, so I can't comment on how popular it is or how easy it is to get pick up matches or suchlike. If that's your thing you'll probably want to check the discussion forums for that.
Right, so.... actual review time now. Where to start? Well, the game looks rather spectacular. They went all out on the graphics, that much is obvious. Everything looks nice and crisp and all the animations move smoothly. More often than not when a game developed like this puts that much focus on graphics it tends to suffer in other areas like performance, but I can't say that's true here. When I bought this my PC was chugging along with an absolutely shameful amount of RAM that meant that most toasters had more processing power than it did, and there was no lag in combat or movement. The closest things I can think of that some people might consider to be issues here are the cutscenes, which are voiced but not animated (You get still images of the people involved in dramatic poses while the lines are spoken) and the way corpses can pile up - if you kill enough people in one small area the bodies tend to stack up and get a bit weirdly floppy and wave limbs wildly and suchlike. Neither thing is an actual game breaking issues though, just something people might not like.
TL;DR: Graphics good and shiny nice.
What next? Gameplay. Well, the UI can be a touch fiddly in a few cases - if a unit gets extra movement, say from a skill that lets it shuffle about a bit after killing someone you need to actually click on the YES I'M DONE WITH THIS UNIT button which caught me out a few times and made me think the game had broken the first time it happened, but once you get used to it it certainly isn't the worst UI I've ever dealt with.
There's a thing called confirmation bias, where people have a tendency to only remember the things they want to be able to use as proof of something, so take this bit with a grain of salt, but I suspect the RNG is stacked in the AI's favour - I definately think I've missed more hits than I should have, and damage rolls have consistently been on the low end. That might just be me though, or it might be a hidden behind the scenes thing to give some much needed help to the AI. The enemy AI isn't amazing. It's functional, but it will never end up giving you one of those stories you can talk about where it did something totally unexpected and wrecked you with a flank attack or something. It's all 'hail diddle diddle, straight down the middle'.
TL;DR: UI slightly fiddly, AI Functional, not amazing.
Ultimately there's a fairly solid little middle of the road game here. It isn't incredible and it wont blow your mind, but what is here isn't bad - they could have scraped together some crappy mobile game and paid a Korean coding sweatshop to port it over later or hired some random developer to vomit up something for whatever number the xbox or playstation is up to this month, but they didn't, they got someone to put together a nice little PC game that is still being patched and worked on regularly, and that should count for something.
All told I'm going to have to quietly change my recommendation to a yes.
