Of Orcs and Men is, at its core, a tactical RPG about the interesting symbiosis between a rogue and a warrior in a fantasy RPG.  The warrior has a stun attack with a high chance of being dodged.  The rogue has an attack which prevents the target from dodging for 5 seconds.  Put them together and you feel clever!  This gameplay works, and we've seen it work in other games.  For example, the original Dragon Age had the exact same symbiosis between a rogue and a warrior and it worked great there.  However....
This is a negative review, but I'll start with the good:
+ Very glad to see some variety in story.  The greenskins as protagonists is an interesting angle.  The story itself is mostly good.
+ Graphics are decent.
+ Combat has enough depth to be interesting, with lots of abilities which synnergize with each other to produce new effects.
The bad:
- The voice actors sound like they're muddling through lines in a second language.  Worse, it sounds like several of the lines are translated literally from the original french, meaning clever local idioms just become nonsense.
- Game was obviously written solely with an xbox controller in mind.  When you reach a hill and have to move your mouse back to look 'up', you have to pull it about three mousepadlengths because the Y coordinate has a different sensativity than the X coordinate.  This cannot be changed in the options.
As I mentioned above, the whole game is about doing clever things with your rogue and warrior TOGETHER.  So you'd assume that, generally, they target the same enemy, right?  Wrong.  Their autotargetting ALWAYS chooses different enemies, so I'm being totally serious when I say 50% of my game time was simply smashing the Q and E keys paging through interminable lists of targets trying to get them to both hit the same guy.  This would be less of a problem if the click selection works, but it doesn't.  The camera is locked 2 feet from the action, usually staring at a wall, and clicking an enemy is just as likely to select the guy 20 meters behind him as it is to select him.
This is a game about combat in which I like everything except the combat.  The combat is awful.  Can not recommend.

UNDER NIGHT In-Birth makes up the trifecta of must-have ArcSys Fighting games on PC right now along with Guilty Gear and BlazBlue. Whereas Guilty Gear is the most stylish of the three with its stylised 3D models and animations while BlazBlue is the craziest in terms of gimmicks and mechanics, UNDER NIGHT In-Birth is the happy medium between the two sporting high quality sprite artwork, a more subdued less crazy gameplay and a soundtrack that easily rivals that of GG and BB's.
In terms of gameplay, Air-dashing which has more or less been a staple that defined anime fighting games is not in UNIEL (though a similar mechanic is still present) making this a more ground-based fighter. Motions and specials have been streamlined to be much easier to perform and learn and with the addition of a smart-combo function, UNIEL is a very easy fighter to pick up and play.
Unlike Guilty Gear and BlazBlue which had very comprehensive tutorials however, UNIEL is lacking in that department so seeking third party help via wikis, videos or a friend is the best a player can do in terms of explanations of mechanics which can be a bit discouraging. Thankfully the aforementioned streamlined controls makes it so that once you get your head around the mechanics and terminology, it's smooth sailing from then on.
While I personally got the game initially because of hype for the upcoming BlazBlue Cross Tag Battle, UNIEL's well balanced cast of characters, clean artstyle and incredible soundtrack makes me excited not just for BCTB but for a potential port of UNDER NIGHT In-Birth Exe:Late[st] as well.

This game is flat out amazing. Soft Circle French Bread did great with developing and is a underrated name in the fighting game business, especially in games like Melty Blood (which I recommend you check out as well). And with the publishing done by the most passionate fighting game developer, Arc System Works, it's one fighting game you need to play.
Presentation
When it comes to graphics, they may seem simple. But they are very pleasing to the eye. Especially with the 3D Backgrounds and stylish looking HUDs. If you're too picky about 3D Graphics, please don't play this game. But if you enjoy really well hand-drawn pixels and 3D backgrounds, this game is great. The cast of 16 diverse characters with great voice acting, appearances, and skins are all unique in their own way and appeal to different fighting styles.
Gameplay
Gameplay is not as simple as it seems. The game of course comes with A (light) attacks, B (medium) attacks, C (heavy) attacks, and D (drive) attacks. But be aware that the characters do separate themselves due to difficulty and control. So choose your character wisely! The GRD and EXS systems are really nice and make the fights more interesting and rewarding. The game modes are full of variety like the Arcade Mode, where you can go through a character's story in a visual novel format with fights sprinkled in. With these game modes and mechanics, the game truly feels complete.
Verdict
Soft Circle French Bread & Arc System Works know fighters. This game needs to be played and needs to receive a lot more attention. Under Night In-Birth is honestly one of the best, if not, the best fighting game ever made. If you have any anti weeb bias, you need to put them aside and play this game.

Revelations is an excellent game. It features both the quality horror atmosphere that the first couple titles in the series are famous for, as well as the improved gameplay introduced in RE4, that ended up steering the series into a different direction.
Fans often complain about the change in tone from RE4 forwards, but both this game and Revelations 2 offer the best of both worlds, horror and gameplay. And these titles are often ignored or shoved aside as "mediocre", when nothing could be further away from the truth. Give it a fair chance and you just might find out that this is one of the greatest titles in the entire series.

This was actually pretty a decent Resident Evil game overall. I think this is because the game actually quite feels a lot like the old RE games, and it truly feels like a survival horror. But the game still focuses a lot on action as well. I thought the game story and the graphics were rather, underwhelming, but I guess I can not really blame them as this game basically started out as a Nintendo 3DS game.
The game actually feels like you are watching something like 24, kind of like a TV series that you would see on TV. And I thought that was an interesting idea.
The gameplay overall is quite well balanced, it is something more like a mix of Resident Evil 3 + Resident Evil 4, with better control overall.
I mean, the game is really good. But, it just does not exactly "stand out" as you'd expect it to be. Maybe Resident Evil: Raccoon City is a bit more fancier graphically, but then again, since it started out as an N3DS game, I can not complain.
And if anything, I thought the final boss was ridiculously hard for no reason. I have a feeling that I do not have good weapons against him, but then again, I don't think I can go back and find the weapons.....the creators should've learned from Resident Evil 5.
Overall, nothing much to say. Not bad, not that amazing, either. Still quite enjoyable though.

Revelations is my new favorite Resident Evil game since the release of RE4. It brings back horror, and some action, just like the first installments. Sure, it's a port of the 3DS version but a very playable (and upgraded) one at that.
The graphics aren't realistic, but I thought they were very well done and I like the way everything looked. The atmosphere was definitely good. The voice acting is also surprisingly good and not too cheesy.
You'll be switching between several characters during the game which keeps things interesting, but the best parts are still the ones that play out on the big ship. You have a special camera that allows you analyze enemies and once the analysis reaches 100% you'll get a free health item. You can keep doing this but once you've captured the same enemy multiple times its progress will slow down. It's a very interesting game mechanic; do you risk getting attacked to analyze that one certain enemy, or do you just kill it and see if you can do it afterwards (which isn't always possible, because enemies disappear just seconds after being defeated).
RER is a lenghty game, even though most of the other RE games take longer to complete. I finished this one in 10 hours, which is the ideal length if you ask me.
In other words; thumbs up for this Resident Evil !

I could sit here and list off things that need to be fixed/updated/changed, but unfortunetly, the developer has said that he will no longer be working on this game, ever again. However, I'll go ahead and tell you why you shouldn't buy this game.
-Multiplayer?
You'd have better luck connecting to someone via a potato and a cracked bendy straw. This game does not have proper multiplayer. If you're like me and have not the slightest bit of insight on network programming, you're♥♥♥♥♥♥out of luck with this. I shouldn't have to look up a "how to" just to play the multiplayer of a game with friends.
-Tutorial?
Not really. Much like the multiplayer aspect, I had to look up a "how to" on... almost everything. From controls, to crafting, to what makes what, etc.. As much as I like games not holding your hand, even Dark Souls taught you the basic controls.
-Story? Character? Setting? Life?
Nope. You're just thrown into a world of caves full of monsters and NPC's that don't have the slightest bit of life to them, or any reason for them to be there other than that they just are. Why are there floating spike boulders and swinging vines holding axe blades? Just 'cause.
-Gameplay? Difficulty?
The inventory is awful. Extremely small, no management options, and, as mentioned before, nothing telling you how to use it. Supplies are frustratingly scarce, requires asinine amounts ingredients to make a thing, and good luck finding/obtaining them. Tired of using a stone pickaxe? Too bad, because now you can only pick caves that only spawn ores that you can't pick with your pickaxe. Have fun trying to get through cave 4 with your stone sword that's nearly broken, because you ain't getting anything better. The game also punishes exploration by having a set time in each cave. Take too much time, and you'll be instakilled by some creature that's twice as fast as you and is pretty much invulnerable.  The towns may have something useful, but only if you have the insane amount of gold they want. Everything is randomly generated, btw.
-Music?
Heh, have fun with the 3-4 looping tracks that are in the game.
If you really want this game regardless of what I have to say about it, fine. It's your money. But at least wait for a sale. There's no sense in buying this game for ten dollars.

Nearly the entire game was just fluff to provide a game around 2 major events concerning Jack.  Really, anything that didn't involve him or Fragtrap was just kind of null and dumb.  I didn't find many other characters memorable or really cool, just one-off gags and/or tools to progress the plot.  Plenty of forgettable and annoying landscapes, characters being pushed along by a forced "you're working for me" and "we have to save the world" theme instead of their own motivation, and no new mechanics since Borderlands 2  (except Ice and oxygen) didn't help.
The oxygen system is beyond unnecessary.  Like... there's no way to put it other than it's dumb and useless.  It takes forever to drain, and when it does drain you just have to find some bubble or geyser to refill it, and if it does run out you don't even die that fast.  Imagine, while playing (for example) Far Cry, you just have to hit the Page Up button on your keyboard every 5 minutes or you start to lose health slowly.  That's not interesting or fun, it's just annoying and a waste of time.
There's 3 major plot points that I found to be the only reason to care about this as a Borderlands installation.  MAJOR SPOILERS AND MY OPINION ON THEM :
Aside from that, there were only a few other small events that were really interesting and fun(ny).  It was just recycled Borderlands 2 stuff but not as exciting.  It's not an awful game in itself, but definitely a letdown compared to its predecessors.

Having read some negative reviews concerning this game, I did not put too much hope into it. Everybody who has played Borderlands 2 knows exactly what will come, and everybody who did not play Borderlands 2 should do so first.
The gameplay is better than in Borderlands 2:
- Cryo weapons are much more funny than slag weapons. You WANT to use them and are not FORCED to use them.
- Laser weapons are a much better ETech replacement. Versatile, strong and good to use. Best addon to the Borderlands line of games.
- The levels are much more diversified... Low gravity, standard gravity. Atmosphere or vacuum. Running across a moon surface or hopping along across the outer hull of a space station using jump pads.
- The Grinder is a good way to improve your gear in the endgame; an alternative to boss farming.
- Vault hunters actually talking to NPCs and each other ingame gives them more personality.
Worse than Borderlands 2 is the story and the NPCs. Except from Springs (because she is first new one you meet) and Pickle (because he is so annoying) I don't remember any one of them. Most of the time, I did not really care why I was doing this mission or that. OK, I get it, Elpis is Space Australia. I understood the joke half an hour into the game, but they keep re-telling it during the whole following rest of it. You need to get the Claptrap DLC to get a good round story ending that fits nicely into Borderlands 2. The biggest story con: there are four original vault hunters, but the story is only told from the perspective of one of them, Athena. The rest don't seem to matter much.
So overall: if you can buy the complete package with all DLC for about 25 €: get it, you'll get your share of fun. But I wouldn't pay full price... the "it should have been the last Borderlands 2 DLC" feeling did not leave me during playing this game.

I'll just make this review quick.
Story is dry, not very appealing.
Quests can be a bit tedious at times.
Game is a bit slow off the bat.
Gameplay is nice, the laser weapons are definitely fun.
Bouncyness of the moon can get a bit annoying, but once you learn how to treat your double jump as extra mobility you soon get used to it.
The characters talk more often and have a bit more depth than the more or less silent protaganists in the previous games who occasionally remark about critical kills or their action skills.
Cryo seems like an acceptable replacement to slag, and I like its function, it can feel a little overpowered at times though.
If you're a fan of the other games, this one does absolutely no justice, its story is lackluster besides the fact you're teetering between being the bad guy and the good guy.
Play as Nisha if you want to just plow through the game without really thinking or have someone with no experience to the other games, her skill is just an aimbot with increased damage, and is generally very lax to play as.
Wilhelm is there for the sake of filling in the backstory of a bossfight that wasn't really that hard in Borderlands 2, and just fits the support class with the obigatory turrets, good for mobbing.
Claptrap is the support basically, if you're not healing the team, you're living by the skin of your teeth with the fragtrap tree, or constantly switching weapons "cuz subroutines r fun."
Athena is the melee character, and generally good all around I'd say.
Jack (The doppleganger) is meant to buff himself based upon the misfortune of others or yet again switching weapons over and over.
Au-Ar-The ice woman, sniper based gameplay, and almost entirely based around the concept of constantly debuffing your enemies, sniping them, and incorporating cryo in to pretty much everything you do, has an entire tree dedicated to co-op if you're into that.
Huh, this review wasn't exactly short, now that I think about it.
I say its good, story is about as indepth as a puddle, but the gameplay is very nice, playing with a friend is heavily recommended as some skills entirely depend on co-op or just have one because friends are nice.
Get it on sale, and try and tell yourself that most of the story isn't canon.

A positive review definitely but but overall a drop in standards compared to Borderlands 1 and 2.
It wasn't all bad  (minor spoilers follow - but a review has to tell you about the game).
THE GOOD STUFF
1)  Lasers.  Accurate, always elemental effects, and coming in a choice of high power or high fire rate by the end these became my default weapon.
2)  Tougher enemy. They are more accurate at long range and their close range fighters are aggressive and fast.  No longer can you stay at range and pick off every enemy with a sniper rifle (although sniper rifles are still very useful in the game).  The AI is far better at using cover too.
3)  New characters.  I played as Wilhelm whose combination of attack drone and heal drone kept me alive through some sticky situations.
4)  There's about half a dozen really good set battles in the game- predominantly the boss battles.
5)  The final level enemies are particularly strong.  Having the correct elemental choice becomes an essential more than an option.  You'll end up choosing your weapons to have a variety of elemental effects immediately available.
6)  The airless game element encourages more aggressive play from the player.  Since dead enemies often drop air tanks there is a greater incentive to get in close.
7) Handsome Jack.  Your now employer is a more stimulating and equivocal personality than in Borderlands 2.
8)  Final battle is suitably epic.
THE BAD STUFF
1)  Confusing map layout.  A couple of early missions I abandoned because I simply couldn't find my way through the map to the destination.
2)  Very few in game spawn points on quitting.  I played through the same quite tough section a dozen times or more trying to find my way through a series of platforms.  Finding the final exit from the map was a lucky guess because at first sight the exit point doesn't look like an exit.
3)  Bad mission layout.  One mission required you to collect and donate 50 ordinary guns but the place where you donated was in the middle of a map and was guarded by hostiles.  It never seemed worth the effort.  Mission start points were often in the furthest corners of the map discouraging uptake.  Early in the game far too much emphasis on platforming.  In one of the early "retrieve the Echo recorders" missions the first recorder was in a location only accessible by jumping into a pressured steam vent and grabbing it.  The Steam vent was next to a lava channel so you died if you got the leap wrong.  There was only one spawn point per map (compared to up to four on Borderlands 2) which were roughly half the size on average of the Borderlands 2 maps so travelling around was difficult.  A racing game which plunged you into inaccessible terrain.
4)  A far greater proportion of my deaths were falling into hostile terrain than in Borderlands 1 and 2.
5)  No mention of Jack's daughter.  Where was she when all this was going down  ?  The pre-credit cut scene fails to take into account that when it happens Jack is guarded by up to four armed to the teeth Vault Hunters.
6)  Puzzles where you have to find your way around inaccessible terrain (I resorted to Google a couple of times) are far more frustrating when you're regularly having to retreat to replenish air which you're expending rapidly in double jumps.
7) Underuse of a mid game enemy - very fast, bullet sponges, good weapon skills.  Only present for one very small segment of the map.
8)  Game was much shorter than Borderlands 2
Borderlands is a great series and Borderlands The Pre Sequel is by no means a total failure.  If the developers went back to making mission start points more accessible players would get more out of the game.  I think in this case far too much use was made of inaccessible terrain and platforming which spoiled my enjoyment.  There's a central section played around a large transit centre/ shopping mall that has no deadly terrain, has air throughout and played closest to the original games and that's what I enjoyed best.
For Borderlands 3: -
1) Decide tone early on.  In Borderlands 2 the players veered from superhero type saviours to sadistic psychopaths rather uncomfortably.
2) Make the vast majority of mission start points easily accessible to the player.
3)  Don't have puzzles which require thought in areas where players can't stay for any length of time.
4) Less inaccessible terrain.
5)  Put in some effort on the story and the NPCs.  From the final (in time) cut scene the narrative is going in a particular direction but don't lose the series' unique collection of oddballs and weirdness.
S.x.

I wrote my initial review on March 7th, 2016, with 14 hours in-game time.  It is now March 12th, 2016 and I have 56 hours under my belt.  Here's what I've learned...
* Wurm Unlimited (which is based on the Wurm Online MMORPG) is a masterpiece of a game.
* It hands nothing to you (except basic tools).  You must work for everything.
* Something you think will take 5 minutes ends up being 4 hours, because you can't stop playing.
* Looting is a non-issue on servers that don't allow thievery.  Lock your stuff up and it's safe.
* It's a massive game world.  You can go anywhere.
* The world is so beautiful and the landscape so extreme that you'll be in awe time and again.
* The graphics settings available are insane.  You can adjust everything.  I cranked it with my 970 GTX.
* The game loads quick and it runs great.
This game is something you can really sink your teeth into and take your time.  It's so rich in depth.  You'll be finding hidden gems (game mechanics) that'll blow your mind; that they thought to add such things into the game.
Coming from almost 500 hours in Rust and being tired of the same old formula (build up, log off, come back later to find you've been looted to oblivion), Wurm Unlimited is like a breath of fresh air.
Word to the wise.  If you're expecting instant gratification, don't buy this game.  If you're not ready to put long hours into Wurm, this game isn't for you.  There is no one to hold your hand.
However, if you're looking for a meat and taters and seconds... no... heapin' helpins... aw hell, the whole cow and the whole potato field, this game is for you.
UPDATE:  I've now spent 245 hours in Wurm Unlimited.  I have my own settlement (Perry on Mythmoor).  The depth of the game is such that it still has much to reveal for me. I'm reaching halfway on my skill levels (50) and I have only scratched the surface.  If you give it a chance, you'll find it addicting and a pure joy to play.  Since everyone is on the server for enjoyment, most are friendly and helpful and become your (new) friends and neighbors; socializing happens naturally.  I assume I'll be spending another 245 hours in Wurm Unlimited.  Probably way more.  In a nutshell, BUY IT!.  Still on the fence?  Look at my screenshots, watch some videos first.
Wurm Unlimited is like a sponge, it'll sap your life from you.  The real world will cease to exist or at the very least become a haze you walk through to get to your next login.

Maybe wait until it is finished.
The base game is a war game set in space, with partially-implemented stubs of other play styles (diplomacy, scientific exploration, civilization management).  Those other options are being developed on an installment plan, as DLC.  Maybe in another year or two, when the game is actually finished and all of the DLC and the base game are bundled into a reasonably-priced package, then I'll come back and play it.
Even as a galactic game of Risk, it's sorely lacking.  The AI is terrible, particularly at empire management, so to make the AI competitive the devs dug deep into the past and used the same fix the very first Civilization game used - let the AI cheat.
And you can't get achievements in anything but Iron Man with no mods, so you can't use mods to fix the worst issues and you can't even reload a prior save if an enemy magically summons an enormous fleet out of the phlogiston itself a week after you declare war...

It's cool if you prefer RP to a realistic 4X game. Since you start with the best military unit in the game and the tech/economy scales linearly (which still somehow makes upgrading your starting corvette worse). Meaning that you basically spend the same amount of credits to produce the same amount of minerals (0.5 credit per mineral per mining building - upgrades just increase the credits converted). There are a few things that scale multiplicatively, but those are few and while helpful don't detract from this feeling that while your empire may be getting bigger, it's not really getting any better.

*Get this game on PS4 if you have one. Some technical aspects of the pc port leaves much to be desired, such as the unnecessarily high bitrate of the cutscene. Get the FAR (Fix Automata Resolution) mod if you want improved framerate and a fix for the fullscreen scaling issues.
Play all the sidequests and main endings and proceed to cry your ♥♥♥♥ing eyes out.
Yes, the game has its flaws. The texture might not look the best, and the cityscape could be bland and repetitive. But really, when you start playing the game and become so engrossed in the characters and story elements, you never really think about those things.
The gameplay feels satisfying, as you murder your way across the map with your different attack combos, weapon loadouts and pod skills. If you can't get into games with horrible gameplay, rest assured.
Story - oh my god the story. There's really no way to talk about this without going into heavy spoiler territory, but just know that please keep going after you finish your first major ending (A). There are 5 major story endings to this game (endings A to E), and each and every one of them is essential to understanding NieR:Automata as a whole. Endings are a bit of a misnomer, in any case, since they are more akin to major chapter breaks in the storytelling. As you move forward in your playthrough, everything will become more and more depressing, and you're gonna love every bloody second of it.
Sidequests - this game does have its faults when it comes to side quests. A lot of the side quests in this game are simple fetch quests, much like the original NieR but to a lesser degree. However, there are also ones that will absolutely wreck you in the best possible way. The side quests are where you get to know your characters better. If you only go through the story without veering off even slightly, the characters might feel bland and empty. It is in the side quests where their personality shine and you get to know them on a deeper level. In my opinion, I think that a lot of character building in side quests should have been placed in the main story instead, but hey, it didn't diminish my love for the characters so eeeeh.
Soundtrack - the soundtrack is brilliant in every sense of the word. Each area of the game has its unique "feel" and the soundtrack conveys it very clearly. An
that inspires a sense of wonder and playfulness? The soundtrack and vocals portray it wonderfully. An
that genuinely feels out of place within the landscape? The soundtrack can also perfectly mimic that impression. The background music even has different versions depending on the scenario. A quiet version plays as you casually roam in the cityscape, a dynamic version plays when you enter combat, a vocal track is added on top of it when it comes to particularly intense moments, and an 8 bit version that plays during certain moments in the game. The best part is, the transition between the different versions is so seemless that you won't even notice. Everything just fits together so perfectly.
All in all, if you think this game is some kind of weeb bait with the revealing outfits and almost deliberate panty shots, you're not exactly wrong. The director Yoko Taro himself even admitted that the characters are designed this way simply because he "just really likes girls". But there's just so much more to this game than what it looks on the surface, and I am sure that you won't be disapointed if you pick it up and play it through to the very end.
Sidenote: The game seems to be designed for controllers. To be more specific, the dodging mechanic feels way smoother with a controller than with a keyboard. Do keep this in mind if you're getting the game, but the game is definitely still playable with mouse & keyboard.
Tl;dr (with a little extra): Great story, phenomenal soundtrack, fantastic voice acting (both English and Japanese), unique and well-developed characters. And the game just fits everything together so perfectly.

On the surface, this is a an action JRPG with scantily clad women fighting against evil robots.
Just like its immediate predecessor, NIER, and the spiritual predecessors, the Drakengard series, the real identity of the game is only revealed layer by layer through multiple playthroughs, each either slightly changing the story or building upon it to create something altogether different.
In the end, NIER: Automata is a game about the meaning and value of life, told through the eyes and thoughts of artificial entities, androids and machines alike. The gameplay is great for the most part, although some parts may appear grindy and frustrating if the wrong choices are made in terms of character building. The music and character design is absolutely beautiful and the underlying story is both sad and wonderful. I played with Japanese voices and English subtitles, which was an awesome combination. All in all, a very worthy successor to the original NIER.
The only issue is the horrendous PC port, but you can (and should) fix this with 3rd party tools. That this is necessary at all is a bit embarassing, sure, but the (easily fixable) technical issues should not deter anyone from giving this game a chance.
Absolutely recommended.
Tip: There are 26 "endings" in total, but only five should be considered "good" or "real" endings (A-E). They are unlocked in sequence by continuing to play the game after an ending was achieved Don't stop playing until you have seen ending E.
Also: Don't bother too much with backtracking for side quests at the beginning of the game. There is a very serviceable fast travel system in place after a couple of hours. Of course you can still enjoy a nice sprint through the world, if you want. :)

Well this game was pretty unique experience. Very good story, cool main characters and great visuals. Also we are being introduced to very well done fighting mechanics. I don't want to say too much, for I think that even talking about some of the gameplay elements would spoil the fun. I bought this game without getting to know what kind of product that is, without reading reviews, without watching videos. I can say, I'm happy about it, because it was really fresh experience. But if you are reading this, you propobly want to know more before buying, so let's get to it.
If you want it short here are pros and cons:
GOOD
-combat system
-story
-main characters
-statistic based, old school RPG elements
-great world design
-nice graphics
-harsh atmoshpere
-great dynamics between two protagonists
-can be really challanging

BAD

The story evolves around an orc Arkail and goblin Styx. This duo is well writen and it's fun to watch how their relations evolve through the game. So, our orcish protagonist is facing a mission: kill the racist Emperor and stop the genocide of the orcs. Styx is being introduced as his guide around the human kingdom. The first part of the game is honestly not a killa. We are moving and fighting around ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s sunken in rain and mud. Quickly we can see the differneces between the two of our protagonists, not only in their appearances or way of thinking. Arkail is a tough warrior, kind of tank i'd say. Styx on the other hand is thief-like chracter, we can use him to silently eliminate some of the enemies before the real fight. After that he can stun or damage armor of the enemies to help Arkail deal bigger damage, and also make his own attakcs more deadly.
After getting through the first parts of the game (that is after getting beyond the Wall) we change monotonous environment and story gets more dynamic. We are constantly hearing some funny talk between Styx and Arkail, which is nice, because game amtosphere does not feel so inflated.
I must say, that if you're a fan of looting, you will be disappointed. There is not that much of equipment to choose from, although i never felt bad because of that, it was just the right amount.
From technincal point of view it's well made product. Sound-wise the game is really great. Especially soundtrack which is kinda unique in its vibes and atmosphere. Graphicly OOAM is also nicely done. Orcish characters are looking amazing, human ones on the other hand not always. Locations are always good looking even if sometimes monotonous as I mantioned before. I didn't get across too many bugs. The most annoying problem I've encounterd was that from time to time one of our heroes, the one we weren't controlling at the moment, liked to get stuck on some obstacles (sometimes even invisible ones...).
Two biggest flaws of OOAM is that it's short (11 hours, goddamn...) and linear. And it's being linear in both cases: story and locations. Non of your choices matter and places you visit are roads from point a to point b. Which is sad, because with that design i'd like to spend much more time sightseeing.
To summarise: this game is kind of a flawed gem. It's well written, has great combat system, awesome music and great visuals. But the construction of the world (tunnel like levels) and story so short... well it hurts a little. However, despite these to thing I hade a lot of fun, and I do not regret those few euros I've spent on this game, and I recommend it. Not to everybody, because it's not a game for everybody. But, if you look for something more ambitious and not-so-dynamic (but awesome!) tactical fighting system does not scare you, "Of Orcs And Man" might be this, what you are looking for.

Of Orcs and Men is an interesting game made by Cyanide studios, which have a track record of making interesting but also deeply flawed games. This time they managed to not screw it up as much as they usually do.
It's an extremely linear RPG with a combat system where you do not have full direct control over your characters. And you can control two characters, an orc who is good for melee and taking damage, and a goblin who you'd prefer to stay at range as he is very fragile.
The story is very much focused on the interaction between these two main characters, while there is a constant overall goal in play, it is much more satisfying paying attention to the developing friendship between the two. The goblin is most certainly the more entertaining of the two, however he does have a propensity towards crude humour which can become a bit tiresome.
In combat you can control both characters and you can switch between them at will, the character that you are not controlling will use the abilities that you queued up for him while you controlled him, and once that runs out he will simply use the basic attack of the stance he is in. This encourages you to actively switch between characters as they are most effective while using abilities. However I found it best to stay in control of the goblin most of the time, as he can very easily get killed if left to fend for himself. The combat is somewhat simplistic but it does have potential for some more advanced play, especially on the higher difficulties.
I came into the game not expecting much, I knew that it isn't going to be anything special, but at the vey least I thought it might be an entertaining game, which it most certainly was. I was most surprised by the story, specifically the interplay between the two main characters, which kept me playing until the end. And I believe that is also the biggest the draw of the game.
7 / 10

He later on meets the unique Goblin Styx (a lone wolf) who's told to show Arkhail the way to accomplish his mission to make an end to this War.
But everything gets out of control and the two find themselves in a ~10 hour long Journey full of twists and mixed up game play: Styx -rather small and fast -  is a master of stealth and you got the option to get 1-3 enemies out of the way quietly before entering a fight. Arkhail on the other hand is big and slow but with powerful attacks when things get real.
So the game play styles of both together were the best possible combination to me in a game like that... though i preferred to play Styx :3
The characters of both could not be more different.. Styx is more grumpy and pessimistic / afraid due big challenges while Arkhail is willing to die for his cause / clan in Honor.
This gets especially clear during several of the amazing cutscenes and dialogues where you got sometimes the option to chose whether Styx or Arkhail answer / choose their own way (for example: Trust someone or Kill stuff -Arkhail / not trust someone and flee - Styx )
I loved this game...it lacks in a lot of things because its very very and I mean VERY linear..not much to explore on 1 path besides the main each mission but it fits the game somehow.. To sum this up.. game play might not be the best but the game plays well, graphics are neither too low nor to high and RPG fans shouldn't bother anyway, Story was interesting though the ending could have been implemented better :D

Tl;dr
If you like turn-based games, have the patience to get into the game and it is OK for you to overlook a number of flaws, then you should try this rather unique game.
Longer version:
Overall, this game is hard to rate and I certainly would not recommend it to everyone as it has several issues:
- The game was released too early. This resulted in lots of bad reviews and is the reason for a second major problem: lack of players.
- as very few people seem to be playing the game, it‘s really hard to find an opponent in multiplayer. Out of the 80 h of time Steam says I spent with this game, probably 20 h I was waiting for a game.
- not only the waiting time for a game is really long, but a match (at least at 50 pts. level) is a serious time commitment. This also applies for singleplayer: you cannot save during campaign battles, if you do not have the time to finish a level, you need to start over.
- the AI is really bad
- not really a downside, but the game has a steep learning curve (including getting used to a rather clunky interface) and the AI is not helpful in improving.
Still I think this is a good game and has lots of potential.
- actually I liked the single player campaign. I am not sure what people expect from a Kickstarter game regarding cut scenes (a complaint in many reviews), but I think they worked quite well in telling the story. While the story is certainly not extraordinary, it kept me playing from one level to the next and I really liked the diversity of the maps. As the enemies in the individual levels are scripted, the dumb AI is not that much of an issue.
- Overall, I think this game is quite unique in bringing a tabletop game to the PC. It may be described as a mash-up of XCOM (turn-based tactics elements), Bloodbowl (positioning your units; not to hide the ball, but your warcaster), and Warhammer (regarding colorful fantasy setting; I have to admit I did not know Warmachine before).
Even though the developers are relatively slow in improving the game, they have been committed to making it better for quite some time and I think they improved it already quite a bit. Overall, I think this game is a solid 7.5/10 with lots of potential.

Alas, this game is plagued by technical and user interface issues. Would not recommend. If given another year of development time, it might have become great even!

Although I have a relative recent graphics cards, this game runs at an average of around 15 FPS (frames per second) with all settings tweaked to the lowest. I will have to say at this point in time, Medieval 2 is my favorite in the series for sure. I have heard people criticize the campaign AI but I genuinely feel it is some of the best campaign AI in the series. My all-time greatest strategy gaming memories come from this title.
I recall a specific example of the amazing campaign AI when one of my long-time allies thought they had a chance at some of my territory and decided to turn on me and try to cut my empire in half. I immediately decimated their armies and took a third of their territory. They were so terrified at being utterly destroyed that I convinced them to give me another third of their territory in exchange for a truce. The end result was that they lost the vast majority of their empire and nearly all of their military strength. I never had to park troops anywhere near my borders with them again. We made peace and went back to being allies with trading rights and they never even thought about expanding again. For over 100 years they were a lesser power that knew their place under my reign as the dominant European faction.
I could go on with further examples but I won't bore you. The battle AI isn't the best in the series but is as good as the base AI in Rome. The mod community is expansive and the base campaign is incredibly well balanced and fun. I have my complaints but overall the game has significantly more positives than negatives. I can't recommend this title enough.

My review of Revelations 2 can be seen here.
(YES Revelations is still active online for those only getting this for Raid mode)
Back on the 3DS I came for the graphics and stayed for the gameplay. I was surprised to find that while Revelations was a handheld title it the best Resident Evil game of 2013 which saw the release of the terrible Operation Racoon City and the linear QTE riddled mess that was Resident Evil 6. Having beaten the 3DS game 100% I couldn't wait to be able to play it on my PC with more content, some slightly nicer visuals, a higher framerate and of course mouse aim. It delivered on everything I expected and a little more. First off, Revelations is insanley well optimized although considering it was first made for and released on the 3DS first it damn well should be. While my current PC was no slouch when I first picked this up (These are my current specs: A GTX 980 SC ACX 2.0, an i7 4790k Devils Canyon and 16 Gigs of RAM.) I've seen it perform very smoothly on a laptop with an AMD A4-5000 1.5ghz, ATI RADEON 8330m 512MB VRAM﻿ and 8GB DDR3-RAM with High textures and everything else on low.
While the absence of the laser and third and firstperson aiming that was present in the 3DS release is a bummer the PC version still trumps it in every other aspect: The characters mouths now move ingame, the common ooze are now more varied in appearence sometimes having malformed arms, an extra enemy has been added, you can pick, choose and swap between different costumes for the main characters the story mode, the Ghost Ship stages in raid mode has been slightly overhauled with more enemies and different enemy placements, there are more characters and costumes for the said characters in raid mode, more variation in the stats for characters and their costumes and more weapon attachments. The game caps at 120 fps when you choose Variable and rarely if ever dips unless you are in an elevator (Which it disguises as the elevator rumbling) or a water lock, but in the context that this happens it's completley understandable seeing as you are still free to move around while it's happening and it's more of a loading issue than a general performance problem as the frame counter remains the same. One thing that I don't understand and that isn't really excusable is why the game doesn't allow 4k or provide non FXAA related anti aliasing.
The audio quality and sound design in Revelations were already superb but what few sounds were compressed are now crystal clear. It's not quite on par with RE5 but asthetically Revelations it trumps it. It does noticeably increase the texture,shader and polygon count though in addition to removing a really ugly bit of water that could be seen out of a window in the 3DS version. It makes it look like what you think it looked like on the 3DS unless you really really squinted. It's also one of the few games where it feels rewarding to get aheivements as you are rewarded with awesome ingame unlockables like an infinite RPG for clearing the hardest mode without being hit. Give it a shot this game is great! I really didn't expect greatness when I first picked this up so that was a REVELATION in its own right, I can't say it's the best Resident Evil game without being super biased but I can say it's a great game in it's own right and one of the better recent entries.
Oh yeah and then there's Raid mode which is basically it's very own games bundled in this one but there's too much in Raid mode for me to cover.

Disclaimer: This review is from a guy that is not good at fighting games (besides smash bros) and doesn't like them that much. On the other hand, I think this should give a fresh review for those who are like me. Now then on to the review---
Review: The first thing I think is worth mentioning is the ease of controls. It is literally the first 2d fightning game (besides smash bros) that I was able to learn the combos of and not button mash. It is very easy to pick up but hard to master. Unlike almost every fighting game out there, that has very difficult and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t comboing such as--up, down, x, a, left, y, up, right, right, x, b~~~~you can do a decent combo with a single button continiously pressed with very minor arrows (up, down, left, right) enabling you to pick up decent combos to give you a fighting chance within minutes of playing the game, without having to look at the combo list and trying to pull it off. It is from the makers of BlazBlue for those who like that. Now onto the story--I haven't played other stories besides the main protagonist Hyde. His story arc is very interesting and his character and storyline is what actually made me want to get this game. If you want a basic geist of the story, check the 'about this game' section of the product page. I'm only saying this because 2d fighting games tend to usually have short stories, so I wouldn't want to spoil any of it. Graphics---The graphics are what you might expect from a fightning game but the visuals and effects have a slight resembalence to Fate/Stay Night. Characters---As I said above, the controls are easy to use, so any character you could basically do alright with during fights after a few minutes of learning their combos. The characters are unique and diverse, which is rarely seen in fighting games. Replay---There is a fair amount of replay by being awarded with points to spend in the custom store for backgrounds, player icons, titles, and color/costume palletes for the characters. Final verdict--8/10. It is worth a pick up if you are a fighting fan, or a guy/girl that doesn't like the genre but would like to if they could find one that's fair to new comers.

This is only my second review since joining Steam.  I’m new and more than a bit shy so I tend to stay quiet but I can’t remain that way when it comes to Wurm Unlimited.
I have been an avid RPer/MMO fan since the first version of Everquest and Asheron’s Call.  I worked on more than one game as a concept artist and graphic designer when the first big name MMO’s came into existence yet still, I have never found the game for me.  SWG was close until … well anyone who played it knows that hellish tale of woe.  When I could no longer find a complex game that offered world building and sandbox appeal, I went to Second Life.  I became a professional builder and even a GM for Linden Labs but I missed the old MMO’s.  Wurm helped me recapture that era once more.
First, let me say this right up front, the game still needs work.  There are a few bugs that I am hoping they iron out someday and the graphics have glitches that need tweaking.  Considering that I am into graphic design, that’s probably just my O.C.D. kicking in.  I see a skin that doesn’t quite meet up correctly and my eye twitches.  The combat is awkward and the game itself doesn’t just have a learning curve, it has a learning cliff.  Please warn your friends not to give up too soon before they enter this game or you'll never hear the end of it.
I have fallen in love with this game.  The depth of realism in the crafting and survival is amazing.  You walk into the world and in order to survive, you have to create everything from scratch but the way its set up makes sense.  If you want to fish, you need to make yourself a fishing pole.  You carve a fish hook or make it from iron you mined.  You create your own fishing line from cotton you gathered growing wild in the fields and you whittled the pole from branches of a fallen log.  From the smallest task like just finding enough food to eat to survive the winter or picking the right herbs to heal your wounds, all the way to creating a vast settlement with your friends, this game has it all.
I was so impressed with the depth and freedom of the game that I have purchased a server and I’m hosting an RP world with some friends.  We are currently rebuilding the settlement towns and this reminds me so much of when I used to buy an island in SL and build a world for people to come RP in.  The best part is, instead of $150.00 a month, this island cost me a one-time fee of $30 bucks.  With the ability to mod and improve the graphics myself or with the help of others, this is the game world I have longed to play in.

The PC issues the game has are more than unfortunate and with official support seemingly non-existant I'm incredibly torn on whether to recommend Nier or not. Thanks to the user created FAR mod however my experience with this game was for the most part without issue. I never experienced any crashes or freezes and frame rate dips weren't too common either, only popping up when just an absolutely insane amount of crap was happening onscreen. Honestly, my weirdest issue was that I wasn't able to play with a controller unless I launched into Steam's Big Picture mode first...which was fine, but odd nonetheless. I'm one of the lucky ones however, most people can't even launch the damn thing.
This is beyond sad, especially when the game being plagued by technical problems is this damn good. This all reminds me of Dark Souls initial PC outing. A game for the ages marred by idiotic technical hiccups. Is that some kind of theme now I wonder? Well it's fitting either way because Nier is the best thing to come out of this industry SINCE the original Dark Souls.
So yeah, I'm going to recommend Nier anyway despite the technical issues. It's that good. The word masterpiece gets thrown around a little too much nowadays for my liking, but I simply can't think of another word to describe Automata, it's a masterpiece. I've never played a game before where I had to actually take several days off from playing to absorb just what the **** the narrative was doing to me. This game LOVES to screw with you, whether it be unexpected 4th wall breaks or shocking plot twists Nier took me to the highest highs and the lowest lows and somehow made a game about talking tin cans into the most human story I've ever experienced in a video game. And it's a story that's going to stay with me for a long, long time to come.
Gameplay wise well, it's a Platinum title so, hell yeah? Fun fact though, that actually turned me off to getting the game at first. Not that Platinum doesn't know their s**t when it comes to gameplay but, I'm just not a fan of hack and slash kind of titles, I think they're fun to play on occassion but I can't see myself ever dropping 60$ on one. So, Nier was something I immediately passed on when I first saw gameplay clips of it. Thankfully I didn't though, as there's so much more to it than what I initially thought there was.
I could go on and on but you get the idea (oh and the music, Jesus Christ the !@#$%^& music). I love this game and I'm going to be playing it for a long time to come still. I just hope the PC version gets some much needed attention, sooner rather than later, because the number of people who have refunded or outright passed on it just from HEARING about the quality of the port is a damn shame. Get your s**t together SE and fix this gem already.

So, after having taken a break from the game being mostly dead, I tried to come back to be plagued by the disease known as 2-step authentication. In order to remove the 2 stage you have to actually already be using the 2 stage. You can contact support to remove it, but that'll take ages and your account actually has to not be locked due to failed logins.
BUT based on what I remember about the game (aside from the dynamic shadows bug causing server disconnects  on certain R9 series cards, numerous latency issues, and lack of general population actually running around doing things) some of the character designs were fairly neat, some of the skills and gameplay mechanics were enjoyable, there were a wild array of builds to play with should you choose, but other beneficial things were hidden behind an annoying and obnoxious paywall.
If you can get a group of friends that actually find this game enjoyable, then go for it, it can keep you occupied for maybe a few hours.  Unless you have this, then you'll probably be better off not bothering, it'll save you from the ridiculous amount of account security shoved down your throat... and there will be ample amounts of NCSoft issues to keep you occupied for a while before actually being able to play the game.  I currently have no friends to play with, no patience left to try and get into an account with nothing worth returning to, and have several other games I can play to get equal or greater enjoyment from, so I'll give this a thumbs down for now. An unusual and intriguing little game that I came to like a lot. This is a title you will either love or hate.
I think of it as a hybrid of action, RPG, hack&slash, strategy and brawler.
The problem with these hybrids is usually that people see one type of game that they like in the list and then complain that it is nothing like their favourite game (see all those peeps comparing it to Dragon Age, Dark Souls, ... and then state that OOAM is rubbish? Yeah well ...)
But, this one really is a mix of action/RPG/hack&slash/strategy/brawler. Don't ask yourself if you like one gamestyle in that list, ask yourself if you would like a mix of all those styles.
You have command over the orc Arkai and goblin Styx. You always control one of them and the other one will either be handled by the AI or by commands from you.
When not in battle, Styx can sneak around and assassinate enemies, which is incredibly fun.
In battle, at any point you can enter "
", which slows down the game a lot and allows to give commands. I found this a much better option than the pause-mode of pure RPG-titles, because it keeps you on your toes.
In strategy mode, you have the option to enter one or more
. For example, you can tell Arkai to taunt an enemy to grab its aggro. But you can also have him first taunt and then follow up with a stunning strike.
This goes for both characters, so in addition to Arkai's taunt and stun, you can order Styx to first poison his daggers and then attack the stunned foe with a destabilizing slash.
It will take a while to get a hang of this combat system, but once you do, you reach a breaking point and are set for the remainder of the game. Be prepared that it will probably require an hour or more to even start to appreciate this title.
You can also give commands by means of hotkeys in the real-time environment, a nice option once you are confident in your abilities.
There is an
but it does not add a lot to the game, as there is actually only very little to loot.
The game comes with experience points for battles won: by the end of the game you will have gained around 22 levels this way. Levelling grants you ability points and skill points.
The
allows you to suit the 2 characters to your preferred playstyle, for example using Arkai as tank and Styx as backstabber, or Arkai as berserker and Styx as ranged support. Skills come in all styles, like light attacks, heavy attacks, stunning attacks, ... This is where the brawler parts kicks in.
However, the freedom in attributing skill points is limited because there are a couple of skills that are absolutely required to win the game. If you don't have a stunning attack on one of your toons by the final level, you have no chance to win for example. The game expects players find such things out on their own.
Also the freedom you have in
is only a farce, because basically you need to dump almost everything into stability (= constitution) to survive the higher levels. Again something that the developers assume you will discover yourself.
Not that all this is actually bad, mind you! In a way the gameplay reminds me a lot of a game of the nineties, where such experimental hybrid of styles, lack of handholding and assumption that the player is smart enough to pick the correct skills were very common. Just ask yourself if that is something you can live with or not.
The biggest negative point is probably that fighting does get repetitive: once you have build your 2 characters as you want them, you are stuck with only a few strategies to handle any situation. Still, the game throws more and more challenging fights at you to keep you interested.
Not a walk in the park but actually not too difficult once you get a hang of the combat system. There are a few parts where you have to solo a bit with one character and you will struggle with a poorly built toon there.
Other than than the only really frustrating bit is the end fight but even there it is a matter of “this needs better strategy” rather than “this is unfair”!
Acceptable. While there are some optional missions or choice-points, you have very little control on the outcome of the story.
The story is developed by means of cutscenes in or between missions and dialogues. Most can be skipped with the escape key, except for one rather frustrating bit at the end.
Extremely linear. There is typically only one path through a level. There is also a map that tells you what to expect in level design from the start of each mission, so getting lost is simply put not possible.
I would have preferred a little bit more freedom in levels, but so be it ...
The levels are all fairly short, which is actually a big plus. You do get some variation in settings and enemies this way.
There are a total of 37 levels. Completing the entire game once, including all optionals, will take about 10 hours at the easiest difficulty. I found this just enough seen the repetitive fighting.
Unfortunately you cannot rebind keys except for shortcuts to skills. Since the combat is for a large part based on cueing commands in strategy mode and not so much on real-time fighting, I don't object at all. You can also use a gamepad.
Note that you can save at any point when not in combat. The game will also save automatically before every fight so you will barely need manual save option. Only exception is the final level, which strangely enough does not autosave at all.
No doubt that we are dealing with a console port. The engine itself is nice and really shows off its quality in backdrops or the glistening of skin for example, but the character models are low-polygloned, texture quality is meh, textures are repeated a lot and lip syncing is awful. On the other hand, this is not a triple-A title so it would not be fair to expect an A+ visual fidelity.
I did find the game surprisingly taxing on my graphics card despite the average graphics. Note that nevertheless I was able to pull the game easily with all setting maxed out. My CPU-use barely rose over 5% at any point. Even video-rendering while playing this game turned out possible.
I also did not experience any crashes, bugs or any other problems running the game.
Basically, any setup with good GPU and VRAM and updated video-drivers will probably be able to run this
Note that the game has a rather small FOV, but you can easily change this yourself (check the forums).
The voiceovers of Arkai and Styx are great - sure Styx is a nasty, backstabbing little coward, but you will come to like this character. The other voices in the game are bleh.
Soundeffects are pretty good although never stand out. The fighting was a bit too quiet to my liking.
The music is fantastic: a combination of raw, tribal rhythms and intense cello!
At one point in the game you have to make a decision as to how to progress your 2 characters. That is basically the only reason to replay this game, because all the others choices you have to make are not really relevant.
Pro:

The short version: This game, overall better than mediocre. The story was interesting; the graphics were fair; the controls were good. 'Of Orcs And Men' had a lot of potential to be a GREAT game, but some of it's bugs and shortcomings bring it down. Nevertheless, I recommend giving it a play-through.
--- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- ---
I will not rehash the concept behind 'Of Orcs And Men'; there are plenty of reviews which lay out the concepts of this title. What will follow is a collection of problems I had with 'Of Orcs And Men'.
Graphics: Character designs for anything that's not a goblin or orc are painfully mediocre. Humans and dogs are bland at best, and many of their animations are very stiff. Shadow quality is poor. Many of the animations, particularly in cut-scenes, can be a bit jittery.
Dialogue: The early game is pretty good. Arkail and Styx were done mostly well throughout the game. Other voice actors are often bland, wooden, or outright BAD. The voice work for the one dwarf in the game is HORRIBLE, sounding as though it may have been "read" by a computer generated voice... it was THAT BAD!
General Combat: Throughout 'OOAM' you will very often find yourself swarmed by small hordes of enemies. This is great, as it lends to the sense of awesomeness of the protagonists. Many of your combat abilities cause crowd control effects, such as stun, which are often necessary to survive some encounters. While it's understandable for some enemies to be more resistant to these effects than others, there seems to be an anti-CC-lock mechanic in place, which seems to prevent MOST enemies from being stunned more that once or twice. This would be great if it worked both ways! I found in some combats, particularly those with magic-wielding Inquisitors, that the enemy's ability to unerringly CC you can easily lead to your death if one of your characters falls, making it impossible for the conscious character to rouse the unconscious one.
A.I. Combat: Arkail and Styx are a team. You can control either character, and whichever you are not controlling is directed by the A.I. when not given a list of specific commands, or when that list runs out. Additionally, if you are scouting ahead with Styx, and get detected, Arkail will not automatically run to his side to fight with him! This can be particularly tricky if there is a bit of distance between the characters. Opening up the command menu will slow time to a crawl, allowing you to issue commands, but you can only move the characters in real time, and you can't control them both at the same time. This often leads to having to run Styx back to wherever you left Arkail, who will be waiting there with a thumb up his .... Adding to the A.I. combat frustration, stuns and other such crowd control effects used against you will not only interrupt the character while trying to execute a command, it will often clear their command queue, meaning they will not resume the queue once the effect has passed. This can often be detrimental, particularly in cases where you've queued a character to perform a vital self-heal.
A.I. Pathing: There are many points where one character will get stuck and not follow the lead character (especially if you're scouting with Styx.) Additionally, there are a few locations where even the character you're controlling won't respond to a given command due to a pathing problem. What's worse, this often leads to enemies (at least the melee variety) completely ignoring that character and ganging up on the other one. If the "invisible" character is Arkail, be prepared to watch Styx meet his doom VERY QUICKLY!
Miscellaneous Issues: 1. While the story for 'Of Orcs And Men' is fairly interesting, some of the conversations can be painfully length, especially in a few of the scenarios where you have died (sometimes multiple times) and are forced to repeat a lengthy bit of dialogue. This can be even more obnoxious if the game won't allow you to skip the dialogue. 2. The armor upgrade system is extremely simple, giving every item in the game a single upgrade. What's more, the game does not give you any sort of preview as to how much this will improve an item. At early stages, when trade points are sparse, it can be quite irritating to upgrade an item only to find your currently equipped gear is still better. At later stages, when you have mages who can supposedly "enhance" your equipment, this could have been made significantly more interesting by adding effects to gear rather than the same enhancements you would get from any other merchant you had dealt with at earlier points. Equipment upgrading was very lackluster. 3. Saving, at later stages in the game, is virtually pointless OR inaccessible, forcing you to rely on autosaves, as you may be forced to soldier on through a series of several combats before the next save. This was particularly obnoxious at the end of the game, as a death with the boss fight would force replaying three or four consecutive combats AND a lengthy, unskippable dialogue scene. 4. Arkail's weapon after loading. It seemed that after every break (quitting the game, and loading it back up at a later time), Arkail's weapon would no longer look like what he had equipped, and would instead look like a simple stick/club. It wasn't until near the end of the game I realized this was because Arkail would somehow unequip his weapon upon reloading the game! This is a minor issue, as you simply have to re-equip his weapon, but this shouldn't even happen in the first place. I also had this happen randomly during play, usually after the occasional cut-scene. 5. At a late point in the game, both Arkail and Styx are each given the choice between two advancement paths which grant access to additional abilities. The game does not give any indication as to what the different advancement paths with grant, so players who are more interested in the abilities they will gain rather than the story reason for selecting a given path will find this lack of insight a bit irritating. 6. Styx is all about stealth, but this option becomes an increasingly less viable option the more the story advances. I found there was almost no point to stealth at the end game. Dogs cannot be assassinated, very few enemies are positioned in ways which allow for stealth kills, and those who are are often extremely weak anyway, so there is not much point to wasting time with sneaking. As a proponent of stealth-based games, I found this highly disappointing. Additionally, the few times where you are forced to play solo as Styx, you are thrust into the combat with no option for approaching with stealth. If you don't build Styx to be tough (focusing on Stamina), this can make for a ludicrously difficult combat.
General Gameplay Weakness: While there are many options available to the player as they advance Styx and Arkail, the best option is to focus on Arkail's defensive abilities and Styx's ranged abilities. Optimally, focusing on Stamina for both these characters will make them extremely tough, and make the game far easier to beat. Essentially, this is the only "right" way to play, particularly at the higher difficulty settings.
--- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- ---
All that said, the game was very engrossing. When I would play, several hours would easily pass, and I didn't want to stop until I had finished.
Great story, great characters, decent combat, all around good game.

I had gotten this game from a friend who had bought the Killer Bundle 3 and he did not want it . He asked me if I was interested in it and upon researching the game I figured I would add the game to my library, download it, and play it at a later time.
I decided to check out the game when my internet went down and was pleasantly surprised by it.

The game is very cinematic graphics wise. You can see that the devs tried very hard to show you a movie story through the cutscenes. The textures are very nice in this game. The skin on the orcs look somewhat realistic and you can see the lighting bounce off it. I personally find it very nice when you can see sunlight bouncing off a character's skin in any game. The rain effects look amazing and it looks as though things are actually getting wet. However, the characters do look a bit stiff sometimes. Lastly, when the characters speak (in the cutscenes) they get a bad case of the rubberlips (notorious in Warcraft 3 where characters' lips would just bounce up and down when speaking)

The music is generic adventure game-like. It's something you would hear and say "Ah, that would sound nice in an action adventure game"
The voiceovers are decent. The best voice actor is the one who voices Styx the Goblin. His character brings a roguelike charm with his monologues and witty lines.
The biggest issue I had with the audio was the mouth synchronization. You are able to hear when the dialogue starts and ends suddenly.

This is where the game really shines. Before playing the game I assumed that it would be a hack and slash action game. The game actually plays like an ARPG (Action Role Playing Game). Upon entering the game I masked my left key hoping that the character would swing his sword around. However upon playing the first 10 minutes of the story (which serves as the tutorial) I found myself slowly understanding how the game works.
The combat system is similar to Dragon Age Origins (or almost any ARPG) in that you can use the spacebar to pause the game and plan your next few moves. Pressing the spacebar also brings up your combat hud. There you can plan up to five of your next moves. Pressing spacebar again will unpause time and your character will do the attacks in the cache.
The level system is fairly simple. There are five attributes that you can put points in. Strength, Agility, Stamina, and Mind. Each attribute has different helpful upgrades. You can also upgrade/unlock new abilities.
You control two character in Of Orcs and Men. Arkail and Styx. While Arkail excels at fighting and tanking damage, Styx has a more stealth/assassin fighting style. Each character has a one unique mechanic. Arkail has a rage system, where if his rage bar fills (by attacking and using special abilities) he becomes uncontrollable and will just pummel at the enemy. Styx can become invisible and will 1 hit kill his next backstab target.
The hud is simple yet visually pleasing.
The one problem the gameplay has is that the targetting system for attacking feels a bit clunky. Sometimes it feels like your character got confused and doesn't know who to hit.

The story is quite simple and might seem a bit cliche.
Humans have enslaved the Orcs and forces them to work as slaves and cannon fodder. However, there is a group of free Orcs that are resisting the humans and are going to take a last stand. It's up to Arkail and his shifty goblin guide to take down the king and free the Orcs.
The game offers some dialogue choices but so far none of them really make any changes to the story.
I love the duo dynamic that exists between Arkail and Styx. They both hate each other when they first meet but grow to respect and even rely on each other.
There are some iffy parts in the script though. I've noticed that the characters love to say "♥♥♥♥" at inappropriate times (inappropriate as in it doesn't really need to be said in the context). Also it seems like the devs/writers/animators tried to give Arkail a signature move/trait (he punches his fists a LOT whenever a cutscene with him ends) but it just ends up feeling very awkward.
I was surprised when I first saw Styx in this game because he actually stars in his own game Styx: Master of Shadows, a stealth game about... well, Styx. When Styx: MaS first came out I was very interested because many people said that it was a Stealth game done right. Upon research, I now know that it is a prequel to Of Orcs and Men.

Overall, I found myself enjoying the game and would definitely have bought it had I known about it. Again, I highly recommend buying it if it ever goes on sale but wait a bit if not. The gameplay is the best part of the game and the graphics are a close second.
This is my first review so please tell me how I can improve and what you liked about the review on my Steam Page. Thank you for reading and it was a fun time playing Of Orcs and Men.

linear game with highly repetitive combat. The story simply ticks all the boxes needed and nothing more though it does have two frankly unnecessary twists: one silly and one bloody obvious. The combat system is, as others have said, a little 'off' though still functional. It's a shame since the developers do seem to have really tried but the game just comes off as a bit boring.
On the positive side the soundtrack was good, if a little repetitive, as were the graphics (both from a prettiness point of view and in terms of art style/matching the setting). The protagonists were also fun enough both individually and particularly when interacting with each other. The Stealth made for a nice change of pace and wasn't forced even in the specific stealth sections. I did enjoy picking off people slowly to make the inevitable fight easier on the big guy. The world
be interesting to revisit as it's just unique enough to interest me but it'd need a less repetitive game (preferably one with a working combat system).
You'll probably get your money's worth if you pick it up on sale but there isn't much replayability unless you
enjoyed it.
It might also have made for a good coop game.

If you liked Limbo, you might like this. It's an extremely similar platformer, which shares a similar silhouetted art style. You also have the the same central mechanic where things kill you by surprise and you have to use what you learned to try again immediately. To offset this, there are ubiquitous silent checkpoints that immediately put you back in the action when you're killed. Also like Limbo, the challenges are bite-sized and are split up by a moody journey through an abstract environment.
I'm interested to find out if this is made by any of the same developers as Limbo due to the extreme similarities. And yet if it is, then this must have been the developer's first attempt made years earlier, because everything about it is just a little bit less interesting and less polished.
Its story is just as artsy-pretentious, unsettling, and obtuse as Limbo, and yet it lacks the same charm. Also, it somehow manages to be even shorter. $10 for a one-and-a-half hour game is criminal considering the caliber of games you can get for that price.
Get it if you loved Limbo and you can find it for a dollar. Otherwise it's probably best avoided.
