stellaris, ah stellaris,
how much i want to like you, how much i want to play you, how hard you are making it for me to enjoy you.
i dont recomend this game, because it is not a full game yet.
it may have the structure and the groundwork, but there is a lot of stuff that is simply missing, or doesnt work, and unlike others im not talking about features like "doomsdayweapons", i am talking about tactical gameplay in a 4 x game, and even worse:
i am talking about strategic gameplay in a 4 x game.
diplomacy is useless, or simply frustrating, dependent on one of the 2 playstyles you choose for your empire (conquering the galaxy, or building a federation). It either boils down to the whole galaxy being in a federation and entangled in defencive pacts against you, or you being in a federation with the rest of the universe. Both options throw the game into a complete diplomatic and galactic stalemante around midgame.
Fleetcombat is simply boring, or frustrating.
War always boils down to "i throw everything i have at everything you have, and whoever defeats the opposing faction instantly wins the war". That is if you are actually able to catch enemy fleets, because the ftl system isnt well thought either and fleets just jump around the galaxy without any real means to snare them in place, which can extend wars extremly long, and be the cause of casualties that arent the players fault, but the fault of badly implemented gameplay mechanics. That leads to bad gamefeel. And ground combat is simply a joke, it may as well just get removed completely, wouldnt it be the only thing to acutally get warscore in wars...
now one might think, hey, what this game lacks in tactical gameplay it surely makes it up with strategic planning?
no. empire building lacks variety (and even worse, depth) as well. there is no real desicionmaking when colonizing a planet if you are a pacifist, sientist, warmonger etc, all buildings are the same, and it always boils down to only 4 types of buildings:
energy generators, mines, sience and food. thats it. nothing more.
Unity is a new ressource in the Utopia dlc, (which can be spend to unlock traditions, which again give your empire boni) but it actually doesnt add anything meaningfull in terms of strategic depth, its just a matter of "oho, i have to waste a potential mining space because else i dont get 4 points out of this planet" (which is absolutely nothing in even the midgame) Its a poorly implemented system that arbitrary slows player progression.
"but what about the roleplaying features? the game is supposed to let me play my own story of my own empire, no?"
Laughtable, althought the latest dlcs and patches aimed to improve the game in that direction, your choices usually (never) dont matter, and it always leads to the previously mentioned playstyles, peace or total war,there are no alternatives. Furthermore, your goverment choices (while trying to offer more diversion for playstyles, simply do the opposite and...) force you to play a certain way.
for example:
if you are a caste system, you have to be a slave empire.
if you are a sience empire, you have to go down the robot path.
if you are a spiritualist, you always have a "single" religion.
and dont even get me started on hiveminds, they are simply just a slapped on thing, instead of a well thought of feature. (although it is confirmed that they are working on improving their flavour, rewriting the flavourtexts and tooltips regarding events and technologies
dont get me wrong, stellaris for the first 1 or 2 times is an alright game, the events tell great stories, and there are alot of small things here and there that are inspired by other sci fi franchises. It is pretty nice when you for the first time discover the "shroud", which basically is the warp from warhammer 40k, or you realise one of the strategic ressources is actually Spice...
but it gets frustrating very fast, and the events simply cant carry gamefeel on their own, not in a 4 x strategy game. Not in a 4 x REALTIME strategy game.
Stellaris has a lot of potential to be a good game, a finished game, but it will be on the basis of a lot of payed dlcs... which i cant support.
dlcs are alright, if the groundgame is finished and dlcs are a means of expanding the game.
dlcs are a scam if the game itself isnt even freaking finished and are a means of updating the game to completion. No, i dont recomment anyone having to buy the base game and potentionally having to pay double or tripple the base price of dlcs, after years of development, to finally get a finished stellaris.
you can either wait and feed the developers (in that case i heavily recommend to look up modders like alpha ash, that fix alot of the problems i mentioned here)
or you dont and play something finished and worth your money
i tried to wait for about a year, but i am not a patient man.

Resident Evil Revelations is an old school blockbuster like I didn’t think it was possible for anyone to make anymore. It somehow feels completely divorced from how big publisher games are supposed to be made today. It probably has to do with its heritage as a 3DS title. Everything about Revelations feels old school, in the style of Capcom from the late 90s and early 2000s.
Whether you like this game or not will depend entirely on your affinity for the older Resident Evil titles. I’ve lost count of how many times I’ve finished Resident Evil 1, and Resident Evil 4 is just a masterpiece, especially on Gamecube with its superior controller. Revelations combines elements of both of them. For some reason the ship you spend the majority of the game on has an interior that seems almost modeled after the Resident Evil 1 mansion, and larger encounters copy the arena style combat of Resident Evil 4 to great effect. I don’t think there’s any game out there which can make you feel as panicky as Resident Evil 4 & 5 when you’re running away from a mob, trying to find a good spot to deal with the masses. Revelations brought those feelings back.
Every imaginable Resident Evil trope is present here. There’s a sci-fi lab near the end, there’s a guy in a helicopter throwing you a rocket launcher to help you fight a boss, there’s a self destruct sequence with a timer ticking down. And it all works. Even the music sounds like proper Resident Evil. It’s a synth orchestra for the majority of the soundtrack, but it tries its best to be as epic as it can. It even has opera singers, exactly in the style of Resident Evil 2.
I had a great time with this game. It put a big smile on my face, and reminded me of why I like this silly franchise so much. If you don’t give a crap about Resident Evil then you will probably not have as good of a time as I did. But if you’ve played a bunch of the games in the series and enjoyed them, then this is a must play.
A final note, the demo is terrible. It’s the opening 15-20 minutes of the game, which are by far the weakest. The second after the demo ends is when the game gets good, and unfortunately they didn’t include any of that in the demo. I got the game because every RE fan who had played it kept going on about how good it was. And they were right.

It's as if a social media and Terraria had a child, and then that child hung too much around with minecraft
Manyland, isn't just a game. It's a set of tools that will help you create literally
you want in this game: Every block, every body... every pixel you'll see on Manyland came from another player's mind. wheter it's a simple solid square block, or an incredibly complex AI (the game let's you mess around with codes and scripts, too). It might seem overwhelming at first, but you'll quickly start having more ambicious projects, projects which will push the limits of your imagination. And Manyland has just the right tools to help you turn those ideas into reality.
The first steps can be confusing: you'll spawn on a "shared area", the welcoming zone for all newcomers, and the "meeting point" for a lot of veterans, too. You're just told to "move around with the arrows, and chat by  typing", so if you're feeling a bit lost, ask other people for help! the community is very thight-knitted, and most people are welcoming.
If you've played Call of Duty, DOTA, Counter-Strike, Minecraft... then you know how people can be horrible little things that won't stop bothering you until they' re sure they ruined your experience. I know Manyland's community isn't even one tenth of those bigger games, but people in here created their own "perfect world", mostly because the game is about sharing your work with other players rather than competing  with them. It's a win-win situation for everyone! Be warned, though, you might form some emotional bonds with people you meet in Manyland...

When it comes to gameplay, the game is a mix between  a social media with platformer elements, with simple controls. As mentioned above, it's pretty straight-forward: you move around with your arrows and chat by typing, in a 2D sandbox. You only use your mouse to draw your creations, and that's about it. Its simple and intuitive gameplay lets you focus your mind of your creations.
Speaking of creations, you'll need a place of your own to display them! Manyland is similar to a "universe", which makes the places you visit "worlds". After getting a bit familiar with the game, you get to create your own world, and build it alone, or with your friends!
Wheter you're a teenager or an older person already, the experience this game has to offer is really worth your time! (If you're still not sure about getting this game, you can always check the free, ads-supported web version of the game!)

Mixed Feelings Mixed Gameplay. Revelations tries to recharge the series by mixing the old with the new. Let's start with the good, no more gun toting zombies, no more cover based ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, no sprinting and sliding around like a jackass. The game brings back some nice things like a setting that is actually a little creepy, at least more so than Africa or Shanghai. The game still forces you to take on a partner, which is an element I wish they'd get rid of. The partner, along with the numberous cutscenes and setting changes remove any feeling of isolation from the environment. Chris and Jill are back together in this one which is nice. Neither one of them has anything interesting to say through the entierty of the game, but what can ya do. There's several  homages to the first game that manage to be subtle and not straight ripping off the past game, which is nice.
The campaign mode is decent and deserves a playthrough if you're a fan of the series. Raid mode is just another mercenaries side game that gets boring very quickly.  You modify your weapons with parts in this game so the base weapons themselves are inherently very similar. One pistol is very similar to another and so forth, so it limits the fun of acquiring new weapons. Raid mode starts fun but then turns into a farm-fest for top gear to kill the same zombies you've been farming for hours. Pointless. The new side characters are all boring except for Rachael whom already feels a bit milked with her DLC. Still though the setting and enemy designs are much nicer in this game than previously.

Revelations is a welcome addition to the Resident Evil franchise. It attempts to go back to its survival horror roots with a tense atmosphere and semi-tank controls. Revelations does not disappoint in that aspect as there are several moments where you do not expect what will be around the corner waiting for you. It really is no secret that Capcom wants to take the franchise into the action/third-person style; and Revelations still has aspects of this as well. It may not be as bad as other Resident Evil games but the game is still quite enjoyable. With the introduction of Revelations comes the Genesis, a device used to show hidden items through-out the environment.
The Genesis adds an interesting layer to the gameplay. The main purpose of the Genesis is to gain additional ammo and herbs. Of course you can also use the Genesis to scan B.O.W.s., whether alive or dead, to gain more herbs with every 100% completion. There are very few healing items in the open world so it is highly advised you use the Genesis as much as possible. Overall the Genesis is an interesting addition to a Resident Evil game but in the end it shows that the game really was made with a handheld in mind.
A few gripes with the game is that the story telling isn’t the best. You are constantly switching back and forth between several people and this tends to mud up the flow of the timeline within the game. Another annoyance is the lack of healing items. There will be quite a few times you run out of them, as you can only carry five, and you only gain a small percentage from scanning monsters. The game also tends to hold your hand when you die, basically telling you what you did wrong and how to overcome it. I wish Capcom didn’t do and let the player figure it out like the past games.
In conclusion Revelations is a must have for any fans of the classic Resident Evil series. It takes a step back to recreate the tense setting and tries to instill fear into the player like the games of old with a few new twists on the gameplay.
Overall I give the game a 7 out of 10.

I was conquering half the galaxy and had built my fleet up to 100k strength in preparation for a war.  The stuttering was already there at that point, but not too bad.  Then one of the "sleeper" empires awakened with a fleet size of 200k.
The game was unplayable from there on out.  I've spent the last 3 days stutter-stepping my way through this game TRYING to finish it.  The lag is horrible enough, but combine that with the fact that I can only conquer 10 planets at a time, once every 10 in-game years, and controlling the galaxy and "finishing" the game is becoming tedious.
Thanks to the stuttering, the game only ticks up a few days every time it unpauses.  Which means I'm sitting here for hours, zoomed in on a distant corner of the galaxy with as little stuff on screen as possible, slowly watching the calendar tick upwards a few days at a time, waiting to declare war so I can take 10 of the remaining, I dunno, 150 planets or so at a time, so I can then repeat this same process for a few more hours again.
Fun game, was really enjoying it, but the fact that they KNOW about this problem and, lets face it, KNEW about it before releasing the game, and STILL it has these horrible issues, it gives me 0 desire to touch this game any longer.
I mean, the game is scripted to spawn in the Awakened empires with their biga$$ fleets.  Its not like I broke the game, the game was coded for this to happen and the game can't even handle it.

Okay, let's be clear here.
I DO reccomend this game, I do NOT reccomend purchasing the Steam version unless you really, really hate ads. I really reccomend checking it out on the web first.
Do you like pixel art? Yes? Do you like pixel art... in a prime number canvas? 19x19 blocks make drawing anything uniform a real pain.
I'm sorry, I love pixel art, but the canvas size absolutely kills the game for me. I can't draw anything uniform.
If you DON'T like drawing pixel art, you can still grab other people's stuff and build with it, or if you don't mind the prime-number canvas, go right ahead and try it on the web. I really don't reccomend the Steam version though.
It's a really amazing idea and should be much better, but it's kinda poorly executed.
It could use a proper sprite-management system and the canvas being resized, and one minor character-sprite-flipping bug fixed. Sadly, the second of these three things would require everything people have drawn to be wiped, pretty much.
Oh, and what'd be REALLY nice is a paintbrush-style thing, rather than a drag-drop copy system. Try drawing something in Everybody Edits, then in Manyland, and you'll see EXACTLY what I'm talking about.

I do recommend this game, but with reservation. The download and install can be a tricky and hard to figure out. Once that is done, the game itself is very arcane and complicated. It is not as intuitive as I would have wanted it to be. You will def. need to alt+tab to google "wurm unlimited" for all of your answers. Do not bother with the in-help game pedia as it is woefully lacking and pointless. There are some glaring glitches and there are MANY CTDs. This is the most unfortunate aspect of the game: it will simply just lock up and it takes FOREVER to close. By forever I mean go pack your lunch for work, shave, and shower and it MIGHT be close to closing and going to desktop. I ended up just doing a hard restart which was 100% quicker, but I know is hard on the system. I have scoured the internet for answers to the ctds but there is really no help beyond the idiotic "check your drivers" "restart your computer" etc. etc. You know, the things that NEVER help but every incompetent fool tells you because they don't know what else to say...
The game is worth buying and playing though despite all the horse manure that comes close to ruining the experience. There are subtle "ah ha" moments that really endear the game. I cannot stress enough to go online for all your questions because you can easily get too frustrated and just quit. The "wurmpedia" is a terrific resource and without it the game would be pointlessly too hard. Last, I HIGHLY recommend setting up your own server and getting to know the game first before going head to head with other players. Also, when you are setting up your own game: don't be afraid to give yourself a very high starting value for all of your attributes and skills. The game is hard enough and you will not feel like you are cheating whatsoever. I didn't do this and it took a very long time to become even average in my skill levels. Even then I still have animals kill me that should never be able to. Also, raise the quality of your weapons as soon as possible (this is called "improve"). You may think just because you have mined, smelted, and forged your longsword after a week straight of hour upon hour grinding that you can now go take on that wolf or bear only to be killed even faster than when using your starting shortsword! It is because you still need to raise the quality of the weapon... I just saved you a LOT of frustration and hours of research. :-) This game is serious and not for quick thrill gamers. It is for the patient, plotting (not plodding), intelligent gamer who doesn't mind making mistakes and learning from them. If you can overlook some glaring flaws, there is a real gem hiding underneath (but you have to raise your mining skill high enough to get to it) ha ha...
Way faster than the original and much better for modification and testing of any developments. Would approve over the main for less grinding and faster pvp/pve and better aspects.

Project Starship is a good example how bullet hell game should not be made.
I love danmaku genre and what is the most beautiful in those games is the fact, that you know all boss moves, enemies scheme and it's all up to you if you have mastered the game or not.
Instead of these Project Starship offers a total randomness. Not only every time there is a different layout of opponents, but also there is no consequence in their arrangement - once there are as many of them that you are not able to see anything and the other time no enemy appears.
Mentioned above visibility is another thing which this game lacks. In a proper made bullet hell, all missles are well visible, so despite of the amount of bullets on the board, you still know what killed you.
I died suddenly many times in Project Starship without knowing the reason at all. I haven't seen a bullet nor an enemy that I could hit. Wtf.
As it comes to missles and obstacles, properly made game always gives you a chance to avoid them. Do you think Project Starship has at least this point? Of course not. Among my short time of playing, there were number of times I hit a solid wall of enemy fire.
Those solid walls happened on so called 'Mad Events', which are nothing more then a sudden random annoying thing. Some of them are easy, some include unavoidable amount of bullets and some of them are just impossible to pass. Personally I don't see a point in them and quickly started to hate this part of the game.
Another thing, after being hit a player should be given few seconds to be able to get their situation. Is it here? Wrong! You can lose your shields one after up to death without even a chance to see what's going on.
There is one more thing worth mentioning - power ups. Letter ones are always good, but there are lot of other various shapes. There is no explanation what they do, but lot of them, if not a majority, instead of helping you, remove your shields and give your ship a weird look. They appear mostly after beating a hard opponent, so they should be a kind of prize, not a punishment. Also it happens that once you get a ton of power ups while another time you get none during a whole level.
So, if you want to try a bullet hell game, avoid this one. Don't be fooled with its low price, you won't get a taste of a danmaku here.

Binding of Isaac.
A common name seen tossed around with my friends, and to be honest, I had not bothered to look at it. It was only recently when I transfered from console to PC that I got the chance to have a browse. Of course, I had to purchase it.
Binding of Isaac follows Isaac, a small child who lived with his mother that watched daily Christian television. After a while, Isaac's mother believes that she hears the voice of God himself. He tells her that she must show her faith by stripping Isaac of everything. Toys, clothes,
God tells Mommy dearest that wasn't enough, and he needs a sacrifice. Isaac escapes his mother by going down into the basement. That starts the game.
First up? This game is f**king amazing. The content in the game is amazing. Based on the Christian faith, there are sweet bits. Like selling your hearts to the Devil to receive items, or fighting the 7 Sins as minibosses. This game is basically a giant mockery towards the faith. The controls are quick, meaning if you hold down the movement buttons too long, that could be game over. The ball squeezing difficulty adds to that control format. Some runs I thought I would win, but I end up dying to a fly or a single blood shot. This game is not forgiving. You die, game over, start again. This ended making me frustrated when I was so close to beating this game and I fell into a fly ridden abyss. Not to mention the fact that almost the entire game is randomised. Some bosses, rooms, items, minibosses, enemies. This stops the player from getting a certain pattern to rooms, and it adds levels of replay value.
However, there are some downsides. Some bosses have a ridiculously easy pattern. One or two fights in, and it's easy to predict what they are going to do. The game also makes you want to give up so easily. Some rooms are so slow, and some runs you just want to quit.
Also, once you think the game is over, nope. You have more.
I recommend this game 100%. And I haven't even finished.

Seems like an alright game, even if there's no mouth movement when characters speak (I can accept that for a budget title). Game play wise it's closer to the new XCOM than Mordheim and I actually appreciate being able to select what units move and when. Camera control is better than XCOM 2 as well (yeah I'm aware you can dl free camera mods, but it's nice that the thought was put in right out of the box here and I won't be corrupting my savegames just to enjoy the privilege). Everything is a little rougher than a triple A title to be sure (and arrg there's a little too much bloom on everything) but there's still a lot of slick animations (mantling for instance). Dunno if I'd be happy to pay 20 dollars for it yet, i got it from the humble bundle after all. I just thought I'd write my review to weight in on a few things.
Most of the critical reviews have nothing to do with the game itself. More than half are protests about dlc policy. A large portion of the remaining critical reviews are are outdated, there are complaints the game doesn't run well but i'm on a mid-tier system and even with everything but lens flare on "Awesome" settings I'm getting some crazy-stupid high frame rates without the fans kicking up to jet engine levels or the celcius climbing.
As for my thoughts on the actual game? The tactical combat itself seems excellent and looks to have a lot of solid systems in place. I particularly like the allocation system because it requires you to make a judgement call, examining the feild in advance to determine whether the warcaster or warjack is going to do you more good this round at the start of your turn, which calls for a bit of a tactical appraisal and a bit of gambling. I also like the ability to spend focus to improve accuracy. I can't recall a turn-based strategy game I've played since Jagged Alliance 2 that let me do something like that and it's been sorely missed.
Since it is reminiscent of XCOM I should probably make a few comparisons about differences since a lot of people will be familiar with that system. While you can select what order you want your units to move in, once you use part of a unit's moves here you have to use all of that unit's moves up at that time or forfeit them. It takes some getting used to but focus can be used to make the system flexible at least. A UI feedback addition I particularly like is that when you're planning to move a unit, visible lines of sight are drawn from the potential location to any potential targets as you hover over the tiles. How many times in XCOM2 have I been shown the damned little targeting icon only to find out I'm illogically not able to hit the target I wanted to hit or once I've moved to that spot I'm not allowed to target any units at all, even though I was told beforehand I would be? Not a problem here, if moving one square over would block my LOS, the line vanishes and you know before you commit. Also you can play the game with any controller if you so please,  though the movement cursor zips around so fast (and the sensitivity is not adjustable) that you might just opt to use a keyboard and mouse even if pads are your thing. The option is still there though.
Maybe it's a matter of not coming into this review with any grudges over kickstarter this or DLC that (and the price of entry I paid can't hurt) but I'm actually enjoying this game quite a bit so I think I'll recommend it.

Warmachine: Tactics had so much potential and that it makes this implementation all that much sadder.  It's been more than a year and a half since the game was released and despite all the patches there has been no real improvement to the fundamental problems.
The UI is a clunky and obtuse mess.  Simple tasks are needlessly complicated to the point that it can be difficult to tell if a bug has occured or if, for example: the character isn't moving because the UI is in some state that precludes moving.  Even just cycling through characters can be difficult.  Hit 'tab', nothing happens, end turn: "You still have characters with actions left".  Hit 'tab' again and they select.
With a little thought Warmachine could have been an X-Com competitor.  Add a few context sensitive menus and a bit of object picking to the mouse and do away with the awful stateful button menus.  The entry to making an attack shouldn't be deciding you'll make a ranged attack before deciding which enemy you're going to make the ranged attack on.  The default enemy chosen when ranged attacking is usually not meaningful.  Let me select the enemy and then select what I want to do to them.
Rather than popping up hints on how to calculate the various 'things' let me hover the mouse over something and show me the modifiers for it.  An obvious reason for why I can't exit a characters turn would be helpful too.  It feels like no effort has been put into user interaction at all; there are problems all the way from the blurred and stretched fonts to the poor - and largely absent - presentation of what's going on on the battlefield: who still has abilities left, what abilities, which enemies etc...  It's all really bad.
Couple the UI with poor voice acting, poor writing, unfinished cut-scenes, a host of bugs  and some dodgy AI and you're left a game that looks nice in screenshots but is almost painful to play.
Spend your time elsewhere, play X-Com or Fallen or Divinity or anything else instead.
Should still be in Beta.

When I saw this game released I was so very excited, I love wargames but I don't have a venue nearby to play, the massive income required to keep up nor the prerequisite skills and time to paint tiny plastic men. I really enjoyed the first dawn of war game and the second was... Fine i guess, but I had really gotten into the Iron Kingdoms, so this was it, my chance to play some Warmachine. The first issue arose immediately, the price, a kickstarter game should not be so ridiculously expensive, but that was OK, I'd just wait for a steam sale like I usually do and play some of the demo while I waited. The second issue peaked it's ugly head above water while playing the demo, the gameplay was an entire city constructed primarily of klunk and the unit selection was puny, but it was only a free demo so I just (incorrectly) assumed that there was a veritable cornucopia of content just behind the locked door, what a fool I was. Even with access to the full game the unit selection was pitiful and the klunk city limits stretched into the horizon, but maybe patches will fix it, thought I, which is where the third issue burst forth from the ground like some horrible cyclopean beast, the same beast which has strangled so many potentially great titles in their cribs, I speak of course of DLC. As other reviewers have no doubt mentioned the DLC is overpriced, even with the newly announced "price cut" each clocks in at $10 and while this may not be as egregious for the Mercs or Retribution bundles (it still is) the Warcaster and Jack bundles are simply ludicrous, 4 units for $10? I would rather not sell my home, but thank you for the kind offer.
So the question still remains, is it good? Is it worth my hard earned dollars/pounds/euro/whatever? The answer, in my opinion is an emphatic but remorseful no. If this game wants to be anything other than a floundering, half funtional cash grab it needs a lot of work, the klunkiness needs to be reduced considerably, the factions need to be expanded and the DLC needs to be added as regular content available upon purchase and expanded as well. If they do enact these changes I truely believe we will have a game which both promotes its source material and allows enthusiasts without an outlet (such as myself) to experiance the world of the Iron Kingdoms. Until then keep an eye on the reviews, you never know, the creators may decide that they don't need to bleed their creation for every cent and give us the game we crave and deserve.

A rather short Limbo-like platform game. Nothing exceptional but not bad at the same time.
In the game you control a robot (that reminds me a dog for whatever reason) that for whatever reason reminds me of a dog. Crash landed on an unknown alien world your quest is to follow your maker and explore the planet. The first thing you encounter is an audio log of the person who gave you free will and you learn that he went ahead of you. Nothing else is explained and you will learn a lot on your way while exploring the planet. To be perfectly honest the plot is pretty thin and after finishing the game I have no idea what the story was really about.
Graphicly this reminds a lot of Limbo. The environment is simple though unlike Limbo with a dash of colour. It also gives the same a little eerie vibe. The only thing standing out is the main character who is quite detailed and because of that a bit out of place. Though you get used to it after a while.
The sound design is pretty good. The soundtrack is a bit eerie and unsettling working well with the game play. Apart from one or two instances where the music goes disco for unknown reason. Luckily it's not more than a couple of seconds at the time. The narrator in form of left audio logs is nice to hear and is a welcomed addition.
Mechanically it's Limbo through and through. Well not entirely but close enough. You move along and solve environmental puzzles along way. There's no fighting, only jumping, climbing and moving blocks and stuff like that. The puzzles are not too complicated and well designed for the most part. The character however while jumping have a tendency to get magnetically pulled towards ledges which was a bit disturbing.
In the end I will say this. If you've enjoyed Limbo you might like this as well. Not as good but pretty good. The story doesn't hold up. Finished it and I have no idea what was it about. Enjoyed it for the most part however and since it's fairly short you'll be done with it before it starts to get annoying.

This is a game where you control a hulking orc and a cunning goblin. The combat is real-time with a pause function, and requires tactical thinking and basically no reflexes, which is a valid design choice. It has RPG elements, and the world it is set in is very grim, with human fanatics having enslaved or exterminated most of your race.
I don't understand the lukewarm reception this game got. It has a unique twist on the dumb old Humans vs. Orcs cliche, and both main characters are interesting and compelling. The combat, at least at the higher difficulties, requires a lot of strategic thought and good planning, and it is just so sweet to see Arkhail break the back of the last imperial soldier at the end of a long fight. On top of everything else, the game looks incredible even on the lower graphics settings. What's not to love?!

A short budget RPG that doesn't overstay its welcome. Tells a neat story with a few twists and turns and stays on course with the story even with the sidequests. Pretty much 100% linear with all missions pretty much being "go there and kill everything", but combat is fun enough to make it not matter.
Each character can also be built in a combination of different ways so there can be replayability if you wanted to try a different combat style. No complaints about the graphics, writing, or voice acting for the most part. Styx is probably the best character I've seen in a long while.
Only thing that really felt wrong about the game are its dead environments. As with other Spiders studio games, towns are full of people that just stand there and do nothing, and you have pretty much zero interaction with the environment besides looting a glowing chest once every couple of maps.
Itemization is interesting in that there are very few items, but most items even from the beginning of the game are completely viable to endgame. Only difference is the stat bonuses they give you, and you customize your gear based on your preferred combat style. Very interesting design choice.
Very good.

I feared this game would be a impenetrable given the rather niche & very nerdy target audience of French Bread doujin games, but it's actually quite friendly for a fighting game casual baby such as myself. I'm someone who's only ever played Street Fighter semi-seriously nearly a decade ago, and who enjoys King of Fighters despite being pathetically awful at it, yet I found it quite easy to jump in. The more unique mechanical aspects of this game, such as the GRD bar that assigns mid-battle power-ups to players based on combat performance, don't create a huge inaccessibility wall - they're a "simple to understand, hard to master" kind of thing. GRD even works in conjunction with the normal special bars present in most other fighters, adding an extra layer of strategy. There is far less to take in before you can properly get started when compared to something like King of Fighters, with its many dashes and dodges; it's more akin to Street Fighter in that regard and it should be easier to get your normie friends to play.
Sadly, the lack of an in-game tutorial is definitely a flaw, especially since the online video tutorial is Japanese-only and the fan-made translation is not perfect, along with the tutorial itself leaving some thinsg out. Nonetheless, it's the best you have. Since I still recommend this game despite this glaring flaw, I will instruct you on how to get the best out of said tutorial. Simply search "Under Night In-Birth Exe Late: Basic System & Mechanics Tutorial" on Youtube and watch both videos while keeping these things in mind: "blocking hitstun" is a strange choice of words, as it simply means "in the process of being attacked while blocking". The numbered inputs such as "1/4/7" refer to numpad directions, so simply look at the right side of your keyboard. KD simply means "knockdown". "Tech" means escaping from a combo by pressing A, B or C and a direction. Force function is B+C.
Netplay is hit-or-miss. Sometimes you'll easily find people to play with, sometimes not so much. I recommend finding at least one friend willing to play with you regularly before buying. Though to be fair, there is still an aspect of online competition even when playing against the computer - in the form of time attack mode, survival mode and whatnot.
Visually, the game's definitely more good than bad. Some of the character designs have a sort of visual novel blandness to them, lacking the unique appeal of the super-iconically designed Capcom & SNK fighters (or at least strong influences; Street Fighter borrowed a lot from Jojo's Bizarre Adventure after all), but they're definitely not tasteless and the stand-out characters are super appealing; my favorites by far being Merkava, an Evangelion Unit 01-like monstrosity with shape-shifting powers and fittingly beastly attacks and animations, and the obviously Cyborg 009-influenced Akatsuki, cameo-ing from the game Akatsuki Blitzkrampf. The animations, though, are where the game shines from a visual perspective. They might not be as mind-blowing as the stuff you'll find in games like Darkstalkers or Garou: Mark of the Wolves, but they're still quite impressive. Even looking at Merkava's idle animations should be enough, with his hyper-fluid and organic breathing animation and his ethereal flowing hair both resembling something out of an anime with particularly high production values.
The Infinite Worth animations are suitably over the top, yet they go beyond mere serviceability with a really cool detail that goes a long way; they are punctuated with brief, snappy, yet fully-animated sequences taking up the entire screen vertically. It's a great way of adding cinematic flair to a game without sacrificing gameplay.
The music hasn't hugely grabbed me, but it definitely adds to the overall cool feeling of the experience.
Overall a fun game, well worth the 7,27€ I paid for it. If you're not reading this review during a sale, then just give it a shot and see if you like it.

The negativity surrounding this game is honestly baffling to me. Don't let my 2.4 hours on Steam fool you, I played this game for months after its release on Xbox 360, and not even in co-op. I love this game, and actually am pretty happy to see that the rating on this game is in the positive.
So, let me first address what I don't like about the game:
-First of all, the music sounds like it belongs in a bad 70s sci-fi film. Which works fine for games like Mass Effect where that is the intended tone. But Borderlands is not 70s sci-fi, it's 80s post apocalypse with sci fi sprinked in. The sound track needs to be rockin guitars, not slow methocial synthesizers. If I could mod the music to be completely different I probably would. Maybe I can, I haven't researched it tbh.
-Some areas are a bit bland and repetitive in appearance. This is sort of to be expected though considering it takes place on a moon. Have you seen the real moon? I am glad they at least tried to make it more interesting than a flat grey wasteland. Plus there is the Helios Station and the Vault towards the end to shake things up a bit. Still, it's not nearly as much variety as BL2 with its sprawling green hills, snow covered expanses, and of course the standard desert wastes.
-Air management is way too easy. I was actually looking forward to the extra challenge of worrying about oxygen, but Oz kits will rarely run out of air and lack of air drains very minute amounts of health so that you can survive for over 2 minutes without air. You can't have both. Air either needs to be more scarce or the penalty for losing air needs to be greater. I have a feeling that they expected more casual players to hate this element if it wasn't so forgiving, and maybe it even had something to do with playtesters. I think they just needed more time to balance the system but had to rush to get the game released at the end.
-This isn't an issue I ever had, but apparently some people didn't realize that some of the narration in the game was taking place in the frame narrative of Athena telling the story to the Vault Hunters. It was confusingly integrated even though I found it to be a clever way to add more jokes to the game, even if some of them were heavy handedly meta.
-Scavs don't really have as much personality as the bandits of Pandora.
-Fire weapons are basically useless until you get back to Helios Station, since enemies will only ignite in air rich environments. It makes sense logically but since when is Borderlands logical?
It's not perfect by any means. But the positives make it very much worthwhile for me:
+Low gravity is so much fun it should be illegal. I actually found myself missing it when I went back to play BL2 it was so much fun. The combat and arenas are very well balanced around this element of the game with plenty of places to jump around to get a new perspective on a battle. Oz kit double jumps and butt bashes fit right in with the other pieces of the Borderlands combat formula. It's fun to play in space which is one of the main reasons I like this game so much. Gameplay should always come first and they really nailed it here.
+Cryo weapons are way cooler than Slag. Theoretically Slag is more interesting from a tactical standpoint, but freezing enemies in a hail of blue fire is very satisfying, especially when you smash them to pieces with your butt.
+Just as much weapon variety as Borderlands 2. In fact, the introduction of lasers means it probably has even more variety! Speaking of which...
+Laser weapons are great. I was happy to see then not include the Eridium weapons, since they tended to eat up standard ammo quite fast. Laser weapons have their own ammo type making them far more viable in combat than a weird laser weapon that consumes 4 bullets to fire. They come in several types, too. My personal favorite is the constant beam variety, but sadly you don't find them all that often.
+Scavs may not be great, but the interesting wildlife of Elpis certainly makes up for it. Rock monsters, Lovecraftian abominations and Threshers keep things relatively fresh. I know Threshers were in BL2 but they fit in much better on Elpis, which makes sense since they revealed that they originated on the moon and are actually an invasive species on Pandora. Also, Dahl makes a really good enemy with their more militaristic appearance and attitude compared to previous corperations.
+The plot is nothing particulatly special, especially since you know how it's going to end from the start. A lot of tension is missing from certain scenes involving Jack himself, but the game still has some twists and memorable moments. The Skipper plot line took me completely by surprise and is actually quite sad. Plus there's something quite nice about watching Jack's facade of heroicism slowly break down as his true character is revealed to the Hunters. You get to see him as an anti-hero for a while before he becomes a full on ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. A glimpse of what he could have been as one of the player characters. All I have to say to the nay-sayers is what were you expecting? How could they have possibly done it any different? The story was already set in stone, what we get is a detailed view of what we already knew which to me is perfectly justified.
The final positive I have about the game will require its own section: The player characters. I think the playable characters in TPS are a huge improvement over the default ones in Borderlands 2. I specify that because Gaige and Krieg are pretty much on par with TPS, actually better in Krieg's case. He's basically the best character ever made. Each character in TPS has a very unique Class Skill, and their skill trees are just as interesting and varied.
Wilhelm: This is the character I played on my own, and honestly he is the best one to play on single player since he has two built in allies. Saint and Wolf are cool, but the meat of playing Wilhelm comes from messing around with his cybernetic implants. He can have a rocket fist, a shoulder mounted laser, mechanical legs that let him shoot and sprint at the same time, and each one of these actually changes his physical appearance and alters his voice more and more until he sounds like the boss he becomes in BL2. I also really like Wilhelm's personality. He comes off like a modern day nerd who grew up to be a grumpy old grandpa type. There's also a lot of jokes at the expense of his complete lack of any defined personality or backstory in BL2.
Athena: I have not played her as much, but essentially she is Captain America. Her shield makes her an interesting choice for players who like to tank, as she can absorb a lot of damage and send it right back at her opponents. She also has a tree dedicated to elemental offenses for those who want to play with fire and ice. Personality wise she's pretty much exactly what you would expect if you played Borderlands. An interesting addition is the fact that she is confirmed a lesbian in this game, as she forms a relationship with Janey Springs.
Nisha: The so-called Lawbringer is probably the most evil character in this game. Jack at least thinks he's doing something for the betterment of man-kind. Nisha is a straight up sexual sadist who derives extreme pleasure from the pain of others. Thank god she went into law enforcement instead of becoming a bandit. Then again, she doesn't seem to be that much better for it. Her playstyle is very DPS heavy, so don't expect to take a lot of hits like the last two characters. Her version of the style is similar yet different from Salvador's, in that she can dual wield any pistol. This can be very handy if you can find the right gun, though on "Fire as fast as you can pull the trigger" guns it really only ammounts to having more ammo before reloading. Her class skill is an aim bot that turns you into John Marston for a while.

What a classic!
It's a great game that makes me reminisce about my childhood. All in all, for modern players who haven't got a PC that can't run a more modern TTW game, curious people who want to play an old TTW title, or people like me who like to reminisce. Plus there is an excellent mod called: The Third Age: Total War, which is basically a Lord of the Rings conversion, which has numerous expansions and an entire campaign, the amount of work gone into the mod is amazing and I highly, HIGHLY recommend it to any LOTR fans. Anyway, back to the base game...
GAMEPLAY:
So like any TTW game, there are two maps, the campaign and the battle map. On the campaign map, you can see all of the main settlements within view and other objects like armies, spies, merchants, diplomats etc... This is where you manage your faction, build structures within your settlements and recruit troops. You move your armies around the map and engage enemy armies or settlements. You can then choose whether to auto-run the battle, or play it yourself on the battle map, where you will move your troops around in real-time, either on an open map or in a siege battle depending on the circumstances.
You have a family tree which evolves throughout the years, some may die from diesease, others in battles and most from old age. Is basically like Crusader Kings, but a lot less in depth. Your faction will have victory conditions which will need fulfilling to complete the game, which will unlock a lot more playable factions.
So yeah, it's a classic TTW game.
GRAPHICS AND SOUND:
Well it's not a very demanding game, so you'll be able to run it on most low budget pc systems. But the graphics definitely aren't terrible! There are some graphic overhaul mods out there too for those of you who have better systems.
Sounds are great for the style and age of the game.
PROS:
- Good in-depth strategy game
- Great battles
- Good amount of unique factions
- Good DLC
- Inexpensive
- Not very demanding in terms of system power
- Awesome mod
CONS:
- Outdated (but still worth playing!)
OVERALL:
It's the perfect game for people who desire a good strategy game for a low-budget system and for those who want to try a classic TTW game too, I also recommend Rome: Total War!

I went into WildStar as someone who has never touched an mmorpg in his life, and I have to say, not a fan. I was hoping this could be a game me and my friends could hop in and have fun on, but it turns out you need 5 players to raid a dungeon. What?! Why 5? That's bs.
Other than that, here's my list of pros and cons.
Pros
+Combat is fun, not anything groundbreaking, but it's alright
+Music is pretty kicka$$, getting a Star Wars vibe from it
+Classes are cool and each offer different strengths and weaknesses
Cons
-Story is awful. It would be alright if it wasn't so jumbled and told poorly.
-Hard to run on lower-ish end hardware. I surpass the minimum specs but yet barely edge out 30 fps on the lowest settings.
-Game is barren and empty. You'd be lucky to find more than 3 people playing in an area at a time.
-Quests are repetative and dull. Go kill this, go get this, go find this, rinse and repeat 100000 times.
My final verdict? If you have a good amount of friends, it's alright. Other than that, avoid WildStar.

- Offline gameplay feels pretty smooth in general
- Celebrations in MyCareer are a great addition. I can dab 50 times a game and still not get tired of it.
- In terms of MyTeam cards, 2K did a pretty good job of putting new and better cards all year long.
- Overall presentation of the game(pre-game, interviews, half time report, etc.) is nice

CONS:
- Archetypes are too limited in their abilities. Sure no more demigods(well there are cheaters so don't worry) on the park, now we're a bunch of bums.
- More annoying animations than ever before(especially the new steal animations and players running into refs all the time)

- Cheaters, lots of cheaters, something you wouldn't see much on consoles
- MyTeam mode has turned into a pay-to-play mode. C'mon 2K, we already paid $60 for the game, let us have fun.
- Despite some interesting cutscenes, MyCareer becomes REALLY dry and boring sooner than I'd expected. Add the grind for badges and attribute upgrades, and the mode turns into a grind simulator.
- Short players still can't play in this game even if they are good players, while tall players are too dominant regardless of their attributes.
- No new or challenging gameplay content in MyTeam at all. They give you domination and weekly/moments challenges. Domination doesn't take long(only took like 1 and a half month for me). The weekly challenges are a joke. The moments challenges were cool until they stopped putting them out halfway through the season.
- Too many overpowered cards in MyTeam. I know 2K releases these cards for profit reasons but c'mon, Hakeem, Kareem, Wes Unseld, KG, Rodman all with high 3 pointer ratings? stop, just stop.
- Bidding in the auction house is broke. If someone bids with 1 second left on the clock, the auction should extend instead of ending right there. It's like someone putting down a bid in real life when the auctioneer is counting down to the last call, and then the auction does not extend, leaving all other bidders no chance to bid again.
-  The auction house is not live, I hate waiting on bids only to realize that they have already expired.
- The graphics had not improved at all since 2K15
- The music is meh. (DONT BOTHER ME, IM WORKING....lol)

Binding of Isaac.
A common name seen tossed around with my friends, and to be honest, I had not bothered to look at it. It was only recently when I transfered from console to PC that I got the chance to have a browse. Of course, I had to purchase it.
Binding of Isaac follows Isaac, a small child who lived with his mother that watched daily Christian television. After a while, Isaac's mother believes that she hears the voice of God himself. He tells her that she must show her faith by stripping Isaac of everything. Toys, clothes,
God tells Mommy dearest that wasn't enough, and he needs a sacrifice. Isaac escapes his mother by going down into the basement. That starts the game.
First up? This game is f**king amazing. The content in the game is amazing. Based on the Christian faith, there are sweet bits. Like selling your hearts to the Devil to receive items, or fighting the 7 Sins as minibosses. This game is basically a giant mockery towards the faith. The controls are quick, meaning if you hold down the movement buttons too long, that could be game over. The ball squeezing difficulty adds to that control format. Some runs I thought I would win, but I end up dying to a fly or a single blood shot. This game is not forgiving. You die, game over, start again. This ended making me frustrated when I was so close to beating this game and I fell into a fly ridden abyss. Not to mention the fact that almost the entire game is randomised. Some bosses, rooms, items, minibosses, enemies. This stops the player from getting a certain pattern to rooms, and it adds levels of replay value.
However, there are some downsides. Some bosses have a ridiculously easy pattern. One or two fights in, and it's easy to predict what they are going to do. The game also makes you want to give up so easily. Some rooms are so slow, and some runs you just want to quit.
Also, once you think the game is over, nope. You have more.
I recommend this game 100%. And I haven't even finished.

2. I played this because of the alluring title. I am still not really sure if it means anything w/r/t the actual game or if they just picked some heavy sounding♥♥♥♥♥♥to draw you in. I guess that's bad but, whatever, I'm not gonna fault some developer for giving their game a wicked sweet name and throwing some eye-stocks sticking out of the ground in the outdoor areas.
3. This calls itself a puzzle platformer but it strikes me as more action oriented ultimately. It had a few tricky bits here and there but didn't strike me as being too terribly challenging overall. I'd call it a satisfying challenge but the game is more about the narrative and exploration than having tough gameplay.
4. A few too many beers helps up the challenge level. That's what I did. Not gonna lie.
5.  The story of this is presented through the locations you progress through along w/ taped audio logs you find along the way.
6. Alex Lewis who did the voice acting on this was excellent. He was just a little over-the-top but that worked well in this case. The audio logs just play right over gameplay so it kinda helps he hammed it up a bit because it helps hold your attention while you are hopping about and trying to stay alive.
7. The main character is a ro-bot but it's pretty clear from the get-go that it's supposed to be thought of as fully sentient.
8. Graphics on this are good but they are the kind of graphics where I see them, I just think, "Oh, this looks like an indie game." Dig all the colors though.
9. The sound design and music are really good. A very low-key ambient techno sountrack  blends in quite well w/ crisp sound effects. It all makes for a good backdrop when those audiologs are playing.
10. The number of checkpoints in this is simply staggering. There is pretty much a checkpoint after every single obstacle. This kinda brings you out of the game a bit. It reminds me of using save-states to cheat through emulated games.
11. Number 11 is not that important.
12. The ending of this is pretty abrupt. Seems like the final sequence is just kicking off and then the game is over.
13. If this game was a bit longer, a bit more involved and maybe a bit more challenging, I think it might stand up as one of the best indie platformers of recent memory. As it is, it's a good game for sure but it feels just a bit unsubstantial. Still, if you got a free evening and just want something to fill it out that you don't have to worry about for weeks to come, this is a great fit.

This game is the first Japanese style game I've played and just...wow. What a way to enter the genre. A truly amazing game. I'd heard from a few people that it was a great game so I took a chance and went ahead and bought it. So glad that I did.
I don't want to spoil the story which is actually a strong point of the game so I will steer clear of any story elements you can't discover within the first 10 minutes. The premise is that humanity has been forced to abandon Earth and escape to the Moon after first contact with an alien race who deployed machine lifeforms to Earth as weapons to wipe us out. The humans then created a race of combat androids to retake earth from the machines. The game centres around the exploits of two of these androids known as 2B and 9S. Oh, 2B ♥.
It's hard to even classify the genre of game this is as the gameplay will often shift from third person actioner, to platformer, to bullet hell, back to third person...and it all just works. The game design is amazing. How the story unfolds, how the areas transition, how the game has you set up so that if you miss something, just keep playing and you'll be able to access that content. And the action itself is amazing with solid upgrade systems and mechanics that once you master you feel like a machine smashing God.
The game does have multiple endings (I never played the first NieR but apparently this is the style of the lead designer) one of which requires revisiting about 60% of the content from the first playthrough and it is 100% worth it! It's more like a continuation until you reach the "final ending".
If you plan on buying it, do yourself a favour, ignore the negative reviews from AMD users who are too hard nosed to go download the excellent FAR Mod which basically fixes any performance issues the game might have had. I don't know about those because I got the mod (it's literally a 1 click install file that autoupdates when necessary, simplicity itself) before I started playing and I've had 46 hours of crash free, 60 fps gaming.
I can say that I am truly satisfied with my purchase and even though I feel like I've finished the game I'll probably be going back to do some completionist stuff (the game lets you do this) and will definitely replay it in the future.

Aesthetics aside, probably the main reason I kept playing was the voice acting. Alex Lewis did such a good job that I had to keep playing to see what happened to the disillusioned spaceman.

The controls are clunky and the AI is far from the best, but Of Orcs and Men tells a story that I haven't seen before in another RPG.  So all and all I enjoyed the game and after a while the combat system grew on me despite its bugs.  It's not great, but it's definitely an interesting take on the genre.  One occassional bit of hilarity comes from the voice acting.  While the main characters are well acted, some of the choices for secondary voices are more than a little off, but they were working with a budge so what can you expect?

For a game released in Oct. 2012 this game feels like it could have come out nearly a decade earlier (aside from its graphics). This is a painfully linear game. The vast majority of it is spent running through brown and gray winding corridors with evenly spaced groups of enemies to encounter. What choices you are able to make, both in moving about the world and within the story, ultimately don't have much real impact. The voice acting for the two main characters, Arkail and Styx, is high quality but the remaining cast ranges from bad to atrocious.
The major selling point for this game, playing from the greenskins' perspective, is implemented with mixed success. The character arcs of Arkail and Styx are both enjoyable. Their personality's balance each other out with Arkail being the brawn and honor type and Styx being the brainy and cautious one. Unfortunately the game follows a lot of stereotypes in terms of orc behavior and in a storyline centering around slaves revolting against power hungry evil rulers. Change the orcs into humans from a warrior tribe led by shamans and very little would change. That makes the story feel more human relatable but also cheapens the greenskins' perspective feature, making it seem like more of a surface change or gimmick.
A lot of reviewers have commented negatively on the excessive use of foul language and I'm inclined to agree. It's not that I am offended by the words but that it feels forced, like a misguided attempt to make the game more dark and gritty. The script is otherwise decent with Styx's dialogue being the best it has to offer ranging down to some of its one dimensional villains being its worst.
I enjoyed the combat during the middle hours of the game but not in the remaining hours. At the start your options are limited before you unlock more attacks and there is a bit of an awkward learning curve. Later on, the repetition got to me as the same strategy that worked early in the game worked all the way through, making most fights feel the same. Styx's ability to stealth assassinate enemies before you are spotted was a feature that I eventually stopped bothering with. I found it wasn't necessary to win most fights, slowed things down and wasn't particularly fun.
Of Orcs and Men's biggest success in my opinion is its soundtrack. It stands out with a unique style that features a lot of cello and drums. As soundtracks often go, not every track is interesting but on the whole I found it catching my ear numerous times throughout the game.
There are situations where I would recommend Of Orcs And Men but overall I didn't find this game to be good enough to recommend to most people. For example, diehard action RPG fans who have already exhausted the higher rated games in the genre might find something worth playing here.

This game is a tricky one.
Pros:
+Very nice storyline (Main reason to buy this game)
+Two nice skilltrees
+Decent graphics
+Nice sounds
+No bugs
Cons:
-Gameplay
I open the gameplay problem a bit.
Think about classic RTS where you look on your characters from the sky, pause the game, give orders and watch the fun from the above. Goood.
Now, in Of Orcs and Men you do the same. The problem is that you play in over-the-shoulder view and you control characters with WASD. It gives you the feeling that you should be able to do some real-time fighting.
The fact that your characters can't really do anything on their own, means you have to control all of their moves using slow-motion, in order to survive. So you can't really do real-time fighting.
That's biggest thing that bugged me throught the whole game and it made the gameplay not-so-enjoyable..

I wanted to love this game, and it has a great deal of potential, however, this team has a serious game breaking controller issue.  The controls are a jumbled mess.  Even with autodetect on a Windows 8.1 system, a licensed and perfectly mapped Xbox 360 controller, and a ton of attempts to adjust the controller settings in the game, it is impossible to engineer a fix for this problem on the user side.  I never really got to play the actual game.  I have no save data, no progress, and no controls to use.  I essentially just idly pranced around and tried to open the menu, which was oddly mapped to L3, until I got stuck again.  In fact, the only 2 inputs that were properly mapped were lateral movement and back (left / right on the d-pad and B).  That's literally all that worked properly with the controls.
I honestly would like a refund for being issued an unplayable game, but I'm not likely to receive one.  The devs won't even acknowledge there's a problem with the PC version of the game.  I believe Steam should pull this game down until the developers acknowledge and fix the problem.  My controller works perfectly fine with all other controller supporting games I own.

This is a great successor to Borderlands 2. It builds on the gameplay of the last game and adds agility via low gravity and boosting as well as oxygen management as a gameplay element. If you enjoyed Borderlands 2 then you will enjoy this as well. It is different enough to not be boring but the core gameplay will be familiar.
The story is a clever backstory that adds depth to the universe in a natural way. It doesn't feel shoehorned in. All the new characters have the Borderlands flair and many familiar faces appear to guide you on your way.
These games run well even on more modest gaming rigs. The style is distinctive and ages well. The controls are flexible and work very well with a Mouse and keyboard, the Steam Controler, or with an Xbox Controler. Like Borderlands 2 the soundtrack is epic and varied enough not to get boring.
I want to give a shoutout to Gearbox and Aspyr for porting these games to Linux. Being able to run it everywhere is awesome.

This game is ADDICTIVE to say the least.
It's a chat.
It's a design your own world 2D reality.
It's a game design kit.
It's all online.
When I tried this game for the first time I was hooked. People were very friendly and always tried to help me out when I was new to the game and lost.
One of the most interesting aspects of this game is that you can try out new game theories and game designs you might have planned, and immediately deploy it for testing as people in the game at any time can visit your "game area", this makes it possible to try out new game design ideas LIVE, how many places can you do that?
You can even to a certain degree - code your own game elements if you don't find the existing game blocks to your satisfaction, there's even some Java script blocks were you can code your own spectacular special effects to add to your game, with the game engine already provided for you - this is an excellent way to try out your javascript stuff and let other people parttake and appreciate your work instantly.
There's a solid sense of community in Manyland, people often get to know each other very closely - young and old, but older people tend to stick to older people while the younger generation plays in their own worlds, sometimes when some great graphics artist come along to play in Manyland - everyone, either young or old can appreciate the work and go exploring trough awesome artwork from all over the world.
There are many community events in Manyland, mostly just created by the community members themselves - this could be weekly or monthly competitions where the prizes are basically just the honor and/or a pixel-pocal ornament with your name on it - maybe you'll get a place in the hall of honors?
Even events similar to the Oscars have been held in Manyland (Called Moscars) where community members who have taken their free time to help newbies and other players, maybe done some outstanding service to the community get voted on by the community itself - everyone is free to parttake, at Manylands events - everyone is invited.
Try it today, but beware - you might never return to the old reality again!

Manyland is weird, complicated, but so compelling. The tools provided in this unique sandbox are some of the most powerful and unwieldy things ever in these kind of games. But it also does a poor job at explaining them, and while I think the game is freaking awesome, it does come short in really being accessible.
Manyland isn't really a video game. It's a straight-up sandbox that lets players create objects and worlds. There's no real PVP or RPG mechanics, or survival; This is all about making things and showing it with other players. Perhaps you want to create a character skin? Or a mountable vehicle? Manyland has a lot of options for those kind of tools, but does put itself at a immense cost;
It's very, very difficult to learn. The game mechanics are explained in tutorials and a whole buncha texts/forum posts, but that's it. For a basic and new player, making things is about as daunting and scary as climbing a skyscraper. When I first played it, I had no idea what to do, because the game didn't boot me to a tutorial world. It gave me a welcome prompt and that was it. Game design wise, it'd be hella-lot more smart to place players in the isolated tutorial areas to start.
My other issue is that the friends list, while functional, didn't let me friend anybody directly. I had to first meet them in the same world in order to add them as a friend. I'd rather to directly add them via username, because I wouldn't want to force my friend online to add him if he wanted to be online later.
This issue can also go with the UI, which is while functional, hard to navigate. There's a ton of menus and buttons you have to click before you find certain maps to play, etc.
But otherwise, it's a pretty dandy game. I've been making cool, social worlds for friends to go on and hang out. Once you understand how everything works, creation makes a lot more sense. Placing and making objects are very intuitive and very efficent; There's a variety of tools to creating objects, and building worlds is as easy as dragging-and-dropping.
What about the community content in this game? It's actually very high in terms of quality. A lot of people have made awesome character skins that resemble pixel art from other games, a lot of the blocks, gamemodes, and objects are very well done. It's a fantastic community to interact with, and that's really the main highlight of this game. The game's hub worlds are filled with a lot of these items too, so it's hard not to explore the game, being amazed at the cool stuff you see. A lot of the folks on the forum are helpful as well, and the developers complement the community back by responding and answering to a user's many burning questions.
What this all leads to is a sandbox that's not perfect, but definitely noteworthy. If you don't want to put the money on the game, you can play it free online, but otherwise, there isn't much to lose if you're really into these kind of games. I expect myself to easily put more hours in this then I originally thought I did.

may look a bit simple and even childish at first, but due to it's complexity it ends being a hard game to explain.
Imagine Terraria in a bigger scale, merged with social games like Habbo or Second Life, and a full engine at our disposal to create almost anything. Interested? I was too, and thankfully the game ended up being better than I expected.
You start off in one of the welcome areas, surrounded by random people without any clue of what to do next. But just like the games I mentioned, there are hundreds of rooms for us to choose. In
they are all divided in categories, such as Art, Cinema, Chat, Adventure, Games, Quest, Music, Party, Horror, Casino, and the list goes on and on.
There is unlimited content thanks to the possibility of creating our own items and character models, and then using them to build something entirely new. Maybe a costume party, a giant pool with robots, minigames, a cinema that actually plays videos from YouTube. There is literally no limit but our imagination.
We can attach items to our body, such as weapons, furniture, vehicles or even wings. And we can swap our character model anytime we want, either by creating one by ourselves or using one that has been already created by another player. There are specific rooms for these items, and luckily we can use a stash/inventory on a side of the screen to save everything that we like and then use it in our room.
We can build a house from scratch, using different types of floor pieces, stairs, ladders, walls, blocks, doors, anything that we can imagine. The game benefits from the online community and we can find people 24/7.
Being able of creating pretty much anything we want it's one of the highlights of the game, and it's something that I haven't seen in a long time. It can be quite hard to understand it at first, but there are plenty of tutorials, both outside and inside the game.
Playing
with a group of friends it's a really fun and addictive experience, and if you're looking for a game that let's you build mini games, items and entire rooms from scratch, this is a must buy. The community it's always helping to improve it, and the devs are very active.

Magicite is a super-fun roguelike, permadeth, pixel-art platformer.
Before talking about the actual game, let's put it into its context. It was released in 2014, two years after Rogue Legacy, and three years after Binding Isaac and Terraria.
Magicite itself fits well into the genre of the above games; it has simple art and crafting like Terraria, and the permadeath of Binding of Isaac and Rogue Legacy, as well as Rogue Legacy's "reincarnation" features. So in that sense, Magicite is nothing new.
What Magicite does differently is boil all of these elements into a simple platformer. The game is fun, you die quickly, rinse repeat and replay.
If you like the genre, you'll like this game.
Also, my hats off to the programmer. Unlike so many games, this game just feels optimized. It runs super smooth on my Macbook, and never even causes the fans to spin. And when I'm running off of battery, the drain is minimal. Well done.

At over ten years old, this game has held up really, really well. It stands up to me as one of the best Total Wars of those I've played (Shogun, Rome I, Rome II, Medieval II, a few mods.) I have spent over 350 hours on it, and so I couldn't possibly not recommend it, certainly in terms of money spent to time played, this is one of the best purchases I have ever made.
Firstly, the good points: Medieval II builds on all the good ideas in Rome I: the gameplay is solid, and the AI is notably smarter than in Rome (not really saying much to be honest. In Rome II it's notably smarter than in Medi II.) The smaller battles generally feel fun and interesting - watching a cavalry charge send enemy peasants flying as the horses and men collide is satisfying on a basic gut level - and there is genuine satisfaction in causing a huge enemy force to rout and sending your men in to run them down. Your generals are fun to manage and it's great watching them develop traits that are influenced by the battles. (For example a general that gets hurt in combat will develop "scarred" traits, increasing his hit points, and one that executes prisoners and sacks cities will devleop "dreaded" traits making him scarier - maybe if he's a real psycho he'll get his own torturer!
Now the negatives: At times the game feels like a lot of good ideas that weren't tested properly. For example, the Pope will threaten you with excommunication (in game terms this translates to a public order penalty, making your cities more likely to rebel, and the worry that he may even ask other Catholic factions to send huge crusading armies to your cities.) The problem is that seemingly no matter what you do, the Pope is likely to threaten you with excommunication for any war against another Catholic factions. Very well, you may think. You'll only war with non-Catholic factions. However, unfortunately diplomacy in this game is totally broken. Thanks to an unfortunate unfixed bug even staunch allies are likely to stab you in the back. Even if you're the greatest power since the Roman Empire and their 'empire' is a loose collection of wooden castles they'll still eventually gather up a mob of peasants to send at your worst-defended city. And when you defend yourself, no matter how nice you are (releasing the prisoners instead of executing them as any Medieval ruler likely would for such blatant treachery) the Pope will tell you not to retaliate or face excommunication.
The alternative is to play as one of the non-Catholic factions, such as the Orthodox Russians and Byzantines, or the Muslim Turks, Egyptians or Moors. Sadly, this brings me to the second great but flawed idea: the Mongols. The Mongols attack with huge armies with amazing generals you are unlikely to be able to match and cannot hope to be better than. It's a great idea - give you a large and powerful enemy to battle as a real challenge, but while it is possible (albeit difficult) to beat them, it's just not very much fun. Usually it's the same endless slog of holding up in a castle, raining fire on them and then feeding them into the meat grinder of your spears.
The final minor gripe is the unit selection. Unlike the Roman world where each culture felt quite distinct in terms of its army makeup, most factions, especially in the early game, feel very similar. In the West it's militia, knights and peasants with bows or crossbows, and in the East cavalry archers. Only Scotland and Denmark really feel unique to begin with.
The Kingdoms expansion really adds more of the same, generally on a smaller and more intimate level. It's four new campaigns and really this is nothing to complain about. In my experience Britannia was a lot of fun to play, while the Crusades and Teutons campaigns were good for one playthrough each. The Americas discovery campaign wasn't great, but might be enjoyable if you want a challenge, either in city management (as the Spanish trying to convert the natives) or on the battlefield (the Aztecs / Mayans, trying to fight a much more advanced military force.)
As much as I've criticised in this review, these minor gripes really can't prevent me from recommending this as one of the best Total War games available, and a must for battlefield strategy fans. Buy this game, you won't regret it (except when you're exhausted at school or work because you stayed up until 3am conquering the Holy Land, because seriously, this game is  a time sink like you would not believe.) As an added bonus, it has a decent modding community who can add real variety to the game.

This hurts you when you need to replenish an army after an attack.
