I hate to post a negative review on what should be a very interesting game -- but after 2.5 hours, I am fed up with the interface.
THE GOOD: The premise of the game is great, and the combat system (which I assume is true to the tabletop version) is refreshingly original.  I especially enjoy the ability to combine volleys of ranged attacks, as well as the dynamic of focus allocation.  The units are sufficiently diverse, and it seems to have all of the elements needed to be great.
THE BAD: The view/interface is terrible.  An ability to see the battlefield is CRUCIAL for this sort of game, but the zoom feature doesn't allow you to zoom out to a level that would be strategically useful.  You're stuck in tunnel vision.  It sounds like a small thing, I know, but it's integral to gameplay.  It'd be like if an otherwise brilliant shooter only allowed you to play in the third person.  No matter how cool the guns are, the game's a flop.
THE UGLY: A handful of annoyingly simple bugs show that not only was this game unforgivably unpolished, but its developers clearly don't care about addressing the issues.

To be honest, I am shocked that this is considered a finished game.  This plays far more like a reasonably far along early access game than anything.  Graphical and sound glitches are everywhere.  Campaign cutscenes are just character models standing *completely* still while the camera pans.  The HUD is atrocious, with no clear way of cycling through troops or immediately telling which troops are still active.  The screen is constantly marked with the version number and framerate, insisting that this isn't even a 1.0 release.  The list continues.
If this game was in early access, I would quickly overlook these problems.  After all, the core game is here and it is pretty solid.  But to call this a finished product is ludicrous.  It's too bad, too.  If you are willing to look past this, the core game is worth a few dollars and a few hours of investment.

TL;DR: if you have a controller and single monitor - this is an excellent game. If you have dual monitors prepare to hate your setup. If you have no controller get something else.
Pros:

Interesting ability/weapons systems
Beautiful music that actually fits the areas it plays
really nice graphics if you have the capabilities for it
somewhere in the Final Fantasy range of advancement (plenty of things to do but overall advancement is slow - yet you feel like you're making a difference the whole time)
"Meh" or can go either way depending on playstyle:
camera follows the player in odd positions sometimes; this gives view of some areas you might not have noticed but can get in the way of combat; it's mostly customizable though

Cons:
Dodge/Counter isn't always responsive and there's no information about it in game, google it to learn.
keyboard and mouse is completely unplayable (the 2-D sections will WRECK you), really have to have 360 degree motion and keyboard isn't even very responsive.
on my dual monitors the game loves to "not start correctly" and freezes the PC the second time it's started. restart PC and then start the game to avoid.
Steam Big Screen never works (will freeze the pc every time)
game doesn't know what screen sizes are. I have it set to 1920x1080 but it always appears 1024x768.
to get full screen you really have to use Alt+Enter. the in-game "fullscreen" mode is unreliable
Steam overlay is broken / doesn't work on this game
alt-tabbing freezes the game permanently (sometimes freezes the pc)
steam controller isn't properly customizable for this game
Summary:
Excellent game but literally the worst port I've ever played... and I've been playing since 1989 across many platforms (mostly pc). If you have a controller then i recommend trying it (use family share for 30 minutes) and you'll know if you like it. If you have dual screen the game itself could be worth the restart each time you want to play... its an annoyance that will affect only a small percentage of players (most people turn their computers off regularly).
note: I'm playing on a GTX-1080, game on SDD, 32G RAM, and nearly 4.2 processing speed... anyone who thinks it's my specs causing the issues doesn't know computers.

I've already played a ton of the 3DS version, so the first thing that I noted was that the keyboard/mouse controls are amazing. They're very responsive and accurate, which helps a lot for getting headshots on the fly against enemies that like to sway around. Moving is fast and easy, too; no more running into walls or standing still while trying to turn sharp corners. Then again, I bet all those "classic-RE-is-the-best-new-RE-sucks" people will hate this new change, since bad controls and bottle-necked game design do such a wonderful job at adding artificial horror, difficulty, and helplessness to games~
Something else that I liked a lot about Revelations was the throwback to Metroid-style open exploration, while staying with solid chapter-progressive story-telling. The recapping of the previous episodes at the beginning of new ones reminded me a lot of a drama, so that was amusing. "LAST TIME ON RESIDENT EVIL: REVELATIONS..." The cutscenes look like they were ripped straight from the 3DS, so the quality on higher resolution monitors probably won't be optimal, but the original quality was pretty damn good already, so it's passable, even at 1920x1080 (the 3DS is actually pretty powerful, believe it or not).
I haven't had a chance to play Raid Mode yet, but I'm definitely looking forward to it. It was pretty much the entire reason for me wanting to play the PC port. It was a blast on the 3DS, so I can't imagine it being any less entertaining, considering the weapons are also more fun, among other positive changes that I mentioned.
events and download support add some nice extra content, as well.
Overall, RE: Revelations is an excellent port with plenty of fun-filled hours available after finishing the story in Raid Mode and various difficulties.

To be honest, although I am recommending this, I don't think you should buy it.
Why not?
The new version of this game (that is currently out in Japan) is coming out in a month or two, and there is hardly anyone playing this game anymore. However, if you have a bunch of friends who you want to play with to get ready for the new one, it's a really well made fighting game. The core mechanics of this game reward fun and exciting gameplay, for the most part. UNIEL is often dubbed "the anime street fighter" because it is pretty ground based, but I think as of right now this game is more enjoyable than SFV. The one question a lot of people have about fighting games before they buy them is if the netcode is stable enough for it to be worth, and honestly, this game has pretty decent netcode. The art style is really cool. All the sprites look really well made and the stages look really cool. The game has unlockable color palettes with currency you get from playing the game too, which is cool. Have I mentioned the soundtrack? The character themes, loading music and everything in UNIEL music wise sounds really really good, and has a lot of personality. Also, maybe just a personal preference, but the lobby screens look really beautiful. The only REAL problems in this game are the lack of story mode (which is forgivable, there is arcade with bits of story in there), and character balance. The top 3 characters in the game, Gordeau, Merkava, and Waldstein, are way ahead of the rest of the cast in pretty much everything. But even then it isn't that huge of a deal. There is just a lot of content for a $30 price tag, which says a lot in the current era of big $50-$60 fighting games. Even Blazblue is $40, and I personally prefer this game to that. Honestly, wait for the new one to come out unless you are getting this with a couple friends. And if you normally don't like anime games but you're willing to try them, start here. UNIEL is a really good introduction to anime, especially since it feels a little like street fighter. Buy the new one on launch. It will be worth it.

Hands down the best anime fighting game series I've ever played. I really can't get enough of it, and I honestly can't wait until they port the next game to Steam.
They put quite a bit of work into the stories behind the characters, even if you have to play the previous game to get most of it. Each character has a really cool personality that's different from all the others and you really will get attached to your main after seeing their different victory quotes after every round you win. It's not terribly complex or anything, more or less just a bit better than what you'd normally expect from an anime fighting game.
The gameplay is literally do or die. When you get good with combos you'll start to realize that once you get one started, it usually lasts long enough to get your opponent to around 25% health. *cough* SETH *cough*
They also have a really cool mechanic. Basically, you have a thing called a Guard Meter at the bottom of the screen between both players' health that fills up as you pressure your opponent and stay close to them. Moving back will make your meter go down. After a certain point, while you have meter, you'll be able to perform something called a Chain Shift. Basically, this consumes your meter to immediately cancel all lag, allow you to cancel into another move, and increases your EXS Gauge based on how much meter you consumed when you performed this. It's the best way to continue your supposed-to-end combos into longer ones.
Then of course, you have the EXS Gauge, which I mentioned earlier. Just like every other super gauge in anime fighting games. By pressing C (on the fight pad) you'll consume part of it to turn whatever move you were using into an EXS variant, which will do much more damage and has more invincibility.
And finally, each character has their own cool cutscene when they do their Infinite Worth, which is their strongest move, consuming 200% of the EXS Gauge. Some last longer than others, but it boils down to the fact that it looks exactly like what you'd want to see from a character's most powerful move.

All in all, I'd give this game a 9/10. It has a couple small points that could be changed, and the netcode is pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥ Other than that, everything else about it is amazing.

This game is enjoyable in it's own.  The platforming works well, the art style is beautiful, and the levels vary quite a bit.  There isn't really a difficulty curve in this game, since it feels like a little harder than your normal platformer.  The story to this game isn't bad, but there are a few major plotholes that don't really make sense.  The voice acting and other sounds have a very professional feel to them.  If you could get this game for around $5-$7 and you enjoyed Limbo or other games like it, I would say that it would definitely be worth your time and money.  It's enjoyable and it's very interesting.

Welcome to Manyland!
I'll try to keep this short and sweet.
Maryland is a cute little browser and Steam app game where you and your friends can meet up, build, roleplay, play games, and whatever else you can possibly imagine!
I have quite a few more hours put into the browser version when a friend told me about Manyland originally. I personally like the ability to log in from your tablet, phone, browser, and have it pop up no issue. What I do wish about Manyland is the ability to log into your Steam account from browser, so I could do the exact same thing, pick it up wherever I may be, without needing to be specifically at my desktop to log in progress and hours for the Steam edition. There's almost no difference, other than the lack of small few second advertisements during loading a zone, and the fact that you're helping out these developers.
One thing I absolutely love is the fact that you can just drop in and without an account, can still interact, play, collect, etc. So I can send a non-Manyland playing friend a link to a world where I've built, and they can see it! That's so awesome. I've yet to interact with anybody apart from my own friends I've sent my world link to, so I can't comment on the community too much. Despite the "no dating" signs everywhere, the main area you spawn in, does feel a bit like 12 year olds trying to hook up.
There is a bit of alt-tabbing or browser tab-opening where you sit there (in my experience) trying to figure things out. There is a help town, but I wasn't placed there to start. There is an outer and inner ring, the difference, I'm still unsure of, but supposedly there's no features taken from you no matter your rank. You rank up by placing/deleting blocks and interacting, so it's a neat concept. Some of the game seems like trial and error, but I personally think that's what adds some fun to it.
My biggest qualm is that, once leaving main areas, no longer are places coherent and beautifully made, but instead, collected spammed blocks of memes and garbage. It's ashame to get 20 feet from the spawn, to be surrounded by Doge and Snoop Dogg gifs. If that doesn't bother you, and you can look past it for the cute little casual game beneath it, go for it. Just open your browser, you've got nothing to lose to try it out! My other qualm is finding worlds that are quality and innovative. I've seen some that I really enjoy, but I can count them on one hand. I hope to see some high quality worlds in the future. Or an easier way to find them.
There is a search in-game, but it seems to be done mostly by popularity, and popularity means cloneable bodies, blocks, etc. for you to collect! So that doesn't necessarily mean you'll get an action adventure game when you're looking for action adventure.
seems to weed out some of this confusion, but it's still hit or miss. Maybe I'm too picky.
Right now I've spent a good 20 hours just running around, collecting assets and building freely, figuring out lighting. In time, I plan on making my own blocks. I've made my first body today, and that was very fun!
Manyland doesn't rely on you being creative in terms of artistic skill. If you lack that, some people are sweet enough to allow you to copy things into your inventory and build with them! All items are player-made, pixel by pixel, and a simple right click will show you who made the original block, as well as who placed or deleted it, so art theft should not be an issue unless copied pixel by pixel.
Anyway, short list:
PROS
-Browser version can log in from phone, tablet, PC, without the requirement of creating an account. (Although logging in will save your items to and from these!)
-You can simply send a link to someone on any device and they can jump right in, Manyland-user or not!
-Wonderful to see an active community.
-Every block/body/pet/etc. is player-made, pixel by pixel!
-Very well monitored and you'd expect to see a whole big phallic world, but nope! Not a single phallic object in sight.
-Able to place blocks made by other players (if they've given the rights to), so you don't need to be artistically inclined to play!
-Able to "snapshot" areas and teleport back to them later!
-Add your friends if they have an account and teleport to them! (Also free to make your location invisible.)
-World permissions for editing/building.
CONS
-Community seems to be geared towards the dating scene, despite various signs everywhere that this is against ToS.
-Have not seen anything questionable, including language. No bullying as of this post.
-Spam, memes, etc trashed around the place in spam areas. World-wipes would feel unfair to those who have built with meaning, but the accumulation of spam, memes, unfinished work, half-deleted areas, etc. gives off a very littered feeling.
-Most worlds I've entered are unfinished, or "littered"-feeling. I can only count on one hand the worlds I truly love at this moment.
It's a sweet little game to sink some hours into, and there's tons to explore. Hope to see some really creative content soon!

In my opinion, this game is wonderful
Stellaris has so many layers, I learn something new each time I load it up. The sheer scope of this game may discourage some potential players but I would encourage you to fail at a few of the mechanics to learn them. You start as a fledgling empire in a vast galaxy. Expand quickly and establish dominance, the early game sets the pace for later. Stellaris begins with familar 4X mechanics, gaining territory, building a fleet, etc but later evolves into a grand strategy game with expansive galactic empires. The customization options are plentiful so you can experiment to your heart's delight on different species and strategies. The game is also beautiful to look at and its comes with an engaging soundtrack to keep you drooling.
The game is not perfect. Paradox seems to be constantly evolving this game and those unfamiliar with thier products should expect tons of DLC. Stellaris is quickly becoming one of my favourites. Watch some Youtube let's plays to get a feel for Stellaris, then engage your warp drive and set off.

Overall I've enjoyed playing this game, but the longer I play the more I begin to see issues that are killing the enjoyment:
- Many of the techs are boring, underwhelming or misplaced in the tech tree. Armour techs are all more or less useless until very late. Techs that give flat 5% production or similar are usable (which kind of tells a lot about the other techs), but so very uninspired. Many of the techs you get early do nothing until much, much later. Overall tech research usually feels like I'm just going for the least bad option for the moment. Also nearly all the weapon/power/shield tech upgrades are just the same with bigger numbers, usually the scaling is fairly linear too. It's just not very interesting.
- For a big part of the early game feels like you just have to do whatever gives you the most mineral production. Minerals are needed for damn near everything early on, which makes early games feel very same ish every game.
- The planet development isn't very interesting. There aren't that many special buildings, usually you just build more power/mineral/research, with maybe a handful of other buildings that are worthwhile. At least assigning planets to AI controlled sectors removes some of that tedium (since it is mostly just pointless busywork), but the AI does manage to screw up planets so that doesn't feel good either.
- Factions feel very unfinished
.. etc. There's a lot in this game that feels sort of unfinished sketch of a system.
I did enjoy the story event, and the feel fo a developing galaxy. It was quite a lot of fun for a while, but I can't really see past the multitude of issues. I'd love to, though, the game does have a lot of promise and I think it *can* get really good with patches.

If you are a fan of both the RTS and Grand Strategy playstyles then this is a very good game for you.
From my experience with the game itself ive found it has 3 major flaws but with a mixture of the fact there is an active modding community scene and the developers are still pushing out content and patches this is a mitigated flaw list.
1. Late Game Relevency
For me this is most likely the biggest issue with the game but it is also a strength, there is late game crisis events that test the galaxy/ your empire to see if it will survive or get consumed by it. the failing in this is that it can either dominate your game or be just a tiny spec on galactic events and lastly the AI's interraction with the event is usually very passive unless it spawns in their empire's space
(this is something that at the time of this writting is being adressed by the developers)
2. Mid Game Emptiness
Very simple negative here that can be adjusted and managed with mods and with the Utopia Expantion but as is the main underlying issue the AI's interractions can be a tad predictable making the midgame a small hurdle to overcome till lategame events.
3. The Sector Management System
To sum this up, you can colonize up to 5 planets baseline before you have to start diverting new colonies into AI controlled sectors, this was the answer to a big problem which would be "what happened if you controlled over 100 planets? Wouldnt it be easier to hand that control to a computer governer like a set and forget system". After many patches trying to address AI behavior and unpredictability the system is better then its inception but it is still in my opinion the games worst failing.
For me tho this isnt a problem i mod the game to give myself unlimited colonization cap the micro management of every aspect of my empire is the point for me, but this is also an opinion i have others may need to have Sectors help regulate their empires.
Now the strengths of the game is what i said at the beginning if you like RTS and Grand Strategy games you will enjoy this but if you are on the fence watch a few videos and see if this is a game for you.

Do yourself a favour and turn off the music in the launcher options before starting the game.
I'm not saying the tracks from Tom E. Morrison are bad work. But having played Wurm Online since 2008, I'll have to say that the music doesn't fit in-game AT ALL. In that regard it's simply bland and generic instrumental music. There is NOTHING that speaks "This is Wurm" in these. It seems like they randomly picked a bunch of tracks from a bag and gave them new, loosely Wurm themed names with no relations.
Here's a most prominent example, the track "Beating the anvil". You would expect to get in some kind of craftsmanship mood, perhaps some kind of smithing. Weapon smithing, blacksmithing, shield smithing, armour smithing, jewelry smithing... okay, not jewelry smithing. In that regard, the track feels NOTHING like ANY sort of craftsmanship except that of the musician who made it, which is completely unrelated and unfitting.
What a darn waste, man... waste of time and money. Compare it the old tracks by Joss Sanglier (21st Century Blues), aka Gurubear (e.g. "The Raven", "Little Miss Jane", "Johnny", "Wind's Last Master", "Blow Wind Blow", "Mol-Rehan Anthem", can be found via Google/YouTube).
Those didn't fit in-game either in my opinion, but at least they had a lot of character, and personality. You could really identify the game within these, he'd sing about Wurm, he'd sing about things in Wurm, about players, places, stories that often really happened someplace in-game in the history of the game. They were strongly Wurm themed. I still listen to those songs to this day.
You're probably not missing out on much otherwise. I'd say you get a much more relaxed experience of Wurm playing Unlimited instead of Online. The difference is very significant in a small number of things. Economy is a big one. In Wurm Online, everything has a tangible value, because the in-game currency can be bought with real money from the developers or other players, and is closely tied to the real life EUR currency. But with perceived tangible monetary values comes longing, desires, possession, ownership, greed, too. You get a fairly sizeable player base, both hostile and friendly, and more drama than you can shake a stick at, for free. A mostly persistent cluster of PvE and PvP servers (wouldn't put all my money on the persistent bet for all servers though), and a decision making from the volunteer and paid staff, and ultimately the CEO, that is incomprehensible in a bigger picture at times, that leaves you disappointed and frustrated.
Honestly, you can only win by playing Wurm Unlimited instead.
You can however, make a free account in Wurm Online, to get a taste of the game first. There's much you can do with all your skills limited to 20 skill points, but there's also "only so much" you can do with it.

I'm always on the lookout for a good bullet hell and this one has just about everything I could want.
Once you get a feel for the items/power-ups and your ship's hit box, this game really takes off. It's very energetic and fun, and I love the way the pilots call out the names of the power-ups. There's controller support which is always nice, although I think the joystick is a little too sensitive so I just stick with the D-pad. Keyboard controls are fine too honestly - just takes a little experimenting to see what works best for you. This was such a great find, definitely recommended for anyone who enjoys bullet hells!

I'm not exactly a bullet hell shooter connoisseur, but I really enjoy Project Starship. It uses a sort of procedural generation scheme that introduces random enemies and powerups each time you play. Still, the enemy fire patterns are predictable once you've gotten to know and identify them. So there's definitely a learning curve and a chance to do better. Some power ups seem  more useful than others, so you might find the game easier or harder depending on what you get. Not sure what a serious player would think, but I really like it as a casual.
The aesthetic is firmly "early 90s arcade". When the game boots up, you can choose to add a CRT filter, which I appreciated on my 27" display. Then you are prompted to insert a coin (just hit the spacebar), chose a character (which changes the qualities of the ship and which character pops up at key moments) and pick either the easy or hard challenge. All the sprites are big and quirky. Enemies include frog legs, skulls, flames and a dozen different types of eyeballs. The projectiles are large and visually fill the screen. This is actually one of the few difficulties I had playing the game: it's not always clear where the hitboxes are. Music, sound effects and occasional voice clips add to the general sensory overload.
Besides the random waves of enemies and occasional boss battle, the game includes "Mad Events". These are announced in huge letters and then the game shifts to a game mode all about dodging. Instead of an enemy firing projectiles, the projectiles just appear and move in a fixed pattern. With nothing to shoot at, your goal becomes to survive for a few seconds. These seem unfair (I hope you got some shield power ups!) but are a useful change of pace.
I gather there is a local co-op option and various extra game modes, but I haven't tried those options yet. The new modes would require me to beat the game. Even on easy, this is a difficult game. For the most part, it seems possible to avoid getting hit, but I'm not nearly good enough or patient enough to get better. Even so, I'm enjoying the experience. It's not as frustrating as most difficult games.
Finally, this game is funny. There's an item called "TV Doesn't Work" that temporarily changes the screen to static. (It also clears enemies and bullets from the screen.) Obviously my monitor hadn't stopped working, but to the extent I was drawn into the fiction that I was playing a game on a CRT, it's an effective practical joke. This is the sort of visual gag that can only make sense in the context of a video game.

Segue uma breve analise minha sobre o jogo:
Pós: Paladins é exatamente um jogo com heróis gratuitos contendo pequenas transações para liberar skins de armas e heróis, assim como ganhar ouros e XP e diamantes, é claro que tudo de acordo com seu rendimento na partida.
O que diferencia Paladins dos demais, e sem dúvida merece comentários, é a inclusão de um sistema de cartas que apoiam o status de nossos campeões, e que recebemos em baús ao subir de nível, junto com algumas skins. Esse sistema de cartas está divido em duas etapas:
1ª) Decks: Compostos por 5 cartas, estas cartas estão separadas em 4 cores: Azul, Verde, Roxo a Amarelo/Lendária;
2ª) Aprimoramento do seu Deck, na loja de itens disponibilizada na base.
Cartas de categoria Azul       → Aprimoramento em Defesa
Cartas de categoria Verde     → Aprimoramento em Curando
Cartas de categoria Roxa      → Aprimoramento em Ofensivo
Cartas de categoria Amarela → Aprimoramento em Utilitários (Chromos e Mais Mortal se Suporte).
Quanto mais cartas, mais opções para montar  Decks personalizados você terá.
Cada carta do Deck vai melhorar status diferentes em cada campeão, seja sua saúde, ou uma habilidade específica, de forma que posso criar diferentes Decks e escolher de acordo com o objetivo e estrategia do Champion escolhido.

If you were to ask me to describe
in as few words as possible, I'd describe it as "incredibly lazy", or perhaps "cripplingly uninspired".
For those of you not in the know,
is a table-top miniatures game created by Privateer Press. It's pretty dang fun, even though I think the game suffers from some pretty severe feature/scale/unit creep.
fails to really capture the feel of the miniatures game, mostly because it's simultaneously obsessive and dismissive about the rules. Clumsily shoehorning in the control phase and facing because they're in the tabletop game, but then forcing everything onto a no-diagnonal square movement grid and giving mooks more than one hitpoint? Please make up your mind, game!
As a result of the game's indecision about whether it wants to be
or
, the game in motion is completely uninspired. Animations are clunky and boring despite the good models and textures, the single player game features mostly acceptable voice work undercut by the least interesting and laziest cutscenes/storyline possible, and game just plays like dropping bricks off a bridge. And that's not even talking about the cluttered and poorly organized UI, which feels like someone looked at XCOM2012 and half-assedly copied their layout before throwing up all over the left side of the screen.
It's pretty clearly Privateer Press Interactive's first rodeo, but Whitemoon is a developer staffed with (minor) folks from some pretty good games. Which leaves me wondering why
looks, feels, and plays like a bad XCOM2012 ripoff with extra steampunk encoggling.
Regardless of my disappointment at this game's poor execution,
. And I got it though a Humble Bundle package that scored me some other games I wanted (

NieR: Automata is an unique experience amidst modern gaming. A gaming marvel from Yoko Taro himself. Originally I expected a lot, but I received more than I could've ever imagined.
So that's it? Was it so that I'd just play it and be amazed 100% of the time? Well, not quite so. It is exellent by all means, but with my high expections I was still blown away by... pretty much everything. The extremely compelling, different and strong story, the gorgeously varied, vast and memorable enviroments and setting, the great and smooth gameplay, the unique roster of characters and their stories and the absolutely 10/10 grade soundtrack...
I wasn't just amazed by it all...
If you seek for what I just described, NieR: Automata is a must-have for you.
Amazing . . . The art style is amazing . . .

Unfortunately, PC port isn't perfect but the game is just too special too avoid it. Exceptional and unique way of storytelling, phenomenal animations, engaging combat system and an interesting approach to  RPG elements such as your character skills customization.
Overall this game is much more than the sum of it's parts. Some scenes will really impress you, some philosophical ideas and questions the game presents will tickle your brain and make you think.
11/10 game overall

Keeping this as short as possible:
First of all, there are multiple story routes in the game, so once you finish the first one, A route, you'll get access to the rest of the routes. So far I've only finished the A route and it took me roughly 18 hours to finish the first route, so the game has quite a lot to offer. However, the main mission part in the route A was a little bit too short, meaning that once you start to have fun with it, it suddenly ends.
As for the gameplay itself, there's really nothing to comblain. Platinum Games knows how to make good battle mechanics and they don't let you down this time either.
For the other gameplay mechanics, there are several different weapon types that you can obtain and each weapon type changes the way you fight. You can also find loot from the world or item drops from the fallen enemies, which you can then use to upgrade your weapons, skills and pods. Pods are basically your second half in the game, allowing you to use range attacks and different variety of powerful skills.
Graphically the game looks decent, though the color scheme makes it sometimes hard to graps your surroundings.
Pros:
+ Gameplay/Battle mechanics
+ Beautiful to watch and listen
+ No autosave function
+ Multiple storylines
+ Characters
Cons;
- Main mission in the "A Route" is little bit too short
- Small delay in subtitles (annoying if you play with Japanese voice acting like I did)
- Boss mechanics little bit too easy and predictable for my taste
- Color scheme
- Makes you desire for sequel
Do I recommend:
Yes. If you've ever played the previous games from the Platinum Games and liked them, you'll like this one too. And even if you're new to Platinum Games titles, this game is a good start to make your acquaintance on them.
Verdict:  8/10 - Really good game

In my entire life, I have never come across of games as unique as Nier. Even though this is a so called sequel to the first game, it still can be seen as stand alone version with hidden easter eggs all around. My wonderful, wonderful friend gifted this to me, and I can never thank them enough for getting me into the world of Nier.
This is one of the most gorgeous and emotional journeys you will come across. Fantastic battle styles and animation, absolutely stunning soundtrack, played at the right time and thus making the finishing blow to your feels, and amazing characterization.
This game has to be replayed 2 times for the full story. First time you get only 1/3 of the complete storyline. Second playthrough is the same story but from the different perspective with added and removed content (once again, it's not the same playthrough and will give you much more insight into the story and characters). Routes A and B (aka these 2 routes) are only the intro into the final route (C&D). And this is where our story trully begins.
Of course, those who played first Nier know of how things ended in the first game, and this follows ending D and E of original Nier (ending E was done as a short story and Nier automata follows it). Basically, it's a pure enjoyment for both old Nier fans and new fans.
The scenery is gorgeous, the levels are done greatly. When you finish third playthrough you get a lot of more benefits for finishing up the game experience, like getting the rest of endings and getting the very interesting side boss fights.
My advice: play three times, make use of the benefits you get, upgrade all weapons and do the thing. You will figure out what i'm saying when you get there.
Gameplay is fantastic. There are hacking games which are made like those 8bit games of old, there are shooter sequences, fantastic boss fights, many battle combinations, choices, in game novels, weapons stories, archives, fishing (you can fish up maaaaaaaany interesting things), etc. This game has everything.
Not all of the side quests are important, but at least 10 give you insight into side characters, and one in particular is important for the main plot. I don't want, of course, to put spoilers and ruin the experience... But do the sidequests. Many fo them are fun and have interesting outcomes. There are also some unmarked sidequests like "gold robots" and "wise machines".
This game is a masterpiece. Honestly. It's a honesly breathtaking story and characterization which you won't regret. At all.
2B and 9S are both well layered characters, as well as A2, and all of the side characters. Pascal, 6O and 21O and Jackass (yes, there is a character named Jackass), all of them are so well written.
As for advice on which language to choose? This is the first time in my life that I have chosen English over Japanese. I usually dislike english voice acting, but they did such a fantastic job on this game I could not play it in Japanese.
I did replay a lot of scenes in Japanese later, and both have fantastic voice acting.
Most notably, 9S in both versions, but I loved his voice much much more in english version.
The reason this game has mixed and mostly positive reviews is for the not so good optimization. I have tried this game on three different PCs. My friend's PC supported it perfectly, my sister's won't even start, and mine had the slow motion effect (for which I blame my graphic card). In order to play this, you either need a really good PC. Or use mods. Up to you.
Also between controller and keyboard: with keyboard, it's playable, but to reach high places or long distances you need a really big ammount of patience, which is ridiculously easier with a controller. Recommendation: controller.

- Do the other endings, they are amazing.
- Collect all the weapons.
- Find a list of important side quests and do those.

Revelations is, by all accounts, a sub-par game. It's not exactly terrific, and all the fan hype about this being a 'return to roots' and 'hope for the future' had me expecting an incredible game. An incredible game it is not; a 6 hour long game that is decent it is.
RE:Rev. plays much like every other Resident Evil game of the modern era, only that the enemy count is much lower, possibly due to the 3DS' technical limitations. Which means this game's absence of action and mayhem is only due to circumstance. You spend most of your time exploring a ship and switching between several characters as the game's plot is unfolded through recollections and various vantage points starring different characters. The new characters are bland and uninteresting, and the game spends more than half the time dragging you through various plot points without ever explaining just what the ♥♥♥♥ is happening. There's even a scene with a character putting on the greatest exposition and display of ''alright I will reveal everything now no really this is how a good writer unfolds a plot'' ♥♥♥♥ery only to have something happen just as he says ''I will reveal everything now''. I'm pretty sure he literally said that word for word.
So the plot and writing is utter♥♥♥♥♥♥(it's Capcom, no surprise there); but the gameplay is somewhat decent. You don't encounter hordes of zombies, the game paces itself more than its full fledged console release bretheren, and there's a bit of atmosphere building at the beginning. But it all feels rather small; the rooms are tiny, the hallways can barely have two creatures standing side by side, maps outside of the ship are pathetically tiny, your arsenal of moves (and movement speed) is a fraction of what it is in the other titles, and chapters can be completed in 20 minutes. It's all down to its handheld origins, but I'll only marginally excuse it because if Persona 4 Golden can be on the Vita and clock in at over 60 hours, RE:Rev. has no excuse.
You won't exactly be scavenging for ammo or herbs (they're everywhere), and you won't be praising its new gameplay innovations. All that is taking place is an RE game that dialed back the explosions and threw in some fairly basic puzzles. About the only scary thing in the game is this one B.O.W. that seems to show up randomly to attack you, which was a nice touch but shows up infrequently and isn't the central plot element in the game as much as a miniscule plot point that no one seems to care about. Missed opportunity.
All in all it's not offensive (as a reviewer put it). Not a bad game, not a great game, barely a good game, a pretty forgettable experience. With all the♥♥♥♥♥♥I'm throwing at it you'd wonder why I filed this under ''reccommend''. Because it's still an enjoyable experience that doesn't drag on due to its length. Like a small pizza that has an interesting, albeit weird flavor; RE:Rev. isn't that great but short enough and decent enough for me to reccomend it. It doesn't overstay its welcome and try to hash out a 90 hour plot out of nothing, and it's over before you start to get bored of it.
PS, this supposedly takes place between RE4 and RE5. Remember in RE5 where there were constant flashbacks and a plot about putting an end to the founder of Umbrella and going to a castle? Yeah, none of that happens here. You're on some boat. It's a simple marketting trick; nothing gets revealed here.

Revelations is rather a movie than a game for me. It is not as exciting as 4, 5 or 6 RE's, but still the story kept me interested and the solid game mechanics are much unchanged. If you decide to pass you won't miss anything critical. Do try it if you are a fan of the series bored waiting for the next big title.

Under Night In-Birth is a fighting game that has lots of potential to become good in the future if more is put into it to improve the game (and I am already aware that UNIst fixes most of the issues I mention in this review, so calm down, take a deep breath, and brace yourselves for a comprehensive review).
First of all, the game system is one of the most outstanding I have ever seen (next to that of KOF XIII, and probably Xrd R's system after that). Incorporating a tug-of-war-like momentum gauge that physically rewards the player in favour? Genius. Now, of course, that's not to say that no other fighting game has something like it. After all, all do in the form of the classic 'super gauge', but that momentum is in the form of theoretical rewards, since the super gauge must be expended in order to be capitalised on, whereas UNIEL's Grind Grid (a.k.a. GRD) buffs automatically the player who has the momentum according to the games' rules.
Other areas in which the game excels are in its relatively less challenging skill caliber requirement for players new to anime fighting games (or even fighting games in general), and the fact that although impractical, extremely-situational high damage combos exist, the game will not restrict your combos (unlike BBCPE) yet you won't die in one combo, and nearly all of them end in a knockdown. Also, the move (not movement) animations of each character reveal their personas exceptionally, in a way that I have rarely seen in fighting games (most of the time it is revealed only in their movement or idle animations).
Some notably good things about the game that aren't necessarily exceptional is the fact that there is a story that is not difficult to follow (and has its dedicated mode, too) and that there are more modes than just Training, Arcade, and Versus modes. I don't like that there isn't a depthful tutorial for this great game so that new entries into the FG scene can be enlightened and encouraged from square one. However, at least there are brief yet comprehensive official tutorials (that are in Japanese! D'x ) for each character on YouTube (and one YouTuber has even subbed most of them for English speakers) and should help with at least learning a character of the player's choice, though the system is not explained well enough in those tutorials, so third-party wikis are almost necessary to fully grasp the game mechanics.
Now, the reason why this game won't be earning the highest mark overall has most to do with both the balancing of the characters (i.e., the meta). I am very fond of games that have a small meta, since it makes it easier to learn all of the matchups (and Xrd R has done this perfectly), but in this case the curve is insanely skewed. Really the only characters seen in the competitive scene on a regular basis are Merkava, Gordeau, Eltnum, Waldstein, Linne (and the occasional troll Akatsuki), all five of which are the top five best characters in the game by overall favourable matchups (according to EventHubs; though my opinion closely matches theirs). Merkava, Gordeau, and Waldstein all have ridiculously long reach, which requires extreme patience, composure, and discipline to work around. This, and the fact that consoles/PC haven't yet received a port for the newest version, are some of the reasons why this game has not received its deserved acclaim in the competitive FGC.
There is also the overpowered-ness of some characters over others (yes, and I am legitimised in using this word, even though OP is overused, typically by novice players). The rule of thumb in this game is that characters with absolutely poor range (like Nanase and Orie) are almost 92% guaranteed to be bodied by characters who either are zoners (like Hilda or Vatista) or have stupid reach (like Gordeau and Merkava). Some trolls online will abuse this rule to keep you out and frustrate you; if you don't enjoy this idea, then either don't play online or reconsider whether this is a good buy (or if you're looking at your computer reading this review and see that I am enjoying this abuse of parentheses, you can either endure through it to the end or I suppose you can downvote this review; though I'm sure that if you've been reading this far you have found it to be at least a little helpful c; ). Fixing this, however, is as simple as resizing the hurtboxes of moves that make this rule law and releasing another version, which I'm sure the company will do if there is enough support. Either way, this is one of the main reasons that the curve is so skewed. And also: putting a shoto-clone character in an anime fighting game? That's like a day-one no-no (this is a note to French Bread to buff Akatsuki, which I hear has already happened in UNIst; please port this game to console/PC).
TL;DR (yeah, I had to use this for once)
Pros:
- Unique and exceptional game system
- Easy-to-follow storyline with a story mode in visual-novel format
- More offline content than just the classic three (Training, Arcade, and Versus)
- Intricate character-defining move animations (something I rarely see in fighting games)
- Great entryway for novice fighting gamers looking to have their first exposure to one (Smart Steer auto combo by pressing A seven times, freeflow gatlings, etc.)
- Has a combo system that allows for freedom without having the traditionally long combos of most anime FGs
- Low skill ceiling compared to mainstream FGs (SF, GG, etc.)
- Small meta
Cons:
- Unbalanced
- No tutorial mode
- Some anime fluff (i.e., fanservice)
- So-so netcode
- Small meta
Overall: 8.8/10 (I'm rating it higher than I would otherwise because of UNIst's improvements from this version, UNIEL)
*EDIT* (20.04.17; time 20:04) - after posting this review, I was looking through UNIEL's discussion forums here on Steam and saw the discussion about UNIst's confirmed forthcoming port to consoles (along with a tutorial mode 0_0). If this excites you, you can brace yourself for the new release along with its proposed improvements, and delay buying this version. Otherwise...well, I don't know what else to say...this is a great game nevertheless.

Ok, so this game may be almost dead (I hope not), but regardless, I'm loving the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of this game.  This game somewhat seems like a standard anime fighter, with just a smaller cast than some of the bigger titles like Guilty Gear or BlazBlue, but it's definitely unique.  This game's unique feature is the "Grind Grid" system, or GRD for short.  It's a mechanic in which both players have access to, but will give an advantage to those who play more offensively, or whose defense outperforms the one on the offensive.  It also discourages overtly unsafe or campy play, so having your throw attempts rejected, backdashing constantly, and having your blockstrings blocked with the barrier lowers your GRD meter.  In short, the GRD system is basically a carry/comeback mechanic, as it can benefit honest, safe offense or defense.
Moving from the gameplay for a bit, the art is amazing, as is with most ASW games, with the usual cast of characters in most anime fighting games: you have your sword-wielding edgy main protagonist, your battle loli who's actually a couple hundred years old, your giant-fist sporting behemoth of a character that moves and hits like a bag of bricks, your bishie-looking a$$hole, and you have your genki-as-♥♥♥♥ female character with the annoying voice.  The game even has two guest characters from two other games made by French Bread (the developers of this game): Sion Eltnam from Melty Blood (some say its a different character entirely cuz the name is spelled Eltnum, but you ain't fooling me, French Bread), and Akatsuki from Akatsuki Blitzkampf.  While you have your usual tropes, there are some characters that definitely break the usual mold, such as a mage teen with a giant♥♥♥♥♥lizard at his disposal and a giant being that to me looks like a fusion between Susaan'o from BlazBlue and Twelve from Street Fighter.  There are also some characters that definitely have movesets similar to characters from other ASW games, such as the blood-controlling Carmine, who has some fullscreen bullcrap that he uses to space much like Yuki Terumi, and Orie, who looks like Mitsuru and literally has a Persona/Stand (which ever you prefer lol).  The roster is small, but fortunately, there's no two characters that have similar properties to another.
As for my impressions when playing, the game plays wonderfully.  A new player can feel safe knowing that mashing standing weak can literally do an auto-combo, but veterans can feel good knowing that there are more options beyond standing weak for combos lol.  The combo system is similar to BlazBlue, allowing for OTG resets that, from what I've played so far, most characters can do, like Hyde (the main protagonist) when using 3C, and relies on a combo meter that, upon depletion, allows the combo victim to ukemi, or 'tech,' out of the combo state.  Each character has their own unique command normals, some can double jump, some can't, and only a few (Eltnum and Akatsuki, from what I remember) can air grab.  As such, you won't have to worry about anyone being a clone of another character in the roster, and can find a variety of playstyles to choose from.
However, I do have a couple of discrepancies.  For one, this game has a very small, but dedicated and helpful community, but if you want to find matches, I'd suggest going to the UNiEL discord server.  You'll find a lot of resources and helpful people on your journey to advance your skill.  Secondly, the price tag of this game is a bit much, so unless you really want a change of pace, I'd wait for it to go on sale.  Finally, the game lacks a tutorial mode, so if you want to learn the game, again, check out the UNiEL discord or go to the Mizuumi Wiki to check on the game's mechanics.
All in all, Under Night In-Birth Exe:Late is a great game, good for newcomers and veterans alike, and is definitely worth a look. 9.25/10

I really enjoyed this game, aside from a couple of nitpicks.
First off, if you want more Borderlands, you'll get that. The story takes place at two times - once after Borderlands 2 and the gameplay, and bulk of the game, takes place in the past after Borderlands 1 and before Borderlands 2.
If you're interested in the story of Borderlands, you'll get a good amount in this game. I really enjoyed finding out the origins of various things, especially how Jack became Handsome Jack, why the mask, how he turned.
You don't play on Pandora, but on Elpis, a moon of Pandora; low gravity and lack of oxygen plays a huge role in the gameplay, but the game is pretty lenient with it.
The four main Vault Hunters all have had a role in Borderlands 2 - Nisha, wielding a magnum who would later go onto be a villain in the 2nd game. Wilhelm, who has a flying bot named Wolf, also went on to become a villain. Athena, fan may remember, appeared in the General Knoxx DLC from the 1st game, and Fragtrap aka Claptrap. Each, of course, has their own set of skills.
There's also 2 DLC Vault Hunters - Jack's Bodydouble and Aurelia the Baroness.
The weapons are mostly standard Borderlands fare, with the addition of laser guns that can shoot any elements and also can deal a great deal of damage.
The ClapTrap DLC is well worth getting as it gives some more background, and is quite fun.
My minor nitpicks with the game in general stem from some of the bosses being a bit TOO hard, at least playing alone even with leveling up, and some of the jumps never seemed to line up, making a bit of rage. Ultimately, I had a fun time, and is well worth playing, especially with friends.

Manyland is a phenomenal MMO, completely based around user-created, pixel-based 'things' which may include platforms, backgrounds, skins for your player, items and so much more. The amount of designs can be counted in the thousands. With these, you can build your very own world.
The editor for designing items and objects is very easy-to-use and fluid, including features such as RGB and supports hexadecimal color codes for specific tones. Each type of creation has limits to how high and wide you can create it, however. When you've created something or you've found a creation you would like to put down, the simplicity and fluidity of placing these creations are very apparant and there's nothing complex about it.
The community are very polite and I have not come across any sour players yet. Simply sitting in the main hub world can find you meeting new people and having fun with the vast amount of items and bodies already created.
I feel the need to also add that the servers are hosted in the United States (as far as I know), however latency is not really a problem at all.
I recommend Manyland for all of these reasons, as well as the unbelievable possibility for countless future creations and interesting worlds. The only real reason to buy on Steam is to play ad-free, however it also comes with 100 free Boosts (visual and cosmetic effects that don't always last longer than 10-20 seconds). Other than that, going to the website itself and giving the game a try is not too bad of an idea. :)

Overall I've enjoyed playing this game, but the longer I play the more I begin to see issues that are killing the enjoyment:
- Many of the techs are boring, underwhelming or misplaced in the tech tree. Armour techs are all more or less useless until very late. Techs that give flat 5% production or similar are usable (which kind of tells a lot about the other techs), but so very uninspired. Many of the techs you get early do nothing until much, much later. Overall tech research usually feels like I'm just going for the least bad option for the moment. Also nearly all the weapon/power/shield tech upgrades are just the same with bigger numbers, usually the scaling is fairly linear too. It's just not very interesting.
- For a big part of the early game feels like you just have to do whatever gives you the most mineral production. Minerals are needed for damn near everything early on, which makes early games feel very same ish every game.
- The planet development isn't very interesting. There aren't that many special buildings, usually you just build more power/mineral/research, with maybe a handful of other buildings that are worthwhile. At least assigning planets to AI controlled sectors removes some of that tedium (since it is mostly just pointless busywork), but the AI does manage to screw up planets so that doesn't feel good either.
- Factions feel very unfinished
.. etc. There's a lot in this game that feels sort of unfinished sketch of a system.
I did enjoy the story event, and the feel fo a developing galaxy. It was quite a lot of fun for a while, but I can't really see past the multitude of issues. I'd love to, though, the game does have a lot of promise and I think it *can* get really good with patches.

I was suckered into buying this game by the large number of positive reviews. I really wanted to like it - I love sandbox games, and this seemed to tick every box for me, but it has some huge problems that most of the reviews I read either didn't mention or glossed over.
Firstly, the UI is appalling. I found it unintuitive and unnecessarily labyrinthine. This is not a game you can load up and figure out how to play as you go along. You need to go to the wiki for even the most basic things, and the UI is so vastly different to most other games within the same genre you need to be prepared to learn a whole new way of controlling your charater and playing a game - a way dreamed up by a committee of insanely pedantic sadists - at least that's what it feels like.
Secondly, progress is laughably slow on default settings. Your starting character is so incapable it might as well be a toddler, and being able to perform even basic actions reliably well seems to require hours of grinding.
Thirdly, while the game is clearly feature-rich this can also make it overwhelming for a new player, since the game makes no attempt at breaking you into the world slowly and carefully in an enjoyable way.
Do not buy unless you are willing to do the following.
1) Devote hours of time to reading the wiki.
2) Print the wiki, or have it on another screen so you can make proper use of it.
3) Spend hours on boring, repetitive tasks (dig some dirt, drop it, dig some more dirt, drop it, repeat for OVER AN HOUR to get digging skill to a useful level).
4) Treat this game like a second job, and spend several hours on it every day, performing mostly boring, repetitive tasks, in order to one day, in several months time, be able to build a semi-decent house somewhere.
If that hasn't convinced you to pass on this, then consider my first half-hour of play.
Minutes 1-10: Face sculpt my character, full of excitement for this new game I'm clearly going to spend hours and hours enjoying.
Minutes 10-20: Explore the labyrinthine UI, trying to work out how the hell to do anything. Seriously, would a bit of context-sensitive left-clicking kill you people??
Minutes 20-25: Give up trying to understand the UI. Venture outside the starting town. Find a sheep. Click "Look after" the sheep. Try and puzzle out what has changed. Click "look after" a small dog. Get told I can only "look after" one animal at a time. Punch the dog.
Minutes 25-30: Trade blows with the dog. For five minutes. Neither of us loses more than one third of our health in that time. Log out and go and read the wiki.
After an hour of exploring the wiki, I'm convinced this game is not for me.

The Binding of Isaac has been my absolute favorite game for a long time. It's dark, challenging but not frustratingly hard to figure out, and utterly addictive. There are a lot of fun items to discover, and seeing all the combinations of item effects you can end up with is an endless source of fun. The music is highly excellent, the graphics are nice, and the story is a delightful twist on a biblical tale. Isaac will provide you with endless hours of gameplay and many, many unlockables. I have played both Mordheium: City of the Damned and Warmachine Tactics. And my reaction as soon as I touched Warmachine was, "THIS GAME IS WAY MORE POLISHED THAN MORDHEIM. HOW IS IT'S RATING WORST!?"
The answer is of course that Warhammer's IP is more popular, so people flock to that. Warmachine did alot of things right. I shall endeavour to explain why I feel this game deseves more love.
THE KEY TO HAVING FUN: Is to understand that this is basically a digital TABLETOP wargame. Expect long turn times, units on a table, and numbers you could care less about reading. That's pretty faithful to the source material, so I can hardly fault the developers. People are upset because the Models' mouth don't move during cutscenes or the controls are weird, or whatever. Who cares.  I treat it as a board game and has loads of fun. If you can keep this in mind and understand that miniatures shouldn't be animated anyway, you won't have much to complain about. Cheaper than buying the actual models right? Of course, if they made this as a pure digital boardgame, it would probably be way better.
Who Would Like this Game: People who like motion blurs, somewhat complex boardgames and tea breaks in front of their computer, have no problem with the dice gods and aren't anal about faithfulness to the source material (2 die, 3 die, who cares?)
Who Would NOT like this Game: People who care alot about perfect animation, smoothness, perfect controls, a thriving multiplayer matchmaking service and a populous community. And video games. None of which applies to this game.
+ Proper ruler Based Movement (none of that WASD FPS nonsense Mordheim gets up to where you can't see what's around the corner- instead, it emulates the ruler based movements of the tabletop fairly well)
+ Small map (thank goodness, otherwise games would take forever)
+ Zoom out for bird's eye view (for proper tactical gauging)
+ Easy to comprehend information bars.
+ Excellent Unit Models, Lots of Factions
+ A kind of still alive Multiplayer (you may want to arrange games through the community groups, play with friends, or campaign. If you want a definitely alive TBS multiplayer, Warhammer 40k: Regicide is what you want).
+ Not a pure RNG game. Positioning is actually somewhat important as are "Combined Ranged Attacks".
Cons
- Motion Blur can be eyewatering. The key, I find, is to just find an angle you're comfortable with and play, the map is small, there's no need to move around as much.
- Stupid control scheme, takes some getting used to, but once you do, it's fine. (I hit tap the X key for unit deactiviation. Saves me time and sanity)
- Long turn times. I move all of my units and attacks. The opponent does the same. You want TEA while you're doing this. Not really a con per se, because this is what a tabletop game is like.
- Annoying numbers and things you have to read. Fortunately it's organized. Fortunately you can just ignore it. I DON'T READ. I zerg Rush and Bayonet the enemy. Like a Baws.
TLDR; Try the Demo, treat it like a board game, not a video game, it doesn't hurt and you have full access to the multiplayer (minus some units).

A fun, quick little jaunt through unique set pieces ranging from the jagged and magical surface of the titular 'Planet of the Eyes' to the deep, dark caverns lurking below, traversed by water and, at times, bouncing 'shrooms. You take on the role of a little robot (inspired by what I believe to be the Polaroid SX-70 line of instant cameras introduced in April of 1972) who comes to after... Surprise!, crash landing on a mysterious, alien planet. Brobot must now follow a bizzare set of recordings left behind on cassette tapes by an eccentric loner, addressed to Brobot himself!
Planet of the Eyes is a very simple side-scrolling platformer most immediately comparable to Limbo in terms of mechanics and gameplay and The Swapper in story, plot and setting. However, PotE never meets the high standard set by either game and tends to fall a hair short in each department above. This is by no means a bad thing and contributes to what makes the game unique. It simply isn't up to par with the delivery of the above games; it does not resonate, it does not leave a mark. The biggest let down is definitely the number of puzzles, the challenge of said puzzles and, inherently, the length of the game. I clocked in a little over an hour playing the game and that's with a good bit of menu idle time while I took a shower.
These puzzles are extremely simple. You won't get stuck on the puzzles; what you will get stuck on is manuevering in platforming sections (and, oh my god, the WATER level). Even then, it doesn't take long to adjust to Brobot's movement. Don't worry if you don't master it, as soon as you get the hang of it you're already two sections ahead or the game is over. I may be influenced in the fact that I got this game via Humble Bundle but I do see the game is currently on sale for $2.49 as of 10/04/16 and the sale ends on 10/15/16. That's a PERFECT price for this game.

Planet of the Eyes attempts to replicate Limbo's success, but lacks the kind of atmosphere and challenge that made Limbo good. It has the simplicity and core puzzles, but beyond that, it is a very bland title.
Playing it I never felt challenged by the platforming or puzzle design, only frustrated with its limitations. Towards the end, you'll encounter rotating arrangements of boxes to traverse. You have to carefully balance your little robot to not slide down on either side of a block, and figure out the right angle to jump off from. It is a matter of timing and precision, yet the controls feel noticeably unprecise in these sections.
This is mostly down to when your robot will find it in himself to latch onto a ledge. The angle of a box has to be just right for it to happen, and even when you feel you should have been able to grab onto it, the automatic system might think otherwise. In reverse, you might end up sticking to ledges when you didn't mean to, and die as a result as well.
That kind of design quirk makes me wonder why the devs couldn't have implemented, I don't know, a button press for hanging on to things? Its not like the game offers more than jump and interact buttons, plus a joke/achievement related dance button. Well, there is the pause menu too, but that, while it has a "Resume" button, doesn't actually pause the game. Oh joy.
A lot of the puzzle-platforming could have been improved simply by requiring my user input, which a ledge-grab action would have helped with. There are a lot of spots where you have to jump from ledge to ledge, and the button-press timing necessary for that would have made them a lot more engaging. The way the game plays now, however, just had me
. Beyond the clean and quirky art style, and the occassional audio log detailing the plot passively, I didn't feel like this was something enjoyable to play. The minimalist sound design adds to that as well.
Compared to Limbo, which it is closest to, everything felt too basic, too simplistic and without real tension. There were a bunch of cool sections with alien wildlife making things difficult for you, but those mostly happened in the earlier parts of the game, and the closer you get to the end, the more it turns into pulling switches to avoid repetitive traps and waiting for platforms to move on their pre-described rotations or ferry you over lava lakes, while you're standing in place until reaching the jump-off point.
It is an utterly inoffensive game, but sadly, that also means it has nothing really going for it to keep me playing.

In retrospect, maybe this game would be better if thought of as an incredibly interactive movie. Next time I play, I will keep that in mind.

I've had the privelege to watch Manyland grow and change over the course of almost 2 years now and I have to say it is an enigma and a joy. Everyone's experience with Manyland is guaranteed to be different - it is so open ended that nearly anything is possible.
There really is no aim to the game unless you give it one. Whether you want to create a messy workshop where other players have to match parts to broken robots, a sunny beach full of partying celebrities and seashell diving, lock your friends in a haunted mansion, an art museum, a cottage in the woods, a space walk, a funhouse... the tools are at your disposal, all you need is imagination. If you'd rather just explore other people's work, that's fine too!
This game is best played with friends, as the adult player base is a little shy - we mostly hide. If you're looking to make friends be sure to come out to Manyday on the 19th of every month.
Despite having only 2 devs and no official moderators, the game is surprisingly well self-moderated and you have to go looking to find anything terribly inappropriate.
